# D E D I C A T I O N

*Whatever the earth holds, whatever the sea and the sky bring forth,*
*Is scarcely enough to satisfy a greedy hunger.*
*To what end will the furious lust of the belly,*
*And the wicked ambition of the throat, finally drag us wretched men?*
*This was not the image of a better world in times past,*
*While the people were simple, and the world was new.*
*When a nation led a long and happy life,*
*Unstained by the marks of innocent blood.*
*When the nourishing earth, with no farmer compelling her,*
*Gave her delights to her master of her own accord.*
*Golden ages most worthy of King Saturn <note>In Roman mythology, Saturn ruled during a "Golden Age" of peace and abundance where labor was unnecessary.</note>,*
*But our crimes forbid those times to continue for long.*
*The Silver ages soon followed, yet whoever compares them*
*To our own customs, would rightly consider them golden.*
*Although a sacrificed victim often fell, its throat cut for God,*
*It was still considered a great sin to place it upon the tables.*
*We are the Iron offspring—oh, the grief!—all things are for the belly,*
*All things have become the prey of a raving throat!*
*What did the oxen deserve—an animal without wicked deceit,*
*And patient in its labors—what did the oxen deserve? <note>The author laments the transition from a vegetarian "Golden Age" to a modern "Iron Age" where even the hardworking ox is slaughtered for food.</note>*</note>

<term>Saturn</term> <note>The ancient god of agriculture; his reign represents a lost utopia.</note>, <term>Golden Ages</term> <note>The first and best age of mankind in classical mythology.</note>, <term>Silver Ages</term> <note>The second age, less perfect than the first but superior to the present.</note>, <term>Gluttony</term> <note>Latin: gula; one of the primary vices criticized in this text.</note>, <term>Lust of the belly</term> <note>Latin: libido ventris; refers to excessive or unnatural appetite.</note>, <term>Oxen</term> <note>Symbol of innocent, productive labor.</note>

<summary>This page contains a Latin elegiac poem lamenting the moral decline of humanity through the classical framework of the Four Ages, specifically criticizing the shift from a peaceful, bloodless existence to modern gluttony and the slaughter of animals.</summary>

# D E D I C A T I O N.

*What have you deserved, you peaceful sheep, a race born*
*to protect mankind; what have you peaceful sheep deserved?*
*But it is not enough to strike down the horn-bearing bull,*
*and the cruel knife is also stained with the blood of the calf.*
*No less is the gentle lamb, snatched from the udder of its dear mother,*
*slaughtered by the hand of the executioner.*
*And you, little chick, not yet happily excluded from your egg,*
*(O truly innocent one) you fill the bellies of men.*
*Indeed, that way of life does not please the Gaetulian lions,* <note>Gaetulia was a region in ancient North Africa, famous in Roman literature for its fierce lions.</note>
*nor does that life please the Armenian tigers.*
*The fiercer beast, content with foliage and green grass,*
*surely scorns bloody feasts.*
*And that beast which is more grim and devours flesh,*
*in turn, hardly even likes to touch the sprouts of the earth.*
*But he who ought to be the rule of life for all other living things,*
*man alone devours both.*
*And if only the examples of the flocks could move him!*
*He has those whom he might imitate so that he might live more mildly.*
*Grim crows and rapacious hawks go hunting,*
*but the gentle dove seeks the charming gifts of Ceres!* <note>Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain; her "gifts" refer to bread or seeds.</note>

# DEDICATION

*Both the wolf and the ravenous bears are sated by flesh,*
*But the doe and the gentle sheep graze upon the pastures.*
*Do not suppose that only the strong creatures feed on blood,*
*While the weaker ones enjoy the herbs and the grasses.*
*Nothing is more spirited than the crested cock <note>The rooster, often used as a symbol of courage and vigilance</note>, and what,*
*Tell me, stands stronger than the warlike horse?*
*But perhaps those bloody feasts suit common souls,*
*Yet they do not befit heroes and demigods!*
*But what was more frugal than the table of Curius <note>Manius Curius Dentatus, a Roman consul famous for his austerity; he reportedly preferred his farm's turnips to Samnite gold</note> in days of old,*
*When he conquered Kings with his strong hand?*
*And Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, another Roman model of virtue who refused bribes and lived simply</note>, preparing for himself a dish of roasted turnips,*
*Remained unconquered by enemies and by bribes alike.*
*But why do I linger on the venerable examples of the ancient Romans <note>original: "Quiritum"</note>?*
*Our dear Fatherland shall provide examples no less noble.*
*O, truly they were Hollanders <note>original: "Batavi," referring to the Batavians, the Germanic tribe regarded as the ancestors of the Dutch</note> once, when by simple food*
*Strength and vigor stood firm in those fearless men!*
*And just as there was no shame in draining capacious cups,*
*Even so, a modest table was held in high esteem.*
*India had not yet sent her spices—those things which,*
*Oh, the grief!—devastate our strength and our ancestral wealth.*

<summary>A poetic dedication praising the virtues of a simple, meat-free diet by citing classical Roman heroes and the rugged ancestors of the Dutch. The author laments how modern luxuries and imported spices from the East Indies have corrupted national strength.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, frugality, Roman virtue, Curius Dentatus, Fabricius, Batavians, Dutch history, temperance, spices, luxury</keywords>

# D E D I C A T I O N.

*Why do we fools now complain of new names for diseases?*
*Those evils dwell within our fine, sumptuous dishes!*
*Use your right, you say, it is necessary that we rule,*
*It is fitting that all things pass under our laws!*
*We flatter ourselves rashly, and proud in our vanity*
*We oppress an unknown race with our nobility.*
<note>The author is likely referring to the animal kingdom or the natural world which humans exploit for food.</note>
*Which, if by chance you wished to compare to our own race,*
*Comes to be preferred by many names.*
*If, however, a more powerful enemy is able to cut the throat*
*Of the weak, and enjoy his strength instead of reason:*
*Let vile souls desire those things; let the ignoble slave*
*Of the belly consider these to be his written laws!*
*Let the peasant, so that he may endure his hard labors,*
*Prepare hard dishes for his barking stomach.*
*But if anyone, born of divine seed, rises higher,*
*Let him rejoice to have raised his head above human affairs:*
*It is fitting for this man, at least, to flee the dire contagions*
*Of foul poison, and to beware the losses of the common crowd.*
*These things my <term>PORPHYRIUS</term> <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who famously advocated for vegetarianism in his work "On Abstinence from Animal Food."</note>, noble in his learned art, strives to persuade*
*His old companion.*

<summary>A poetic dedication arguing that human diseases stem from gluttony and the consumption of meat, invoking the philosopher Porphyry to advocate for a more disciplined, "divine" lifestyle over base physical appetites.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, Porphyry, vegetarianism, gluttony, disease, Neoplatonism, temperance</keywords>

# DEDICATION

*If anyone should think these are merely the dreams of a secular philosopher,*
*And now wishes to place no faith in his books,*
*Who does not know of that man, for whom the cheaper food of locusts*
*And honey, which drips from the trees onto leaves, were enough?* <note>A reference to John the Baptist’s ascetic lifestyle in the wilderness.</note>
And that for the followers of Christ to never touch the feasts of the meat-market,
Was considered a work of holy religion!
But why should I praise things which we do not think should be imitated;
That cause does not depend upon my own judgment.
Yet if that matter were indeed within my own judgment,
I would wish to live by that law forever.
Being noble-hearted and content with the goods which the Fatherland provides,
Let the Dutch table <note>original: "mensa Batava"</note> give me its magnificent feasts.
And let me care nothing for the gifts of the Western or Eastern worlds,
Where the glutton seasons unknown foods with his art.
Truly, God cuts the regions of the heaven and the wide lands
With mountains and the sea and with rivers.
Each nation is circumscribed by its own limit, so that
It might learn to be content with the goods given within.
Whatever it may be, we praise the old ways, but we use the years
Which a good birth-fortune and God have granted us.

<vocab>Dedication, Dutch (Batavian), Western, Eastern, God, Fatherland</vocab>

<summary>A poetic dedication contrasting the extreme asceticism of biblical figures with a modern preference for the local bounty of the Dutch Fatherland. The author argues that God divided the world into nations so that people might be content with their own native resources rather than seeking exotic luxuries.</summary>
<keywords>asceticism, John the Baptist, Dutch identity, providence, nationalism, moderation, geography</keywords>

# DEDICATION.

*Now the famous city of* DEVENTER <note>original: "Daventria," the Latin name for the city of Deventer in the Netherlands</note> *has offered hospitality to the peaceful Muses,*
*and has nurtured men of the highest standing in the arts.*
*From every side, the eager student once approached this "Athenian" city on the IJssel,* <note>original: "Salicas Athenas." The river IJssel was known in Latin as the Sala; calling a city "Athens" was a common humanist compliment for a center of learning.</note>

*Now also... but why should my Muse be a burden to the modesty*
*of those living, when I alone am failing?*

# TO THE UNBIASED READER

->SENDS GREETINGS<-

# JACOBUS DE RHOER.

At last, therefore, I have finished weaving the web, an undertaking that seemed almost an ill-omened thing when I first approached it. For most distinguished men had indeed frequently set their hands to the "golden" books (as they are commonly called) of *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, but always with frustrated effort. Those who had pledged their labor to the Tyrian Philosopher seemed, as the saying goes, to ride the horse of Sejanus <note>A proverbial expression for something that brings ruin to its owner</note>, or to have married Fulvia, a wife fatal to her husbands. I learned that MERIC CASAUBON was among their number from his notes on DIOGENES LAERTIUS, Book II, Segment 7. That THOMAS GALE promised the same in his notes on *Iamblichus: On the Mysteries*, Section V, chapter 4, and that DAVIS, LAKEMACHER, and LA CROZE—all most excellent men—held the same intention, is a well-attested fact. But perhaps no one employed a better preparation for this matter than JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS, Rector of the Gymnasium of Schweidnitz in Silesia. He certainly indicated himself that he had many collations of manuscripts ready at hand: and among them even a Vatican copy, ancient and elegant, as we know from the *Treasury of Letters* of the illustrious LA CROZE, Volume III, page 225. That same LA CROZE had shared his own observations and those of PETITUS with THOMAS. Those notes of PETITUS, however, were very few, and unless they were better than those I touched upon regarding Book I, § 42, he would have deserved little credit regarding our *Malchus* <note>original: "Malcho"; Malchus was the original Semitic name of Porphyry</note>. THOMAS also received the observations and emendations of GALE, which he had smeared with his own hand onto a copy of the Author, as the *same Treasury of Letters*, Vol. I, p. 340 and Vol. II, p. 122, informs us. Besides these, he used many aids, which can be understood from his own letters given to the most learned SIBER (which you will find at the end of this Edition). It was not permitted for me to be so fortunate as to hope for those unpublished notes; yet even so, they pointed out this path which had to be traveled if I wished to find any assistance. Receive now in a few words what I have set in motion and achieved in that matter.

Since I most vehemently desired the Vatican copy I just mentioned, I persuaded myself that it could not be better pursued than through PETER WESSELING, a man of admirable erudition, for whom we have not yet finished mourning—on account of the loss our literature suffered, and I especially in the death of an excellent Teacher, who (as they used to say of *Porphyry’s* teacher, *Longinus*) was "a certain living library and a walking museum" <note>original: "βιβλιοθήκη τις ἦν ἔμψυχος καὶ περιπατοῦν μουσεῖον"</note>. Nor had I supposed this rashly, though the outcome was not very successful. I will subjoin part of the letter in which that most kind man indicated this to me: *"I do not know if it was signaled to you that I had asked Cardinal Librarian ALBANI to order an inquiry into whether the sheets of the Porphyrian book in the Vati-"*

For the Illustrious SWIETENIUS <note>Gerard van Swieten, 1700–1772, a famous physician and librarian to Empress Maria Theresa</note> saw to it that this was written back to me: *I cannot be persuaded that Porphyry’s little book "On Abstinence from Animal Food" <note>original: "περὶ ἀπ. ἐμψ." (peri ap. emps.)</note> ever existed in the Augustan Library; for although I have searched and investigated as diligently as possible both formerly and especially now, I have not yet found it; for which reason it truly pains me greatly that I cannot write back more joyful news.*

Nor did I have better success through a Parisian friend whom I tasked with shaking out the Royal Library and that of the Benedictines; for that most learned man indicated to me that, besides the version by B. FELICIANUS, nothing was found there that was rare or that I lacked—even though *Thomas* testifies in the same Letter that he possesses variant readings from a Parisian Royal Codex.

But what I had sought in vain in France, I found in Holland. I owe the greatest thanks to that most Excellent Man, no less illustrious for his erudition and merits than for his honors, G. MEERMAN <note>Gerard Meerman, 1722–1771, a renowned Dutch book collector</note>, who pointed out to me that in that literary treasury which he had acquired for himself from France, there was also a manuscript codex of Porphyry’s work. With an incredible zeal for promoting literature, he offered it for my use so that I might compare it with the printed editions. The codex is paper, in a smaller folio size, not indeed very ancient, but of good quality. The title is as follows: *Three books of Porphyry the Philosopher on Abstinence from Animal Food; furthermore, the Life of Pythagoras and a small volume concerning Alexander.* <note>original: "Πορφυρίου Φιλοσόφου περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων βιβλία τρία. ἔτι δὲ καὶ Πυθαγόρου βίος καὶ περὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου μικρὸν τεῦχος."</note> You see that the subject matter is incorrectly indicated, and three books are mentioned when there are, in fact, four. That mutilated little work on Alexander the Great does not bear a name, but it is by Arrian, though it contains only thirteen chapters of the first book. Then there is added: *Naulot of Coila <note>Jean Naulot, a 16th-century scholar</note> read this in the year of Christ the Savior 1573.* <note>original: "Ταύτην ἀνέγνωκε Ναυλὼτ ὁ Κοιλαδεὺς ἔτει Σωτῆρος Χριστοῦ (α. φ. ο. γ.) 1573."</note> and it is written thus again at the end of the Codex, except that there he is called *Naulot of the Valley*. On the top of the page is read: *Parisian College of the Society of Jesus.* I noticed that this Codex agrees in most respects with the Leipzig one (of which I shall speak presently); indeed, almost the same scholia <note>Ancient marginal notes or explanations</note> are read in the margin there. And I often rejoiced to find the Leipzig reading confirmed where it had seemed truer, and often even conjectures—born of myself or others—were confirmed, although in many matters it still left me in uncertainty.

Britain also provided some help. For since I believed that DAVIS <note>John Davies, 1679–1732, President of Queens' College, Cambridge</note>, a most outstanding man, had set his hand to this work, and would not have attempted it without the help of manuscript codices, I consulted the library catalogs to see if anything could be hoped for from there. There were, however, only two manuscript codices in the Bodleian Library which *Davies* had ordered to be compared with the printed editions. *But not without a sense of regret, which returned to him from money spent without fruit, as HUDSON writes to J. C. WOLF in the La Croze Treasury, Vol. II, p. 99.* Certainly one of the codices was recent...

<note>original: "Galeo"</note> Gale’s advice, in the notes to Iamblichus’ *On the Mysteries* V, 4. Most truly <note>original: "La Crozius"</note> La Croze wrote to <note>original: "Moshemium"</note> Mosheim in Volume III of the *Treasury of Letters*, page 225: *I warn again that Porphyry’s book will never be pleasing to the Learned of all nations, unless it comes forth together with the version of <note>original: "B. Feliciani"</note> Benedictus Felicianus, which will also be found very convenient in many places for correcting the Greek text.* I have followed that advice, and thus that most inept version by F. de Fogerolles, and that of Joannes Valentini—which is only slightly better—had to give way to Felicianus. For although he is said to be insufficiently concise and redundant, and not to have achieved that clarity which such length requires, by the celebrated <note>original: "P. D. Huetio"</note> Pierre Daniel Huet in *On Famous Translators*, Book II, page 222; and though I would not say he perfectly possesses all those qualities which make a true translator—namely, scrupulousness in explaining meanings, faithfulness in expressing words, diligence in showing the "color" <note>the stylistic tone or "flavor" of the original</note>, clarity, elegance, and that which corresponds to the Author and his character, and other things of this kind—nevertheless, he is commended for most of them and snatches the palm <note>wins the prize</note> from the others. He also made use of a much better manuscript than others did, though even that one was not fully cleansed of errors, and therefore he frequently bears witness to the integrity of the writing. I often grieved that, content to have expressed the sense, he left the reader in doubt as to which specific word he had found in the source. I also wish he had not followed the bad example of translators who force the Author’s verses into meter, for from that it is usually uncertain what they actually read.

I come now to the Editions. A work never sufficiently praised—to speak with <note>original: "L. Holstenio"</note> Lucas Holstenius in his *Life of Porphyry*, chapter 8—that great glory of Italy, <note>original: "Petrus Victorius"</note> Piero Vettori, brought to light at Florence in the year <term>1548</term> <note>original: "cIɔ. Iɔ. XLVIII."</note> together with the same author's <margin>Saxius, *Onomasticon*, Part III, p. 587.</margin> *Sentences Leading to the Intelligible* <note>original: "πρὸς τὰ νοητὰ ἀφορμ."</note> and Michael of Ephesus’ *Scholia on Aristotle’s Four Books on the Parts of Animals* <note>original: "σχολ. εἰς τέσσαρα τοῦ Ἀριστ. περὶ ζώων μορίων"</note>. Vettori added some observations, but these are occupied almost entirely with Eusebius, and he did not even compare all the places which that author had taken from Our Author, and sometimes did so not very accurately—for example, in Book IV, section 11—not even mentioning that Porphyry had derived all those things from Josephus into his own fields.

That First Edition was followed by F. de Fogerolles, Counselor and Physician to the King of France, who, having made a Latin version from the Greek copy, illustrated with scholia and prefaces (as he says), published it at Lyon in France (not Leiden <note>original: "Lugduni Batavorum"</note>, as <note>original: "Weinrichius"</note> Weinrich thought in *Leipzig Miscellany*, Vol. IV, p. 176) in the twentieth year of the preceding century. What he achieved he tells us in the Dedicatory Epistle (which I did not wish to prefix in its entirety to this Edition, lest I abuse your patience, Gentle Reader <note>original: "L. B." / "Lector Benevole"</note>); I will speak in his own words: "We undertook at our leisure to translate the Greek writer Porphyry, rescued from the shadows; in which version we preferred to express the flow of the meanings rather than the words. For it is difficult (says Saint Jerome) when following foreign languages not to fall away somewhere; it is also arduous to preserve the same beauty in a translation of famous sayings: something is signified by the property of a single word; I do not have the means with me to express it: and while I seek to fulfill the meaning by a long circuit, I scarcely measure out short spaces. Add to this the twists of hyperbaton <note>a figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed</note>, the dissimilarities of cases, the varieties of figures, and finally the very property of the language itself, which if I interpret word-for-word, sounds absurd; if, out of necessity, I change something in the order or the speech, I shall seem to [fail] the duty of a translator..."

He includes a quote from Fogerolles justifying a sense-for-sense rather than word-for-word translation style.</summary>

...departure. As far as the integrity of the Greek text and the diligence applied in purging the readings is concerned, I will not deny that Petrus Victorius <note>Pietro Vettori (1499–1585), a famous Italian Renaissance scholar known for his editions of Aristotle and other Greek texts.</note> applied so much study in emending them that he seems to have brought much aid to Porphyry: although he did not erase all the stains, nor was he able to restore several mutilated passages which crept in through the ignorance of former times and the fault of the copyists. I, however, have found a great number of errors after him, a series of which has been noted by us in the margin of the work, and we do not doubt that a greater number can be noted by another in the future.

He had also added a *Synopsis of the Pythagorean Abstinence* expressed in verse, and a *Double Dissertation, on Heroic Virtues and Christian Abstinence*. Nor have I neglected these observations, since I did not think them equally foolish everywhere. Yet, what should be judged concerning the man's industry, let <term>HOLSTENIUS</term> <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661), a German humanist and geographer who served as the Vatican librarian.</note> say in the passage cited: <term>BERNARDUS FELICIANUS</term> *expressed it excellently in the Latin language: which being neglected, recently in France some unknown person, with a most foolish version, or rather a perpetual delirium, most wretchedly contaminated an excellent work. So that among all types of evils, with which an angry deity has hitherto pressed the spirit and name of Porphyry, I would easily lead this as the chief one: that he fell into the hands of such a bad physician.*

The last edition, as far as I know, is that of <term>IOANNES VALENTINI</term> <note>Jean Valentine, whose Cambridge edition appeared in 1655.</note>, which appeared with his new translation at Cambridge in the fifty-fifth year of the previous century. He added *Brief Notes*, as he calls them, which ought also to be read here; except that I have omitted one or two passages in which he was correcting the errors of the typesetters. Wrongly do <term>P. PETITUS</term> <note>Pierre Petit (1617–1687), a French scholar and physician.</note> in *Observations* Book I, chapter 5, and others attribute this version to <term>L. HOLSTENIUS</term>. Indeed, what should be decided concerning Valentini's merits, you will best gather from his own preface. He complains that he was destitute of all aids, and had not even seen the Latin interpreter mentioned by <term>HOLSTENIUS</term>. He was able to procure no manuscript codices, and used only the Florentine and French editions. The worst thing is that he everywhere stuffed into the text readings which he himself had hammered out, and, corrupting the healthiest passages, he thrust in those things which had been born in his own brain. He was the first to describe these books into sections or paragraphs, since <term>FOGEROLLAEUS</term> <note>François Fogerolles, a physician and philosopher who edited Porphyry in 1621.</note> had already prefixed the arguments <note>Summaries or outlines of the chapters.</note>, which <term>VALENTINI</term> mostly followed; nor were these to be wiped out by me, both because of the use they can provide, and because they are sometimes illustrated in the notes.

Aided by these supports, I have devoted my labor to the books which the Philosopher <note>Porphyry (c. 234 – c. 305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> wrote to *Firmus Castricius*, his friend and fellow student, to recall him from error and to refute those things with which <term>Heraclides Ponticus</term>, <term>Hermachus the Epicurean</term>, and others, and specifically <term>Claudius of Naples</term>, had defended <term>meat-eating</term> <note>original: "κρεωφαγίαν" (kreophagian)</note>.

In establishing the text, I followed the Cambridge Edition, yet in such a way that I erased what he had rashly poured in, and where he clearly erred, I substituted truer things—never, however, unless the authority of the manuscripts supported it. Those words of the most polished <term>D'ORVILLIUS</term> <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> in the Preface to *Chariton* please me: that learned and wise men today seem by no means able to deserve better of ancient writers than if they oppose themselves with all their might to the license with which now the skilled and unskilled, young and old, in disturbing...

<note>original: "Praefatio"</note>

...they often abuse even the healthiest passages by summoning corrections. If anything appeared disjointed or corrupt, such as those instances where one must rely solely on the "oars of the mind" <note>An idiom for using one's own intellect or intuition when external evidence is lacking</note>, I have indicated it in the notes. In cases where a passage could be restored by changing punctuation marks or the so-called accent—as happens not infrequently—I have acted with less hesitation, for the Author runs no risk from such changes.

The primary consideration had to be the language and style. And here, indeed, the style leans toward the Attic manner of speaking <note>Atticism: a refined, classical Greek style favored by later scholars</note>, yet it is somewhat harsh, being adapted to the period and the subject matter. The expressions themselves are often elegant and do not depart from the example of the best writers, as has been observed throughout the notes. However, transpositions, or *hyperbata* <term>hyperbaton: a figure of speech where the natural order of words is disrupted for emphasis</term>, are far too frequent. For although the Greek and Latin languages are not subject to that slavish and uniform word order and sequence found in modern tongues, one is still not permitted to mix and confuse everything, unless we wish to sin against the elegance and clarity of composition—as D'Orville <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a famous Dutch classical scholar</note> rightly noted elsewhere. Neglect of this fact has often given birth to corrections that were not at all necessary. For this reason, he does not care for those who come to these exercises more to "correct" than to read. Often, I have transcribed the full and undiminished credit for a suggested emendation to others who saw the same thing before me; as no one with a modicum of refinement is ignorant that such credit ought to be given in a book of this quality. Nor have I sought out opportunities to correct other authors, unless a passage presented itself naturally which I could not do without. For I do not follow the counsel of those who love to display their "adversaria" <note>Commonplace books or collections of miscellaneous notes</note> everywhere, which is truly to subject a single author to a heap of miscellaneous observations.

While I had to wander through various branches of learning with this Learned Author, I had to be careful not to linger on "commonplaces," as they are called, while those public granaries stand open to everyone daily. Nor do I deny that I have engaged with these books without a sense of pleasure. To each his own is beautiful: to me, those writers are beautiful who hand down memorable events, customs, rituals, religions, and precepts for living—a genre in which everyone knows our *Malchus* <note>Malchus was the original name of the philosopher Porphyry</note> excels. Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), author of a monumental history of philosophy</note> spoke well of him in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, Volume II, page 257: *it cannot be said how much knowledge of ancient doctrine and history he acquired for himself, which Authors he read, excerpted, and whose fragments he preserved. If he had been permitted to use these rightly—notwithstanding his mediocre judgment and the vanity of the superstition and the detestable, deceptive philosophy he followed—we would perhaps have no one in all of antiquity whom we would place above Porphyry.* Furthermore, no one will understand the rituals of our religion and Church—as they once were and from whence they drew their origin—unless he has him and the other Platonists as teachers. Truly, those who occupy themselves with great zeal over some trivial writer seem to me to act no differently than if someone were to take up some cold and tasteless "nania" <note>A funeral dirge or a nonsensical song</note>—of which this age is so fertile—to illustrate and explain it for themselves several centuries later.

Yet I experienced a more laborious task than I had expected. For just when you think yourself well-versed in the doctrines of Plato and Pythagoras, darkness is suddenly poured over you by the "later Platonists," as they are called. For after the Pythagorean Philosophy had infused itself into the Platonic, those men—although they consider nothing more divine or excellent than their own leader—often [treat] their master...

they report, as it seemed to be required for the sake of religion. I recall that **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the influential Christian theologian.</note> noted this somewhere regarding our Author. Indeed, even those very men not infrequently disagree among themselves, as you will see observed in the proper place. And yet, in these books you may find many things which—whether you consider the formulas of speech or the precepts themselves—might seem not much removed from our own sacred teachings. No one who knows the Author and remembers what he plotted against the Christians will wonder at this. For this was common to him along with other philosophers of this family <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists.</note>: while taking many things from the Christians (through whom, however, they did not wish to appear to have made progress), they strove to deceive them with this commentary, as if the disagreement were not so great; and to show their own followers that it was not necessary to seek from the schools of Christians those things which were praised as more wholesome in our religion, since those same things were handed down by the Philosophers. I recall this was excellently observed by the distinguished man, J. L. MOSHEIM in his *Dissertation on the Church Disturbed by the Platonists*. I wish that, besides those other things which the celebrated ERNESTI <note>Johann August Ernesti (1707–1781), a famous German rationalist theologian and philologist.</note>, that splendid light of Germany, recently advised on this matter, those who love to compare the tablets of the New Testament with writers of this kind would call it to mind; lest they allow themselves to be led into error by the similarity of words, since those authors signify entirely different things by sayings of this sort.

But I also had to compare ancient authors—**Plato**, **Josephus**, **Plutarch**—from whom Porphyry took many things, and the fragments of others which he used had to be sought out. No light labor also had to be given to the ancient Theologians who had inserted Porphyrian passages into their own works: **Eusebius**, **Cyril**, **Theodoret**, and **Jerome**. No one will wonder that the latter <note>St. Jerome.</note> took many things from our Author in his books *Against Jovinianus*, who remembers that both championed almost the same cause, but with a different purpose. Let us hear the man himself in Book II, 7: *What is it to us, whose conversation is in heaven <note>original: "quorum conversatio in coelis est" — a reference to Philippians 3:20.</note>, who [are] above Pythagoras... who subdue the resisting flesh, which drags us toward the incitements of lusts, by fasting? The eating of meat and the drinking of wine, and the filling of the belly, is the nursery of lust.* Therefore, the more frequently I found those men in citing testimonies, the more easily the true reading could be restored; if many had remembered them, they would not have rashly disturbed Porphyry's writing, or they would have healed it with a more suitable remedy.

You understand now for the most part, Kind Reader <note>original: "B. L." for "Benevole Lector".</note>, who it was who created this leisure for us. In his native tongue he was called **Malchus**, which was also his father's name. But since that fell upon Greek ears as unusual and "barbarous," **Longinus**, his teacher, called him **Porphyry**, from purple <note>The Greek "Porphyrios" means "clad in purple."</note>, a truly royal color; for that is what "Malchus" signified in the dialect of the Syrians <note>Malchus is derived from the Semitic root for "King."</note>. But I must not dwell on his life, as the most learned L. HOLSTENIUS has dealt with him with great effort in his *Dissertation on the life and writings of Porphyry the Philosopher*.

Therefore, I have not sought out judgments and testimonies, being content—as had been done by previous Editors—to prefix the Philosopher's life and the index of his Works from **Eunapius** and **Suidas**, together with the version of **Felicianus**, who added a few things from Eunapius which other Editors had left untouched.

# P R E F A C E

<note>P. VI-</note>

By FABRICIUS <note>original: "BRICIO" / "FABRICIO"</note> also, in Volume IV of the *Greek Library*, it was published; therefore, it was not necessary to increase the size of this edition. The distinguished Johann Brucker also dealt with this subject with great diligence in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, Volume II, page 236. He did not leave untouched the question that has been debated among the learned: whether the Philosopher <note>Porphyry, the 3rd-century Neoplatonist</note>, after having given his name to the Christian religion, later defected from it, as some writers of Ecclesiastical History seem to indicate. Reflecting on this, the learned J. F. Thomas had decided to prefix to his edition a Dissertation on *Porphyry’s Apostasy* <note>The act of renouncing one's religious faith</note>, in which he intended to demonstrate that Christian rites were known and familiar to our Philosopher, but that he had not, as La Croze and others believed, defected from the Christian religion to Platonism. See *The Treasury of La Croze*, Volume I, page 341. That attempt indeed lacked success, as was just mentioned; however, the letters remain in which Thomas and Siber, both eminent men, discussed this argument. These were made public in Volume I of the *New Leipzig Miscellany*, and I wished to append them to this edition so that Thomas's plan might be honored.

I would almost believe that Porphyry simulated for some time a mind not alienated from the Christian religion—as those crafty men were accustomed to do—even adapting his formulas of speech and the doctrine itself to the precepts of the Christians, so that they might better circumvent the cautious. From this arose the persuasion that the Philosopher had given his name to those sacred rites, but then recoiled from them as the cause of Platonism demanded. And for that reason, perhaps, the Emperor Constantine willed in a public edict that the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, whose views on the nature of Christ were declared heretical</note> be called *Porphyrians*; I see that the learned disagree on the reasoning for this nickname. The matter itself is handed down in *Socrates' Ecclesiastical History, Book I, chapter 9*, and in the *Last Law of the Theodosian Code regarding Heretics*, and *Law 6 of the Justinian Code regarding Heretics, Manichaeans, and Samaritans*. Certainly, if one punctuates the text differently than is usually done, as it seemed fit to the renowned Heineccius: *But just as the Arians are named after Arius, by the law of Constantine of divine memory, they are called Porphyrians after Porphyry, on account of the similarity of their impiety.* The Emperor wished to take care lest the credulous be deceived under a plausible name. Other causes may indeed be added, which can be read in Socrates; however, in that law, it is expressly handed down so that they might not abuse the title of "Christians." For Arius had also wished to be counted among the number of Christians, but the ancient theologians everywhere exclude him from it.

Finally, there were also those who thought that Porphyry had given his name to the Christian religion toward the end of his life, which they gathered from Jerome’s *Chronicle*; but the falsehood of this opinion has long since been demonstrated.

I have detained you long enough now, Best of Readers; however, I wish you to know one more thing: I have placed a Latin translation alongside the Greek text and added notes at the bottom of each page to consult your convenience. Let the renowned Perizonius state the reason for this practice in the Preface prefixed to *Aelian*. In the solemn formula: farewell and look with favor. Given at Deventer <note>original: "Daventriae", a city in the Netherlands</note> on the very Kalends of April <note>April 1st</note>, 1767.

# THE PREFACE OF PIERO VETTORI

---

# PIERO VETTORI
### *To those devoted to the Greek arts, written in the Greek language.*

The Prince of our Republic <note>Referring to Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence</note> is not of the sort of men who, captured by the splendor of a shadowed honor and the desire for empty glory, wish to keep noble and useful things for themselves alone, or to stand above all others by the mere possession of them. On the contrary, he considers those things to be true goods which are held in common, and which can be obtained by all who show themselves worthy of them. Just as he has often declared this to us in many ways, so now he will make it known to many nations through this plan of his. For he has resolved to publish the ancient writers sought out with the greatest diligence by his ancestors—and rescued at great expense from the ruins and fires of the most cruel wars in Greece—and thus to provide for the benefit of students and the memory of learned men. These authors wished to benefit posterity through their labors and excellence of mind, and spent their entire lives in these cares and studies; yet, having long suffered an unjust fate, they lay hidden in darkness. Just as the authors themselves were exposed to various misfortunes, so too they bore no fruit, or very little, for those eager for the noble arts. 

Nor has he decreed only to bring into the light those who have not seen it for many centuries, but also to give out once more—thoroughly cleansed with the greatest care and restored to their full integrity <note>literally "increased by their limbs"</note>—not a few who have already been printed in faulty and mutilated forms, using the help of that same collection and the abundance of most faithful manuscripts. This is the task now being applied to; and work is being done so that such an honorable and pious will of the Prince may be brought to completion, in accordance with his dignity and the utility of students. Meanwhile, desiring to give some specimen of this work which is being woven, and to be the first to bring such joyful news to the ears of the learned, I have, as it were, run ahead before the preparation for so great an undertaking was finished, and have seen to the publishing of this small volume. 

In this volume are contained the four books of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a Neoplatonist philosopher of the 3rd century AD</note> *On Abstaining from Killing and Devouring Living Creatures*, which are greatly celebrated even by our own authors; and likewise another small book of his in which certain subtle and weighty questions concerning divine matters are contained, according to the decrees of Plato; as well as the explanations of Michael of Ephesus <note>A 12th-century commentator on Aristotle</note>, one of the later interpreters of Aristotle, on the four books *On the Parts of Animals*.

<summary>Piero Vettori introduces a new edition of Greek philosophical texts, praising the patronage of the Medici for rescuing ancient manuscripts from destruction and making them available to the public. The volume includes works by Porphyry on vegetarianism and Neoplatonism, alongside Michael of Ephesus's Aristotelian commentaries.</summary>

# P R E F A C E.

The books of the Tyrian philosopher <note>original: "Tyrii philosophi"; referring to Porphyry of Tyre, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist</note>; and his precise discussion of those matters, once superstition is removed, will be wonderfully useful on account of the manifold and varied exposition of hidden and elegant subjects. He also makes frequent use of examples from ancient writers—now lost to the passage of time—either to confirm his own opinions or to refute the judgments and customs of those same authors. Indeed, the small book in which he wished to encourage the perception of things that are discerned only by the mind and by reason is entirely "golden" <note>original: "aureolus"; a term of high praise for a small but perfect work</note>; and it encompasses much obscure doctrine in few words. I also thought that the brief explanation by the Ephesian <note>original: "Ephesii"; likely referring to Michael of Ephesus, a 12th-century commentator</note> regarding the books of that excellent author would not be unwelcome. I am well aware that he was by no means equal to Porphyry in dignity or learning; however, because those Aristotelian books are partly obscure and very difficult, and because they are illustrated by no other Greek author that I know of—excepting the paraphrase by Metochites <note>Theodore Metochites, a Byzantine scholar and statesman</note>, which has not yet been printed—no better or more learned work should be expected in any respect.

Regarding the integrity of the text and the diligence applied in refining the reading, I will not deny that the books of Porphyry were in a terrible state due to the ignorance of former times, and were greatly corrupted by the faults of copyists. Nevertheless, by comparing many manuscripts, we have applied so much effort to correcting them that we seem to have brought them much aid. Although we were not able to erase every blemish, nor restore several places that were crippled or diminished, our faithfulness and diligence were certainly not lacking. We have also provided this same care in the scholia <term>scholia: explanatory notes or comments inserted into the margins of ancient manuscripts</term> of the Ephesian, to their great benefit. Farewell, you talented and learned men, and expect more and better things shortly from the liberality of our most humane Prince and his extraordinary love for you.

# THE PREFACE OF P. VICTORIUS,

->which he placed before the notes.<-

### TO THE STUDIOUS.

Since I had consulted several respected manuscripts to assist Porphyry—who was in a poor state everywhere and neglected—and had rendered him better in many parts, I attempted to see if I could bring him aid by another route, which I have found to be quite useful. For I knew that Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian historian and exegete.</note>, his contemporary, had often taken testimonies from this work in his books *The Gospel Preparation* <note>original: "προπαρασκευῆς εὐαγγελικῆς" (Praeparatio Evangelica)</note>. Although Eusebius—not without cause—attacks him and harasses him with every kind of insult, he was nevertheless captivated by the Author's erudition. He adduces many passages, especially from these books, by which he either proves what he wishes to confirm, or teaches that Porphyry felt falsely and wickedly about some matter. For Porphyry was hardly fair to our piety <note>The Christian faith.</note>, which was already spreading widely and taking firm roots; he was, in short, violently hostile to the Christian name. However, in these specific books, he touches upon nothing that might harm it; rather, he aligns wonderfully with our institutions and morals. For just as he approved with his whole soul the religion handed down from his fathers and stood bravely by it against adversaries, so he showed himself to be a most temperate man. He was content with a very meager diet; indeed, we can truly say that he stood forth as a most bitter enemy and censurer of the vices of the belly and the throat, and that while still living, he flew away from the prison and chains of the body. Moreover, beyond the fact that he came from the excellent discipline of that most grave man and the most severe house of Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism and Porphyry's teacher.</note>, this is clearly understood from the many most holy precepts collected by him in this work. This, I believe, was the cause of the preservation of this subtle writing, filled with great learning, while other labors of his—by the merit of a more wicked index <note>Referring to the imperial decrees and church condemnations that ordered the burning of Porphyry's anti-Christian writings.</note>—have perished and been deleted from all human memory. I therefore attended diligently to all the passages cited by Pamphilus, and when I encountered many great differences in the readings, I preferred—since Porphyry was already printed and the script found in him retained—to note all the variations here. For not even in Eusebius are all things preserved purely and with integrity, although not a few seem to be read better there. I believe this happened because the writings of Pamphilus were held in great honor among Christians, as they bring much light to our affairs and diligently refute the empty rites of the nations. Porphyry’s books, however, lay idle for a long time due to the just hatred he had stirred up against himself on another account, and they were almost consumed by neglect and filth. Furthermore, I am not unaware of the custom of the ancients, who used no small liberty in placing examples from other authors; if they retained the meaning, they often did not care for the words themselves or their order. Therefore, thinking this the safer path, I have noted whatever difference I could perceive in that writer regarding the testimonies sought from these books, and I have even occasionally indicated briefly toward which side I more incline.

He notes that while Porphyry was an enemy of Christianity, his philosophical writings on temperance survived because of their moral value.</summary>

# I. VALENTINE’S
## PREFACE.

It is not in my nature, friendly Reader, to disparage the labors of others, even if they were completed under an unlucky omen. However, so that you may understand why I have undertaken a new version of Porphyry’s *On Abstinence*, listen for a moment to the Distinguished Lucas Holstenius <note>A prominent 17th-century German humanist and geographer</note> complaining thus in his *Dissertation on the Life and Writings of this Philosopher*: *“Porphyry wrote four books 'On Abstinence from Eating Animals,' a work never sufficiently praised, which Bernardus Felicianus rendered excellently into the Latin language. This being neglected, someone or other recently in France—with a most foolish version, or rather a continuous delirium—has most wretchedly contaminated this excellent work. Among all the types of misfortunes with which an angry Deity has hitherto oppressed the spirit and name of Porphyry, I would easily consider this the foremost: that he fell into the hands of such a poor physician.”* I wished to try, good Reader, whether I might act as a physician somewhat more successfully. Nevertheless, I have prepared this interpretation destitute of all assistance. I did not even happen to see the Latin interpreter mentioned by Holstenius. I was able to obtain no manuscript codices, although I sought them diligently. I had only two printed editions: the Florentine, and the French one which follows it <term>step for step</term> <note>original: "κατὰ πόδας" (kata podas)</note> even where that other one wanders most wretchedly in error. I hope, nonetheless, that infinite passages have been healed by us, partly from Plutarch, Josephus, and Eusebius, and partly from our own conjecture; so much so that there is perhaps only one or two places about which anyone might strongly complain. For what remains, I shall close with the words of the Most Learned Petavius <note>Denis Pétau, a French Jesuit theologian and scholar</note> in his *Letter to the Reader* prefixed to Epiphanius: *“I would wish you, Kind Reader, to approach this study of ours in such a way that you understand that we have not been entirely without fault here; but if you find errors in it, you should balance them with the many good points—if indeed I have many good points—or with equal or fewer points, and enjoy the latter while granting pardon to the former.”*

<header>THE DEDICATION OF G. B. FELICIANO.</header>

# TO ALVISE MICHIEL

### GIOVANNI BERNARDO FELICIANO SENDS GREETINGS. <note>The "S." stands for "Salutem," a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>

---

How much zeal was always applied by the ancients to the regulation and composition of morals can be clear to anyone who considers the ancient method of philosophizing. Indeed, all the schools of the philosophers are seen to have been held more for the sake of establishing a way of life than for the sake of contemplation and theoretical knowledge. This is declared both by the ancient discipline of Pythagoras and later by the instruction of Socrates, from whose disputations every method of living civilly and morally emanated. Many others, and especially those two splendid lights of wisdom, Plato and Xenophon, handed this down to posterity most seriously and elegantly in their literary monuments. For since a desire is implanted in man by nature not so much for *finding* happiness as for *attaining* it, the Philosophers did not think it was enough if they labored in finding happiness, unless they also devised a way by which we might be able to reach it. 

Just as the investigation of the nature of things fortifies for us a path toward finding the first cause of all and the first author of all, God; so the integrity and purity of life, which we fashion within ourselves by imitating the goodness of God, makes us fit to possess Him. Indeed, the supreme power of goodness and uprightness can easily be perceived from this: that no action or speech—not even among the wicked—has authority unless either uprightness, or at least some appearance of uprightness, underlies it. For in truth, whatever is not stabilized and supported by the solidity of uprightness, no matter how much genius and craftsmanship it is composed with, it must eventually appear to everyone as it truly is—vain and ridiculous—and be held in contempt. 

Wherefore, most illustrious Alvise, although you excel in nobility of birth, wealth, and genius, you have nevertheless considered that your life must be established so moderately and holily that you have embraced in a wonderful manner this part of philosophy which looks toward morals—which you have been accustomed to call the "soul of philosophy"—as befits one who is truly good, and *a branch fashioned by Zeus entirely upon truth*, <note>original: "πᾶν ἐπ’ ἀλαθείᾳ πεπλασμένον ἐκ διὸς ἔρνος" — a Greek poetic fragment likely referencing Pindar or a similar lyric style, emphasizing divine and truthful origin.</note> as that famous man says. This you display both by the most tranquil type of life which you lead, and by the most noble thoughts with which you daily keep your soul raised up from the disturbances of the world and the filth of the common crowd. For this reason, since those writers have also greatly pleased you who would track down the truth not only with subtle and sharp disputations, but...

<summary>In this dedication, Giovanni Bernardo Feliciano praises Alvise Michiel for prioritizing moral philosophy and the "integrity of life" over mere theoretical study. He argues that true happiness and a connection to the divine are achieved through the imitation of God's goodness and the practice of virtue.</summary>

<keywords>Alvise Michiel, Giovanni Bernardo Feliciano, moral philosophy, Socrates, Plato, Xenophon, virtue, happiness, ethics, Pythagoras</keywords>

# D E D I C A T I O N

...they might also simultaneously instruct and purify the life of man in such a way that they might lift our minds toward that <note>original: "τὴν ὁμοίωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν"</note> **likeness to God as far as is possible**, as Plato desired. You encouraged me repeatedly, and even by your own right imposed upon me and commanded me, that if I could find anything of this sort among the ancient authors, I should rescue it from the darkness and see to it that it was brought into the light. I, however, although distracted by other occupations and deterred by the awareness of my own modest learning, nevertheless decided I must not fail to obey your commands, at least in some part. This was especially true since I regard the one who gave the command with the greatest respect and veneration, and I saw that the things commanded were of such a nature that engaging in their investigation could not be anything but extremely useful. Therefore, having undertaken the task, I sought out several Greek authors of this kind; and I wished to begin the publication with this work by Porphyry, thinking that its reading would be pleasant to many, both because of the author's name and the subject matter of which he treats.

For Porphyry is held in such high renown in both Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy that he can easily attract students of philosophy by his name alone. Moreover, the work itself is filled with varied and manifold learning; for while he treats the abstinence from eating animals, he handles it not so much in a Pythagorean manner as in a Platonic, and finally, a theological manner. For although he pursues certain arguments concerning the injustice done to animals and the power of <term>unclean demons</term> <note>The author refers to the Neoplatonic belief that eating meat attracted lower, malevolent spirits to the soul.</note> which is secretly drawn in from bloody feasts of this kind—following the decrees of the Pythagorean and Platonic schools and others of that sort—nevertheless, all things look toward this goal (as he himself also seems to interpret): that by diminishing nourishment, the bond of the soul, which is the body, may be thinned and weakened. Thus the mind, released from the disturbances of the passions, may be able to ascend more freely to contemplate and enjoy divine things. Furthermore, by removing delicate feasts, a more easily obtainable diet does not distract care from more serious matters, and every occasion for gluttony is cut away. This has no other purpose than to demonstrate that the principle of fasting and abstinence is proven not only by divine law, but also by natural law. However, so that all things might be more clearly understood, we thought it not irrelevant to also translate the *Life of the Author* written by Eunapius and place it before the work itself. Farewell.

# THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY.

## THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY.

### FROM THE COMMENTARY OF EUNAPIUS,
->*In which he collected the lives of the Sophists and Philosophers.*<-

Tyre was the homeland of Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrios"</note>, the foremost city of the ancient Phoenicians, and his ancestors were of no small distinction. Having received the appropriate education, he advanced and improved so rapidly that he became a pupil of Longinus, and within a short time, he became an honor to his teacher. At that time, Longinus was a kind of living library and a walking museum <note>The term "museum" here refers to a shrine of the Muses, a place of high learning</note>, and he had been entrusted with the task of critiquing the ancient authors, just as many others had been before him—most notably Dionysius of Caria. 

In the city of the Syrians, Porphyry was originally called Malchus <note>original: "Malchos"</note>; this name signifies "King" <note>Malchus is derived from the Semitic root *MLK*, meaning king</note>. However, Longinus renamed him Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrios," meaning "Purple"</note>, alluding to the royal color of the imperial robes, thus adapting his name into Greek. Under Longinus, he was trained in the highest branches of learning; like his master, he reached the very summit of grammar and rhetoric. Yet he did not stop there, but applied himself to mastering every branch of Philosophy. Indeed, Longinus was by far the best of all men of that time in every respect. A great multitude of his books are in circulation and are held in wonder; if anyone criticized one of the ancients, their opinion did not prevail until the judgment of Longinus had confirmed it. 

Having been brought up in this primary education and being looked upon with admiration by all, Porphyry desired to see the great city of Rome, so that he might take the city by storm through his wisdom. As soon as he arrived there and entered into the company of the great Plotinus, he forgot all other teachers.

->* * * *<-

...and he devoted himself entirely to that man <note>Plotinus</note>. Being insatiably filled with that instruction, and with those fountain-like and divinely-inspired discourses, he was satisfied to remain a listener for some time, as he himself says. Then, overcome by the sheer magnitude of the doctrines, he came to loathe his own body and the very fact of being human. Having sailed to Sicily across the strait and the Charybdis <note>A dangerous whirlpool in Greek mythology, located in the Strait of Messina</note>—where Odysseus is said to have sailed—he could not bear to look upon a city or even to hear the sound of a human voice. In this way, he cast aside everything in him that felt pain or pleasure. Stretching himself out toward Lilybaeum <note>Modern Marsala; one of the three capes of Sicily that points toward Libya</note>, he lay there wasting away and starving himself to death, refusing food and avoiding the path of men.

But the great Plotinus did not keep a "blind watch" <note>original: ἀλαοσκοπίην — a Homeric term for failing to notice something</note> over these events. Following in his footsteps, or rather searching for the youth who had fled, he came upon him as he lay there. He provided him with a wealth of arguments to call back his soul, which was just then on the verge of flying away from the body, and he strengthened the body to retain the soul. Thus, Porphyry was restored to life and arose. Plotinus then set down the words he had spoken into a book of his writings.

While other philosophers hide their secret doctrines in obscurity—just as poets do with myths—Porphyry praised the remedy of clarity. Having tasted it through experience, he brought these matters into the light by writing a commentary. He himself then returned to Rome and applied himself to his studies with such zeal that he even appeared in public for demonstrations of his learning. The fame of Porphyry was attributed back to Plotinus by every marketplace and every crowd; for while Plotinus seemed heavy and difficult to hear because of the celestial nature of his soul and the oblique, enigmatic style of his discourses, Porphyry was like a "Chain of Hermes" <note>A metaphor for a golden chain of communication reaching from heaven to earth</note> leaning down toward men. Through his varied learning, he announced everything in a clear and pure manner. He himself says (though it seems he wrote this while he was still young) that he never encountered any of the public oracles; yet in this very book he records, and after these...

He busies himself with many other such matters, regarding how one ought to take care of these things. He also says that he chased away and cast out a certain demonic Nature <note>original: "daimonion tina Physin"</note> from a certain bathhouse; the locals used to call this spirit "Causathas." Now, his fellow students (as he himself records) were among the most excellent: Origen <note>Not the famous Christian father, but Origen the Neoplatonist, a fellow student of Plotinus</note>, Amerius, and Aquilinus, and indeed some of their writings are still preserved. However, not a single word of theirs remains in common use: for there is much that is unrefined <note>original: "akytheron," meaning lacking in grace or charm</note> in them, even if their doctrines are sound, and it runs through their discourses. 

But Porphyry himself praises these men for their skill. He himself pursues every grace of style, yet he alone points out and proclaims the greatness of his teacher <note>Referring to Plotinus, the founder of Neoplatonism</note>. He left out no form of education. Indeed, one might wonder to oneself and marvel at what was more greatly studied by him: whether it was those things tending toward the material of rhetoric, or those leading to grammatical precision, or those dependent upon numbers <term>Arithmetic: the study of discrete quantity</term>, or those leaning toward geometry, or those inclining toward music. 

As for his philosophical works, neither his logic is easily grasped, nor is his own particular reasoning easy to reach. Let his works on Physics and <term>Theurgy: "god-working" or rituals intended to invoke the presence of the divine</term> be left to the rites and mysteries. Thus, the man himself became a sort of all-mixed thing <note>a "pantoriges," or a universal genius</note> directed toward every virtue. One might look upon the beauty of his words more than his doctrines, or perhaps more upon the power of his speech. 

It appears he also engaged in marriage; a book is circulated addressed to Marcella, who became his wife. He says he married her—even though she was already the mother of five children—not so that he might have children by her, but so that those already born might receive an education; for the children had previously belonged to the woman by a friend of his. He appears to have reached a deep old age. At any rate, he left behind many theories in his later books that were contrary to those he had previously worked out. Concerning these, one can only suppose that as he progressed, he changed his opinions. It is said that he departed this life in Rome.

# THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY

->FROM<-

# EUNAPIUS.

Porphyry was a Tyrian by birth—Tyre being the leading city of the ancient Phoenicians—and was born to parents of noble standing. Having received a liberal education, he made such progress that, after becoming a student of Longinus <note>Cassius Longinus (c. 213–273 AD), a famed rhetorician and philosopher</note>, he soon brought great honor to his teacher. In those days, Longinus was regarded as a kind of living library and a walking museum. He had devoted his mind to the critical study of ancient writings, following in the footsteps of many others before him, most notably Dionysius of Caria <note>likely referring to Dionysius of Halicarnassus</note>, who was the most celebrated of them all. 

Now, Porphyry was originally called Malchus <note>original: "Malchus", from the Semitic root 'MLK' meaning king</note> in the language of his Syrian homeland, a word which signifies "king" in the idiom of that people. Later, his name was changed by Longinus to Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius", derived from the Greek word for purple</note>, a reference to the purple color of royal robes. Under Longinus's discipline, he applied himself most diligently to the study of fine literature. He reached the very summit of grammatical knowledge, just as his master had, and mastered rhetoric as well—though he was not particularly inclined toward that field by nature. He became highly accomplished in every branch of philosophy. Indeed, Longinus was easily the foremost of all who flourished at that time; a great abundance of his books survives and is held in high admiration. So great was his authority that if anyone found fault with something in the ancient writers, they did not feel they could trust their own opinion until it was confirmed by the judgment of Longinus.

When Porphyry had been trained in this manner in his early education and had become conspicuous to all for his talents, he was seized by a great desire to see Rome, so that he might take hold of that city with his wisdom. As soon as he arrived there, he entered into the company of the divine Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD)</note>. Forgetting all others, he devoted himself entirely to him. Applying himself with insatiable greed to that discipline, he spent a long time drawing from that sacred fountain of divine disputations. Later, however, overcome by the sheer magnitude of these contemplations, he began to pursue his own body with hatred and to feel distressed that he was a human being. Consequently, after he had sailed to Sicily and crossed the strait of Charybdis <note>The famous whirlpool in the Strait of Messina</note>—where Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> is also said to have traveled—he could not bear to see a city or even hear the voice of men; so much...

He had utterly cast off all sense of pain and pleasure; and so, having set out on a steady journey toward Lilybaeum <note>Modern Marsala; one of the three capes of Sicily</note>—which is one of the three promontories of Sicily that faces toward Libya—he cast himself down there. He lay there groaning and enduring, refusing all food, and, as the saying goes, "shunning the tracks of men." <note>A reference to Homer’s description of Bellerophon in the Iliad, wandering alone in grief.</note> Yet this empty searching did not keep the great Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism and Porphyry's teacher</note> away from these events. For he followed immediately—whether because he had a premonition of what would happen, or because he was searching for the young man who had fled—and found him lying there. He devised words for him that might both recall a soul just about to fly away from the body and strengthen the body to retain it. And so, having recovered his spirit, Porphyry rose up. Plotinus later recorded the words he had spoken in a book, among those of his writings that still exist. 

But since philosophers used to hide their secrets with obscure speech, much like poets do with myths, Porphyry—who had approved of the remedy of clarity and tasted it by experience—published these ideas to the light, illuminating them with his commentaries. He himself then returned to Rome and devoted his leisure to the study of oratory, even appearing in public for the sake of display. Nevertheless, every assembly and every gathering attributed Porphyry’s glory back to Plotinus. For Plotinus, on account of the celestial power of his soul and his hidden, enigmatic way of speaking, seemed heavy and difficult to perceive. Porphyry, however, like a kind of "Homeric Chain" <note>A metaphor for a golden chain connecting heaven and earth; here meaning he links high philosophy to human understanding</note> let down to men, expressed everything with ease and transparency through his varied learning and knowledge. 

And he himself says—though perhaps he had written these things when quite young—that he had encountered no public oracle. In the same book, he discusses many other matters regarding what care should be taken of such things: how he had put to flight and cast out a certain demonic nature from a bathhouse, which the locals call *Causathan*. <note>original: "Caufathan"</note> His fellow students, as he himself writes, were quite outstanding: Origen, Amelius, and Aquilinus. Their writings exist, yet no beauty is seen in them, even though their dogmas and opinions are correct and they persist in their words. Porphyry, however, praises the eloquence and dignity of these men, even while he himself surpasses them all in grace; he alone makes his teacher manifest and proclaims him, having omitted no branch of learning. Indeed, anyone might wonder and doubt what subject he seems to have studied most: whether those pertaining to the faculty of oratory, or those which make for the exact inquiry of grammar; those belonging to arithmetic, or those pertaining to geometry or music. Likewise, regarding philosophy, it is uncertain whether he spent more effort on the things of reason <note>Logic and theory</note> or the things of administration <note>Ethics and practical life</note>. For those matters regarding natural and divine contemplation are so sublime that they seem fit to be left to sacred rites and mysteries. Thus, that man stood out as a being perfectly harmonized for every virtue. At one moment, one might admire his words more than his dogmas; at another, his decrees and opinions more than his power of speech. He appears to have taken a wife, for a book is circulated addressed to his wife Marcella, whom—although she was already the mother of five children—

# THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY FROM SUIDAS <note>Suidas, or the Suda, is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>

Porphyry, the one who wrote against the Christians; who was properly called *Basileus* <note>original: "Basileus" (King). Porphyry is the Greek translation of his Semitic name, Malchus, which also means King.</note>. A Tyrian philosopher, a student of Amelius (who was himself a student of Plotinus), and the teacher of Iamblichus. He lived during the times of the Emperor Aurelian and continued until the reign of the Emperor Diocletian. He wrote a vast number of books—philosophical, rhetorical, and grammatical. He was also a pupil of Longinus the Critic.

*   **On Divine Names**, 1 book.
*   **On Principles**, 2 books.
*   **On Matter**, 6 books.
*   **On the Soul**, addressed to Boethus, 5 books.
*   **On Abstinence from Animal Food**, 4 books <note>A key text in the history of vegetarianism.</note>.
*   **On the Command "Know Thyself"**, 4 books.
*   **On Incorporeal Beings**.
*   **On the Fact that the Sects of Plato and Aristotle are One**, 7 books <note>Porphyry was famous for trying to harmonize the teachings of these two different philosophical schools.</note>.
*   **On the History of Julian the Chaldean Philosopher**, in 4 books.
*   **Against the Christians**, 15 books.
*   **On the Philosophy of Homer**.
*   **Against Aristotle, on the Soul being an "Entelechy"** <term>Entelechy: a technical term for the realization or complete expression of a thing's potential</term>.
*   **Philological Histories**, 5 books.
*   **On Genus, Species, Difference, Property, and Accident** <note>This work, known as the *Isagoge* or Introduction, became the standard textbook on logic in the Middle Ages.</note>.
*   **On the Sources of the Nile according to Pindar**.
*   **On the Benefit derived from Homer by Kings**, 10 books.
*   **Miscellaneous Inquiries**, 7 books.
*   **On the Preface of Thucydides**.
*   **Against Aristides**, 7 books.
*   **On the Art of Minucianus**; and many other works, especially on astronomy; among which is an **Introduction to Astronomy** in three books, and **Grammatical Problems**.

This is that Porphyry who set in motion an insulting tongue against the Christians. Porphyry, the enemy of the Christians, was from the Phoenician city of Tyre.

<meta>This page continues the biographical front matter, specifically providing the entry for Porphyry from the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia. The catchword ΠΟΡ- (POR-) refers to the beginning of Porphyry's name in Greek.</meta>

# AN ACCOUNT OF HIS LIFE AND A LIST OF HIS WORKS FROM THE SUDA.

Porphyry of Tyre, a city in Phoenicia, was a philosopher who was called "King" <note>original: "rex"; a translation of his Semitic birth name, Malchus</note> in his native language. He was a disciple of Amelius, a student of Plotinus, and the teacher of Iamblichus. He was also a student of the critic Longinus. He wrote a great many books, both philosophical and also rhetorical and grammatical: one *On Divine Names*; two *On Principles*; six *On Matter*; five *On the Soul*, addressed to Boethus; four *On Abstinence from Eating Animals*; four *On the Saying of the Wise Man, "Know Thyself"*; a work *On Incorporeals*; seven volumes on the fact *That the Schools of Plato and Aristotle are One and the Same*; four volumes *On the History of Julian the Chaldean Philosopher*; seven volumes *On Aristotle’s Categories*, addressed to Gedalius; and one volume *On the same Categories* in the form of questions and answers. He also wrote *On the Philosophy of Homer*; a work proving *That according to the Opinion of Aristotle the Soul is <term>entelecheia</term>*, that is, a "perfection" or "actualization" <note>original: "ἐντελέχεια"; a core Aristotelian concept describing the full realization of a potential</note>; five volumes of *Philosophical History*; a work *On Genus, Species, Difference, Property, and Accident* <note>This is the famous "Isagoge" or Introduction to logic</note>; *On the Sources of the Nile according to the Opinion of Pindar*; ten volumes *On the Utility Kings can Derive from Homer*; seven volumes of *Miscellaneous Questions*; seven volumes *On the Introduction of Thucydides*, addressed to Aristides; a commentary *On the Rhetorical Art of Minucianus*; and many other works, especially on astronomy, among which is an *Introduction to Astronomy* completed in three books, as well as grammatical questions. He flourished under the reign of Aurelian and lived until the times of Diocletian.

### SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT.

*The first book is divided into three parts: the first of which contains the preface to Firmus Castricius, who had fallen away from Pythagorean principles to the eating of flesh. Sections 1, 2, etc. The second embraces the arguments by which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> and the Stoics (Section 4, etc.), the Epicureans (Section 7, etc.), and Claudius of Naples (Section 13, etc.) teach that living creatures may be rightfully killed. The third part contains several matters which Porphyry sets forth for a fuller understanding and explanation of the subject at hand. Section 27, etc. First...*

**ANIMAL FOOD.**] <note>original: "ΕΜΨΥΧΩΝ"</note> *Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation* XVII. 8: "Of existing things, some are soulless <note>inanimate</note>, and others are ensouled <note>animate</note>. The soulless are stones, wood, and such things; the ensouled are plants and animals." <note>original: "τῶν ὄντων τοίνυν τὰ μὲν ἄψυχα..."</note> Nor is the opinion of Plato different, see *Julian, Oration* VI, page 193 B, or that of Aristotle, *History of Animals* VIII. 1. Our author, however, and other Pythagoreans signify *animals* specifically by this word. Compare:

<column-break/>

*Samuel Bochart, Hierozoicon* I. 1. Hence the "life of a plant" and the "life of an ensouled being" are distinguished by our author in his *Sentences on the Intelligibles*, Section 12. Therefore, "we shall not extend the principle of justice toward plants," <note>original: "καὶ πρὸς τὰ φυτὰ παρατενοῦμεν..."</note> since it is impossible to live without them, as is said below in Book III, Section 18. Yet he does not teach that plants should be harmed recklessly, but discusses that matter in another place.

# PORPHYRY

*...it is established that he does not impose this burden of abstinence upon everyone, but only upon those who desire to lead an Intellectual life <note>original: "vitam Intellectualem"; referring to the life of the mind or spirit</note>. §. 27, etc. Indeed, the alienation of the soul from those things which stir the senses and from bodily matters greatly promotes this life. §. 30, etc. Among these things, food also holds a place. §. 33, etc. For since there are various things rushing into our senses which disturb the soul, §. 33. we must beware of the contagion of them all as much as possible. §. 35, etc. Nor is it fitting for us to involve ourselves in them, following the example of the Philosophers, etc. §. 36. And since food has no small importance in this matter, §. 38. account must also be taken of it. For what some say—that they can be mixed with sensible things and yet not be disturbed by them—is a slippery argument, §. 39, etc. And it is one by which many have been deceived and entangled in foul lusts. §. 42, 43. Therefore, one must look out for all those things which are accustomed to move the mind, §. 43, etc. And moderation must also be observed in foods. §. 44, etc. Which he further proves by the example of the Epicureans. §. 49, etc. Since this is not a great task, nor too troublesome (§. 55.), it is by no means to be refused: especially since, though we may attempt and endure all things, we ought to consider it a success if at last we are permitted in any way to enjoy God. §. 56. to the end.*

A ritual formula used in ancient weddings and initiations.</note> nor as Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who taught the transmigration of souls and advocated for a bloodless diet.</note> did, having lamented his former life to return to a better one; such an approach seemed to me both unrefined and far removed from rational persuasion.
