->**Notes on the Greek and Latin Text**<-

4. *By the flight from evil...*] The ancients were accustomed to use this expression in weddings and initiations. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> says: *"I fled the evil, I found the better." It is applied to those who have come from a worse state to a better.* See Kuster there and the writers of proverbs. Presently, the Leipzig manuscript <note>original: "cod. Lipſ."</note> is faulty in reading "having flayed" instead of "having lamented," and then "returning to the better." This last is not so bad and is supported by the Meermann manuscript.

5. *According to Empedocles.*] See Book II, section 31. — VALENTINI.

6. *Found to be.*] Something seems to be missing before "found to be." For example, "for the purpose of teaching" or "for the purpose of correction." — REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a 18th-century German scholar.</note>

7. *From what things into what things...*] A nearly identical expression occurs in Psellus' *On Demons*: "exchanging what things for what things." — VALENTINI. In Aristotle, "from what things into what things," and other formulas of this kind are very frequent. See T. Gataker on Antoninus, Book X, section 26.

1. *As I reason.*] The construction gapes and falters. For "I would say" follows. Therefore, either something is missing, or it should read "For I, reasoning to myself... I would say," or "For it appears to me, reasoning to myself..." — REISKE. Certainly, these do not respond to the rules of the Grammarians. I would almost believe this is from the number of those things which they call "confusion of syntax" or "forgetfulness," which many have taught is not infrequent among the Greeks. No one even slightly cultured is ignorant that this occasionally happened to the Latins as well: at the beginning of a longer period, they would place a case for which they intended to supply a corresponding verb, but it slipped their mind.

2. *Health.*] The words "for the sake of" or "on account of" can indeed be understood, as they are often omitted. I nevertheless think "striving for" or "desiring" is missing. — REISKE. The Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts give a different spelling for "health," which are often confused. Our author, however, prefers the former.

3. *To change.*] The Leipzig manuscript reads "to have changed." The scribe intended the past tense, which is correct, for he is speaking of a past time; although the same scribe a little later writes "to contribute." — REISKE. The Meermann manuscript also has "to have changed," but a little later "to be contributing."

# PORPHYRY

And you yourself, when you were living among us, used to acknowledge that a meatless diet <note>literally: "fleshless way of life"</note> contributes to a balanced endurance of the labors required by Philosophy. Indeed, it is easy to know by experience that you were speaking the truth when you said these things. Therefore, it seems to me that you have run back to your former transgressions <note>original: "peccata" / "παρανομήματα" — referring here to the eating of meat</note> either because you were led astray by a deception—thinking that it makes no difference to Wisdom <note>term: Prudence/Wisdom (Phronesis) — the practical application of philosophical knowledge</note> whether one eats in this way or that—or perhaps for some other reason unknown to me, which inspired a greater fear in you than the impiety of breaking your commitment. For I would never say that you held the ancestral laws of that Philosophy you once admired in such contempt because of a lack of self-control or a fear <note>see margin note 5 regarding the correction to "desire"</note> of gluttonous greed. Nor would I say that your nature is inferior to that of certain common people <margin>6</margin>. For there are those <margin>7</margin> who, having accepted laws contrary to those by which they previously lived, endure the cutting of their own limbs <note>likely a reference to circumcision or ritual scarification</note> and would sooner abstain from certain animals they used to feast upon than they would from human flesh.

->§ 3.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>4. The Fear etc.]</margin> So below in § 9: "They suspended an irrational fear." *Clement of Alexandria*, Miscellanies Book II, p. 412 B: "Wherefore it seems to me the Law divinely and necessarily suspends Fear." <note>original: "ἐπαρτᾶν" — to hang over or suspend, as a threat</note>

<margin>5. Lack of self-control and fear [desire] etc.]</margin> In the margin of the French edition, "desire" <note>original: "πόθον"</note> was substituted for "fear" <note>original: "Φόβον"</note>. The sense of the passage seems to require this. VALENTINUS. *Plutarch* in the Symposiacs, Vol. II, p. 667 F: "For we call people 'fish-eaters' and 'delicacy-lovers,' not those who delight in beef... but those who are always hanging around the fish-market." But the term has a much wider application. *Clement of Alexandria* says rightly in The Instructor, Book II, p. 146 B: "Gluttony <note>original: "ὀψοφαγία"</note> is nothing other than excess in the use of delicacies. And 'throat-madness' <note>original: "λαιμαργία"</note> is a mania concerning the gullet." Hence "delicacy-eating" and "throat-madness" and similar terms are usually joined together. The manuscripts agree in a manifest error here, giving "fear" instead of "desire."

<margin>6. Common people.]</margin> See Book II, § 61. VALENTINUS.

<margin>7. Who [accepted] contrary laws...]</margin> *Sextus Empiricus*, Outlines of Pyrrhonism, III. 24: "For a Jew or an Egyptian priest would sooner die than eat swine's flesh." Our author also mentions the Jews below in II. 61 and IV. 13. He seems, however, to be referring to the history of the Maccabees, as *Fabricius* also thought in the Greek Library, Book IV, ch. 27, p. 201.

§ 3. Since some who arrived also recounted the arguments you were accustomed to make against those who abstain <note>from eating meat</note>, I felt not only distressed, but truly indignant and angry. It is shameful that you allowed yourselves to be deceived by such cold and utterly stale sophistries, and that you suffered yourselves to overturn an ancient <term>doctrine</term> <note>Greek: dogma; a settled principle or belief</note> that is dear to the gods. Therefore, I thought it would be worth my while not only to demonstrate our own position as it truly is, but also to collect and refute the arguments of our adversaries. These opposing views are far stronger than those you mentioned—in their abundance, their force, and their general preparation. I shall show that the truth is not defeated even by those arguments which seem weighty, let alone by stale and superficial trifles. ->The followers<- of Epicurus directed the bulk of their opposition against the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles, which you have earnestly striven to emulate. ->The followers<- of Epicurus directed their contradiction against the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles: whose rival you have desired to be at this present time. # On Abstinence, Book I.

->**Chapter 5**<-

<column-break/>

...we should consider that both men and gods look upon us, while we also maintain a relationship with other brute animals that have no direct dealings with us. We should not use some for labor and others for food, judging them to be entirely foreign and excluded from our society, as if they were outside the human commonwealth. For he who wishes to behave toward them just as he does toward men—sparing them and doing them no harm—attributes to justice a burden it cannot bear <note>The author argues that extending full human rights to animals might make the practice of justice impossible for humans.</note>. In doing so, he destroys that which is possible, and by introducing foreign elements, he takes away and ruins what is proper to justice. For it follows that either we must act unjustly by not sparing them, or if we do spare them and refuse to use them, we will be unable to carry on our lives. In the end, we would live the life of beasts ourselves if we were to reject the use of beasts.

§ 5. For even if I pass over the infinite multitude of Nomads and Troglodytes <note>Cave-dwellers; ancient authors often used these groups as examples of "primitive" diets.</note> who recognize no other nourishment but flesh: for us, who seem to live mildly and humanely, what work of the earth, what work of the sea, what...

<column-break/>

...considering that both gods and men look upon us, and having a natural relation even toward the other beasts that do not belong to us. And we should not use some for work and others for food, deeming them alien and dishonored from our fellowship as if from a city-state. For he who treats these as he treats men, sparing them and not harming them, attaches to justice that which it cannot bear, and destroys its potential; he corrupts what is proper to it by adding what is foreign. For it becomes necessary for us either to act unjustly by not sparing them, or, if we do not use them, life becomes impossible and without resources; and in a certain way, we shall live the life of beasts if we give up the utility derived from beasts.

§ 5. For I leave aside the undiscovered myriads of Nomads and Troglodytes, who know flesh as food and nothing else; but even for us, who seem to live gently and with love for mankind, what labor is left of the earth, what...

---

<margin>
4. **By what is foreign.**] In the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, it is incorrectly written as "of foreign things."
1. **For I leave aside the Nomads etc.**] You may read these things in *Plutarch*, Volume II, page 964 A. More will be said concerning the customs of these nations in Book IV, section 21. Instead of "of numbers" (*arithmōn*), the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* codices have "in number" (*arithmō*); which some also prefer in *Plutarch*, and which the learned *Reiske* restored in his *Observations on Plutarch’s Short Works*, page 548.
2. **Is left of the earth.**] "Of the earth" (*gēs*) is missing in the *Leipzig* manuscript, which is an error. Perhaps it should be read "is left upon the earth" (*epi gēs*). — REISKE.

# PORPHYRY

...in the sea, 4 what clear art, what ornament of our way of life would be left to us, if we were so disposed toward other animals as if they were our own kin, 5 and if we conducted ourselves toward them harmlessly and with reverence? 6 For it is no small task to say—indeed there is no remedy, nor any cure for the poverty that destroys life— 7 unless we possess justice, and unless we preserve the ancient law and boundary 8 as, according to Hesiod, Zeus divided the natures and established each of the races separately,

<column-break/>

for what distinguished art, what ornament of our livelihood would be left, if we were so affected toward other animals as if they were related to us, such that we conducted ourselves harmlessly and piously toward them? Indeed, we shall be able to provide no remedy for such great want—which takes away all life and justice—unless we preserve the ancient law and definition. Since, as Hesiod says, when Jupiter <note>The Latin translator uses the Roman name Jupiter for the Greek Zeus.</note> had distinguished the natures, and had established each genus of animals separately,

<column-break/>

3. **Which in the sea etc.** [Plutarch: *in the mountains*] **art — if toward kin etc.** Plutarch says: *if we learn to conduct ourselves harmlessly and with reverence toward all animals, as is fitting for rational beings and those of the same race, it is no small task to say.* VALENTINUS. <note>Valentinus is the editor comparing Porphyry's text to a similar passage in Plutarch.</note>

4. **What clear art.** *Active* or *busy* is the art which will be exercised. It could also be read as *some activity of art* so that it corresponds to the next phrase, *some ornament of life.* REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774) was a famous German physician and philologist known for his critiques of Greek texts.</note> *Clear* <note>original: "enarges"</note> and *active* <note>original: "energes"</note> are frequently confused; some would prefer to render the former in St. Paul, 1 Cor. 16:9, but against the evidence of the manuscripts. Often also *fate* <note>original: "energeia"</note> is used for *activity*. See Bengel on Paul’s epistle to Philemon, 6. Iamblichus also speaks of *active art* in *On the Mysteries* II:2. Yet I would not dare to proscribe the common reading, which Felicianus also read. Immediately after, instead of *we are disposed*, Reiske preferred *being disposed*.

5. **Harmlessly — let us conduct ourselves.** To *conduct oneself reasonably* refers to mild and gentle treatment, as in Diodorus Siculus IV.53; the opposite of which is to *conduct oneself bitterly, violently* etc., concerning which see the Great Interpreter there.

6. **For to say is no task.** Instead of *to say*, the sense requires *it remains* or *it is left*, or since it is punctuated this way in the Leipzig Manuscript: *for to say the task —* one might conjecture: *for there remains, so to speak, no task.* "There is left absolutely none, if it is permitted to say, the work." REISKE. In Plutarch, these things are read in a slightly different way, yet we have *it is no task to say then, no remedy* etc. In our author

<column-break/>

therefore, I would wish it to be retained as well. He is accustomed quite often—as are others—to omit the word *is*, which if you insert it, the sentence seems clear. However, Meermann distinguishes it in the same way as the Leipzig manuscript. In the Bodleian manuscript, the word *for* was unfortunately missing.

7. **If we have justice.** Perhaps: *if, holding fast to justice, we do not preserve the ancient law and boundary, by which according to Hesiod...* REISKE. Consider with me those words of Plutarch: *therefore no remedy, nor any cure for the poverty that either destroys life or destroys justice do we have* etc. You should know that the oldest editions have it thus (for the Cambridge editor first brought forth *if* <note>original: "ei"</note> instead of *or* <note>original: "ē"</note>), and it is read no differently in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts: and you will admit that I have rightly driven out the corrupt writing and restored to Porphyry his own *or*.

8. **Let us preserve as according to etc.** In Plutarch it is read thus: *Let us preserve, by which according to Hesiod, having divided the natures and established each of the races separately, to the fish indeed...* It seems that *Zeus* is missing in Plutarch. *By which, according to Hesiod, Zeus...* etc. or *by which* in Plutarch should be changed to *as*. I had not deliberately translated Plutarch's words before, and the false punctuation in Porphyry caused me to not interpret it entirely correctly. If you remove the period at *Let us preserve* and *each*, and add only a comma, everything will become clear. The version of the verses from Hesiod is Grotius's: from *On the Law of War and Peace* I, I: 11. Porphyry changed the end of the third verse. For in Hesiod it is read (*Works and Days* 277): *it becomes much better —* VALENTINUS.

§ 6. Moreover, for those with whom there is no mutual dealing of acting justly toward us, there is likewise no account of acting unjustly on our part toward them. Those who reject this reasoning leave no other way for justice to enter, not even a narrow path. For that which we have already said—that our nature, which is not self-sufficient but in need of many things, would be barred from the help of other animals—is nothing other than to utterly destroy life and shut it up in a state that is difficult, lacking all tools, and destitute of necessary things. Furthermore, they say that those first men did not live very fortunately; for superstition <note>The author uses "superstition" here to refer to an excessive or irrational scrupulousness regarding what one may eat.</note> does not contain itself within the boundaries of animals, but eventually even breaks into the realm of plants.

# PORPHYRIUS

<column-break/>

...writing, nor without the record of those things which still endure and are by nature suited to be passed down; but rather by the consent of those <margin>1</margin> who were to use them. For it was by the wisdom of the soul, not by bodily strength or the tyrannical <margin>2</margin> enslavement of the masses, that those who introduced such things to the multitude excelled. They brought some to a rational understanding of what is useful—those who previously perceived it without reason and often forgot it—while others they struck with awe through the greatness of the penalties. For there was no other remedy to use against the ignorance of what is beneficial than the fear of the punishment defined <margin>3</margin> by the law. Indeed, this alone even now restrains ordinary men and prevents them from doing what is unprofitable, whether publicly or privately. For if everyone were able to see and remember what is useful in a similar way, <margin>4</margin> they would not—

<column-break/>

<note>The Latin text here is a contemporary translation of the Greek column to the left, which has been integrated into the English translation above for readability.</note>

---

<column-break/>

1. *Those who use them.*] By a peculiar expression, those who observe a law, or those for whom a law is passed to be observed, are said to "use the law" <note>original: "χρῆσθαι νόμῳ"</note>. *Plato* in the *Minos*, page 565 C: "nor do they themselves always use the same laws." *Thucydides*, Book V, chapter 105: "We neither established the law, nor were we the first to use it once it was laid down." These passages shed light on those words of *St. Paul* in *1 Timothy 1:8*: "The law is good, if one uses it lawfully." Those words "now and suited to be passed down" are missing in the *Lipsius* manuscript.

2. *Enslavement*] <note>original: "Δουλεύσει"</note> Should be read as "Subjugation" <note>original: "Δουλώσει"</note>, meaning oppression. For the original term refers to the "state of slavery" which is endured, not that which is imposed upon the weak by the powerful. *REISKE* <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. The illustrious *Abresch* also favored this, and rightly so.

<column-break/>

3. *By the law.*] Elsewhere he uses "under" <note>original: "ὑπὸ"</note> the law. But the former is not to be condemned; it is put for the latter a hundred times, and thus one has everywhere taken the place of the other. See regarding that confusion *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus IV, 46*; *D'Orville* on *Chariton VI, 4*; and many others.

4. *They would have no need of laws.*] A most true sentiment. Hence: "laws did not exist among men as long as they were happy," below in Book III, 16. And the law "left the Brahmans to be their own legislators, and was revered as something superior to itself," Book IV, Section 18. *St. Paul, 1 Timothy 1:9*: "The law is not laid down for the righteous man." Here the interpreters will measure out the sayings of others on this matter "by the whole sackful," as the saying goes. Yet *Philo* is beautiful on this...

# On Abstinence, Book I.

If men were able to keep in mind what is truly beneficial, there would be no need for laws; instead, they would of their own accord avoid those things which are forbidden and perform those which are commanded. For the consideration of what is useful and what is harmful would be sufficient to encourage the flight from evil and the choice of good. But the imposition of punishment is directed toward those who cannot perceive what is beneficial: for them, the threat of terror hanging over them forces them to master the desires that drag them toward useless actions, and thus by force keeps them in their duty.

§ 9. Hence, the legislators did not wish even involuntary homicide to be entirely free from all punishment, so that they might not only give no occasion to any to willfully imitate the deeds of those who acted unwillingly, but also to take care that many such things should not happen <note>The author argues that even accidental deaths must be punished to maintain a high standard of public caution.</note>

<column-break/>

they would have no further need of laws; but by their own choice they would avoid forbidden things and do what was commanded. For the contemplation of the useful and the harmful is sufficient to provide for the avoidance of the former and the choice of the latter. But the <gloss>5</gloss> raising up of punishment <note>original: "ζημίας ἀνάστασις"</note> is for those who do not foresee what is advantageous. For the threat hanging over them forces them to master the impulses that lead to unprofitable actions, and by force compels them to do what is necessary.

§ 9. Since even involuntary homicide was not established by the legislators as being outside of all punishment; so that they might not grant any pretext to those who might choose to willfully imitate the actions of those who act involuntarily; but rather so that <gloss>2</gloss> such a thing might not be unguarded or neglected,

---

<margin>I ought to add a passage from Philemon <note>A Greek New Comedy poet</note>, because it is similar to ours. Thus he says in Fragment page 290:
> O how wicked a thing is the nature of man
> Entirely, for it never had any need of law. <note>The commentator notes the irony that if man were good, law would be unnecessary.</note>

5. *Raising up of punishment.*] Perhaps it should be *uprising*, and then *for it is a necessity to master*. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a noted 18th-century philologist</note>. *Anastasis* [Raising up] is a threat accompanied by bitterness and boldness, as *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says. For it is said that *anateinesthai* [to stretch up] is used properly of those who lift a staff, which is the gesture of those threatening. Hence *anastasis* and *epanastasis* are often used in threats. See: *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus* XIV, 3. Next, *Lipsius* reads: "those not yet seeing."

1. *So that they might not grant.*] It seems that "not" <note>original: "οὐχ’"</note> is missing before "so that," to which "but so that" in line 29 would respond. VALENTINUS. Perhaps "not only, so that no..."</margin>

*grant.* REISKE. *Not so that* had already been written in the margin by *Fogerolles*, and indeed it is customary for our author and others to say *not so that* instead of *not only*. However, in this place, it seems to me that *not only* is suppressed by ellipsis <note>A grammatical omission where the meaning is understood</note>. For Greek writers are accustomed to this, as in *Gospel of John* XII, 44. and *V. D.* on *Xenophon of Ephesus, Miscellaneous Observations* Vol. X. p. 201. Latin writers follow the same manner of speaking, who say *non* [not] for *non modo* [not only], followed by *sed* [but]. *Corte* gathered a harvest of examples on *Sallust, in the Jugurthine War* XIV, 23. For *ekdōsi* [give out], which was a printer's error in the *Cambridge* edition, I have restored *endōsi* [grant]. *Meermann* incorrectly reads *involuntary* [plural].

2. *Might be unguarded.*] Thus *Valentinus* correctly; previously it was incorrectly read as *was* [past tense], which was also in the *Bodleian Manuscript*.

# PORPHYRY

...so that many things happen that are truly involuntary. For this was not beneficial either, for the same reasons that we said it was forbidden for men to destroy one another in a voluntary manner. Therefore, since among involuntary acts, some occur due to an **unpredictable cause** <note>original: ἀσάθμητον αἰτίαν</note> and one that cannot be guarded against by **human nature**, while others occur due to our own negligence and **lack of attention to the difference** <note>original: ἀνεπίσατον τῆς διαφορᾶς</note>, [the legislators], wishing to prevent the **indolence** <note>original: ῥᾳθυμίαν</note> that harms those nearby, did not leave even the involuntary action unpunished. Instead, **by the fear of penalties**, they curtailed the great frequency of such errors. And I think...

<column-break/>

...[they feared] that things might occur which were truly involuntary. For neither was that advantageous, for the same reasons for which we said it was also forbidden that men should willfully destroy one another. Wherefore, since among involuntary acts some are committed from an uncertain cause, and of such a kind that cannot be avoided by human nature; others from our negligence and carelessness, not noticing how much a thing matters: in order to prevent others from being harmed by our inertia, they did not leave even the involuntary action unpunished; but by the terror of punishments, they restrained the abundance of this kind of sin. And...

***

3. *Unpredictable cause.*] "Cause" can be explained as the cause of things which can neither be foreseen by the sharpness of the mind nor guessed at by conjecture. I fear, nonetheless, that the word is less than suitable. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar.</note>. The word *asathmētos* [unpredictable/unstable] was excellently illustrated by *D’Orville on Chariton* VI, 4, where he taught that it is very frequently applied to *Fortune*, *the masses*, and *human nature*. Nothing should be added to those remarks.

4. *Human nature.*] Our author [Porphyry] uses this phrasing below quite often, but he never says *anthrōpeia physis* [an alternative form of "human nature"]. *M. Thomas* prescribes that the latter should be said, not the former. But the notes of the *Famous Duker on Thucydides* III, 40 and *Wesseling’s Observations* I, 30 will show you by what right they teach this. There is, therefore, nothing unusual in those words of *St. James* III, 7: "has been tamed by human nature." However, the other term seems to have a greater mark of antiquity. Compare the learned *Pierson on Moeris*, p. 26.

5. *And lack of attention to the difference.*] "The lack of attention to the difference" is the thoughtlessness and blindness of a quarreling anger, when he who brawls, carried away by the heat of rage, does not sufficiently collect himself, nor foresee what he is preparing or what he is doing, but is borne along blindly and, inflamed by the glow of a raging mind, perpetrates those things which he may regret having done. <term>REISKE</term>. The conjecture of the Learned Man is ingenious, as he preferred *unstable destruction* <note>original: ἀνεπίστατον τῆς διαφθορᾶς</note>. The *Cambridge Editor* had added the article "the" before "lack of attention." But neither the earlier editions nor the manuscripts recognize it. Often, both in our author and in others, you may find the article sometimes added and sometimes neglected, in which matters we must attend to the usage of the writer.

6. *Harms those nearby*] Either "the" <note>original: τοὺς</note> must be read simply instead of "them" <note>original: αὐτοὺς</note>, or if that is kept, it should read "them and those nearby" <note>original: αὐτοὺς καὶ τοὺς πλησίον</note>, meaning both the parties in the strife and the rest of the citizens. <term>REISKE</term>. The *Lyons* and *Cambridge Editions* had substituted "the" for "them," but since all the *Manuscripts* agree on "them" <note>original: αὐτοὺς</note>, I do not doubt but that by the fault of the scribes, two words which ought to have been distinguished—"again those" <note>original: αὖ τοὺς</note>—coalesced into one. I have the *Meerman manuscript* in agreement. This happens quite often to this little word in our author and others, as will be said elsewhere. The translator rendered the word *rhathymia* as "inertia"; nor is that bad. However, it has a broader meaning, and signifies a vice of the soul devoted to worthless things, and hence also encompasses the vices flowing from there. See *Perizonius on Aelian’s Varia Historia* IX, 9.

7. *By the fear of penalties*] The *Leipzig manuscript* reads "the penalties of cattle" <note>original: τῶν βοτῶν ἐπιτιμίων</note>; a monstrous corruption. It is the same whether the common reading is kept and "the great part" <note>original: τὸ πολὺ</note> is taken for the multitude, frequency, or commonness [of the error]: or whether one reads...

# On Abstinence, Book I.

Indeed, I believe that even those killings permitted by law were required to be atoned for through certain customary expiations for no other reason than this: those who first established these rites wished to distance men as far as possible from voluntary acts of violence. Since people required some form of prohibition from every side, the founders acted so that men would not slip so recklessly into committing acts that are not beneficial. Therefore, those who first observed this did not only establish legal penalties; they also introduced another kind of "irrational" terror, declaring that those who had killed a human being in any manner whatsoever were contaminated <note>original: "contaminatos"</note> unless they had purged themselves with certain sacrificial atonements. For in this way, the irrational part of the soul, being educated in various ways, arrives at a proper state of gentleness.

<column-break/>

And I, for my part, [maintain] that even killings permitted by law require the customary satisfactions through purifications for no other cause—according to those who first beautifully introduced these things—than the desire to keep men as far as possible from voluntary action. For common men everywhere needed something to prevent them from readily doing what is not advantageous. Hence, those first [legislators] who were conscious of this did not only ordain punishments, but they also suspended another irrational fear over them, proclaiming that those who had killed a man in any way were not "pure" <note>original: "καθαροὺς"</note> unless they made use of purifications. For the foolish part of the soul, having been guided like a child <note>original: "παιδαγωγηθὲν"</note> in various ways, came into a settled state of refinement.

---

<column-break/>

...they took away much <note>original: "ἀφείλοντο πολὺ"</note>; in two words, *they greatly detracted from the error.* <term>Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note></term> Well said and relevant to our subject is <term>Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies <note>original: "Stromata"</note></term> Book II, p. 376: "For those whom reason does not capture, fear tames."

8. **By those who first [introduced]... beautifully.** <term>Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, renowned Renaissance humanist.</note></term> [suggests] "by" <note>original: "ὑπὸ"</note> (which <term>Reiske</term> approved, to vary the style) "those who first [introduced]... badly" <note>original: "κακῶς"</note>. The <term>Meermann</term> and <term>Bodleian</term> manuscripts also prefer "by" and "badly." The oldest editions also have "first" <note>original: "πρώτων"</note>, which was changed by <term>Valentin</term> to "firstly" <note>original: "πρῶτον"</note>, but I have restored it to its place. However, "badly" <note>original: "κακῶς"</note> was previously read incorrectly instead of "beautifully" <note>original: "καλῶς"</note>, unless perhaps it was "not badly." We shall mention elsewhere how these words were commonly confused.

9. **Being conscious of this.** <term>Reiske</term> says: I am unwilling to change "being conscious" <note>original: "Συνειδότες"</note> because of the multitude of examples from which I believe I have understood that the ancients were accustomed to use "being conscious" in place of "having observed" <note>original: "συνιδὼν"</note>. I shall bring forth some of these examples regarding <term>Polybius</term> if the fates allow. See the notes on <term>Polybius</term>, Book I, p. 104. Next, for "suspended over" <note>original: "ἐπήρτησαν"</note>, the <term>Bodleian</term> manuscript gave "placed above" and <term>Lipsius</term> gave "detached." Both are faulty. Our author speaks this way also above in section 2; see there.

10. **Guided like a child in various ways.** A beautiful turn of phrase. The irrational part of the soul is called a "child" <note>original: "παῖς"</note> by the Philosophers, over whom a "tutor" <note>original: "παιδαγωγὸς"</note> must preside; to rule and moderate it is "to act as a tutor" <note>original: "παιδαγωγεῖν"</note>, and the thing itself is "tutelage" <note>original: "παιδαγωγία"</note>. See below in section 44: "Some allow the child to do what he wants by himself; others leave it to the tutor." So also in Book III, 26 and elsewhere. <term>Heraclitus</term> in *Homeric Allegories*: "Just as if reason, acting as a tutor, aroused his capacity for concern." <term>The learned Palairetus</term> compares this passage with Paul's letter to the Galatians 3:24, where with similar elegance the Law is called a "tutor" <note>original: "παιδαγωγός"</note>.

11. **Devising beforehand, etc.** The construction of the words seems quite perplexed. In the translation, I believe we have followed the sense, even if not...

# PORPHYRY

...devising various ways to tame the irrational impulse of desire <gloss>12</gloss> from the very beginning by those who served the multitudes; among these [rules] is also the requirement not to kill one another without judgment.

§ 10. Regarding the other animals, those who first defined what we ought and ought not to do reasonably did not forbid us from destroying any of them. For in their case, utility was achieved through the opposite action. For it was not possible to be safe unless they attempted to ward off <gloss>1</gloss> [the animals] while living together with one another. And some of the most refined men of that time <gloss>2</gloss>, remembering how they themselves abstained from killing [each other] because it was useful for their safety, instilled in the rest a memory of what happens in the—

<column-break/>

—namely: while they apply various modes of taming to the irrational incitement of desire, those who from the beginning cultivated the peoples: one of which is also that they should not kill each other without a trial.

§ 10. But regarding other animals, those who first established for us what things were to be done, or not done, rightly forbade the killing of none: since indeed utility in these matters arose for us from the contrary action. For it could not happen that they were safe, unless they had tried to repel the attacks of the beasts among whom the men lived. Since therefore some of those who were then the most elegant remembered that they had abstained from mutual slaughter for the reason that it contributed to the safety of others in common societies, the outcome of the matter—

<column-break/>

<margin>
*Not the form of the words. The word* "the" [Greek: τὰς] *must be deleted, and thus it may be interpreted more literally: to those who first ruled the multitude, inventing certain things for the wild, etc.* VALENTINUS. <note>Valentinus refers to a specific grammatical correction in the Greek text.</note> *The word* "the" [τὰς] *is rightly absent from the Leipzig manuscript; it was inserted by Valentinus.* "Desire" [ἐπιθυμίας] *is in the genitive case in this place.* REISKE. *Valentinus had taken it from Fogerolles, who had ineptly added that* "the" [τὰς] *in the margin; all others agree on* "the" [τῆς].
</margin>

<margin>
12. "Taming of those who served the multitudes."] *Perhaps it should read:* "the tamings of those who from the beginning adorned the multitudes." *The meaning is this: when those who, at the beginning of the human race, first instructed and polished the peoples with a noble cultivation of mind, laws, and customs, skillfully devised ferments and soothings of desire against the force and impetus of brute lust.* REISKE. *I would also prefer* "adorned" [διακοσμησάντων], *although I know what can be said in defense of the common reading.* Arntzen. <note>Scholars are debating whether the original Greek meant "serving" the people or "ordering/adorning" the people.</note>
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
"To serve" [Διακονεῖν] *takes the dative, as no one is unaware. In a ministry of this kind, the voice is also quite appropriate, just as* "to tame," "to act as an envoy," *and* "to serve" *are joined in Pollux IV: 28. Here, however, there seems to be another reason. Abresch preferred* "those who inhabited," *as if it were read in this order: devising tamings (by) those who from the beginning inhabited the multitudes...*

1. "This living together."] *In place of* "this" [τοῦτο], *Fogerolles had substituted* "them" [αὐτὰ] *in the margin, which Valentinus accepted, but against the faith of all manuscripts. It seemed to Reiske that something was missing between* "to ward off" *and* "this." *To me, it seems that* "this" [τοῦτο] *was born from* "those" [τοὺς] *through a shorthand of letters. And that also pleased the learned Abresch.*

2. "As they themselves abstained."] "They themselves" [Αὐτοί τε] *without* "as" [ὡς], *which seems to have crept in wrongly from the end of the preceding word* "refined" [χαριεσάτων]. REISKE. *The Leipzig manuscript reads* "abstained." *Moreover, those who are polished and refined are called* "the most elegant" [χαριέσατοι]...
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

they recalled: so that by abstaining from those of a kindred race, they might preserve a fellowship which would greatly assist in the individual safety of each person. Furthermore, this separation of men gathered into one place, and their abstinence from mutual harm, was useful not only for repelling the attacks of animals of a different species, but also for warding off other men who might approach for the purpose of doing harm. And for some time indeed, for this reason, those who came together into the same community for their necessities abstained from one another, and they brought some utility to both of the goals mentioned. But later, as time progressed, and kinship became more widely spread through mutual procreation, and thus external animals were driven out—

<column-break/>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

-> C 2 <-

<meta>catchword: ui- / θος</meta>

...be killed. For none of those animals which the laws permit to be killed is of such a kind that, if allowed to increase to an excessive abundance, it would not bring harm to mankind; yet, if maintained in a moderate number, it provides certain uses for human life. For the sheep and the ox, and all such creatures, if they remain in a moderate state, offer certain benefits for the necessary conduct of our lives; but if they should fall into a great redundancy and exceed in number beyond what is fitting, they would undermine our lives: the oxen indeed turning to violence, inasmuch as they are endowed by nature with sufficient strength and robustness for that purpose; and the sheep by grazing upon the food that springs from the earth for our sake. For this reason, the slaughter of this kind of animal was not prohibited: so that a multitude of them might be left which serves our use and which can be easily managed. For it is not as with lions and wolves, and all others called wild beasts—both small and large—where no multitude can be found which, if left alone, would assist...

<column-break/>

...for, so to speak, there is no such thing among those permitted by the law which, if allowed to reach an excess of abundance, would not become harmful to us. But when maintained at the current population, it provides certain necessities for life. For indeed the sheep and the ox and every such creature, being in moderation, brings certain benefits toward our necessary way of life; but if it falls into every kind of profusion and possesses a great excess <gloss>3</gloss> beyond the established limit, it would ruin our life. The one [the ox] even turning toward strength <note>original: ἀλκὴν; referring to physical force or aggression</note>, since <gloss>4</gloss> it shares in a nature well-suited for this. The other [the sheep] merely consuming the food sent up for us from the earth. Therefore, and for this reason, it was not forbidden to destroy even such animals, so that a population advantageous for our use might be left behind, and one that would be able to be easily controlled. For it is not as in the case of lions and wolves and simply those called wild animals, <gloss>5</gloss> likewise both small and large, it is not possible to take any multitude...

In a like manner, *established gentleness* at the end of section 9 is also to be understood. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist.</note>

The celebrated <term>Valckenaer</term> <note>Lodewijk Caspar Valckenaer (1715–1785), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> clearly explained the proper and improper use of the voice in his *Observations on Ammonius*, Book II, 2. § 12. <gloss>1</gloss> For reasons similar to those already stated, one must consider that the regulations regarding the eating of living beings were determined by those who originally <gloss>2</gloss> established these laws. # On Abstinence, Book I.

->C 3<-

Let everyone take notice: some people, thinking that certain matters are of no consequence, overlook them; others hold contrary opinions about these same things, and judge that which does not contribute to the universal good to be useful everywhere. From this it happens that they sometimes decree things that do not suit everyone, provided they have found things that are profitable to themselves and contribute to their mutual utility. Of such a kind are the regulations established among most nations concerning the eating and slaughter of animals <note>original: "de animalium esu & caede"</note> due to the specific nature of their region; which certainly ought not to be observed by us, since we do not inhabit the same place. If, therefore, just as among men, a certain compact <note>term: pactum — a formal agreement or social contract</note> could have been made with the rest of the animals concerning slaughter—so that they would not kill us, nor we kill them indiscriminately—justice would have been rightly extended that far; for it would have been sufficient for our security. But because it was in no way possible for those creatures which are devoid of reason <note>original: "expertia rationis"</note> to have a communication of laws and justice:

<column-break/>

...some do not perceive these things as applying to everyone. Instead, some, believing them to be among the "indifferent" things <note>term: adiaphora — in Stoic philosophy, things that are neither morally good nor bad in themselves</note>, pass them over. Others hold the opposite opinion about them, and some think that things which are not universally beneficial are beneficial everywhere. For this reason, they cling to things that are not applicable. Even if, in some cases, they discover what is advantageous to themselves and what has a common utility—among which are the regulations concerning the eating and destruction of living beings <note>original: "τὰς ἐδωδὰς τῶν ἐμψύχων"</note> ordained in most nations because of the particularity of the land. It is not necessary for us to abide by these, because we do not inhabit the same place. If, then, they were able to make a certain treaty, just as with men, so also with the rest of the animals, regarding not killing—so that they would not be killed by us without judgment—it would be well to extend justice to that point; for it would be stretched toward security. But since it was among the impossible things for those animals that do not receive reason <note>original: "λόγον"</note> to share in law...

---

REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. Valent: had added *than*, but against the authority of all the others, and therefore we have restored the old writing. # On Abstinence, Book I.

It is argued that it is according to nature for man to eat meat, just as it is contrary to nature for him to eat it raw. <note>The author is exploring the philosophical argument that humans are biologically "meant" to eat meat, but only when transformed by fire.</note> Hence, after the discovery of fire, it came about that they arrived at what was suited to their nature by admitting meat once cooking was applied. For lynxes are "eaters of raw flesh" <note>original: *crudiuori*</note>; and that famous line was spoken as a reproach: *Indeed, you would devour Priam raw* <note>Homer, Iliad 4.35</note>; and: *Tearing the raw flesh, he devoured it with a full mouth*—as if, clearly, the eating of raw flesh is attributed to the impious. But this is considered human: *The attendant placed chargers full of various meats here and there.* <note>Homer, Odyssey 1.141</note> At first, therefore, they did not feed upon animals, because

<column-break/>

it is natural for man to eat meat, but contrary to nature to eat it raw. Therefore, when fire was discovered, they reclaimed what was natural by accepting meat through boiling. # On Abstinence, Book I.

->D<-

Whether they have attacked us or not, we kill them so that no evil may come to us from them. For there is no one who, if he sees a serpent, does not immediately kill it to the best of his ability, lest he himself or any other human at all be infested by its bite. This is done not so much out of hatred for the beast as out of the benevolence of man toward man. Since, therefore, war against wild beasts is just, we nevertheless tend to abstain from many animals that live among humans. Hence the Greeks eat neither dogs nor horses, nor likewise asses, because the tame versions are of the same genus as the wild ones; yet they eat swine, and also poultry. 8. **The Phoenicians and Jews.**] Concerning the Jews, more will be said immediately. It was also a solemn custom for the Phoenicians to abstain from pigs. Hence, among the gifts which the Emperor Elagabalus <note>A Roman Emperor of Syrian/Phoenician origin known for introducing Eastern customs to Rome.</note> used to scatter, were "all animals that are tame, except for wild ones, and excluding pigs; for he abstained from these according to Phoenician law," according to **Herodian** <note>A Greek historian of the Roman Empire.</note> Book I, 6. §. 22. But see **Bochart's** *Sacred Zoology* <note>original: "Hieroz:" referring to Samuel Bochart's 1663 work on animals in the Bible.</note> Vol. II. chapter 57. page 702.

9. **At all in those places.**] Tacitus, Plutarch, and others—about whom we do not speak here—fluctuate greatly in defining the causes why the Jews so abhorred the pig. However, **Petavius** (in his notes on Julian's Oration v. p. 91) and **Castellanus** (on the eating of flesh, Book IV, ch. 4) observe that the history of the pigs into which the sacred text <note>The Bible.</note> narrates demons were sent proves the falsity of the reason our author [Porphyry] brings forward. Truly, that cannot be forced from the Gospel. Read what the incomparable **Bochart** argued in *Sacred Zoology* II. c. 57. p. 697. This genus of beasts was not found in Judea, not because the region was unsuitable for rearing them, but because it was not permitted to rear them through religion.

10. **Nor now in Ethiopia.**] **S. Bochart** (in the cited place, p. 703) concludes from this that the Ethiopians also abstained from pigs. However, **Aelian** (History of Animals XVII, 10) relates from Dinon that a "four-horned pig" <note>original: "ὗς τετράκερως"</note> is born in Ethiopia. **Bochart** also reviews other nations which had the same institution. To those, the people of Comana are added from **Strabo** (according to Diodorus Vol. I. p. 380). I, an eminent man, add the Cretans, about whom **Athenaeus** writes in Book IX, 4; and the Galatians of Pessinus, "who do not touch pigs," according to **Pausanias** in his *Description of Greece* (Achaica, p. 430).

<column-break/>

11. **Just as therefore a camel**] Greece did not abound in camels, wherefore a Learned Man <note>original: "V. D." for Vir Doctus.</note> in his notes on **Diogenes Laertius** (found in Philostratus' *Life of Apollonius* Vol. I, 13) restored the word "apples" <note>original: "μήλοις"</note> in place of "camels" <note>original: "καμήλοις"</note>, which I see is approved by **Olearius**. Regarding other peoples, the opposite is brought forth. **Jerome** (Against Jovinian, II. 7): "The Arabs and Saracens and all the barbarians of the desert live on the milk and meat of camels; because an animal of this kind, due to the climate and sterility of the regions, is easily both born and nourished among them." Instead of "therefore" <note>original: "οὖν"</note>, **Reiske** preferred "on the other hand" <note>original: "αὖ"</note>. Shortly after, the word "the" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> before "animals" <note>original: "ζῶα"</note> had been wrongly omitted in the Cambridge edition, which I have restored to its place from the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts and the old editions.

12. **Nor the Egyptians.**] The Egyptians abstained from pigs, as many teach, but they agree very little in defining the cause of the matter. See **Bochart** in the place cited a little earlier. However, **Herodotus** (II, 47) says they were sacrificed to the Moon and Bacchus <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Osiris in this context.</note>, and I believed those sacrifices were discussed in the same work (ch. 45). A Great Man <note>Likely a reference to a specific scholar like Scaliger or Bochart.</note> thinks that passage is corrupt and should be understood as referring to sheep, which Herodotus teaches the Mendesians sacrificed. **Strabo** (Book XVII. p. 552) contradicts this regarding the Nitriote Nome: "among these alone in Egypt is a sheep sacrificed." **Plutarch**, however, affirms that only the Lycopolitans eat sheep (Vol. II. p. 380 B). In any case, Egyptian Theology was not the same throughout the whole kingdom, nor through all time.

# PORPHYRY

...they are accustomed to restore themselves by the eating of flesh. That Pythagoras did not hold a healthy opinion is indicated by no small sign: for none of the wise men were persuaded by him, neither any of the Seven Sages, nor the Natural Philosophers who came after. Indeed, not even the wisest Socrates, nor those who followed from Socrates, accepted it.

§ 16. But come, let us suppose all men were persuaded by this doctrine. What fate then would befall the offspring of the animals? <gloss>1</gloss> For it escapes no one's notice how many young a sow or a hare produces. Add to this all the other animals without exception. From where, then, will their pasture come? And what will the farmers suffer? For when their crops are being destroyed, they will not <gloss>2</gloss> kill the destroyers. ...they have been accustomed to restore themselves by the application of meat as food. For that Pythagoras did not think rightly, there is no small evidence. § 16. But come, let us grant that all men have complied. To what point will the propagation of animals proceed? For it is hidden from no one how many a sow bears, and a hare. <columns>2</columns>

...those things which ought to have been separated have grown together into one. Regarding the fattening of athletes, more will be said later. <note>The translator is likely referring to the common argument that athletes need meat for strength.</note>

<margin>4. *The wisest Socrates.*</margin> Socrates was judged *the wisest* <note>original: "sapientissimus"</note> not only by the consensus of men, but even by the oracle of Apollo, as Valerius Maximus says in Book III, 4. Indeed, the ancients everywhere look back to that oracle:
->*Of all men, Socrates is the wisest.*<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀνδρῶν δ’ ἁπάντων Σωκράτης σοφώτατος.</note>
Consult now Markland on Maximus Tyrius, Dissertation XXXIX. It is therefore no wonder that the ancients, as they loved to distinguish each of the Philosophers by some illustrious surname, gave to Socrates the title of *The Wise*. On this matter, read Holstenius in the *Life of Porphyry*, chapter 6.

<margin>1. *For it escapes no one's notice how many young a sow or a hare produces.*</margin> Those curious about nature discuss the fecundity of the sow and its causes. Consult the learned men on Aelian's *On the Nature of Animals*, XII, 16. Regarding that of hares, see Rittershusius on Oppian's *Cynegetica*, Book III, verse 522, and the learned men on Herodotus III, 108. Next, the Meerman manuscript reads *the other animals*.

<column-break/>

<margin>2. *They kill.*</margin> The reading *they kill* <note>original: "ἀποκτείνουσιν"</note> holds well. For we are imagining that the peasants [do not] kill the beasts. Reiske and Valentinus had inserted *they will kill*, but I do not dare to move the common reading, in which all the manuscripts agree, although Felicianus seems to have read it otherwise. Plutarch illustrates this matter beautifully, showing that the eating of flesh was introduced by necessity, lest there be an excessive multitude of living creatures, since the oracle also warned that the fruits should not be destroyed in that manner, in *Symposiacs* VIII, 8. But more on this later.

There would be no refuge for the hungry against famine; there will be no retreat against the cruel assaults of hunger, for although all things will be full of food, no one will use them, wherefore everyone must necessarily perish of hunger. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century German physician and philologist.</note>. # On Abstinence, Book I.

...are they driven? But if they enter into bodies voluntarily, out of a love for youth, it must be admitted that they must travel through every species of animal; thus, we should consider that the slaughter of animals is actually pleasing to them, as it procures for them a swifter return into human form. For if their bodies are eaten, it can cause them no distress, since they have already been separated from them and long to be within the nature of a man. Indeed, we must believe that just as much pain as they feel when leaving a human body, they feel an equal amount of pleasure when they are released from other bodies. This is because it allows them to return more quickly to man, who holds sovereignty over the other living creatures just as God holds it over men. Therefore, a sufficient reason for killing them is that by killing them, we prevent them from harming men. For if the souls of men are immortal while those of brutes are mortal, we do not act unjustly by killing them. But if their souls are also immortal, we actually benefit them by killing them; for we do this to grant them a swifter return into human nature.

§ 20. But if we are taking revenge, we do not offend, but rather punish those who cause offense.

->Which-<-

<column-break/>

...they entered into nature. But if they did so voluntarily, and through a love of youth <note>original: "νεότητος ἔρωτι"</note>, and through every form of living thing, then being killed would be a favor to them. For the return to the human state is swifter; and the bodies being eaten would not instill grief in the souls, as they have been released from them; and their desire would be to come into the nature of a man. Thus, as much as they might grieve leaving the human state, so much would they rejoice leaving other bodies. For the return to man is swifter—man, who rules over all irrational creatures as God rules over men. Therefore, there is sufficient cause to kill other animals insofar as they do harm by killing men. If the souls of men are immortal, but those of irrational creatures are mortal, we men do not act unjustly by killing the irrational ones; just as we benefit them, if they are indeed immortal, by killing them: for we do this to facilitate the return to human nature.

§ 20. But if we defend ourselves, we do not act unjustly, but we pursue those who act unjustly—

# P O R P H Y R Y
<note>original: "PORPHYRII" — This refers to Porphyry of Tyre, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his treatise "On Abstinence from Animal Food."</note>

...we proceed. Thus, if their souls are immortal, we actually benefit them by killing them <note>Porphyry is likely summarizing an opponent's argument here: that releasing a soul from a body is a favor</note>. If, on the other hand, the souls of irrational animals are mortal, we commit no impiety by killing them. And if we act in self-defense, how can we not be acting justly? <margin>1</margin> We kill the snake and the scorpion even if they have not attacked us, so that no one else might suffer at their hands, defending the common race of mankind. <margin>2</margin> As for those creatures that attack humans, or the animals that live with humans, or our crops—how could we not be justified in killing them?

§ 21. But if someone considers <margin>1</margin> this to be an act of injustice once and for all, then he must not use milk, nor wool, nor eggs, nor honey. For just as you do a man an injustice by stripping him of his clothes, so you do to a sheep when you shear it; for that is the sheep's clothing. And the milk was not <margin>2</margin> produced for you, but for the offspring that were born. The bee, too, collected that food for itself, which you take away to make a luxury for yourself.

<column-break/>

Therefore, if their souls are immortal, we benefit them by inflicting death. If they are mortal, we do nothing impious. But if we are even taking revenge, how is it that we do not act quite justly? For we kill the serpent and the scorpion, even if they do not yet provoke us, helping the common race of men, lest another suffer some evil from them. Moreover, those things which invade men, or harm those things which dwell with men, or lay waste to the fruits of the earth—how are they not deservedly to be removed from our midst?

§ 21. Furthermore, if anyone should think this is altogether an injustice, he must use neither milk, nor wool, nor eggs, nor honey. For just as you act unjustly if you despoil a man, so if you shear a sheep, you inflict an injury: for that which you pull off is the sheep's garment. Milk also was prepared not for you, but for the offspring already brought forth. The bee also gathered that nourishment for itself, which you, having snatched it away, turn into a delight for yourself.

# On Abstinence, Book I.

I will set aside for now the religion of the Egyptians, who believe that we act unjustly if we do violence even to plants. <note>The author is likely referring to Porphyry’s discussion of the Egyptian priesthood's strict dietary laws.</note> If, however, these things are truly brought forth for our sake: then the bee, serving us, produces honey, and the fleece grows upon the sheep so that it may provide us with both ornament and warmth.

§ 22. Furthermore, we sacrifice animals while practicing piety toward the gods themselves: and among them, Apollo is called the "Wolf-Slayer" and Diana the "Beast-Slayer." <note>original: "lycocidus" and "fericida"</note> For even the demigods and all the heroes who excelled us in lineage and virtue approved the eating of living creatures to such an extent that they even offered to the gods "twelve-fold sacrifices" and "hecatombs" <note>A hecatomb was a grand public sacrifice of one hundred oxen.</note>—

<column-break/>

—which you have prepared; and I have kept silent regarding the discourse of the Egyptians, because we act unjustly even when touching plants. But if these things have come into being for our sake, then the bee, serving us, works the honey, and the wool grows upon the sheep; for us, it is an adornment and a protection from the cold.

§ 22. And performing acts of piety for the gods themselves, we sacrifice living beings; and of these gods, Apollo is called the Wolf-Slayer; and Artemis, the Beast-Slayer; since even the demigods and the heroes, surpassing us in both birth and excellence, approved the offering of animate beings, as—

---

<margin>
You may see. Before an aspirated vowel, the "movable N" <note>A grammatical feature in Greek where an 'n' is added to the end of a word to avoid a clash of vowels.</note> is often neglected, of which several traces remain, and perhaps more would remain had they not been erased by the scribes, as noted well by *D'Orville on Chariton, Book II, ch. 1, p. 156.*

3. *Because even of the plants etc.*] See the note on § 18. If this pleased the Egyptians, it is no wonder that the same persuasion remains today among the Indians, who are, as is thought, colonists of the Egyptians; on which matter see the *Celebrated La Croze in History of Christianity in India, Book VI, p. 434.*

4. *Works the honey.*] A specific expression, just as "work" <note>original: "ergon"</note> and the Latin *opus* are used for the honey which bees fashion. See *Spanheim on Callimachus' Hymn to Jove, 50.* Well known are those lines of *Phaedrus, III, 13, 9:* "pour your work into the wax," where the *Interpreters* provide more. Bees are said to "work the honeycomb" in *Aelian, Various History, XII, 45.*

5. *For us, an adornment and warmth.*] Those lines of the poet come to mind, from *Metamorphoses XV, 117:*
> *What have you deserved, sheep, a placid flock, born*
> *to protect men, you who carry nectar in your full udders?*
> *You who provide your wool to us as soft garments:*
> *and help us more by your life than by your death.*

The phrase *of the sheep* was wrongly absent in the *Meermann* manuscript.
</margin>

<column-break/>

1. *Wolf-Slayer - Artemis Beast-Slayer.*] Slightly different in *Plutarch, On the Cleverness of Animals, p. 966 A:* "just as Apollo is called Wolf-Slayer, so Artemis is called Deer-Shooter." Regarding this title of Apollo, there is a notable passage in the *Scholiast on Sophocles' Electra, 6.* Diana, moreover, is usually called *Beast-Slayer, Beast-Slaying, or Rich-in-Beasts.* See *Spanheim on Callimachus' Hymn to Diana, 12.* However, you will find our specific term <note>original: "theroktonos"</note> more rarely; though it rests in the Lexicons only on the authority of Hesychius, it is defended by this example of ours by *Alberti on Hesychius under "Beast-Slayer."*

2. *Since.*] Furthermore, *then, next, often "since" is used for "thereupon."* — *REISKE.*

3. *Demigods and the heroes*] "Do you not know that the heroes are demigods?" to speak with *Plato in Cratylus, p. 274 D.* Certainly elsewhere the *demigods* are the same as the *Heroes*, as the *Scholiast on Homer's Iliad, A. 4* and many others teach. *V. G. Cuper, once a distinguished ornament of our Athenaeum, III. Observations: 16.* But it is not necessary to distinguish between them in this passage.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry's argument regarding the origins of animal sacrifice and the dietary laws of Pythagoras, specifically addressing the philosophical justifications for abstaining from meat.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

->On Abstinence from Animal Food<-

...so that they even established the practice of sacrificing to the gods "twelve-fold" offerings <note>original: *δωδεκηΐδας* (dodekeidas); a sacrifice of twelve animals</note> and hecatombs <note>a grand sacrifice, literally of one hundred oxen</note>. Indeed, Hercules is celebrated for many things, and among them for this: that he was a "devourer of oxen." <note>original: *βουφάγος* (bouphagos)</note>

§ 23. Now, to claim that Pythagoras was looking far into the future when he established his safety measures—trying to drive men away from cannibalism <note>original: *ἀλληλοφαγία* (allelophagia); literally "eating one another"</note>—is simply foolish. For if all men in the time of Pythagoras were eating one another, it would be nonsensical to try to pull them away from eating other animals just to keep them from eating each other. In fact, such a rule would likely have the opposite effect: it would encourage them by suggesting that eating one another is no different a sin than feasting on the flesh of pigs and oxen. On the other hand, if they were not cannibals at that time, what was the need for such a doctrine? But if for himself and his companions...

<column-break/>

...he instituted these sacrifices of twelve sheep and a hundred oxen. Hercules, truly, among other things, was celebrated with that praise: that he used to eat oxen.

§ 23. If anyone truly says that Pythagoras, by this decree of his, wished for nothing else than to provide a distant precaution lest men eat each other, it is clearly a stupid suggestion. For if in the time of Pythagoras all men were eating each other, that institution is absurd which deters them from the slaughter of other animals in order to keep men from mutual eating. Indeed, it would rather incite them to the contrary, while it shows that eating each other is the same sin as if they were to feed on the flesh of oxen and pigs. But if they were not eating each other at that time, what was the need for an institution of this kind? But if for himself...

---

<margin>4. *And to sacrifice to the gods twelve-fold.*] The word "And" is missing in the *Leipzig* edition; then the *Meerman* manuscript has "to kill" instead of "to sacrifice." For *dodekeidas*, *Felicianus* reads *dodekoidas*. The *Bodleian* manuscript has *dodekeidas*. In *Suidas* they are called *dodekides*. See also *Hesychius* under *dodekades* and *dodekeida*, and the "Learned Man" in the same place. Shortly after, the *Meerman* manuscript reads "celebrated among these."</margin>

<margin>5. *He was a devourer of oxen.*] That Hercules was a glutton is declared by almost all poets and writers, as *Athenaeus* says in the *Deipnosophistae* [Banquet of the Learned], Book XI, 1, bringing forth evidence of the matter. Rightly, therefore, they called him "ox-eater." See *Casaubon* at the cited passage and *Spanheim* on *Callimachus' Hymn to Diana*, 148. This passage can be added to another in the Greek Epigrams, where *Alberti* noted this word occurs in his notes on *Hesychius* under *bouphagos*.</margin>

<margin>1. *Driving away from cannibalism.*] Some have handed down the tradition that in the earliest times men devoured each other. See the *Fragment of Athenion* in *Athenaeus*, XIV, 23, and the notes on this fabulous commentary by *Wesseling* in his edition of *Diodorus Siculus*, Book I, 14. Regarding the word itself, one may consult *J. Alberti* on *Hesychius* under *Allelodotai* [Given to one another].</margin>

<margin>2. *To feed on flesh.*] The *Leipzig* edition has "fleshes" [plural]. It is much the same, and I do not know if it is better. Certainly, the plural would stand out in this place, and the verb "to feed on" <note>original: *ἐμφορεῖσθαι* (emphoreisthai)</note> is constructed equally with the accusative as with the genitive case. —REISKE. In the middle voice, it is rightly constructed with the accusative; if with the genitive, it should be understood as passive. Others have already advised this. See *S. Bergler* on *Alciphron*, Book I, Epistle 35. The *Meerman* manuscript also has "fleshes" here, but a little earlier it has the worse reading "would turn them."</margin>

<margin>3. *But if they were not.*] Although the singular *en* [was] occurs here and there for the plural *esan* [were] in *Pindar*, *Homer*, and others, I would prefer *esan* in this place. —REISKE. Unless "cannibalism" <note>the noun</note> was corrupted into "cannibals" <note>the people</note>...</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.
## E 2

->**Column 1 (Latin)**<-

...to him and his companions he ordained this law, it is indeed a shameful argument: for it indicates that those who lived with Pythagoras were suffering from this mutual savagery of eating one another. <note>The author is arguing that if Pythagoras forbade eating animals to stop cannibalism, it implies his followers were prone to it.</note>

§ 24. Add to this that the very opposite of what he aimed for would happen. For if we were to abstain from living creatures, not only would we be deprived of such wealth and pleasure, but we would even lose the fields themselves, devastated by wild beasts. Indeed, the whole earth would be occupied by serpents and birds: so that plowing could only be done with difficulty, and whatever was sown would be immediately snatched away by birds, and what barely reached maturity would be utterly consumed by four-legged animals and perish: and finally, men would be reduced to such a lack of food that they would be forced to attack one another.

§ 25. It is added that the gods also, in many...

<column-break/>

->**Column 2 (Greek)**<-

...to his companions he gave the law, it is a shameful premise; for it proves those living with Pythagoras to be eaters of one another.

§ 24. <gloss>1</gloss> On the contrary, the opposite of what he intended would happen. For if we abstain from living beings, we will not only fall short of such wealth and pleasure, but we will also lose the plowed lands, they being destroyed by the wild beasts; the whole earth will be overtaken by snakes and winged creatures; so that the plowing happens with hardship, and the things sown <gloss>2</gloss> are immediately gathered up by the birds, and the things brought to completion are all consumed by the four-legged animals. Such a lack <gloss>3</gloss> of food occurring, a bitter necessity will overtake us to turn upon one another.

§ 25. And furthermore, even the <gloss>1</gloss> divine...

---

<margin>I notice that this suspicion is confirmed by the *Meerman Manuscript*. Presently in the *same* and the *Florentine* edition it was, "of this doctrine." And then in the *Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts*: "the premise is shameful." Either is better than the common reading. Here, however, instead of "companions" <note>original: ἑταίροις</note> it gave "others" <note>original: ἑτέροις</note>. This is a frequent confusion.</margin>

<margin>1. "On the contrary... would happen."] For "would happen" <note>original: συμβήσεσθαι</note> we have restored "will happen" <note>original: συμβήσεται</note>. —VALENTINUS. The future infinitive can be preserved by understanding "We say." —REISKE. Unless "it was going to" <note>original: ἔμελλε</note> fell out before "would happen," which seemed likely to the Illustrious *Abresch*.</margin>

<margin>2. "Immediately by the birds..."] Perhaps "immediately then" <note>original: εὐθὺς τότε</note> instead of "immediately" <note>original: εὐθύστε</note>; the particles "te" and "tote" are not rarely permuted with each other. —REISKE. Presently, "to be completed" <note>original: τελειοῦσθαι</note> is the solemn word for fruits that have reached maturity. "Fruit being completed" and "complete" is said by *Theophrastus in Causes of Plants, Book II, p. 307, and often elsewhere*.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>3. "Of food occurring."] Thus correctly in the *Leipzig Manuscript*; previously it was read as "of mortals" <note>original: βρότων</note>. In the same way we have already corrected it above.</margin>

<margin>1. "Divine prescriptions etc."] I approve of "gods" <note>original: θεοὶ</note> by *Valentini*, but I would prefer the "te" to be absent, or it should read "men" <note>original: μὲν</note> because of the following "de." —REISKE. *Vogeroll* had also already corrected "Gods," and the *Bodleian Manuscript* confirms it; it is uniquely true. "To prescribe" <note>original: Συντάσσειν</note> and "prescription" <note>original: σύνταξις</note> are technical terms in medical matters, just as they call "compositions" <note>original: συνταγὰς</note>. *Aelian, Varia Historia IX, 13*: "The doctors therefore prescribed <note>original: συνέταξαν</note> a medicine for him." And so "to ordain" <note>original: προστάσσειν</note> in the same author, II, 37. *Artemidorus, Interpretation of Dreams, Book IV, 24*: "Regarding prescriptions, that the gods prescribe <note>original: συντάσσουσι</note> treatments for men, it is vain to seek." *Gataker* has other notes on *Marcus Antoninus V, 8*.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

...and they have given instructions for many <gloss>2</gloss> to use animal products for the sake of healing and remedies. History is full of accounts of how the gods themselves commanded certain people both to sacrifice animals to them and to consume the flesh of those sacrifices. During the return of the Heraclidae <note>The "descendants of Hercules," a legendary group of Greeks who conquered the Peloponnese</note>, those who campaigned against Laconia <gloss>3</gloss> with Eurysthenes and Procles, being in a state of extreme want of necessities, ate serpents, which the earth then brought forth as food for the army. To another army, suffering from hunger <gloss>4</gloss> in Libya, there fell a cloud of locusts. <gloss>5</gloss> In the...

<column-break/>

...gave instructions concerning beasts for the sake of assistance and remedy. Histories are full of instances where they commanded that certain animals be sacrificed to them and that the people themselves should eat the sacrificed meat. Moreover, in the return of the Heraclidae, those who had made an expedition into Laconia with Eurysthenes and Procles, being placed in a shortage of necessary things, ate serpents, which the earth brought forth for the nourishment of the army. In Libya also, a cloud of locusts fell upon another army laboring under starvation...

---

<column-break/>

<gloss>2. For the sake of healing... from beasts.]</gloss> I would prefer the word "of" <note>original: "τῆς" instead of "τὰς"</note>. A little later, "to sacrifice to them," etc. although the interpretation I gave can perhaps be sustained, it is better thus: *then to slaughter wild beasts for them, and then to eat the slaughtered ones.* For the word "to partake" <note>original: "προσφέρεσθαι"</note> occurs in this sense more than once in Porphyry. VALENTINUS. Correct. Previously he had given "to immolate." Felicianus also does well: you may find it thus a hundred times, not only in our author but in others. See *Menage on Diogenes Laertius III, 48* and *Kuster on Iamblichus' Life of Pythagoras p. 172*, who accurately explains the difference between "to offer" and "to partake of food" <note>original: "προσφέρειν" and "προσφέρεσθαι τροφὴν"</note> and similar terms.

<gloss>3. With Eurysthenes and Procles.]</gloss> It ought to be read "Procles." See *Pausanias p. 160* and *Sylburg in the notes to that place.* VALENTINUS. "Procles" is also in the *Leipzig Manuscript*. The *Bodleian* has "Proskelos," which seems to have intended "Procles," and so also *Felicianus*, although in Greek he is called not Procles but *Prokles*. He is the same one who is elsewhere called Patrocles. For as to the fact that *Davies on Cicero's On Divination ch. 43* thinks Strabo and Plutarch should be corrected, and "Procles" rewritten instead of "Patrocles," I cannot allow myself to be persuaded of that, because they are not the only ones by whom he is so called. But that is not the business at hand now. Others also touch upon the history itself. Many, however, write that not Eurysthenes and Patrocles, the sons of Aristodemus, but Aristodemus himself occupied the ancestral kingdom.

<column-break/>

So the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> themselves in *Herodotus* and others, whom *Meursius* ordered to give testimony in *On the Kingdom of Laconia ch. 6*, many testify that those Lacedaemonians ate snakes, whence they were called *ophiophagoi*, "snake-eaters." The same *Meursius* explains the matter and the cause in *Laconian Miscellany Book III, 2.* Presently, *Meermann* misses the word "nourishment."

<gloss>4. In Libya... a cloud of locusts.]</gloss> *Jerome, Book II against Jovinian ch. 7:* Again, *it is the custom for Eastern and Libyan peoples to eat locusts, because clouds of locusts are found throughout the deserted and hot vastness of the wilderness.* They testify the same regarding other nations. Read *Bochart, Sacred Zoology II, 4. 7.* *J. Ludolph, History of Ethiopia I, 13*, understands that genus of living things to be the "little birds" <note>quails</note> which we know the Hebrews used in the desert; however, in that matter some things can still delay agreement. Moreover, he says elegantly "a cloud of locusts" <note>original: "νέφος ἀκρίδων"</note>, as in *Livy*, "a cloud of locusts" <note>original: "nubes locustarum"</note>. In both languages this is a very common way of speaking. *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus Book III, 29* and the interpreters on the *Apostolic Epistle to the Hebrews IX, 1* have raised a "cloud" of examples.

<gloss>5. In Gadeira.]</gloss> "And this also in Gadeira." Immediately read "Bogos," for so it is also in Strabo p. 1183. Others call him "Bogoas," "Boguas," and "Bogud." Concerning the slaughter of Boguas, see *Cassius Dio p. 611*; concerning him, note *Fabricius at p. 343, 44* and the *Index to Dio under Bogud.* REISKE.
