# On Abstinence, Book I.

-> E 3 <-

...a cloud of them presented itself. In Gades <note>Modern Cádiz, Spain</note> also, something of this sort is said to have happened. Mogus was a king of the Mauritanians <note>People of ancient Northwest Africa</note>, who was killed at Mothona by Agrippa. He was attacking the temple of Hercules, which was very wealthy in that place. Now, it was the custom for the priests to sprinkle his altar daily with blood. That this was done not by the design of men, but by the god, the occasion itself declared. For when the siege was being drawn out for a long time, and all the sacrificial victims had already failed, the priest, lacking both resources and counsel, beheld a dream of this kind. He seemed to himself to be standing between the Her-

<column-break/>

In Gades this also occurred. Mogus was king of the Maurusians <note>Mauritanians</note>, who was slain in Mothone by Agrippa; he made an attempt upon the temple of Hercules, which was most wealthy. It is the law for the priests to bloody the altar every day. That this happens not by the will of men, but according to the god, the occasion then demonstrated. For as the siege was prolonged, the sacrificial victims failed. The priest, being in a state of helplessness, saw a dream of this sort. It seemed to him that he stood in the middle of the pillars of Her-

***

6. *Mogus — in Mothone.*] Both names are corrupt <note>original: "corruptum est," meaning the spelling in the manuscript is likely an error</note>. For they ought to be written *Boguas* or *Bogas* and *Methone*. See Dio Cassius, Book 50, and Strabo, Book VIII. Dio relates in Book 48 that Bogud (or Bogus) crossed into Spain and harassed it. Therefore, the temple of Hercules which he mentions seems to be that in Gades. Strabo notes that it is well known this city is called *Gadeira*. VALENTIUS. Regarding *Mogus*, learned men rightly refer to him as *Bogos*, as in Strabo, who relates that these things happened during the Actian War <note>The war between Octavian and Mark Antony, 32–30 BCE</note>, when this Bogus followed the party of Antony. I would not say the word *Methone* is corrupt, although it is called *Methone* by others. For it seems it was later called Mothone, as Casaubon has already observed.

7. *He made an attempt.*] The use of this word is well enough known. The Leipzig Manuscript has a slightly different spelling. This is incorrect, except that the final letter "n" was rightly absent, as Reiske advised. That manuscript frequently omits that letter, unlike the printed editions; it is not worth the effort to note this in every place.

8. *That [it was] not by the will.*] So it was read in the older editions, and confirmed by the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts. Therefore, the word "still" was rashly ejected by Valentius. Moreover, the phrase "it happens according to the god" is beautiful, which Wetstein illustrates in his notes on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, 8:27. Recently, from the Leipzig manuscript and the authority of the translator, I restored the word "for" where it was previously missing.

9. *Being prolonged.*] The active form of the verb "to prolong" is more common than the middle form used here. However, I would not wish to cast doubt on the common reading for that reason. REISKE. Excellent. Verbs often occur in the middle or deponent form where the active is more common. These things should be noted rather than changed, especially in writers of a later age.

10. *The priest.*] A little later he calls him the "High Priest." Nothing is more common than for the High Priest of the Jews, Romans, etc., to be designated by both names. There are many examples in sacred and secular literature. I add nothing to the diligence of the great Wesseling on Diodorus. Among the Latins, "Pontifex" is used for the highest overseer in Livy, Florus, and others.

11. *He saw a dream.*] "To see a dream" and similar phrases are frequent among the Greeks. Among the Latins, dreams and night visions are also said "to be seen." Recently, the Leipzig manuscript read "middle" in the neuter rather than the masculine.

# PORPHYRY

-> Of Hercules <-; then, directly opposite the altar, he saw a bird perched <gloss>12</gloss> and attempting to fly toward him. For this name is brought forth everywhere in this way on coins and ancient inscriptions, and *Spanheim* <note>Ezechiel Spanheim (1629–1710), a famous Prussian diplomat and numismatist.</note> thinks it should be restored on their authority in his *Dissertation on the Use and Excellence of Coins, II, p. 125.* Yet there is not enough cause for *Felicianus* to bring forth the Roman name in this way, despite what *Spanheim* advised in that same place.

<gloss>16. It is necessary to sacrifice a cow.]</gloss> Perhaps "it was necessary" <note>original: "χρῆν" for "ἔχρην"</note>. For in Porphyry’s time, those sacred rites had long since ceased. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist.</note>. *Plutarch in his Life of Lucullus, p. 497 F.* indicates that it was a black heifer. And *Appian, Book I:* "when the festival arrived in which they sacrifice a black cow."

<gloss>17. Opposite the city.]</gloss> After "opposite," it seems that "on the mainland" <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἠπείρῳ"</note> has fallen out of the text.

# PORPHYRY

...it would be a long task to relate. That it is not impious to kill and eat animals is shown by the fact that Pythagoras himself acted thus. While the ancients gave athletes milk to drink and cheese soaked in water to eat, and those after them rejected this diet and gave athletes dried figs for nourishment, Pythagoras was the first to set aside the ancient custom and give meat to those in training, finding that it produced a far superior strength and power. Some also record that the Pythagoreans themselves laid hands upon living creatures <note>original: "ἐμψύχων" / "animantibus" — referring to ensouled beings or animals</note> when they sacrificed to the gods. Such are the arguments found in the works of Clodius, Heraclides Ponticus, and Hermachus the Epicurean, and—

<column-break/>

3. **And Pythagoras himself etc.**] This Pythagoras was different from the Philosopher; he was the son of Eratocles, who wrote books on athletic matters. However, Porphyry relates that the Philosopher <note>The famous Pythagoras of Samos</note> gave assistance to Eurymenes, a Samian athlete, and that by the Philosopher's advice he ate a certain weight of meat every day, and thus acquired great bodily strength. It is no wonder, therefore, that these two men named Pythagoras are often confused. Compare *Iamblichus* in the *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 5, and the *Learned Men* <note>original: "V. D." / "Viri Docti"</note> on *Our Author* <note>Porphyry</note> in the *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 15, where this custom of using soft cheeses, dried figs, etc., is further explained. See also *Spanheim* on *Julian's* First Oration, page 103. But the Philosopher did not forbid the use of meat even to athletes, as is said elsewhere. Note also the transpositions of words, familiar to our author, so that the sense may be clear to you.

<column-break/>

4. **Some also record etc.**] Some report that Pythagoras himself rejected the use of meat and wine. Indeed, *Eudoxus* says in *Our Author's Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 7, that he not only abstained from living things, but would not even approach cooks or hunters. However, they teach that he did not abstain from all living things entirely, but very rarely used meat from sacrificial victims, and even then, not indiscriminately from any part. See *Rittershusius* on *Our Author's Life of Pythagoras*, number 34. And so *Iamblichus* records in the *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 21, that the Pythagoreans also used the meat of animals which it was lawful to sacrifice.

5. **Clodius and Heraclides etc.**] Above in section 3, "a certain Clodius of Naples" is mentioned, not without a note of contempt. *Heraclides Ponticus*, according to *Diogenes Laertius*, had written *On the Pythagoreans*, which are the books our author refers to. See *Menage* on *Laertius*, Book VIII, 4. No other *Hermachus* occurs to me than that Epicurean about whom *Fabricius* writes in the *Greek Library*, Volume II, page—

1. # PORPHYRY

-> [On Abstinence from Animal Food] <-

...not for athletes of the body, nor for soldiers, nor for sailors, nor for orators, nor for those who have chosen a life of practical affairs. But for a man who has reflected <note>Greek: *λελογισμένῳ* - one who uses reason</note> on who he is, where he has come from, and where he ought to hasten to, and who has changed his views regarding food and other duties compared to the standards set by other ways of life, 6 we would not utter a single word <note>original: *γρύξαιμεν* - literally "to grunt" or "mutter like a pig"</note> to those others or their like. For indeed, in this common life, the same advice is surely not given to the sleeper and to the one who, if it so happens, 7 [strives for] this throughout his life...

<column-break/>

...neither to soldiers, nor sailors, nor orators, nor finally to the rest who have established a busy life, can any persuasion of this kind be brought. But only to those who consider both who they are and where they have come from, and who have proposed for themselves a different standard for food and other duties than the custom of others. For to the others, not even a word of this kind should be made. Since indeed, even in this common life, the same warning is not applied to him who sleeps, and [does] so through his whole [life]...

---

<margin>
Line 6. *Hear therefore: swine and boars, and stags, and the rest of the living creatures were created so that soldiers and athletes, sailors, orators, and diggers of mines and other men enslaved to hard labor might have foods for which strength of body is necessary.* Where Martianay <note>Jean Martianay, a Benedictine scholar</note> could have supported the reading of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, who quoted Porphyry in his polemic against Jovinian</note> from our text against those who do not want to tolerate the word *orators* there. It is also clear from this that the word *sailors* <note>Greek: *ναύταις*</note> is wrongly omitted in the *Leipzig Manuscript*. That Jerome indeed looked back to our author can also be gathered from the fact that those things which follow, *But for a man who has reflected...* etc., he expresses clearly a little later. Otherwise, our religion [requires] *not a boxer, not an athlete, not sailors, not soldiers, not diggers, but a follower of the study of wisdom, who has dedicated himself to the worship of God, and knows why he was created, why he dwells in the world, and where he hastens to depart.* However, there is no mention of orators here, and since that class of men seems hardly to belong to this category, it could be doubted whether they ought to be read in our author. But because of those things which Martianay noted regarding Jerome, nothing should be changed. If you desire to be taught which were called the *vulgar arts* <note>Greek: *βάναυσοι τέχναι* - manual or "low" trades</note>, consult Lacerda and Perizonius on Aelian’s *Various History*, VI, 6.
</margin>

4. **Who he is and where he has come from...** A noted formula concerning those who used to question arriving strangers. *Plato at the beginning of the Phaedrus: "My dear Phaedrus, where are you going and where have you come from?"* There are innumerable examples. Philologists will provide many for those words of *John in the Apocalypse VII, 13: "Who are they and where did they come from?"* The poet said, *Aeneid VIII, 114: "What is your race? Where is your home?"*

5. **And other duties...** The *Leipzig Manuscript* correctly gives *having changed* <note>Greek: *ἐξηλλαγμένῳ*</note>, from which it is clear that a little later one should read *having proposed* <note>Greek: *ὑποτιθεμένῳ*</note>. To one looking at those things, following those purposes and plans which differ from the institutions of other men, as much in food as in other duties. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century philologist</note>. The older editions and the *Bodleian* as well as the *Meerman Manuscript* agree on the plural *changed things* <note>Greek: *ἐξηλλαγμένα*</note>; then *having proposed* must follow, as anyone can see.

6. **We would not utter a single word.** Thus correctly the old editions and the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts. That first *an* <note>a Greek particle indicating potentiality</note> was first ejected by Valentinus, which however is often accustomed to be repeated in the same sentence. *Gryzein* <note>to grunt/mutter</note> is proper to piglets, as the ancient Grammarians teach; see them praised in P. Horreus, *Observations on Herodotus*, p. 261. From here it is transferred to dogs, and even to men. See Hesychius and what the learned men say there. Generally, therefore, it is said instead of "to speak." *Plato in the Euthydemus, p. 209 B: "And I thought I had suffered justly because I muttered."* Such is that phrase *Is it possible for you to mutter?* which Suidas cites from Aristophanes.

7. **This throughout his life.** *Bodleian Manuscript* has *of this*; *Meerman* has *to this*. Presently here and in the *Leipzig* manuscript, *having been prepared*. Then the "and" before "all" is missing in the *Leipzig* and other manuscripts.

# On Abstinence, Book I.

-> F 2 <-

One man might strive for a course of life where he prepares sleep-inducing aids from every side; another, struggling earnestly to repel sleep, provides everything that makes for wakefulness. For the former, so that he may devote himself to drunkenness, gluttony, and surfeit, he must be advised to choose for himself dark rooms, a soft and wide bed—and as the poets say, a "rich" one—and to take every soporific drug that induces lethargy and forgetfulness, whether by smelling, anointing, drinking, or eating. But for the other man, just as his drink should be sober and free of wine, so his food must be prescribed as so thin that it nearly approaches fasting. Furthermore, his house should be bright, filled with thin air and capable of sharpening the senses; he must also be commanded to be moved by the vigorous motion of cares and thoughts—

<column-break/>

—striving for a life prepared with sleep-inducing things from every side, and the one who is eager to repel sleep and has arranged everything about himself for wakefulness. But for the one, it is necessary to suggest drunkenness, gluttony, and surfeit <note>original: "plenitudinem" / "πλησμονὴν"</note>, and to advise him to choose a dark house and a soft, wide, and rich bed, as the poets say, and to bring to him every narcotic drug that produces idleness and forgetfulness, whether it be inhaled, smeared on, or taken as food or drink. But for the other, the drink should be sober and wineless, and the food light and tending toward a state of fasting, and the house bright and partaking of thin air and spirit, with the stirring up of cares and anxiety—

<margin>
The Manuscripts read this correctly, for neither the earlier editions recognize it. Reiske thought "and everything" <note>original: "πᾶν δὲ τὸ"</note> should be read. Abresch also wanted this.

8. **And surfeit [suggested]**: This word is used particularly regarding the immoderate use of food and drink. *Strabo, Book 15, page 492:* "From surfeit and luxury they fell into insolence." *Julian in the Misopogon, page 340 C:* "By accident, not by surfeit." And so it is used often. Not otherwise is *Paul to the Colossians 2:23:* "to the satisfying <note>or surfeit</note> of the flesh." As our author joins "drunkenness and surfeit," so also does *Theophrastus in On the Senses, page 495.*

# On Abstinence, Book I.
-> F 3 <-

and we are filled with drowsiness and sleep: especially since the place in which we dwell is so exceedingly sluggish <note>original: "ueternosus"; likely referring to the material world or the physical body</note> that it brings a rheum to the eyes, and by its exhalations leads everyone into a heavy stupor and forgetfulness. If, therefore, the legislators established their laws with the intention of leading men toward a contemplative life, lived according to the mind and intellect, then we must certainly obey them and fully accept what they have handed down regarding diet. But if they framed their sanctions looking toward the "natural life" (which is called the middle path), and toward those things which the majority of the common people could agree upon—who are accustomed to regard external things and those pertaining to the body as either good or evil—why should anyone, by bringing forward the laws of these men, attempt to subvert that life which om-

For friends are accustomed to include themselves in the same severity of admonition as those to whom the exhortation pertains. <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>.

Bergler</term> on <term>Alciphron</term>, Book III, Epistle 46. Presently the <term>Bodleian manuscript</term> wrongly has "we may spend time" <note>Greek: διατρίβωμεν</note>. And the <term>Meerman manuscript</term> has "full" <note>nominative</note> instead of "full" <note>genitive</note>.

4. **We must surely, in obedience.** <term>Reiske</term> preferred "it was necessary" or "it would be necessary." The <term>Bodleian</term>, however, wrongly has "to those obeying."

5. **As the goods or evils.** The words "as the" <note>original: "ὡς τὰ"</note> are either plainly to be deleted as a mistaken repetition of "to whom the" <note>original: "οἷς τὰ"</note>, or changed to "all things," meaning whatever they see as external and accidental, and likewise what pertains to the body, they hold among goods or evils. After "likewise" a comma could be placed. The meaning is: the common people decide concerning the things of the body just as they do concerning external and accidental things, that they are either good or bad. <term>Reiske</term>.

6. **Citing the law.** Thus correctly <term>Valentinus</term>. The <term>Lipsian</term> and <term>Meerman</term> codices confirm this. The <term>Florentine</term>, <term>Leiden</term>, and <term>Bodleian</term> codices wrongly have "of the laws."

7. **Written and --- established.** The <term>Lipsian</term> wrongly has "for somewhere" and "established" <note>plural</note>, which is also in the <term>Meerman</term>. Among the ancients, laws were inscribed on tablets

# PORPHYRY

->...is superior to every written law set before the multitude, and who chiefly pursues the unwritten and divine law? For the matter stands thus:<-

### § 29.
The contemplation that makes us happy does not consist in a gathering of words or a multitude of learned disciplines <gloss>1</gloss>, as someone might suppose <gloss>2</gloss>, nor does it receive its increase from the quantity of such discourses. For in that case, nothing would prevent those who have collected every branch of learning from being happy. But as it stands, <gloss>3</gloss> not only does every branch of learning fail to complete this contemplation, but even the knowledge of those things which truly exist <gloss>4</gloss> cannot provide it, unless a way of life that is kindred and conformed to those truths is added. For since they say there are three ends for us, just as there are for every goal <gloss>5</gloss>...

<column-break/>

...is superior to every written law published to the common people, and follows most closely the unwritten and divine law? For this is how the matter holds.

### § 29.
That contemplation which renders us happy is not established in a multitude of sciences and disciplines, as anyone might imagine; nor does it take its growth from their increase. For in that way, there would be no obstacle to those being happy who had sought out all disciplines from every side. But it is so far from the case that every discipline perfects contemplation, that not even the knowledge of those things which truly exist can provide this, unless an institution of life also added, which is cognate and conformed to those very things. For since there are three ends for us, as they say, just as in every goal...

---

...were accustomed to be placed in a public location—at Athens in the Acropolis, the Prytaneum, or the Forum; at Rome in the treasury, etc.—and to lie there. Hence it arose that a "law set" <note>original: νόμος τεθεὶς</note> or "lying" <note>original: κείμενός</note> for someone is said to be a law which pertains to someone, or which is passed for someone's sake. I see twenty or more examples already collected by interpreters regarding those words of *St. Paul in 1 Timothy 1:9*: "The law is not laid down for the righteous," to which I would add as many others that are ready at hand, if I wished to abuse both my leisure and yours, Reader.

1. **A gathering of words and learning, etc.**] A golden sentiment and one which our author frequently brings forward. Let Christians hear from the mouth of a man hostile to the Christian name a truly Christian dogma, as we say with *T. Gataker* <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar and theologian</note>, who brought similar points from others (and did not forget us) in his notes on *Antoninus 1:9*.

2. **As someone might suppose.**] Instead of "as" <note>Greek: ὡς</note>, the *Bodleian* manuscript mistakenly has "who" <note>Greek: ὅς</note>. Shortly after, in the *Leipzig* manuscript, it was "consisting."

<column-break/>

It seemed to *Reiske* <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German philologist</note> that it should read "consisting according to the same": a number of reasons and doctrines gathered into one and the same place. Then he also wanted "those having gathered."

3. **Not only.**] See the note at the *Beginning, § 9.*

4. **Concerning those things which truly exist.**] See page 86 (Book II, § 43) and Porphyry's *Sentences* § 36, and pages 28 and 45 of this book. VALENTIUS: "Exist" <note>Greek: ὄντων</note> was not in the *Leipzig* manuscript, but in the margin was written: "Note <note>original: σημ / σημείωσαι</note> that happiness is not in knowing many things, but in living according to virtue." REISKE: *Meermann* places the same Scholion <note>an ancient or medieval marginal note</note> a little earlier.

Or does he refer to those words of Pythagoras? # On Abstinence, Book I.

->**The Goal of the Intellect**<-

...that we may attain the contemplation of that which truly is: so that its attainment, according to the faculty within us, may effect a kinship between the contemplator and the thing contemplated. For one does not return to anything other than that which he truly is; nor does kinship and union occur with anything other than that which he truly is. He himself is truly the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς". Porphyry follows the Neoplatonic idea that our highest self is the divine Mind</note>: therefore, the end <note>The "telos" or ultimate purpose of life</note> will be nothing other than to live according to the Intellect. Toward this end, literature and external disciplines serve as a means of purification for us, but they do not constitute happiness itself. For if happiness were defined by the acquisition of disciplines, it would be possible for us to reach the goal while neglecting both food and actions. But since we must be purified by both reason and deeds to be transformed from this present life into another—

<column-break/>

—the goal for us is to attain the contemplation of being, with that attainment effecting, according to our power, a union between the contemplator and the contemplated. For the return is not to something else, but to one's true self; nor is the union with something else, but with that same true self. And that true self is the Intellect. Thus the goal is to live according to the Intellect. Toward this, both discourses and external studies hold a purifying role for us, but they are not the fulfillment of happiness. Hence, if happiness were defined by the mere grasping of discourses, it would be possible to reach the goal while being indifferent to both foods and the types of deeds performed. But since it is necessary to exchange the present life for another, having been purified through words and deeds,

---

<margin>In the Life of Pythagoras, number 39.</margin> Does he touch upon the three principal opinions of the philosophers regarding the "highest good"? Namely, the Peripatetics, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, to which he joins and explains the Pythagorean dogma. *Those around Aristotle define the end as living according to virtue,* as found in *Clement of Alexandria:* Miscellanies, Book II, page 415. Zeno the Stoic does not depart from this, page 416: *He considers the end to be living according to virtue.* Regarding the "tranquility" <note>original: "εὐθυμία" (euthymia)</note> of Epicurus, it is spoken of elsewhere. Indeed, he indicates above in Book I, section 3, that he is dealing with those philosophers.

6. *One's true self.*] The following words suggest that *himself* <note>original: "αὐτὸν"</note> should be read. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century critic</note>. Presently, the word *other* was missing in the *Leipzig* manuscript, though a blank space was left. For the word *toward*, the *Bodleian* manuscript incorrectly has *into*.

7. *And that true self is the Intellect.*] Previously these words

<column-break/>

were joined together, which we have now distinguished for the first time based on the authority of the *Leipzig* manuscript. <term>Reiske</term> also approved of this, and had added the note: *That "Himself" is the mind truly worthy of that name.*

8. *Hold a purifying role for us.*] By the order of the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, I have placed a comma after *us*, which was previously placed before that word. For *role* <note>original: "τρόπον"</note>, <term>Reiske</term> conjectured *place* <note>original: "τόπον"</note>. The *Bodleian* has *turning*. Presently, the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts read *if indeed in the grasping of discourses* instead of the standard reading. For *fulfillment*, it seemed to *Valentinus* that the plural *fulfilling things* should be read, but without a sufficiently just cause.

9. *And foods.*] *And what kind of foods, and what kind of deeds.* Having no concern for the burden, *whatever we might eat, and whatever we might do.* The word *what kind* <note>original: "ποιὸς"</note> in this place means "of whatever sort." <term>REISKE</term>.

# PORPHYRIUS

->Let us consider what kind of reasoning and what kind of actions will establish us in this state.<-

§ 30. <margin>1</margin> Would it not be the case that those things which separate us from the objects of sense and the passions <note>The Greek *pathe* refers to emotional disturbances or sufferings of the soul.</note> associated with them, and which lead us up toward an intellectual life—one free from imagination and passion as far as possible—would be the things we seek? <margin>2</margin> And would not their opposites be alien and worthy of rejection? Indeed, I believe it follows that we must grant this, especially as the latter withdraws us from the former and drags us down. For we are like those who have come to, or departed for, a foreign <margin>3</margin> nation; not only are we exiled from our own people, but we have also, in that foreign land, been filled with <margin>4</margin> passions and customs and alien laws, and have acquired a leaning toward them. Just as—

<column-break/>

we ought: come then, let us consider what reasons and what works may lead us to that state.

§ 30. Would it not seem that those things which separate us from things exposed to the senses, and from their disturbances, and raise us to an intellectual life, void of imagination and suffering, are of this kind? And that the opposites are truly alien and to be cast away, and all the more so because while they call us away from the former, they entice and drag us down to the latter? I certainly think these things must be granted. For we are similar to men who, having set out for foreign nations, are not only driven out from all their domestic affairs, but have also been so imbued with the disturbances, customs, and foreign institutions of the external region that they are greatly inclined toward them. Just as—

***

<margin>1. **Is it not then the case...**</margin> This was the previous reading, but *Valentinus* <note>Benedetto Valentini, a 16th-century editor.</note> removed the word "not." The old writing is also upheld by the *Meermann* and *Leipzig* manuscripts; the latter, however, mistakenly has "me" for "men," though "men" was there previously, for the letter "n" had been erased by an idle hand. Further on, for "these things," the *Bodleian* manuscript has "this."

<margin>2. **Withdraws from the one.**</margin> I suspected something was missing, and therefore I interposed the word "the." VALENTINUS. This correction by Valentinus is to be rejected. "The" is well-placed; "of one thing" is understood—it leads us away from that one thing. "Toward which" twists and weighs us down toward this other thing. REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist.</note> We do not begrudge the suspicion of *Valentinus*, but he should not have stuffed "of the Mind" into the text; the passage is healthier than a fish.

<margin>3. **Come to or departed for a nation.**</margin> In the *Leipzig* manuscript it is "to a nation either having gone willingly." This is elegant and

<column-break/>

true, and I accept what is given voluntarily. But that is not enough; the other member of the sentence is missing; add "or having been carried away unwillingly." Those who betake themselves to another people either do so of their own accord or are transferred against their will, having been ordered to migrate. It could also be more briefly emended as "to a nation either to those willing, or to those [unwilling] having departed." It is always necessary to oppose will and necessity, or compulsion, against each other. REISKE. The first edition is in exactly the same way as the *Leipzig* manuscript, with which the *Meermann* manuscript agrees. *Fogerolles* followed this, except that he placed "either" after "willingly." Either "having come" is true, or perhaps when "willingly" had been changed into "having come," it happened that this "either" crept into the text.

<margin>4. **Passions and customs.**</margin> Only *Valentinus* had "character" <note>original: *ethon* (character) vs *ethon* (customs)</note>, which I did not dare to receive, although I am not unaware that "passion" and "character" are often joined—

# On Abstinence, Book I.

Just as if someone wished to return home from a foreign land, they would not only be eager to make the journey, but would also take great care—in order to be welcomed by their own people—to cast off whatever they had acquired from foreign customs. Such a person would call back to memory those things which they once possessed but had forgotten, and without which they could in no way be admitted by their kinsmen. In the same way, if we are to return to those things which are truly our own and proper to us, we must cast off everything we have contracted from our mortal nature, along with the <term>affection</term><note>original: "affectu" / "προσπαθείας". This refers to an emotional or physical attachment to worldly things that "glues" the soul to the body.</note> by which we pursue them. It was from this very attachment that our <term>descent</term><note>The Neoplatonic belief that the soul "falls" or descends from a divine realm into a physical body.</note> originally occurred. We must remember our blessed and eternal essence and strive with all our might to return to those things which lack all color and quality <note>i.e., the pure, non-physical forms of the divine realm</note>, employing two forms of meditation: one by which...

<column-break/>

<margin>
...are joined, and that the former signifies *disturbances of the soul and affections*, while the latter signifies *disposition and character*: on which matter see *Perizonius on Aelian's Various History, Book IV, ch. 3.* Furthermore, the letters epsilon (ε) and eta (η) are frequently confused in this word and many others.
</margin>

</margin>

<margin>
6. *To cast off everything.*] *The Leipzig manuscript reads "to have cast off."* Soon, instead of "possessing," *Reiske* conjectured that "there" should be read, *the things which he forgot there.* "There" meaning in the foreign land. Then, the same author preferred "we are about to" instead of "we might be about to."
</margin>

<margin>
7. *The descent occurred &c.*] He speaks of the descent of the soul, and its return or ascent. See: *Iamblichus in the Protrepticus, p. 12* and *Holstenius on the Life and Writings of Pythagoras*, where he discusses this book *On Abstinence*. VALENTINUS: See how excellently these things can be applied to our own religion <note>Christianity</note>.
</margin>

...can be applied. Nor neglect to compare the sayings of *St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 4:18 and 5:1.* <note>"While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen..."</note> *Plato* also writes beautifully in the *Phaedrus, p. 1222*: "No poet here has ever sung, nor ever will sing worthily of the region above the heavens... for the essence that truly exists—colorless, shapeless, and intangible—is visible only to the mind, the pilot of the soul." *Proclus* uses these words in *Platonic Theology, Book IV, ch. 10, p. 196.* Moreover, those things which our Author discusses regarding the descent and return of the soul must be explained from the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, which the Platonists followed: that the soul descended from heaven into bodies, and returns there at last after being freed from earthly affection by various purifications, as we know from *Iamblichus and others*. Our Author wrote a book on that return of souls, just as *Plotinus* wrote on the descent of the soul into the body. # PORPHYRY

-> [Page 50] <-

...one way, by which we shall cast aside everything material and mortal; and another, by which we may achieve our return and prevail, ascending by a contrary path to that by which we descended to these things. For we were, and still are, intellectual substances <note>original: *νοεραὶ οὐσίαι* / *intellectuales substantiae*; referring to the soul's true nature as pure mind</note>, being pure from all sensation and irrationality. However, we became entangled with the sensible world <note>the world perceived by the five senses</note> through the weakness of our eternal association with the Intelligible <note>the higher realm of pure thought and forms</note>, and through a certain power directed toward the things found here. For all those faculties and powers that operate in conjunction with sensation and the body sprouted forth <note>original: *ἐβλάστησαν*; a botanical metaphor for the growth of lower soul-functions</note> because our soul did not remain within the Intelligible. It happened not unlike the corruption of the earth, which often, when the seed of wheat—

<column-break/>

—is cast down, [produces weeds]. <note>The sentence is interrupted by the column break and the start of the critical notes.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>
*apei-*, a blank space having been left for the last syllable; from which it seemed to **Reiske** <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German physician and philologist</note> that in the manuscript from which the *Leipzig* copy was transcribed, the word was *apeiron* <note>meaning "infinite" or "boundless"</note>.
**8. By which we descended to these things.**] The *Lyons* and *Cambridge* editions preferred "by which [we came] *unto* these things." However, among Greek and Latin writers, the preposition is often omitted in the latter position. Yet I do not doubt that we should read from the *Leipzig* manuscript "by which *here* we descended," or from the *Meerman* manuscript "by which *also here* we descended." For, as the illustrious **Reiske** also rightly noted, "here" <note>original: *ἐνταῦτα*</note> is the proper word in this context, concerning this life which we now lead among men in this world, just as "in this place" <note>original: *τῇδε*</note> is used a little later.
**9. We became entangled with the sensible.**] The word "sensible" <note>original: *αἰσθητῷ*</note> is missing in the *Leipzig* manuscript, which is an error. Perhaps it should read: "it was entangled with the sensible and the irrational." **REISKE**.
**10. They sprouted forth.**] In the *Leipzig* manuscript it is *eblastēsan* <note>sprouted</note>; I do not know if this is the true reading. It is certainly not displeasing; if it is accepted, the passage seems to be constituted thus: "the vices of the soul, not remaining in the Intelligible, sprouted forth." The verb for "sprouting forth," bringing forth, or pushing out—like a bud from a vine—seems to require the following simile drawn from wheat. **REISKE**.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
**They sprouted forth.**] All editions and manuscripts agree on this reading, except that some have *eblasthēsan* instead of *eblastēsan*. Only the *Valentian* manuscript gave *eblaphthēsan* <note>were damaged</note>, and that so confidently that, although providing no warning, they adopted it into the text. It is true that words are often confused, on which matter see **Muretus**, *Various Readings* III, 14. But what we have given here is uniquely true. This type of metaphorical language is very common. **Plato**, *Epistle VII*: "from which all evils have burst forth and sprouted for all." **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**, Book IX: "to seek a cure for sprouting evils." Conversely, concerning virtue, **Theophrastus** in **Plutarch’s** *Life of Agis*: "virtues being produced and sprouting." Regarding the sentiment itself, also metaphorically: "lawless excesses, drunks, and corruptions sprouted forth," etc. Instead of "in the Intelligible" <note>original: *ἐν νοητῷ*</note>, the *Leipzig* manuscript had *enoētōn*.
**11. Of wheat.**] Perhaps "of wheats" or "wheaten." If the latter is admitted, "the seed" will be added by what they call apposition. **REISKE**.
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

->G 2<-

...if it receives seed, it produces oats <note>original: *auenas* / *αἶρας*. Likely referring to darnel or wild oats, often used as a metaphor for weeds or inferior growth</note>. In the same way, this occurs through a certain depravity of the soul; it does not destroy the soul's essential substance by the procreation of an irrational nature, but through this nature, the soul is joined to mortality and dragged away from its own proper state toward that which is foreign to it.

§ 31. Therefore, if we desire to return to our original state, we must first strive with all our might to withdraw from sensation and imagination, and from the irrational quality that follows them, as well as from the passions associated with them—at least as far as the necessity of our physical birth <note>original: *generationis* / *γενέσεως*. Refers to the state of being embodied in the material world</note> permits. Next, we must correct those things pertaining to the intellect, securing for it peace and quiet from the war it wages with its irrational nature. We should do this so that we do not merely hear about the intellect and intelligible things, but also, as much as lies within us, enjoy the contemplation of it. Thus, restored to an incorporeal nature, we may truly live with it, and not—

<column-break/>

<gloss>12</gloss> produced oats. This happens through a certain wickedness of the soul, which does not corrupt <gloss>13</gloss> its own essence by the birth of unreason, but through this is joined to the mortal, and is dragged down to the foreign from the familiar.

§ 31. So we must practice, if indeed we are eager to return to the things of the beginning, as much as is in our power, to stand apart from sensation and imagination, and the unreason that follows these and the passions according to it, insofar as the <gloss>1$</gloss> necessity of birth does not press upon us. We must articulate the things according to the mind, providing for it peace and quiet from the <gloss>2</gloss> war of unreason; so that we might not only hear about the mind and the things of the mind, but also, as much as is possible, <gloss>3</gloss> be enjoying the contemplation of it, and being established in bodilessness, and living with truth—

<margin>
12. *Produced oats.*] A charming metaphor, just as the earth is often said to "give birth" among the Latin writers. Our author uses the same style of speaking below in Book IV, 17. Note that famous passage of the *Apostle* in Hebrews 6:7: "the earth bringing forth herbs." Hence the fruits which pertain to life are called *births* <note>original: *γεννήματα*</note>. *Diodorus Siculus* (V, 17) calls wine "the births intended for nourishment," and who does not know the "birth of the vine" <note>original: *γέννημα ἀμπέλου*</note> so often discussed in the *Gospels*? Therefore, *M. Thomas* incorrectly <note>original: *ἀδοκίμως*</note> applies this to certain fruits. On this "incorrectly," see the many notes of the Learned Man. *Bodaeus a Stapel* explains what "oats" <note>original: *Αἶρα*</note> are in his notes on *Theophrastus's History of Plants*, VIII, 7.

<column-break/>

<margin>
13. *Its own essence.*] *Valentinus* restored "of itself" <note>original: *Αὐτῆς*</note>, which also pleased *Fogerolles*, but it goes against the consensus of others. Recently *Lipsius* read "joined toward the [masculine]," which is poor.

1. *Necessity of birth.*] See the note at § 41.

2. *War of unreason.*] These words are certainly corrupted. *Valentinus* and *Fogerolles* preferred "of unreason." It seems probable to me, along with *Reiske*, that the author intended "from the war *against* unreason."

3. *Be enjoying the contemplation of it.*] *Reiske* suggests: "Let us be intellectual [or intelligible], enjoying some of its contemplation."
</margin>

4. *We must strip off &c.*] I would not altogether condemn the word *apoluteon* <note>original: ἀπολυτέον - "must be released"</note>, yet *apekduteon* <note>original: ἀπεκδυτέον - "must be stripped off"</note> or *apobleteon* <note>original: ἀποβλητέον - "must be cast away"</note> seems more appropriate. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note> I prefer *apoduteon* <note>original: ἀποδυτέον - "to undress"</note>. It suits the metaphor of garments and is confirmed by *Felicianus* and the words that follow. This style of speaking is exceedingly elegant and frequent among philosophers and even sacred writers. *Our author* <note>Porphyry</note> in *The Cave of the Nymphs* says "the body is a tunic for the soul," where you may compare the two. *Goensius*, a flower of the learned youth. In this place, Porphyry attributes several tunics to man: this exterior visible and fleshly one, and the interior ones with which we are clothed within, etc. These signify our body, its affections, and depraved habits. *Our author* below calls the body "the last and outermost tunic of skin," Book II, § 46. *Saint Jude* speaks of "the tunic spotted by the flesh" in verse 23, where the commentators diligently illustrate this mode of speaking. To this also pertains that saying of *Cassian* in *Clement of Alexandria*, Miscellanies Book III: "Cassian considers the tunics of skin to be the bodies." No less are the affections and depraved habits "tunics": *Philo* testifying, some said the wise man strips off the "tunic of vainglory" last of all. In *Stobaeus*, Sermon 45:

<column-break/>

"we strip off the last tunic of glory at death itself." *Athenaeus*, Book II, ch. 15. Just as "vainglory is the last tunic of the soul," which the *Brahmins* <note>Ancient Indian philosophers</note> said must be cast aside, in *Origen*, Philosophumena ch. 24. The same metaphor for the same matter is in *Tacitus*, History IV, ch. 6: *"Even for wise men, the lust for glory is the last thing to be stripped away."* Elegantly, therefore, *Justin Martyr* says of sins in the *Dialogue with Trypho*: "we have stripped off all the filthy evils with which we were clothed," and a little later, "filthy garments, that is, sins."

5. *Naked and without tunics.*] <term>LIPSIUS</term> <note>Justus Lipsius, noted humanist scholar.</note> had written at this place, in the same ink and hand as the rest: "Note how the Theologian also says this," meaning *Gregory Nazianzen*. <term>REISKE</term>. He continues in a style of speaking which he knew was very common among Christians. You might almost say he had before his eyes those things read in *Paul*, 1 Corinthians 9, Hebrews 12:1, and other places. *Meermann* added the same note as Lipsius. Presently, the later "upon" seems to have arisen from repetition.

6. *Upon the [Olympics] of the...*] I would prefer "upon" to be absent, and presently "and of which, without." <term>REISKE</term>.

7. *Not to eat...*] Perhaps "not to eat meat nor..."

# On Abstinence, Book I.

->G 3<-

For to not eat, or to refuse gifts of money, is a manifest and outward act; but the hidden and secret thing is to not even desire them. Therefore, along with the outward actions, one must also withdraw from the affection <note>original: *affectione* / *προσπαθείας*; the emotional "clinging" or attachment to an object</note> by which we are carried toward them. For what does it profit us to withdraw from the acts themselves if we remain pinned and fastened to the causes from which those acts spring?

§ 32. This withdrawal can be achieved either through force <note>i.e., through sheer willpower or external constraint</note> or through persuasion and reason, while the affections gradually waste away and—as one might say—are consigned to oblivion and die off. This is indeed the best kind of withdrawal, as it ensures that nothing remains clinging to that part from which the separation was made. For that which is torn away by force, even in these sensible things <note>physical objects perceived by the senses</note>, always leaves behind either some small part or a trace

<column-break/>

For example, not eating, or not taking money when offered, were among the visible things. But not even desiring them is among the less visible. Thus, along with the deeds, one must stand apart from the attachment and the passion toward them. For what is the use of standing apart from the deeds while being nailed to the causes from which the deeds arise?

§ 32. And the withdrawal might happen with force, but it might also happen by persuasion and according to reason, through a fading away and, as one might say, a forgetting of them and a death. This indeed happened to be the best withdrawal, not leaving behind a longing for that from which it was torn. For that which is torn away by force, even in sensible things, brings with it either a part or a trace of the tearing—

---

<margin>Taking money when offered: REISKE. Instead of "or," the Leipzig manuscript 2 and then the Bodleian manuscript have "of the things set forth" instead of "set forth." Not bad.</margin>

8. *To desire, of the...*] This precept also corresponds remarkably well to our Holy Scriptures. Read what the best interpreters have noted regarding the Gospel of *Matthew*, chapter V, 28 <note>"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."</note>. I cannot be more wordy on a well-known matter.

9. *To be nailed*] Because sensation happened to be "as a nail of the soul to the body," as is said below in § 38. Hence this beautiful metaphor, *to be nailed*, is used in that sense quite often by our author in § 57, etc. *Plato* in the Phaedo, page 63. A: *"Every pleasure and pain, having as it were a nail, fastens the soul to the body and pins it there."* *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> uses the same manner of speaking in the Life of Pythagoras, 32, looking back to Plato, as *Kuster* has already seen there. Again, *Iamblichus* in On the Mysteries, Section II, 6: *"And it fills with passions that nail those who behold them to the bodies."* There is a similar elegance in those words of *Clement of Alexandria* <note>An early Christian theologian</note> in the Stromata, Book II, page 407. A: *"Every pleasure and pain pegs the soul to the body,"* which are also related to Plato.

1. *Not leaving behind a longing for that from which it was torn.*] In the *Leipzig* Codex it is "not defeated." It seems it should be read as "not by a lack of that thing" from which we are torn away against our will. Or rather: "it is not that the soul is defeated by that from which it was torn—not that abandonment of a beloved thing when the soul allows itself to be torn from it with the greatest difficulty and cannot bear the longing for it." REISKE. "Not a lack" according to the *Meermann* manuscript; from which, following the stroke of the letters, I conjectured "not a lack (or a state of wanting)"—*chētis* meaning privation. *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> defines *chētei* as "deprivation." The Lexicographers and the illustrious *Bast* in Critical Observations, chapter 50, cite a passage of Plutarch for this word, but in truth it is Plato's in the Phaedrus, page 1217. C. The conjecture of the illustrious *Abresch* is ingenious: "and it is not defeated by that..." or "it is certainly not defeated by that." It could also be "not..."

# On Abstinence, Book I.

...passions are excited, and the entire irrational power, becoming more thickened <note>original: "crassior"</note>, drags the soul downward and turns it away from its proper love toward that which truly exists. Therefore, one must withdraw from these things to the best of one's ability. This withdrawal must be managed by excluding the passions that arise from the senses and the irrational power. Now, the senses arise from those things which are either seen, or heard, or perceived by taste, smell, or touch. For the sense has stood within us as a kind of "metropolis" <note>A mother-city or capital</note> for a foreign colony of passions. <column-break/>

—the passions are aroused, and the entire **irrationality** <note>original: "ἀλογία" (alogia)</note>, becoming thickened, brings down the soul and turns it away from the love of true Being. One must therefore stand apart from these things as much as possible. These departures occur through the avoidance of the passions related to the senses and those related to irrationality. <margin>
...and indeed. For we know that the Greeks frequently subjoin the particle *te* <note>and</note> to another word for joining, as in Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians 1:30. In that place, it does not seem necessary to refer the word "wisdom" to the Lord Christ, as noted in *Baffius, Critical Observations I, 1.*
</margin>

4. <term>Thickened irrationality <note>original: "Ἀλογία παχυνομένη"</note></term>] "To thicken" is elegantly transferred to the soul. Eating living things is said to "thicken the mind" in Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius I, 8.* Hence "thick" men are called stupid or senseless, as is known from *Suidas* and others. Learned men have many notes of this kind on *Matthew 13:15*: "the heart of this people has grown fat" <note>or "thickened"</note>. Our author below in section 38 speaks of "thickening the bond." From this, the ancient theologians took the idea: "The sinning soul is thickened, but virtue thins it." *Origen, Selections on the Psalms, p. 699.* See also the Latin commentators who speak of a "fat wit" <note>original: "pingue ingenium"</note> and similar things.

5. <term>The departures through avoidances <note>original: "Αἱ δὲ ἀποστάσεις διὰ τῶν ἐκκλ."</note></term>] The *Lipsius* and *Meermann* manuscripts read "exclusions." Diogenes Laertius (VII, 116) calls a rational avoidance a "reasonable declination." Do not fail to compare this with the beautiful passage in *Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation XVII, 7*, for it is too long to write out here.

6. <term>Now, the senses etc. <note>original: "Αἱ δὲ αἰσθήσεις &c."</note></term>] Jerome refers to this and the following in *Against Jovinian, Book II, 8*: *"Through the five senses, as if through certain windows, vice finds entry to the soul. The metropolis and citadel of the mind cannot be captured unless the hostile army rushes in through its gates. The soul is weighed down by the disturbances of these, and is captured by sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch."* If anyone is delighted by the circus, the contest of athletes, the mobility of actors, or the beauty of women, etc. Instead of "smellable things" <note>original: "ὀσφραντῶν"</note>, the *Lipsius* manuscript has "things pertaining to smell."

7. <term>For as it were a metropolis etc. <note>original: "Οἷον γὰρ μητρόπολις &c."</note></term>] A beautiful type of comparison. Thus, history is called the "metropolis of Philosophy" in *Diodorus Siculus, Book I, 2*, because the precepts of life proceed from there like colonies from a mother-city; see *Wesseling* for many other examples. Of similar elegance is that saying of *Diogenes*, who called "the love of money the metropolis of all evils," in *Laertius's* life of him. The best interpreters usually compare this with the saying of *Paul in 1 Timothy 6:10*. The same "love of money" is elegantly called the "citadel of vice" by *Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor II, 3.* And in *Stromata VII, p. 718*: "Pleasure is the metropolis of vice." "Greed is the metropolis of evils," *Palladius, On the Life of John Chrysostom, p. 45.*

8. <term>Fuel flows in... <note>original: "Ὑπέκκαυμα εἰσρεῖ τ. π."</note></term>] Similarly, *Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration XVIII*: "the fuels of the passions." And "the fuel of desire" in *Clement of Alexandria, Stromata Book II.*

# On Abstinence, Book I.

...they depart, they are carried away as if driven by madness: others, on the contrary, are rendered effeminate and transformed in every possible way. Furthermore, as for the use of perfumes or fragrant breaths <note>original: "odorati flatus"</note>, which offer their charms to their lovers, there is no one who does not know how much they fatten the irrational power within the soul. For what could anyone say concerning the disturbances admitted through the sense of taste? Especially since a double bond is woven therefrom: one which is fattened by the passions arising from tasting, and the other which is rendered heavy and powerful by the filling of the body with foreign substances. For poisons <note>or "drugs/medicines"; original: "venena"</note>, as a certain...

<column-break/>

...having stripped away reason, causes them to be carried away in a frenzy, while others are made effeminate, twisting in all sorts of turnings. 6. For concerning the sufferings through taste, what could one even say, since here especially a double bond is entwined: one which the passions fatten from the act of tasting, and the other which we make heavy and powerful from the stuffing of ourselves with foreign bodies. <margin>To be deleted. Perhaps "they cause those who have completely stripped off their reason (or their reasonings) to be carried away in a frenzy." REISKE.</margin>

5. **In a frenzy.** <note>original: "Oistroumenous"</note> Thus it was previously read: "It causes them to be carried away in a frenzy." A French interpreter had noted "furthermore" <note>original: "loipon"</note> in the margin of the book; I noted "as if" <note>original: "hoion"</note>. Both crept into the text. However, I judge the latter to be more true. VALENTINUS. It seems to me it should be read as "so as to make" or "as they make." The passionate things heard are such "as to make them be carried away in a frenzy," etc. Or "as they make," etc. "From whom is it hidden?"—which can also be referred here from what follows. It is indeed a mild remedy.

6. **Uses of incenses or [foul-smelling] breaths.** Perhaps "incenses or the foul use of breaths." This "sweet-smelling" <note>original: "euodeis"</note> was a conjecture of the French interpreter and ought to have been omitted. For I thought there was no need to change "foul-smelling" <note>original: "dysodeis"</note>, but that "uses of foul-smelling incenses or breaths" could be tolerated. VALENTINUS. Perhaps "sweet-smelling uses of incenses, and breaths which [trade] their own desires"—the word "sweet-smelling" <note>original: "hedysodes"</note> is indeed rare for "fragrant" <note>original: "hedyosmos"</note>, and the construction "sweet-smelling uses of incenses" is rare for "uses of sweet-smelling incenses." Yet it seems...

<column-break/>

...Porphyry used that diction, which that age produced, harsh, affected, and often monstrous, to have given that which we have set down. REISKE. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, Book II, 8: *“The sweetness of odors, and diverse incenses, and balsam, and kyphi, vine-flower, musk, and the skin of a foreign mouse, which is suitable for the dissolute and for lovers, no one except the dissolute denies.”* One might suspect he read "sweet-smelling breaths." For "uses" <note>original: "chreseis"</note>, it seemed rightly to the learned Abresch that "graces" <note>original: "charites"</note> should be restored (and the first hand in the Meermann manuscript had given this), and presently "which" or "which at least."

All agree on the feminine "how much" <note>original: "hosen"</note>. Moreover, he elegantly said "to fatten irrationality," just as "to fatten the bond," "passions," and similar phrases are familiar to the Philosophers. "To fatten the bond of the soul," Julian, *Oration VI*, p. 198; which our author calls "to thicken the bond" in section 38, concerning which word see above.

# PORPHYRY

One of the physicians once said that it is not only the medicinal preparations of the medical art, but also the daily foods and drinks we consume for nourishment, that transmit a far more deadly force to the soul than the poisons prepared by pharmacies to bring about the dissolution of the body. Furthermore, the sensations of touch—which all but turn the soul into a physical body—often provoke it to fall into inarticulate noises, as if it were already mere flesh. From these sensations, memories, fantasies, and accumulated opinions arise, stirring up a swarm of passions: they fill the soul with fears, desires, angers, loves, charms, griefs, envies, anxieties, and diseases of similar disturbances.

§. 35. Therefore, the struggle to be purified of these things is great, and the labor to be freed from the constant dwelling upon them—both by night and by day—is immense.

<column-break/>

<note>The Latin column mirrors the Greek text above, emphasizing that the "deadly power" (letifera uis) of food is more dangerous to the soul's health than physical poison is to the body.</note>

One physician said that it is not only those things compounded by medicine, but also the foods and drinks habitually taken for daily nourishment, from which a deadly power is diffused into the soul, more so than the destruction brought to the body's dissolution by poisons. Now indeed, touches—rendering the soul almost corporeal—often cause it to break out into inarticulate sounds, as if it were now becoming a body. From all these things, memories, imaginations, and opinions are gathered, and an innumerable flock of perturbations is excited, filling the soul with the diseases of fears, lusts, angers, loves, allurements, pains, emulations, anxieties, and disturbances of this kind.

§ 35. And for that reason, it is difficult to be purged of these; a very great labor must be undertaken if we wish to be liberated from the meditation upon them, since by day...

---

<margin>That this "variety of foods" is the single cause of diseases is noted in <note>original: "τῶν ἐδεσμάτων τὴν πολυειδίαν"</note> Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, Book II, page 140 B.</margin>

9. **And into inarticulate noises]** I do not understand this passage. It is obscure what those "inarticulate sounds" are into which the sense of touch might run. Or, if we prefer the reading *to fall into* <note>original: "ἐμπίπτειν"</note>, it suggests being carried away and dashed against them, like a ship against rocks. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>. I understand these as the "clatter and tumult" into which the soul falls through that sense. Jerome refers to this in *Against Jovinianus*, Book II, 8: *"The touch of foreign bodies and the burning desire for women is neighbor to insanity. Because of this sense we desire, we grow angry, we exult, we envy, we emulate, we are anxious... especially since touch depicts for itself even past pleasures, and by memory forces the soul to suffer along with it, and in a way to practice what it is not actually doing."* Lipsius does not have the word *but* <note>original: "δὲ"</note> before *touches*. Meermann wrongly reads *into articulate* <note>original: "εἰς ἄρθρους"</note>.

10. **A swarm of passions]** Below in Book II, 62, he calls it a "swarm of evils." Hesychius defines "swarm" <note>original: "ἑσμὸς"</note> as a "multitude," where learned men have noted many things of this kind.

11. **Loves, charms]** Below in Book II, 42, "erotic things" and "charms" <note>original: "Φίλτρα"</note> are also joined. The word *philtron* is used sometimes for a drug given for the sake of love, and sometimes for conjugal love or the love shown toward children. This is a well-known matter; see Wolf on Libanius, Epistle 76. Meermann mistakenly reads *fear, desire*.

I. **The labor to be freed]** Lipsius reads "a laborless labor to be freed" <note>original: "πόνος ἄπονος"</note> as a correction, for previously he had written...

# PORPHYRY

And it was far from the city, a place that was also, as they say, 3 unhealthy. Others even went so far as to not spare their own eyes, out of a longing for internal, undistracted contemplation. But if anyone thinks that by living among men and filling his senses with the passions <note>The Greek term *pathe* refers to emotions or disturbances of the mind triggered by external stimuli.</note> belonging to them, he himself can remain unaffected, he deceives himself and those who believe him; he fails to realize that 4 he has largely enslaved himself to the passions by not distancing himself from the multitude. For it was not in vain, nor 5 by misrepresenting the nature of things, that the one among the philosophers spoke, saying: 6 "These men, I suppose, from their youth..."

<column-break/>

it was in a desert place, and far from the city, and was even considered somewhat unhealthy, as they say. Indeed, it is well known that there were some who, out of a desire for internal contemplation, so as not to be distracted, did not spare their own eyes. But if anyone, while mingling with men and satisfying his senses with their own affections, thinks he will remain impassive, he deceives both himself and others whom he has persuaded; nor does he notice that by the very fact that he is not alienated from the multitude, he has surrendered himself most greatly to the power of the passions. For it was not rashly, nor by lying about the nature of philosophers, that he asserted—the one who said: "These men, indeed, from childhood first [travel] the path into..."

->**Notes and Commentary**<-

<margin>3. *Unhealthy.*</margin> Others also indicate this. *Aelian, Historical Miscellany IX, 10:* "Plato [chose] the Academy, which was said to be a sickly place." The *Interpreters* say more on this matter. If these things are true, it must be said that Cimon <note>An Athenian statesman who famously beautified the city.</note> achieved little, who "adorned the city, turning the Academy from a waterless and parched place into a well-watered grove, furnished by him with clean running-tracks and shaded walks," according to *Plutarch, Volume I, page 487 C.* Recently, the *Cambridge* edition had omitted the word "the" <note>original: "τῶν"</note> against the faith of previous editors and my own manuscripts.

<column-break/>

<margin>4. *He has largely enslaved...*</margin> It is better to take "enslaved" <note>original: "καταδεδούλωται"</note> in the active sense. This is common. VALENTINUS. This latter point is very true, but I would prefer to understand "himself" <note>original: "αὑτὸν"</note> as implied. The force of the middle voice is well known, and how pointlessly it is read in *Lucian's Solecist*: "to be enslaved happens to another, but to enslave happens to oneself." *Duker on Thucydides III, 70* and others have shown this. The sense, therefore, is: "he has largely enslaved himself to [the multitude] by his lack of alienation." To these last words *Reiske* had added: "properly not—*alienation from the common people.*" "Non-alienation" <note>original: "οὐκ-ἀλλοτρίωσις"</note> is treated as a single word, and was written as such in the *Meerman* manuscript. Note the Grammarians' figure of "under one" <note>original: "τοῦ ὑφ’ ἕν" — a hyphenated concept.</note>.

<margin>5. *Misrepresenting the nature.*</margin> "One who misrepresents." Plato is meant, whose noble passage is read in the *Theaetetus.* REISKE. Excellent. To "misrepresent" <note>original: "καταψεύδεσθαι"</note> with the genitive is used everywhere by the Greeks to mean "to lie about someone, or to rashly attribute something to someone." Thus "to misrepresent human nature" appears below in *Book IV, 21.* Other examples are given by *Perizonius on Aelian, Historical Miscellany XII, chapter 36.*

<margin>6. *These men, I suppose, from their youth...*</margin> These words up to...

# On Abstinence, Book I.

They do not even know the way to the marketplace, nor where the court of law, or the council chamber, or any other public assembly of the city is located. As for the laws and decrees that are spoken or written, they neither see nor hear them. Indeed, the strivings of political factions for office, the meetings, the dinners, and the revels with flute-girls <note>original: "psaltriis" (Latin) / "αὐλητρίσι" (Greek) — female musicians often present at banquets</note> do not occur to them even in their dreams. Whether something has happened well or ill in the city, or if some misfortune has befallen someone from their ancestors—whether men or women—it escapes the philosopher's notice more than the "pebbles of the sea," as the saying goes. And of all these things, he does not even know that he does not know them; for he does not abstain from them for the sake of gaining a reputation. In reality, only his body remains and dwells in the city, while his mind, considering all these things to be small and worth nothing at all—

<column-break/>

—from their youth, first of all, they do not know the way to the marketplace, nor where the courtroom or the council-chamber is, or any other common assembly of the city; and as for laws and decrees, whether spoken or written, they neither see nor hear them. The zeal of political clubs for offices, and gatherings, and dinners, and revels with flute-girls, does not even enter their dreams as things to be done. Whether something has happened well or ill in the city, or if some evil has come to someone from their ancestors, whether on the side of the men or the women, it escapes his notice more than the so-called "measures of the sea" <note>original: "χόες" — a Greek unit of liquid measure, here used proverbially to mean something impossible to count, like the sands or drops of the sea</note>. <margin>Toward the end of the Section: these words are taken from Plato, in the *Theaetetus* 127 <note>Modern citation: Theaetetus 173c-d</note>, from which many others have also drawn into their own works. *Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book V, p. 596. 7. **The zeal of political clubs.**] We have taken care to edit it thus. Previously it was read as *spoudaite* <note>a corruption in the Greek text</note>. Not only the authority of the *Meermann* manuscript, but also *Plato*, and those whom I said described him, command it so. Instead of *hetaireiōn* (of clubs), *Clement of Alexandria* and *Eusebius* have *hetairiōn*. We have said above that "ei" and "i" were frequently confused in these matters because the sound was almost the same.

8. **In the city.**] Thus it is correct. Only the *Cambridge* manuscript had *en omi*, but *Plato* and the others go against it. Then I restored *tōi k.* (to someone) instead of *to k.* (the), which was read previously. It is correctly published as *tōi* in *Eusebius*, and it must be restored to *Plato* and others. The *Florentine* edition and the *Leipzig* manuscript command the same, except that in the latter, instead of the enclitic *tōi*, it was written as *tῷ*. This is also in the *Meermann* manuscript. Instead of "from ancestors," *Theodoret*—but he alone—has "among ancestors." *Plato* and *Eusebius*, however, have "or on the side of the men."

9. **It escapes his notice.**] Both the *Leiden* and *Cambridge* editions wanted *autous* (them, plural). But *Plato* and the rest contradict this. The editors did not remember that it is a common usage for Attic writers and others to very often transition from the plural to the singular. The *choes* (measures) are rendered as "sands of the sea" by the translator of *Plato*, p. 64. A little later, the *Meermann* manuscript has *archetai* (begins) instead of *apechetai* (abstains); this is an error.

# On Abstinence, Book I.

he says, it occurs to him. Much less, therefore, is he likely to be indignant if he is deprived of some broth or a small piece of meat; rather, he will hardly give any care to these things at all. He will not consider these matters as anything but small and insignificant if he abstains, but great and harmful if he partakes. For since he has examples in the nature of things—that the divine is the most blessed, while that which lacks divinity is the most miserable—he will present himself as similar to the former and dissimilar to the latter. He will establish a life suitable to that which he wishes to resemble: a life content with a very slender diet, and one that is minimally filled with mortal concerns.

<column-break/>

<note>This is the original Greek text of the passage translated into Latin on the left.</note>
...he says, it approaches him. Hardly then would he be vexed at being deprived of broths and bits of meat, or would he attach himself to these things at all? Would he not rather deem them small and nothing in their absence, but great and harmful in their introduction? Since there are examples standing in reality—the one divine and most happy, the other godless and most wretched—he will make himself like the one and unlike the other, living the appropriate life of that which he resembles: a life simple, self-sufficient, and least filled with mortal things.

---

->§ 38.<-

<note>The following section contains scholarly debates on the specific Greek wording used by Porphyry, comparing different manuscript versions and previous editors' opinions.</note>

...he ordered it to be repeated, so that it reads *he does not know, he knows, but* etc. It is a frequent occurrence that the "senseless tribe of scribes" <note>original: "insulsa librariorum natio"</note> neglected a syllable, or even an entire word, which had preceded it.

3. *Or would he attach himself to these things at all.*] In place of *prosthēsetai* <note>original: "προσθήσεται" - will add/attach</note>, the previous translator had substituted *prosthēsetai*. But either it should not be changed, or the whole should be read as: *or if he will not attach himself at all*. VALENTINUS. <note>Referring to the scholar Pier Vettori/Victorius</note> Perhaps *prosthēsetai* means he will admit to himself, adopt, or embrace. REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, a famous 18th-century philologist</note> All agree on *prosthēsetai*. For *prosēsetai*, which is in the *Leipzig* manuscript, was the same. This would be from the verb *proïēmi* <note>to send forth</note>, which does not seem to fit this place. If it descends from *prosiēmi* <note>to let come to oneself</note>, it should be read as *prosēsetai*, which pleased the celebrated Abresch, whose words deserve to be recorded here as much as possible. In compounds of this kind, where the simple verb begins with a *sigma* (s), the omission of the second *sigma* in the preposition *pros* is almost the most frequent error. Thus, in Henri Estienne's *Thesaurus*, it is wrongly held as *prosernizomai*, and he, just like Salmasius in Hesychius, wants it replaced with *prossernizomenos* for *prosernizomai*. Longus, Book IV, page 133: *prossernizeto*, and he did not want to leave the enclosures. See Gataker on Marcus Aurelius, pages 107 and 199. *Dilucidationes Thucydideae*, page 380. These are the words of that learned man. *Prosēsesthai* in this place, meaning *to strike against*,

<column-break/>

->§ 38.<-

*to be a weariness and a burden*, as is often the case among the Greeks, is explained by Reiske in his *Opuscula* of Plutarch, page 390. The Greeks are accustomed to use this meaning with the dative case. Here it can be taken in the same sense as a little before, or simply *these things happen to him, or come into use*. Regarding this use of the word, see Gataker on Marcus Aurelius VI, 46. Instead of *scholē* <note>meaning "hardly" or "scarcely" in this context</note>, which is superior, the *Leipzig* manuscript wrongly has *scholē* <note>with a different accent</note>. Meermann's manuscript has *scholē*.

4. *And not all things etc.*] In place of *panta* (all), I would prefer *mallon* (rather). And thus the whole passage is established: *but rather, having considered that he will be harmed little by abstinence but greatly by the introduction of these things*, with the examples standing within. *And will he not be made like*, with the rest thrown in as a parenthesis. One could also read *in the closest proximity* <note>original: "en tō anchista hestōtōn"</note> instead of *in reality* <note>original: "en tō onti hestōtōn"</note>, from which "to the" is gathered, *you stand nearby*. REISKE.

5. *Examples standing in reality.*] Valentinus had corrected this to *in the mind*. No one will change anything who remembers that these are the words of Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, page 129 D: *examples standing in reality, the one divine and most happy, the other godless and most wretched... becoming like the one, and unlike the other, living the appropriate life of that which they resemble.*

# PORPHYRY

§ 38. For as long as someone is troubled <note>original: "διαφορῆται" - to be distracted or anxious</note> about foods, and argues that this or that must be eaten, and does not consider that—if it were possible—one should abstain from all nourishment entirely, such a person is merely advocating for their own passions. They are "hunting for reputation" <note>original: "δοξοκοπεῖ" - to seek vain glory or be obsessed with mere opinion</note>, acting as if there were no difference in the very things they are disputing. Now, the philosopher will not take himself out by force <note>This refers to the Neoplatonic prohibition against suicide; one must wait for the soul to be naturally released.</note>. For he who is forced out nevertheless remains in that place from which he is being violently removed. Yet, he will not think it a matter of indifference if he makes his bond <note>The "bond" refers to the physical body which chains the soul.</note> thicker. Therefore, granting only what is necessary to nature, and ensuring that even this is light and provided through lighter foods, he will reject everything beyond this as tending toward pleasure.

<column-break/>

§ 38. For as long as anyone disputes about foods, and contends that this also must be eaten, and is not of the opinion that, if it could be done, one should assert that all nourishment whatsoever must be abstained from; he seems to patronize his passions boastfully and in vain: as one who thinks it matters nothing in those things about which he disputes. But he who practices philosophy will not withdraw himself from these things by force: for he who is compelled by violence is nonetheless accustomed to resist in that place from whence he is unwillingly led away: yet he will not think, if he renders the bond thicker for himself, that he is doing something that matters nothing. Wherefore, exhibiting to nature only that which is necessary, and that being exceedingly light, and by the lightest foods possible, he will refuse whatever exceeds this limit, as if for the sake of pleasure.

<margin>
It is the same, and has just as much value as *accommodating oneself to another*, or finally, adopting the reading of the *Leipzig manuscript*, *being filled*, one should read *being filled with mortal things*, or *being filled with mortal food*. REISKE. A little before, instead of *likely*, the Meerman manuscript wrongly has *yielding*.
</margin>

1. *Is troubled.*] To be troubled <note>original: "διαφορεῖσθαι"</note> in this place is not *to disagree*, but to be distressed in mind, to labor, not to be at peace whether a thing exists or not, or whether it happens in this way or another, but to think it matters much to oneself how a thing happens or does not happen. Therefore, *to be troubled* is the same as *to differ* <note>original: "διαφέρεσθαι"</note> a little later. REISKE. The illustrious Abresch preferred *both to be troubled and* or *to differ and*. Instead of *foods* <note>original: "βρωτῶν"</note>, the Meerman manuscript has *mortals* <note>original: "βροτῶν"</note>, by a frequent error, as we saw above.

2. *That this also must be eaten.*] *That this must also be eaten*. REISKE.

3. *Hunting for reputation*] This is a rarer word. It is said of a vain opinion which occupies someone fruitlessly, like other compounds of this origin. In *Plutarch's Life of Pericles*, p. 154 E, instead of *hunting for reputation* and *reputation-seeking*, some manuscripts prefer our word and *reputation-seeking*. Several authors use this latter term, as does our author below in Book II, 52, which see.

<column-break/>

4. *The philosopher [will not take] himself out.*] Holstenius in *The Life of Porphyry*, chapter 8, and the learned editor of *Hierocles on the Golden Verses*, p. 260, as well as others, explain *to lead oneself out* as *to take one's own life*, in which sense our author is accustomed to use it, as we shall say regarding Book II, § 46. It could be understood here as *detachment*, when one withdraws oneself from the senses and leads the soul out, as it were, from the body, so that it is not hindered by its mass and passions—a doctrine he emphasizes everywhere. Nevertheless, the nature of the expression is the same.

5. *Making the bond thicker.*] See above, § 34, and below in § 47 he calls it the *thickness of the bond*.

6. *Through lighter [foods].*] Perhaps *nourishing through the lightest [foods]*, namely *nature* or *the body*. REISKE. Soon, instead of *tending toward*, the Bodleian manuscript wrongly has *stretching together*.
