# PORPHYRY

It is one thing to be present, and another to believe oneself not to be present by withdrawing one's attention. <note>The Greek text here has a disputed reading between "withdrawing" and "applying" attention.</note> Certainly, no one will show that Plato concedes this point, unless one were to demonstrate that Plato was deceiving even himself. For he who voluntarily gives himself over to the consumption of food, to spectacles seen through the eyes, and to social gatherings and laughter, is—by that very act of settling into them—present in the same place where the emotion is. But he who is intent upon other things and stands apart from these, is the one who, through his lack of experience in such matters, provides a cause for laughter not only to Thracian servant girls but to the rest of the crowd as well; and when he is forced into such situations, he falls into every kind of hesitation—not because he lacks his senses, nor because he perceives things with exactitude <insert>but only with his irrational side</insert>.

<column-break/>

It is one thing to be present, and another to think one is not there by attending to something else. No one will show that Plato grants this, unless they wish to show he deceived himself. He who of his own accord gives himself to eating, shows, meetings, and laughter, is, by that very surrender and approach, in the place where the affection is. But he who is intent on other things and stands apart from these, is that man who, due to inexperience, offers laughter not only to Thracian maids but to the rest of the crowd; and when compelled, he falls into total hesitation: not because he lacks sense, or because he perceives exactly, but only in an irrational way.

***

3. *By withdrawing one's attention.*] It would be better to read *by applying one's attention*. VALENT. <note>Referring to the scholar Pier Vettori/Victorius.</note> Reiske agreed with this, and rightly so, though I know what can be said in defense of the common reading. The Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts also have "the." The Bodleian manuscript is quite faulty here. Then the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts have "deceiving," which Fogerolles had also published.

4. *To spectacles voluntarily seen through the eyes, etc.*] The word "through" is missing in the Leipzig manuscript. I am troubled by this passage and cannot easily free myself from the difficulty. For what then? Are there other "spectacles" <note>original: "theai"</note> which do not happen through sight? Is the word "spectacle" so ambiguous, like "something heard" <note>original: "akroama"</note>, so that just as the latter signifies any show (even though properly it refers only to things delighting the ear), so "spectacle" might be any show even if it does not delight the eyes alone? I do not like the word "social gatherings" <note>original: "homilias"</note>; I would prefer "chatterings" <note>original: "samylias"</note>, which fits better with "laughter." I also wonder if "sight" <note>original: "opseos"</note> hides the word "mockery" <note>original: "skopseos"</note>. Did the author perhaps write: "and into voluntary spectacles and the pleasures of mockery, chatterings, and laughter"? REISKE. I understand these "spectacles" to be those mentioned above in § 33, which are very different from that contemplation mentioned in Book II, § 34, where he says of the Gods: "that they truly nourish us through the sight of them." The word "social gathering" is very broad and encompasses all

<column-break/>

meetings and almost everything that happens in the daily usage of life. They therefore join "gatherings" and "associations." See the authors cited by Alberti on Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians 15:33. <note>"Bad company ruins good morals."</note>

5. *Providing laughter.*] This refers to the stories told about Thales and his clever servant girl. <note>Thales of Miletus famously fell into a well while looking at the stars, prompting a Thracian maid to mock him for wanting to know the heavens while not seeing what was at his feet.</note> I have Plato as my witness, who, after telling that story, continues in the *Theaetetus* (p. 127 A): "he provides laughter not only to Thracian girls, but to the crowd." Eusebius excerpted this from Plato, among other things, in his *Preparation for the Gospel* (p. 603). That woman is said everywhere to have been "Thracian" by race, but Origen in his *Philosophumena* (ch. 1, p. 878) indicates this was her proper name. Since it was common for maids in the past to take their names from their fatherland, there is no reason to trouble this reading as a certain learned man did in his *Critical Additions*, which I see Wolf has already noticed.

6. *Not because he lacks his senses.*] Instead of "but," it seems "inasmuch as" should be read. But this place is somewhat intricate. What if he wrote: "inasmuch as he does not show himself exactly, nor again exactly, but in his irrational part," as if showing himself neither entirely foolish and slow, nor on the other hand a spectator and judge of things.

§ 41. But what need would there be to waste away the affections and to die as far as they are concerned, and to meditate upon this daily: if it were possible that we might operate from the intellect, and occupy ourselves with mortal matters without any inspection of the intellect, as some assert? pertain. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note> As below in § 41. *for it is not possible*, with which place the illustrious <term>Elsner</term> compares *The Gospel of Luke* 13:33: and so throughout.

1. **To wither the passions, and to die.**] *To wither* <note>original: "Μαραίνειν"</note> is used metaphorically regarding the affections. Our author uses "through withering" <note>original: "διὰ μαράνσεως"</note> below in III, 26. and IV, 3. — and "death" <note>original: "θανάτου"</note> above in § 32. as it is joined here with "to die." Elsewhere he calls it the **Death of the Philosophers**, which by others, such as **Pythagoras** in the *Golden Verses*, is called the "release from evils." They recommend that philosophical death everywhere at the end of Book II: "we who have made 'dying' our daily practice in life." What sort of death that is, he teaches in *Sentences on the Intelligibles* § 9: "Death is indeed twofold; one is well-known [physical]... the other is that of the Philosophers, where the soul is released from the body." Pythagoras took that custom of subduing and taming the body like an enemy from the Egyptians, and from them it was propagated to other nations, especially the Indians, where it has not yet fallen into disuse; on which matter see <term>La Croze</term> in *Christian History of India*, Book VI. Truly, because interpreters are accustomed to crowd these types of passages when they find something similar in the New Testament, for example in the *Epistle to the Romans* 6:2, those who have experience in ancient philosophy understand by what right that is done.

2. **Some have asserted.**] <note>original: "Τινες ἀπεφαίνοντο"</note> Perhaps it should be *as some have asserted*. The word "as" <note>original: "ὡς"</note> perished in the collision with the end of the word "oversight." <term>REISKE</term>. Most truly, and so the translator has it. Previously it was read as *some were showing*; yet

<column-break/>

the traces of the true reading were in the *Leipzig* manuscript: *some were fleeing*. More correctly <term>Meermann</term>: *some have asserted*. Unless it was in the singular: *someone asserted*. In which way <term>Marsilio Ficino</term> seems to have read it, for he translates: *as someone declared*, so that it refers to the following saying of Epicharmus. However, the preceding syllable had absorbed the "as," as happens a hundred times. You could also read it as *of some oversight*, which pleased <term>Abresch</term>.

3. **For the intellect sees** etc.] A famous saying of Epicharmus: *The intellect sees, and the intellect hears; the rest are deaf and blind.* **Jerome**, in *Against Jovinian* II, 9: *That the mind sees, and the mind hears, and that we can neither hear nor see anything unless the sense is intent upon those things which we discern and hear*, is also an ancient opinion. We shall say more at Book III, 21. where Plutarch praises the saying, but with the author's name suppressed.

4. **Why not also frequently** etc.] "Frequently" <note>original: "Πολλάκις"</note> in this place does not mean "often," but "for example," as I use it here. <term>REISKE</term>. For the word "you are" <note>original: "εἶ"</note>, the *Leiden* edition had substituted "he might be," which I know not where they received it. For the *Florentine* edition also has "you are." However, both wrongly have "being with." <term>Abresch</term> preferred "frequently being with." Those things which follow—*which are not even honorable to speak of*—are frequently used in cases of this kind; <term>Wetstein</term> teaches this, and does not forget our author, in his notes on *Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians* 5:12.

# On Abstinence, Book I.
->I 3<-

...acts, which are not even honorable to speak of? For these are everywhere the passions of the "child" within us <note>The "child" is a Platonic metaphor for the irrational or impulsive part of the human soul</note>. But will you assert that because these things are shameful, the soul is not dragged down toward them? Yet what is this distinction you make? That you cannot be affected by some things unless you attend to them and are present with them, while you allow yourself to pursue others even while you are free to perceive intelligible things? <note>The "intelligible" refers to the higher realm of thought and divine truth, contrasted with the physical world</note> For it must not be said, of course, that some things are considered shameful by the many, and others not at all. For all things are shameful insofar as they pertain to the life that must be led according to the intellect. One must abstain from all things no differently than from sexual pleasures, except that a small amount of food must be granted to nature due to the necessity of generation <note>original: "generationis," referring here to the maintenance of life and the physical self</note>. For wherever there is sense-perception and the grasping of it, there a withdrawal from the intelligible necessarily occurs. And the more the motion of the irrational part is incited, the more the power of thought fails. For it is not possible...

<column-break/>

...which are not even honorable to speak of? For these were everywhere the passions of the **child** within us, <gloss>5</gloss> and insofar as they are shameful, the soul is not dragged down toward them. For what is this distribution of lots, that it is impossible to suffer some things without being present with them, but to allow the completion of others while remaining with the intelligible? <gloss>7</gloss> For it is not because some things are assumed to be shameful among the many, <gloss>8</gloss> and others are not; for all things are shameful in relation to the life according to the mind, and one must abstain from all, just as from sexual pleasures. A little food should be granted to nature because of the necessity of **generation**. <gloss>9</gloss> For where there is sensation and the perception of it, there is the departure from the intelligible. And as much as there is a stirring of the irrational, by so much is there a departure from thinking. For it is not possible here...

<gloss>5. The child.]</gloss> We spoke on this at section 9. <term>Jerome:</term> <note>Saint Jerome, early Christian scholar</note> Book II against Jovinian, chapter 10: *Another comparison of the soul and body is placed by the philosophers: saying the body is the child, and the soul is the pedagogue (teacher).*

<gloss>6. And insofar as they are shameful.]</gloss> Something indeed seems to be missing here, but the passage is nevertheless complete. This is the characteristic brevity of Porphyry, saying the same as if he had said "and by how much more shameful these passions are, by so much more the soul is not dragged down toward them." So a little later "as much as the irrational," where "more" is again omitted. <term>Reiske.</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century philologist</note> "As much as" is often said by the Greeks through ellipsis <note>omission of a word</note> for "as much more." See <term>the celebrated Duker:</term> on <term>Thucydides</term> VI, 89. "To be dragged down" is used metaphorically of the passions, often in our author and others. See above section 30, and Book IV, section 20. Instead of "these" in the <term>Leipzig manuscript</term> there was "them," which <term>Reiske</term> preferred.

->and being carried toward that place, while being here, to be there. For we do not direct our attention with a part of ourselves, but with our whole being.<-

**§ 42.** 1. The belief that one can be affected according to the senses and yet simultaneously act toward the intelligible <note>Greek: *noētois*; things understood by the mind rather than the senses</note> has led many, even 2. among the barbarians <note>A term used by Greeks/Romans for non-Hellenic peoples, often including Jews and Christians</note>, to fall headlong into ruin. These people, out of a spirit of negligence, have advanced into every form of pleasure, claiming 3. that it is possible for one who is occupied with other things to allow themselves to use the irrational part of their nature. Indeed, I have already heard some who, in defense of their own misfortune, argue in this manner—

<column-break/>

—it is possible that we are carried here and there at the same time, and while we are here, we are also able to be present there. For attentions are not made by a part of us, but by the whole.

**§ 42.** For this opinion—that anyone, while all their senses are being affected, can still be free for intelligible things—has carried many even of the barbarians headlong and destroyed them. These people, poured out into every kind of pleasure through negligence, asserted that they were indulging themselves because, while they were attending to other things, they could also use their irrational faculties. Now indeed I have heard some, when they were patronizing their own unhappiness, in this—

***

—it is necessary: because we are born such that we cannot help but indulge ourselves in this. <small>REISKE.</small> So above in § 31: *the necessity of generation* <note>original: "hē anankē tēs geneseōs"</note>. Plato and others very often speak this way. Our author calls it *the necessity of mortal nature* <note>original: "tēs thnētēs physeōs anankēn"</note> in § 45. Just before "to perceive" <note>original: "noein"</note>, the word "of the" <note>original: "tou"</note> was wrongly missing in the Florence and Leiden editions.

1. *The belief that etc.*] Jerome expressed this in *Against Jovinianus*, Book II, chapter 9: *But if anyone thinks that he can enjoy an abundance of food and drink and still be free for wisdom—that is, to live in luxury and not be held by the vices of luxury—he deceives himself.*

2. *Led many of the barbarians headlong.*] *P. Petit, Miscellaneous Observations, book 1, chapter 5*, is excessive in explaining and amending this passage. He says it was badly translated by Holstenius (note a frequent error, about which I speak elsewhere) and that he could not amend or complete it. He thinks it refers to Solomon, King of the Hebrews, and that he is called a "barbarian." He suggests Porphyry had read those words of Solomon: "vanity of vanities" etc., and had also seen the passage where Solomon boasts of his wealth and magnificence. From this, he concludes that Solomon held the heresy that a wise man could be free for mental contemplation and bodily pleasures at the same time. He thinks that after the word "saying" <note>original: "legontes"</note>, Solomon's words "vanity etc." were lost and the passage should be reconstructed in that sense.

<column-break/>

Who does not see that these ideas are far-fetched, and there is no need for such circuitous reasoning? Nor do I subscribe to the learned *Thomasius*, who (*Treasury of Lacrozian Epistles, Vol. I, p. 341*) thought the Epicureans were being touched upon here. I would hardly think he wished to include them under the name of "barbarians," for he usually speaks of them more mildly. As that word is used most widely, and pertains peculiarly to the Jews and Christians, it should be taken here in that broad sense. *Led headlong* <note>original: "Exetrachēlisen"</note> is a term taken from the wrestling school. The word was excellently illustrated by *Perizonius on Aelian's Varia Historia XII, 58* and *V. D. Miscellaneous Observations Vol. III, p. 242*. From there, it means in any way to *cast someone down headlong, to ruin them.* "To lead youth headlong" <note>original: "ektrachēlizein tēn neotēta"</note>—*Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 13. A.; Alciphron III, 40; Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book IV, p. 173. D.: "they led the multitudes and the common people headlong."* Compare also *Wetstein on the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. IV, 13*, though that passage does not belong here. *Meermann*, with the order of letters disturbed, wrote "exetrachilēsen." Just now I have restored "hou" <note>of which</note> on the faith of the *Leipzig* manuscript; previously it was read as "hoi" <note>who</note>.

3. *And to be able etc.*] In the *Leipzig* manuscript it is "tōn," which leads us to the tracks of the true reading. By deleting "kai" <note>and</note>, which seems to have been born from the "s" of the word "legontes" <note>saying</note>, and changing "tōn" to "tō," I think it should be read: *saying, that by being able to perceive* (understand "someone") *even while being occupied with other things, they allow themselves to use the irrational part* (understand "themselves"). <small>REISKE.</small> "Tōn" was also in—

# On Abstinence, Book I.

In this manner, they say, foods do not defile us at all: just as the sea is not polluted by filthy currents. For we have mastery over all things, just as the sea is superior to all liquids. But if the sea were to close its mouth so as not to admit those things which flow into it, it would indeed be great in itself, but in relation to the world it would be considered small, as it would be unable to contain filth. But where there is an abyss of power <margin>10</margin>, they receive all things and are defiled by nothing. Deceiving themselves with such arguments, they acted in accordance <margin>11</margin> with the delusions by which they were deceived; instead of freedom, they plunged themselves into the abyss of misery and were drowned. This is what made some of the Cynics <margin>12</margin> "all-craving" <note>original: *pantorektas*, meaning those who follow every appetite</note>, as they clung to the cause of their sins, which we are accustomed to call "indifferent" <term>indifferent: *adiaphoron*, a Stoic term for things that are neither morally good nor evil, such as food or wealth</term>.

§ 43. But a man who is cautious and suspicious of the enchantments of nature—

<column-break/>

and by that [filth] it is oppressed and overcome, yet the whirlpool <note>or deep water</note> is not stained. Thus, eating overcomes and oppresses the meager; but for those in whom there is a whirlpool and an immense breadth of liberty, all things are taken in as nourishment and bring no stain. Those men, therefore, deceiving themselves with such follies, even acted according to their errors: and having thrust themselves from liberty into the whirlpool and depth of unhappiness, they were suffocated. This also was what led some of the Cynics to desire and devour all things, when they applied their minds to the cause of errors, that which we have been accustomed to call "indifferent."

§ 43. But a cautious man, who holds the deceptions of nature in suspicion—

<note>Critical Commentary by the Editors</note>

As *Abreschius* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, 18th-century philologist</note> rightly noted. It is well known how widely the use of this word extends.

8. **And is enslaved.**] The French translator noted in the margin "is muddied" <note>original: *tholoutai*</note>. But "is enslaved" <note>original: *douloutai*</note> is read correctly enough, as it seems to me. —VALENTI. Either "is muddied" must be read, or "is shown" is a corruption. —REISKE. *Valenti*, however, had placed "is muddied" in the text. "Muddy water" is said a thousand times. The reading "muddied" could be confirmed by a beautiful passage suited to our subject from *Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 33, 5*: "Just as winter rivers muddy the safety of works and order, so also the soul is unsettled by the immoderation of passions," etc. Yet I hardly dare to condemn the graceful metaphor of "being enslaved," especially since that word preceded it.

9. **Overcomes those who possess little.**] Of the little (namely, of filth or defilements) they do not get the better; *eating a few kinds of food cannot overcome impurities.* That is, when we shrink from many kinds of food but stop within a few, then we cannot help but contract filth from the eating of those few kinds. —REISKE.

10. **They receive all things.**] In the *Florence* and *Leyden* editions, it was incorrectly written "they were receiving." For "of power," *Abreschius* preferred "extraordinary."

11. **By which they deceived.**] Namely, themselves, which preceded. A learned man preferred "they were deceived" or "they suffered," which would suit the verb "they acted." In the *Florence* and *Leyden* editions, it was "deception." Meermann has "they had been deceived." He meant "they deceived themselves," which I think is true.

12. **Made them all-craving, as they clung etc.**] "Clinging to the cause" —REISKE. I was reshaping it to: "as the causes of their errors were persistently clinging to them." This is the Greek *prosplékesthai*, a word the lexicons are ignorant of, but which *Gataker* <note>Thomas Gataker, English scholar</note> defends with suitable authority in his notes on *Marcus Aurelius, Book 10, 7*. But you will not find the word "all-craving" <note>original: *pantorektēs*</note> in those authors, though it is used by others like *Anacreon, Ode 10, 11*.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the relationship between the soul and the body, specifically focusing on how the soul must govern the body's irrational impulses to maintain temperance.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

Whoever observes the nature of the body and understands that it has been fitted to the powers of the soul like an instrument, is not ignorant that its harmony is such that if it is struck from without, and that very stroke is perceived, the emotions will resonate whether we wish it or not. For perception is nothing other than the sound itself. But the soul cannot resonate unless it has been turned entirely toward the sound, and has directed its presiding eye toward it. For since the irrational faculty is by itself unreflecting, and is in no way able to judge to what extent, or how, or from where, or toward whom it acts, but wherever it leans it is very much like horses without a charioteer, it is impossible for it to manage anything properly with external things, or to know the occasion and measure of nourishment, unless the eye of the charioteer is present, who mo- <note>The text breaks mid-word; "mo-" likely continues as "moves" or "moderates" on the next page.</note>

<column-break/>

<note>original: Greek</note>
...of [perception], having examined the nature of the body, and knowing how it has been joined like an instrument to the powers of the soul, he knows that the passion is ready to speak, <gloss>1</gloss> whether we wish it or not, when the body is struck by things from without, and the stroke arrives at the point of perception. For perception happened to be the "speaking"; but it is not possible for the soul to speak unless it is turned entirely <gloss>2</gloss> toward the sound, and shifts its presiding eye toward this. In general, since the irrational part has no power to judge the "how much," and "how," and "from where," and "toward whom," being by itself unobservant, wherever it might lean, <gloss>3</gloss> it is like horses without a charioteer; it is impossible to manage anything fittingly toward <gloss>4</gloss> external things, or to know the timing and measures of food, unless the <gloss>5</gloss> charioteer...

However, a little before, the Bodleian reads very poorly <note>original: "hermosan"</note> instead of <note>original: "etoimon"</note> [ready].

<gloss>2. Toward the sound.]</gloss> Perhaps "toward the stroke." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>

# PORPHYRY

...of a presiding eye standing over it, which regulates the movements and acts as a charioteer to that which is, in itself, blind unreason. But he who removes the oversight of reason from the irrational faculty, and permits it to be carried along according to its own nature—whatever sort of man he may be—by allowing desire to proceed as far as it wishes in its own movements, and likewise with anger: such a man would surely make the "virtuous man" <note>Greek: *to spoudaion*</note> and his rational deeds appear to us as something unrestrained by the presiding reason during the activities of the irrational soul.

->§ 44.<-

...should moderate and rule the motions of that which is blind of itself. Truly, he who takes away the presidency of reason from the irrational faculty, and allows it to proceed by its own nature: whatever kind of man he is, who so indulges both desire and wrath that they may advance as far as they wish in their motions: he will surely present himself to us as an excellent example of virtue, and show his deeds to be endowed with reason, once he has withdrawn himself from the moderation of presiding reason in the operations of the irrational faculty. <note>The translator here is using heavy irony to show that a man without reason is the opposite of virtuous.</note>

->§ 44.<-

**Notes on the Text:**

**Line 5.** *Golden Verses:* which are circulated under the name of *Pythagoras*, verse 69:
"Establish as charioteer the best Mind from above." <note>Original Greek: Ἡνίοχον γνώμην στήσας καθύπερθεν ἀρίστην.</note>
*Hierocles* in his commentary on the *Golden Verses*, p. 298: "As a charioteer, still touching and overseeing the body; but the erotic <note>unless you prefer 'supervisory'</note> eye is stationed above the charioteer." And more is found there by R. W. (in that passage I defend the reading "contemplative eye" <note>Latin: *theoretikon omma*</note>, as it was previously read). *Heraclides Ponticus* also explained this from Plato; see him in *Gale’s* "Mythological, Physical, and Ethical Works," p. 432. I omit many others.

**Line 6. Allowing as far as, etc.** *Reiske* preferred the infinitive "to allow." <note>original: *synchōrēsai*</note>. Presently, they translate *thymon* as "wrath," and certainly "desire" <note>epithymia</note> and "anger" <note>orgē</note> are joined even below in § 44. The use of the word is very well known, as is the way they distinguish between *thymos* (spiritedness/anger) and *orgē* (rage), which you may see joined a hundred times. I would believe, however, that these words of Porphyry are to be explained from Platonic doctrine, which attributed two parts to the soul: the **Rational** <note>logikon</note>, which was believed to reside in the head, and the **Irrational** <note>alogon</note>. They further divided the **Irrational** into the **Spirited** <note>thymikon</note>, located in the heart, and the **Appetitive** <note>epithymētikon</note>, which has its seat in the diaphragm. This is a well-known matter from *Plutarch's* "Opinions of the Philosophers," IV, 4; *Heraclides Ponticus* in *Gale*, and others. Hence, "Mind" <note>Nous</note> and "Soul" <note>psychē</note> are distinguished by our Author and others, though in such a way that you may doubt whether they mean two distinct natures or two 

<column-break/>

faculties of a single nature. Distinguished men like *C. Vitringa* (Observations, Book III, ch. 4) and others are accustomed to use this distinction to illustrate *Paul* in 1 Thessalonians 5:22 <note>"May your whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless..."</note>. That learned man <note>Latin: *V. D.* for Vir Doctus</note> in his notes on *Nemesius's* "On the Nature of Man," p. 2, thinks this was the doctrine of the early Christians—to attribute spirit and soul to man—but that they let it go in order to more surely crush the error of the Apollinarians <note>A 4th-century heresy regarding the nature of Christ's soul</note>. Nor does that supreme man *H. D. Gaubius*, the "Hippocrates of Leiden," seem to me to wander far from this in his second Oration on the "Government of the Mind": that there are two principles of acting in the soul, and these are very different from each other; or that there are two parts, one participating in reason, the other devoid of it. The unlearned ought not to quibble at these things, but first weigh what the ancient Christians and Philosophers intended.

**Line 7. Will make the virtuous man.** I do not think "the man" <note>ton</note> should be substituted for "the thing" <note>to</note>, which the previous translator did; but I judge that instead of "unrestrained" <note>akathekton</note> we should read "easily restrained" <note>eukathekton</note>. **VALENTIUS:** I approve of "the man" <note>ton</note>. Truly, he will present the good man to us in an excellent way, and the institutions proceeding from him as remarkably consistent with reason, if he presents one whose brutish principle does not allow its affections to be governed by reason. **REISKE:** The learned *Abresch* preferred: "Well indeed will he [show] us the virtuous man... [who is] unrestrained by the presiding [reason]."

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the governance of the soul, specifically contrasting the virtuous man with the common person in their approach to physical desires and food.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

§ 44. For in this regard the honorable and upright man is seen to differ from the wicked: the former everywhere has **reason** <note>original: "rationem" / "logon"</note> standing by him to restrain and govern the faculty that lacks reason. The latter acts without reason, neglecting it in whatever he does. Therefore, the latter is called ill-advised and irrational, being dragged along by his irrational faculty. The former, by contrast, is well-advised and rational, one who masters every reckless appetite. Indeed, the fact that most people err in speech, action, desire, and anger—while the good act rightly—stems from this: the former have permitted the "child" <note>The "child" represents the impulsive, unthinking part of the human soul.</note> within them to do whatever it wishes on its own; the good have handed the leadership to the **tutor** <note>original: "paedagogo". In antiquity, a pedagogue was a guardian who supervised a child's conduct.</note> and govern their actions according to his precepts. From this it follows that both in taking food and in other bodily works—

<column-break/>

§ 44. And yet, in this way the virtuous man appears to differ from the base man: the one has reason present everywhere, commanding and driving the irrational part like a charioteer. The other, however, neglects to act with reason and acts without it in whatever he does. Wherefore the one is called irrational and carried away by unreason; the other is called rational, and a master over everything irrational. Thus, this tendency to err occurs in the majority of people in word, deed, desire, and anger; conversely, the virtuous succeed because the former allowed the child to do what it wants by itself, while the latter gave control to the tutor, and with him they govern their own affairs. So it is also in the matter of food, and in other things pertaining to the—

---

<margin>
Doing [these things] by reason, namely the things themselves. If you adopt the masculine "the" <note>original: "ton"</note>, the sense seems to stand well. However, all the manuscripts agree on the neuter "the" <note>original: "to"</note>, and it can be explained in this way: "he will do the virtuous thing beautifully" (or "well"). "To do well" is a known formula for those praising a matter, found in Demosthenes and others. I remember this has been shown more than once by philologists regarding the New Testament. However, these things are to be taken ironically, as "well" <note>original: "kalos"</note> is often used in irony. "The virtuous" <note>original: "to spoudaion"</note> denotes any excellent thing worthy of our study. See Perizonius on Aelian, *Varia Historia* II, 13.
</margin>

1. *But the other [acts] many things... etc.*] Perhaps: "the other acts many things, yielding (that is, permitting) to the irrational part, and with this he does what he does." *The other man, the wicked one, does many things, having made room for recklessness, or, since he has given himself over to the power of blind and dull recklessness, driven by which he performs all his affairs.* <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar.</note>. You could also read: "the other acts many things, neglecting reason, and with that (namely the irrational part) he does what he does," as I see <term>Gataker</term> <note>Thomas Gataker, an English critic and theologian.</note> already wished on *Marcus Aurelius IX, 3*. Or rather: "the other, neglecting to leave many things to be done by the rational part."

<column-break/>

2. *To err therefore [because of] this.*] <term>Reiske</term> conjectured "therefore *because of* this." Moreover, the word "and" <note>original: "kai"</note> before "angers" was not in the <term>Lipsius</term> manuscript. <gloss>Compare to Longinus page 369: "therefore because of this," etc.</gloss>

3. *They allowed the child, etc.*] We have provided an illustration of this phrasing in the preceding sections. It was noted in the <term>Lipsius</term> and <term>Meerman</term> manuscripts: <insert>Note that he calls the irrational power of the soul a "child."</insert>

<summary>This page discusses the Stoic and Platonic concept of the soul, comparing the irrational impulses to a child and the guiding reason to a tutor or charioteer. It argues that self-control in diet and behavior stems from submitting the "child" to the "tutor" of reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s philosophical argument regarding the soul's control over the body, specifically focusing on the metaphor of the charioteer and the necessity of abstinence from meat and bodily pleasures.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

In the activities or enjoyments of the body, when the charioteer <note>The "charioteer" is a Platonic metaphor for the rational mind or intellect (Logos) governing the soul.</note> is present, he defines what is proportionate and timely. But when he is absent and—as some say—occupied with his own affairs, if he keeps our attention with him, he does not allow the irrational part of the soul to be affected by passion or to act at all. However, if he allows this attention to remain with the "child" <note>The "child" refers to the lower, irrational part of the soul that requires constant supervision.</note> without his guidance, he destroys the man, who is then dragged away by <margin>4</margin> the folly of the irrational.

§ 45. Therefore, for serious men, abstinence from both meats and the pleasures and actions of the body is more appropriate than engagement with them. For in touching bodily things, one must descend from one's own character to the training of the irrational element within us. This is even more necessary regarding food, for the irrational part is not capable of calculating what will result from it. By its very nature, the irrational is unable to recognize what is not immediately present. If it were possible to be as free from foods as we are from visible objects when they are removed (for it is possible to be occupied with other things by putting to <margin>1</margin> sleep...

<column-break/>

...in the operations or functions, let the present charioteer prescribe the measure and the opportunity. But when he is absent and, as some say, vacant in his own thoughts, if he has held our attention with him, he permits the irrational faculty neither to be moved nor to work anything at all. But if he should allow our attention to be present with the "child" without himself, he loses the man, since he is dragged headlong by irrational madness.

§ 45. Wherefore it is fitting for upright men that, regarding the pleasures and actions which exist through the body, they should abstain from foods more than from touch. This is because, although while we touch bodily things it is necessary to descend from our own habits to instruct the irrational faculty which is in us, the same must be done even more in the taking of food. For the irrational part cannot consider what will happen because of them; it is of such a nature that it perceives absent things in no way at all. For if we could be as free from nourishments as we are from things exposed to the sight when they are withdrawn—since, when the images of those things are put to sleep...

---

<margin>4. *The folly of the irrational.*] I confidently restore the reading "of the irrational" (*tou alogou*), whereas previously it was read as "of the reason" (*tou logou*). Someone might perhaps want "ignorance of the reason," as these words are swapped a hundred times; but since he says below "the irrational is unable to recognize what is absent," and the *Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts* as well as the translator agree on "irrational," I do not doubt this came from our pen. Next, do not wonder that "more" (*mallon*) is joined with a comparative; the Greeks do this a hundred times: see *Wetsten* on Paul's Epistle to the Philippians 1:23, and the Latins do no differently. "More clearer" and similar things, on which see the learned men on *Justin, Book III, chapter 2.* Then, in the phrase "and of those through the body," the *Leipzig manuscript* had wrongly omitted "and." Then also "of enjoyment" and "of touch," both erroneously.</margin>

<margin>1. *Putting to sleep from them.*] So it was read, but I have restored "putting to sleep" (*koimisanta*). The matter itself, as well as the authority of the Translator and the *Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts*, absolutely demands it.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

->K 3<-

It might be permissible for others to direct their minds elsewhere: it could happen conveniently enough that once we had indulged the necessity of our mortal nature for a little while, we might immediately emerge free. But since a delay of time is drawn out while food is both cooked <note>original: "concoquitur"; referring to the ancient medical belief that digestion was a form of internal cooking</note> and distributed through the body, and since even before that, assistance is sought from sleep and rest and other forms of leisure—and after certain effects from the digestive temperament and the secretion of waste are completed—it is necessary that a "pedagogue" <note>term: pedagogue (Greek: paidagogos). Originally a slave who supervised a child's conduct; here used metaphorically for Reason governing the body's needs.</note> be present. This guide, choosing for himself things that are light and offer no hindrance, grants those to nature. For since he foresees what is to come, and how great a hindrance it would be if he were to yield to desires, he judges it unfair that for the sake of a brief pleasure—perceived only in the act of swallowing while we take in food—he should overwhelm us with such a heavy burden.

§ 46. Not without reason, therefore, does logic [cast out] that which is excessive and superfluous...

<column-break/>

...[having lulled to sleep the fantasies arising from them] it would have been moderate, having yielded to the <gloss>2</gloss> necessity of mortal nature for a short time, to be immediately set free. But since there is a need for a lingering of time, and for digestion, and for distribution, <gloss>3</gloss> and for the cooperation with these things that comes from sleep and quiet and other idleness—and after these things, for the specific temperament resulting from the distribution and the passage of waste—it is necessary for the pedagogue to be present. He, having selected for himself the light and unhindered things, <gloss>4</gloss> will permit these to nature, foreseeing the future and <gloss>5</gloss> how great the hindrance would be. If he were to yield to the desires, he would introduce to us a burden <gloss>6</gloss> not easy to carry for the sake of a little pleasure, which [men] <gloss>7</gloss> perceive in the act of receiving food into the throat for swallowing.

§ 46. Not without reason, then, does reason [or logic] secrete the much and the superfluous...

---

<margin>...they command. With the same elegance, Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Book IX, p. 596) uses the phrase *to lull the sedition to sleep*. Lucian in *The Tragic Jupiter* uses *to carry away anger*; Aeschylus in *Eumenides* (line 835) says *to lull the rage to sleep*. This is said without observing the distinction that Critics make between these words. I omit more examples, especially the elegances of the poets. A little before, the Meermann manuscript has *epilogikon* instead of *epilogistikon* <note>referring to "logical" vs "calculating"</note>.</margin>

<margin>2. *Necessity of nature.*] Above, he calls it the *necessity of generation* <note>or "becoming"</note>. See the note at § 41.</margin>

<margin>3. *And for the [cooperation] with these.*] Reiske suggests either *toward this* or *toward these*. To me, it seemed it should read *before*, and I see this is approved by the Meermann manuscript.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>4. *Will permit these.*] Perhaps it should be *the other things* (that is, *ta alla*) *he will permit*. Reiske. The Lipsian and Meermann manuscripts have *will permit*, but incorrectly.</margin>

<margin>5. *How great the hindrance [if he] yields.*] For *how great*, understand *it will be for himself*, or *for reason*. Reiske.</margin>

<margin>6. *Not easy to carry.*] The Florentine manuscript had *being well and beautiful*, which Fogerolles indeed followed, though he corrected it in the margin. The word itself is elegant; concerning it, see Hesychius and what the interpreters have noted regarding him.</margin>

<margin>7. *They perceive.*] Namely, *men*. Or rather, *the desires*. However, he ought to have said *we perceive*, because he placed *to us* before it. Reiske.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

->**On Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

Having judged [these matters], he restricts what is necessary to a small amount. He does this so that, by not providing [excess], he might not <gloss>1</gloss> have troubles <note>original: "pragmata" - meaning business or bothersome affairs</note> due to needing more; nor by making things elegant <note>referring to a lavish table</note>, <gloss>2</gloss> would he need more servants; nor by eating would he be seized by more pleasures; nor by being overfilled would he be filled with much laziness; nor by being stuffed with a heavier burden <gloss>3</gloss> would he become sleepy; nor by being filled with things that fatten the body, would he make the bond <note>the body as the "prison" or "bond" of the soul</note> stronger, but himself more sluggish and weaker for his own proper duties. Let some man, therefore, <gloss>4</gloss> show us—one who strives as much as possible to live according to the intellect, and to be undistracted by the passions of the body—how a diet of meat is easier to obtain...

<column-break/>

...excluding [excess], he contracts that which is necessary into a small and narrow space: lest either by supplying [too much] he undergoes troubles while requiring more; or by seasoning sumptuous meals he requires more people to serve them; or by eating he is affected by more pleasures; or by saturating himself he is filled with much idleness; or by stuffing himself with a heavier pack he falls into sleepiness; or by filling himself with things that fatten the body, he renders the bond stronger and himself more sluggish and weaker for performing his own duties. Let someone show us, therefore, who studies to lead a life according to the intellect as much as possible, and desires to be disturbed and distracted as little as possible by the affections of the body: [whether] a meat-based...

---

<column-break/>

1. *To have troubles.*] *Pragmata* are *business affairs, troubles*. Therefore, "to have pragmata" is *to be involved in troubles or troublesome business*; just as "to provide pragmata" means *to cause trouble for someone*: "to provide labors" is said in *Matthew 26:10*. Hence "to have" and "to provide" troubles are elegantly joined in *Alciphron: Book III, Letter 30*, where *Bergler* notes: Epicurus in *Diogenes Laertius p. 795* says: "That which is blessed and immortal neither has troubles itself, nor provides them to another." Instead of "due to the [fact]," some editions incorrectly had "due to this."

2. *Nor by making things elegant.*] The learned *Abresch* in *Dilucidations on Thucydides p. 381* contends we should read "elegant" [euprepē]. This is also preferred by the *Leipzig manuscript* and *Reiske* following it. These words could very easily be confused, as happens very often. In *Diodorus Siculus I, 45*, instead of "elegant temples," some manuscripts incorrectly have "fitting." In *Euripides' Suppliants*, instead of "elegant," *Markland* wanted "seemly." Likewise in *Lucian's Dialogues p. 84*, the illustrious *Hemsterhuis* illustrates the power of this word excellently. However, "elegant" things are called *splendid, magnificent*, just as an "elegant table" is a *table furnished with magnificent and sumptuous feasts*, as already noted by *H. Stephanus in the Thesaurus*.

<column-break/>

3. *Being filled.*] The *Bodleian manuscript* has "having been filled." The *Leipzig* has "being filled" [without the 'm']. There is often variation in this word, for sometimes it is written *empíplasthai*, sometimes *empímplasthai*. The same happens with other words where the letter M is sometimes added, sometimes not. Read *D'Orville's Elegancies on Chariton, Book V, ch. 2*. Our author loves to add that letter to the word.

4. *Some man, striving etc.*] Thus we have punctuated this for the first time. So does the translator, and also the *Leipzig manuscript*, which however incorrectly gave "who" [hos] for "as" [hōs]. On the faith of the same manuscript, I have restored "undistracted" [aperispastos], for which previously was read "unstable" [aperistaton], but which *Foggerolles* had already corrected in the margin. *Meerman* wanted the same, giving "uncircumstanced." The word in...

<meta>catchword: ni- (likely continuing "nisi" or a similar Latin term on the next page)</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

...the eating of all fruits and vegetables is either more abundantly available or more cheaply prepared; it brings less pleasure and is lighter in concoction <note>The ancient physiological process of "cooking" or ripening food within the stomach via heat</note> and digestion. It irritates the desires less, and contributes less to the passions and the physical strength of the body than a diet sought from inanimate things <note>original: "inanimatis," referring here to plants/fruits which lack a "sensitive soul" in Neoplatonic thought</note> and those which require no labor from cooks.

§ 47. But if neither a physician, nor a philosopher, nor a trainer <note>original: "alipta," a specialist in a gymnasium who oiled and trained athletes</note>, nor—

<column-break/>

—meat-eating <note>original: "ἡ κρεωφαγία"</note> [is compared to] dishes made from tree-fruits and vegetables, the preparation of the latter is cheaper than that of inanimate things <note>The commentator Reiske suggests this should perhaps read "animate things" (meat) to make sense of the comparison</note>, and they generally do not require cooks. It is, in itself, unpleasant when compared to the inanimate diet, but lighter in digestion than the other, and in the distributions <note>The process of nutrients being sent from the stomach to the rest of the body</note> to the body, it is faster than the distribution from vegetables. It excites the desires less and contributes less to the thickness <note>or "passion"</note> and strength of the body than the inanimate diet.

§ 47. But if neither any of the physicians, nor of the philosophers, nor a trainer—

---

<margin>
*Wetstein* illustrates this: on 1 Corinthians 7:35.
</margin>

5. **Meat-eating** ----.] *Florence, Lipsius, &amp; Meerman manuscripts:* "meat-eatings" (plural). We have seen these terms vary frequently.
§ 15. **Tree-fruits** <note>original: "’Ακρόδρυα"</note> properly refers to those covered with a harder shell (nuts), but from there, all fruits of trees are generally so named. See *Bodaeus à Stapel* on Theophrastus's *History of Plants*, Book III, chapters 12 &amp; 15; and this usage is frequent in *Diodorus Siculus*, as noted by *Wesseling* on Book V, chapter 43.

6. **And the preparation is cheaper etc.**] *Jerome*, *Against Jovinian*, Book II, 10: *“The preparation of vegetables, fruits, and legumes is both easier and does not require the art and expense of cooks; it sustains the human body without care, and when taken moderately (since that which has no stimulants for the throat is not greedily devoured), it is concocted with a lighter digestion.”*

7. **Of the inanimate.**] Perhaps it should be "of the inanimate, fire, and cooks." This is a comparison and adaptation of the eating of foods sought from inanimate things, which need neither fire nor cooks. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar</note>.

8. **In itself compared.**] Perhaps "unpleasant both in itself and when compared." Both viewed on its own and compared with. <term>REISKE</term>. It seems it should read "compared to the *animate*" <note>meat</note>, and at the end "than the *animate* diet." This was pleasing to *Abresch*, a distinguished man,

<column-break/>

unless in this place you prefer "unpleasant." I shall speak of this immediately.

9. **And in the distributions.**] *Valentin* had given "and in the distributions" against the evidence of all others. See on § 15. However, *Valentin &amp; Lipsius* correctly have "those into the body," for which the *Florence &amp; Leiden* manuscripts had "of that into the body."

10. **Faster.**] Thus *Valentin* is correct, from whom *Lipsius* does not differ. *Meerman* gives "faster than that of vegetables." In the *Florence &amp; Leiden* manuscripts, it was "faster." Soon after, *Reiske* preferred "into thickness" <note>original: "πάχος"</note> referring to the *thickness and mass of the flesh*, because a little later he calls it the "thickness of the bond" <note>referring to the body as a bond to the soul</note>. But in the previous sections, he had called them "the passions of the body."

11. **Of the inanimate diet.**] Either it must be read as "animate diet," and a little before "compared to the animate." For as these are now read, they do not provide a suitable sense. They could easily have been confused, for since the ancients wrote *ampsychos* for *empsychos* <note>living/animate</note>, it happened that one occasionally took the place of the other. See *D’Orville* on *Chariton* VIII, 1. Or perhaps a little before, "unpleasant" for "unpleasant." *Let someone show me how meat-eating is joined with pleasure or sweetness if it is contended against an inanimate diet, and how that is lighter... contributing [less] than the inanimate diet.* The word "but" is then repeated, as is often the case among the Greeks.

# PORPHYRY

...and as no <gloss>1</gloss> ordinary person <note>original: ἰδιώτης / idiotes; referring to one who lives a common life without philosophical discipline</note> has ever dared to say: why do we not willingly withdraw ourselves from this bodily burden? Why do we not, by such <gloss>2</gloss> withdrawal from many things <note>Reiske suggests this refers to the specific list of distractions that follows</note>, set ourselves free? For it is not from one thing, but from ten thousand, that a person is delivered who accustoms himself to be satisfied with the very least. He is freed from an abundance of wealth, from the service of many slaves, from a multitude of furnishings, from a state of sleepiness, from the intensity and frequency of diseases, from the need for physicians, from the incitements to lust, from thicker vapors <note>referring to the "heavy" humors or breaths thought to arise from digesting meat</note>, from a flood of waste products, from the <gloss>3</gloss> thickness of the bond <note>the "bond" is the physical body; see section 38</note>, and from that physical strength which rouses one to external actions—in short, from an <gloss>4</gloss> Iliad of evils <note>a proverbial expression for a vast series of disasters, referencing the woes of the Trojan War</note>. From all these, a soulless <note>i.e., vegetable-based, lacking a "nephesh" or animal soul</note>, simple, and easily procured diet delivers us, providing peace to the <gloss>5</gloss> reasoning power that provides for our salvation. For <gloss>6</gloss> Diogenes says that thieves and enemies do not come from those who eat barley-cakes, but from those—

<column-break/>

—who eat meat. <note>The text breaks mid-word "car-", completed as "carnivoris" or "carnibus" (meat-eaters) in the following page.</note>

***

<margin>
1. **Ordinary person.** "Idiotes" in passages of this kind refers to those men who lead a common life and do not organize it according to any particular system to care for their health. See: *Casaubon on Athenaeus, II, 8.*

2. **Withdrawal from many things.** Perhaps "from those many things" which he immediately enumerates. —REISKE.

3. **Thickness of the bond.** See section 38.

4. **Iliad of evils.** *Diodorus Siculus in the Eclogues, page 534:* "All Sicily was possessed by confusion and an Iliad of evils." See also *Wesseling* there. In Latin, *Ilias malorum*. *Cicero, Letters to Atticus, VIII, 2:* "An Iliad of evils threatens." Compare with the proverb collectors.

5. **Provides for our salvation.** The reading "to the reasoning power living for salvation" was in the *Leipzig* manuscript. "Living" (zōnti) likely arose from the following word "providing" (ekporizonti).

6. **Diogenes says from the barley-eaters.** *Jerome, Against Jovinian, Book II:* "Diogenes asserts that tyrants and the overthrows of cities, and wars—whether foreign or civil—are stirred up not for a simple diet of vegetables and fruits, but for meats and the delicacies of feasts." Regarding how cheap a kind of food he himself was content with, see *Aelian, Varia Historia, XIII, 26*, where *Kuhn* thought the word "mazan" (barley-cake) had fallen out because of this passage in our author. *Julian* also mentions this saying, though in a slightly different way, in *Oration VI, page 198 D.*
</margin>

<summary>Porphyry argues that a simple, meatless diet liberates the philosopher from physical ailments, social burdens, and mental distractions, citing Diogenes the Cynic to claim that social strife arises from luxury rather than simple living.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from Book I of Porphyry's "On Abstinence from Animal Food," specifically focusing on how a simple diet aids the intellectual life.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

those who eat meat become slanderers and tyrants. Now, once the cause of our many needs is removed, and the great quantity of things taken into the body is withdrawn, and the heaviness of those things being digested is lightened, it follows that the eye <note>The "eye of the soul," a common Platonic metaphor for the intellect.</note> becomes free, escaping tranquil from the waves and the corporeal smoke.

§ 48. This is a matter that requires neither proof nor demonstration, because of the evidence inherent in the thing itself. Hence, not only those who strive to live according to the intellect, and who establish such a life as their goal, judge this abstinence to be necessary for them to achieve that end; but also every philosopher, I believe, judging that frugality is suitable for conducting a civic life, would more highly approve of that life which is content with few—

<column-break/>

—slanderers and tyrants come from the meat-eaters. But when the cause of needing many things is removed, and the multitude of things introduced into the body is taken away, and the weight of those things being distributed is lightened, the eye becomes free, anchored outside the smoke and the wave of the body.

§ 48. And this needs neither reminder nor proof, because of the clarity present therein. Wherefore not only those who have been eager to live according to the intellect, and have set the life according to it as their goal, see the abstinence from these things as necessary toward that goal, but also almost every philosopher, I think, preferring simplicity <note>original: εὐτέλειαν (euteleian), meaning cheapness or frugality.</note> over extravagance, would rather accept the man who is satisfied with little, than the one—

---

<column-break/>

<margin>For Diogenes says that tyrants do not come from those who eat barley-cakes, but from those who dine sumptuously. Not without cause does *Homer* call just men "milk-eaters" <note>original: γαλακτοφάγους (galaktophagous)</note>, as *Clement of Alexandria* notes in *The Instructor, Book I, p. 98. D.* Compare *Didymus on the Iliad, IV, 6.*</margin>

<margin>7. *The cause of needing being removed.*] Exactly as this mode of living brings about "needing nothing" in *Philostratus, VIII, 12.* see there; *Olearius.* Presently he calls the nourishment, food, and drink forced into the body "things introduced" <note>original: εἰσαγόμενα (eisagomena)</note>, as is customary. *Hierocles* in *The Golden Verses, p. 174:* "one must set a measure for the filling of things introduced." Wherein R. W. was not forgetful of our author. *Meermann* has "the [cause] of the many."</margin>

<margin>8. *Being taken away — being lightened.*] In place of "being taken away" (plural), the French translator substituted "being taken away" (singular). I do not know why, for "of us" ought to be understood, to which the plural refers. VALENTINUS. The *French translator* had also substituted "being lightened" (singular). *Reiske* rightly approves of both. However, the Greek manuscripts agree in the common reading.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>9. *The eye becomes free, etc.*] *Fogerolles* preferred "the body" <note>original: σῶμα (soma)</note>. Wrongly. Plato and the Platonists often mention the "eye of the soul." *Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras, 16:* "He purified the soul, and redirected toward the intelligible that divine eye, which is better to be saved, according to Plato, than ten thousand fleshly eyes." And *Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor, Book II, p. 139. C.* not differently than in this place, the abundance of food and luxury are said to "hold down the discerning eye of the soul." *The same, p. 186. C.* Moreover, he speaks elegantly of "smoke and wave." <meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the virtues of a simple diet, specifically citing the unexpected support of the Epicureans for frugal living.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...content with little, rather than that which requires much. Furthermore (and this might seem incredible to most people), we find that those who believe pleasure to be the goal of philosophy <note>Porphyry is referring to the Epicureans, who are often misunderstood as gluttons, but here he defends their actual practice of moderation.</note> actually assert and value this principle. For most of the Epicureans, beginning with their founder himself, appear to have been satisfied with a simple barley cake and fruits; they have filled their writings with descriptions of how little Nature truly requires, demonstrating that her necessary needs are sufficiently healed by a thin and easily obtainable diet.

§ 49. For he says, "The wealth of Nature is limited and easy to procure..." <note>A famous quote from Epicurus's *Principal Doctrines*.</note>

<column-break/>

...although it may seem common, it is nonetheless not better. It appears Porphyry gave it this way, comparing **frugality** with **extravagance**, and would rather approve of a life lived with little and satisfied with little, than one requiring more. Certainly, in the *Leipzig* manuscript, instead of "a life with little," it reads "a life in words." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske was a 18th-century German scholar known for his editions of Greek texts.</note> The word "before" was also in the oldest edition and the *Meermann* manuscript, and I have therefore restored it to its proper place.

2. **Those saying this etc.**] Perhaps: "We find those very people saying and valuing this who otherwise state and embrace the exact opposite." <term>REISKE</term>

3. **Those who think pleasure is the goal etc.**] He means Epicurus and those who followed him. They established **Pleasure** as the highest good, which for them was "cheerfulness" and "freedom from disturbance"—neither suffering in the body nor being troubled in the soul. Not a bad thing in itself, but they used the word poorly, since in common usage it signified a different kind of pleasure, as is well known. See, however, *Perizonius on Aelian's Varia Historia IV, 13 and Book IX, ch. 12.* *Reiske* preferred the reading "those who, by Zeus, think pleasure is the goal." In earlier editions, "those who philosophized" was written as "those who played the sophist."

4. **Satisfied with barley cake and fruits.**] Epicurus himself used to say that he was ready to compete with Jupiter for happiness, provided he had "barley cake and water." See *Aelian, Varia Historia IV, 13* and *Julian, Oration VI, p. 195 B*: "not even a barley cake, of which Epicurus says that if he has plenty, he does not fall behind the gods in terms of happiness." *Jerome* refers to our author in *Against Jovinian II, 11*: "**And what is wonderful, Epicurus, the defender of pleasure, filled all his books with vegetables and fruits, and says we must live on cheap foods.**" I am not surprised. For in this way, the body and mind can best be kept to their duty, and thus "freedom from disturbance" <note>original: *ataraxia*</note> could be promoted. Recently, the *Meermann* manuscript mistakenly gave "citizens" instead of "thin/simple."

1. **For he says.**] The *Leipzig* manuscript does not do badly with "He says." Epicurus, I suppose, whose saying this is, taken from his *Principal Doctrines*. A little later, however, it has "They say," in which it deviated from consistency. <term>REISKE</term> Excellent. Such is that saying of Epicurus...

# On Abstinence, Book I.

-> L 2 <-

...arise from empty opinions; these are infinite and of such a kind that they can only be satisfied with great difficulty. For those things which are easily supplied—having a simple nature of both fluids and solids—are accustomed to well and abundantly remove all distress of the body arising from want. All other things, however, which fall into luxury, are said to involve a desire that is not necessary, nor of the kind that arises from some necessary pain. Instead, such desires arise either from a mere annoyance <gloss>felt from the absence of the thing</gloss>, or entirely from the pleasure of its presence, or from empty and false opinions. None of these relate to a natural deficiency which, if not satisfied, would be able to dissolve our constitution. For those things which—

<column-break/>

—are [easily] provided are sufficient for these ends. <note>The Greek text here mirrors the Latin on the left, quoting Epicurean doctrine.</note> But the desire arising from empty opinions was both indefinite and difficult to provide. For that which troubles the flesh according to need is well and sufficiently removed by things easy to provide, which have a simple nature of fluids and solids. But the rest, as much as has fallen into <gloss>2</gloss> extravagance, they say does not have a necessary appetite, nor does it arise necessarily from something painful, but rather arises from <gloss>3</gloss> that which either causes grief or merely "stings" <note>original: νύττοντος (nyttontos); refers to a sharp, poking sensation of desire</note> in its absence; or it arises entirely from that which gives joy; <gloss>4</gloss> or entirely from empty and false dogmas, <gloss>5</gloss> which relate to no natural lack, nor to that which dissolves the constitution through its absence. For even the most ordinary things are sufficient—

---

<margin>
In *Diogenes Laertius* <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers</note> Book X, page 798: "The wealth of nature is both limited and easy to provide, but that of empty opinions falls away into the infinite." And page 790: "That which is natural is entirely easy to provide, but that which is empty is difficult to provide." Since this was also read in the *Florentine* and *Leiden* editions, and was confirmed by the translator and the *Meerman manuscript*, I did not hesitate to restore to the author his own words. Immediately following, instead of "was" [ην], *Reiske* <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note> conjectured "of us" [ημων] or "at the same time" or "together."
</margin>

2. **Fallen into extravagance.**] I would prefer "fallen away into" [ekpeptoken]. This usage is unknown to no one. And so it is in the saying of Epicurus, which I just praised: "falls away [ekpiptei] into the infinite." Our author certainly has that in mind. Instead of "they say it has," *Reiske* wanted "it has by nature."

3. **Either causes grief or stings.**] Perhaps "either does *not* (or may not) cause grief." The word "indeed" [men] is badly missing in the *Leipzig* edition. *REISKE.* The metaphorical use of the word "to sting" [nyttein] is very frequent. *Diodorus* (XIII, 58) says "to receive stings in the soul," just as *Themistius* (Oration XIV, p. 171) says "it stung the mind." With these can be compared "to be stung in the heart" in *Luke*, Acts of the Apostles II, 37. Often "to sting" and "to grieve" are synonyms; *D'Orville* <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville, a Dutch philologist</note> taught this beautifully in his notes on *Chariton*, Book VI, 5, and he was not unmindful of our Author.

<column-break/>

4. **Or entirely from —**] The second "entirely" [holos] is missing in the *Leipzig* edition. If "entirely" ought to be absent, it would be more convenient in the first position. *REISKE.* However, the *Meerman manuscript* also does not have the second one, nor did the translator read it.

5. **Which relate to no natural lack.**] Either "which" [he] should be read, or rather "in which way" [hei]. Both, together with "relate," refer back to "appetite." *REISKE.* I have corrected what was previously read as "or" [ē] into "in which way" [hēi], as the *Meerman* manuscript rightly has it. In the *Florentine* edition, "lack" [elleimma] was faultily written with one 'l', which the *Leiden edition* followed according to its custom.

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

...to maintain those things <gloss>6</gloss> which Nature necessarily requires. These things, both because of their simplicity and their scarcity <note>meaning they are required in small amounts</note>, are easily obtained. Furthermore, for one who partakes in the eating of flesh, there is also a need for inanimate foods <gloss>7</gloss>; but for one who is satisfied with inanimate things, <gloss>8</gloss> the task is half as easy, and the preparation requires very little expense.

§ 50. For they say <gloss>1</gloss> that one ought not to first prepare the necessities and then treat Philosophy as an afterthought; rather, one should first prepare the soul to be truly confident and then <gloss>2</gloss> take hold of daily needs. For we would be committing our affairs to a poor counselor if, without Philosophy, we attempted to measure and prepare what is necessary for Nature. Therefore, while practicing philosophy, one must also provide for these things, and as far as...

<column-break/>

...which nature necessarily requires. Moreover, because of their cheapness and small quantity, they can be easily acquired. Furthermore, he who uses the eating of meat also has need of inanimate things for food. But he who is content only with inanimate things, for him it is available at half the effort, and requires very few expenses for the preparation.

§ 50. For they say it is not proper that when someone has prepared the necessities, he should then apply philosophy as if it were an addition: but that first, having legitimately acquired endurance and virtue of mind, he should then manage his daily needs. For we would surely commit our affairs to a bad counselor if, without philosophy, we wished to measure and prepare for ourselves what is necessary for nature. Wherefore, by philosophizing, one must also provide for these...

---

<margin>6. *To maintain these things etc.* Perhaps it should read *this nature.* <note>original: "ταύτην. naturam puta"</note> Then I would also wish the period to be changed to a comma and read: *but those things which Nature necessarily requires, these indeed—* where the second *indeed* <note>original: "δὲ"</note> is elegantly redundant, being nothing other than a non-necessary repetition of the first, of which type of repetition very frequent examples occur. Just as the Latin *vero* <note>meaning "truly" or "indeed"</note>: *those things which nature truly needs necessarily, those are indeed very easy to obtain.* <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note></margin>

<margin>7. *But for one satisfied with inanimate things.* <term>Jerome, Book II against Jovinian, chapter 11:</term> *Those who eat flesh also require those things which are not of flesh; but those who make use of a simple diet do not require meat.* A little before, <term>Meermann</term> <note>referring to a manuscript variant</note> reads *partaking in meat-eating.*</margin>

<margin>8. *From a half.* Perhaps it should be: *from a half the necessity is left behind, and this is easily provided and requiring little expense for the preparation.* <term>REISKE</term></margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>1. *They say.* But after you have acquired for yourself true constancy of mind and certain confidence, which allows itself to be shaken by no fears of future want, only then should you undertake the care of performing daily business and seeking food. This meets the argument of the adversaries, which ends at the word *preparation.* <term>REISKE</term></margin>

<margin>2. *To take hold of daily [needs].* This means to cling to them most tenaciously, to study nothing further. Thus *to cling to things that are not fitting* above in § 12; *to cling to the diet* in § 56; *to cling to salvation* and similar phrases, concerning which that light of the literary world recently, <term>P. Wesseling</term> <note>Petrus Wesseling, a Dutch scholar</note> on <term>Diodorus Siculus II, 12.</term> I would prefer to connect the word "genuinely" <note>original: "gnosios"</note> with what follows.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

It is necessary: namely, as far as the intensity of care toward those things permits. However, insofar as anything is taken away from that focus, so that it does not dominate the perfect purification <note>original: "perfectae purgationi"</note>, one must not approach the preparation of wealth or food. § 51. # PORPHYRY

->**On Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

...the disturbances that follow from it. Indeed, the Philosopher must also possess the hope <gloss>3</gloss> that nothing necessary for life will fail him. Readily available goods sufficiently preserve this hope, whereas costly things make it difficult to maintain. Certainly, the majority of men, even though they possess much, toil without end as if their resources will fail them <gloss>4</gloss>. Remembering that no amount of wealth, even if all the riches in the world were collected, has the natural power to provide a significant release from the soul's distress, makes one content with what is easily obtained and most simple. On the other hand, even the most moderate and ordinary things—which are entirely easy to provide—remove the physical discomfort of the body. Even if such things should fail, they do not disturb the man who practices for death. Furthermore, the pain <gloss>5</gloss> caused by great want...

<column-break/>

...which follow from it, can in any way compensate for the trouble. Add to this that since it is necessary for the philosopher to be of such hope that he believes nothing will be lacking to him in life: hope of this kind is preserved by things easily obtained, just as it is weakened and diminished by sumptuous and luxurious things. For this reason, it happens that most people, although they possess much, never cease to labor as if wealth will always be lacking to them. However, so that we may be content with the cheapest things and those which are most easily acquired, it helps most if we keep in mind that there is nothing which has any power to bring about the calming of the mind's disturbances—at least those of any importance—even if all riches were gathered together. To soothe the discomfort of the body, however, any things, even the most modest and those which can be easily supplied from anywhere, are sufficient. Even if these should be lacking in some small measure, they cannot disturb him who [meditates on] death...

<column-break/>

<margin>To one contemplating, or something similar. "It becomes unprofitable" is the same as "it appears to be so." To one thinking of the impediments, it immediately appears that the preparation of so many and such great things is not worth the effort. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note></margin>

<margin>3. "That nothing will fail."] Later writers often use this word <note>original: "ὑπολείπειν"</note> for "to be lacking" or "to cease to be supplied." <term>REISKE.</term> This precept corresponds excellently to our own religion. We have the warnings of the Lord Christ against vain anxiety about the future in <term>Matthew, chapter VI.</term></margin>

<margin>4. "They toil without end."] That is, in vain. Thus "vain and endless labor" is found in Plato. <term>Alciphron, Book I, Letter 2</term> uses the same formula as our author: "we toil fruitlessly and without end." See <term>Bergler.</term> <note>Stephan Bergler, known for his editions of Alciphron.</note></margin>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from the previous section regarding the necessity of food versus the pursuit of luxury. The text is presented in parallel Latin and Greek columns, followed by scholarly philological notes.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

...he meditates constantly. Furthermore, the pain that arises from a deficiency <note>i.e., hunger</note> is far milder than that which results from overfilling, unless someone deceives themselves with empty opinions. Moreover, a variety of foods not only fails to remove the disturbances of the soul, but it does not even increase the pleasure of the body; for pleasure reaches its limit as soon as the removal of pain is achieved. Thus, the eating of meat neither dissolves any actual distress of our nature, nor does it provide anything which, if left undone, would have led to pain. Instead, it offers a violent sort of gratification which is quickly mingled with its opposite. For it does not contribute to the preservation of life, but only to the variety of pleasures—not unlike sexual matters or the drinking of foreign wines, without which nature is still able to endure. For those things without which nature cannot persist are very few indeed, and are of such a kind that they can be obtained easily, with justice, with liberality, and with much quiet and leisure.

<column-break/>

...of mildness than that which involves repletion, unless one deceives oneself with empty opinions. And the variety of foods, far from releasing the disturbances of the soul, does not even <gloss>6</gloss> increase the pleasure in the flesh. For this too has its limit once the removal of pain is accomplished. Thus, the practice of meat-eating did not relieve any annoyance of nature, <gloss>7</gloss> nor did it provide anything which, if not completed, would have resulted in pain. Rather, it possessed a violent charm that was quickly mixed with the opposite. For it did not contribute to the <gloss>8</gloss> permanence of life, but to the variety of pleasures; it is similar to sexual acts or the drinking of foreign wines, without which nature is able to remain. But the things without which it could not endure are altogether few, and are able to be provided easily and with justice, freedom, stillness, and much ease.

Now, it is recovered through the thinnest and meatless diet <note>original: "ἀσάρκου διαίτης" (asarkou diaitēs) - literally a diet without flesh</note>, so that by this it would also remain; and if food from inanimate things <note>i.e., plants</note> does not contribute to the strength of a Milo <note>Milo of Croton was a famous 6th-century BCE wrestler known for his immense strength and for eating vast quantities of meat</note>, nor generally to the increase of power, yet neither strength nor the increase of power is necessary for the Philosopher, if he intends to attend to contemplation and not to 2 outward actions and excesses. § 52. Indeed, we shall find that meat does not contribute to health, but is rather an impediment to it. For it is necessary that those things by which health is restored are the same by which it is preserved. It is restored, however, by a very thin diet and one free of meat; wherefore it is brought about that by the same diet it may endure. But if food sought from inanimate things does not bring the strength of Milo, nor does it act at all toward the increase of forces: yet neither strength nor the increase of forces is needed by the philosopher, who is to be at leisure for contemplation, not for actions and intemperance.
