1. *For by those means through which health is recovered &c.*] Jerome expressed this in Latin in *Book II against Jovinian, 11*: <note>original: "Quibus ergo cibis recipitur sanitas..."</note> "By whatever foods health is regained, by these it can also be kept, lest anyone think that diseases are stirred up by vegetables: But if vegetables do not provide the strength of that famous Milo of Croton &c." Regarding the strength of Milo, all things are well known. I recall those words of *Cicero in On Old Age, chapter 10*: "Milo is said to have entered the stadium at Olympia while carrying a living ox on his shoulders; would you then prefer this strength of body, or the strength of Pythagoras's intellect to be given to you?" For the word "health" <note>original: "ὑγείᾳ"</note> which preceded, others write <note>original: "ὑγιείᾳ"</note>, and our author loves that form. We have spoken of this elsewhere. There was a note added in the *Meerman manuscript*: <margin>Note that the necessary things are few and easy to provide, but the unnecessary things are the opposite.</margin>

2. *Actions and excesses.*] There was one who preferred "disturbances" <note>original: "ταράξεσι"</note>, as in the following section the "undisturbed state of the soul" is mentioned. Unless "actions and excesses" is, by a known figure of speech, made into "excessive actions." I understand this to refer to those who follow the "practical life," concerning whom see above in § 27.

3. *And the enjoyments &c.*] What "enjoyments" <note>original: "Ἀπολαύσεις"</note> properly are, what the "enjoyable life" is, and who "enjoying men" are, will be discussed below at Book III, § 18.

4. *Nothing to us.*] A very common formula, which he uses also below in Book II, 43. <note>original: "τί πρός σε"</note> "What is it to you?"

# PORPHYRY

...be consumed, just as happens with countless animals that humans do <gloss>2</gloss> not eat. But as long as this varied and all-encompassing folly persists among men, <gloss>3</gloss> there will be countless people who will greedily devour these things.

One must maintain health, not out of a fear of death, but for the sake of not being hindered in attaining the goods that come from contemplation <note>Greek: *theoria*, the philosophical act of seeing or understanding divine truths</note>. The primary preserver of health is the undisturbed state of the soul and the orientation of the mind toward that which truly exists. For much of this influence reaches as far as the body, as our companions have shown by experience. <gloss>4</gloss> Indeed, some who suffered from gout <term>arthritis: a disease of the joints</term> in both feet and hands—so severe that for <gloss>5</gloss> eight whole years they had to be carried—struck off the disease at the same moment they cast away their wealth and turned their gaze toward the divine. Thus, along with their money and their anxieties, they laid aside the sickness of the body as well.

<column-break/>

...be consumed. This is what usually happens in the case of innumerable animals which humans do not eat. But if this varied and manifold foolishness persists among men, there will also be innumerable people who, devoted to gluttony, will gorge themselves on these things.

Furthermore, health is not to be preserved through the dread of death, but for this reason: that we may not be impeded from pursuing those goods which arise from contemplation. Its chief preserver is the imperturbable and tranquil constitution of the soul, and the attention of our mind toward that which truly is. For there is much that reaches from the soul even to the body, just as our friends have taught by experience. Those who labored under a joint disease <note>Latin: *articulari morbo*, referring to gout or arthritis</note> which had so violently seized their hands and feet that they had to be carried for eight full years, expelled the illness as soon as they rejected their riches and betook themselves to contemplating divine things. For together with their money and cares, they also laid down the malady of the body.

# PORPHYRY

...not the mere filling of poverty’s void, but to taste and experience pleasure <note>original: "γεύσασθαι" / "percipiat"</note> so that it might pass through all things, and to set as a limit that which is necessary rather than that which is indefinite. For in this way, even in this matter, it is possible to have attained the available good through self-sufficiency <term>autarkeia: the Stoic and Epicurean ideal of being self-contained and independent of external needs</term> and likeness to God. Thus, the body itself will not desire more, nor will it crave more time as if it would add a greater good to itself. In this way, one will truly grow rich, measuring wealth by the natural limit and not by empty opinions. Thus, one will not hang upon hopes of the greatest pleasure—which has no certainty of coming to pass and is most turbulent—but will remain in the self-sufficiency of what is present and what has already occurred. For one will not be in agony, lest...

<column-break/>

...is, so that he perceives not the filling of hunger, but the pleasure of this satiety, so that he reaches toward all these things. Nor should he set as a limit that which is undefined, but that which is necessary. For thus it will happen, that the body also will follow the good which can happen to it, out of sufficiency and out of the likeness which it has to God. Thus neither will it desire the use of a longer time as if it might bring an increase to its good. Thus he will truly grow rich, while he measures riches by a natural limit, not by vain opinions. Thus he will not always be suspended by the hope of the greatest pleasure, which as it has no certain outcome, is likewise most turbulent: but he will now be established in the sufficiency of the present and the past, so that concerning the future, as if to remain longer...

->remains, let it not be a source of anxiety.<-

§ 55. Come now, I ask you, how is it not absurd if a man who is suffering, either oppressed by some heavy external calamity or caught in chains, does not even think of food, nor labor over how it might be provided: but if it is set before him, he takes only what is necessary: yet he who is truly a prisoner, afflicted by internal calamities <note>The "internal calamities" refer to the passions and the soul's entanglement with the material body</note>, seeks out a display of banquets and procures a variety of them, by which he strengthens his own chains and makes them thicker? How can these be the actions of men who have recognized what they have suffered, and not rather of those who delight in their sufferings and are ignorant of the evils in which they are placed? # PORPHYRY

->**On the Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

...being ungrateful for their present life, and full of immeasurable turmoil, they yearn for what is absent to find fulfillment. For no one among those who have reached such a state comes to desire silver tables and couches, perfumes, cooks, fine vessels, garments, and banquets of every multitude, variety, and extravagance because all their inner disturbances are easily resolved; rather, it is from a sense of uselessness <note>original: ἀχρησίας; the translator notes this may also mean "dissatisfaction"</note> regarding their entire present life, and...

<column-break/>

...they recognize their own misery. For since their present state of life is ungrateful to them, and they are driven by an insatiable agitation, they affect a longing for absent things even unto surfeit. Indeed, there is no one among those who have surrendered themselves to every abundance of luxury and variety who is led to seek out silver tables and couches, ointments, cooks, furniture, clothing, and sumptuous dinners because he has all his disturbances pacified. Rather, it arises from the unpleasantness of the present life and an indefinite [longing] for types of goods...

***

<margin>
Wetstein uses and illustrates the phrase "and in those things in which they are" in his notes on Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians 4:11.
</margin>

5. **Full of immeasurable turmoil.**] Our author uses this expression again a little later. The word *aplatos* <note>immeasurable/terrible</note>, although it might seem poetic, is not unusual to other writers, but is often confused with the word *apletos*, which means nearly the same thing. To say no more, the industry of those most excellent men J. P. D'Orville (on Chariton, Book 8, ch. 2) and P. Wesseling (on Diodorus 2.49) has already addressed this.

6. **To find fulfillment.**] Thus in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts, as two words. Others write it as one word, *eisplerōsin*.

7. **Easily resolved... regarding disturbances.**] Reiske is suspicious of the word "disturbances" (*thorybous*). Gataker excellently illustrated the word *eulytos* <note>easily dissolved/resolved</note> and explained its nature in his notes on Antoninus 3.5. One will be stuck here if they do not consider the habit of construction and transposition which our author is accustomed to use: "For no one of the men (who have) come to a desire for silver tables... and a multitude of perfumes... comes (to them) because of the fact that all things for him [are resolved] etc."

8. **Tables and couches.**] These are very often joined together, and therefore I rewrite "new tables" as "couches" following Gronovius on Polyaenus 8.16.2. Not only silver, but sometimes golden couches and tables are mentioned, on which matter see D'Orville on Chariton 8.6, p. 706.

<column-break/>

9. **And cooks.**] These also pertain to luxury. A cook was at first a cheap slave, but truly when gluttony began to require various arts, every most skillful cook became of the highest price; much has departed from ancient customs, where people bought horses more dearly than cooks. This is a well-known matter; see, however, Corte on Sallust, *Jugurtha* 85, and Wesseling on Diodorus, Vol. 2, p. 609.

10. **And garments.**] He understands soft and delicate clothes. Seneca writes elegantly of them: *I see silken garments, if they can even be called garments, in which there is nothing to protect the body or even modesty; having put them on, a woman can hardly swear with a clear conscience that she is not naked.* (On Benefits, Book 7, ch. 9). They are mentioned everywhere by those who describe the luxury of the ancients.

11. **Of men having come.**] Perhaps "of men who are well-off" <note>Latin: hominum fortunatorum</note>. But there are still other things in this passage which I cannot resolve. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German physician and philologist.</note>

12. **Uselessness regarding the present life.**] The word *achrēsias* <note>uselessness</note> can be defended: "because one is unable to use life in its present condition." However, from what precedes, it seems better to read *acharstias* <note>ingratitude/dissatisfaction</note>. <term>REISKE</term>. Excellent. *Achristias* was also pleasing to Abresch. The mixing of these two words is frequent, regarding which see Reiske’s *Observations on Aristides*, p. 385. Ingratitude and uselessness, which word a little...

# P O R P H Y R Y

For surely, if we must be cured of a disease, we endure all things with earnestness—being cut <note>original: "τεμνόμενοι" - referring to surgery</note>, being bloodied, being burned, drinking bitter medicines, being purged through the bowels, through vomiting, and through the nostrils, and even paying fees to those who treat us in this way—should we not then reasonably endure all things for the sake of the internal disease? (As those who are competing in the contest for immortality and communion with God, from which we are prevented by our communion with the body). Even if it were necessary to endure these things with pain, we should certainly not follow the laws of the body, which are violent and opposed to the laws of the mind and the paths of salvation. But since we are not now philosophizing about the endurance of pain, but about the rejection of unnecessary pleasures, what excuse remains for those who wish to shamelessly defend their own lack of self-control <term>intemperance: the inability to restrain one's physical desires</term>?

->§ 57.<-

<column-break/>

What must be done? For it is not only to be freed from a bodily disease that we must endure so many things—while we are cut, while we are bloodied, while we are burned, while we drain bitter medicines, while we are purged through the bowels, through vomiting, through the nostrils, and moreover, fees must be paid to those who so affect us—but truly for the cause of the internal disease, where our contest is for immortality and for having fellowship with God (from which we are prohibited by our fellowship with the body). Should we not endure all things, even if it were necessary to suffer pains and afflictions? Nor should we rightly follow the laws of the body, which are violent and oppose the laws of the mind and the ways of salvation. But since we are now philosophizing not about tolerating pains but about rejecting unnecessary pleasures, what further excuse remains for those who impudently wish to protect their own intemperance?

->§ 57.<-

# P O R P H Y R Y

The more one is established far from every material manifestation, the more it is fitting for the person approaching him to be in every way pure and holy, beginning from the body and ending at the inner self, assigning to each part, or to all things present, the purity that is natural to each. But perhaps no one would speak against these points; yet one might wonder how we place abstinence in the category of purity, even though in sacrifices we are accustomed to slaughtering sheep and oxen, considering this sacred rite to be both holy and pleasing to the gods. Therefore, since a long discourse is needed for the resolution of this problem, we must take up the subject of sacrifices from a different starting point.

# PORPHYRY THE PHILOSOPHER

# P O R P H Y R Y

->S U M M A R Y  O F  A R G U M E N T S<-

*Porphyry first provides a preface; and briefly sets forth the order in which the matters in this second book are to be treated. § 1. He afterwards approaches the refutation of an argument of the greatest weight (as it seemed to some), which endeavored to prove the lawful use of animals for food based on their use in sacrifices. § 2, etc. He then explains the entire business of sacrifices. § 5, etc. Namely, by what steps the practice eventually arrived at the slaughter of animals. § 6, 7, etc. For what reasons it was introduced. § 9, 10, etc. He reviews several of the arguments of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle's successor; Porphyry relies heavily on his lost work "On Piety" here.</note> against the slaughter of animals. § 12, etc. He proves that the nature of animals and fruits is different. § 13. He shows that God is most greatly delighted by things easily procured and of little expense. § 15. Nor does any of those reasons for which we perform sacred rites to the Gods have a place regarding animals. 24. Therefore, the true cause why we sacrifice them is our own intemperance and pursuit of pleasure. § 25. He returns later to demonstrate the beginnings of sacrifices. § 27, etc. How, having started from fruits, the license of sacrifices eventually progressed even to humans. § 27, 28, etc. He afterwards adds several reasons why one ought to abstain from animals. § 31, etc. He teaches most excellently what things and what kind of things it is fitting to sacrifice. § 33, etc. He illustrates his own sentiment by reviewing the opinions of the Pythagoreans § 36, and the Platonists § 37. Wherein he surveys the various types of Gods, their natures, and their duties. § 37, and 38. He recounts many things concerning good and evil Spirits <note>original: "Genii" - intermediate beings between gods and humans.</note>. § 39, etc. Indeed, that the evil ones are greatly delighted by the smoke-smell <note>original: "nidore" - the smell of burning fat/meat</note> of sacrifices made from animals. § 42. Therefore, a pious man ought to refrain from them. § 43. To which he finally and seriously exhorts: since it contributes greatly to chastity and holiness. § 44, etc. Which things are even simulated by enchanters. § 45. They are hinted at by the external symbols of all sacred rites. § 46, 47, etc. Arguments for ani-*

§ 4. For if <gloss>1</gloss> these matters are not confused, but are distinguished in the proper manner, most of the opposing arguments are found to be vain. 3. *All wickednesses.*] Thus all the manuscripts, except for the *Bodleian: wicked (feminine plural)* which was placed in the margin by *Fogerolles* and approved by *Valentini*. A little before, after *being*, the *Leipzig* edition had erroneously omitted *and*.

4. *Fall before the contentious.*] *Fogerolles and Valentini* restored *fall upon/encounter*. It is well known that these words are confused a thousand times, as also below in Book III, 26, where I nevertheless defend the common reading. Nor is it different in this place: *fall before* means it falls forward, or incurs the eyes of its own accord. There is a significance in the word that argues for a sudden and spontaneous appearance. Hence, in a bad sense, *precipitously* means headlong or inconsiderately, and *to fall forward* signifies rashness in the impulse of acting. <note>See Gataker on Marcus Aurelius, I, 17, and Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus, XV, 65.</note>

5. *We will clarify the inquiry.*] Thus correctly in the earlier *Editions* and also the *Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts*, which *Valentini*—I know not by what authority—had changed into *we will discern*. Gataker illustrates the word itself <note>See Gataker on Marcus Aurelius, X, 12; Cicero to Atticus, VII, 8: "we will clarify this more philosophically," where some read "we will discern," but wrongly.</note>

<column-break/>

# PORPHYRY

...[as we proceed] we shall record; aiming as much as possible for a symmetry and style appropriate to the subject. The matter stands thus:

§ 5. It seems an almost immeasurable time has passed since that most learned race of all mankind—as **Theophrastus** says—who inhabit the most holy region created by the **Nile**, first began to sacrifice to the celestial gods, starting from the hearth...

<column-break/>

...maintaining that proportion, as far as possible, which is most suited to the proposed argument. The matter, therefore, is as follows:

§ 5. It is a nearly countless time since the race of men, the most learned of all (as Theophrastus says), who inhabited the most holy region founded by the Nile, first began to sacrifice to the celestial gods from the hearth and home, not...

---

<margin>
To aim for symmetry: *Diodorus Siculus* said this quite often, as the great *Commentator* <note>likely referring to Peter Wesseling</note> teaches regarding Book I, ch. 8, who did not forget our author [Porphyry].
</margin>

1. **An immeasurable time...** — These words and those following, up to the phrase "but the antiquity etc." near the end of this section, were transcribed from our author by **Eusebius** in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, p. 28. Eusebius partly provides help in reading Porphyry and partly expects it from him. In the *Meerman* margin it is noted: "Note that Theophrastus speaks of bloodless sacrifice."

<margin>
2. **Most learned race.**
</margin>
He means the **Egyptians**, whose wisdom is praised everywhere. He calls them "the most learned of all" below in § 26. The term *logioi* <note>original: λογιωτάτοι</note> refers to those who are wise and skilled in a particular matter. Thus, "the most learned of the priests" and similar phrases are found in **Plutarch** and others. **Wesseling** (on Diodorus II, 4) and the **Philologists** (on Lucian) will satisfy you on this point.

<margin>
3. **As Theophrastus says.**
</margin>
He praises Theophrastus frequently in the following parts of this book, which I suspect were taken from the same work. But out of the many books he wrote, I will discuss which one is meant at § 11.

<margin>
4. **By the Nile.**
</margin>
The *Lipsian* manuscript lacks the article "the." It signifies **Egypt**, but why does he say it was "founded by the Nile"? Does he mean the King, who is called *Neileus* in Diodorus Siculus (I, 63) and *Nilus* by others, from whom the city of Nilus in Egypt also took its name? So it seems to **Fabricius**. But although I would easily grant that this king deserved well of the Egyptians, 

<column-break/>

it cannot be conveniently said that he "founded the region." I would prefer, therefore, to understand it as the **river**. The Author speaks from the conviction of the ancients (though the reasons of the great **Bochart** suggest this is false), who believe that Egypt, or rather its lower part, was born from the alluvial deposits and accumulated silt of the river; hence they call it the *gift of the Nile*. **Heliodorus** says the river itself is "the savior of the upper part, and both the father and creator of the lower." See **Olear** on Philostratus and **Wesseling** on Diodorus, who shows that the expression "to found a region" <note>original: κτίζειν χώραν</note> was used very broadly among the Greeks.

<margin>
5. **From the hearth.**
</margin>
In Eusebius it is "at the hearth," where the most learned **Vigerus** translates it as "at the domestic hearth." And certainly more correctly than I did with "from Vesta." **VALENTINUS**. See the *Scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps*: the meaning is that the first of all to whom sacrifices were made were the celestial gods, and in these very acts, the beginning of the sacrifice was made from **Vesta** <note>The goddess of the hearth</note>. **REISKE**. Excellent. **Phurnutus** <note>Cornutus</note> says: "Wherefore the Greeks began from her as the first in sacrifices, and ended with her as the last." Therefore, it should also be restored in Eusebius, where Vigerus did not see how this proverbial "from the hearth" <note>original: ἀφ’ ἑστίας</note> fit here. It fits because of where the proverb originated. **Plato** in *Cratylus*: "Let us begin from Vesta according to the law." Read the cause explained there.

6. *Neither of myrrh nor of cassia.*] We ought not to dwell too long on "commonplaces," as they are called. Yet I cannot restrain myself from adding those lines from *Ovid, Fasti, Book I, line 337*:

7. *A ladder of error.*] In Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note>, who cites this passage in the first book of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, it is read as "a seeker of error, a *mazer*" <note>original: πλάνης ἐρευνητὴς μαζὴρ</note>. However, I would not advise anyone to correct Porphyry thus. For I fear these may have been the notes of some not very skilled person who believed that "ladder" <note>klimaktēr</note> meant what he expressed in two words. I myself feel differently, and I think "ladder" here signifies—if the reading is intact—the origin of error, and as it were a certain ascent and step. However, since it is read that way in the magnificently printed Parisian volumes of Pamphilus, I have seen a manuscript in which only the latter of those words was read. <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian philologist</note>. In Eusebius it is read differently: *and man becoming a curious seeker of error, offered to the gods the first-fruits of a necessary life with many labors and tears.* Which the translator rendered thus: *when man, having been made a curious investigator of error, offered to the gods the first-fruits of a necessary life after the drops of many labors and tears.* The words as they are read in Porphyry can be conveniently rendered as I have already interpreted them, if "becoming" were written as "surviving." <term>Vigerus</term> <note>François Viger, a Jesuit scholar</note> thinks that "seeker" in Eusebius is a gloss <note>an explanatory note that crept into the text</note> explaining the word *mazēr*. <term>VALENT</term>. Either "surviving" or "becoming master of." <term>REISKE</term>. <term>MEERMANN</term>. "Ladder" <note>klimatēr</note>. I had long ago restored "error and *mazēr*," which <margin>Suidas III. 336.</margin> anyone can see how easily it could have been born from "ladder" <note>klimaktēr</note>. I was much rejoiced when I noticed this was confirmed by *Eusebius*, in whose work, however, the word "seeker" is to be held as a gloss (as that troublesome race of scribes is often accustomed to substitute a more frequent word for a less frequent one, which then creeps into the text). I conclude this mostly from our author; not, as *Vigerus* preferred, because *mazēr* is the same as "seeker," for otherwise those two words are also usually joined. See: *Bergler on Alciphron I, 11 and Sylburg on Clement of Alexandria p. 814.* But if "and *mazēr*" displeases you, "ladder" <note>klimaktēr</note> is certainly preferable. Not what *Valentinus* had given. And indeed, the older editions of *Felicianus* and the *Leipzig Manuscript* agree on "ladder" <note>klimaktēr</note>.

...but of the green herb, as if they were lifting up with their hands a kind of downy bloom of fertile Nature. <note>original: "χλόης... χνοῦν" - referring to the fine, soft growth of young plants.</note> For indeed, the earth brought forth trees before animals; and long before the trees, it produced the annual budding grass. —the herb itself, which they had plucked with their hands like a certain downy growth of fertile nature. <margin>10. page 34. B. and *Theodoret:* in his *Sermon on Sacrifice:* where he intends to show that Porphyry thought sacrifices were foreign to true piety, and that he had stolen these ideas from the Sacred Scriptures: "but of the green herb, as if lifting up a kind of downy bloom of fertile Nature with their hands" etc. *Diodorus Siculus (Book I, 43)* also touches upon this most ancient custom of the Egyptians: "wherefore even now, men remembering the utility of this herb, when they approach the gods, they pray while holding a branch of it in their hand." *Wesseling* touches upon these Porphyrian passages there.</margin>

<column-break/>

13. **Welcoming with sacrifice.**] An elegant word, just as "to welcome with gifts" <note>original: "δεξιοῦσθαι δώροις"</note> is used in *Aelian (Varia Historia, Book I, chapter 32)* and elsewhere. *Hesychius*, looking to that usage, defines "to welcome" as "to bring to oneself." See the celebrated *Alberti* on that point.

14. **Through the fire rendering honors immortal.**] The word "Through" <note>original: "Διὰ"</note> is not in *Eusebius*; while both versions can be approved, *Viger* rightly notes there that our reading is easier to understand. *P. Wesseling*, in his notes on *Diodorus Siculus (Book II, 20)*, declares the force and power of the verb "to immortalize" <note>original: "ἀπαθανατίζειν"</note> excellently, as is his custom; he teaches that "to be immortalized" is said of all those who attain immortality in any way, from which he illustrates our phrase "to immortalize honors."

15. **We maintain, etc.**] Thus in Pamphilus: "they maintained [the fire] immortal in the temples as being [like the gods]." VICTORIUS. *Eusebius* has "they were maintaining." VALENT. These things ought to be explained according to the custom of the ancients, who nourished eternal fires in honor of the Gods. Thus, besides the hanging lamps, *Spanheim* (in *Vesta and the Greek Prytaneis*) shows from this passage that an altar and a fire always burning were consecrated to Vesta by the ancients. But our author does not restrict these things to Vesta alone.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

From those things which were burned from the earth—that is, from *incense-burning* <note>original: "thymiasi"</note>—they named the altars *incense-burners* <note>original: "thymiatēria"</note>, as if you were to say "vessels for fumigation," and they called the act *to sacrifice* <note>original: "thyein"</note> and the offerings *sacrifices* <note>original: "thysias"</note>. We, however, do not interpret these terms correctly, as if they surpassed the later sin <note>The "sin" refers to the later introduction of animal slaughter</note>; for we call that worship which appears to be offered to the gods through the slaughter of animals a *sacrifice* <note>original: "thysian"</note>. Indeed, those ancients had such great care that the old custom should not be violated, that against those who neglected the old ways and introduced new ones, they employed a curse <note>original: "execratione"</note>, and named those things with which we are now accustomed to fumigate *aromatics* <note>original: "arōmata"</note>, which is to say, "cursed things" <note>The author suggests a folk etymology linking 'aroma' to 'ara' (a curse)</note>. And anyone might observe this use of ancient fumigations from the fact that many even now [offer] chopped pieces of fragrant wood...

<column-break/>

...most similar. And from the burning of the products of the earth, they called them both *incense-burners* and the act *to sacrifice* and *sacrifices*. We, however, misinterpret these, as they deviate from the later error, by calling the service that seems to be done through animals a *sacrifice*. So much did the ancients care not to transgress the custom, that against those who left behind the ancient way and brought in another, they uttered curses, and called the things now used for fumigation *aromatics* <note>original: "arōmata"</note>. One might see the antiquity of the aforementioned incense-offerings by looking at the fact that many even now still sacrifice chopped pieces of fragrant [woods]...

---

<margin>16. **Sacrifices — deviate.** There, the printed text had "sacrificing" and "signifying." However, the manuscript I saw does not differ at all from the author's reading in the first part. **VICTORIUS.** I conjectured it ought to read "revealing." **Eustathius** confirms this, where "signifying" is found. **VALENTINUS** also cites "revealing," as does **Graevius** in *Notes on Hesiod* ch. 8. But I do not dare to proscribe a beautiful metaphor in "deviating" and similar words. To **Reiske**, "as" here seems to be the same as "towards," and he reads: "those deviating." Or if "as" is taken for "as if," he reads: "confirming," as if confirming and stabilizing the more recent impiety.</margin>

<margin>17. **Having cursed.** Better there "having cursed" <note>original: "arasamenous"</note>. **VICTORIUS.** In other editions it was "about to curse," and so also in the Leipzig and Meerman Codices, whence **Reiske** conjectured it should read "cursing." This scholium was added in the margin of the Leipzig manuscript: *Why incense-offerings are called "aromatics" and how those sacrificing through them were either cursing or praying. For from this they say prayer is a "curse" <note>original: "aran"</note>.* And so also the Meerman, except that there it is "sacrificing" instead of "having sacrificed." Where "aromatics" were so named should not be investigated here. **Bodaeus à Stapel** on Theophrastus' *History of Plants* IV, 6, derives it from "I pray," but such is the infirmity of human memory that at IX, 7, being inconsistent with himself, he fetches it from elsewhere. A little before, instead of "having introduced," the Leipzig Codex has "introducing," which **Reiske** deservedly preferred because of the preceding "neglecting." It is no different in **Eusebius**.</margin>

<margin>18. **Fragrant woods.** Secular writers record that trees, especially fragrant ones, were used in sacred rites in olden times; the use of frankincense is more recent for them. **Pliny**, *Natural History* XIII, 1: *In the times of the Trojan War, supplication was not made with frankincense; they only knew the smell—or rather the soot—of cedar and citrus wood rolled in smoke during sacrifices.* We know of an older use of this from the Sacred Scriptures. But this is not the place for dealing with these matters. As for the fact that **Spencer** [claims] the law by which God ordered cedar wood to be burned with the heifer...</margin>

19. *Along with the original grass...* Perhaps "after the original grass." And soon, instead of "their leaves," *Lipsius* correctly reads "its leaves" <note>original: "autēs"</note>, meaning the oak's. REISKE. The *Meermann Codex* also confirms "its." The same soon reads "incense" <note>original: "thumiamata"</note> instead of "sacrifices" <note>original: "thumata"</note>.
20. *From the nuts.* Perhaps "from the fruits." REISKE. Excellent. "From the beginning, sacrifices of fruits were made to the gods." Below in § 27: "In ancient times it was through cakes and fruits, as we have shown." Also § 59. "Nut" <note>original: "Karyon"</note> has a very wide meaning, like the Latin *nux*. It denotes every fruit covered with a hard shell, and hence even *Walnuts*, because men, having long been nourished by acorns, finally discovered a tree that bore nuts, and having tasted the sweet flavor, called them "Jupiter's acorns" <note>original: "Iovis glandes"</note> on account of their excellence. But see *Bodaeus à Stapel* on *Theophrastus, History of Plants* III, 15. I ought to mention this because of what follows. *Casaubon on Athenaeus* II, 12, also teaches that "nuts" <note>original: "Karya"</note> embraces every kind of tree-fruit.
21. *Enough of the oak, he said.* A well-known proverb, often explained by ancient critics. He uses it also in IV, 2. Compare *Casaubon on Theophrastus:*
</margin>

*Characters of Ethics*, page 313. *Eusebius* against Marcellus I, 3, who explains the origin of the saying. *Libanius*, Epistle 1082, and there *Wolf* and *Alberti on Hesychius* under the letter V. But "there is enough of those things just as there is of the oak," as I might say with *Julian* in the *Misopogon*, page 346 A.
1. *The fruit of Demeter after the legume, etc.* Elsewhere they usually use the plural: "legumes" <note>original: "ta chedropa"</note>. And so our author does below in III, 18. They call by this name all pod-vegetables which are gathered and plucked by hand from which bread is not made. By another name they are called *ospria*. *Pollux* VI, 60: "There are also the *ospria* which they also named *chedropa*." Some do distinguish them, but without necessity. See *Bodaeus à Stapel on Theophrastus, History of Plants* VIII, 1. Indeed, whenever *chedropa* is said simply, *ospria* seem to be understood, for you may find them sometimes added. *Suidas* shows from *Thucydides* that the ancients used it even in the singular, as happens in this place. Our author says that barley was discovered first after the legumes; therefore mortals were first fed on barley. *Artemidorus*, Book 1, *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 71: "Barley loaves are good for all, for the story goes that this was the first food given to men by the gods." Next, *Reiske* preferred "the first appearance of barley" in the genitive or feminine plural.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

they used, which they called <term>barley-groats</term> <note>original: οὐλοχυτεῖσθαι; referring to the ritual sprinkling of whole barley</note>. Then, when they had broken the grain and ground it into food, they hid the tools of its manufacture in a secret place, as if they were sacred, because they had provided divine assistance to human life. From that ground-up sustenance—which they considered blessed above all previous forms of diet—they made the first offerings into the fire for the gods. For this reason, even now at the end of our drink-offerings, we are accustomed to use ground sacrificial cakes, thereby testifying to that ancient increase of incense, not

<column-break/>

mankind [performed] the sacrifices. But later, <insert>3</insert> after they had crushed the grains and ground the food into meal, they hid the tools of the labor—having provided divine help to their lives—in a secret place, <insert>4</insert> and approached them as if they were holy. <insert>5</insert> Because this "milled life" <note>A metaphorical term for a civilized life supported by agriculture</note> <insert>6</insert> was deemed more blessed than the former, they first offered a portion of the ground food into the fire for the gods. Whence even now, <insert>7</insert> toward the end of the burnt offerings, we use <insert>8</insert> ground sacrificial cakes; testifying indeed to the fact that what is being done [preserves] from the beginning...

<margin>
*Theophrastus:* These are praised; I ought to add a brief note <note>original: scholion</note> which is read under the name of *Didymus* regarding the Iliad, Book 1, line 449. <term>Barley-groats</term> <note>original: οὐλοχύτας</note>: these are barley grains mixed with salt which they poured over the animals being sacrificed before they were killed, either for the sake of a great invocation, or making a memory of the ancient way of eating. For as Theophrastus says in his book *On Discoveries*, before men learned to grind the fruit of Demeter <note>grain/wheat</note>, they ate the grains themselves in this way. From this you might almost guess the passage was taken from that book of *Theophrastus*, though it does not seem so. I will speak on this at section 11.
</margin>

3. **Crushed—ground the food into meal.**] To be "crushed" <note>original: Ἐρείκεσθαι</note> is said of fruits or legumes *only lightly bruised*; hence the terms "bruised," "broken," and others. To be "ground" <note>original: Ψαίεσθαι</note>, however, is *to be reduced to flour by a mill*. Immediately he calls them "ground sacrificial cakes," which by another name are elliptically called <term>psaista</term>, or ground fruits. In Latin, these are *molae* or *liba*: handfuls soaked in flour and oil, which the poorer people offered to the Gods in place of drink-offerings. *See Kuster* on *Aristophanes'* Plutus, 138, and *D’Orville* on *Chariton* VI, 7.

4. **As if they were holy.**] I would prefer "as if they were holy themselves." VALENTIUS. An error of the typesetter, who in the *Victorius* edition had given "priests" <note>original: ἱερεῖς</note> instead of "holy things" <note>original: ἱεροῖς</note>, was foolishly propagated in subsequent editions. *Felicianus* and the manuscripts are correct.

<column-break/>

5. **The milled life.**] See *Casaubon* on Athenaeus, Book 14, chapter 12. VALENTIUS. In previous *editions* and the *Leipzig* and *Meerman manuscripts*, it was "milled" <note>original: ἀληλεμένου</note>. However, the "milled life" <note>original: ἀληλεσμένος βίος</note>, or *a life of grinding*, was so frequent among the ancients that it passed into a proverb. It is opposed not only to the life of the first men, who are believed to have lived on acorns, but also to those who, being next to the first, ate fruits that were not milled but only lightly bruised. This matter is certain from what *Paullus Leopardus* in *Emendations* XI, 4, and *Petrus Wesseling* on Diodorus I, 17, have taught.

6. **Blessed than the former.**] Than the former. Specifically: the life. Then, after "fire," it seems that "placing" or "sending" or "gifting" is missing. REISKE.

7. **Of the burnt offerings.**] *Reiske* preferred "sacrifices." He uses the word again below in section 59; see there. This passage fits that of the poet in Iliad 9, line 220:
> And he cast the sacrificial offerings into the fire.

8. **Ground sacrificial cakes.**] What these were has just been said. Since the most ancient men won the favor of the Gods with these alone, that honor was thereafter held for antiquity, so that after everything else, they offered ground cakes as a gift most pleasing to the Gods. Go to *Casaubon* on *Theophrastus'* Ethical Characters, page 231, who explains these things beautifully. In the *Florentine edition* and the *Leipzig* and *Meerman manuscripts*, it was incorrectly written "late-ground."

# PORPHYRY

...the increase of the nine types of incense <note>original: "θυμιαμάτων αὔξησιν"</note>; yet they did not perceive for what reason we perform each of these acts. Starting from these beginnings, as fruits and even wheat became more abundant for us, the first-fruits of cakes <term>pelanoi: sacrificial cakes made of meal and honey</term> and all other remaining things were added to the sacrifices for the gods. People gathered many flowers, and mixed in no fewer of these, if they possessed anything beautiful in life or fitting in scent for divine perception. Some of these they used for wreaths <note>original: "σέφοντες" - literally 'honoring' or 'crowning'</note>; others they gave to the fire, offering other divine drops of wine and honey. Furthermore, having discovered oil for human needs, they offered the first-fruits of this as well to the gods who were the causes of it.

§ 7. To all these things, the procession of the Sun and the Hours, which is performed in Athens even to this day, seems to bear witness—

<column-break/>

—not understanding, however, for what reason we were doing each individual thing. Proceeding from here, as other fruits and now wheat were supplied more abundantly, the first-fruits of wheat porridge and all other things were employed in sacrifices to the gods: while men culled flowers from many sources and mixed in other things, if they seemed to have anything beautiful in life, and which excelled in scent for the divine sense: and of these, some they used for garlands, others they burned having been cast into the fire. Where they had also found divine drops of both wine and honey, and likewise oil for human uses, they made a sacred offering from these also to the gods who were the authors of them.

§ 7. To all of which, the procession of the sun and the hours which to this very day at Athens—

---

<margin>9. *The increase of incense.*] Either there is a fault in the word "increase" <note>Greek: αὔξησιν</note>, or rather something seems to be missing. "The simplicity of the incense (or sacrifices, as in the Leipzig Manuscript) from the beginning, which afterwards proceeded and grew into an increase of luxury." Thus testifying by that rite to the original meager nature of the offerings, which later advanced and grew into sumptuosity and splendor. REISKE. "Sacrifices" <note>Greek: Θυμάτων</note> appears in the Meermann Manuscript, whereas conversely at the end of § 5 it is "incense" <note>Greek: θυμιάματα</note> where others have "sacrifices."</margin>

<margin>10. *For us, and of the... etc.*] It would be easy to substitute "at the same time" <note>Greek: ἅμα</note> for "but" <note>Greek: ἀλλὰ</note>, which are exchanged for each other a hundred times. One might also think of adding "not only." But the common reading holds well, and the simple "but" has the same value as "not only... but also." I have compared examples of this matter in Polybius. Therefore the fault does not seem to be here, but in the word for "wheat" <note>Greek: πυρῶν</note>, and one should read "means/resources" <note>Greek: πορῶν</note>. REISKE. Clearly the Cambridge Editor had rashly inserted "on the one hand" <note>Greek: μὲν</note> after "us"; Reiske has skillfully explained the "but also," unless you prefer "nay even" or "furthermore."</margin>

<margin>11. *Now of cakes.*] In the Leipzig and Meermann Manuscripts, this Scholion <note>ancient marginal explanation</note> was added: "Pelanoi: cakes made of fine flour, or it is the thinnest meal, suitable for sacrifice. Or fruits softened with honey. Or certain first-fruits for the gods. Or the foam solidified around the body, and the solidified and dried gummy tear, such as frankincense and gum, and the obol <note>small coin</note> which is the seer's fee." You may read almost the same things in Suidas under "Pelanoi," which the celebrated Ruhnken illustrates in his Lexicon to Timaeus, suspecting they were taken from Boethius’s Platonic Lexicon.</margin>

<margin>12. *Some they used for wreaths.*] See § 16 near the end. VALENTINI. "Some," namely the flowers. It is said not only "to honor a statue with flowers," but also "to honor flowers," meaning to place wreaths on the head. Therefore this reading seems to hold well here. But in the next line I approve the reading of the Leipzig Manuscript, "those," namely the "drops." But in such a way that the punctuation at line 23 and the "but" <note>Greek: δὲ</note> are omitted according to the prescription of that same manuscript, and a comma is placed after "oil." And yet even so, the sentence is a little harsh and more intricate. For which reason—</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

...is celebrated, it seems to bear witness: in which not only other herbs but also grass, likewise oak and the berries of the strawberry tree, service-berries, tri-

<note>original Greek: πομπῇ, Ἡλίου τε καὶ Ὡρῶν. πομπεύει γὰρ εἰλυσπόα ἄγρωσις ἐπὶ πυρηνίων ἡγηρίας, ὄσπρια δρῦς...</note>
...procession of the Sun and the Seasons. For there is carried in procession the <term>agrostis</term><note>Couch-grass or a similar wild grass</note> wound around [something], upon the kernels of the <term>hegeteria</term><note>A ceremonial loaf or branch carried in festivals</note>, legumes, oak...

---

I would prefer to acquiesce to the common reading on this condition: that "of those worshipping" and "of those giving" be read, on account of the preceding "collection of flowers." If this is admitted, everything in this passage will be plain and easy. **REISKE.** The punctuation has rendered the passage obscure. I have followed the distinctions of the first **Editions**, which **Valentinus** had disturbed, who had therefore inserted "but" after "divine."

1. **Of the Sun and the Seasons.** Many maintain that the <term>Thargelia</term><note>An Athenian festival in honor of Apollo and Artemis/the Sun</note> were celebrated among the Athenians in honor of the Sun and the Seasons, in which the first fruits of the crops were carried around. However, those cannot be considered here, but rather the <term>Horaea</term>, in which we read of solemn feasts dedicated to the Seasons, who stood by the Sun and presided over the times of the year; **Casaubon** contends this is the meaning here in his notes to *Athenaeus* XII, 20. Yet there is nothing there from which the rites that follow can be illustrated. We read that such sacred rites were generally celebrated in the <term>Pyanepsia</term><note>A bean-cooking festival in autumn</note>. See the *Scholiast on Aristophanes* at *Knights* 725 and at *Plutus* 1056, and there the Great **Hemsterhuis**.

2. **Wound-grass agrostis.** This passage, if any other, has certainly caused me trouble. **Meursius** cites these words in *Greek Festivals* under "Thargelia" thus: "for there is carried in procession mud, grass, agrostis upon the kernels of the leader," etc. Having weighed everything, I conjecture it ought to be read: "agrostis wound around the suppliant-branch of kernels, legumes, oak, etc., and the <term>palathe</term><note>A cake of pressed fruit, usually figs</note> leader," as I have seen to it being printed. For **Meursius** in the cited place proves this procession was made to the Sun and Seasons in the Thargelia and Pyanepsia. In the Pyanepsia, moreover, an olive branch, which is called a "suppliant-branch" by **Eustathius**, was carried forward. See **Meursius** there. This suppliant-branch, as it seems, had berries, around which **Porphyry** says the agrostis was wound, although all others say it was wool. Therefore, perhaps better: "wool wound upon the kernels of the suppliant-branch." *Palathe* is perhaps a <term>gloss</term><note>An explanatory note that accidentally entered the main text</note> for "the leader." Concerning the use of the pot in the same festival, see **Meursius** on the Pyanepsia. That <term>orthostates</term> is the name of a cake, and that it is imposed from its shape [upright], is clear from Pollux. **VALENTINUS.** I find it necessary to leave this passage to those who abound more in leisure. To me, hurrying now, these few things occur spontaneously to mind, which will be, unless I am mistaken, plain and open. In "eilyspoa" lies a scholium. It seems someone wrote in his manuscript next to "agrostis" this 

<column-break/>

admonition: "a species of grass" <note>original: εἶδος πόας</note>, by which he would teach that *agrostis* is a certain *kind* of herb. It happened afterwards that this "species of grass," deformed into "eilyspoa," was thrust into the text. The second "hegerias" [or "hegerias" as it is in the Leipzig Manuscript] should be removed from verse 32, as it is a faulty spelling of the word *hegeteria* in verse 35. This later spelling of the same word is just as faulty as the first. But in verse 33 it invaded a foreign place; in verse 35 it holds its own place, that word being easily emended. For read "then" (that is, *eita*, namely "there was carried in procession") "etria." Then were carried forward *etria*, a kind of very thin cake made from the flower of wheat. If I knew for certain that *pyrenion* was once said of a dish, or a wooden carrier made in the manner of a pine cone or nut, or a pyramid, I would suspect it should be read "upon a pyrenion." But let this conjecture vanish into the breezes. **REISKE.** I observe that my manuscripts offer no help here, and the **Bodleian** omits everything from the word "agrostis" all the way to "pyrinon." **The Illustrious Abresch** in *Dilucidations on Thucydides* p. 390, conjectures it was "winding grass" (in *Theocritus* "low-spreading grass") "agrostis upon the kernels of the leader" or "for the leader" — "Cakes or Cakes, a pot standing upright." **Valentinus** had corrected it to "wound around." *Moeris the Atticist* p. 204: "ilyspomenos" in Attic, "eiloumenos" in common Greek. Where concerning this word the Learned Man (it is more correctly said *eilyspasthai* than *ilyspasthai*, See: **The Erudite Heringa** obs. c. 26.) Was it "eiloumene," that is, "being woven"? Concerning which word see also **Alberti** on *Hesychius* under "Elissomene." Or rather "a bundle, grass, agrostis." *Hesychius*: "Eile: the stalk of legumes." That certainly comes close to the writing and the matter being discussed. But there are enough conjectures. You choose. "Grass" and "agrostis" are well distinguished: the former is grass which cattle and quadrupeds eat, the latter is what physicians use, although this distinction is not permanent, as **Wesseling** rightly observes on *Diodorus* I, 43.

3. **Upon the kernels of the leader.** I think it was written *hegetrias* for *hegetorias* (for it is said both ways). For *pyrenion*, however, I would want *pyrinon* [of wheat] or *pyrinon*. They call *pyrenas* or *pyrinas* (for they are confused everywhere) the kernels by which, in fruits, the exterior and surrounding flesh is sustained...

# PORPHYRY

->**114**<-

...oaks, 4 arbutus berries, barley, wheat, 5 a pressed fruit cake, a "leader" cake, 6 a flat cake made of wheat and barley flour, 7 "upright" cakes, 8 and a pot. But when the first-fruits of the sacrifices, which were available to men, 9 moved far away from lawlessness, the adoption of the most terrible sacrifices was introduced, so that—

<column-break/>

wheat, barley, bundles of dried figs, and cakes made from wheat and barley flour, sweets, and even pots of legumes were customarily brought forward. Indeed, while the offerings made in sacrifices kept men far from injustice, the adoption of wicked victims was introduced, of a cruelty—

---

<margin>
<note>This note discusses botanical classifications.</note>
...is held, such as are found in cherries, olives, etc. Read *Bodaeus à Stapel* on *Theophrastus: Historia Plantarum III, 17.* Indeed, everything in a nut or a pine cone, or anything else that becomes fit for eating, as *Casaubon* teaches on *Athenaeus II, 16.* He signifies, therefore, what kind of *hegetoria* <note>original: ἡγητορίαν; a sacrificial cake</note> he wishes to be understood here.
</margin>

4. *Arbutus berries.* <note>original: Μιμαίκυλα</note>] What these are is known from the Lexicographers. Regarding the various spellings of the word, see *Valesius* on *Pollux VII, 144.*

<margin>
5. *Pressed fruit cake, leader cake.* <note>original: Παλάθη ἡγητηρία</note>] Unless this is a single phrase, *palathe* and *hegeteria* can be distinguished. The former pertains to the custom of the ancients, who, when they had dried figs, plums, and other things of that sort, used to thicken them into a mass and arrange them in various shapes and call them *palathai*. Consult *Wesseling* on *Diodorus XVIII, 67.* However, in *Suidas*, *palathe* is also *a type of herb*. And *Casaubon* (under the entry *Hegetores*): *the palathe of figs; a palathe is a mass of figs.* Certainly, a mass of dried figs that was carried in a procession is usually called *hegeteria* or *hegetoria*, *because they considered this the first civilized food.* <note>original: ὅτι ἥμερον τροφὴν πρώτην ταύτην ἡγήσαντο</note> See *Kuster* on *Suidas* and *Casaubon* on *Athenaeus III, 2.* For the fig was first discovered at Athens (while others previously fed themselves on acorns or other fruits, on which matter see *Aelian: Varia Historia III, 39.*), and thus a better way of living was introduced. See *Aelian: V. H. III, 38.* and *Meursius: Attic Lectures II, 13.*
</margin>

<margin>
6. *flat cake...* <note>original: φθόϊς</note>] This seems to be a nominative plural. And for *orthosatais* <note>upright</note> read *orthosatai kai* <note>upright [cakes] and</note>, and for *chytros* <note>pot</note> read *chytroi* <note>pots</note>. Thus three types of cakes are designated, encompassed by the general name of *etria* <note>honey-cakes</note>. *Phthois, orthosatai, chytroi.* What the differences between them were is not easy to say. Therefore, having removed foreign elements, the order of this passage runs roughly as follows: *processions of wheat (or wheaten flour), legumes, acorns, arbutus berries, barley, pressed cakes, honey-cakes made of wheat and barley flour, upright cakes, and pots.*
</margin>

<column-break/>

It seems the last kind received its name from the oil and honey poured over those cakes. These are the things which extemporaneous meditation suggested to one in a hurry; if they are not so polished and perfect as to leave nothing of doubt or obscurity, they nevertheless do not seem likely to be entirely useless or irrelevant. **REISKE.** I distinguish *phthois* and *orthos*. The ancient critics teach us that the former word is pronounced as one syllable by the Attics, but is a disyllable for others. I read it therefore as *phthois* (in the plural, as the Attics are accustomed). See *Suidas* and *Spanheim* on *Aristophanes: Plutus 676.* Then *orthosatai*, *a certain kind of sacred bread*, as *Pollux* says, *VI, 73.* which is certainly just as good as *Valesius's* *orthosates*, which he had substituted in the text.

7. *Pot.* <note>original: Χύτρος</note>] I would by no means dare to condemn this, on account of the manifold use of pots in sacred rites. See *Suidas* under the entry, and the *Scholiast on Aristophanes' Plutus 1198*, where a very timely scholion for this passage occurs in the margin of the Leiden manuscript, which *Hemsterhuis* published: *those who dedicate something in temples, or establish them, had a custom of bringing pots full of gruel and fine flour, or of cakes and ground legumes.*

8. *But when the... &c.* <note>original: Πόῤῥω δὲ τῶν</note>] You may read these words all the way to the end of this section also in *Eusebius: Preparation for the Gospel, Book I, p. 29 and Book IV, p. 151.* *Theodoret* also has a part of them in his *Sermon on Sacrifices*.

9. *Moved away.* <note>original: Προεχουσῶν</note>] In *Eusebius* it is printed as well as written in two places as *proiouson* <note>proceeding</note>. Specifically in the first and fourth of those books. **VICTORIUS.** Better in *Eusebius Book 3, Chapter 14: proiouson.* **VALESIUS.** Reiske preferred *proelthouson* <note>having gone forward</note>. The common reading *proechouson* <note>standing out/surpassing</note> can be defended, that is, *surpassing*; however, besides *Eusebius*, *Theodoret* also has *periouson* <note>being around/surviving</note>. Next, what *epeisagesthai* <note>to be introduced</note> means in this place is illustrated by *Wetstein* on the *Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews VII, 19.*

For some men became *atheists* <note>original: "ἄθεοι"</note>, that is, entirely alienated from the gods; others might rightly be called *evil-minded* <note>original: "κακόφρονες"</note> rather than *god-hating* <note>original: "κακόθεοι"</note>, because they considered the gods to be base and in no way superior to us in nature. Therefore the Divinity, as **Theophrastus** says, being indignant at both of these, seems to have imposed the appropriate punishment. Insofar as some men have become *godless*, others might justly be called *evil-minded* rather than *believers in evil gods*, because they lead themselves to believe the nature of the gods is mean and nothing better than ourselves: thus some appear to have become *non-sacrificers*, making no first-fruit offering of their possessions to the gods; while others are *evil-sacrificers* and have touched unlawful victims.

---

...almost, by a certain play of wit, the inhabitants are called *Thoes* <note>Greek: "Jackals"</note> by the author, with respect to the name of that city, in much the same way as the Trojans are compared to Jackals in *Homer's Iliad, Book 11, line 474*, where *Didymus says: "he spoke the words Thoes and Troes as similar and with the same ending."* And this is all the more likely because he had already spoken of this carnivorous animal above in Book I, chapter 13. If anyone, however, discovers a people called "Thoes" on this coast, I will most quickly remove my conjecture with a single stroke of the pen. The barbarian King of the Tauri, *Thoas*, is well known from *Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris, line 30.*

<margin>2.</margin> *'Snatched away -- they were.'*] A people is said to be *snatched away from among men* when they are completely destroyed. Those expressions "to be snatched away" or "to make snatched away" are common, as is "to be carried off," regarding cities which are not only suddenly captured but even overturned from their foundations. There is a sense of violence and speed in this matter. *D'Orville* beautifully examined the nature of this word in his notes on *Chariton, Book III, 7 and IV, 6.* The Greeks also say "to be pulled up" or "to be displaced," which we had above in Book I, 26; the distinction between these words is often scarcely <column-break/> noted. Compare the celebrated *Valckenaer on Herodotus, Book IV, chapter 204.*

<margin>3.</margin> *For insolence, etc.*] Those verses from *Hesiod's Works and Days, line 133*, were previously corrupted in this way: --- *nor to see the blessed ones, etc.* and *as is the custom for the immortals, etc.* VALENTINUS. These were also found corrupted in that manner in the *Bodleian, Leipzig, and Meerman manuscripts.* Thomas Canter had already corrected these from Hesiod in his *Various Readings, II, 24.*

<margin>4.</margin> *Regarding the Bassarae indeed.*] *Valentinus* does not have the word *de* <note>Greek: "indeed" or "truly"</note>, unlike all the others, both printed and manuscript. *Tauri* is written with a capital letter, as *Felicianus* well expressed it, contrary to what was usually done. He means the Tauri, a people of Scythia, who were formerly infamous on account of the human sacrifices made to Diana. The matter is very well known from ancient authors and the writings of Christians, who often cast this as a reproach against the pagans. See: *Minucius Felix, Octavius, chapter 6, and the commentators there.*

<margin>5.</margin> *To the [frenzy] of human [sacrifices], etc.*] The *Leipzig manuscript* reads *the... to these added*, and it was also thus in the *Florence* edition, which the *Lyon* edition followed.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 10. In Icarus <note>original: "Ἐν Ἰκάρῳ" - a deme or district in ancient Attica</note>, a part of Attica, they first killed a goat because it had nibbled on a grapevine. Likewise, Diomus, who was a priest of Jupiter Polieus <note>The "City-Protector" aspect of Zeus/Jupiter</note>, is said to have been the first to slaughter an ox, following an incident of this kind: While the Diipolia <note>A very ancient Athenian festival in honor of Zeus Polieus</note> was being celebrated, and the fruits had been prepared according to ancient custom for the rite, an ox approached and tasted the sacred meal <note>original: "pulte" / "πελάνου" - a thick sacrificial cake or porridge</note>. The priest, aided by the help of others who were present, killed the animal. Among the Athenians, these specific causes are cited; different stories are usually told among other peoples. Yet all are full of wretched—

<column-break/>

§ 10. In Icarus in Attica, they first laid hands on a goat because it cropped the vine. Diomus was the first to slay an ox; he was a priest of Zeus Polieus. During the celebration of the Diipolia, when the fruits had been prepared according to the ancient custom, the ox approached and tasted the sacred sacrificial cake. Taking as his accomplices the others who were present, he killed it. Among the Athenians, such specific reasons are given, while others are told among other peoples. But all are full of—

---

<margin>
The term *chernips* <note>original: "χέρνιψ"</note> refers to "water for the hands." In this passage, however, as is common in other authors, it should be understood as lustral water <note>holy water used for ritual purification</note>. See the notes by Duker on Thucydides, Book IV: 97. Regarding what they called the *chernibon* and *cherniba* <note>vessels for holy water</note>, the learned Pierson will also teach you beautifully in his notes on the Attic Moeris, page 414.
</margin>

1. **In Icarus.** Meursius corrects this to *Icarium*. See under the People of Attica, *Icaria*. VALENTIUS: Correct, and so reads Reiske.

2. **They laid hands on.** Felicianus rightly translates this as *interemerunt* <note>Latin: "they destroyed/killed"</note>. Xenophon in the *Expedition*, Book VII, page 403: "if anyone resists, we will attempt with your help to lay hands on them <note>original: "χειροῦσθαι" - to subdue or kill</note>." Otherwise, to "lay hands on" wild beasts means to *subdue* or *tame*, regarding which usage see Wesseling on Diodorus, V, 39.

3. **Cropped the vine.** Thus Valentius rightly restored it, and before him Fogerolles. Suidas defines "cropped" <note>original: "Ἀπέθρισεν"</note> as "sheared off." In this passage, Kuster did not act with the best faith; read Abresch, who most skillfully restores it in *Animadversions on Aeschylus*, II, 8. Consult also Barnes on the word in Euripides' *Helen*, line 1204.

4. **Of Zeus Polieus.** There was no city among the ancients that did not have some peculiar God or Goddess to whose care it especially committed itself. Hence, "City-Gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ πολιεῖς"</note> and "City-Keepers" <note>original: "πολιοῦχοι"</note>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

There was a great scarcity among them of this animal, which is otherwise very useful. Therefore, while they both ate bulls and slaughtered them in sacred rites, they spared the females for the sake of breeding. They ordained it as a <term>piaculum</term> <note>an act requiring expiation or a religious crime</note> if anyone should lay hands upon them. In this matter, it was undoubtedly utility and practical use that determined what was considered piety and impiety within one and the same species of cattle. Since these things are so, Theophrastus—who truly wishes to act with piety—rightly forbids the sacrifice of animals for these and other similar reasons.

<column-break/>

<note>original: Greek text of the passage above</note>
...this animal being useful, it was scarce among them. Therefore, they both tasted and offered first-fruits of the bulls. But sparing the females for the sake of offspring, they legislated that touching them was a defilement; and indeed, based on utility, they defined the pious and the impious act regarding one and the same genus of oxen. Since these matters stand in this way, Theophrastus reasonably forbids those who wish to be truly pious from sacrificing living creatures, employing these and other such arguments.

->§ 12.<-

->§ 12.<-

Our author <note>referring to Porphyry</note> mentions the Egyptians and Phoenicians quite often. See the end of this book, and Book IV, 7. *Jerome, in his second book against Jovinian, chapter 7: "In Egypt and Palestine, because of the rarity of cattle, no one eats a cow."* *Herodotus* testifies that the Barcaeans, Cyrenaeans, and the nomadic Africans from Egypt as far as Lake Tritonis abstain from eating the cow. Others say the same of different groups. See *Bochart, Hierozoicon II, 32.* It is therefore not surprising that even today the Brahmins of India—disciples of the ancient Egyptians, as some believe—abstain from cows, for which reason they abominate European Christians. See *Jablonski in the Prolegomena to the Egyptian Pantheon, p. 20.* Learn from our author the "secret of the State," the true cause of this abstinence. For since Egypt was not very fertile in animals, greater consideration was rightly given to the females than the males (not unlike how, during the recent plague, the most provident Fathers of our Country took measures). A matter useful to the public was later turned into a superstition, and thus gave occasion for the worship of beasts. It will not be a regret to have read *Mosheim's notes on Cudworth’s System, p. 918*, which our author could have defended excellently. *Wesseling, in his notes on Herodotus II, 41*, observes that this superstition lasted until the times of the Emperor Constantius. We ought not to dwell here on the opinion of *Spencer (Ritual Laws II, 15)* that God once willed a cow to be slaughtered so that the Hebrews might be led to contempt and hatred of the Egyptian cow-worship.

§ 12. First, because it was out of a greater necessity <note>original: *anankēs*</note>—as we have already stated—falling upon us, that they first began these sacrifices. Furthermore, one must render thanks and returns for benefits to different beings in different ways, according to the merit of the kindness. To those who have performed the greatest services for us, we owe the greatest returns, drawn from the most precious things—especially if they themselves are the providers of those very things. Now, the finest and most precious things with which the gods benefit us are the fruits of the earth. § 13. But perhaps someone will say that we also take something from plants when we make offerings of fruits to the gods. But that taking is not similar: for it is not done to the unwilling. We must, therefore, abstain from animals in sacrifices. § 15. And indeed, the outcome of the event itself testifies that these things please the gods more than those which require great expense. For when once that Thessalian was immolating oxen with gilded horns and hecatombs to the Pythian Apollo, the Pythian priestess asserted that the man from Hermione had been more pleasing to her—

2. *Cultivated fruits*] Perhaps read as "certain ones." REISKE <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>. Where *Lipsius* and *Meerman* have "from the earth," it is not bad.
</margin>

1. *The gods [more] than the costly.*] The word "more" is understood, the absence of which is not unusual in this kind of word order. > But the grain-cake of the far-famed man of Hermione was pleasing to me. <note>original: "Ἀλλά μοι εὔαδε χόνδρος ἀγακλυτοῦ Ἑρμιονῆος."</note>

These were the sacrifices of the poorer sort, hardly different from those, as is also clear from what is read below in § 17. The wealthy threw *incense* and other offerings of that kind onto the altar, and they observed that they should offer either the *incense* or the *fruits* with the tips of their fingers, as *Casaubon* writes on *Theophrastus' Characters*, p. 232. Indeed, it was customary for this to be done with three fingers. *Ovid*, *Fasti* II, 573.
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

...sin, who had offered cakes from a small basket using only three fingers. When that man, because of what had been said <note>referring to a previous oracle or divine statement praising the small gift</note>, threw all the rest of his belongings into the fire upon the altar, the divinity spoke again, saying that he had made himself twice as unwelcome by doing so as he had previously been pleasing. Thus, that which is easily provided is dear to the gods; the divine power looks more to the spirit and character of those who sacrifice than to the abundance of the victims.

§ 16. Theopompus <note>A Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> has also recorded similar things. He says there was a certain man of Magnesia in Asia, who was exceedingly wealthy. Since he possessed a great abundance of cattle, he was accustomed to perform many magnificent sacrifices to the gods every year, partly because of his great wealth and partly because of his piety—

<column-break/>

—cakes from the small bag with his three fingers. But when he, because of what was said, cast all the rest into the fire upon the altar, the voice said again that he was twice as much hated for doing this as he was formerly favored. Thus, the inexpensive is dear to the gods, and the divine looks toward the character <term>ethos</term> of those who sacrifice rather than the quantity <term>plethos</term> of the things sacrificed.

§ 16. Theopompus relates similar things, saying that a man of Magnesia from Asia came to Delphi; he was very rich and owned many flocks. He was accustomed to make many grand sacrifices to the gods every year, partly due to his prosperity—

---

<margin>
*And he places three grains of incense with three fingers beneath the threshold.*
Compare Bodaeus à Stapel on Theophrastus's *History of Plants*, Book IX, chapter 4. Therefore, the man from Hermione was content with that kind of sacrifice which the wealthy were accustomed to add to others, and which they properly called "to sacrifice additionally" <note>original: ἐπιθύειν (epithyein)</note>, as will be discussed in another place.

</margin>

The syllable *ma* (in the word *soma*, "body") was born from the final letter *n* of the word *toson* ("so much") and the *a* from the start of the following word *apechthoito* ("he might be hated"). REISKE. Excellent. Fogerolles and Valentinus have already corrected it to "twice as much." It was no different in the Bodleian Codex. Rightly, therefore, Needham restored it thus. I was unwilling to allow "the body" <note>original: τὸ σῶμα (to soma)</note>, which used to be read, to remain any longer.
</margin>

<column-break/>

—ancient sages repeat a hundred times. I will only bring forward Plato in the *Alcibiades* (page 459 B) because it is a most beautiful passage: *For it would be a terrible thing if the gods looked to our gifts and sacrifices, and not to the soul, if one happens to be holy and just. Much more so, I think, than to these costly processions and sacrifices.* And consider that which happened to the widow in the Gospel, Mark 12:43. Note also the elegant wordplay <term>paronomasia</term> between "character" <note>original: ἦθος (ethos)</note> and "quantity" <note>original: πλῆθος (plethos)</note>, which ancient authors often like to pursue. Among others, Alberti has much on this matter regarding Luke 8:30. Such is the case in § 19: "dear to God" <note>original: θεοφιλεῖς (theophileis)</note> and "costly" <note>original: πολυτελεῖς (polyteleis)</note>.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

-> R <-

And when he had quickly arrived at Methydrium <note>A small town in Arcadia, Greece</note>, at first, having observed the smallness and humility of the town, he so despised the matter that he did not think any private individual there, nor even the entire city, could worship the gods more excellently or magnificently than himself. Nevertheless, he approached the man and requested that he explain the manner in which he worshipped the gods. But Clearchus spoke thus: "I indeed always sacrifice to the gods with the greatest diligence at the appointed times; while every single month at the new moons <note>original: "nouiluniis"</note>, I crown and adorn Mercury, and Hecate, and the rest of the gods whom our ancestors left to us, and with frankincense for them, and cakes, and—

<column-break/>

And when he had quickly arrived at Methydrium, at first he looked down upon it, the size of the place being small and humble, thinking that not only could no private citizen, but not even the city itself, honor the gods more magnificently or beautifully than he did. But nevertheless, having met the man, he asked him to tell him in what way he honors the gods. And Clearchus said that he performs and zealously offers sacrifice at the proper times, every month at the new moons crowning and cleansing the statues of Hermes <note>Mercury</note> and Hecate, and the rest of the sacred objects which his ancestors left behind, and honoring them with frankincense and barley cakes—

***

I ought to have warned there, we have the same form in *Plato:* in *Gorgias:* p. 327. E. concerning other Teachers: *Abresch:* Dil: Thuc: Auct: p. 282. In this place *Meermann* more correctly reads: *to desire.*

6. **Of small ---- size of the place.**] The word *magnitude* <note>original: "μέγεθος"</note> here signifies nothing other than the *space and circuit* of the town, and is a term common to both a great thing and a small one. Therefore the comma is rightly absent from "being" in the *Leipzig Manuscript.* I will not hide, however, that it seems to me Theopompus gave it thus: "being humble in respect to the size of the place." REISKE. *Pausanias* says in Book VIII, p. 475 & 512: "Methydrium is no longer a city, but a village contributing to the Megalopolitan district." For from the time Megalopolis was founded, it degenerated into a village. Compare the Learned Men on *Thucydides:* V, 58. "Small of size" seems to be a species of oxymoron, about which kind of speaking the Learned Men have said much. The opposite, "cities greatest in size," was elegantly said by *Aelian:* V. H. III, 18. Read other examples

<column-break/>

in *Wesseling:* on *Herodotus:* I, 19.

7. **Every month etc.**] A most ancient Athenian law: *to sacrifice at the New Moons,* which sacred rites were called *monthly* <note>original: "ἐπιμήνια"</note>. See: *Petit:* Laws of Attica, Book I, 1. p. 158. Hence *Plato* in *Laws:* VIII. p. 905. B. says: "there are twelve festivals for the twelve gods. Whichever tribe is named after each, for these there are monthly sacrifices." Therefore, since that custom was very frequent among the gentiles long before the age of Moses, God formerly willed that victims be sacrificed to Him at the new moons, lest the Israelites, being more addicted to ancient customs, should sacrifice to the deities of the Nations, as it seemed to *Spencer:* on Ritual Laws: III, 4.

8. **To honor with frankincense.**] It was written in the margin of the *Leipzig* & *Meermann Manuscripts:* <margin>Frankincense <note>original: "λιβανωτός"</note> is the aroma produced from the incense tree. Barley cakes <note>original: "ψαιςὰ"</note> are meal moistened with oil and wine from the scrapings of the mill, which they burned for the gods; and sacrificial cakes <note>original: "πόπανα"</note> are flat, thin, and round cakes.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

...and with round sacrificial cakes. <note>original: "ποπάνοις" / "placentis"</note> Every year I perform public sacrifices, omitting no solemn festival. In these very festivals, I worship the gods not by slaughtering oxen, nor by cutting up sacrificial victims, but by offering whatever happens to be at hand. I make it a point, however, to offer the firstfruits to the gods from all the seasonal fruits <note>original: "καρπῶν καὶ τῶν ὡραίων"</note> that are received from the earth; some of these I set before them, and others I consecrate by fire. <note>original: "καθαγιάζειν" / "adolere"</note> Because I am devoted to self-sufficiency, I have never even considered the sacrifice of oxen.

§ 17. It has been recorded by certain historians that when the tyrants, after defeating the Carthaginians, <note>A reference to the Battle of Himera (480 BCE) where Gelon of Syracuse defeated the Carthaginian forces.</note> [offered] a hecatomb... <note>A hecatomb is a grand sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>9. *And with sacrificial cakes.*] See the celebrated Rhunken’s notes on Timaeus’s Platonic Lexicon under *Popana*, where the reading matches the cited scholium, except that "pastries" <note>original: "πέμματα"</note> is used instead of "flat-cakes." Suidas and Photius also prefer this in their manuscript lexicons. Compare Suidas under *Anasatoi*, where the interpreter incorrectly says *popana* are also called *placentae* (cheesecakes), an error corrected by the elegant Toup in his *Emendations of Suidas*, p. 36. The word migrated into Latin; see Juvenal, Satire VI, 540: *"Osiris corrupted by a thin sacrificial cake."* Frankincense and the *popanon* cake are joined in Menander, below at section 17, where more is said.

10. *Of fruits and seasonal things.*] REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note> notes that *seasonal things* <note>original: "ὡραῖα"</note> also includes those things produced annually from animals at fixed times. However, *seasonal fruits* are properly all fruits coming from the earth which were used according to the season of the year—spring, summer, etc.—as they were born in their own hour <note>original: "ὥρᾳ"</note> or rather reached maturity. For the text speaks of mature fruits, not immature ones as the Learned Gentleman <note>original: "V. D." - Vir Doctus</note> suggested in his notes on Diogenes Laertius II, 32. This is certain from what Graevius and Wesseling have taught.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>11. *To consecrate.*] Perhaps it should read *kathagizein*: to burn to ashes, to consume by fire. REISKE. Felicianus also translated this as *adolere* (to burn/worship), and certainly *kathagizein* is frequently used for victims placed on the altar and consumed by fire. See Wesseling on Diodorus IV, 23. These words are very often confused with one another. For an example, see what the Learned Gentlemen observed on Pollux I, 26.

12. *Considered the sacrifice of oxen.*] REISKE notes that before "considered" <note>original: "προνοεῖσθαι"</note> the word "not" or "nothing" is missing. Unless you take "considered" in the sense of "taking precautions against" or "avoiding," as found in Henri Estienne’s Thesaurus.

1. *The tyrants.*] I believe Porphyry is referring to the history found in Diodorus Siculus, Book XI, and Herodotus, Book VII, concerning Gelon and his allies. VALENTINI. Diodorus (XI, 24) records Gelon’s affairs with the Carthaginians, but nothing there fits this specific passage. Herodotus (VII, 65) relates that Gelon reported a victory over the Carthaginians and sent money to Delphi.

2. *Having presented hecatombs.*] "To present" <note>original: "Παραστῆσαι"</note> is the proper technical term for sacrifices. We saw this in section 25...</margin>

...among themselves, and in a spirit of rivalry after the Carthaginians had been defeated, they brought forth distinguished Hecatombs <note>A "Hecatomb" was originally a sacrifice of one hundred oxen; here it refers to any massive, expensive animal sacrifice.</note> to Apollo.
