<meta>This page continues the discussion of Porphyry's "On Abstinence from Animal Food," specifically focusing on the superiority of simple offerings like incense over bloody sacrifices. It references fragments from the comic poets Antiphanes and Menander.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

The proof of this is that whenever people sacrifice hecatombs <note>A "hecatomb" was originally a sacrifice of 100 oxen, but came to mean any large-scale public sacrifice.</note>, after all these things, incense is placed on top as the very last act.

As if to say that while many other things are consumed alongside,
Being a vain expense for their own sake,
This small thing itself is what is pleasing to the gods.

And Menander says in *The Grouch* <note>original: "Dyscolus," a famous play by Menander rediscovered in the 20th century.</note>:
The incense and the sacrificial cake are a pious offering;
This the god accepted when the whole was placed upon the fire.

<column-break/>

Supplying the proof of this matter,
For when someone has made a sacrifice from a herd of oxen, he says,

After everything, the vapor of incense is added to the altars
Last of all: so that the ample abundance of the rest
Might display nothing but the glory of those offering them,
And vain expenses: but that which is brought in at the last place,
That small bit is seen to please the gods.

Indeed, Menander also in *The Morose*—that is the name of the play—speaks thus:
From this comes the pious offering of incense and libations,

Which, cast into the flames, the god accepted in its entirety.

---

->§ 18.<-

<margin>From the law of the meter, it appears either that the ancients wrote *libanotos* (incense) with an 'o', or that in poetry they used 'o' and 'a' interchangeably. The argument of the matter is this: when they sacrificed hecatombs, incense is offered last of all and placed upon the altar. REISKE.</margin>
*As in Antiphanes, etc.*] There were various men of this name: the one signified here is he whom most think was from Rhodes, concerning whom see *Fabricius, Bibliotheca Graeca II, 22.* *Athenaeus* also praises this comedy in Book X, 11 (where he teaches it was a conversation of women, and there was no reason why *Dalechamps* thought it should be read as *Amystiden*) and Book 13. This *Mysis*, or "the initiated woman," seems to have taught a form of divine worship that was celebrated not with pomp and immense costs, but with a pure and holy mind. For it is credible that the Comic poet in this play wished to prick and rub raw the corrupt laws and ceremonies of sacred rites, as was well observed by the distinguished Tibertius Hemsterhuis in his notes to *Pollux X, 67*, who did not forget this fragment. Now as to the verses themselves, Valentini has stated what Hugo Grotius's opinion was; however, it is not for nothing that instead of "was placed upon" (*epetethē*), one reads there

<column-break/>

->§ 18.<-

"was sacrificed upon" (*epethuthē*). Certainly, "to sacrifice upon" would fit best here. Compare what is said in § 59. In any case, it does not seem probable to me that all those words which the Author introduces are by Antiphanes, until he reaches Menander. I am persuaded that most of them were taken from the poet, but not expressed in a continuous series. If the judgment of my ears does not deceive me, those words "the proof of this is" seem to belong to the philosopher rather than the Comic poet. I will not be anxious about the meter for this reason: if you note that in those verses Grotius was not always consistent with himself, I would wish you to remember that this Great Man everywhere took greater care for the meaning than for the measure. Furthermore, the word "the" (*ta*) before "such things" was missing in the *Meerman* manuscript, in which a <insert>marginal note</insert> was added: "Sopater also says this in his *Excerpts of Histories*." And it is the same in the *Leipzig* manuscript, but there instead of "says," it is "brings forward."

7. *Menander in The Grouch, etc.*] In the *Fragments of Menander, p. 52*, it is read thus:
- - - - - - the incense is a pious thing
And the sacrificial cake. This the god accepted upon the fire

Certainly, it should have been read here as "kerameiois," but we have said elsewhere that *ei* and *i* are confused a hundred times in this sort of thing.

5. **Elaborately worked.** <note>original: "Περιέργως εἰργασμένα."</note> You will easily understand what kind of things these were if you consider the force and power of the word *periergazesthai* <note>to take needless trouble</note>. It is, in fact, *to work on something with excessive care*. Hence it is commonly said of extreme and immoderate zeal spent on a matter, from which *periergon* began to denote whatever involves excessive and superfluous labor. Let students consult *Perizonius on Aelian's Varia Historia II, 44*; the prefix *peri-* <note>around/excessively</note> usually functions this way in other compounds.

These things ought to be explained by the use of wool in the sacrifices of the ancients, as *wool and fleece* are often joined together. Presently *olais*, that is *oulaîs* <note>barley groats</note>, for the ancients used the letters *o*, *ō*, and *ou* interchangeably; and *oulaì* are the same as *olaì krithaì*: grains of barley not yet crushed by the millstone. — REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century German physician and philologist</note>

4. *There was a mixed medley of all fruits* etc.] Incorrectly in *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch jurist and scholar.</note>:
*In which there was a mixed medley of all fruits in husks.*
Better in *Clement of Alexandria*, although with the order slightly disturbed: *There was a mixed medley of all fruits.* which might seem more poetic. The term *pankarpia* <note>original: παγκάρπια; a sacrificial offering of all kinds of fruits.</note> perhaps displeased the scribe, who was unaware that many words of this kind are expressed in both ways. The Lexicographers teach what *oulai* <note>original: οὐλαὶ; sacrificial barley groats.</note> were. It comes to the same thing whether you write it that way or as *holai* <note>meaning "whole" or "entire".</note>. Neglect of this observation caused a Learned Man to cast blame on *Lucian*, from which *D’Orville* <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville, an 18th-century classicist.</note> frees him in his notes on *Chariton IV, 2*. The meter in this passage requires the latter.

5. *of the tawny bee* etc.] In *Clement*, "of oil" is published instead of "of the olive," and "yellow" instead of "tawny." But the poets love the latter, as in a fragment of *Antiphanes* in *Athenaeus X, 15* and below in section 21. In the *Scholia on Euripides*, which praises this little verse, it is read as "of the tawny bee" etc. *Valckenaer* <note>Lodewijk Caspar Valckenaer, a Dutch classical scholar.</note> thought that this proceeded from Sophocles, not without cause; see his notes on *Euripides' Phoenician Women, p. 622*. He elegantly calls honey the "tool of the bee." "Tool" instead of "work." See the *Scholia on Euripides* in the place cited. Poets everywhere call it the "works of the bee," see the note on I, 21. Note also the use of honey in sacred rites, which they believed was most pleasing to the gods. See *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus V, 62*. This was otherwise than what pleased the Hebrew lawgiver <note>A reference to the prohibition of honey in certain Jewish burnt offerings (Leviticus 2:11).</note>, but that does not pertain to this passage.

6. *And there were venerable... of those* etc.] In the most ancient times, it was customary for the sacred objects of the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people of the far north who worshipped Apollo.</note> to be sent to the island of Delos—sheaves of grain—and this was done with solemn pomp and dancing. *Amallai* denotes sheaves of grain, and we read that the Athenians performed rites to

<column-break/>

*Amallophoros* <note>The "Sheaf-bearer."</note> Ceres <note>The Roman name for Demeter, goddess of the harvest.</note>. Specifically, however, sheaves of barley are understood, the first-fruits of barley: for those whom our Author calls "sheaf-bearers," *Servius* in his notes on the *Aeneid XI, 858* calls "barley-bearers." But you may read quite diverse accounts of these things, depending on whether the authors drew from the ambitious narratives of the Athenians or from elsewhere. For me, the distinguished men whom I see summoned to this matter by the interpreter of *Herodotus IV, 33* have spared me further labor. Since Delos, having been previously devastated, perhaps recovered some splendor under Hadrian, it might be doubted whether that rite had already fallen into disuse in Porphyry's time or not? You might conclude the former from this passage, and yet below in section 28, he speaks of those rites as if they were still celebrated in his own time. From this, it can be made probable that while the other monuments of Delos were in bad condition, the altar mentioned there had not been violated. See the arguments of the Learned Man in *Miscellaneous Observations Vol. VII. T. I. p. 83*. Certainly, I do not know from where it could be proven that the Emperor Hadrian granted the Athenians the right to administer those rites according to the ancient custom. *Plutarch* at least (T. II. p. 1136. A.) says that in ancient times those rites were sent to Delos with the use of flutes, pipes, and lyres. Since *Aelian* (V. H. III, 1), who is later than him, speaks of that matter as something observed even at that time, it must be understood as referring to the previous century.

# PORPHYRY

...offering these sacrifices as dear to the gods, rather than those that are merely expensive. But as it stands, people believe that if they are clothed in a splendid garment over a body that is not <gloss>9</gloss> clean, it is not sufficient for the purity required of sacrifices. Yet, when some have <gloss>10</gloss> brightened their bodies along with their clothing, while possessing a soul that is not clean of evils, they go toward the sacrifices and believe it makes no difference. This is as if God does not rejoice most in the most divine element within us when it is in a pure state, seeing as it is of a nature akin to His own. At least in Epidaurus <note>A major religious center in ancient Greece, famous for the sanctuary of Asclepius</note>, this inscription was posted <gloss>11</gloss> for those entering within the fragrant temple:

->One must be pure who enters the fragrant temple;<-
->And purity is to think holy thoughts.<-

<margin>The word "most slender" <note>original: λετάτας</note> is treated as a single word by Reiske. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a Church Father</note> took these passages from our author in Book IX *Against Julian*, page 310, where he gave the phrase "sacrifices dear to God." Regarding the matter itself, see § 15. Just as Porphyry does, Clement of Alexandria says in *Stromata* VII, page 719: "It is necessary, therefore, to offer sacrifices to God that are not expensive, but dear to God."</margin>

<margin>9. **Clothed in a clean [garment].** Valentinus had given "clothed in a clean [thing]" <note>original: καθαρὸν</note>. But the earlier editions and the Lipsius and Meermann manuscripts have "clothed in a clean [garment]" <note>original: καθαρὰν, feminine to match 'veste'</note>. In Cyril it is "having been clothed." This is a slight matter, but it makes a great difference whether you read "clean" in the feminine or masculine. The older editions and the Meermann manuscript gave the former, except that the scribe wrote "lyre" <note>original: κιθάραν</note> by a slip of the pen. The translator of Cyril does not differ: "now if we have been clothed in a splendid garment, *not a clean one*." Certainly, a "splendid" garment and a "clean" one differ, just as "white" and "clean" are distinguished below in § 45. The Pythagoreans used clothing that was "white and clean." See Iamblichus in *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 21. The former refers to the color and external brilliance, the latter to the material,</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>or if it were polluted by any other thing that did not suit the sacred rites. The Latins call the former "white," "bright," etc., and the latter "pure" or "chaste." Both are used in sacred rites. See Broukhusius on Tibullus I, II, 27. The words that follow prove that "clean" <note>original: καθαρὰν</note> is the true reading here.</margin>

<margin>10. **Having brightened, not...** Cyril has "Being brightened, or clean," where one should rewrite "not clean," and then "being disposed" instead of "of those being disposed." Also, "was inscribed" <note>original: προσεγέγραπτο</note> is wrongly placed there for "was posted" <note>original: προεγέγραπτο</note>; for those words differ. Note also the construction "clean of evils." The Greeks are accustomed to use that mode so that the thing signified by that case is excepted and excluded. We have the phrase "a place clean of evils" in Plato's *Theaetetus*, page 129, from which Plotinus took it in *Enneads* VI. 9, page 768, and Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel*, page 606. Read other things of this kind in R. W. on Hierocles' *Golden Verses*, page 252. A little after, "just as not even to the divine." Meermann manuscript.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 20. Moreover, it can be clearly seen that God is not delighted by the abundance and magnitude of sacrifices, but by a pious simplicity. This is evident from our daily food; whatever is served to us, we are all accustomed to offer a small libation <note>A ritual pouring of a drink as an offering</note> to the gods before we taste anything ourselves. Though that offering is small, the estimation of that small gift is the greatest of all. Furthermore, since Theophrastus has shown through many ancient ancestral customs of various peoples—

<column-break/>

§ 20. That God does not rejoice in the bulk of sacrifices, but in whatever happens to be offered, <gloss>1</gloss> is shown by our daily nourishment; no matter what kind of food is set out, everyone begins the meal by offering a small portion before enjoying it. Though it is small, there is a certain great honor in this small thing above all else. Through many <gloss>2</gloss> ancestral traditions <gloss>3</gloss> of each people, Theophrastus demonstrated <gloss>4</gloss> that in ancient times—

<note>The following section contains scholarly commentary on the Greek and Latin text, discussing various manuscript readings and corrections.</note>

We think that instead of *emphamen* (we say), *embamen* (to step in) should be read. "Purity" etc. were separated from the rest. Unjustly indeed, as I have judged. Therefore, I have restored it to its proper place. VALENTINUS. The more people who mention the inscription, the more certainly we can restore the true writing. Just as we provide it here, so also does *Clement of Alexandria in Stromata, Book V, p. 551,* although the meter was not preserved there; and *Cyril in Book IX, p. 310, Against Julian,* where instead of *naoio* (of the temple), which has occupied all editions of Porphyry, you should restore *nēoio*. For that, and *hagneiē* (purity) (for previously it was read as *hagneia*), belongs to the dialect. In the *Leipzig Manuscript* it was *emphamena hagneia*. In the *Bodleian and Meerman Manuscripts* it was *emphamenai*. This almost agrees with that ancient *emphamen* or *emphamen* which was read before. Learned men have illustrated this matter in notes to *Clement* and *Aelian, Varia Historia II, 31,* and many others.

1. **It is shown from etc.**] This "from" is suited to the infinitive "to begin," or rather, as I think it should be read, "to be content with." I would also prefer the word "clear," for "to be content with" would better suit the word "clear," but "from the" responds more aptly to the word "clear." Therefore, I will arrange the passage thus: *It is clear from the fact that whatever kind of daily food is offered to him (God), he is certainly more content with that than with delicacies themselves. Granted, let that which is served repeatedly be small. And yet.* — REISKE. Instead of "of this" in the older *Leipzig and Meerman* editions (which had *protōn* for *pro tōn*), the *Manuscript* had "these," and instead of "of the daily" it had "those daily," which *Fogerolles* supplemented in the margin as "those touching [the food]." Both he and *Valentinus* replaced "to begin" with "to offer first-fruits." But "to begin" is often used for "to offer first-fruits." "It shows," namely God shows. "It shows that from the," was pleasing to the *Celebrated Abresch.* It is a known custom, derived even from the heroic ages, that before guests filled themselves with food, they offered the first-fruits to the Gods.

2. **Theophrastus.**] Does he mean the books of Theophrastus *On History* or *Historical Commentaries* mentioned by *Diogenes Laertius V, 47* and others? I would prefer the books *On Piety*, the same ones mentioned above in § 5 and 11 and below in 26; in all of those, he speaks of sacrifices. *Fabricius (B.G. III, 9, 16)* thinks the *History of Divine Matters* is referred to, but those things which follow shortly after at the beginning of § 21 were sought from those records I mentioned, as I shall show from *Photius's Lexicon* under the word *Mito*.

3. **Ancestral [customs] of each.**] It is well known that the word "customs" is frequently omitted in this phrasing. The *Bodleian Manuscript* gives "paternal," as those words are usually confused since they mean almost the same thing. Certainly, authors much wealthier in vocabulary than the Grammarians often disregard their rules on the distinction between them, using both "paternal laws" and "ancestral laws." However, Porphyry uses "ancestral" again below in IV, 22, and they certainly tend to call the manners and institutions of the ancestors "the ancestral" rather than "the paternal." Consult the *Learned Men on Thucydides VIII, 76.*

4. **That in ancient times.**] The word "the" is not in the *Leipzig Manuscript*.

# PORPHYRY

...that the ancient custom of sacrifices consisted of the fruits of the earth—having stated even earlier that grasses were used—he now explains the ritual of libations in this manner: The ancient sacrifices among most peoples were "sober" <note>original: *nephalia* (νηφάλια), meaning wineless offerings</note>. Sober offerings are those that consist of water libations. After these came libations of honey; for we received this liquid fruit, prepared by bees, as the first of its kind. Then came libations of oil. Finally, at the very end, came the later practice of libations of wine.

§ 21. These matters are attested not only by the pillars inscribed in the *kyrbeis* <note>triangular or square tablets, often of wood or bronze, used in ancient Greece to display laws and sacred rites</note>

*Lipsius:* Perhaps the word "still" <note>Greek: *eti* (ἔτι)</note> does not mean "yet" in this passage, but "as." For example, "as ancient as possible." Instead of "having said" <note>Greek: *eipon* (εἰπὼν)</note>, by a slight change I once conjectured "annual" <note>Greek: *epeteion* (ἐπετείων)</note>, which would refer to the fruits, or "annual grass," as Theophrastus says above in § 5, a passage to which Porphyry refers. The words "to explain," "explanation," and "interpreter" <note>Greek: *exēgeisthai, exēgēsis, exēgētēs*</note> are peculiarly used by our author and others regarding the interpreters of ceremonies, or even of omens and prodigies. <margin>
5. "Sober among..." etc.] What these "sober" sacrifices were, Suidas in his entry on "Sober Sacrifice" and a hundred others have taught. However, while it is true that the older the worship of the Gods, the simpler it was, I would not want to affirm that the order which Malchus <note>another name for Porphyry</note> relates was exactly observed. Potter felt the same in *Grecian Antiquities* II, 4. A little before, Meermann reads "and the ancient things," and soon for "the liquid [fruit]," that manuscript and Lipsius read "of the liquids," which rightly pleased Reiske; then the same manuscripts read "the later things," which I approve, and so does the oldest edition. That phrase "above all," "besides all these," or "finally," is illustrated by Wetstein on Luke XVI, 26, not forgetting this passage.

<margin>
1. "By the pillars in the *kyrbeis*."] I thought these words could perhaps be read better as "by the pillars in Kyrbe, which are of the Cretans," etc. For first, although I knew that *kyrbeis* among the Athenians were wooden or stone pyramidal blocks on which laws regarding sacred matters were written, yet I nowhere find in those *kyrbeis* anything described pertaining to the Corybantic rites <note>ecstatic rituals associated with the goddess Cybele</note>, nor, what is more, do I find that those rites ever publicly prevailed among the Athenians. I know what can be said about the *Metroum* <note>the temple of the Mother of the Gods</note>. But even that does not seem to prove this clearly enough. Furthermore, "in-kyrbeis" <note>Greek: *enkyrbesin*</note> as a single word occurs nowhere. And if it were admitted here without precedent, I do not see how it could be conveniently translated. That Kyrbe is a town in Crete is clear from Stephanus' *On Cities* under "Hierapytna." I could also prove with many arguments, if it were worth the effort, that the Corybantes were transferred from Phrygia to Crete, and those rites were likewise sent there. So that it is fitting enough to say that in Phrygia there are the "original writings" <note>Greek: *tau-grapha*</note> of the Corybantic rites, and in Crete the "copies" <note>Greek: *antigrapha*</note>. But I decide nothing in this matter. Let the learned judge. VALENT. A not inept conjecture concerning that city is in Meursius' *Crete*, chapter 10.
</margin>

<margin>
Strabo says the city was founded by Corybas (Book X, p. 325), but it is clear that the word *kyrbeis* <note>triangular wooden tablets for laws</note> came to our author's pen from Theophrastus, as cited in Photius's unpublished Lexicon: "*kyrbeis* are triangular axles or... it is said to be named from being peaked (*kekoryphōsthai*) at the top... but Theophrastus says they are named after the Cretan Corybantes. For they are, as it were, copies of the Corybantic rites." This passage is of great value to us, because it teaches that these are also the words of Theophrastus, from whom Porphyry draws much both just before and in the preceding sections. These were taken from Theophrastus's book *On Piety*, as the most learned David Ruhnken—a distinguished man—kindly pointed out to me in correspondence. I learned this from the Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Birds* (line 1354): "*Kyrbeis* are named from the Corybantes, for they were their invention, as Theophrastus says in *On Piety*." Do not say that I act in bad faith by writing "Theophrastus" in the Scholiast, when in all editions "Theopompus" is read. It is clear enough from my arguments that there is no place for Theopompus here. Therefore, the book *On Piety* should be deleted from the catalog of the works of the historian Theopompus, where Meursius, Vossius, and others—deceived by a corrupt reading—placed it. Thus far the celebrated Ruhnken. To the same scholar, it seemed that the word "pillars" (*stēlōn*) should be ejected from the text, as it had crept in from a gloss <note>a marginal explanation that accidentally entered the main text</note>. If the decision were mine, I would rewrite it: "by the [sacrifices] from the *kyrbeis* and pillars." Plato joins them thus in the *Statesman* (p. 555 B): "writing on *kyrbeis* and pillars." Eusebius in *Life of Constantine* (I, 1): "others engraving lines on *kyrbeis* and deep pillars." The illustrious Abresch, who held the same opinion as I, added from Themistius (Oration 30): "how it is necessary to perform sacrifices, those from the *kyrbeis* and the pillars, according to the writings." For so Taylor established it in his work on the *Cyrbe*.
</margin>

From Pollux, Suidas, and a hundred others, all these things are widely known: among later writers especially, all monuments testifying to the memory of some matter are called thus. See Hemsterhuis on Pollux (VIII, 128). Furthermore, in the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts, it was written: "*kyrbeis*: triangular tablets in which the laws concerning sacred and civil matters were kept; *axones* were square ones, in which private laws were kept." In the margin of the Bodleian manuscript, it was corrected to "on the *kyrbeis*." Regarding the most ancient custom of handing down famous discoveries, laws, and other things to posterity on columns, stones, walls, and bronze tablets, nothing need be said here. However, let the student note that by *stēlas* <note>pillars</note> one should not understand columns properly so-called, but stones which were mostly square, artistically polished and smoothed. Their use spread from the Egyptians to other nations, on which matter see Jablonski in *Egyptian Pantheon* (V, 5).

2. **The ones from Crete, etc.**] Who the Corybantes <note>armed, rhythmic dancers who worshipped the goddess Cybele</note> were has been excellently investigated and demonstrated by learned men; see Wesseling on Diodorus (III, 55). *Antigrapha* are copies. Attic writers love the plural number even when speaking of a single copy. On this matter, see Thomas Magister and other grammarians. See Wolf on Libanius (Epistle 1044). However, more recent writers do not always reject the singular number. Plutarch in *Life of Alexander* (Vol. I, p. 668 B): "he writes a letter of which there is a copy (*antigraphon*)." But see the learned men on Moeris the Atticist (p. 7). As our author uses it, "copies of a pillar" in Demosthenes (*Against Leptines*, p. 378). Instead of the word "the" (*ta*), the learned Ruhnken preferred "certain" (*hatta* or *tina*).

3. **Nor was there any, etc.**] These seven continuous verses of Empedocles are also cited by Athenaeus in the *Deipnosophistae* (Book XII), near the beginning of the book, where he discourses on pleasure. In his version, these are varied, because the third verse is halved, thus:

# On Abstinence, Book II.

...thinking. But after Mars <note>The Roman god of war; the Greek text uses Ares.</note> and turmoil, and every kind of battle and occasion for war invaded: then for the first time it came to pass that no one abstained from the slaughter of their own kind. Furthermore, these matters must be considered in this way: just as we believe that, although a kinship exists among humans, those evildoers who are driven by the impulse of their own nature and depravity to inflict harm on anyone should be killed and punished; so too among the animals lacking reason, it is perhaps appropriate to kill those which are unjust by their own nature and malicious, incited to harm and attack the human race. However, to kill the rest, which are endowed with no such cruelty for harming, is without a doubt unjust, no differently than killing men who are not injurious. § 23. Should we then sacrifice to the gods those animals that deserve to be slaughtered? And how could that be right, if they are evil by nature? For it is no more fitting to offer such things than to offer those that are mutilated <note>original: ἀνάπηρα (anapēra) - referring to animals with physical defects which were traditionally forbidden in sacrifice</note>. <margin>1</margin> Indeed, by doing so, we would be making an offering of evils <margin>2</margin> rather than performing sacrifices for the sake of honor. Namely, that there is some justice for us. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German physician and philologist known for his commentaries on Greek texts.</note>. In the following section, "certain other things." The Grammarians have much to say about this little word, distinguishing between *atta* meaning "whichever" and *atta* meaning "certain ones." See <term>Duker</term> on <term>Thucydides</term> II, 100 and <term>Alberti</term> on <term>Hesychius</term> under the letter V.

<margin>1. Often, however, by some mystical reasoning of the rites, they would immolate victims mutilated in some part. The Spartans also did this, but for another reason, concerning which see <term>Wesseling</term> on <term>Petit's</term> *Attic Laws*, Book I, page 74. Instead of "in this way" <note>original: οὕτω</note>, <term>Reiske</term> preferred "these" or "them."

For example: "how shall we say this?" <term>REISKE.</term> The structure is rather intricate due to the use of *hyperbaton* <note>a rhetorical figure where the natural word order is disrupted</note>, which our author is too fond of. If you construe it as "having agreed that we must not kill those doing us no harm... nor sacrifice," then the word "so that" <note>original: ὥστε</note> is redundant or implies a consequence. If you use "so that," then the word "but" <note>original: δὲ</note> is vacant. Furthermore, for the word "if" <note>original: εἰ</note>, the <term>Florentine</term> edition had "who" <note>original: οἳ</note>, which <term>Fogerolles</term> had also corrected, but whose dullness failed to see it was a typesetter's error.

...even if some of them <note>referring to animals</note> must be killed?

§ 24. Furthermore, there are three reasons for which it is thought that one should sacrifice to the gods. For we believe that offerings should be made to the gods just as they are to good men: either for the sake of honor, or out of gratitude, or because of a need for blessings. We honor the gods either when we strive to be delivered from evils and prepared to attain good things; or when, having been treated with some benefit, we conduct ourselves gratefully; or for the sake of obtaining some advantage; or led solely by the veneration of their goodness. —nothing, <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν</note> is it nevertheless proper to kill some of these others?

§ 24. For otherwise, there are three reasons to sacrifice to the gods: either for honor, or for gratitude, or for the need of good things. For just as we think it necessary to offer first-fruits to good men, so we do for the gods. We honor the gods either seeking the averting of evils and the preparation of good things for us, or having previously received a benefit, or so that we might obtain some help, or according to the pure estimation of their good disposition. So that even of the—

---

<column-break/>

4. *And to kill nevertheless...*] Read *ge* <note>a Greek particle</note>. The word *mē* <note>"not"</note> was badly intruded by the translator. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note> notes: *meanwhile, however, it is fitting to kill some of the animals.* The illustrious <term>Abresch</term> also preferred *ge*. Regarding this particle, which is often redundant in the middle of a sentence or takes the force of "and," and is confused with *ge*, read <term>D’Orville</term> on Chariton, Book IV, ch. 4, p. 419. The earlier editions also did not recognize *mē*; therefore, it has been deservedly sent into exile. <term>Valentinus</term> wanted *mē* to be read after *atta* <note>"certain things"</note>.

1. *Three reasons to sacrifice to the gods.*] <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in *On the Mysteries*, Book V, ch. 5: *But I tell you my own doctrine concerning sacrifices, that they should never be performed for the sake of honor alone, just as we honor benefactors, nor for the sake of acknowledging favors for the good things the gods have given us, nor for the sake of first-fruits or the exchange of certain gifts.* He calls these reasons "vulgar" and derived from common human custom. You see, therefore, by what right the Distinguished Man <note>likely referring to a previous commentator</note> writes that those views of <term>Iamblichus</term> are refuted by our Author <note>Porphyry</note> in this place. Rather, he confirms them, but argues that it does not follow from them that living beings must be slaughtered.

2. *Having previously received a benefit.*] The word *Paschein* <note>"to experience/suffer"</note> is of the middle voice. It is used either simply for "to be affected," or for "to suffer something evil," but with the addition of the particles *eu* <note>"well"</note> or *kakōs* <note>"badly,"</note> etc., it is reduced to a specific sense. Often—

<column-break/>

—our Author uses it thus, never simply for "to be affected by good." Nor is it usually said so by others, and if ever it seems to be said, it is understood from the context in what sense it should be taken, as in <term>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</term>, Book VII, p. 456, in which place the Learned Man uses it to prove the opposite. However, "to experience something" is frequent in <term>Dionysius</term> for "to be affected by a thing." Not otherwise in <term>Josephus</term>, *Antiquities*, Book III, ch. 13. I shall therefore expect more certain things from the interpreters of <term>Paul's Letter to the Galatians 3:4</term> to establish that usage.

3. *Or so that we might obtain etc.*] The words *or so that we might obtain* seem to be deleted. For their force is already in the preceding words *the preparation of good things.* Presently, one or the other *tēn* <note>"the"</note> should be deleted, but rather the second seems better to be deleted. <term>REISKE</term>.

# PORPHYRY

If animals are to be offered as first-fruits to the gods, they must be sacrificed for one of these reasons <note>Porphyry is outlining the traditional Greek reasons for sacrifice: honor, gratitude, or need</note>. For whatever we sacrifice, we do so for one of these purposes. Would our god <note>original: "ὁ ἡμῶν θεὸς"</note> then consider himself to be receiving honor when we are shown to be acting unjustly through the very act of offering first-fruits? Or would he not rather consider such an act, performed through these first-fruits, to be a mark of dishonor? Indeed, by killing animals that have done no wrong in the act of sacrificing, we acknowledge that we are committing an injustice. Therefore, no other living being should be sacrificed for the sake of honor. Furthermore, we should not sacrifice them to return thanks for benefits received. For he who wishes to give a just return for a benefit, and a worthy repayment for kindness, ought not to provide this by doing evil to anyone.

<column-break/>

If animals are to be offered to the gods, they must be sacrificed for some reason of this kind: since we are accustomed to make sacrifices to the gods for one of these reasons. Will God then be thought to receive honor from us if we appear to act unjustly from the very moment of the offering? Or will he not rather think himself treated with ignominy by that sacrifice? But if, in sacrificing, we slaughter animals that offer no offense, it is granted that we act unjustly. Therefore, for the sake of honor, none of the other animals should be sacrificed to the gods. Nor should they be sacrificed so that we may return thanks for benefits. For he who wishes to render worthy thanks for a benefit and kindness ought not to return them by means of injury to another. For it is no more...

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**Column 1**<-

...he will appear to act with no more grace than a man who, having stolen something from another, wishes to honor a third party with the loot. <note>original: "furatus, eo honeſtare alium uelit"</note> Likewise, it is not fitting to slaughter animals for the sake of obtaining some protection from the gods. For he who seeks to obtain a benefit from another by acting unjustly falls under the suspicion that he will feel no true gratitude for any benefits received. Thus, even for those desiring some favor, animals are not to be sacrificed at all. For although we might perhaps be able to act in such a hidden way that it remains undiscovered by any man, it is in no way possible for us to remain hidden from God. If, therefore, one must sacrifice for the sake of one of these reasons, yet for none of these reasons should animals be slaughtered, it is manifest that animals are not to be sacrificed.

**§. 25.** But while we attempt to erase the truth of these matters through the pleasures we enjoy from the sacrifices, we hide the truth from ourselves, not from God. For—

<column-break/>

->**Column 2**<-

—for he will no more seem to make a return, than if someone, having snatched the property of his neighbor, should crown certain people <note>original: "στεφανοίη τινὰς"</note> as if returning thanks and honor. But neither is it for the sake of some need for good things. For he who hunts for good treatment through an unjust action is suspected of not being likely to feel gratitude even after receiving the good. So that even when a benefit is hoped for, one must not sacrifice animals to the gods. And indeed, one might perhaps hide this action from men, but it is impossible to hide from God. If, therefore, one must sacrifice for the sake of something, but it must not be done for the sake of any of these things, it is clear that one must not sacrifice animals.

**§ 25.** For by trying to wipe out the truth about these things with the enjoyments derived from the sacrifices, we hide it from ourselves; for certainly not from—

**10. Should crown certain people.** "To crown" <term>stephanoun: to bestow a crown or prize</term> is generally to give or affect with a reward; or properly to give for the sake of honor. On the contrary, *Eusebius* ends the testimony there which he had taken from our author. Those words "For by..." etc. are not read there. Let students note the phrase "to wipe out the truth" <note>original: "ἐξαλείφειν ἀληθὲς"</note>. Properly it means *to smear over*: to scrape away the wax with which tablets were covered, and hence in a general sense *to cancel, to delete*.

# PORPHYRY

For oxen and sheep, and in addition to these, deer and birds—and even those who share in no cleanliness but provide us with enjoyment, the fattened hogs—we slaughter for the gods. <column-break/>

For from those animals which provide no human use for life, and bring no delight in the enjoying of them, we employ none as a sacrifice to the gods. <margin>3. *Under the pretext of the divine.* Perhaps: "truly slaughtering and skinning them for our own enjoyment, but feignedly under the pretext of the divine." *Epi prophasia* means by way of a pretext, or under a cover. REISKE.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

...if they were to command us to sacrifice, we would surely abandon the undertaking. 4 For they do not feast upon the flesh of the sacrificed animals, but burning them entirely as whole-offerings <note>original: "holocausts"</note> at night, and pouring much honey and wine over them, they consume the sacrifice quickly, so that the all-seeing one <note>The Sun</note> might not become a spectator of the dread deed. And they do this while fasting during the intervening days; and throughout all this time, being philosophers by race, they converse with one another about the divine. But at night they perform the contemplation of the stars, looking toward them, and through...

<column-break/>

...if they wished us to sacrifice, we would undoubtedly desist from the business. For they do not banquet on the flesh of the sacrificed victims, but they consume the entire host—having been cast into the fire—quickly at night, with much honey and wine additionally poured on, lest the sun, who gazes upon all things, be made a spectator of the crime. And they do this while occupying themselves with fasts on the intervening days, and through that whole time, as they are philosophers by race, they talk among themselves concerning God; but at night they contemplate the stars, while they look up at them, and with certain...

<column-break/>

...which I later saw Vigerus <note>François Viger, a 17th-century scholar</note> agreeing with me. I had also supplied the word <term>manner</term> <note>Greek: τρόπον</note>. Eusebius confirms this. VALENT. The reading <term>sacrificing living things</term> <note>Greek: ζωοθυτοῦντες</note> is also in the Bodleian and Meerman manuscripts, and truly so, in my opinion. Then, after the word <term>itself</term> <note>Greek: αὐτὸν</term>, if you adopt <term>manner</term> from Eusebius, everything is explained. However, instead of <term>if</term> <note>Greek: εἰ</note>, the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts had <term>into</term> <note>Greek: εἰς</note>; and in the former, <term>sumon</term> instead of <term>suron</term>. Both are incorrect.

4. **For they do not feast, etc.** Vigerus writes that Theophrastus (quoted in Eusebius) speaks of unknown and false things, but I doubt if he is correct. I admit these details poorly suit all Jews. Learned men have long ago shown that it was their custom to prepare feasts from the remaining parts of the victims. But these remarks of our author—or rather of Theophrastus—seem to pertain solely to the **Essenes** <note>An ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period</note>. I said so immediately, and the following parts confirm it. No one who has investigated their affairs is ignorant of the fact that they differed greatly from other Jews in matters of religion. The celebrated Mosheim uses this passage in his notes on Cudworth to settle the controversy that has long exercised scholars: whether the Essenes sacrificed victims or not? In this matter, Josephus and Philo seem to disagree. They did indeed offer victims, but not in the Temple, because they avoided all use of meat. Furthermore, Philo speaks of the Essenes who lived in Egypt, others of those in Syria, as our author does here, which he explicitly indicates at the start of the section. Finally, it must be noted that these men were divided into many classes and sects, and not all taught the same things. I would wish more to be read in Mosheim. I only add now that they departed from the religion of their ancestors in many ways, and while living among the Gentiles, they adopted certain ideas of the Philosophers—especially of **Pythagoras**—which recommended themselves by an appearance of sanctity.

5. **Honey and wine.** We have the Divine Law which forbade this to the Jews in Moses, Leviticus 2:11. Regarding them, see also Plutarch, *Symposiacs* IV, 5: <note>original: "furthermore, they do not offer honey in their sacrifices, because it seems to spoil the wine when mixed."</note> This was different from the custom of other nations, as mentioned above.

6. **The all-seeing one might become a spectator.** This signifies the Sun, <note>original: "who sees all and hears all"</note> as the poet says in *Odyssey* XII, 323; and the man from Sulmo <note>Ovid</note>, "who hears and sees us." *Metamorphoses* IV, 769. The term <term>all-seeing</term> <note>Greek: πανόπτης</note> is often used by Aeschylus and others. See Cuper, *Harpocrates* p. 114. It seems the Essenes thought of the sun somewhat more magnificently than was proper, which you may also gather from the testimony of Josephus below (IV, 12), where there is more.

7. **During the intervening days.** Eusebius and the Meerman and Leipzig manuscripts read <term>of these days</term>.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s critique of animal and human sacrifice, specifically discussing the transition from human victims to animal substitutes, and the subsequent decline into gluttony.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

->now, not only in Arcadia at the Lycaean festivals, nor only in Carthage to Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Phoenician god Baal Hammon</note> do they all publicly perform human sacrifices, but also in a periodic cycle, for the sake of preserving the memory of the legal custom, they sprinkle kindred blood upon the altars, even though the sacrifice <note>original: "θυσίας" (thysias); some scholars suggest "ὁσίας" (hosias), meaning 'divine law'</note> among them excludes from the sacred rites—by the proclamation of the lustral vessels—anyone who is responsible for human blood. From that point, therefore, moving forward, they made the bodies of other animals a substitute in their sacrifices for their own bodies; and again, through a satiety of the lawful food, falling into a forgetfulness of piety, they embarked upon an insatiable—<-

<column-break/>

custom even until now, not only in Arcadia at the Lycaean rites, nor at Carthage to Saturn, do they all publicly slaughter human victims. But even from an annual circuit, in memory of the institution, they sprinkle the altars with kindred blood, although the sacrifice among them keeps him away from the sacred rites, by the boundary of the purifications and by edict, if any author of human blood and slaughter should stand forth. From there, however, having progressed, they substituted the bodies of other animals for their own in sacrifices. Afterwards, when by a satiety of lawful food they had come into a forgetfulness of piety, with a certain insatiable desire—

3. **In Arcadia.** See: Pausanias <note>Greek traveler and geographer</note> pages 600 and 678. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist</note>. Many others have taught what the <term>Lycaea</term> <note>An ancient festival involving a transformation myth and alleged human sacrifice</note> were, such as <term>Potter: Greek Archaeology II, 20.</term>

4. **But in a periodic cycle.** I would prefer "but also in." <term>REISKE.</term> <term>Meermann</term> reads "according to the cycle." For "cycle" <term>Abresch</term> offers an ingenious conjecture: "in passing" or "incidentally." But there is no variation in the manuscripts here or in <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Early Christian historian who quoted Porphyry</note>.

5. **They sprinkle kindred blood.** In the fourth book of <term>Eusebius</term>, it is printed as "they always sprinkle kindred blood." Incorrectly, in my opinion; for that adverb of time is not read in the written manuscript of that author. <term>VICTORIUS.</term>

6. **The sacrifice excluding etc.** In a note to Psellus, <term>Gaulminus</term> cites these words as if they should read "from the sacred lustral vessels, if anyone etc." and for "numbered" <note>original: "ἀριθμείου"</note> he restores "joined" <note>original: "ἀρδμίου"</note>, that is, a friend or relative. I prefer the more general word "human" <note>original: "ἀνθρωπείου"</note>. <term>VALENTINI.</term> I would prefer "divine law" <note>original: "ὁσίας"</note>. Although their own native religion, amid the sprinkling of lustral water, excludes by the voice of the herald all those who are guilty of "human blood" <note>original: "αἵματος ἀνδρομέου"</note> or human slaughter. "Lustral vessels" <note>original: "περιῤῥαντηρίοις"</note> can mean the same as "in the lustral vessels," though I would prefer the latter if I had the choice. <term>REISKE.</term> I see the things I was working on have already been taken up by others. "Divine law" <note>original: "ὁσίας"</note> appeals to me, see <term>Acts of Trajan 1. 83.</term>

<column-break/>

as below in this paragraph: "although... divine law presided over these things." These words are often confused, as a <term>Learned Man</term> <note>original: "V. D." (Vir Doctus)</note> wished to rewrite "sacrifice" there; and certainly "divine law" <note>original: "ὁσίας"</note> ought to be restored from <term>Eusebius</term> in place of the common "sacrifice" <note>original: "θυσίας"</note> in our author below in section 34. But the common reading has something to defend itself. These things pertain to the custom of the ancients, when a <term>lustral vessel</term> <note>original: "περιῤῥαντήριον" - a basin for ritual purification</note> was placed at the temple entrance, and no "profane person" <note>original: "βεβήλῳ"</note> was allowed to pass beyond it. Before the sacred rites began, a herald cried out in a loud voice that famous "Away, away, [you profane]" etc. Those who were guilty of slaughter belonged especially to this class. On the word for lustral vessel, which has three meanings among the Greeks, see <term>Bourdelot on Heliodorus Book II, p. 53.</term> The opposite is "to pass within the lustral vessels," <term>Aristides Vol. I, p. 62.</term> For "numbered," <term>Fogerolles</term> had corrected it to "human or numbered." <term>Valentini</term> suggests "human or numbered" (on which word see <term>Learned Man on Hesychius and Suidas</term>); I prefer the former.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**On the transition from plant offerings to animal sacrifice**<-

...they were led by greed to taste and eat everything. This is exactly what commonly happens now with food derived from all kinds of fruits. For when they have relieved their natural hunger by consuming them, they seek an excessive fullness and prepare many things for food that exceed the limits of temperance. Hence, as if they were presenting no mean sacrifices to the gods, they proceeded to eat them; and from the beginning of this practice, the eating of animals was added by men to their nourishment from fruits. For just as in ancient times they offered fruits to the gods, and after the sacred rite <note>original: "sanctimoniam" / "hosian"</note> they joyfully ate of those same things: so when they had sacrificed animals, they thought they ought to do the same for themselves. Although in ancient times, holiness <note>The author argues that true ancient piety did not involve blood sacrifice.</note> was not thus...

<column-break/>

...leaving nothing untasted or uneaten. This is what now happens among all people regarding food from fruits. For when they have eased their necessary want by the offering, seeking the excess of satiety, they labor to produce many things for eating that lie outside the bounds of self-control. Hence, as if making these things no dishonorable sacrifices to the gods, they were led to taste them. And through the beginning of this practice, the eating of animals became an addition to the food from fruits for men. Just as, therefore, in the old days they offered the first-fruits to the gods and gladly tasted of the offerings after the sacred rite, so having begun the sacrifice of animals, they thought they should do the same thing, even though in the ancient time holiness did not thus...

***

<margin>Notes on the Greek text and philology</margin>

...into forgetfulness <note>Latin: "into oblivion"</note>, the opposite of which is *so that they might not come to the thought of this* in **Thucydides** III, 46. *Entering into greed* has grounds to defend itself, yet I would prefer with **Abresch** *entering into greed* <note>The commentator is debating the specific Greek case ending for "greed"</note> as in *they gave themselves over to impudence* in **Homer's** *Odyssey* X, 424 and elsewhere. Regarding *leaving behind*, **Fogerolles** also well suggests *omitting*. We know those prepositions are frequently confused in compound words. But the use of a participle instead of a finite verb might also offend someone. This must either be derived from Greek usage, where "they are" or "they were" is understood after the participle, about which the Learned have said much, or the sense must be suspended until the following *they were led*. But then, the word *hence* which precedes it would be empty, though that little word seems to introduce the cause of the things he had discussed. Finally, participles crowded together without a connecting link ought not to weigh down a weak stomach <note>A metaphor for a reader's patience or a critic's sensibility</note>. **Gronovius** on **Arrian** IV, 6 and **Wesseling** on **Diodorus** XIII, 14 show that this is not unusual for the Greeks.

8. **Among all.**] That is, *between and among all*. **Abresch** noted from **Plato** page 492: *one might find these (namely, states) among the barbarians.*

9. **They labor.**] There was a time when I suspected the word meant *they devise* or *excogitate*, although the common reading can return to the same meaning. Next, for *the things to the gods*, perhaps read *these things* or *such things*. **REISKE**.

10. **Holiness not thus ordaining these things.**] Why "holiness" <note>Greek: "hosia"</note> should be changed into "sacrifice" <note>Greek: "thysia"</note> by the illustrious man in his notes on **Chariton** IV, 5, I do not understand. "Holiness" denotes the whole of religion, in which word "judgment," "action," or a similar noun is understood. The words that preceded, *after the sacred rite*, sufficiently defend the common reading. And, as every...

# PORPHYRY

...holiness having ordained these things, 11 but honoring each of the divine beings with fruits; 12 for with these, both Nature and the entire perception of the human soul were pleased, 13 and the altar was not moistened with the unmixed <note>original: *akritoisi*</note> slaughter of bulls. But this was the greatest defilement among men, 14 to tear away the life-spirit 15 and devour the noble limbs.

->§ 28.<-

<note>The following is a Latin translation of the Greek verse above, likely provided by the 18th-century editor for clarity.</note>
...had instituted these things. But they worshipped the gods with fruits, in which both nature and every sense of the human soul delighted.

> *But the altar did not shudder with any slaughter of bulls:*
> *But mortals then thought it a great crime,*
> *To devour the very limbs once the life of the cattle was snatched away.*

->§ 28.<-

***

To remove any doubt for you, *Cyril, Book IX Against Julian, p. 307 A* (among whom the things that follow, up to those words "wherefore the Pythagoreans" etc., are also read) proceeds in exactly the same way. I also return our reading to *Suidas* under the entry *kyrbeis* — "of him who defined the substances" <note>original: *ousias*</note> — "and the *kyrbeis* <note>Ancient tablets or pillars inscribed with laws.</note> held the substances." Learned men there wish for "sacrifices" <note>original: *thysias*</note>, and that could be defended from the *Scholiast on Aristophanes' Clouds, 450*, but it is not said there simply as it is in Suidas. *Brabeuein* <note>to ordain/govern</note> signifies to establish by will, to dispense, and to govern in general; we know this manner of speaking is derived from the distributors of prizes. *See D’Orville on Chariton IV, 5 and Reiske on Polybius Book II, p. 140.* Boissius shows in *Animadversions ch. 25* that it is frequent in Josephus for "to give" or "to attribute."

11. **But from the fruits —]** Perhaps "but honoring each of the divine powers among them with the fruits," but "honoring each of their own deities with an offering of crops." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a famous 18th-century German philologist.</note>

12. **For with these.]** Cyril has "to these." *Eusebius* agrees with our text, having excerpted this place up to the end of paragraph IV in *Preparation for the Gospel, p. 151 C.*

13. **Of bulls, etc.]** In Eusebius it is "unmixed" <note>original: *akrētoisi*</note>. I suspect *akrētoisi* was in the original author. In the third verse, "having torn away" <note>original: *aporrhēsantas*</note> to eat. As far as the latter variation is concerned, the matter is certain in the printed edition: but in the manuscript truly "having slaughtered" <note>original: *aporrhaisantas*</note> to eat. For this is the true reading. Since indeed in the words of Porphyry cited by Eusebius before the verses of the Agrigentine poet <note>Empedocles</note>, there are two differences in the printed version, the manuscript does not depart from the reading which

<column-break/>

is now in our author. For "both nature" <note>original: *hē te physis*</note> is also read there, and "was pleased" <note>singular verb</note>, not the plural "were pleased." <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Pietro Vettori, a Renaissance scholar.</note> Our author also praises this first verse above in § 21, and *Stephanus* has this and the following in *Philosophical Poetry p. 30.* Instead of "indiscriminate" <note>original: *akritoisi*</note>, *Scaliger* preferred "unmixed" <note>original: *akrētois*</note> there. In *Eusebius* it is *akratoisi*, which comes to the same thing, for the 'eta' is a matter of dialect. *Viger*, however, prefers *akritois*, and thus it is also read in *Cyril* in the place cited. I once suspected *akrētoisi* was born from *arrhētoisi* <note>unspeakable</note>.

14. **Having torn away the life-spirit — noble]** I had restored "having torn away" <note>original: *aporrhēsantas*</note> and "noble" <note>original: *ēia*</note>. Later I found that Viger in *Eusebius* had once determined the same. <term>VALENTINI</term>. For *aporrhēsantas*, one must read *aporrhaisantas* <note>slaughtering</note> in the present, and either *eedmenai* or *ededmenai* for *edmenai*, and this for *edesthai* — *to eat, to consume.* For *ēia* <note>noble/provisions</note> I would prefer *ēpia* — *to eat soft, sweet, pleasant things.* <term>REISKE</term>. The illustrious *Ruhnken* wished to rewrite it: "Having broken off the life-spirit, to eat the goodly limbs." I would believe *aporrhaisantas* <note>slaughtering</note> to be uniquely true, which learned men found in *Eusebius*. *Cyril* and *Stephanus* confirm this in the places cited. Nor omit the fragment in the same, p. 24: "Having slaughtered the life-spirit, they eat the dear flesh." See *Sextus Empiricus, IX Against the Rhetoricians, p. 580* and Fabricius there. In the *Bodleian Manuscript* it was *aporrhēsantes*. I, fortified by so many authorities, did not hesitate to restore to Porphyry his own. In the preceding verse, for "was" <note>original: *esken*</note>, *Cyril* has "they held."

15. **To eat the noble limbs.]** For "to eat," I restored the Ionic form *eedmenai*. The authors just praised order this. I would not dare to condemn *ēia* <note>noble/goodly</note>; it can...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the history of animal sacrifice and the virtues of a bloodless diet, specifically referencing the practices of the Pythagoreans and the sacred traditions of Delos.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 28. This may be observed from the altar which is even now preserved at Delos; because no animal is offered or slaughtered upon it, it has been named the "Altar of the Pious." Thus, they did not only abstain from slaughtering animals, but they also judged those who had dedicated the altar, and those who used it, to be endowed with piety. For this reason, the Pythagoreans, having received an instruction of this kind, abstained from the eating of animals throughout the entire course of their lives. However, whenever they offered some animal to the gods as a sacrifice in their own stead, they were accustomed to eat only from that specific portion, while living entirely estranged from the tasting of any others. But we do not act in this way; instead, being filled beyond measure in—

<column-break/>

§ 28. 1 One may observe this from the altar still preserved today at Delos; since nothing is brought to it by them, nor is any animal sacrificed upon it, it is called the Altar of the Pious. 2 Thus, they did not only abstain from animals when sacrificing, but they also imparted the reputation of piety to those who established it, and likewise to those who used it. Therefore, the Pythagoreans, having accepted this, abstained from the eating of flesh <note>original: "ζωοφαγίας" (zoophagias) - literally the eating of living things</note> throughout their whole life. 3 But when they might set aside a portion of an animal for the gods as a first-fruit offering in their own stead, they tasted of this only, and lived truly untouched by the rest; but not so with us; 4 being filled—

---

<margin>
Consult *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> & the *Scholiast on Homer: Iliad: N.* 103. & *Odyssey: B.* 289.
1. *One may observe &c.*] This is correct. The *Florentine* edition and the *Lyons* edition which follows it are incorrect in reading *θεωρίζαι*. *Cyril: Codex Meermann* & *Leipzig* agree with our reading. We spoke of the Delian Rites above in § 19. It is well known that the altar of Apollo the Progenitor <note>original: "Γενέτορος" (Genetoros)</note> was never stained with the blood of victims (and thus should not be confused with the Horned Altar of Apollo, concerning which there is an elegant inquiry by the Illustrious *H. I. Arntzen: Miscellanies: chapter 2.*). *Iamblichus* in chapters 5 & 7 relates that Pythagoras visited and honored that altar; for it was his custom to worship at bloodless altars <note>original: "ἀναίμακτους βωμοὺς" (anaimaktous bomous)</note>, as is clear from the same chapter 24. I pass over *Clement of Alexandria* and others dealing with that altar, cited by *Spanheim on Callimachus' Hymn to Apollo* 60. & *on Delos* 266. *Lomeier: on Purifications* 24. and others, who abundantly explain why it was called *of the Pious*. For upon it were offered wheat, barley, and cakes without fire <note>original: "πόπανα ἄνευ πυρὸς" (popana aneu pyros)</note>, as we know from *Diogenes Laërtius*.
</margin>

...of which kind many other altars are mentioned as being "without fire" or "bloodless" and distinct from "fire-altars," about which nothing should be said here. The conjecture of the Celebrated *Michaëlis* in *Exercise I on the Victims of the Heart and Brain* § 30 is ingenious: that Pythagoras imitated the Delian Apollo, and composed the laws of his table according to the customs of that altar, so that he might demonstrate himself to be the progeny of Apollo.
2. *Not only.*] *Not only* <note>original: "Οὐ μόνως"</note> is in the *Leipzig Codex*, a little better than what is in the common speech. I would prefer *οὐ μόνον* [not only]—REISKE. To be sure, *μόνος* was in the older *Cambridge* editions; they agree with the *Leipzig Codex*, but *Cyril* has *οὐ μόνον*. *Iamblichus: On the Mysteries IV, 7.* and others also use *μόνας*.
3. *Set aside a portion for the gods.*] Perhaps *ἀπομερίσειαν* [to set apart], and the comma should be moved immediately and placed after "the truth." *If we wish the truth, the Pythagoreans did not eat their victims, but only tasted them.*—REISKE. And the *Meermann* manuscript distinguishes it thus.
4. *Being filled.*] *Codex Bodleian & Meermann* read *ἐμπιπλάμενοι*. See Book I, 46.

It contrasts the restrained, symbolic participation in sacrifice by the Pythagoreans with the excessive meat consumption of the author's contemporaries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument against animal sacrifice, transitioning from general moral claims to a specific historical anecdote regarding the origins of the 'Bouphonia' festival in Athens.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

...and having arrived at this point, we have proceeded into a most lawless custom in these matters throughout our lives. For neither should the altars of the gods be stained with slaughter, nor should men touch such food, just as they must not feed upon the flesh of their own bodies. Instead, that lesson for all of life must be adopted, which is still preserved in Athens.

§ 29. For in ancient times, as we also said previously, when men offered the fruits of the earth to the gods, but did not sacrifice animals nor consume them for their own nourishment, it is said that during a certain public sacrifice being celebrated at Athens, a certain Diomus or Sopatrus—who was not a native by birth, but farmed land in Attica—witnessed an event. While the <term>pelanos</term> <note>A thick, sacrificial cake made of grain and liquid</note> and the offerings were lying clearly upon the table so that they might be sacrificed to the gods, one of the oxen coming in from work...

<column-break/>

...proceeded into a most lawless custom. For neither are the altars of the gods to be imbued with slaughter: nor should men use food of this kind, in the same way that they must not eat the flesh of their own bodies. But that example of life must be made, which even yet is accustomed to be observed at Athens.

§ 29. For anciently, as we have also said above, when men offered fruits to the gods, but neither sacrificed animals nor took them for food, while a certain public rite was being celebrated at Athens, they say a certain Diomus or Sopatrus—who was not indeed a native, but cultivated fields in Attica—because an ox, coming from its labor, approached the table where the sacred meal and other libations had been placed to be sacrificed, [ate] some of them...

---

<margin>
1. *But not animals.*] See what we noted regarding those words "but not," Book I, 41.
2. *Abusing for food.*] The Greeks use the compound verb <note>original: *katachresthai*</note> for the simple "to use," although you may see translators everywhere incorrectly rendering it as "to abuse," as in Paul, 1 Corinthians 7:31, and others. So also Worth in his edition of Tatian, p. 6. See also Huet on Origen’s Select Works on the Psalms, p. 528. It is true, however, that it is often turned toward a worse sense, as in this place and elsewhere.
3. *Diomus or Sopatrus.*] Above in § 10 he calls him *Diomus*. The Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Clouds* 979 calls him *Bauwon*, but there it should be rewritten as *Thaulon*. See Suidas under *Bouphonia* and *Thaulon*. Meursius had already corrected the name in *Attic Readings* VI. 22.
4. *Of the cake and the offerings.*] The Lyon and Cambridge editions had given *thymematon* <note>incense-offerings</note>. Often indeed the tribe of copyists perverts the more unusual form *thyema* <note>sacrificial offering</note>; see this excellently supported and explained by the illustrious Ruhnken in his notes on Timaeus' Lexicon under *Thuyemata*. Here, however, nothing should be changed, for all the manuscripts agree on *thylemata* <note>sacrificial cakes</note>. And so Victorius himself gave it, but the laziness of editors had not noticed the error of the typesetters. Regarding the word itself, it was discussed above. Those *thylemata* were placed "upon the table." "For there are tables in the temples on which they place the offerings," as the Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Plutus* 678 says.
5. *One of the oxen coming from work.*] Pausanias in his *Description of Attica* p. 43 says it was an ox "which they keep ready, having prepared it for the sacrifice." You might easily think the animal was killed with the best justification. But if you remember that the ox was a plowman...
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book II of Porphyry's "On Abstinence," specifically recounting the myth of the first slaughter of an ox in Athens and the subsequent institution of the Bouphonia festival.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

-> V 2 <-

returning from his work, had eaten some of the offerings and trampled others. They say that the man, becoming excessively enraged at what had happened, snatched up an axe that was being sharpened nearby and struck the beast. When the ox died from the wound, and the man’s anger had subsided, he realized what a terrible deed he had committed. After burying the ox, he took it upon himself to go into voluntary exile, fleeing to Crete under the charge of impiety. However, when a great drought and a resulting barrenness of crops afflicted Attica, they decided to consult the oracle on behalf of the state. The Pythia <note>The high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracles.</note> responded that the exile in Crete would provide a solution for these troubles: if they punished the killer and raised up the dead in the same fat <note>original: "adipe". This refers to a cryptic oracular command regarding the restoration of the ox.</note> in which it had died: that

<column-break/>

coming in from his work, he ate some things and trampled others. He, being exceedingly provoked by the event, snatched an axe that was being sharpened nearby and struck the ox. When the ox had died, and he had calmed down from his anger, he reflected on the nature of the deed he had performed. He buried the ox, but taking up a voluntary exile as one who had committed an act of impiety, he fled to Crete. While droughts took hold and a terrible infertility occurred, they collectively questioned the god. The Pythia proclaimed that the fugitive in Crete would release them from these things, provided they punished the murderer and raised up the dead one in the very trough <note>original: "σιάλῳ" (sialo). There is significant scholarly debate in the footnotes below as to whether this means a feeding trough, fat, or a threshing floor.</note> in which he died—

---

<column-break/>

returning from work, you will judge otherwise. It is well known how diligently the Athenians and others took care that this should not happen. See § 31. "Work" <note>original: "ἔργον"</note> refers to *rural labor*, just as the farmer is said "to work" <note>original: "ἐργάζεσθαι"</note>, and the "plowing ox" is mentioned below in § 30. Who has not illustrated this?

6. **An axe.** <note>original: "Πελέκεώς τινος"</note> Perhaps it should be "the axe" <note>original: "πέλεκυν"</note>, for "being sharpened" <note>original: "ἀκονωμένου"</note> is not passive here, but middle voice: *someone nearby sharpening his own double-axe for himself*. — REISKE <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>

7. **Taking up a voluntary exile.** <note>original: "Φυγὴν δὲ ἑκούσιον ἀράμενος"</note> He says the rite originated from the fact that the first man who killed an ox had fled. I note this because *Pausanias*, describing the same event, adds: "I do not write the alleged reason for these things." Therefore, Pausanias should be clarified by our author [Porphyry].

8. **They questioned the god.** <note>original: "Ἐπερωτῶσι ---- τὸν θεόν"</note> A proper expression for those who consult an oracle. Regarding a similar calamity, *Diodorus Siculus, Book III, ch. 59* says: "And the earth becoming barren, they questioned the god about the deliverance from evils." *Ibid. in Excerpts p. 550:* "In the face of misfortunes, he questioned [the oracle] at Delphi." *Thucydides I, 118:* "Sending to Delphi, they questioned the god." More examples are at hand, which I will not use now.

9. **Died in the trough... will be, etc.** <note>original: "Ἀπέθανεν σιάλῳ ἐν ἔσεσθαι"</note> Perhaps: *in the very labor in which he died, it would be better*. <note>original: "ἐν ᾗπερ ἀπέθανεν ἐργασίᾳ λῶον ἔσεσθαι"</note> That is: *if they resurrected the dead and set him to that work in which he expired, it would benefit them*. — REISKE. An Oedipus <note>A metaphor for a riddle-solver.</note> is needed to explain the oracle of the "Loxian" <note>A title for Apollo, meaning "The Slanting" or "Ambiguous" one.</note>. Instead of "he died" <note>original: "ἀπέθανεν"</note> in the *Florence, Leiden, Leipzig, and Meerman Manuscripts*, it was written "he died," but *Fogerolles* rightly corrected it. For "will be," the same man restored it, and *Valentinus* followed: "to be helped by the threshing floor" <note>original: "ἄλῳ ὀνήσεσθαι"</note>, in which I confess I find much charm. But since "trough" <note>original: "σιάλῳ"</note> is found in all copies, I suspected it meant: *that he [the fugitive] would be in the trough in which he died*. That is, *he would be the one to expiate the crime*. Or "this would be," meaning the calamity could be removed in that way. *Abresch* tried: "there would be a harvest in the trough where he died," or "a harvest by the iron [axe] where he died," or "a harvest in the coffin where he died." Whichever you choose, "ambiguity" <note>original: "λοξότης"</note> will remain. If the first, one must think of the rich sacrificial feasts which the ox had devoured, and which became the cause of his death.

...that it would be so <note>original: ἔσεσθαι</note> if they both tasted of the dead animal and did not restrain themselves. Therefore, an inquiry having been held and Sopatrus being discovered along with the deed, Sopatrus—thinking he would be delivered from the trouble <note>original: δυσχολίας</note> surrounding him as one under a curse—told those who came to fetch him that an ox must be slaughtered by the city. When they were at a loss as to who would be the striker, he offered this to them: if they would make him a citizen and share in the slaughter. ...and the hay and herbs with which the oxen are distended and fattened. The notion of *fatness* is established from *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek physician</note> *V. Foes: Oec. V.* <term>sialos</term> <note>Greek: σίαλος, meaning fat or grease</note>. If the word for "iron" <note>Greek: σιδήρῳ</note> is hidden in the syllable *si*, the oracle may have intended that the ox should fall by iron, and thus be raised onto its feet, stuffed with hay, by some iron instrument. If by a "rope" <note>Greek: σερᾷ</note>, a *skin* will be indicated; and finally it is added that it must be eaten, not, as Diomus had done, buried in the earth. If they did this, there would be a "threshing floor" <note>original: ἀλωὴν ἔσεσθαι</note>. *See Hesychius* <note>A 5th-century lexicographer</note> *under the word* <term>Aloē</term> <note>Greek: Ἀλωή, meaning threshing floor or garden</note> and the *Scholiast on Theocritus* cited there. Or finally, the author perhaps left it as "in which [vessel] there would be a threshing floor." The syntax of "having punished" and "to those having tasted and not having restrained" seems to be the same as that discussed in *Clarification of Thucydides, p. 833.* These are the views of the Illustrious Man; for my part, being of a doubtful mind in these intricacies, I do not wish to waver or fluctuate any longer, leaving the learned reader to choose for himself. For "having tasted" <note>original: γευσαμένοις</note> I have restored the spelling <note>original: γευσαμένοις</note> because the older editions and all my manuscripts demanded it.

10. **And not restraining.]** "And not restraining the murderer." REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. *Fogerolles* had corrected it to "and not [holding] the murderer."

11. **Sopatrus with...]** Instead of "having been discovered" <note>original: ἀνευρεθέντος</note>, it should be read with the *Leipzig manuscript*; though "having been discovered" is doubtful,

<column-break/>

there is no doubt that "with" <note>original: μετὰ</note> can be questioned. *Sopatrus being found together with the crime*, or *caught in the act*, can easily produce this meaning: both that Sopatrus is the one guilty of the deed, and the whole deed as it was perpetrated in order. However, I would prefer to read "accessory to the crime" <note>original: μεταίτιον</note>. REISKE. I have removed a most foul error which had occupied all editions: "having been discovered" <note>original: ἀνευρεθέντος</note>. But MEERMANN <note>Gerard Meerman, a Dutch jurist and book collector</note> is correct, following the *Leipzig manuscript*. "With" <note>original: μετὰ</note> can signify "after," in which sense it occurs with the genitive both in our author and in others. See *D'Orville on Chariton III, 4.* But nothing prevents him from simply saying that while they were occupied in searching, Sopatrus was found.

But perhaps "difficulty/peevishness" <note>original: δυσκολίας</note> is better in the *Leipzig* and *Meermann* manuscripts, which was also conjectured by *Abresch*, who cited a passage of *Pausanias p. 57. 70.* Yet the common reading has that by which it can defend itself. The word is indeed not found in the Lexicons I consult. But neither do they have "difficult/peevish" <note>original: δύσχολον</note>, even though *Theophrastus* joins "bitter and difficult" in *On Odors p. 545.*
