§ 30. They selected water-carrying virgins to bring water for those who were to sharpen the axe and the knife. Once the axe and knife were sharpened, one person handed over the axe, another took it and struck the ox, and yet another slaughtered it. After they had flayed it, everyone feasted upon its flesh. Afterward, however, having sewn the hide back together and stuffed it with hay and straw, they raised the ox up in the same form it had when it was alive, and they yoked it to a plow as if it were working. When this was done, they summoned all who had participated in the act to a trial for murder. When the water-carriers accused those who had sharpened the tools, and those who had sharpened them accused the one who had handed over the axe, and he in turn accused the one who— <note>The Latin text breaks off mid-word: "iu-" for "iugulavit" (slaughtered).</note>

<column-break/>

§ 30. 1. They selected water-carrying virgins; these bring the water so that they may sharpen the axe and 2. the knife. When they had sharpened them, 3. one person handed over the axe; another struck the ox, and another slaughtered it. After those who followed had flayed it, everyone tasted of the ox. When these things were performed, they sewed up the hide of the ox and, 4. having stuffed it with hay, they stood it up, having the same appearance it had when living, and yoked it to a plow as if it were working. 5. Holding a trial for the murder, they called all those who shared in the deed to a defense. When the water-carriers blamed those who had sharpened the tools more than themselves, and those who sharpened them blamed the one handing over the axe, and he blamed the one who slaughtered— <note>The Greek text breaks off mid-word: "σφά-" for "ἐπισφάξαντα" (the one who slaughtered).</note>

---

<margin>
*What the crime was*, consider that which he had committed, or rather *as if being under a curse* <note>original: "ὡς ἐναγὴς ὢν"</note>. On account of the preceding *Sopatrus the lawgiver* <note>original: "Σώπατρος νομ."</note> or *as if not being under a curse*. Or, as I would prefer, *as if the whole people were under a curse, since the entire population would contract the guilt of the crime.* <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist.</note>
</margin>

1. **They selected water-carrying virgins.**] Carrying water was the work of women. *Xenophon: Expedition of Cyrus, Book IV, p. 330* mentions "women carrying water." The same custom existed in the Orient, as the sacred scriptures show, and today among the tent-dwelling Arabs. Compare *The Learned Man on the Gospel of John IV, 7.* You may observe everywhere that this was the work of virgins, as in this place; see *Homer: Odyssey VII, 20; Athenaeus XIII, 6, etc.* That our word is common and of good repute is shown by *Hemsterhuis on Pollux VII, 130.*

2. **The knife.**] *Felicianus* rightly translates this as "knife" <note>Latin: "cultrum"</note>; others wrongly as "sword." It often happens with this word <note>Greek: "μάχαιραν"</note> that it signifies a larger knife. See *Xylander on Plutarch’s Theseus p. 3* and *Alberti on the Gospel of Matthew XXVI, 51.*

<column-break/>

3. **One person handed over the axe.**] The common reading can be defended. I would prefer, however, "someone handed over the axe, and another struck," or "they handed over the axe, and another struck." <term>REISKE</term>. The older writers preferred "to give back" <note>Greek: "Ἀποδιδόναι"</note>, but our word is also correct, as these terms are confused a hundred times. See *D’Orville on Chariton VIII, 4*, who did not forget this passage. Recently, instead of "of those" <note>Greek: "τῶν δὲ"</note>, the earlier *Leipzig and Meermann editions* had "of those indeed."

4. **Having stuffed.**] The vocabulary of *Henri Estienne* <note>A famous 16th-century lexicographer.</note> can be increased by this word. It is the same as if he had said "sufficiently swollen," as the prefix "apo-" often functions in compounds. So below in IV, 8, "to bear witness," "to marvel at," concerning which see *The Illustrious Abresch: Readings on Aristaenetus p. 290, and elsewhere.* Recently, instead of "having it," *Reiske and Abresch* rightly preferred "the same thing which..."—that is, "the same."

5. **A trial.**] There was a note in the margin of the *Leipzig and Meermann Manuscripts*: "A strange and playful trial."

...slaughtered it, and the one who did this deed threw the blame upon the knife; $^6$ against which, being voiceless, they pronounced a sentence of murder. From that time until now, during the <term>Diipolia</term><note>A festival in honor of Zeus Polieus, "Zeus of the City."</note> at Athens on the Acropolis, those appointed perform the sacrifice of the ox in the same manner. For having placed cakes and parched grains upon the $^8$ bronze table, they drive around the $^9$ oxen that have been selected; the one that tastes the offerings is the one slaughtered. And there are families of those who perform these acts even now. Those descended from Sopatrus, who struck the blow, $^{10}$ are all called "Ox-strikers"; those descended from the one who drove the oxen around are called "Goaders." Those descended from the one who cut the throat they name "Carvers," because of the feast that results from the distribution of the meat. Then, having stuffed the hide, when they come to the—

For when the gruel and cakes have been placed on the bronze table, they lead the grazing oxen around: and whichever of them tastes from the table, they sacrifice. And the families of those who do these things still exist: from Sopatrus who wounded the beast, those who are called "Ox-killers"; from him who drove them around, those named "Goaders"; and from the slaughterer, those whom they call "Dividers," from the banquet which was established from the division of the flesh. 6. *Against which, being voiceless —*] The ordinary construction requires *against it*, but the common reading is nevertheless good, and should be referred to that form of speech about which I argue in the notes to Polybius, p. 117. 5. <term>Reiske</term><note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German scholar and physician.</note>. It is a well-known custom that the Athenians held trials against inanimate objects, and that by the law of Draco, as *Pausanias* writes, Book VI, p. 364. He notes that the custom took its origin from this event, Book I, p. 53. Trials held against brutes also belong here. Examples can be sought from sacred literature, legal scholars, and others, which I do not wish to heap up, because those things which learned men observed in the notes to *Pollux* IX, 120 and *Kuhn* on *Aelian's Varia Historia* VIII, 3 are sufficient.

The "Ox-striker" is the one who strikes the oxen being sacrificed with an axe on the neck, as the *Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius* II, 91 says. Compare the learned men on *Hesychius* regarding the terms *Boutes*, *Boutypos*, and *Bouphonia*.

§ 31. Thus, in ancient times it was not holy to kill animals that were helpers to human life; and now, one must likewise take care against doing this. And just as previously it was not pious to slaughter these for sacrifices, so now it must not be considered holy to kill animals of this kind for the sake of eating. If, however, this must be done for the sake of expiation toward the gods, nevertheless, all this pollution from the bodies must be rejected, lest the nourishment—

<column-break/>

<note>original Greek: "τὴν κρίσιν ἀχθῶσιν, κατεπόντωσαν τὴν μάχαιραν"</note> ...they are brought to judgment, they sink the knife in the sea.

§ 31. Thus, in the old days it was not holy to kill animals that work together with our lives, and now this must be guarded against. And just as before, it was not holy for men to touch these <note>i.e., to eat them</note>, so now one must not consider it holy to touch animals for the sake of food. If, then, this must be done because of a sacred rite toward the divine, yet at least this entire suffering <note>or "affection"</note> from the bodies must be sent away from oneself, so that the nourishment—

---

<margin>
11. *Brought to judgment.*] A term proper to those who are led to plead a cause or to punishment. In Latin, *this is "to lead" (ducere)*. Examples are found everywhere. See *Staveren on Nepos: XIX, 4.*

12. *They sink the knife.*] We have just spoken of the judgment. *Herodotus and others* use this form of the word; more often it is said as *katapontizein* (to throw into the sea). See *D’Orville on Chariton: I, 5.* Much rarer is that of *Nicolaus of Damascus, Excerpts by Valesius p. 445:* "the men... he drowned as if they were godless." Compare *Wesseling on Diodorus: XIV, 112.* A milder judge is used for the two-edged axe in *Pausanias Book I, p. 53:* "the axe was immediately acquitted after being judged."

1. *To kill the helpers, etc.*] *We have this animal as a partner in labor and the cultivation of the field,* says *Pliny: VIII, 45.* *A farmer and a sharer in human toils,* says *Aelian, Varia Historia V, 14.* It is no wonder, then, that the Athenians and others took such diligent care not to rashly slaughter an ox, especially a plow-ox, although later this was not always so rigidly observed in sacred rites. On which matter see the Learned Men on *Aelian.* Hence the poets say that men of the Golden and Silver Ages did not eat oxen, and attribute it finally to the Bronze or, as others say, the Iron Age. I will not dwell on a well-known matter. As for what our author says happened in the Diipolia <note>An Athenian festival</note>, *Thebes used to sacrifice bulls to Apollo of the City in ancient times,* according to *Pausanias Book IX, p. 559.*
</margin>

2. *Must be guarded against doing.*] *Phylattein* is *to observe someone or something*, so that he does not do it, or it does not happen, or even so that he does something, or it happens. I add nothing to illustrate the use of the word beyond what has long been observed. See just now *D’Orville on Chariton: V, 2. p. 442.*

3. *To men —*] To men, for the sake of holiness (or sacrifice or first-fruits), to touch animals. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. *To touch* is *to eat, to feed upon.* It has been stated elsewhere: "he touched food" in *Chariton I, 13*, where the Celebrated Commentator says more. But the Greek word, like the Latin *Tangere*, generally means *to harm or injure*, properly by touching. See the Learned Men on *1 John 5:18*, in which sense it can be conveniently explained here.

4. *Sacred rite.*] *Felicianus* gave *Expiation*; below in IV, 8, *Sanctification.* The word has a very broad meaning and encompasses the worship of the Gods and even sacrifices. See *Rittershusius on Porphyry’s Life of Pythagoras: 6* and *Valesius on Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History V. p. 102.*

5. *But that at least —*] The phrasing is brief and abrupt; the full sense would be: "but this at least, it must be known and observed, that—" or more briefly, "but remember at least that—" <term>REISKE</term>.

# PORPHYRY

-> On Abstinence from Animal Food <-

...sustenance obtained from sources where it was not fitting <note>original: *proseke*</note>, we would have this act of violence as a constant companion in our own lives. For indeed, if nothing else, we would all benefit greatly at least in terms of a mutual truce <note>original: *ekecheiria* — a cessation of hostilities</note> toward one another. Certainly, for those whose senses recoil from touching animals of other species, it is evident that their minds will abstain from harming those of their own kind. Perhaps, then, it would be best of all to abstain immediately from now on. But since no one is without sin, it remains for us to heal <note>original: *akeisthai* — to remedy or medicate</note> our previous errors concerning food through purifications for the future. This would likewise happen if, having placed the horror before our eyes,

<column-break/>

...from where it is not appropriate, it becomes a kind of provocation for us to inflict violence upon one another. For even if the matter held no other evil in itself, it would certainly bring it about that we are rendered more ready to invade one another. For those whose feelings turn away from harming foreign creatures, it is clear that their minds will refrain from injuring their kinsmen. Therefore, it would perhaps be best of all if we abstained immediately for the future: but since there is no one who is free from sins, it remains that the sins of our ancestors in the taking of food be at least left behind for posterity through expiations. This, moreover, would be achieved if, with the crime before our eyes...

But the Grammarians have often taught that the imperfect is used for the present. Above at the end of section 12: "it was not fitting to take away." So too "it reached," "it was proper," and similar terms, concerning which see *D’Orville on Chariton, Book VIII, 2. p. 670.*

Perhaps it will please others more. — VALCKENAER. It does not please me. The common reading is, as they say, "healthier than a fish" <note>a Latin idiom meaning perfectly sound</note>. He understands the impulse to inflict force. Felicianus translated it well.

The word *ekecheiria* (truce) is very well known from *Suidas* and other lexicographers. Learned men have illustrated its proper and improper use in notes on *Thucydides IV, 58.*

REISKE: "To be dedicated" <note>Greek: *anakeisthai*</note> is fine, provided it is understood as coming not from the verb "to lie" <note>keisthai</note>, but from the verb "to heal" <note>akeisthai</note>—*to repair, to amend, to cure, to correct.* A little later, "concerning food." *Akeisthai* and *iasthai* (to heal) are not infrequently used this way, and that word alone must find a place here; it is confirmed by what follows, "remedy" <note>akos</note>, and below, "to heal injustice." Rightly, therefore, Abresch in *Diluc. Thuc. Auct. p. 390* reads "it remains to heal." And Ruhnken in his *Humane Letters* emends it to "to heal." He himself in section 60 imitates "to heal the injustice," as he does everywhere, following Plato’s *Republic II, p. 424 C*: "by sacrifices and incantations, if any injustice... to heal." Phrynichus in the manuscript notes on Timaeus p. 84 looked to this passage of Plato. $^+$ Thus says the Learned Man. Since, therefore, not even a letter was changed, I have separated what was previously read as one word (*anakeisthai*) into two words (*ana keisthai*). The translator did not understand the passage. I would not dare to condemn those words "concerning food." The Greeks are accustomed to using the second and fourth cases <note>Genitive and Accusative</note> indiscriminately in such matters. See *Abresch, p. 387.*

</margin>

# PORPHYRIUS

The hearth of mankind; and it is necessary that all of us, reclining upon her as our nurse and mother, should sing her praises and love her dearly as the one who gave us birth. For by doing so, when we reach the conclusion of our life <margin>2. *The conclusion of life.* The translator Felicianus gave "change of life"; this is a term for the end of life, *death*. The Scholiast on Thucydides II, 42 says: "conclusion is death." Aelian in *Historical Miscellany* I, 14: "when regarding the conclusion of life," and IV, 14: "to conclude life," and so he says it quite often. <note>original: "καταστροφὴ ὁ θάνατος"</note></margin>, we might again be deemed worthy of entry into heaven and the company of the entire race of the celestial gods. These gods we now see, and we ought to honor them for the fruits of which they are the co-authors for us, by offering the first-fruits of the existing crops—and this applies to everyone, though we do not consider all of us to be worthy <note>The text suggests a distinction between simple offerings of grain and the more complex, often "unclean" rites of animal sacrifice.</note> to perform sacrifices to the gods. For just as not everything should be sacrificed to them, so perhaps sacrifice is not pleasing to the gods when performed by everyone. These, then, are the main points from Theophrastus <margin>3. *We might be deemed worthy of entry into heaven, and the etc.* Perhaps: "we might again be deemed worthy to ascend into heaven to the entire [race] of the gods." Those whom we do not see now, we must or ought to honor with those things of which they are co-authors with us. In this way, one might smooth out this rugged passage. *Reiske says: "For thus it would happen; that we return to heaven to the universal race of the heavenly Gods, whom although we do not yet see now, we ought nevertheless to decorate with those things whose production they share with us."* There is a confusion of structure, common in our author, which perhaps obscured the sense. They could be explained in this way: "deemed worthy into heaven" (using "into" for "in," unless it was originally so, but corrupted by what follows) "and to honor again the whole... those whom" (using "whom" for "the ones who" as is frequent) "now seeing" (Valentinus wrongly substituted "they see") "with these things" (Fogerolles and Valentinus correctly amended this to mean "that we honor them") "of which fruits they are co-authors, offering first-fruits indeed and all etc." That "and" is missing from the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts and the old editions. And in the Leipzig manuscript, something else was there before "fruits," in place of which another hand, it seems, substituted "fruits," the earlier reading having been obscured.</margin> regarding the necessity of not sacrificing animals, excluding the myths that have been inserted, and with a few additions and abridgments made by us.

->§ 33.<-

The hearth and Vesta <note>The translator here equates the Greek "Hestia" with the Roman "Vesta," both representing the hearth and the stability of the Earth.</note> of the human race. And we all ought, reclining upon her as our nurse and mother, to celebrate her with praises, and just as a parent, to love and cherish her. For thus, having attained the change of life, we would be made worthy, so that the way might lie open for us again into heaven to the universal assembly of the celestial gods. Looking up to them now, we ought to venerate them with those things which they supply to us as fruits, and all should worship with the first-fruits of them; yet we should not think that all are fit to perform sacrifices to the gods. For just as all things are not to be sacrificed to the gods, so it must be judged that perhaps sacrifices are not made pleasing to the gods by everyone. This, therefore, is the sum of the reasons why animals are not to be sacrificed, excepting the stories which have been interspersed, and with a few things added briefly by us, from Theophrastus.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 33. For my part, I would not attempt to dissolve the established customs that have prevailed among various peoples; for it is not my present purpose to discourse upon the nature of the state. However, since the laws under which we live permit us to honor the Divine even through the simplest and inanimate things, we shall choose that which is most frugal. Thus, we shall sacrifice according to the law of the city, and we ourselves shall take care to offer a fitting sacrifice, approaching the gods pure in every respect. For in general, if sacrifice holds the status of "first-fruits" <note>original: "ἀπαρχῆς" (aparchēs) - the first portion of a harvest dedicated to a deity</note> and an expression of gratitude for those things we have received from the gods for the uses of life, it would seem most absurd if we, who abstain from living beings, were to make offerings to the gods from them. Surely the gods are not inferior to us, such that they should require things which we ourselves do not need. Furthermore, it is not holy to offer first-fruits from a food from which we ourselves abstain. For we have understood that such is also the custom of men—

<column-break/>

§ 33. <note>This column contains the Greek source text for the Latin passage provided on the left.</note> I do not come to destroy the prevailing customs among each people. For it is not set before me now to speak concerning the constitution. But since the laws in which we live as citizens have granted us the right to honor the Divine even through the most simple and soulless things, choosing the most simple, we shall sacrifice by the law of the city, and we ourselves shall be diligent to make the <gloss>1</gloss> fitting sacrifice, approaching the gods pure from all sides. And altogether, if the value of sacrifice is that of <gloss>2</gloss> first-fruits, and a thanksgiving for what we have from the gods for our needs, it would be most irrational for those who themselves abstain from living things to offer first-fruits of these to the gods. For the gods are not worse than us, <gloss>3</gloss> so that they themselves should need these things, while we do not need them; nor is it holy to give a first-fruit of food from which we ourselves abstain. Since we have also understood such a custom of men—

---

<column-break/>

1. *Fitting sacrifice... approaching.*] In the Leipzig manuscript it is *to make the fitting [sacrifice] to approach*; regarding those who approach the gods for the sake of religion, it is a frequent expression, as with the Latin *adire* <note>to approach/address</note>, or *to approach the Gods*, as I shall say later.

2. *From the beginning...*] These two words are to be contracted into one, and joined in a single embrace, so that it is <term>aparchēs</term> <note>first-fruits</note>; the sacrifice has the value of an offering of first-fruits. Or, the force and meaning of sacrifice is this: that by offering it, we wish to declare that we are returning to God the first-fruits of a thing received from Him. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist</note>. <term>Felicianus</term> <note>Giovanni Bernardino Feliciano, 16th-century translator of Porphyry</note> is correct: and therefore I did not hesitate to fuse into one the two words which were previously read as separate.

3. *So that they themselves should need these things.*] The word *autoi* <note>themselves</note> is correct, although previously *autōn* was read, which was also in the Bodleian and Meermann manuscripts. For *deōntai* <note>they might need</note>, which is also in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts, it was previously published as *deontai*. This is also acceptable, although it fights against the rules of the Grammarians. The sentiment itself—that God does not stand in need of our gifts—he frequently introduces in these books. Others also frequently introduce it. Compare <term>Kortholt</term> <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a Lutheran theologian</note> on *Justin's Apology I, page 9.*

The scholarly notes debate the specific Greek phrasing of "first-fruits" and the theological concept of divine self-sufficiency.</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

-> X 3 <-

...nor that which is within, if it has been defiled by the passion of the soul. But we worship him with a pure soul and with pure thoughts concerning him. It is necessary, therefore, that having been joined with him and made like unto him, we should offer our own mental elevation as a sacred victim to God: which is at once our hymn and our salvation. In the contemplation of this God, then, which is void of passions in the soul, the sacrifice is perfected. But for those gods who are his offspring, the intelligible gods, a hymn expressed in words is now also to be added.

<column-break/>

...nor that which is within, when it is defiled by a passion of the soul; but through pure silence and pure thoughts about him, we worship him. It is necessary then, having been joined and made like him, to bring our own elevation <note>original: "anagoge," a lifting of the soul</note> as a holy sacrifice to God, the same being both a hymn and our salvation. In the passionless contemplation of this God by the soul, this sacrifice is performed. But to his offspring, the intelligible gods, the hymnody of speech must now be added.

---

<margin>
5. *Through pure silence.*] This is a well-known formula for commanding silence in the sacred rites of the ancients. The Pythagoreans and Egyptians especially worshipped God with silence. See *Our Author* <note>Porphyry</note> in *The Cave of the Nymphs* p. 266 and *Iamblichus* on the *Mysteries* VIII, 3. And to whom is their Harpocrates <note>The Egyptian god of silence</note> unknown? *Proclus* in *Platonic Philosophy* II, 11: "but in silence to hymn his ineffable nature, which is the cause of all causes, existing before all causes without itself having a cause." I do not know whether those things read in *Psalm 65:2* <note>In the Vulgate/Septuagint numbering; "To you silence is praise"</note> ought to be illustrated by that sacred silence. If you further observe that Our Author hereafter opposes this silence to "hymnody of speech," and that the common reading is found in two places in *Eusebius* and *Cyril*, you will perhaps judge the reading sufficiently firm, even though *Felicianus* read "of the soul," which alone pleased Gale in his notes on *Iamblichus*. Those who understand the nature of sacred rites know that the commands of *Iamblichus* (Mysteries VII, 4) to use "speech kindred to the gods," or the fact that the Pythagoreans prayed with a clear voice (as *Clement of Alexandria* teaches in *Stromata* Book IV), do not stand in the way.
</margin>

<margin>
6. *We worship him.*] In *Eusebius* (Book IV), by whom this whole passage is called as testimony, it is "let us worship." And in the first part of the following page, "by the contemplation of the soul of God." However, since it is read thus in the printed editions, the manuscript does not differ from the author's reading; as in the three following variations, the manuscript agrees with the printed *Eusebius*. For in the second page it has "offspring," and in the third "first-fruit" in the nominative case, which I think is more true. Likewise "it holds the essence together into being," with great variety, which I approve. VICTORIUS. *Cyril* also has "we worship." But the same later has "it is therefore necessary." It is an excellent precept, which Our Author and others often emphasize. R. W. collected testimonies in his notes on *Hierocles* on the *Golden Verses* p. 30. We know the divine man <note>St. Paul</note> commends "rational worship" in Romans 12:1.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
7. *Elevation.*] The transfer of our souls, called away from fleeting things, toward divine and immortal things. Commonly "the elevation of the heart to God and abstraction." REISKE. See *Budé*, and what *Stephanus* takes from him in the *Thesaurus*, and what *Gale* disputes against *Iamblichus* on this passage (Mysteries V, 22). *Cyril* has "guidance" and then "to bring to," and so *Eusebius* in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, but not in the other place. Instead of "being a hymn," *Cyril* has "hymning."
</margin>

<margin>
8. *In the passionless [contemplation] of the soul.*] "In passionlessness" is published in *Eusebius* (P.E.); it wanders further in the *Demonstration of the Gospel*, where it is "in the passionlessness of the virtue of the soul." These should be corrected from here. There are also things similar to this passage in P.E. Book III, p. 122. C. Moreover, the word "the" before "God" is found in neither *Eusebius* nor *Cyril*.
</margin>

9 For a first-fruit offering is made to each according to what they have given, and through those things by which they nourish us and sustain our very being. Just as a farmer <gloss>10</gloss> offers the first-fruits of his sheaves and tree-fruits, so we shall offer to them the first-fruits <gloss>11</gloss> of our thoughts and of the beautiful things concerning them, <gloss>12</gloss> giving thanks for the contemplation they have granted us, and because they truly nourish us through the sight of them, being present with us, appearing to us, and shining upon our salvation.

§ 35. But now, many of those who have been eager to practice philosophy shrink from doing this; <gloss>1</gloss> seeking reputation <note>original: δοξοποιοῦντες; literally "making an opinion" or "chasing glory"</note> rather than honoring the Divine, they hover around <gloss>2</gloss> the cult-images, having neither considered where they ought to go (or not go), nor being eager to learn from the divinely-wise—

§ 35. But now indeed, even many of those who have studied philosophy refuse to do this: but chasing glory rather than worshipping the deity, they are occupied around statues: nor is any consideration held by them as to where they must arrive, or must not: nor with any zeal—

9. **For a first-fruit to each.**] This entire passage is read thus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, chapter 12: "For a first-fruit to each, of the things which essence <note>original: οὐσία (ousia)</note> has given, and through which it nourishes us, and sustains essence into being." The sense is the same as that which the words show as emended by me in Porphyry. VALENTINUS. Correctly "first-fruit" <note>original: ἀπαρχὴ</note> in Eusebius, and from there our author is to be emended. And so also in those things which follow, as well noted by *Victorius* and *Valentinus*. The latter "into" <note>original: εἰς</note> is therefore to be deleted, which the Meerman manuscript also did not have; but the same hand, it seems, which wrote the rest had written it above the line. And for "sacrifice" <note>original: θυσίαν</note> one should write "essence" <note>original: οὐσίαν</note>, which words are often confused. See at § 27.

10. **Of sheaves and tree-fruits.**] What the "tree-fruits" <note>original: Ἀκρόδρυα</note> were, we said above in Book I, 46. He rightly joins "sheaves" to them, on which matter see *Viger* on Eu-

<column-break/>

<margin>sebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, page 10.</margin>
11. **Of thoughts and of.**] Perhaps "thoughts of the beautiful things concerning them." The "and" <note>original: καὶ</note> is not in the *Leipzig Manuscript*. REISKE.

12. **Giving thanks.**] The writers of the New Testament, who so often allowed the use of this word, introduced nothing new. *Artemidorus, IV, 3:* "both sacrifice and give thanks." And 13: "the poor give thanks to the gods." The great *Wesseling* will give other examples in his notes on *Diodorus, XX, 34*; however, *Pierson* notes in his work on *Herodian the Grammarian*, page 441, that it is sought in vain in the writings of the ancient Attic authors. A little later in the *Leipzig Manuscript* it is "both being present with." Not bad.

1. **Seeking reputation.**] Or perhaps "hunting for glory"? <note>original: δοξοκοποῦντες</note> which word he also uses above in Book I, 38, where see. But all manuscripts and the translator agree on the common reading. The Lexicons are ignorant of it, but *Polybius* uses its compound; see *Reiske* on his *Excerpts*, page 607.

2. **Hover around cult-images.**] *Suidas* and *Hesychius* explain "cult-images" <note>original: Ἀφιδρύματα</note> as the statues of the gods.

6. **"Nor from a blood-stained hearth..."**] We spoke above concerning the bloodless altar of Pythagoras. Let the Grammarians teach what an *eschara* <note>Greek: $\dot{\sigma}\chi\acute{\alpha}\rho\alpha$, a hearth or low altar</note> properly is. Albert in his notes on Hesychius, Valckenaer in his *Animations on Ammonius*, and the Scholiast on Euripides' *Phoenician Women* (line 647), with the note of that most elegant man, treat this abundantly. Instead of "from" <note>$\dot{\alpha}\phi'$</note>, Valentinus had corrected it to "upon" <note>$\dot{\epsilon}\phi'$</note>, and for "outside" <note>$\stackrel{\prime}{\epsilon}\xi\omega$</note> he corrected it to "goes out" <note>$\dot{\epsilon}\xi\grave{\iota}$</note>; both are incorrect.

7. **"But he knows, being concerned with piety..."**] In the three verses that follow, three variations of the writing are found in the same author <note>Eusebius</note>, who cites them in his fourth book; I judge these should be preferred to this reading. For first, "he of piety" is read there: yet our manuscript does not differ from the printed one in this, and as it were applies itself to the author's reading, although it is clearly disturbed in this part, for it has: "he knows that when of piety," and below "but to daemons," "but either to the good." At the very end, "of those needing them." **VICTORIUS.** See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, p. 153 C, where Viger writes that our "that" <note>$\stackrel{\prime}{o}\tau\iota$</note> can be approved instead of "since indeed" <note>$\stackrel{\prime}{\alpha}\tau\epsilon$ $\delta\grave{\eta}$</note>. But that which is in Eusebius is uniquely true, for it is also thus in the Leipzig Codex. To those words "not to gods is it sacrificed, but to daemons," Abresch had well added this from the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10:20: "But that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils <note>daemons</note>, and not to God." See also what our author says below in section 58. Those words "and to others" I cannot digest. Eusebius is correct; the "the" <note>$\tau\grave{\alpha}$</note> in "transcribe" had erroneously fallen out in the Meerman manuscript.

8. **"And of those, how far..."**] I cannot explain these things.

<column-break/>

The sense seems to require: "and how far it is necessary for those needing their help to proceed." <note>Latin: *& quo ad progredi deceat eos, qui eorum ope egeant.*</note> **REISKE.** Victorius gave the reason. "Of him" <note>$\alpha\dot{\upsilon}\tau o\tilde{\upsilon}$</note> could indeed stand, namely "to sacrifice." However, I have greater faith in Eusebius. Compare Viger there, who preferred: "and how far, of those needing the same things." For the Theologian knew not only whose part it was to sacrifice to them, but also "how far," namely "the sacrificing is." To what extent they ought to proceed in sacrificing.

9. **"Let it be laid down as 'blessed'..."**] A marginal note in the Meerman manuscript: "In the Ionic dialect, instead of 'auspicious' <note>$\epsilon\stackrel{\prime}{\upsilon}\phi\eta\mu\alpha$</note>, and they say 'to pray' <note>$\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\xi o\mu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$</note> instead of 'to speak auspiciously' <note>$\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\phi\eta\mu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$</note>." We have "let it be laid down as blessed for me" according to Herodotus in Plutarch, from where Theodoret excerpted it in his *Discourse on Oracles*, p. 625; and it is frequent in others, for it was like a proverb. See the learned men on Magister Thomas under "To pray," and Wesseling on Herodotus II, 171; they have spoken of it abundantly.

He has "unblamable" <note>$\dot{\alpha}\nu\epsilon\mu\acute{\epsilon}\sigma\eta\tau o\nu$</note> instead of "in the middle" <note>$\dot{\alpha}\nu\grave{\alpha}$ $\mu\acute{\epsilon}\sigma o\nu$</note>, but agrees on "to indicate" <note>$\mu\eta\nu\acute{\upsilon}\epsilon\nu$</note>, for which either "he indicates" or, as Reiske preferred, "he will indicate" or "he is able to indicate" should have been said, unless this is Porphyrian brevity. "Setting forth... to indicate," namely "it is necessary," etc.

11. **"Setting forth..."**] Perhaps "having been set forth." **REISKE.**

# PORPHYRY

...to reveal the matters set before us; and they speak as follows:

§ 37. <gloss>1</gloss> The first God, being incorporeal, immovable, and indivisible, and <gloss>2</gloss> not being in any place, nor bound within himself, has no need of anything from the outside, as has been said. <note>original: "ὥσπερ εἴρηται" - referring to earlier arguments in the text that the supreme being is self-sufficient.</note> Furthermore, neither does the Soul of the World <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a central Neoplatonic concept of a spirit that animates the entire universe.</note> need anything external; for though she possesses three-dimensional extension and is by nature self-moving, she is naturally inclined to choose to move herself and the body of the world in a good and orderly fashion according to the highest principles. She has received the body into herself and embraced it, although she herself remains incorporeal and free from all passion. <gloss>3</gloss> To the remaining gods—the world itself, and the fixed and wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>—which are visible and composed of soul and body, thanks must be returned in the manner already described, through inanimate sacrifices. <note>Porphyry argues that higher gods should not be honored with animal slaughter, but with "unbloody" offerings like incense or grain.</note> There remains for us, then, the multitude of invisible beings, whom

<column-break/>

I believe I must offer an explanation. For they speak in this manner:

§ 37. Indeed, the first God is incorporeal, immovable, and indivisible, and is neither in any place nor bound within himself; he lacks nothing from without, just as has been stated. Moreover, the Soul of the World itself lacks no external thing: since she has it within herself to be complete in three dimensions and to be moved naturally from within herself; and by nature she proposes and chooses to move herself and the body of the world well and orderly by the best reasons, and she has admitted the body into herself and embraced it, although she herself is considered incorporeal and devoid of all affection. # On Abstinence, Book II.

### Page 171

Those whom Plato called "undifferentiated daemons" <note>original: "daemonas indistinctos". The translator is discussing how Plato uses the term 'daemon' generally for a variety of spirits.</note>. Among these, those who have been specifically named by men receive honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship from their respective followers. However, those who for the most part have not been specifically named, receive names and secret veneration from some people in various villages or certain cities. The rest of the multitude is called by the common name of "daemons." Regarding all of them, men are persuaded of this: that if they become angry because they are neglected or defrauded of their established worship, they will inflict injury; on the other hand, they will act as benefactors to those who have rendered them propitious through vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other such things.

§ 38. But since the knowledge concerning them is confused and leads to much slander, their nature must be distinguished in this discourse—

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek version of the text above.</note>

—whom Plato called "undifferentiated daemons." Of these, some having been named by men, obtain honors equal to the gods and other service among each group; others, for the most part, have not been named at all, but by some in villages or certain cities, they obtain both a name and worship in secret. The rest of the multitude is thus addressed by the common name of "daemons." There is such a conviction concerning them all: that they might even do harm if they were angered by being overlooked and not obtaining the customary service, and again, they might act as benefactors to those who appease them with prayers, litanies, sacrifices, and the following rituals.

§ 38. Since the notion concerning them is confused and proceeds into much calumny, it is necessary to distinguish—

<margin>4. *“Plato called them undifferentiated daemons.”*] Fogerolles and G. Cuper (Observations III, 16) read this as *“daemones idiosolous”* <note>Greek: ἰδιοσόλους</note>. Indeed, one is called *idiosolos* who is sent to protect or manage some specific matter. Felicianus and Marsilio Ficino seem to have read *“undifferentiated”* <note>Greek: ἀδιαςόλους</note>, for both gave the Latin *indistinctos*. Therefore, I must not attempt anything against the evidence of the manuscripts. He says that Plato calls those who are distinguished from the Gods he had enumerated "daemons" in a general or indiscriminate sense, and we have immediately seen that this is true. This is confirmed by what follows: *“The rest of the multitude is thus addressed by the common name of daemons.”*</margin>

<margin>5. *“Honors equal to the gods.”*] Thus *“honors equal to the gods”* <note>Greek: τιμαὶ ἰσόθεοι</note> is found in Diodorus Siculus (I, 90) and others. Learned men have most diligently illustrated this style of speaking in notes on Paul’s letter to the Philippians (II, 6). However, it does not always signify honors equal to the divine in every respect, as in that fragment of Menander (p. 238):
> Law assigns to parents honors equal to the gods
as the learned man observes there.</margin>

<margin>7. *“With prayers.”*] Read *“those”* <note>Greek: τοὺς</note>. Be careful not to refer *“those”* to *“them”* <note>Greek: αὐτοὺς</note>, for it refers back to *“those who appease.”* **REISKE.** They [the ancients] maintained that daemons do not ward off the evils they have brought upon cities and peoples until they have been appeased. # PORPHYRY

...by reason of their nature. For perhaps it is necessary, as they say, to reveal the source from which error concerning them has arisen among men <gloss>1</gloss>. We must therefore make a division in this manner. Those souls which, having sprung from the whole, govern great parts <gloss>2</gloss> of the regions below the moon <gloss>3</gloss>, leaning upon a spirit <term>pneuma: a subtle, airy substance or "spirit-body" that connects the soul to the physical world</term> but ruling over it according to reason—these must be considered good daemons <note>original: "daimones". In the ancient world, a daemon was a mediating spirit, not necessarily evil like the modern "demon."</note> who manage everything for the benefit <gloss>4</gloss> of those subjects under their care <gloss>5</gloss>, whether they preside over certain animals, or assigned fruits, or even those things that exist for the sake of these, such as moderate rains and winds...

<column-break/>

...we must distinguish. For perhaps it is necessary, they say, that the source from which error concerning these beings has fallen upon men should be made manifest. Therefore, a division must be used in this way: Whosoever souls, having arisen from that universal whole, govern the great parts of the places which are below the moon, leaning indeed upon a spirit, but themselves ruling over it according to reason: these are to be esteemed as good daemons, and those who procure all things for the utility of those whom they preside over: whether they preside over certain animals, or certain fruits, or those things which exist for the sake of these: of which kind are rains and winds.

---

<column-break/>

1. *Concerning them, to reveal.*] The translator whom we have followed distinguishes the text well here, differently than was previously customary.

2. *Of the regions below the moon.*] They commonly assign this tract of space to the daemons: *between the highest ether and the lowest earths, positioned in that intervening space of air (divine middle powers) through which both our desires and our merits pass to the gods.* Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. 101. Who, on p. 103 of the same work, says the Daemons were allotted the regions of air bordering the earth, and no less confined by heaven. Learned men have brought together many things of this kind from the decrees of the Jews and Philosophers to illustrate Paul’s letter to the Ephesians 2:2, where the evil genius is called the *ruler of the power of the air*. *Sextus Empiricus:* other souls also *inhabit the region below the moon*. On which matter see *Needham* on Hierocles’ *Golden Verses*, p. 437.

3. *Leaning upon a spirit.*] This passage is very obscure; from p. 82, 18 it appears that for the Platonists, *pneuma* (spirit) is the principle of evil, madness, and blindness. Almost nothing occurs to me in my haste that fits the matter, unless we think this is something: *resisting that spirit.* *Resisting that spirit which rushes blindly.* Then the word

<column-break/>

*antereidos* (resisting) would be derived from *eris* (strife). —REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German physician and philologist.</note>. I understand it as that subtle, spiritual *pneumatic* body which they attributed to Daemons, concerning which see § 39 and 42. Just as *daemons having acquired a spirit* are mentioned by *Tatian: Oration to the Greeks, 20*, and at the end of this section, *to rule over the continuous spirit*. *Marsilio Ficino* <note>The famous Renaissance Neoplatonist who translated Plato and Porphyry into Latin.</note> in his version retained the Greek word *apereidomenai* and translated it as *leaning upon*, or *clinging to*, or *placed upon the spirit*. Similarly, *images flowing from all things* in *Synesius:* whenever they encounter the psychic spirits — they lean upon these, and rest as if upon a perch. *On Dreams*, p. 138. In the *Leipzig Manuscript* it was *which things we saw in the spirit*.

**10. *But as for those souls etc.***] The sixteen following lines are placed by the same author [Eusebius] in the same book. However, the writing in these places differs from that which is now found in the author [Porphyry]. *For this reason* <note>original: *διὰ τοῦτο*</note> is used with the middle word removed. For where the printed version of Pamphilus <note>referring to Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*</note> has *mostly mastered* <note>original: *πολὺ κεκράτηνται*</note>, the manuscript copy has *and are mastered* <note>original: *καὶ κρατοῦνται*</note>, just as in Porphyry below it says *even themselves* <note>original: *καὶ αὐταὶ*</note>. Likewise, *but rather in shapes* <note>original: *ἀλλ’ ἢ ἐν σχήμασι*</note> is a phrase added to the discourse. And immediately: *and their forms characterizing their spirit.* But what is read in the printed text, *that which is by the souls*, is faulty, and should be read in the dative case as *to the [souls]*, as I found written in the manuscript of Eusebius. That phrase *and to be changed* is true, and it is necessary to correct Porphyry accordingly. Just as in these two names being preserved more integrally: *those who allot more to the passionate part [of the soul] inhabit the region near the earth, where there is nothing of evils etc.* in the following line, *having*, which was erroneous in the author. Since what follows varies in the same printed book, and it is read there *being removed from the natural happiness derived from the better [source]*, I do not think it should be accepted; nor do I think that reading is in any way to be preferred to ours. — **VICTORIUS**. The passage in **Eusebius** is *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 4, p. 171 C. Soon, instead of *and these* <note>original: *καὶ αὗται*</note>, **Abresch** rightly corrected it to *even themselves* <note>original: *καὶ αὐταὶ*</note>. **Lipsius** wrongly suggested *to do evil* <note>original: *κακοεργεῖν*</note>.

**1. *Invisible and completely imperceptible.***] **Eusebius**: *both invisible and completely*. **Iamblichus** is so similar to our author in *On the Mysteries*, Section 1, 20, that he seems to have taken it from him: *For the spirits are both invisible and in no way graspable by sense.* **Apuleius** teaches the same in *On the God of Socrates*, p. 106: *who says the bodies of Spirits are visible to no one by chance, unless they show their appearance by divine will.*

**2. *Clothed in a solid body...***] Exactly as many Christians attributed subtle bodies to Angels, regarding which see § 42. Soon a distinction is made in **Eusebius** after *more*: *their forms being modeled and characterizing their spirit, sometimes... sometimes...* The earlier editions of **Porphyry** have *being modeled*, and so also the **Meerman Manuscript**. If, however, after that word...

<margin>
If we wish to distinguish the [textual] difference, as was usually done, it is necessary to restore "modeled" <note>Greek: ἐκτυπούμενοι</note>, which *Valentinus* therefore received into the text. You could also read "modeled forms" <note>Greek: ἐκτυπουμένας μορφάς</note>, so that it refers to "all," but *Viger* preferred this for *Eusebius*. *Gale* on *Iamblichus' Mysteries p. 208* notes "imprinted forms" <note>Greek: ἐντετυπωμένας μορφάς</note> is used by *Eusebius* in *Preparation for the Gospel Book III*. But *Eusebius* also says "demons imprinted in many shapes" in *Book IV*, referring to this very passage. Therefore, one should read it the same way in both places. For "sometimes" <note>Greek: τοτὲ</note>, the *Bodleian Manuscript* had "at some time" <note>Greek: ποτὲ</note>. In earlier editions it was "then" <note>Greek: τότε</note>, but what I have given is from *Eusebius* and is uniquely true. *Abreschius* also saw this beautifully. Finally, compare this passage with what *St. Paul* says in *1 Corinthians 11:14* concerning Satan, who "transforms himself into an angel of light," where scholars find many things of that kind.
</margin>

3. **For it is likely that something flows... and is nourished.** *Eusebius* reads "and is changed" <note>Greek: καὶ τρέπεσθαι</note>, and *Viger* and *Victor* wished to correct it here in that way. To me, it seems *Eusebius* should be amended from our author [Porphyry]. He attributes "not eternal" to the demons because something flows away and admits nutrition. Demons, there-

<column-break/>

-fore, are not everlasting <note>Greek: αἴδιοι</note> because they require food, as *Aristotle* says. Just so, our author [Porphyry] says below that their spiritual nature "is fattened and strengthened by the steam of sacrifices." "To flow away" <note>Greek: ἀποῤῥεῖν</note> is a common word in this matter. *Iamblichus* in *Mysteries V, 10*, speaking on the same subject—though not entirely agreeing with Porphyry—says: "For if there is any body surrounding the demons, which some think is nourished by sacrifices, this is unchangeable and impassive, so that nothing flows from it, etc." See *V. Gale* on this. I notice what might be said in favor of "changed" <note>Greek: τρέπεσθαι</note>, but he who reads the preceding will not expect "it is likely to be changed" here. The learned know those words are often confused. The words from "it is likely" up to "the bodies" are missing in the *Bodleian Manuscript*; *Eusebius* also poorly reads "those of the good."

# PORPHYRY

...allotting more of the passionate element to the region near the earth. There is, therefore, no evil they do not attempt to perform. For possessing a character entirely violent and treacherous, and being deprived of the protection <note>original: φυλακῆς</note> that comes from the superior divinity, they mostly make intense and sudden attacks like ambushes; at one moment trying to remain hidden, and at another employing brute force. 

Hence, the sufferings caused by them are sharp and swift; but the cures and the corrections provided by the superior divinities seem to be slower. For everything that is good, being easy to guide <note>original: εὐήνιόν, literally "well-reined"</note> and steady, proceeds with order and does not overstep what is necessary. If you hold this opinion, you will never fall into that most absurd error of supposing that evil comes from the good, or that

<column-break/>

good comes from the evil. <margin>These spirits are unstable; hence, being more subject to passions, they occupy the place neighboring the earth. There is no evil they do not try to bring about. They have violent and deceitful habits: and since they have been deprived of the guardianship of a better spirit, they make vehement and sudden assaults as if from ambush: now they strive to hide, now they bring open force. Whence the evils that come from them are swift: but the remedies and corrections procured by the better spirits seem therefore to be slower: because everything that is good, since it is easily directed and uniform, progresses by order and does not miss the proper opportunity.</margin>

§ 40. For this also must be established as one of the greatest harms inflicted by malevolent spirits <note>original: "maleficis daemonibus." In Neoplatonic thought, these are lower spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern hellish sense, but entities that crave the energy of animal sacrifices.</note>: that while they themselves are the cause of the calamities that occur around the earth—such as pestilences, barrenness, earthquakes, droughts, and other things of that kind—they persuade us that the authors of these things are actually those who are the causes of the exact opposites, that is, of fertility and prosperity. Thus, they withdraw themselves from the blame of the calamities. Their first priority is to remain hidden while they do harm; secondly, they induce us to offer supplications and sacrifices to the beneficent gods, as if it were they who had been angered. These and similar things they do—

<column-break/>

—and [they attribute] good things to the wicked. For not only is the reasoning absurd in this way, but the majority of people, adopting the basest assumptions about the gods, pass them on to the rest of mankind.

§ 40. They exempt themselves from the blame, and they busy themselves with this first: to remain undetected while doing wrong. After this, they turn us toward prayers and sacrifices to the benevolent gods, as if they were the ones who were angry. <gloss>2</gloss> These and similar things they do, [turning us away]—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Porphyry’s treatise on the nature of malevolent spirits (daemons) and their deception of humanity, followed by philological commentary comparing the text to Plato and other classical sources.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

They act thus because they wish to turn us away from a correct understanding of the gods and toward themselves. For they delight in all things done so inconsistently and incongruously; and as if putting on the masks of the other gods <note>original: "personas subeuntes"</note>, they take advantage of our lack of wisdom. They win over the masses by inflaming human desires with passions, and with longings for wealth, power, and pleasures, as well as with empty vanity <note>original: "inani gloria"; the Greek text notes "xenodoxiais" (hospitality/strange opinions) but the Latin and notes suggest "kenodoxiais" (vainglory)</note>, from which seditions and wars grow, and things akin to these. And what is the most serious of all...

<column-break/>

...it is not the property of cold to heat, but of its opposite <note>original: "ψυχρότητος τὸ θερμαίνειν"</note>, which are found there. Since that most learned writer was not content with that one example, but added another, he brought in something different from the former and passed on to other matters, if we wish to trust the opinion of the author himself. However, so that the whole matter and where the error remains may be more easily perceived, I will cite the whole passage from Plato: *For I do not think it is the work of heat to cool, but of its opposite. Certainly. Nor of dryness to moisten, but of its opposite. Quite so. Nor indeed is it the work of the good to do harm, but of its opposite.* <note>Quoting Plato's Republic, Book I, 335d</note> Therefore, either Porphyry thought it sufficient to place the former, or if he also cited the later example, which is more likely (for the end of the later part, differing in no way from the end of the former, could have provided an opportunity for a scribe to err), one must consider whether he varied the words and the opinion of the author, or the example; and, as it came to mind, added something suitable for proving the same point. For there are also other variations from the reading of Plato in this testimony taken from there. Moreover, the passage is taken from the first book of the *Republic*: below, *most just indeed... since it would not even be divine.* With two tiny changes, which I nevertheless did not want to omit indicating, and this also remains in the written copy of Eusebius: the word "but" <note>Greek: "δὲ"</note> is placed where it is in Porphyry. <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Pietro Vettori (1499–1585), a famous Italian philologist</note>.

<column-break/>

3. **For in all these things etc.**] Those words of Minucius Felix in chapter 27 concerning Daemons harmonize excellently: *They disturb life, they disquiet sleep; creeping also into bodies secretly, they terrify minds and distort limbs, so that they may force men to worship them; so that, fattened by the steam of altars or the sacrificial victims of cattle, they may seem to have cured what they had previously constricted.* See more on those snares of the daemons there. Compare also Gale to Iamblichus II, 10; III, 31; and V, 20, who irrigated his own fields from our author <note>meaning he drew heavily from Porphyry's work</note>, having much to say about the fraud of spirits, how they put on the appearance of better deities and lie that they are those whose form they bear.

4. **To inflame the desires of men with passions etc.**] I have seen to it that "to inflame" <note>Greek: "ἐκκαίειν"</note> is printed instead of "he inflames." For "hospitality" <note>Greek: "ξενοδοξίαις"</note>, Eusebius reads "vainglory" <note>Greek: "κενοδοξ."</note>. For "the" <note>Greek: "ὁ"</note> I had restored "which" <note>Greek: "ὃ"</note>; I later found it thus in Eusebius. <term>VALENT</term> <note>Likely the scholar Henri Valois (Henricus Valesius)</note>. It is most certain that "to inflame" is correct, which Eusebius protects in two places, as do the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts. It is elegantly said "to inflame desires with passions." Indeed, "to desire" and "desire" are used particularly of Venusian [sexual] longing, as has often been observed. However, love is well distinguished from lust: *Let us say this man desires, but does not love* (Maximus of Tyre, XXVII, 4).

5. **With longings for wealth.**] Good Spirits are also "givers of wealth" (Hesiod, *Works and Days*, 146), to which he refers...

# On Abstinence, Book II.
## Signature Z 2

->§ 41.<-

First, proceeding from these [lower spirits], they even persuade men of similar things regarding the greatest gods, to the point that they subject even the highest God to these accusations—namely that He is the one, as they say, who turns all things upside down <note>original: "sursum ac deorsum conturbant." A Greek idiom for total chaos or subversion.</note>. This happens not only to the unlearned, but also to many of those engaged in philosophy; and this occurs for a mutual reason. For those practicing philosophy, who have not withdrawn from the common path of the masses, fall into the same errors as the multitude; and conversely, when the masses hear things that agree with their own opinions from those who appear to be eminent, they are further confirmed in holding such views about the gods.

<column-break/>

...the most terrible thing, they ascend from these [lower matters] and persuade people of similar things even concerning the greatest gods, to the point of subjecting even the best God to these accusations, by whom they say all things have been turned upside down. This has been experienced not only by private citizens, but also by not a few of those who spend their time in philosophy. The cause has become mutual; for those among the philosophers who did not stand apart from the common current <note>original: "κοινῆς φορᾶς" (koines phoras). Refers to the popular trend or "drift" of public opinion.</note> ended up in the same place as the masses. And again, the masses, hearing things in harmony with their own opinions from those who seem to be wise, were strengthened to think even more in such a way regarding the affairs of the gods.

<margin>He cites *Plutarch* Vol. II, p. 417. But also below in § 42, like others, he says the desire for riches proceeds from them. 6. **And concerning the &c.**] This is good in *Valentinus* and agrees with *Eusebius*. Earlier editions had "and the things concerning the gods," where "the things" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> was badly repeated from the previous line. Soon after, the *Lipsius* Manuscript mistakenly had "to these accusations" <note>original: "τοῦ τοῖς ἐγκλ."</note>. Also, I restored "by whom" <note>original: "ᾧ"</note> from *Eusebius*, for which "the one who" <note>original: "ὁ"</note> was being published. Then "up and down" <note>original: "ἄνω καὶ κάτω"</note> was found in *Pamphilus*, which *Vigerus* approves.

7. **Has become mutual.**] The learned *Abresch* had noted the passage in *Aristides* Vol. I, p. 7: "to do... through one another."

8. **From the common current.**] Elsewhere he calls the "common current" the common opinion of men. Book IV, 9 & 16. Nor is it said differently in this place: that common impulse by which men are usually carried along. Therefore, it is not necessary to derive this from the meaning of "abundance" or "multitude," and hence to take it as "the common herd of men," as *Fabricius* does in his notes on *Sextus Empiricus*, *Against the Logicians*, Book VII, p. 379. What follows, "they ended up in the same place"—

<column-break/>

—*Abresch* illustrated this with those lines from *Aeschylus' Libation Bearers*, 208: "to come to the same point as..."

9. **And again the masses.**] Previously it was read as "again these things" <note>original: "πάλιν αὐτὰ"</note>. But they must be read separately <note>as "πάλιν αὖ τὰ"</note>, as I have seen to it being published. *Eusebius* and the *Meerman* Manuscript are correct. Very often in this formula, "again" <note>original: "αὖ"</note> has merged with the following "the" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> through the fault of scribes. See *Markland* on *Maximus of Tyre* XXVI, who also restores it in this place. I doubt, however, whether it should also be rewritten in *Longinus*, *On the Sublime* II, 5, where they want "again the" instead of "these things." This formula is also corrupted in our author below in III, 22; see there.

10. **From those who seem.**] "From those who seem to be wise" appears twice in *Eusebius* p. 172 D and 173 D, which might seem to have arisen from a gloss <note>A "gloss" is a marginal explanation that a later scribe accidentally moved into the main text.</note>, for "those who seem" <note>original: "οἱ δοκοῦντες"</note> is also said simply of those who are in high esteem or distinguished by authority. The learned man [V.D.] has much to say on *Paul's Epistle to the Galatians* II, 2. Elsewhere, however, Malchus <note>Porphyry's original name.</note> is accustomed to add what kind of "seeming" people are understood. Soon after "concerning," the "the" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> ought to be deleted, which *Eusebius* also does not recognize. A similar error was driven out a little earlier. From the same source, you could have "yet" <note>original: "ἔτι"</note> instead of "upon" <note>original: "ἐπὶ"</note>.

# PORPHYRY

§ 41. For the art of poetry has further inflamed the preconceived notions of men, by employing a style of speech designed to cause astonishment and enchantment—a style capable of casting a spell and inducing belief in things that are utterly impossible. <margin>1. <note>original: "Ἀδυνατωτάτων δυναμένῃ"</note> From this, correct the reading in *Eusebius* to "having been made." The error arose because the word "made" had just preceded it.</margin> Yet we ought to be firmly persuaded of this: that the Good never harms, nor does the Evil ever benefit. For it is not the property of heat, as **Plato** says, to chill, but rather the property of its opposite; <margin>2. <note>original: "Ὡς φησὶ Πλάτων"</note> See the recently published fragments of *Hierocles*, p. 208 (VALENT.) and *Needham* on *Hierocles*, p. 284. *Sextus Empiricus* also took this from Plato, as did *Iamblichus* in *On the Mysteries*. Regarding the doctrine itself which the Author emphasizes—that God can affect no one with evil since He is Himself good—read *Gataker on Marcus Aurelius, II, 11*.</margin> likewise, it is not the property of the Just to cause harm. Surely the Divine is by nature the most just of all things, <margin>3. <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ ἂν ἦν θ."</note> Earlier editions, along with the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, read "since nothing would be." More correctly, *Eusebius* reads "since otherwise it would not be." The word "since" here means "otherwise," as is very often the case. I add nothing to the diligence of *Johann Albert* on *Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, 5:10*.</margin> otherwise it would not even be Divine. Therefore, this power and lot <note>The "power" to do harm</note> must be cut off from the <term>beneficent spirits</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθοεργῶν δαιμόνων" (agathoergon daimonon). In Neoplatonism, "daemones" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. For a nature that is inclined to and desires to do harm is the opposite of a beneficent one. And opposites can never exist within the same being. While these <note>harmful spirits</note> ruin the mortal race in many respects, and sometimes in great matters, <margin>4. <note>original: "Καθ’ ἕνα μὲν γὰρ ---- οὐχὶ"</note> *Valentini* included these words in parentheses as if they referred to men, unlike *Felicianus*, who referred them to the Spirits; the latter's reasoning seems better to me...</margin> on an individual basis, there is never a time when the good spirits do not alleviate our troubles, but they even give signs beforehand—

<column-break/>

§ 41. For poetic eloquence has even further set fire to the opinions of men, since it uses a style of speaking adapted to induce admiration and amazement, and of such a kind that it can soothe minds and create faith in things that can least of all exist. Yet we should hold it as a firm persuasion that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever help. For it is not the nature of heat, as **Plato** says, to make things cold, but of its opposite; so it is not the nature of the just man to bring any injury. Moreover, the divine power is surely by nature the most just of all things, otherwise it would be nothing. Therefore, this force and fate must be severed from the beneficent spirits. For the faculty which is accustomed to harm by nature, and wishes to do so, is without doubt the opposite of the beneficent; and opposites can in no way exist in the same subject. Since, therefore, those [evil spirits] harm the mortal race of men in many parts, and sometimes in the greatest, the good spirits never cease their duties individually: but [they warn of] dangers—

<summary>Porphyry argues that the Divine and good spirits are inherently incapable of causing harm, refuting poetic myths to the contrary. He cites Plato to demonstrate that a thing cannot produce an effect opposite to its own nature (e.g., heat cannot chill).</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

They demonstrate to us, as far as they are able, the dangers hanging over us from evildoers, showing them through dreams, through a divinely inspired soul, and through many other signs. Thus, if someone were capable of distinguishing the things signified, they would recognize and guard against every fraud. For they signify to all, but not all perceive what is signified; nor can everyone read what is written, but only those who have learned their letters. Nevertheless, all deceptions <note>original: "praestigiae" / "γοητεία" (goēteia) - referring to sorcery or illusions</note> are performed through the contrary demons. For those who procure evils through sorceries and charms especially venerate these demons and the one presiding over them.

<column-break/>

-> § 42. <-

...unless, as *Abresch* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch (1699–1782), a Dutch philologist</note> preferred, you wish to read "there is not when" instead of "not indeed."

5. **Hanging over... dangers.** *Valent.* following *Fogerolles*, corrected the Greek to "encountered." I would prefer "impending" <note>original: "ἐπηρτημένους" (epērtēmenous)</note>. Among the Greeks, this is commonly used for impending danger, punishment, and similar things. "To hang fear over" occurred to us above in Book I, chapters 2 and 9.

6. **Showing through dreams.** They believed the highest God was "all-seeing" <note>original: "παντοδῆ" (pantodē)</note> and signified future things to men through demons. See *Davies* on *Maximus of Tyre*, Dissertation 19. This also happened through dreams. *Apuleius* in *On the God of Socrates*: "as a province is assigned to each, even for the confirming of dreams," etc. See also *Justin Martyr*, Apology I, 17. Likewise, the Jews believed certain dreams proceeded from demons, on which matter see the best interpreters on *St. Paul* to the Ephesians 2:2. Next, "to distinguish" <note>original: "διαιρεῖσθαι" (diaireisthai)</note> means to discern or judge with the mind. See *Bos*, Critical Observations, chapter 6, and the learned discussion on this word by *D'Orville* on *Chariton*.

7. **To know every [danger].** It would be better to read "everyone would know," as I have restored. **VALENT.** The former was very true (and the first hand had given it so in the *Meerman* manuscript), but instead of "would know" from the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* codices, I read "might know." *Abresch* had beautifully attempted to reach the truth by conjecture; however, the *Meerman* manuscript wrongly gives "might guard against."

8. **Nevertheless, through the contrary [demons] etc.** *Eusebius* <note>Early Christian historian</note> has these words up to the end of § 42 in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV. *Cyril* <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> has the same, and a little more, in *Against Julian*, Book IV. *Theodoret* also uses most of these in his *Sermon on Angels and Demons*, but he praises these as if taken from *Porphyry’s* books *On the Philosophy from Oracles*. This happens quite often, that he mixes different passages of Porphyry together. For example, in the *Sermon on Sacrifices*, he praises certain things from the books to which we have devoted this work, which in the *Sermon on Oracles* he says were drawn from the books *On the Philosophy from Oracles*. However, it could sometimes happen that the same things were said in different places. In *Theodoret*, "sorcery" <note>original: "γοητεία" (goēteia)</note> ought to be restored from our author in place of "need."

<gloss>1.</gloss> Through the working of wonders.] *Cyril* <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note> has: "for these are able to deceive through the working of wonders, through them etc." *Theodoret*: "working wonders and through this preparing charms and love-potions." Instead of "these," *Eusebius* has "there are." What our author asserts regarding the magical arts of Daemons, others also bring forward, wishing them to have taught men magic and other evil arts. See those praised by the Learned Men on *Minucius Felix*, chapter 26. A little before, *Meermann* mistakenly wrote "full" [singular] for "full" [plural].

<gloss>2.</gloss> Falsehood is their nature.] So says *Lucian* and others regarding evil Daemons, and Christians regarding evil angels. In the margin of the *Meermann* manuscript is added: "Note that the daemons pretend to be gods."

<gloss>3.</gloss> Presiding power.] Above he called him "the one presiding." "The great leader of the daemons" in *Iamblichus, Mysteries* III, 30, and "over the daemons" IX, 9; on which see *Gale*. Instead of "to seem" [infinitive], *Theodoret* and *Eusebius* in one place (p. 171 B) have "it seems," but in another (p. 173 D) "to seem," following "he wishes," which preceded it.

<gloss>4.</gloss> Libations and the smell of fat.] Well and to the point, *Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation*, page 26 C: "The daemons themselves somewhere confess their own gluttony, saying: 'For libations and the smell of fat are the honor we have received.'" These words are taken from *Homer’s Iliad* IV, 49 and XXIV, 70. Those two are also joined in *Iliad* IX, 496, which passage *Plato* uses in *Republic II*, page 595. Regarding the word "knissa" [smell of fat], see what the *Scholiast on Homer* (Iliad I, 317) teaches from *Porphyry*. *Arnobius* (Book VII, beginning, p. 212) says they are fed on fat-smells.

<gloss>5.</gloss> The spiritual nature is fattened.] *Eusebius, Cyril,* and *Theodoret* say "the spiritual and bodily [nature]." *Gale* on *Iamblichus, Mysteries*, p. 210, reads "spiritual body," or "bodily and spiritual." Ibid. p. 267: the Platonists call that subtle and thin body which they attributed to spirits "spirit" and "spiritual." See above, § 39. *Apuleius* (*On the God of Socrates*, p. 108) calls Daemons "animals with aerial bodies." <margin>Dionysius’s Epitome to Lacaena, page 54.</margin>

<gloss>7.</gloss> Is strengthened by etc.] Instead of "fat-smells," *Eusebius* has "sacrifices," who, since he follows our author (and with *Cyril* confirming our text), seems in need of correction. It was believed that the immortal gods were fed by vapors and the smell of victims—

<meta>This page continues Porphyrius’s argument regarding the nature of sacrifice and the purification of the soul, specifically addressing the distinction between ritual sacrifice and the consumption of meat.</meta>

# PORPHYRIUS

We exert every effort to become like God and those beings who surround Him. This likeness is achieved through <term>impassibility</term><note>original: "apatheia" – a state of being undisturbed by passions or emotions</note>, a clear and distinct understanding of those things which truly exist, and a life directed toward those same realities. Conversely, we strive to become unlike evil men and demons, and generally unlike anything that delights in what is mortal and material. Therefore, in accordance with the words of Theophrastus, we too shall offer sacrifice. With this, the <term>theologians</term><note>Porphyry likely refers to ancient priestly authorities or Orphic/Pythagorean writers</note> have also agreed, knowing that to the extent we neglect the purification of the soul’s passions, to that same extent we are joined to a wicked power; thus, it becomes necessary to appease even that power. For as the theologians say, for those who are bound by external things and do not yet rule over their passions, it is necessary to turn away the malice of this power; otherwise, they will never find rest from their labors.

§ 44. Thus far, let the matters pertaining to sacrifices be explained. Now, regarding what we said from the beginning—that it is not necessary to assume that if animals must be sacrificed, they must also be eaten—we shall demonstrate that one must not eat of animals, even if it is sometimes necessary that they be sacrificed. For all the theologians agree in this: that one must neither touch

<column-break/>

We exert every effort to become like God and those who are around Him, so that we may be made similar to Him: this occurs through impassibility, and a distinct perception of those things which truly are, and a life tending toward these very things: but that we may turn out dissimilar to evil men and demons, and altogether to everyone rejoicing in mortal and material things. Therefore, according to those things which were said by Theophrastus, we also shall sacrifice. With whom the Theologians also have agreed, since they have known that as much as we have neglected the cleansing of the affections of the soul, so much are we joined to a depraved power: so that it is necessary for us to soften even that power. For just as the Theologians say, for those who are bound to external things, and do not yet master their affections, it is necessary for them to avert the mischief of this power also. Otherwise, they will never cease from their labors.

§ 44. Up to this point, however, let those things which pertain to sacrifices be explained. Now, because we said from the beginning, it is not necessary that if animals are to be sacrificed, we should immediately think they are also to be eaten: we shall demonstrate that one must not eat from animals, even if sometimes it is necessary that they be sacrificed. For all theologians agree in this—

---

<margin>3. *Said by Theophrastus*] The earlier editions, the Leipzig and Meermann Manuscripts, read "to Theophrastus." I spoke above regarding the passage of Theophrastus. A little before, the word "truly" was badly missing before "beings" in the Meermann manuscript.</margin>
