# On Abstinence, Book II.

They believe that from those sacrifices which are performed for the sake of averting evils, nothing at all should be tasted; rather, they assert that these must be treated as purifications. For they say that no one should return to the city, nor enter a private home, unless they have first cleansed both their garments and their body in rivers or springs. For this reason, even those to whom they have permitted the act of sacrificing are commanded to abstain from the victims; and before they sacrifice, they must purify themselves through fasting, and especially through abstinence from the flesh of living creatures. For they say that purity and chastity <note>The Latin 'castimonia' here refers to ritual holiness or "state of grace."</note> serve as a guard for the sake of caution: like a divine symbol or seal, so that a person may suffer no harm from those beings whom he approaches to appease. For by being in a state contrary to the things he is performing—and more divine, because he is clearly purer in respect to both the body and the emotions of the soul—he remains unharmed, with ritual purity cast about him like a defensive bulwark.

->§ 45.<-

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text of the passage translated above.</note>
...one must [not taste] of the things sacrificed in the averting rituals, but must use them as purifications. For they say one should not go into the town, nor into one's own house, without first cleansing clothing and body in rivers or a spring. Thus, even those they permitted to sacrifice, they charged to abstain from the victims, and to hallow themselves beforehand by fasting and especially by abstinence from ensouled beings <note>original: "ἀποχαῖς τῶν ἐμψύχων" - referring to the core theme of the book: vegetarianism as a spiritual requirement.</note>. For purity is a guard for the sake of caution, like a symbol or a divine seal, to ensure one suffers nothing from those beings whom one approaches and appeases. For being in a state opposite to the deeds he performs, and more divine because he is purer in body and in the passions of the soul, he remains unharmed, having wrapped himself in purity like a fortress.

->§ 45.<-

***

1. *And must use them as purifications.*] A "purification" <note>original: "Καθάρσιον"</note>, namely a sacred rite, is called an *expiatory lustration*. See *D'Orville on Chariton, VIII, 1.* The custom itself—that after performing these rites, they did not return home before purifying their clothing and body with river or spring water—is well known from those who have written on the Lustrations of the ancients, and *Casaubon on Theophrastus, p. 292.* Indeed, the "averting" victims <note>original: "ἀποτρόπαιοι" - sacrifices meant to turn away evil spirits or bad luck.</note> were believed to pollute those who touched them. *Marsham (Chronicus Canon, Sec. IX, p. 208)* compares these with established sacred rites, though according to his own judgment.

2. *Like a symbol or a divine seal.*] *Abresch* preferred "And like a symbol." However, the author rightly calls the purity of the mind such, just as *Psellus* established that there are *divine symbols in souls*

<column-break/>

which put demons to flight. Compare the notes by *Elsner on the Revelation of John, IX, 4.* The nature and use of this word was excellently explained by *Casaubon on Athenaeus, III, 32.* The words *for the sake of caution... from those* are missing in the *Meerman* manuscript.

3. *Than the things he performs.*] The word "than" <note>original: "Ἢ"</note> seems as if it should be deleted. [The sense is] enjoying a condition very different from the nature of the things he is currently doing. For he is occupied with slaughter, and therefore also in the company of evil spirits who delight in slaughter; but he himself is most foreign to all these things. It could also be read as *being situated in the things he performs*, meaning *most foreign to these things, even in the midst of those very acts he then performs.* — REISKE. I understand this to refer to those evil spirits of whom he had spoken. *Performs* <note>original: "δρᾷ"</note> refers to *performing sacred rites* <note>original: "sacra facere"</note>.

# PORPHYRY

<columns>
§ 45. For this reason, even among sorcerers <note>original: γοήτων / praestigiatores - refers to practitioners of "low" magic or trickery</note>, such precaution has seemed necessary; however, it cannot be effective at all times. <gloss>1</gloss> For it is for the sake of licentiousness that they trouble evil spirits. Thus, purity did not belong to sorcerers, but to divine men and those steeped in divine wisdom; it brings protection everywhere to those who practice it through their kinship with the divine. Would that sorcerers also used it continually! For then they would no longer desire to practice sorcery, being excluded by this purity from enjoying those things for the sake of which they act impiously. Hence, <gloss>2</gloss> being full of passions, and abstaining for only a short time from impure foods while remaining filled with inward uncleanness, <gloss>3</gloss> they pay the penalty for their lawlessness against the whole of nature—partly at the hands of those very beings whom they provoke, and partly <gloss>4</gloss> by that Justice who oversees all mortal things, both deeds and thoughts—

<column-break/>

§ 45. Whence even to jugglers and charmers the necessity of this kind of precaution extends: yet it does not have power in them perpetually, because they invoke evil demons for the sake of outrages and lust. Wherefore, chastity <note>Latin: castimonia - ritual purity or abstinence</note> does not belong to charmers, but to divine men, and men imbued with divine wisdom: which indeed, from the conciliation with the gods, is accustomed to bring protection to those who use it. For would that the jugglers also used it perpetually: for they would no longer wish to pursue their charms: since they would be drawn away from enjoying those things for the sake of which they act impiously. Whence, since they are full of disturbances, and for a little while abstaining from impure foods they are filled with uncleanness, they pay the penalties of the crime which they commit in their entire operation, partly from those very ones whom they irritate, and partly also from Justice who [oversees] all mortal things and works...

<margin>
*To act, to perform sacred rites.* <note>original: "cere, sacris operari"</note> This kind of speaking is well known, illustrated a hundred times in both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note>. See § 59. *Athenaeus, Book XIV, 23:* "The ancients called sacrificing 'to do' <note>original: δρᾶν</note>."

1. *For because of licentiousness...*] The translator gave "of outrages and lust" <note>original: Flagitiorum & libidinis</note>. Indeed, *aselgeia* <note>Greek: ἀσελγεία</note> has a very wide meaning and embraces every impotence of the soul. Philologists have dealt with this word most diligently in the *Epistle to the Romans 13:13* and *D'Orville on Chariton V, 6.*

2. *Being full of passions, filled.*] Paul also joins these in *Romans 1:29*: "being filled with all unrighteousness... full of envy," etc. where see *Kypke*. "Full of passions" and similar phrases occur a hundred times. *Compare D'Orville on Chariton V, 8.*

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**A a 2**<-

...observes both deeds and counsels. Therefore, the purity of a divine man is both internal and external. Just as he strives to abstain from the passions of the soul and from those foods that incite the passions, so he enjoys the food of divine wisdom. He reconciles himself to the likeness of God through right thoughts concerning Him. He is one who is consecrated by an intellectual sacrifice <note>original: *intellectuali sacrificio*; referring to a mental or spiritual offering rather than a blood sacrifice</note>, approaching God with a white garment—which is truly the bright purity of the soul’s freedom from passion <term>impatibilitatis; the state of being unaffected by worldly suffering or emotion</term> and the lightness of the body. He does not approach God burdened by foreign and external juices in the body or by disturbances in the soul.

§ 46. For surely, it is not the case that in temples dedicated to the gods by men...

<column-break/>

...justice. Therefore, the purity of a divine man is both internal and external. He strives to be "fasting" from the passions of the soul and "fasting" from those foods that stir the passions, while "feeding" upon divine wisdom. He makes himself like God through correct thoughts about the Divine. He is a man consecrated by the intellectual sacrifice, approaching God with a white robe—the truly pure state of the soul’s freedom from passion—and with a lightness of body, not burdened by alien and foreign juices <note>original: *χυμῶν* (chumōn); referring to the bodily humors or fluids affected by diet</note> or by the passions of the soul.

§ 46. For surely, if in the temples set apart for the gods by men...

---

### [Critical Commentary]

<columns>2</columns>

*Eusebius* in his *Praise of Constantine* says the eye of Justice is the overseer of human affairs. I see these and other points already praised by *Kuster* in his notes on *Suidas* regarding the "Eye of Justice." *Synesius* in *On Kingship*, p. 19: "The justice of God sees all and hears all."

5. **Fasting from...** The phrase "fasting from passions" (for the word "from" seems unnecessary to remove) may be compared with that famous and solemn maxim of Pythagoras, if I am not mistaken: "to fast from wickedness." *Reiske* <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. *Caelius Rhodiginus* thought this a great and divine saying of Empedocles. To "feed on wisdom" and similar phrases are well known from the Lexicographers.

6. **A man being consecrated.** The form *hierōmenou* is more common, from the verb "to be a priest." It seems the word "man" should be removed as it was placed just above. *Reiske*. Grammarians note a distinction between *hierasthai* and *hierousthai*: the latter is used for things being consecrated, the former for those performing the office of a priest. See *Duker* on *Thucydides* V, 1. I thought *Thomas Magister* meant that *hierasthai* and *hiereuesthai* are said of sacrifices, but only *hierasthai* is said of priests. But interpreters contend the reading there is corrupt. *Eusebius*, perhaps regarding this, says in *Demonstratio Evangelica* I, p. 29: "those consecrated to the God over all, not with cattle-sacrifices... but with right dogmas of true piety." Our author and others repeat this so often that there appears no reason to think he received this from *Paul* in *Romans* 12:1.

7. **A white and pure garment.** Compare the observations at § 19. The white garments of those performing sacred rites are very well known. *Clement of Alexandria* rightly says in *Stromata* IV: "External adornment and purification happen for the sake of a symbol." Thus, white clothes are fitting for priests, according to *Artemidorus* in *The Interpretation of Dreams* II, 3. The *Meermann* manuscript reads "of the body," but then incorrectly reads "winter" instead of "juices."

8. **Burdened.** The Florence and Leiden editions read *bebarumenou*. It comes to the same thing. Both *bareisthai* and *barunesthai* commonly mean to be weighed down, to be sluggish, or to languish; it is attributed to the soul which becomes sluggish through immoderate food, drink, cares, etc. Such is that passage in *Luke's Gospel* 21:34: "lest your hearts be weighed down." On which many learned men have commented.

1. **For surely...** This entire paragraph...

# PORPHYRY

...and <gloss>2</gloss> the sandals on one's feet must be clean and unstained; but in <gloss>3</gloss> the temple of the Father—this world—should one not take care to keep the <gloss>4</gloss> outermost garment, this skin of ours, pure, and to dwell within the temple of the Father with a pure heart? For if the danger lay only in its being defiled, one might perhaps overlook it and be careless. But now, since every perceptible body carries emanations of material demons, along with the impurity arising from flesh and blood, there is present a power <gloss>5</gloss> dear and welcoming to this impurity, due to their similarity and kinship.

§ 47. Wherefore the theologians rightly [advocated] for abstaining—

we ought to wear clean shoes, free from every stain: but in the temple of the father, which is this world, should no care be taken that our outermost tunic of skin be preserved pure, and that we enter it pure and bright? For if the danger consisted only in its defilement, it might perhaps be permitted to neglect it. But since every sensible body brings with it certain flows of material demons, it happens that, together with the impurity which exists from the eating of flesh and blood, a power friendly and familiar to it is also present because of their likeness and kinship.

<note>The following are scholarly annotations provided by the editor of this edition.</note>

1. Cyril took this from our author <note>original: "Cyrill: Adv. Iulian. L. IX. p. 310."</note>. Instead of "by men" he uses "from men." Well said: "set apart for sacred things." For "to set apart" <note>original: "aphorizesthai"</note> is properly said of those things which are designated and dedicated to God, as specifically of a portion of a field which was separated from the rest of the estate for divine use. Just as a field consecrated to God is called "set-apart land" <note>original: "ge aphorismene"</note> by the Alexandrian elders in Leviticus 27:21. Hesychius defines it as: "sacred precincts, temples, groves, or places set apart in honor." See also Salmasius on Solinus, p. 767, and the learned man on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans 1:1.

2. **The sandals on one's feet... unstained.** Who is unaware of the ancient sacred practice of walking barefoot <note>original: "nudipedalia"</note> and the Pythagorean precept: "Sacrifice and worship barefoot"? He is believed to have taken this from the Hebrews. See Moses in Exodus 3:5 and the Book of Joshua 5:15. The same custom existed among certain ancient Christians, regarding which see Bingham’s *Antiquities of the Christian Church* III, p. 342; nor has it fallen into disuse today among the Indians and other nations. Suidas explains "unstained" <note>original: "akēlidōton"</note> as "spotless" or "undefiled." Compare the learned man on Hesychius under that word. To our point, Synesius in Epistle 105 says: "It is fitting for a priest to be unstained in all things."

3. **In the temple of the Father, the world...** The Leipzig Manuscript has "neō" for temple; that is indeed the Attic form, but our author did not swear by those laws, and a little later he spells it with an "a" <note>original: "naō"</note>. However, he uses the Attic style below in § 54. Heraclitus beautifully illustrates the matter itself in an Epistle: "Do you not know that God is not handmade, nor has he a base from the beginning, nor a single enclosure? But the whole world is his temple." Even in the sacred scriptures, this whole universe is viewed as the temple of God. The prophet Malachi signifies this in chapter 1:11.

4. **The outermost garment, this skin of ours.** I spoke of this above in I, 31. Seneca, Epistle 92: "What I said of clothing, consider me to say of the body: for nature has surrounded the soul with this also, like a certain garment; it is its covering." A little later Cyril has "it was possible even to overlook."

5. **A power dear and welcoming.** These are well joined, as below "Dear and welcoming" in § 53. "Dear and welcoming things" in Eusebius. Indeed, "welcoming" <note>original: "prosēgoron"</note> refers to that which is joined and friendly, hence it is opposed to "that which is at war," as Markland teaches on Maximus Tyrius, Dissertation XI; thereby shedding light on our author.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

-> Aa 3 <-

...they should apply the foremost care toward abstinence. And the Egyptian <note>original: "Aegyptius". Referring to the philosopher Plotinus, as noted in the commentary below.</note> revealed these things to us, bringing forward a most natural cause which experience had confirmed. For since a base and irrational soul, which has been violently snatched away and has deserted the body, remains near to it—just as the souls of men who perish by a violent death are also accustomed to linger by the body itself (which is why one is forbidden from violently casting oneself out of the body)—since, therefore, the violent slaughter of living beings forces the souls to take delight in those things which they have left behind; and since the soul is in no way prevented from being there where something kindred draws it; for which reason many have even been seen to lament:

<column-break/>

...they took care regarding abstinence. And the Egyptian <note>original: "ὁ Αἰγύπτιος"</note> revealed these things to us, rendering a most natural cause which he had proved from experience. For since a base and irrational soul, having left the body, being snatched away by force, remains with it, seeing as even the souls of men who have died by force are held back near the body (and this is a deterrent against leading oneself out by force). Since, then, the violent slaughters of animals force the souls to linger fondly in those things which they leave behind, and the soul is by no means barred from being there where its kinship drags it down, whence also many have been seen mourning. And those of the unburied...

---

1. *The Egyptian.*] This is Plotinus. REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, a noted 18th-century scholar.</note> For he had his homeland in Lycopolis in Egypt; since there were two cities of this name, it seems that the one situated in the Thebaid is meant. *Fabricius: on our author in the Life of Plotinus, Greek Library IV, 26.*

2. *For since the soul.*] The adverb *since* <note>original: "ἐπεὶ"</note> in a period quite circuitous and ambitious, is repeated twice for the sake of picking up the speech again, like a signpost for a reader about to go astray—once at line 26, then again at line 37. Immediately, instead of *which the body* in the *Leipzig* manuscript there is *or*; he intended *if*, which is the true reading. REISKE. *The Meerman manuscript also has "or".*

3. *Snatched by force.*] Thus it was published, but I have restored *stripped/despoiled.* <note>original: "συληθεῖσα"</note> It is well done by the *Leipzig & Meerman* Codices, which preserved the true writing for us, which is confirmed by *Felicianus & Marsilio Ficino*, who gave *exspoliata* [despoiled]. Many illustrate this very doctrine which our author introduces concerning the unhappiness of the souls of those men who perished by violent slaughter. See *Fortunio Liceti on the Secret Lamps of the Ancients, Book III, ch. 7.*

4. *Where.*] This is an indication of an argument brought forward to demonstrate the truth of the proposed opinion: soon a verb is missing before *and are held back—*

<column-break/>

—for example: they are fled, they roam, they wander, or something similar, or the *and* should be deleted. REISKE.

5. *And the [deterrent] against...*] It was more correctly read previously as *which also [the deterrent] against.* And so it was in the *Leipzig & Meerman* Codices. *To lead out by force, to lead oneself out, to lead oneself out of life, out of living,* etc. They say these things of those who snatch life from themselves by force; for the soul is *the true man*, as he says in section 47. See: *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus III, 33. and V. D. on Xenophon of Ephesus, New Miscellaneous Observations p. 52.* Our author rightly refutes this opinion, who himself had once thought about killing himself, as we know *from the Life of Plotinus, ch. 2.* Pythagoras forbids *departing from the guard-post and station of life without the order of the commander, that is, of God. Cicero: On Old Age, ch. 21.* This was seen otherwise by the "People of the Porch" <note>The Stoics, who famously permitted suicide under certain rational conditions.</note>, so to speak, and others, although even they did not think death should be hastened rashly. But concerning the dogma of Pythagoras, read *Holstenius in the Life of Porphyry, ch. 8. and V. D. on Hierocles in the Golden Verses, p. 260.*

6. *In those things which they leave.*] Namely *the bodies*, which I am inclined to think should be added. REISKE.

7. *And those of the unburied [remain] etc.*] Concerning the soul—

The souls of the unburied also remain beside their bodies; sorcerers <term>venefici: those who use potions or magic</term> abuse these souls for their own service, compelling them by detaining either the whole body or some part of it. Since, therefore, they observed the nature of a wicked soul, and the kinship <gloss>8</gloss> and pleasure it is accustomed to have toward the bodies from which it was torn away, they rightly avoided the eating of flesh. <margin>On depraved and unpurified souls, see *Plato* in the *Phaedo*: page 61. D. "Such a soul is weighed down and dragged back again into the visible world... wandering, as is said, around monuments and tombs." <note>original: "ἡ τοιαύτη ψυχὴ βαρύνεταί τε καὶ ἕλκεται..."</note> So also the souls of those who perished by a violent death; hence the necromancers <term>nekromanteis: those who consult the dead</term>, who consulted souls about the future, were accustomed to spend the night in sepulchers. See *Elsner* on *Matthew VIII*, 28. It was believed those souls retained the remains of their old filth, on which matter see *Gale on Iamblichus*: *On the Mysteries* II, 5. and many others. Lawgivers prudently made use of this persuasion—that such souls do not rest before the corpses are buried—for their own purposes, so that murders would not be committed safely and easily: a point beautifully handled by the learned *Warburton* in *The Divine Legation of Moses*, Book II. page 368.</margin>

You do not lack authority in a manifest matter. *Lipsius* and *Meermann* are correct.</margin>

namely, they devour the hearts of crows, or moles, or hawks; for they believe that these animals possess a soul that sits beside them and prophesies like a god, and which, at the moment the body is ingested, glides into them as well.

§ 49. Justly, therefore, the philosopher—who is the priest of the God who is over all—abstains from all eating of animate beings. ...devouring, such as the hearts of crows, or moles, or hawks, they possess the soul present and oracular like a god, and <gloss>3</gloss> entering into themselves along with the insertion of the body.

§ 49. Reasonably then the <gloss>1</gloss> Philosopher, and priest of the God over all, abstains from all food of living souls, striving alone to approach <gloss>2</gloss> the only God through himself, without the annoyance of those things that follow along, and he is devout, having <gloss>3</gloss> searched out the necessities of Nature. <margin>
Iamblichus says in *The Mysteries* III. 14 that certain drinks bring the power of prophesying; see there the notes by Gale. Regarding the parts of animals believed to contribute most to divination, read the same author on III, 22; for they thought the spirit entered into crows, hawks, and other birds. Eusebius touches on the futility of this in *Demonstratio Evangelica* Book V, p. 209; see also his work *Against Hierocles* p. 918. C. They primarily ate the heart because it was the symbol of the soul. Read the learned discussion by the celebrated Michaelis in his *Dissertation on the Heart and Brain*. Moreover, the phrase "the most sovereign parts" <note>original: τὰ κυριώτατα</note> was missing in the Meerman manuscript.
</margin>

<margin>
3. *Entering into themselves.* <note>original: Εἰσιοῦσαν εἰς ἑαυτοὺς</note> The Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts have "into them" <note>original: εἰς αὐτοὺς</note>, which I prefer. An "insertion" <note>original: ἔνθεσις</note> is what the Latins call a morsel or a mouthful. "Eating in an orderly fashion, you make the insertion," according to the delightful Antiphanes in Athenaeus IV, 17.
</margin>

<margin>
1. *Philosopher, and priest of God.* <note>original: Φιλόσοφος, καὶ θεοῦ ἱερεὺς</note> Just as pious and holy men are often called "priests of God" in the Sacred Scriptures. The Stoics used to say that "only the wise man is a priest." This is a very well-known matter.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
2. *Through himself to approach God.* <note>original: Διὰ τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ θεῷ προσ.</note> The older editions and the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts read "through his own god" <note>original: διὰ τ. ἑ. θεοῦ</note>, which Reiske approved, as if it said "through the god within himself" <note>original: διὰ τοῦ ἐν ἑαυτῷ θεοῦ</note>—that is, through his internal divinity or spirit. However, the word "to God" <note>original: θεῷ</note> is supported by what preceded ("to approach God alone") and what follows in § 52 ("he himself... approaching God through himself"). I almost believe these words strike at the Christians. For the Lord Jesus is the priest who saves "those who approach God through him," as is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews VII, 25. Porphyry had undoubtedly read this passage.
</margin>

<margin>
3. *Having searched out.* <note>original: Ἐξισορικώς</note> All editions and even the Meerman manuscript (though in that one 'i' and 'e' are confused everywhere) read *exisorikos*, but in Valentinus's edition it was a printer's error. Perhaps also in the Victorian edition. The Leipzig manuscript and Suidas are correct: "having searched out, having investigated, having narrated." This is confirmed by Herodotus.
</margin>

<margin>
4. *The [priest] of some...* <note>original: Ὁ τινὸς τῶν</note> Perhaps "whoever of the particular..."
</margin>

# P O R P H Y R I I
### On Abstinence from Animal Food

<column-break/>

...just as a priest <margin>A priest of a specific temple. <note>original: "μέρος ναῶν ἱερεὺς"</note> Reiske suggests "a priest of some specific god," referring to local deities as opposed to the priest of the God over all. <note>The manuscript notes a scribal error in the Meerman codex: "merchant" instead of "experienced."</note></margin> is experienced in the consecration of his god's statues, and in the mystic rites, initiations, purifications, and similar matters; so the priest of the God who presides over all things is skilled through experience in the fashioning of His "statues" <note>Porphyry likely refers to the cultivation of the soul or virtues as the true "statues" of the Supreme God.</note>, and in the purifications and other means by which he is joined to that God.

§ 50. <gloss>1</gloss> Now, if the priests and inspectors of sacrifices <term>hieroskopoi|diviners who examine the entrails of sacrifices</term> in this world <margin>1. "The priests of those here." Perhaps "the priests of the temples here." <note>original: "τῶν τῇδε ναῶν ἱερεῖς"</note></margin> command both themselves and others to abstain from tombs, <gloss>2</gloss> from unholy men, from women in their menstrual period, from sexual intercourse, <margin>2. "Unholy men, etc." In antiquity, those polluted by such things were barred from sacred rites. Compare the notes on Book IV, 16. These might seem to touch upon the Mosaic laws; a note in the Meerman manuscript says: "I believe he is speaking of the divine Moses."</margin> and <gloss>3</gloss> from sights that are shameful or mournful, and from listening to anything that excites the passions—<margin>3. "Shameful sights and sounds." Just as Julian the Emperor instructed that a priest approaching the gods should neither say nor hear anything shameful.</margin> (since it often appears that even the presence of impure people disturbs the inspector of sacrifices, which is why they say that sacrificing at an improper time brings greater harm than profit)—<gloss>4</gloss> then surely the priest of the Father himself will not endure to become a tomb for dead bodies? <margin>4. "Will he endure to become a tomb?" A beautiful turn of phrase frequent in both Greek and Latin. Regarding a man devoured by wild beasts, Lucretius (Book V) wrote:
> He provided living food for wild beasts, devoured by their teeth,
> Seeing his living entrails buried in a living tomb.
Gataker notes many other examples, such as Marcus Aurelius (VI, 21): "He is buried in the bodies of those who are fed." Dandamis in Palladius says similarly...</margin>

<column-break/>

...of his statues, and of the sacrifices, ceremonies, expiations, and similar things he is skilled: so the priest of the God presiding over all is expert in the experience of His images, of the expiations, and of all other things by which he is joined to Him.

§ 50. But if the priests and sacrificers of those who are here command both themselves and others to abstain from graves, and profane men, and menstruating women, and sexual intercourse, and even from a shameful or mournful spectacle, as well as from hearing those things which move the passions: because frequently, on account of the presence of even impure persons, something appears which disturbs the sacrificer and the soothsayer: whence they also say that sacrificing unseasonably brings greater loss than gain: shall then he who is the priest of the highest Father endure to become himself a tomb of dead bodies?

<column-break/>

<summary>Porphyry argues that if ordinary priests must maintain strict ritual purity to avoid disturbing their divinations, the priest of the Supreme God must maintain even higher purity by refusing to turn his body into a "tomb" for dead animals.</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**B b**<-

...himself full of defilement, while he strives to be an associate of the superior being? <note>original: "cum praestantiore" / "τῷ κρείττονι". This refers to the Divine or the gods.</note> Is it not enough that we take the portions of death into this life of ours through the fruits of the earth? But it is not yet the place to treat of these things. For we must return to a more exact distinction of those matters which pertain to sacrifices.

51. For someone might say that we would be doing away with a great part of divination—that which is customarily performed through the entrails <term>exta: the internal organs of a sacrificial animal, used for omens</term>—if we abstain from the slaughter of animals. But such a person might as well kill human beings, since the future is seen even more clearly, so they say, in their entrails; and many among the barbarians practice divination through human entrails <note>original: "aruspicianam" / "σπλαγχνεύοντες"</note>. But just as it was a mark of injustice and cruelty <note>original: "immanitatis" / "πλεονεξίας"</note> to kill one’s own kind for the sake of divination, so it is unjust to slaughter an irrational animal for the sake of prophesying. Now, whether the gods show these signs, or spirits <term>daemones: in the Greek sense, intermediary spirits between gods and humans</term>, or the soul as it departs from the animal through...

<column-break/>

<note>The following section translates the scholarly annotations provided at the bottom of the original page.</note>

---

<column-break/>

Concerning the Brahmans: page 43. *“And you become walking tombs of dead animals.”* <note>A famous Pythagorean sentiment regarding meat-eating.</note>

5. **The superior being.**] Felicianus translates as *with the more excellent*. I suspect, however, it is better rendered as *with God*. The term *superior* <note>Greek: "κρείττον"</note> is used for a *divine power*, but most especially in the plural <note>Greek: "κρείττονες"</note> they are the *Gods*. See *Bos: Animadversions on Lucian, chapter 15.* Presently, the Leipzig Manuscript omitted the word *the*; then Abresch preferred the phrase *from the fruits*.

1. **Divining through humans.**] Abresch suggests *through human beings*. I believe the manuscripts that have the form *they practice divination* <note>Greek: "σπλαγχνεύονται"</note> hold the true hand of the Author, though I know how the common reading can be defended. Note the "anthropomancy" <term>divination by human sacrifice</term> of certain nations, or the custom of divining through human victims. Concerning the Gauls, see *Diodorus Siculus, Book V, 31.* Concerning the Lusitanians and others, see *Olearius on Philostratus’s Life of Apollonius of Tyana, Book VIII, 15*, where you will see that Elagabalus, that most foul of bipeds, also established this practice. Nor were Christians treated any better by the Roman Emperors. Concerning Julian, see the *Scholiast on Gregory Nazianzen, Invective II, page 61.* For others, see the Learned Men on *Justin’s Apology I, 24.*

2. **Injustice and cruelty.**] Felicianus gave *Injustice and cruelty* <note>Latin: "Iniustitiae & immanitatis"</note>, in which sense the word *greed/cruelty* <note>Greek: "πλεονεξία"</note> is also used elsewhere in Porphyry. These terms are well joined, because *to be greedy* is *to inflict injury*...

The commentary provides historical context on "anthropomancy" (human sacrifice) among ancient cultures and the Roman Empire.</summary>

# PORPHYRIUS

->How the divinity answers a question through the signs in the entrails <note>original: "σπλάγχνοις" / "extorum" - referring to extispicium, the practice of reading animal organs</note> is not the subject of the present inquiry.<-

§ 52. However, for those whose lives are tossed about by external things, we permit them—having once committed an impiety against themselves—to be carried along wherever they are already drifting. But if we are describing a **Philosopher** <note>The "Philosopher" here is a technical term for one seeking a life of pure reason and detachment from the physical world.</note>, one who stands apart from external affairs, we rightly say that he will not trouble the spirits <note>original: "δαίμοσι" / "daemonibus" - here meaning lesser divine beings or mediators</note>, nor will he have need of soothsayers or the entrails of animals. For this man has practiced withdrawing from the very things for which divinations are performed. He does not enter into a marriage, so as to trouble the soothsayer about the wedding; <gloss>2</gloss> he does not engage in trade, nor does he consult about a slave, nor about <gloss>3</gloss> his advancement <note>original: "προκοπῆς" - progress or promotion</note> or any other <gloss>4</gloss> vanity <note>original: "δοξοκοπίας" - literally "glory-striking," seeking public reputation</note> common among men.

<column-break/>

<margin>To harm someone in any way. Thus "to be wronged" and "to be defrauded" correspond to each other in Thucydides, Book I, 77. A little later in the Lipsius and Meermann manuscripts: "the soul."</margin>

1. **But if we are describing a Philosopher etc.**] *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian who quoted Porphyry extensively to argue against paganism.</note> also takes testimony from here in the same book. These are the variations in the reading: in that text, "the soothsayer" is written in the dative case, and in the following line "concerning theft" is used, not "concerning advancement" as it is here. For where the text above has "he has practiced," the reading there is "it has been a care," which is an error. This is also confirmed by the authority of the *Eusebius* manuscript: VICTORIUS. Up to those words at the end of § 52, "and instead of a soothsayer etc." *Eusebius*, Preparation for the Gospel, IV. p. 166. D.

2. **Trouble the soothsayer.**] *Eusebius*, as just mentioned, uses the dative case. *Heraldus* cites our author this way in his notes on *Arnobius*, p. 233; but he had read it in *Eusebius*, for he also cites other errors found in *Eusebius* but not in *Porphyry*, such as "it has been a care" and "theft."

<column-break/>

Our author uses both constructions: with the accusative in I, 49 and II, 45, and with the dative a little earlier, "to trouble the spirits." You may find it both ways a hundred times. See the celebrated *Alberti* on *Hesychius* under the letter E. The same logic applies to "to disturb." *Luke* in Acts 15:19 joins it with the dative, others use both.

3. **Advancement.**] The word "theft" in *Eusebius* has already been corrected by learned men. Perhaps the slip arose because minor Greek grammarians think this word is "unapproved" <note>original: "ἀδόκιμον" - not used by classical Attic authors</note>; it has long been shown by scholars that they are gravely mistaken, and that it denotes *any kind of increase*. It is well known that "to advance" <note>original: "προκόπτειν"</note> is said particularly of those who *make progress in the study of virtue*; *Jens* and *Alberti* (on 2 Timothy 3:9) investigate where this manner of speaking was derived from. For "other," the *Meermann* manuscript incorrectly has "to others."

4. **Vanity.**] Regarding the word "to hunt for glory" <note>original: "δοξοκοπεῖν"</note>, see the notes on Book I, 38. *Suidas* defines "glory-striking" as "vainglory." The same under "to court the people": "courting the people" is also called "glory-striking."

<summary>Porphyry argues that a true philosopher has no need for divination or animal sacrifice because they have detached themselves from the worldly ambitions (marriage, money, status) that such rites are meant to serve. The philological notes compare Porphyry's text with citations in Eusebius, debating specific Greek word choices like 'advancement' versus 'theft.'</summary>

5. **Will reveal the truth.**] Thus "the clear" (saphes) stands for "accurately and truly" in *Pindar*. And "clear Phoebus" in *Sophocles* stands for "the true one," as the ancient critics explain. See *Alberti on Matthew 20:31 and Suidas.* Presently, instead of "we say" (legomen), it should be read as "we were saying" (elegomen) from the *Eusebius and Meerman Manuscripts*, for it refers back to those things said previously.

6. **In the true [entrails] etc.**] To better perceive the meaning of this word, it helps to note what is written in the margin of the *Leipzig Manuscript* as a memory aid: "that God is established in the entrails of the one living according to virtue." It seems to refer to p. 90, 23. *Reiske.* The same scholion <note>A marginal note or explanatory comment in a manuscript.</note> was written in the *Meerman* manuscript. The ancients used to say God was in the entrails because they believed He signified future things through them, as if there were a certain sign in them called "God," which, if it appeared whole, showed the Divinity was propitious. He refers to this when he says God is established in the "true entrails" of the wise man. See *Olearius on Philostratus VIII, 15.* *Gataker* does well to compare this with "the divinity established within in the depths" in *Marcus Aurelius III, 16*, just as the Apostle wishes our bodies to be temples of God. And "the Word of God dwelling in the true entrails" is said by *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book IV, p. 170 D*, who certainly refers to this passage.

-> Confidant of great Jupiter <-

Shortly before, in our author's text in *Pamphilus*, "entirely there" (holōs ekei) should be rewritten instead of "wholly there" (holōs ekei) as it is published.

1. **If some [necessity] should press.**] *Leipzig MS*: "if something of [necessity] should press." Incorrect. It is established, however, that it should be read: "if indeed something of [necessity] should press." *Reiske.*

2. **Through dreams and signs and divine voices.**] I have restored to Malchus [Porphyry] his own words, for all manuscripts agree on this reading. Only the *Valentian* had neglected "and signs." "Ossa," or in the Attic dialect "Otta," denotes a certain divine instinct by which men are taught, whence "ossesthai" and in Attic "otteuesthai" means to be [led] by a certain secret instinct...

# PORPHYRY

and through omens <note>original: ὄττης (ottēs). Porphyry refers to divine signs or voices</note> good spirits <note>original: δαίμονες (daimones). In this context, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> run before us to signal what is about to happen, and what is necessary to guard against. For one must only depart from evil, and recognize that which is most precious in the universe, and consider everything good in the universe to be a friend and approachable. But wickedness and ignorance of divine matters are a terrible thing, accustomed to looking down upon and dragging down <note>original: ἐπισύρειν (episýrein). This implies a dismissive or slanderous dragging of a reputation</note> those things which it does not know. Since Nature does not cry out these things with audible voices, but being intellectual in essence, she initiates those who revere her into the sacred mysteries through the intellect. Furthermore, even if one accepts the ritual of sacrifice for the sake of foreknowing the future, it does not follow from this that it is necessary to eat and accept flesh, just as a sacrifice performed in any way to either gods or spirits does not introduce the eating of meat. At any rate, history shows not only that others—

<column-break/>

and through a vision, they may announce beforehand what is to happen and what is to be avoided. One must only stand apart from evil: and recognize what is most precious and most honorable in the universe, and that everything good in the universe is friendly and affable. But it is a wonder how much wickedness and lack of skill in divine matters is accustomed to promptly despising and condemning those things which it has not known. Nevertheless, to those who are fit to hear, Nature cries out: who, since she is intellectual, initiates through the intellect those into the sacred rites who worship her. Add to this that even if someone should admit the rite of sacrificing for the sake of foreknowing future events, it does not follow from that, however, that meat must also necessarily be eaten; just as a sacrifice which is otherwise made either to gods or to spirits does not immediately introduce the eating of flesh. # On Abstinence, Book II.
## Bb 3

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who wrote extensively on piety and botany.</note> mentioned this, but he also handed down to memory many other things concerning the slaughter of humans, which the ancients used to practice; yet it does not follow from this that humans ought to be eaten.

§ 54. Since these instances are indeed many and various, I think these few which I shall subjoin will be sufficient to prove this point. For in Rhodes, on the day before the Nones of July <note>July 6th</note>, a human was sacrificed to Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus; the translator uses the Latin name here.</note>. And when that custom had persisted for a long time, it was afterwards changed into a more civilized manner. They would detain someone condemned to death by public judgment in prison until the Saturnalia; when the solemn day arrived, they brought him outside the gates opposite the shrine of Aristobula <note>A title for Artemis meaning "Best Counselor."</note>

<column-break/>

Theophrastus mentioned this, but he also handed down the memory of many more, such as those of old who sacrificed a human, and surely because of this humans are not to be eaten.

§ 54. And that we do not say these things simply, but from a full history, these examples are sufficient to demonstrate. For in Rhodes, on the sixth day of the month of Metageitnion <note>An Attic month roughly corresponding to late summer; the Latin text above equates it with July.</note>, a human was sacrificed to Cronus. This custom, which prevailed for a long time, was changed. For they held one of those publicly condemned to death until the festival of Cronus; and when the festival was at hand, they led the man outside the gates opposite the [shrine] of Aristobula—

---

1. **And that these &c.**] In the same book <note>Referring to Eusebius's "Preparation for the Gospel."</note> are read twenty-three verses which follow here in succession; I will note the variations in them. The first difference is tiny, for "having given wine to drink" is written there in the genitive case, and so forth: in the verse "of the crow," in which the diversity of reading remains, since he mentions this town again later in the same book. In the penultimate line of this page "they were sacrificing." In the second item of the following page by the same reasoning "they were sacrificing," not "they were being sacrificed," as in both places here. Moreover, where it is read below "and the Dumatii of Arabia," it is written there "Dumates. Those of Arabia." In the last verse "of Latiarius" with a letter changed, not "Latiarius." Wrongly, I think, for the written book of Eusebius agrees with Porphyry. VICTORIUS. <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian philologist.</note> Almost to the end of § 56, Eusebius transcribed this. See also his "In Praise of Constantine." Cyril, Theodoret in his "Sermon on Sacrifices," all use these passages of Porphyry. But also Clement of Alexandria in his "Exhortation" and many others deal with that dire kind of sacrifices. However true those things may be

<column-break/>

which he says—that even if they are sacrificed, it does not follow that humans must also be eaten—you should observe that these things were nevertheless mostly joined together. Compare Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus III, 24.

2. **For he was sacrificed &c.**] Eusebius also relates these and the following things in "In Praise of Constantine" and Theodoret in "Sermon on Sacrifices," but there it is read "it was changed into a custom." On the matter itself, read Meursius in "Rhodes" I, 16.

3. **And when the festival was at hand—**] Note the custom, that when a feast day was imminent, they would inflict punishment on the accused, for it was not permitted on the feast day itself. Hence Socrates in Plato's *Phaedo*: "the festival of the god prevented me from dying." From this, the Gospel history of Matthew 27 can be illustrated. Note also that the punishment was inflicted "outside the gates," which was a very frequent custom of old. Compare the learned commentator on the Epistle to the Hebrews 13:12. The most honorable Cuper teaches the same regarding the Romans and indicates the cause of the matter in "Observations" IV, 19.

4. **Of the seat of Aristobula.**] See Meursius on the "People of Attica" in the section on Melite. VALENT. <note>Likely a reference to the scholar Valentin Rose or similar commentator.</note> Of the Rhodians.

# PORPHYRY

<note>original Greek: βούλης ἕδους... / original Latin: lae uini potione...</note>
...of the seat of [Artemis] of Good Counsel, having given them wine to drink, they would slaughter them. In the place which is now called Salamis, but was formerly named Coronis, in the month of Aphrodisius according to the Cypriot calendar, a human being was sacrificed to Agraulis, the daughter of Cecrops <note>The legendary first king of Athens</note> and the nymph Agraulis. This custom continued until the times of Diomedes. Then it changed, so that the human was sacrificed to Diomedes. Within a single enclosure stood the temple of Athena, and that of Agraulis and Diomedes. The one 

<column-break/>

who was to be sacrificed, being led by the youths, would run three times around the altar. Then the priest would strike him with a spear in the stomach, and thus...

---

...by whose example Themistocles built a temple at Athens to Diana <note>Artemis</note> of Good Counsel, concerning which see *Meursius*, *On the Piraeus*, chapter 9.

5. **Having given them wine to drink.**] Following the custom of the ancients, which commentators use to illustrate the sour wine <note>original: posca</note> which the soldiers gave to the Lord Christ, *Matthew 27:48 and Mark 15:36.*

6. **In the place which is now Salamis, etc.**] *Meerman* incorrectly writes *Koronidion*, where the "on" was attached from the following syllable. In *Eusebius* it is *Koroneia*. See *Viger* there. Just as our author writes, so also does *Cyril*: see also *Theodoret*, *Sermon on Sacrifices*, page 589. *Stephanus of Byzantium* writes that *Korone* is a part of Salamis. But *Meursius* shows in *Cyprus* I, 20, that the city was called this in ancient times, which Teucer later enlarged and named Salamis after his homeland. Regarding the Cypriot month *Aphrodisius* and others, read the same author, chapter 24.

7. **A human was sacrificed to Agraulis, daughter of Cecrops, etc.**] I wish the illustrious man <note>referring to a specific scholar</note> had proved in his *Chronological Canon*, Century 8, that Cecrops introduced human sacrifice to Cyprus. Certainly, you cannot force that conclusion from this passage. And I remember others reporting much milder things concerning the sacrifices of Cecrops. *Barnes* reads *Aglaurus* for *Agraulus*, and shortly after *Aglauridis* for *Agraulidis* in his notes on Euripides' *Ion*, line 23. But those names are frequently used interchangeably. *Alberti* in his notes on *Hesychius* under *Agraulus* has saved us the trouble. On the matter itself, read *Meursius*, *Attic Readings* VI, 3, who corrects the error of those who confuse Agraulis, the daughter of Cecrops, with Minerva <note>Athena</note>, who was also surnamed *Agraulus* or *Aglaurus* by the Athenians. Porphyry calls the wife of Cecrops *Agraulis*, others call her *Agraulus*. See *Meursius*, *On the Athenian Kingdom* I, 11. For "so that to Diomedes," *Meerman* reads "as to Diomedes."

8. **Within a single enclosure, etc.**] This word is used specifically for the circuit of a temple. The Greeks properly called the *peribolos* a certain measure of land that was vacant around temples and enclosed by a wall. The Latins call it the *conseptum* <note>enclosure</note> of the temple. From this, it began to be used more broadly to mean the temple itself. See *Salmasius* on *Solinus*, page 8, and the famous *Stosch*, *Antiquities of Thyatira* I, 7, 20. For "times" just above, in Cyril it is "seasons," and for "human" he has "man."

9. **Being sacrificed.**] The earlier editions of *Eusebius* and the *Leipzig Manuscript* all have *sphagiazomenos* <note>being sacrificed</note>. In *Cyril* it is *sphazomenos* <note>being slaughtered</note>. *Meerman* incorrectly has *sphagiazomenos* <note>with a different accentuation</note>.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->...and so, having been cast upon the piled-up pyre, he was burned whole.<-

§ 55. Diphilus, the King of Cyprus, who lived in the times of Seleucus the "Theologian" <note>original: *theologus*; here referring to a writer on divine genealogies or a mystic</note>, abolished this custom, changing the sacrifice to the immolation of an ox. The deity <note>original: *daemon*; in the Neoplatonic sense, a spiritual being or tutelary spirit</note> accepted the ox in place of the human, signifying beyond doubt that the power of both acts is of equal value. Likewise, in Heliopolis of Egypt, Amosis abolished the law concerning the slaughter of humans: as in the li—

<column-break/>

—thus he would offer him as a whole burnt offering upon the constructed pyre.

§ 55. Diphilus, the King of Cyprus, abolished this decree, having lived during the times of Seleucus the Theologian, changing the custom to the sacrifice of oxen. And the deity accepted the ox instead of the human. Thus, the deed is of equal value. Amosis also abolished the law of manslaughter <note>referring here to ritual human sacrifice</note> in Heliopolis of Egypt. To whom <insert>the catchword "To whom" indicates the start of the next section</insert>

***

10. *Burned as a whole offering on the pyre.*] *Eusebius:* in both places, both in *Preparation for the Gospel* and *On the Life of Constantine*: "constructed" <note>original: νηθεῖσαν</note>. *Cyril:* "kindled" <note>original: ἀφθεῖσαν</note>. In the other passage *Eusebius* has "they burned whole," but in the *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, as here in the singular: "he burned whole." *Cyril* also has this. He uses the word again below in Book IV, § 15. It could have been "he sacrificed whole," which pleased the illustrious Abresch, as above in § 26. For "Diphilus," *Eusebius* incorrectly has "Diiphilus."

1. *In the times of Seleucus the Theologian.*] Concerning Seleucus the Theologian, or magus (for he seems to have been the same person), read *Fabricius, Greek Library, Vol. I, p. 77.* Reiske notes that in the Meerman manuscript it is "against Seleucus." There were several of this name. See *Gale on Iamblichus' Mysteries, p. 297* and *Viger on Eusebius*, to whom in *Preparation for the Gospel, Book V, p. 203*, he is called a "wonderful theologian and an initiate of secret mysteries." Such men were formerly called Orpheus, Linus, and others; and following their example, even more recent figures were so named, on which matter see *Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus, IX, Against the Physicists, p. 593.* The Meerman manuscript incorrectly has "nation" <note>original: ἔθνος</note> for "custom" <note>original: ἔθος</note>; the same manuscript deletes the word "the" before "human."

2. *He abolished the law.*] Thus, immediately, "to abolish a decree." "To break customs" appears above in § 33, which can be added to a hundred other examples collected by the learned man on *Matthew 5:17.* In *Eusebius* it is "and also in Heliopolis," and it is the same in the Meerman manuscript.

3. *Of Egypt, concerning the slaughter of humans.*] *Herodotus* denies that the Egyptians sacrificed human victims, but others affirm it along with our author. See *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus, I, 88.* Indeed, we know from *Athenaeus, Book IV, ch. 21* that Seleucus wrote *On Human Sacrifice among the Egyptians*.

<column-break/>

However, Gale notes on *Iamblichus' Mysteries, p. 278* that they did not observe this dire custom except in the most severe calamities; and perhaps it did not pervade all of Egypt, but held sway in only one or two cities. For why would Amosis not have removed it everywhere his empire extended? Certainly Manetho, and our author following him, who speak only of Heliopolis, would not have been silent on this. *Plutarch, however, Vol. II, p. 380*, reports from Manetho that living humans were also burned in the city of Idithya. There, for "Idithya," I rewrite "Ilithyia," otherwise called "Eileithyia." *Stephanus of Byzantium* says: "Eileithyia, an Egyptian city." Nor is it necessary to conclude from this that they disagree because *Plutarch* indicates these rites were made to Diana, while our author says to Juno, a matter which will be discussed immediately.

4. *Amosis.*] In *Eusebius' Praise of Constantine*, it is rendered "Amoses." Elsewhere it is also "Amasis." There is variation everywhere in these names. See the *Translators of Diodorus Siculus, I, 60*, and the one who elegantly shows how it happened that this name is reported so diversely, *Bos, Animadversions on Josephus, 27*. Nor is there less variation in the name of that Amosis in whose reign the Hebrews are believed to have exited Egypt. See *Perizonius, Egyptian Origins, 18.* Our author here is called "Amasis" by *Philostratus in Life of Apollonius, V, 42*, where he is called a "lion" because he joined gentleness with a royal nature, being the one who authorized the removal of human sacrifice, as *Olearius* writes there.

Indeed, three were sacrificed in a day, in whose place Amosis <note>The Pharaoh Ahmose I, who reportedly abolished human sacrifice at Heliopolis</note> ordered an equal number of wax images to be substituted. In Chios also, they used to offer a sacrifice to Dionysus the "Raw-Eater" <note>original: "Omadius"</note> by tearing a man to pieces; and also in Te—

<column-break/>

5. *To which Manetho bears witness.*] I would prefer, following Eusebius: *as he bears witness*. In Plutarch he is called *Manethon*; by others also *Menethos*. The Learned know that this name is pronounced in various ways, though *Manethon* is generally approved by them. See Fabricius, *Greek Library* III, 20, 1, where much is said about him and about the book *On Antiquity and Piety* which is praised here.

6. *They were sacrificed to Juno.*] Our author and others indicate these rites were made to Juno, as many speak of that Egyptian Goddess. And yet Herodotus (II, 50) testifies that Juno was entirely unknown to the Egyptians; but he speaks of the Juno of the Greeks, whom the Egyptians truly did not know, while others speak of the Juno of the Orientals, who was customarily confused with Venus. Compare the celebrated Jablonski in *Egyptian Pantheon* I, 1, 4. From Plutarch, as I was just saying, you may gather these sacrifices were offered to Diana, but she who is Eileithyia <note>The Greek goddess of childbirth</note> among the Greeks is Lucina, Diana, and Juno to the Romans. And so our author could explain Eileithyia by the name of Juno, on which matter see Jablonski, Book III, 3, 7.

7. *Pure calves and marked with a seal.*] Hence the priests were called *sphragistae* <note>sealers</note>, who marked the ox to be sacrificed by impressing a seal. See Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 363, and what will be said below in IV, 7. The celebrated Wesseling uses this passage to restore the reading "pure male oxen" in his edition of Herodotus II, 38.

8. *Three were sacrificed in a day.*] That three men were sacrificed every single day to Juno at Egyptian Heliopolis is also handed down from our author by Theodoret in *Sermon on Sacrifices*, p. 589, and Eusebius in *Oration in Praise of Constantine*. Instead of "to be placed upon" <note>original: "ἐπιτίθεσθαι"</note>, Viger (on Eusebius, p. 11) wanted "to be substituted" <note>original: "ὑποτίθεσθαι"</note>, as being sufficient...

<column-break/>

...and substituted in place of the living. Incorrectly. Eusebius in both places defends the common reading: "to be placed upon," namely, upon the altar.

9. *Sacrificed — to Dionysus the Raw-Eater.*] "And they sacrificed" is found in Eusebius. For *Omadius* <note>Raw-Eater</note>, the Leipzig Manuscript has *Omadeius*. Eusebius in another place is exactly like our author, and so again in *Preparation for the Gospel*, p. 163, except that he adds "tearing limb from limb." But in the *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, he uses "Omadius Dionysus." Cyril (p. 129) does not add this surname. I do not doubt that *Omadius Dionysus* is the same as *Omestes*, the "Eater of Raw Flesh." For to him they sacrificed living men, as Arnobius says. We have examples in Plutarch where he says this cruel rite was performed for the "Raw One." He was indeed believed to delight in raw flesh. Below (IV, 19), he calls these "the raw-eating feasts of Zagreus." It is no wonder, then, that the Bacchants were also accustomed to eat raw flesh, on which matter see Barnes on Euripides' *Bacchae*, 139. *Omophagia* <note>The ritual eating of raw flesh</note> is the name given to this by Clement of Alexandria: "the Bacchants celebrate Dionysus with *omophagia*." See Meursius, *Greek Festivals*, Book VI. Our author also uses this epithet in the *Orphic Hymns* LI, 7, and as learned men rightly judge, in Hymn XXIX, 5, where "Ormadius" is printed. In both places a distinguished man translates it as "the Porter" <note>Latin: "baiulum"</note>; I would think it means "raw-eater," which can also be gathered from the following verse: for in the rites mentioned there, we saw solemn feasts of this kind. Nor do I understand by what right that surname of "Porter" fits Dionysus, whom [they describe as] tender...

Indeed, among other nations that cursed custom lasted long after; it is far from the truth, as some wish to claim, that human sacrifices ceased everywhere after the birth of the most mild Savior. Read *Fabricius: Library of Antiquities, ch. XI, 3*.

finally the learned *Viger* was despairing in this matter. I thought it would be too difficult for a little man like me to resolve what such a Giant could not suffice to explain. In the *Leipzig Manuscript* it is "Ephicrates." and a little before in the *Meerman Manuscript* "the same sacrifice." not a bad reading.

**11. Dumatii.**] Perhaps *Dumathii*, as it also seemed to *Viger* in his notes on *Eusebius* and to *Abresch*. *Stephanus of Byzantium* says: "Dumatha, a city of Arabia. The citizen is a Dumathenian." In *Eusebius's* "In Praise of Constantine," *Valesius* prefers "Dumathenians."

**12. Which they use as a cult image.**] *Maximus of Tyre*, Dissertation VIII, 8: "The Arabs worship, though I know not what. But I saw the statue; it was a square stone," where see *Davis*. This is the *Dysares* of Arabia mentioned in *Tertullian's* Apology ch. 24; not Mars, as it seemed to *Suidas* under "God Ares," but Bacchus. *Huet* in "Demonstratio Evangelica" IV, 3, thinks it was an image of Moses. Today also the Arabs at Mecca worship a black stone, which *Selden* (On the Syrian Gods II, 4) says he does not know if it is that square stone mentioned by *Maximus*. But see what *Bochart* opposed to this opinion in "Phaleg" II, 19. Certainly in this place, the most distinguished *Cuper* (on *Lactantius* p. 11) rightly judged that the same stone of Bacchus is signified, since that altar served in place of an image, and the shape of an altar fits well.

<column-break/>

**13. Phylarchus moreover etc.**] In *Eusebius* (Preparation for the Gospel p. 156 B and 164 A) it is wrongly published as "Philarchus." Then in the other *Eusebius* passage, "In Praise of Constantine," it is "before going out to wars." In the *Leipzig Manuscript* it is "polemi-", that is, "polemias" <note>hostile forces</note>. Moreover, in both that and the *Meerman Manuscript*, this scholium <note>marginal comment</note> was added: "that the Bulgarians also did this before receiving holy baptism."

**14. Killed the daughter of Erechtheus and Praxithea.**] *Eusebius*, "In Praise of Constantine": "The Athenians remember the Leokorae, and the daughter of Erechtheus being sacrificed," where see *Valesius*. *Cyril* against *Julian* p. 128 and many others record that Erechtheus himself sacrificed his daughter to the Daemons <note>spirits/divinities</note>. But these accounts are not in conflict. It is also known that some testify the girl (indeed some want it that two offered themselves) offered herself voluntarily to be slaughtered. See *Meursius* "On the Kingdom of Athens" II, 13, who also discusses the name. As for the testimony of Demaratus in *Stobaeus* Sermon 38, where she is called Proserpina, since I see that name attributed to her nowhere else, I suspect in that author it was "sacrifice to Persephone," not as published "sacrifice Persephone." For *Clement of Alexandria* in "Protrepticus" p. 27 says she was sacrificed to Pherephatta <note>another name for Persephone</note>.

**15. But even now.**] "But even now at least." *Eusebius*, *Leipzig* and *Meerman Manuscripts*. But as in this place, so *Eusebius* in the other "In Praise of Constantine."

**16. The Great City.**] See de la Cerda on *Tertullian's* "On the Spectacles" n. 93. VALENT. He understands Rome, according to the custom of his age. See *Valesius* on *Eusebius* p. 256. It was also a solemn epithet, regarding which see *Vitringa* on *Revelation* XVII, 18 and *Fabretti* on the *Theodosian Code* Vol. VI, p. 292. We know many cities were designated by this title.

<insert>At Rome</insert>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->Cc 3<-

Finally, when all other food had been consumed, they turned upon one another and by lot ate their fellow soldiers who were drawn. When Hamilcar <note>Hamilcar Barca, the Carthaginian general</note> finally defeated them and took them into his power, he had them trampled to death by elephants; he judged it a violation of divine law for such men to ever mingle with other human beings again. Nor did he himself ever admit the eating of humans simply because some had dared to do it; nor did his son Hannibal, when someone advised him as he led his army into Italy to accustom his troops to eating human flesh so that they might never be overcome by a lack of food. Therefore, just because famine and wars were the cause of our beginning to use other animals for food, it does not follow that the same should be practiced for the sake of pleasure. In the same way, we have never accepted the eating of human flesh. Nor, because they sacrificed animals to certain powers <note>original: "potestatibus" / "δυνάμεσι" — referring to spiritual or divine entities</note>, should they therefore be eaten. For even those who sacrificed humans did not, for that reason, also [eat] their flesh—

<column-break/>

—and they even rushed upon one another, eating their fellow soldiers by lot. But Hamilcar, having taken them captive, trampled them under his elephants, as it was not holy for them to mix with other men any longer. And neither did he accept it because some had dared <gloss>3</gloss> cannibalism <note>original: "ἀνθρωποφαγίαν"</note>, nor did his son Hannibal, to whom someone suggested while he was campaigning in Italy that he should habituate the army to cannibalism so they would not lack nourishment. Therefore, since <gloss>4</gloss> famines and wars have been the causes of eating other animals, one ought not to accept this practice for the sake of pleasure, just as we did not welcome cannibalism. Nor, because they sacrificed <gloss>5</gloss> animals to certain powers, was it necessary to eat them. For those who sacrificed humans did not taste the flesh for that reason—

***

3. *Cannibalism.*] The *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts incorrectly read "human-slaughter" <note>original: "ἀνθρωποσφαγίαν"</note>. And so again a little later, "to habituate the army to human-slaughter," and then "we welcomed human-slaughter."

4. *Famines and wars.*] The *Bodleian* manuscript reads "plagues and wars" <note>original: "λοιμοὶ κ. π."</note>. It is noted elsewhere that these words are frequently confused. Here, what we have given is the only true reading. There are many examples of those whom the extremes of war, dire circumstances, and the long poverty of a terrible siege forced to protect their lives with human flesh, as Juvenal says of the Vascones in *Satire XV, 95*. Strabo affirms the same regarding the Celts, Iberians, and others in *Book IV, page 39*. The same advice of Critognatus is found in Caesar's *Gallic Wars, Book VII, chapter 77*. Athenagoras says this happens "according to some most bitter calamity" in *On the Resurrection of the Dead, page 63*, where Rechenberg indicates what the interpreters of natural law determine on this matter. A little later, for "human" <note>original: "ἀνθρωπίνων"</note>, the *Meerman* manuscript has "man-like" <note>original: "ἀνθρωπείων"</note>. See the note on Book I, 9.

5. *To certain powers.*] So again a little later he mentions "the powers in the universe." But see the note at section 34.

->of human affairs. But that the act of sacrificing does not necessarily imply that one must also eat the animals has been demonstrated through these arguments.<-

### Section 58.
1. Those who have thoroughly studied the powers within the universe have confirmed—and this is even attested by the <term>theologians</term><note>Porphyry often refers to ancient poets like Orpheus or Egyptian priests as "theologians."</note> themselves—that bloody sacrifices are not offered to the gods, but rather to <term>daemons</term><note>In the Neoplatonic sense, daemons are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. 2. ### Section 58.
Indeed, it has also been confirmed by the Theologians themselves that sacrifices of this kind, which consist of flesh and blood, were customarily offered not to gods but to daemons by those who had explored the nature of the powers that exist in the universe. For it is established as an assertion by these same authorities that some of these daemons are malevolent, while others are good and kind, and will bring no disturbance upon us if we offer the first-fruits only from those things on which we feed and which nourish either the body or the soul. Accordingly, if we merely add this—to show that the least depraved and perverse opinions of any men do not wander from a right view of the gods—[we shall finish] the book.

***

1. **That it is not even to the gods.**] I will not neglect to note here even certain slight variations in the text. For since this passage is also cited in another book by the same author <note>original: "eodem in libro eiusdem auctoris"</note>, it is written there as *not to the gods* <note>original: "οὐ θεοῖς"</note>, and a little later *they were bringing* <note>original: "προσῆγον"</note>. Below, *and they will not trouble* <note>original: "καὶ οὐκ ἐνοχλήσουσιν"</note>, although the conjunction is absent from the manuscript of <term>Pamphilus</term>, nor is the article *the* <note>original: "ὁ"</note> used in its place as it is in Porphyry. **Victorius**. The word *But* <note>original: "Δὲ"</note> is not in the **Meermann** Codex. Up to the words *offering first-fruits* etc., most of these things are read in **Eusebius** page 153 C. **Cyril** also has many of them in *Against Julian*, Book IX, page 306 D. A little before, the word *and* <note>original: "καὶ"</note> before *to eat* was missing in the **Leipzig** and **Meermann** Codices. The reading *they were bringing* from **Pamphilus** is also found in **Cyril**. On the matter itself which our author and others bring forward, see **Gale** on **Iamblichus**' *On the Mysteries*, page 270.

<column-break/>

2. **Evil-doers, others good.**] These are well contrasted. Just as among the Latins, *Good Juno* and similar terms are used for *propitious* deities. See **Spanheim** on **Julian's** *Orations*, I, page 295. **Abresch** is correct regarding *who will not trouble*; the construction of this word was discussed above.

3. **We shall bring the book to a close.**] To the learned man [commenting] on **Diodorus**, page 5, it seemed that *paragraphesomen* <note>original: "παραγράψομεν"</note> should be written instead. For *paragraphein* means *to limit or finish*, whereas *perigraphein* means *to cancel or mark around with signs* to indicate that the text between those signs should be deleted. I would not deny that one of these words has occasionally wrongly occupied the place of the other; the learned **Abresch** gives examples in *Dilucidationes Thucydideae*, page 367. However, the metaphor is drawn from those things which we define by drawing a line around them <note>original: "circumscribendo" - to circumscribe</note>.

that is, according to the custom of the fathers, <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ ἔθος τῶν πατέρων"</note> he seems to refer everything back to ancient custom. This ancient custom, as we have demonstrated, consisted of cakes and fruits. From this, the terms for sacrifices, <note>original: "θυσίαι" (thysiai)</note> offerings, <note>original: "θυηλαὶ" (thyēlai)</note> and altars <note>original: "θυμέλαι" (thymelai)</note> were derived; and the very word for "to sacrifice" <note>original: "θύειν" (thyein)</note> was connected to the word for "to burn incense," <note>original: "θυμιᾷν" (thymian)</note> and to what we now call "to offer upon the altar." <note>original: "ἐπιθύειν" (epithyein)</note> For what we now call "to sacrifice," they used to call "to perform" or "to work." <note>original: "ἔρδειν" (erdein)</note>

# On Abstinence, Book II.
-> D d <-

...superstition, luxury, and the belief that the gods can be bribed with gifts or that injustice can be redeemed through sacrifices. For what other reason did some offer "triads with golden horns" <note>original: *terniones auricornes*; a specific ritual offering of three animals</note>—which is an offering of three victims—while others performed "hundred-oxen" sacrifices, that is, hecatombs? Indeed, Olympias, the mother of Alexander, used to sacrifice thousands of every kind of animal. Is it not because costly displays, once they begin, lead entirely into superstition? For when a young man learns that the gods delight in magnificent expenses and, as they say, in banquets of oxen and other animals, how can he possibly be expected to practice self-restraint? In what way would he think such sacrifices are pleasing to the gods, if he did not also believe he was permitted to act unjustly in all things? Since he believes he can buy his way out of all his sins...

<column-break/>

...superstition, luxury, and the notion that the divine can be bribed, and that injustice can be healed <gloss>2</gloss> by sacrifices. Otherwise, where did the "triads with golden horns" <gloss>3</gloss> come from, or the hecatombs? Olympias, the mother of Alexander, <gloss>4</gloss> used to sacrifice a thousand of everything, for once extravagance leads the way toward superstition, <gloss>5</gloss> it knows no bounds. When a young man perceives that the gods rejoice in lavishness and, as they say, in the feasting <gloss>6</gloss> upon oxen and other animals, <gloss>7</gloss> how could he ever be willing to be temperate? Believing that by offering these things he is doing what is pleasing to the gods, will he not think it is permitted for him to act unjustly, intending to buy his way out of his...

<margin>
2. *To heal injustice.*] He imitates his beloved Plato; see the passage cited above at § 31. Euripides uses the phrase "to heal injustice" in *Orestes* 651, as do others. Herodotus used "to heal the error," on which see Wesseling's commentary at V, 91.
</margin>

<margin>
3. *Triads with golden horns.*] This type of sacrifice is very well known from the Scholia on Aristophanes' *Plutus* 280 and many other sources. However, the Etymologist explains "triad" slightly differently under that entry. Compare Hemsterhuis on the aforementioned passage of Aristophanes.
</margin>

<margin>
4. *Sacrificed a thousand of everything.*] VALENTINI: I would prefer to read "five thousand at once," meaning she sacrificed 5,000 at one and the same time. REISKE: "Five" is a dull and absurd conjecture in this context. "Everything" is correct. It means "a thousand of each kind," such as a thousand oxen, as many sheep, and likewise pigs and goats, and so on. FELICIANUS: Correctly rendered as "thousands of whatever kind." "Everything" here means "of every genus." This is exactly like the phrase "to sacrifice a hundred of everything" which Strabo (Book III, p. 107) and Athenaeus (Book IV, 10) praise from Pindar. On both passages, see Casaubon, whom the learned editors of Herodotus (IV, 88) have already called to testify.

However, the reading is changed in four places; it is preserved more faithfully there, if I am not mistaken. The first difference is "how could he ever," which is clearly better. As for what is here—"he will benefit himself by acting unjustly"—it is undoubtedly correct, whereas in that other place it is read incorrectly in the plural possessive "of them," though our manuscript copy confirms our current reading. Further down, "the best first-fruit for the gods," and in the last verse "couches," with only one letter varied in the middle syllable of that noun. This, however, changes the meaning significantly and makes it better: and immediately "gifts of arrangements."

</margin>

<margin>
7. *Everything.*] VALENTINI: In place of "everything," I later found "how could he" in Eusebius, and "ever" in another source.
</margin>

8. *They have no need, etc.*] See what we said at § 33. He stated in § 15 that <note>original: "Deum τὸ τῶν θυόντων ἦθος, ἢ πρὸς τὸ τῶν θυομένων πλῆθος βλέπειν"</note> "God looks to the character of those sacrificing, rather than the quantity of the things sacrificed." You have already frequently observed that the word *approach* <note>original: "προσίεναι"</note> carries the meaning of obedience, veneration, and religious worship. The *Meerman* manuscript incorrectly gives "of the greatest things" instead of "the greatest." In the margin it read: <note>original: "Ζῆ ὅτι ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸ ἦθος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀφορᾷ, καὶ οὐ πρὸς τὸ θῦμα"</note> "Note that God looks to the character of the man, and not toward the victim."

9. *How shall he not be self-controlled, holy, and just.*] Just as below he joins "prudently and temperately and holily" (Book IV, 21). Exactly as here "temperate, just, holy" are used by St. Paul in Titus 1:8. *Wetstein* compares these passages, just as he compares what follows immediately with the Gospel of John 4:24. "Temperance, justice, and holiness" <note>original: "σωφροσύνη, δικαιοσύνη & ὁσιότης"</note> are joined in this way by *Plato* in the *Lysis*, page 494.

VALENTINI. Previously it read "of moderate things." The *Leipzig* and *Meerman* editions of Eusebius are no different. I suspect the original was "a moderate thing."

It is the same in the *Meerman* manuscript. In the edition of Eusebius, "indeed" is printed.

3. *Rising from one's seat and reclining.*] The *Eusebius* manuscript has "rising up and reclining," not "the giving of contributions." VALENTINI. The *Leipzig* manuscript correctly has "reclining" <note>original: "κατακλίσεσι"</note> from the verb "to recline." But in the word "requests" <note>original: "δεήσεσιν"</note> it incorrectly agrees with the common reading. The translator correctly guessed "gifts" <note>original: "δόσεσιν"</note>. "Contributions" <note>original: "συντάξεις"</note> are taxes levied on everyone, which all pay unwillingly. REISKE. These readings are absurd, but they can be corrected with a little effort from Eusebius. Compare these notes by the celebrated *Wetstein* on the Gospel of Matthew 23:6. The *Meerman* manuscript agrees with the *Leipzig*.

For the good man knows best what ought to be sacrificed, and from what things one must abstain, and what things should be pursued, and from which things the first-fruits <term>primitiae: the first portion of a harvest or sacrifice offered to a deity</term> should be offered to the gods. Wherefore Plato says that it is fitting for the good man to sacrifice and to always converse with the gods with prayers and offerings and sacrifices, and with every service; but for the evil man, his great labor concerning the gods is in vain. For the good man knows what must be sacrificed, and from what he must abstain, and what things must be brought forward, and from what things the first-fruits must be given; but the base man, bringing honors to the gods out of his own disposition and from the things he himself has been eager about, is impious rather than pious.
