4. *If you remember &c.*] Grotius translated this in *Excerpts from Valent.* p. 911, whom [the editor] has followed. For *Philinus, a favor from you*, it previously read *To love: exchange a favor*. From which the writing of the *Leipzig Manuscript* does not depart much: *I have long since received [it], you love [me], exchange the favor*. I am not ignorant of where a pretext for these readings might be sought; however, I prefer the common reading. The *Meerman Manuscript* gives *curse the favor* instead of *long since*, and the *Bodleian Manuscript* gives *again*.

5. *For it was for this reason &c.*] The earlier editions wrongly had *before you I deposited*. *To deposit a favor with someone* is used as if for a *deposited gift* (for that is the proper meaning of *katatithenai*, whence a favor deposited in this way is elegantly said by the Greeks *to be laid up*). We have this usage in *Luke, Acts of the Apostles 24:27*, see the interpreters there, and *Wolf on Libanius, Epistle 215*. But in those examples, it is constructed with the dative case. Just as our author [uses it] in *Demosthenes against Neaera p. 864 B*: *to deposit a favor with the woman herself*. Likewise *On the Liberty of the Rhodians p. 145 B*: *to deposit a great service with him*. Which Aristides said as *unto someone* (Vol. I, p. 38) and Chariton (IV, 5, p. 72), where D'Orville diligently illustrates this manner of speaking. Reiske advised that in the upper verse, the article *the* before *favor* should be adopted from the *Leipzig Manuscript*, and that in this verse the meter requires the form *heneka* [because of].

6. *Satisfied by these things.*] A question mark should be placed after *these things*. For it is a speech in the form of a negative question. —REISKE.

# PORPHYRY

...that the philosopher should not merely go along with the crowd; for this is neither pleasing to the gods nor profitable to men. Instead, he judges that the philosopher must proceed on the right path, taking no account of any danger or any infamy from the common people. For it would indeed be an absurd thing if, while the Syrians will in no way taste fish, nor the Hebrews swine, nor most of the Phoenicians and Egyptians female cattle—and even when many kings applied force, they resolved to undergo death rather than violate their ancestral customs—we, out of terror, should [betray] the laws of nature and divine precepts...

### Section I.
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial N inside a square frame with floral and geometric patterns.</image-desc>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Book II regarding the ethical treatment of animals, transitioning now into a formal defense of justice toward non-human beings based on their possession of reason.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book III.

### Section 1.
...he used to say <note>original: "aiebat"; likely referring to Epicurus or a similar hedonistic philosopher mentioned previously</note> that our happiness is situated in pleasure, provided that the intellect maintains dominion over all things. We, however, even if all the wolves and vultures were to praise the eating of flesh, will never concede that they speak justly, so long as man remains harmless by nature and abstains from procuring pleasures for himself through the injury of others. Therefore, let us pass over to the discussion concerning justice. Since those who oppose this decree assert that justice only extends toward those similar to ourselves, and for that reason exclude irrational animals from all rights regarding men: come now, let us set forth the true and simultaneously **Pythagorean** opinion on this matter. We shall demonstrate that every soul which participates in sensation and memory is also rational. For if this is demonstrated, it will be established—even according to the opinion of our opponents—that justice pertains to all animals. We shall briefly relate those things which have been handed down in the records of the ancients.

### Section 2.
Since, therefore, there is a twofold "reason" or "speech" <note>original: "ratio, seu oratio"; translating the Greek *logos*</note> according to the opinion of the **Stoics**, the one being internal—

<column-break/>

...that our happiness is situated in pleasure, provided that the mind maintains dominion over all things. We, however, even if all the wolves or vultures approve of meat-eating, will not concede to them that they speak justly, so long as man is by nature harmless, and inclined to abstain from providing pleasures for himself through the harm of others. Therefore, moving into the discourse concerning justice—since those who argue against us have said that this must extend only toward similar beings, and for this reason they strike out <gloss>4</gloss> the "irrational" animals—come, let us preserve the true and at the same time **Pythagorean** glory <gloss>5</gloss> by showing that every soul which shares in sensation and memory is rational. For once this is proven, we shall reasonably extend justice toward every living creature, even according to their own principles. We shall speak by briefly abridging the works of the ancients.

### Section 2.
Since there are two kinds of reason <note>original: "logos"</note> according to those of the Porch <note>The Stoics</note>, <gloss>1</gloss> the one being internal—

---

<margin>4. *They strike out the animals.*] *To strike out* <note>original: "Diagraphēin"</note> is to draw a transverse line through something, and hence to erase something or remove it from the midst. See the discussion on the nature of this metaphor by the illustrious **Reiske** in his notes on the *Excerpts of Polybius, p. 766*, and **Casaubon** on *Athenaeus II, 22*.</margin>

<margin>5. *Every soul, etc.*] This was indeed the foundation of the Pythagorean <term>abstinence</term> <note>original: "apochē"; the ritual or philosophical act of refraining from animal products</note>, and is therefore frequently emphasized by our author. Hence in the *Life of Pythagoras* he says *all things produced with souls are of the same genus*, as we have seen in another place.</margin>

<margin>1. *The one internal, the other expressed.*] A most common distinction in the writings of the Philosophers and the ancient Christians. *Internal reason* <note>original: "logos endiathetos"</note>, or *thought-based*, and *expressed speech* <note>original: "logos prophorikos"</note>, *discourse*, or *word*. The ancients placed Mercury in charge of both, on which matter see **Tollius**, *Italian Journey, p. 153*.</margin>

<summary>Porphyry begins Book III by arguing that if animals possess sensation and memory, they must also possess reason (logos), thereby entitling them to justice under the Stoics' own definitions. He introduces the crucial distinction between internal thought and external speech.</summary>

# PORPHYRY

->**On Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

Since there are two kinds of reason <note>original: "λόγος" (logos) - meaning both thought and speech</note>, one internal <note>original: "ἐνδιάθετος" (endiathetos) - the reason arranged within the mind</note> and the other external <note>original: "προφορικός" (prophorikos) - the reason expressed through voice</note>, and again, one being correct <note>original: "κατορθωμένου" (katorthomenou) - perfected or virtuous reason</note> and the other faulty, it is necessary to distinguish which of these they <note>The Stoic philosophers</note> deprive animals of. Do they mean they lack only "correct" reason, and not reason in an absolute sense? Or do they mean they are entirely devoid of all reason, both that which stays within and that which proceeds outward? They certainly seem to attribute a total deprivation of reason to them, not just the deprivation of "correct" reason. For otherwise, other animals would not be "irrational," but would still be "rational" beings, just as almost all humans are according to their own standards. For according to them, only one or two "wise men" have ever existed in whom reason is truly perfected; all other men are "depraved," even if some are making progress while others are held in a flood of depravity. Yet, despite this, they consider all such humans to be equally rational. It is only because of their excessive self-love <note>original: "φιλαυτίας" (philautias)</note> that the Stoics claim all other animals are ir-

Furthermore, one is "right" and the other "depraved." It seems we must distinguish which of these they deny to animals. Do they say they lack only "right" reason, and are not absolutely devoid of all reason, or do they say they lack every kind, both that which is within and that which proceeds outward? They clearly seem to attribute a total deprivation of all reason to them, not just of the perfected kind. For otherwise, the other animals would not be considered irrational, but rational, no differently than almost all men are held to be by them. Indeed, since in their opinion only one or two "wise men" are found in whom "right reason" is seen, all the rest would be depraved, even if some progress slightly and others are detained, as it were, in a fusion of depravity. <margin>In place of "which" (ὃ), as was previously read incorrectly, both manuscripts have "the things which" (ἁ). The truth is "but" (δ). No less certain is "is about to" (μέλλει), which is supported by the authority of the Leipzig and Meerman Codices.</margin>

6. **What of this?**] Namely, "what great thing is this?" or "what is this to the present matter?" as seen below in Section 4. This is a solemn formula in interrogations. See Demosthenes, *On the False Embassy*: "If the Phocians are not present, what of it?" and others often. After "that of the Indians," Fogerolles ineptly supplied "understood the dialect." # On Abstinence, Book III.

The speech of the Syrians, for example, or the Persians, seems unformed and inarticulate to us, just as the voice of other animals seems to all humans. For just as we perceive only a certain sound and noise when we are unskilled in the speech of, say, the Scythians—so that they seem to us to be making a clanging noise and explaining nothing articulately, but rather using a single sound, now longer, now shorter—and that variety of sound falls upon our ears with no meaning at all; yet to them, their own speech is easily understood, just as ours is to us, and carries much distinction: in the same way it happens with the other animals. 11. **Apollonius of Tyana.**] *Philostratus*, in his life of Apollonius, narrates the same thing as our author, except that Porphyry puts a swallow in place of a sparrow, and says a donkey with a load fell instead of grain being spilled by a boy. # PORPHYRY

->**On the Intelligence of Animals**<-

...call out in one way; when they invite others to feed, in another; when they greet one another kindly, in another; and when they challenge one another to battle, in another. Indeed, the diversity is so great that the distinction is extremely difficult to observe due to the sheer number of variations, even for those who have dedicated their entire lives to such observations. For instance, augurs <note>diviners who interpreted the flight and cries of birds</note> who study the calls of the crow and the raven have noted the differences up to a certain number, but have omitted the rest as being beyond human grasp. However, when these birds speak to one another, their meanings are clear and distinct, even if they are not known to all of us. If they are seen to imitate us, to learn the Greek language, and to understand those who look after them, who would be so shameless as to deny they are rational beings <note>original: "logika"</note> simply because he himself does not understand what they are saying? Ravens and jays, for example—

<column-break/>

...call out: they are heard to cry in one way when they invite others to eat; in another when they receive each other kindly; and in another when they provoke one another to fight. And indeed, there is such a variety that the distinction among them is very difficult to observe because of their multitude, even for those who have spent their whole lives in this kind of business. For the augurs of the chatterings of the crow and the raven, having made observations up to a certain number, omitted the rest, as they were things that could not easily be perceived by a human. But when they are not speaking among themselves, they signify things clearly, even if those things are not known to all of us. But if they are seen to imitate us, to learn the Greek language, and to understand those in charge of them, who will be so impudent as to not concede that they are rational, for the reason that he himself perceives very little of what they say? For ravens and magpies, and—

---

<margin>
Scholiast on Euripides: "Snakes came and licked their ears, and thus made them so sharp of hearing that they alone could hear the counsels of the gods and became the highest of prophets." More on this matter can be read in Bochart, *Hierozoicon* I, 1, 3, and Olearius on Philostratus' *Life of Apollonius of Tyana* I, 20.
</margin>

4. **Challenge to battle.** *Porphyry* speaks fully here. Elsewhere, the word "challenge" <note>original: "prokaleisthai"</note> is commonly used on its own when the discussion concerns a provocation to a contest or war. I only cite *Kuhn on Aelian, Varia Historia I, 24.* A little earlier, the word "to" <note>original: "eis"</note> before "food" was wrongly omitted by *Meermann*.

5. **But when to one another...** The Leipzig Manuscript adds "not" <note>original: "mē"</note> after "but." Without doubt, the word "indeed" <note>original: "men"</note> is hidden within it; those two words are often swapped for one another. If this is admitted, the passage could be restored as:

<column-break/>

"whatever they indeed utter to one another is clear and distinct." With this assumed, the word "if" before "they are seen" can keep its place. But if we arrange the passage thus: "but when they indeed utter to one another things that are clear..." then the "if" must be removed. It matters little which path you follow. —REISKE. The reading of the *Leipzig* manuscript was also expressed by *Meermann* and the translator. Correctly, in my opinion. However, the *Leipzig* manuscript errs a little earlier by omitting "and" before "raven," and *Meermann*, confusing the vowels again, writes "having been laid down" in the feminine. *Wetstein* compares this to the "distinct speech" <note>original: "eusēmon logon"</note> of *Paul in 1 Corinthians 14:9.*

6. **Ravens and jays, etc.** *Persius, in his Prologue, line 8:*
> Who taught the parrot its "hello" <note>original: "chaire"</note>
> and taught the magpies to attempt our words?

# On Abstinence, Book III.

->**On the Speech of Animals**<-

Both redbreasts <note>original: "erithaci"</note> and parrots imitate human beings; they remember what they hear, and while being taught, they listen to and perceive the instructor. Indeed, many of these birds have even pointed out and revealed those committing crimes within a house by using the words they had learned. Furthermore, the Indian hyena, which the natives call the *corocotta* <note>A mythical or semi-mythical creature often identified in antiquity as a hybrid of a hyena and a lioness or dog, famed for its mimicry.</note>, speaks in such a human-like manner even without a teacher that it is accustomed to frequent houses and call out to anyone it recognizes can be easily overpowered. For it imitates the voice of the person's dearest friend, or someone whom the person called would absolutely obey; the result is that the Indians, although they know of this trick, are deceived by the similarity, and obeying the voice, they go outside and are consumed and perish. Now, if not all animals—

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text of the passage translated in the first column.</note>

Both redbreasts and parrots imitate humans and remember whatever they hear; when being taught, they obey the teacher, and many have reported those doing wrong in the house through the things they were taught. And the Indian hyena, which the locals call the *Krokottas*, speaks so humanly even without a teacher that it even visits houses and calls whoever it sees is easy for it to master; it imitates the voice of the person's most beloved, and whoever the one called would entirely obey. Thus, even though the Indians know this, they are deceived by the likeness and are destroyed as they go out and obey the voice. But if [it] does not imitate all—

<margin>Where he speaks of other birds of this kind and the singular cleverness of certain ones.</margin> **Casaubon:** Not forgetting our own. 7. **The Indian hyena which they call the Corocotta.** The *Corocotta* is a species of hyena which some write is born from a dog and a wolf, others from a hyena and a lioness. See **Wesseling** on Diodorus Siculus, Book III, 35. Some distinguish between these animals, yet both attribute to them that cunning malice which our author mentions. See **Aelian**, *On the Nature of Animals*, VII, 22. Most report that the hyena is not entirely ignorant of human speech, but they attribute the imitation of the voice especially to the *crocuta*. There are many testimonies to this matter, but **Vossius** in *On Idolatry*, Book III, 59, argues they are false. The **Leipzig Manuscript** has *korottan*, and it is also written this way in the small index added to the margin: "concerning the Indian hyena, which is also called the *korokotta*." **Meermann** has the same, except in the margin it is "concerning the I. H. or *korokotta*," and this should not be rashly rejected. For although the word is commonly pronounced with three syllables, **Aelian** (in the place cited) also calls it *korottan*. **Felicianus** also gave *Corocottam*, and **Salmasius** observed (on Capitolinus in *Antoninus Pius*, ch. 10) that it is almost always found written this way in Latin books of better quality.

8. **Speaks humanly.** <note>original: "Φθέγγεται ἀνθρωπικῶς"</note> **Diodorus Siculus** (III, 35) called this "imitating the dialect of humans." Above in section 3, we encountered "to speak like a dog or an ox."

This is poor and ambiguous, so that you do not know whether he wanted "it imitates" or "to imitate." # PORPHYRY

And if not every animal is quick to learn our language, what of it? For not even every human is quick to learn or imitative—not just of the voices of animals, but not even of five of the dialects found among men. Some animals, perhaps, do not speak because they are not taught, or because they are hindered by the physical organs of their voice. At any rate, while we were in Carthage <note>original: Καρχηδόνα / Carthaginem</note>, a tame partridge flew to us; we raised it, and as time went on and it grew accustomed to us, it reached such a degree of tameness that we perceived it not only wagging its tail and attending to us and playing with us, but even calling back in response to our voice. As far as it was able, it answered us in a different way than partridges are accustomed to call to one another; it did not speak when I was silent, but only called back when I spoke to it.

<column-break/>

they imitate, and not all are fit for learning our speech, what does it matter? For neither are all men docile, or apt at imitating the voices of other animals, nor even any five of the languages that exist among men. To omit the fact that some of these animals perhaps do not speak either because they are not taught, or because they are hindered by the unsuitability of the organs of the voice. We indeed, when we were at Carthage, raised a certain tame partridge which had flown to us; in the course of time it was brought to such tameness that it would not only play, fawn, and coax, but would even cry out in turn at our voice, and as far as was possible even respond, in a different manner than when partridges are accustomed to call one another. For it did not emit a sound while I was silent, but while I was speaking and calling, it emitted its voice in turn.

-># On Abstinence, Book III.<-

§ 5. Furthermore, even among animals that lack a human voice, some are recorded to have obeyed their masters as promptly as any human being. For instance, the Roman Crassus <note>Likely Licinius Crassus, a wealthy Roman statesman</note> had a moray eel so accustomed to him that it would come to him whenever it was called by name. Indeed, it affected his spirit with such affection through its obedience that, although he had previously borne the loss of three children with moderation, he wept for the eel when it died. Many have also handed down to memory that the eels in Arethusa <note>A famous fountain in Syracuse, Sicily</note> and the *saperdae* <note>A type of small salted fish, possibly a perch or herring</note> near the Maeander River <note>A river in modern-day Turkey known for its winding path</note> listen to those who call them. Therefore, the internal thought of the speaker—whether it reaches the tongue or not—is undoubtedly the same. For this reason, I do not see how it is not absurd if we wish to call only the human voice "speech" simply because it is perceived by us, while we reject the voices of all other animals. For it is just as if the crows should judge that only their own speech exists, and consider us irrational because we do not speak clearly to them; or if the inhabitants of Attica <note>The region of Athens, known for the "purest" Greek dialect</note> should say that only the Attic voice is speech—

<column-break/>

§ 5. It is recorded that even among those without a voice <gloss>1</gloss> some obey their masters so readily that no <gloss>2</gloss> human among acquaintances could do better. At any rate, <gloss>3</gloss> the moray eel of Crassus the Roman, being called by name, would approach Crassus; he was so affected by this that he mourned it when it died, though he had previously borne the loss of three children with moderation. <gloss>4</gloss> And many have recorded that the eels in Arethusa and the *saperdae* around the Maeander obey those who call them. Is not the mental impression the same as that of the speaker, whether it reaches the tongue or not? How then is it not thoughtless to say that only the human voice is "reasoned speech" because it is intelligible to us, while rejecting that of other animals? For it is similar to if crows claimed that their own voice was the only one, and that we were "without reason" <term>aloga: lacking the faculty of speech or reason</term> because we do not utter sounds that are clear to them; or if the Athenians said that only the Attic dialect was speech, while others—

# PORPHYRY

->On Abstinence from Animal Food<-

...they considered others to be "irrational" <note>Greek: *alogous*, meaning both "without speech" and "without reason"</note> simply because they lacked the Attic dialect. And yet, an inhabitant of Attica would sooner understand the meaning of a crow than that of a Syrian or a Persian speaking in their own hissing and Persian tongues. But surely it is absurd to judge what is rational or irrational based on whether a speech is easily understood, or based on silence and voice. For by that logic, one might say that the God over all things, and the other gods, are not rational because they do not speak in this human way. Yet the gods signify their will while remaining silent; and the birds understand them more quickly than humans do. Having understood, they report these things as best they can, acting as heralds for the various gods to mankind. Of these, the eagle belongs to Zeus, the hawk and the crow to Apollo, and the stork to Hera...

<column-break/>

<margin>
See Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals*, Book 8, Chapter 4. Note the variations in the Meerman manuscript regarding the word for "calling" or "speaking." Abresch suggests a correction regarding the phrase "upon the tongue," which is confirmed by the Meerman codex.
</margin>

<note>Scholarly Commentary on the Text</note>

5. **By not speaking.**] Reiske suggests the reading: "By speaking nothing," or rather, "one might say they are not even rational because they do not speak." The Meerman manuscript uses "thus" instead of "so." The Leipzig codex had a slight error in the particle used here.

6. **And understanding, etc.**] The Leipzig and Meerman codices use the form "having understood." As I mentioned above, birds were believed to be aware of the future and to be the heralds and interpreters of the gods. Indeed, these and other animals have a closer fellowship with God, and they teach humans those things which God has revealed to them—as Celsus says in Origen’s *Against Celsus*, Book 4, where more is written on this subject. Hence, a bird is called a "messenger"

<column-break/>

in Apollonius Rhodius, Book 3, line 1111. Euripides calls them "heralds of the gods." See also Plutarch and Spanheim’s notes on Callimachus’s *Hymn to Jove*. After the word "can," the Meerman manuscript adds: "now that he pursues, now that he has captured, and of the wanderer, that he wanders." These words appear again in their proper place shortly after, though the first part is omitted there.

7. **Of which the eagle is Zeus’s.**] Valentinus suggests "as" would be more suitable than "of which." While "of which" can be defended, I suspect it arose from the ending of the preceding word. It was fitting to consecrate the eagle to Jove; it is a truly royal bird. Diodorus Siculus writes: "The Thebans honor the eagle because this animal is thought to be kingly and worthy of Zeus."

8. **And to Apollo the hawk and the crow.**] Just as the eagle is to Zeus, so these birds were sacred to Apollo (or the Sun) among the Egyptians and other nations. From coins...

# On Abstinence, Book III.

->...the stork; the rail and the owl are sacred to Minerva <note>Athena</note>; the crane to Ceres <note>Demeter</note>; and others to other deities. Furthermore, those among us who are observant and spend their lives in the company of certain animals come to understand the meaning of their voices. For instance, the hunter, by the variation in the barking, perceives whether the dog is seeking the hare, has found it, has caught it, or is wandering aimlessly. Likewise, the cowherd knows from the various lowing of the ox whether it is hungry, thirsty, weary, incited to mate, or seeking its calf. The lion also expresses threats by its roaring, just as the wolf indicates its distress by howling. Even by their bleating, it is clear to shepherds what the sheep require.

§ 6. Nor does the human voice escape their notice, whether men are angry or speaking soothingly,<-

<column-break/>

->...the stork; and of Athena, the rail and the owl; and of Demeter, the crane; and so others for others. Moreover, those of us who observe and those who are reared with them recognize their utterances. The hunter, certainly, perceives from the "performance" <note>original: ὑποκρίσεως (hypokriseos) - here meaning the specific modulation or "acting" of the voice</note> of the barking dog, now that it seeks the hare, now that it has found it, now that it pursues, now that it has caught it, or when it is straying, that it is lost. And the cowherd knows now that the cow is hungry, or thirsty, or weary, or in heat, or seeking the calf. And the lion by roaring shows that he threatens, and the wolf by howling that he fares badly, and the bleating sheep do not escape the shepherd's notice as to what they need.

§ 6. Therefore, the voice of humans does not escape them either,<-

<margin>The scholar *Cuper* <note>Gisbert Cuper, 17th-century philologist</note> proved this by the testimonies of the ancients and explained the causes of the matter in his work on Harpocration, page 70. Certain things regarding the hawk will also be mentioned below in Book IV, 9.</margin>

9. **And so others for others.**] It seems the word "as" <note>original: Ὡς</note> should be deleted, and then read "others for other things." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century critic</note>. Or, as was pleasing to *Abresch*, "as others for other [gods]." <term>MEERMAN</term> deletes the word "and" before "of us."

10. **The hunter, certainly—**] *Sextus Empiricus* <note>Skeptic philosopher</note> argues for the same cause in *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* I, 14, page 21: "And we hear the dogs uttering one voice when they are defending themselves against someone, another when they howl, and another when they are beaten, and a different one when they wag their tails."

11. **Performance.**] *Hypokrisis* in this place is a certain composition and modulation of the voice, varying according to the affection of the mind. <term>REISKE</term>.

<column-break/>

12. **Now that the cow is hungry.**] Either "now" <note>original: νῦν μὲν</note> must be deleted, or if it is kept, it should read "now that the cow is hungry, and now that it is thirsty, or weary." He uses "now" <note>original: νῦν δὲ</note> to mean "at another time" below, as in "now eagles and the swan." <term>REISKE</term>. See at § 16.

13. **The lion by roaring — the wolf by howling.**] He uses the words which are properly accustomed to be applied to these beasts, about which we spoke above. However, there is nothing unusual in those words in *1 Peter 5:8*: "as a roaring lion," as *L. Bos* beautifully demonstrated regarding that passage.

14. **And the bleating sheep.**] So below in Book IV, § 7: "those which they call *bais*." Other plurals of this kind are also found, which it suffices to have mentioned. Consult *D'Orville* on *Chariton* IV, 7, page 423, who uses our examples.

# PORPHYRIUS

-> [On Abstinence from Animal Food] <-

...not when people are angry, nor when they are being friendly, nor when they are calling out; it is not the voice of one pursuing, nor of one begging, nor of one giving—not a single one of these—but rather, the animals obey all these voices in a way that is appropriate to each. This would be impossible to do if that which is similar in intelligence did not act upon its like. They are also calmed by musical melodies, and stags, bulls, and other animals become tame <gloss>1</gloss> from a wild state. <gloss>2</gloss> Even those who vote against the rationality of animals <note>referring to the Stoics, who denied animals possessed reason</note> say that dogs understand dialectics <gloss>3</gloss> and make use of the "syllogism of multiple disjunctions" when tracking prey and arriving at a three-way crossroads. For they reason that the beast must have gone either this way, or that way, or the other way; but since it went neither this way nor that way, it must therefore have gone the remaining way, along which the dog then pursues. But it is easy for [the critics] to say that animals do these things by nature, because no one taught them. As if we ourselves were not also allotted reason by nature, <gloss>4</gloss> even if...

<column-break/>

...whether they call, or drive them away, or wish to ask for or give something: rather, they are seen to comply appropriately with all such vocalizations. This could happen in no way unless that which is similar in intelligence responded to its like. Even stags, bulls, and other animals are soothed by certain modulations of the voice, and are rendered tame from their wild state. Add to this that even those very people who decree that other animals are irrational assert that dogs are, in a certain way, capable of dialectics <note>the art of logical discussion</note>, especially regarding the proposition they call "disjunction from many," as when they reach a three-way path while tracking wild beasts. For they say the dogs reason thus: the beast went either this way, or that way, or the other way. But it went neither this way, nor that way: therefore it fled the other way. Once they have gathered this, they are accustomed to throw themselves into a run in that direction. Although the response is ready for them—that dogs have these things implanted by nature because they were taught by no one—it is as if we ourselves also [possessed reason only by nature]...

***

<margin>1. *From a wild state, etc.*] Clar. had added a note: *Abresch:* This passage is in Eustathius's commentary on Homer's *Iliad*, Book I, page 284, last line. A little before, the words "nor of one begging" are mistakenly missing in the *Leipzig* Manuscript.</margin>
<margin>2. *Even those who...*] The *Leipzig* manuscript gives "For even those who...", which I would not reject; and the Meerman manuscript says the same.</margin>
<margin>3. *And make use of the [syllogism] of multiple disjunctions, etc.*] Taken from Plutarch, in whose works you may also read these things in Volume II, page 969 A. On the traces of reason found in brute animals, many authors have written much. See those praised by *Fabricius* in his notes on Sextus Empiricus, I, 14. More on this matter at section 7. Then Meerman on the formula "neither this nor that," which is discussed elsewhere.</margin>
<margin>4. *Even if we assume some...*] I do not understand this passage. I once suspected it should read: *or as if we did not assign names to them by some reason because...* or *as if we did not impose names on other animals by some other reason, because we enjoy a natural faculty for that thing.* But the meaning does not seem to become much better or clearer. In the meantime, nothing better occurs to me. REISKE. All manuscripts agree on "themselves" [autoi], as *Felicianus* also reads. *Holstenius*, however, had corrected it to "to them" [autois].</margin>

-># On Abstinence, Book III.<-

# PORPHYRIUS
## Book A

-> [The soul] which he has chosen to cut down like a stone. But indeed Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Pythagoras, Democritus, and all those who took care to grasp the truth concerning them, recognized <note>original: ⁸ ἔγνωσαν</note> that which participates in reason. <-

**§ 7.** It must also be demonstrated that there is within them an internal and mental reason <note>The "internal word" or "disposed reason" (logos endiathetos), as opposed to spoken language.</note>. It appears that the variation, as **Aristotle** also says somewhere, does not differ in essence, but is observed in the "more and the less." Just as many people think that the nature of the gods differs from ours, with this difference being not according to essence, but according to the precision, or lack thereof, of their reason. And as far as perception is concerned, and the rest—

<column-break/>

-> [The soul] which she herself does not fear to strike and bruise just like a stone. But truly Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Pythagoras, Democritus, and all who have studied to investigate the truth concerning them, judged that the other living beings also participate in reason. <-

**§ 7.** For it remains for us to demonstrate that reason and the speech which is disposed inwardly in the mind are also present in them. Moreover, the diversity seems to be, as Aristotle himself also says, not in essence, but in that which is considered as "more and less." In the same way, some are of the opinion that the gods also differ from us, so that the distinction between us and them is understood to be established not in substance, but in a more or less exquisite reason. And indeed, as much as pertains to the senses, and—

***

<margin>
*Aelian: V. H. IV, 19* calls this their "history." A well-known title of an Aristotelian work, *History of Animals*, or *Inquiry into Animals*, or simply *On Animals*, concerning which see *Periz: on Aelian: at that place.*
</margin>

8. **That which participates in reason.**] Perhaps "that part of them which participates in *spoken* reason," because of what follows. The word "to grasp" <note>original: ἑλεῖν</note> is derived from the hunt. *Reiske.* "The reason" <note>original: Τὸν λόγον</note> in the *Lips.* and *Meerm.* manuscripts is an error. "To grasp" means to hold an opinion or to *judge*. Philosophers are accustomed to use this for the dogma they follow. See *Steph: Thesaurus.*

<margin>
1. **It must also be demonstrated that there is within them...**] There are many among the ancients who thought that reason was common to animals and humans, even among the Jews and—what you might wonder at—the Christians, as is clear from Lactantius and others. See *Scheff: on Aelian: V. H. I, 6.* Among more recent writers, not a few have established the same. *Wolfius, on Origen: Philof c. 9*, praises many who took up this argument to elaborate upon it. More recently, that most excellent man **S. H. Reimarus** disputed most sagaciously concerning the genius of beasts. The celebrated **Mosheim**, in his notes on *Cudworth: Intellectual System p. 1159*, explains Porphyry's dogma, where more may be found on this matter. However, what that distinguished man says—that Porphyry judged the souls of brute animals to be equal to human souls—is not to be taken too strictly. Certainly, he felt with his mentor Pythagoras "that all things produced with souls should be considered of the same genus," as he says in *Life of Pythagoras 19*; or "that a share of the rational belongs to all ensouled beings," as seen below in § 23. He therefore thought the souls of animals were "of the same essence" <note>original: ὁμοουσίους</note> as ours, not indeed according to substance, but according to the "more and less" of their participation in reason, as **Holstenius** well noted on the earlier passage of our author. This is what he expressly signifies in this place.
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book III.

Almost everyone concedes that, regarding the rest of the instrumental arrangement of both the sensory parts and the entire flesh, other animals are disposed no differently than we are. For they share a likeness with us not only in the natural affections and movements that exist within them, but there is also a great communication between us and them in those things which happen contrary to nature and are morbid. Nor should anyone of right mind assert that they are devoid of reason and speech <note>original: "rationis atque orationis"</note> simply because of the diversity of their physical habit and form; for even among humans, one beholds a great variety of this kind according to the diversity of races and peoples, and yet one concedes that all are nonetheless rational. To come to the point: the donkey, for instance, is accustomed to be seized by a dripping of phlegm <note>a "catarrh" or cold</note>, which, if it flows down into the lungs, destroys and kills it just as it does a human. The horse becomes suppurated <note>filled with pus or abscessed</note> and, like a human, is consumed and wastes away. Likewise, stiffness <note>tetanus</note> invades the horse, and po-

<column-break/>

-ssesses the same organization, both in terms of the sense organs and the <gloss>3</gloss> flesh, as we do—nearly everyone has conceded this. For they share with us not only the natural passions and movements observed through these parts, but also those things seen in them that are contrary to nature and diseased. A person of sound mind would not say that they are incapable of a rational disposition because of the difference in their bodily condition, seeing as even among humans there is a great variation in condition <gloss>4</gloss> according to races and nations, and yet we grant that all are rational. The donkey is indeed seized by catarrh, and if the disease flows into its lungs, it dies just like a human. <gloss>5</gloss> The horse also becomes abscessed and wastes away, just like a human. And <gloss>6</gloss> tetanus seizes the horse, as do gout, fever, and rabies,

# PORPHYRY

->**On Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

<margin>as: 5</margin> Animals are not deprived of this <note>original: "ταύτης" (tautēs); referring to sensory perception</note> simply because they are not human, nor do they lack reason for that reason. For if that were the case, the gods would also be deprived of reason because they are not human—or we ourselves would lack it, if only the gods were truly rational. Indeed, in terms of sensation, animals actually seem to possess an advantage. For what man sees as far <margin>6</margin> (not even the legendary Lynceus <note>A mythological hero of the Argonauts famed for his keen sight, said to be able to see through trees and underground.</note>) as the dragon <note>original: "δράκων" (drakōn); in antiquity, this often referred to a large serpent or watchful guardian, derived from the verb "to see."</note>? This is why the poets use the word *to see clearly* <note>original: "δρακεῖν" (drakein)</note> to describe sight. And the eagle, <margin>7</margin> even from a great height, does not fail to spot the cowering hare. Who has sharper hearing than the cranes, who <margin>8</margin> can hear from such a distance that no human could even see that far? In the sense of smell, almost all animals have such an advantage that things hidden from us strike them clearly; they can recognize each kind of creature even from a scent left in a footprint. Thus, men use dogs as guides, <margin>9 who</margin>

<column-break/>

are necessary because they are not human. Just as reason is not to be taken away from us simply because the gods are rational. On the contrary, it is evident that we are far surpassed by other animals. For what man is there—even if he were the Lynceus mentioned in the fables—who can see as much as a dragon? From which the poets even derived the word *to see* <note>original: "δρακεῖν" (drakein)</note>. Truly, the eagle, looking down from the high air, does not miss the doe. Who hears more acutely than the cranes? They are accustomed to perceiving sounds from such a distance as men cannot even see. For in smell, almost all other animals so far excel humans that those things which are hidden from us do not escape their keenness; indeed, they recognize each individual thing specifically by smelling the very footprint. Whence even men are accustomed to using the guidance of dogs so that they may understand where to go for the boar,

one must go out to find a boar or a deer: indeed, the state of the air affects us slowly, but is felt immediately by other animals, so that we take from them the signs of coming storms. Furthermore, they possess such an exact distinction of flavors that they discern what is morbid, healthy, and poisonous better and more exquisitely than any human physician is able. Now, Aristotle <note>referring to Aristotle's "History of Animals" or "On the Soul"</note> asserts that those beings endowed with more vigorous senses are also more prudent. # PORPHYRY

...one body is, <gloss>13</gloss> so to speak, healthier, and another less so, and in disease likewise there is a great difference; and just as there are <gloss>14</gloss> natural aptitudes and lack of aptitudes <note>original: "εὐφυΐαις καὶ ἀφυΐαις" — terms usually referring to innate talent or physical disposition</note> in bodies, so it is in souls: one is good, another base; and of the base, one is more so, another less. Even among the good there is not the same equality; Socrates, Aristotle, and Plato were not good in the same way, nor is there identity even among those of the same school of thought. Therefore, even if we possess more intellect than the other animals, we must not for that reason strip the animals of their intelligence. Just as partridges are not to be deprived of the power of flight because hawks fly better than they do; nor are other hawks to be thought lacking flight because the <gloss>15</gloss> dove-killer <note>original: "φασσοφόνος" — likely the peregrine falcon or a similar raptor</note> excels them and all others. One might grant, then, that the soul sympathizes with the body, and is affected by it whether it is in a good or bad state, but that the soul changes its own nature—that is impossible.

<column-break/>

...in the same class of bodies, both in the fitness for health or the susceptibility to disease, there is a great diversity: so in souls also, some are found good, others wicked: and of the wicked, some are more so, others less so, and in the good also there is not the same parity. For Socrates, Aristotle, and Plato are not good in a similar way. Furthermore, not even in those who hold the same opinion is there an entirely identical conformity. Therefore, if we also understand more than the rest of the animals, the intelligence of the rest of the animals must not be taken away for that reason. Just as partridges are not to be deprived of flight because hawks fly more powerfully than they; nor are other hawks to be judged to lack flight because the one called the "dove-killer" stands out above them and all others. Someone might therefore concede that the soul has a certain consensus with the body, so that it is indeed affected by the body being well or ill-disposed, but its nature nevertheless [does] not [change].

---

<margin>13. *As a healthier body.*] Either "as" <note>original: "ὡς"</note> should be deleted, or it should read "so to speak, healthier" <note>original: "ὡς εἰπεῖν, ὑγιεινότερον"</note>. As if to say, or rather thus: .. in each one, so to speak, in its kind, one is healthier. — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>.</margin>
<margin>14. *Natural aptitudes and lack of aptitudes.*] These pertain to the habit and nature of the body. Elsewhere they are usually transferred to the soul, whence Plato and others called the excellence of character "good natural aptitude" <note>original: "εὐφυΐαν"</note>, and he who was strong in it was called "well-endowed" <note>original: "εὐφυὴς"</note>. The opposite is "lack of aptitude" <note>original: "ἀφυΐα"</note> and "unfit" <note>original: "ἀφυὴς"</note>. So our author in the *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 1, where see Holstenius: but I spoke of this word above at Book I, section 11.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>15. *The dove-killer of all.*] Homer: *Iliad* Book 15, line 238:
- - - - - - - - - - - like a hawk
swift, the dove-killer, which is the swiftest of winged things.
From there the Author of the *Life of Homer* took it, in Gale’s *Opuscula Mythologica, Physica et Ethica*, page 320. So the hawk is called the "lightest of winged things" in *Odyssey* Book 13, line 87. Regarding the speed of these birds, Bochart has much in *Hierozoicon* II, 29. Aelian calls it the "dove-slayer" <note>original: "Φασσοφόντην"</note> in *History of Animals* XII, 4. A little after, "as" <note>original: "ὡς"</note> before "instrument" <note>original: "ὀργάνῳ"</note> is missing in the Leipzig edition.</margin>

<summary>Porphyry argues that differences in the degree of intelligence between humans and animals do not negate the existence of animal intelligence, using analogies of health and the varying flight speeds of birds. The marginalia provide philological commentary and classical citations from Homer and Aelian to support the text's descriptions of predatory birds.</summary>

does not change. But if the soul is only affected in conjunction with the body, and uses it as an instrument, it will be able to perform many actions through that body—if it is organized differently than ours—which we ourselves cannot do; and while it will be affected in a certain way according to the body's condition, it will not change its own nature.

§ 9. Therefore, it must be demonstrated that the rational power of the soul exists in other animals as well, and that they are not lacking in <term>prudence</term><note>original: "prudentia" / "φρονήσεως" (phronēseōs); refers to practical wisdom or the ability to act with foresight.</note>. For first, every creature knows perfectly well whether it is weak or strong: and for this reason, it guards against some and uses others for its own defense. Indeed, the leopard protects itself with its teeth; the lion with its claws and likewise its teeth; the horse with its hooves; the ox with its horns; the rooster with its spurs; the scorpion with its sting. Furthermore, the serpents in Egypt defend themselves with spit, whence they are also called <term>ptyades</term><note>original: "πτυάδες"; derived from the Greek word for "to spit."</note>, that is, "spitters": and with this, they aim at and blind the eyes of those attacking them; and so it is clear that each uses a different means to maintain its safety. us. But if it [the soul] only suffers in sympathy with the body, and uses it as an instrument, it would perform many things through it—being organized differently than in us—which we are unable to do, and it would suffer in sympathy according to how the body is disposed, yet it would not alter its own nature.

§ 9. That there is, therefore, a rational element in them, and that they are not deprived of wisdom, must be shown. First, each knows whether it is weak or strong, and so some things it guards against, while others it employs, as the leopard uses teeth, the lion claws and teeth, the horse the hoof, the ox horns, the rooster the spur, and the scorpion the sting. 3. **As much as it knows what is for its advantage.**] The Leipzig manuscript has "as much as is advantageous," without the word "for." This is correct. In some books it was "as much as is advantageous," in others "as much as is suitable"; then, the two readings being confused, the common version arose. One could also read "everything which it knows to be advantageous (or suitable) for itself." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist known for his textual criticism.</note>

To me, indeed, it does not seem to be so. I would rather prefer that "the" together with "dwelling" be omitted entirely and the sentence end at "of them." <term>REISKE</term>. *Felicianus* also seems not to have read it: nor is it in the Meerman manuscript. But *Aristotle*, whom our author praises, says: "Among wild birds, dwellings are devised for their lives and the safety of their offspring." *History of Animals*, Book IX, chapter 11.

# On Abstinence, Book III.

[It is not the case that] there was a time when it <note>the animal soul</note> was irrational; rather, as soon as it existed, it also emerged as rational. Nothing could prevent it from being so, even if it did not acquire its reason through formal instruction. Yet in animals, just as in humans, there are many things that Nature has taught them, while others are acquired later through training. For they learn some things from one another and, as has already been said, some things even from humans. They are also endowed with memory, which is the most essential part for the attainment of reasoning and wisdom. Furthermore, even vices and envies <note>original: "invidiae" / "φθόνοι"</note> are observed in them, although they are not as widespread as they are among humans; for their vices are much lighter than those of men. This is something we can easily observe from the following: if a man were to build a house, he would never lay its foundations unless he were sober and in his right mind; nor, if he were constructing a ship, would he lay the keel unless he were of sound mind; nor [would a farmer plant a vine...]

<column-break/>

<note>The following section contains the Greek source text for the passage above, followed by scholarly philological notes.</note>

...there was a time when it was irrational, but as soon as it was, it was also rational, and it is not prevented from being rational just because it did not take up reason through teaching. However, in other animals, just as in humans, Nature taught them most things, while learning provided others. They are taught some things by each other, and others, as we said, by humans. And they certainly possess memory, which happens to be the most sovereign element for the acquisition of reasoning and prudence. There are also vices and <gloss>1</gloss> envies in them, even if they are not <gloss>2</gloss> so poured out <note>i.e., widespread</note> as in humans; for their vice is lighter than that of men. For instance, a man who is a builder of a house would not lay <gloss>3</gloss> foundations unless he were sober, <gloss>4</gloss> nor would a shipwright lay the keel of a ship unless he were healthy [in mind], nor <gloss>5</gloss> a farmer...

<margin>1. Envies in them.]</margin> This might not seem so certain or well-proven. *Plutarch, Volume II, Page 537 B:* "Envy, however, occurs only toward humans. It is not likely that envy arises in wild beasts toward one another." However, others disagree, and among them *Theophrastus* wrote a book *On Animals Said to be Envious*. See *Menage* on *Diogenes Laertius V, 43* and *Fabricius, Greek Library III, 9, 12.*

<margin>2. So poured out.]</margin> For "poured out" <note>original: "κέχυνται"</note> I have taken care to restore "made small/thin" <note>original: "κεκάνυνται"</note>. VALENTINUS. *Fogerolles* also preferred this, but wrongly. I have followed what all the manuscripts prefer: "poured out" <note>original: "κέχυνται"</note> (except that *Valentinus* mistakenly gave "κέκυνται"). Why they should be troubled by this, I cannot figure out. *Bellinus Felicianus* translates as "widely open" or "widely spread," as above in section 2: "those having a pouring out of depravity." See there.

<column-break/>

<margin>3. Lay foundations.]</margin> To "lay a foundation" <note>original: "Καταβάλλεσθαι θεμέλιον"</note> is used by the *Writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews 6:1*, where *Wetstein* has cited this passage and many others.

# PORPHYRY

...if a man cultivates a field, he plants a vine <note>original: "ἀμπελον φυτεύσαι" / "uitem conferet"</note> without necessarily focusing his mind solely on that; yet almost all men engage in procreating children while drunk. But the other animals do not behave this way. They generate life for the sake of offspring, and for the most part, once the male has made the female pregnant, he does not attempt to mount her again, nor does the female tolerate it. 

<margin>Gospel of John, Chapter 15, verse 1. See Grotius's commentary there. <note>A reference to the "True Vine" imagery, likely comparing human and divine cultivation.</note></margin>

The extent of human insolence and intemperance in these matters is evident. Among animals, the mate recognizes the labor pains of the other, and in many cases shares in the labor, just as roosters do; some even help in hatching the eggs, as male pigeons do. They also take care to find a place where they are to give birth. And once each has given birth, it cleanses both the newborn and itself. If one observes closely, one would see that all things proceed with order and reason. 

<margin>6. "Neither does he mount." The Learned Man <note>likely referring to a previous editor</note> thought the word "men" <note>the Greek particle μὲν</note> should be deleted. I do not think so. Writers often insert this little word and similar ones for the sake of filling out the sentence, though they have not always escaped the criticism of learned men.</margin>

<margin>Read D'Orville on Chariton, Book 6, chapter 5.</margin>

For they also run to meet their nurturer with wagging tails <note>original: "σαίνειν" / "blandiendo"</note>, recognize their master, and signal the presence of an intruder.

<margin>7. "Encountering." Perhaps it should read "And by Zeus, encountering." — REISKE <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, a famous 18th-century textual critic.</note></margin>

### § 11.
Who is ignorant of how gregarious animals <note>animals that live in herds or colonies</note> maintain justice toward one another? This is seen first among ants...

<column-break/>

...if he should till a field, he brings together the vine, unless he turns his mind especially to that: but for the procreation of children, almost all men are vacant <note>distracted or idle</note> through drunkenness. But the other animals do not carry themselves so: they fruitify for the sake of progeny, and most of them, when they have rendered the female pregnant, neither do they themselves attempt to go in further, nor if they should attempt it, does the female endure it. In which matter, how much human shame and lack of self-control exists is a doubt to no one. And in other animals, one recognizes the birth-pangs of the other: and many even labor together, just as the poultry; some sit on the eggs together, like doves; and they have a care for seeking out the place where they are to bring forth. Likewise, each one, when it has brought forth its brood, purifies both itself and the offspring brought into the light. In which things, if anyone observes rightly, he will notice that all things proceed by order and reason. For they also meet the parent with fawning, recognize their master, and point out the snares of strangers.

### § 11.
That those which are of a flocking nature observe the law which is among themselves, no one is ignorant. For that is seen both in ants and...

-># On Abstinence, Book III.<-

...is most clearly evident in bees and other similar creatures. Who is ignorant of the chastity of wood-pigeons <note>original: "palumbium"</note> toward their mates? For if they happen to be pressed by an adulterer, and the mate discovers it, they strike him down and kill him. Who has not observed the justice of storks <note>original: "ciconiarum"</note> toward their parents? For a certain proper virtue excels in each animal, for which it has been made fit by nature; so that neither the nature nor the stability of these virtues ought to take away from them their rational power. For that point <note>that they lack reason</note> could perhaps be proved if the works of virtue and rational skill <note>original: "rationalisque solertiae"</note> were not clearly seen. Although we do not understand how these things are done, because we are unable to penetrate into their thoughts, they are not therefore to be condemned by us in such a way that they are thought to be entirely lacking in reason. For since we cannot penetrate into the mind of God in any 
way...

<column-break/>

...each of these, and this is also true of bees and similar creatures. And who is unheard of <note>unaware of</note> the temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sophrosynen)</note> of wood-pigeons toward those they live with—who, if they are even victims of adultery, kill the one who committed the adultery if they catch them—or the justice of storks toward those who gave them birth? For in each animal a certain specific virtue stands out toward which it is naturally inclined; therefore, neither nature nor the constancy of these traits removes reason from them. For one would have to prove that their works are not those of virtue and rational dexterity <note>original: "λογικῆς ἐντρεχείας" (logikes entrecheias)</note>. But if we do not understand how these things are practiced because we cannot enter into their reasoning, we shall not for that reason accuse them of irrationality. For no one is able to penetrate into the mind of God...

1. ...which seems to be later. <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist.</note> It often happens among the ancients that they join an adjective or pronoun of a different gender to a substantive. This seems to have arisen because another word expressing the same thing was being observed in the writer's mind. This matter has been insisted upon so many times that I would not wish to add even a single example from Greece or Latium. In this place, "race" <note>original: "γένος" (genos)</note> or something similar can be understood.

2. *The temperance of wood-pigeons, etc.*] "Of temperance" <note>genitive case</note> because of the following word "unheard of." <term>Reiske.</term> <term>Fogerolles</term> <note>François de Fogerolles, a 17th-century physician and translator of Porphyry.</note> had also corrected it thus: rightly so, unless you wish to repeat "who is ignorant" from the previous lines. For then it seems one should read "or who is unheard of... regarding the storks." <term>Aelian</term> discusses the chastity of wood-pigeons in *On the Nature of Animals*, Book III, 44, who also records that they punish adultery with death. More on this matter in <term>Samuel Bochart</term>, *Hierozoicon*, part II, Book I, chapter 4.

<column-break/>

3. *Or that of the storks...*] Rather, "or who [is unheard of] regarding the storks," as was just said. <term>The Celebrated Abresch</term> <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch (1699–1782), a Dutch philologist.</note> agrees with me. The ancients everywhere proclaim the piety of the stork. "Regarding storks, then, it is a common story among many that they are fed in return [by their young]," to speak with <term>Aristotle</term>, *History of Animals*, Book IX, chapter 13. A little later, "we take away" is erroneously written in the *Leipzig Manuscript* instead of "being taken away."

4. *Rational dexterity.*] "Rational dexterity" <note>original: "λογικὴ ἐντρέχεια"</note> is rational—if I may put it so—skill, or the use of reason. It often denotes skill mixed with some malice, yet not always, but is also taken in a good sense. Thus <term>The Celebrated D'Orville</term> <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a Dutch classicist.</note> explains the passage we have at hand in his notes on Chariton, Book II, chapter 6, page 195.

5. *For no one [can penetrate] into the mind of God, etc.*] Not entirely foreign to this passage is that saying of **Saint Paul**...

§ 12. One might justly wonder at those who establish justice based on reason, and who call those animals that do not share in human society "wild" and "unjust," yet do not extend the reach of justice to those animals with whom a social bond does exist. <margin>See Romans 11:34: "For who has known the mind of the Lord?" <note>original Greek: "τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου;"</note> where *Jo. Alberti* cites secular authors on this sentiment. Porphyry often treats religion as something unfathomable to the human mind. See Job 11:4, 1 Corinthians 2:10 & 11, etc.</margin>

6. *The works of the sun, etc.*] It ought rather to be read "of God" <note>Greek: "θεοῦ"</note>. However, "of the sun" <note>Greek: "ἡλίου"</note> can be sustained, though it is not as convenient a reading. VALENTIUS. Pythagoras, Plato, and others held the sun and other celestial bodies to be Gods, which they believed were rational <note>Greek: "λογικὰ"</note> and endowed with mind, as has been said elsewhere. *Plato* calls the sun and moon "great gods" in *Laws* VII, p. 901. *Julian* in Epistle 51 calls the sun "the great Sun, the living image, endowed with soul, mind, and the well-doing of the intelligible father." Therefore, although the Pythagoreans (from whom the Stoics received it) believed God was diffused through all nature, they held the sun and other celestial bodies to be the primary image of Him. "For the entire rational order, along with the incorruptible body natural to it, is an image of the whole Creator," to speak with *Hierocles* on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, p. 18.

<column-break/>

1. *Up to these [sharing] fellowship.*] Should be read with the article "the" <note>Greek: "τῶν"</note>. REISKE. Certainly, unless you understand "the gregarious ones" <note>Greek: "τῶν συναγελασικῶν"</note>, of which he began to speak in § 11. *Lipsius:* "sharing fellowship" <note>Greek: "κοινωνούντων"</note> is from a correction by the same ancient hand.

2. *Extending to whom.*] That word "to whom" <note>Greek: "οἷς"</note> has no value; therefore it seems it should be deleted. VALENTIUS. "To whom" should be deleted as a faulty repetition of the last syllable of the preceding word "extending" <note>Greek: "ἐκτείνοντας"</note>. REISKE. Let him who can digest stones endure these things as they were previously published! "To whom" used to be connected with the preceding "extending." If you place a punctuation mark after that word, the sense becomes convenient: "For just as for humans, for whom life vanishes if society is removed, so it is for those animals." It has often been said that our author loves these kinds of transpositions.

3. *Placed in need of humans—*] Perhaps it should be: "placed both humans in need of them in the use..."

# On Abstinence, Book III.

And it seems that Nature established humans in their state of need for this very reason: so that a common right <note>original: "commune ius," referring to the concept of natural law or justice</note> might be engendered both for them toward us, and for us toward them. If there are some animals that act wildly toward humans, it is not to be wondered at. For that which is said by Aristotle is true: if, he says, an abundance of food were available to all, they would exercise no ferocity either toward one another or toward humans. Indeed, all their friendships and enmities exist for the sake of food—however meager and necessary—and for the sake of their dwelling place. For if humans were reduced to that same scarcity of necessary things by which other animals are oppressed, how much more fierce and monstrous must we judge they would become than even those creatures that seem wild? War indicates this, in which men do not abstain even from devouring one another. Furthermore, even without war and famine, they do not fear to kill and eat the tame animals that live among them.

<column-break/>

...and [Nature] established humans in the need for them, making justice innate both for them toward us and for us toward them. If any are wild toward humans, it is nothing to wonder at; for the saying of Aristotle was true: that if all possessed an abundance of food, they would not behave wildly toward one another or toward humans. For the sake of this food—even though it is necessary and cheap—their enmities and friendships exist, as well as for the sake of their territory. If humans were shut up in such want as the animals are, how much more wild would they have become than those that seem wild? Both war and famine show this; where they do not even spare the taste of one another, and even without war and famine, they devour the animals that are reared with them and are tame.

# PORPHYRY

§ 13. But someone might say that while animals are indeed rational, they have no relationship <note>original: "σχέσιν" (schesin) - a technical term for a moral or social connection</note> toward us. And yet, it was by first assuming they were irrational that people denied this relationship; they made them out to be irrational, and then they derived our lack of community with them from their own needs <note>i.e., the human desire to use animals for food or labor</note>, rather than from the nature of reason itself. Our goal, however, was to demonstrate that they are rational, not whether they have made formal agreements with us. For even among humans, not everyone enters into a contract with us, yet no one would call a person "irrational" simply because they have not made such an agreement. Furthermore, many animals have even served humans, and as someone rightly said, although they serve through the ignorance and injustice of men, they have—through their own wisdom and justice—turned their masters into their own servants and caretakers. <note>Porphyry suggests that by being useful, animals compel humans to feed, shelter, and protect them, effectively making humans their "stewards."</note> Moreover, their vices are clearly visible, and it is from these that their rational faculty is most clearly revealed; for—

<column-break/>

§ 13. But indeed, someone might say that they are rational, yet they have no regard for us. First, they made them irrational, and from the fact that they were irrational, they asserted that they had no relation to us. Then, they claim that our fellowship with them is based on the utility we perceive in them, not on reason. But our purpose is to show that they are rational, not whether they have any pact with us; since even among men, not all are joined to us by a pact, and yet no one would say those who do not agree with us are therefore irrational. But many of them have even served men, and as a certain person said quite rightly, although they served out of the ignorance and injury of men, they themselves, out of wisdom and justice, rendered their masters their own ministers and managers. And indeed, their vices are plain to see, from which the rational faculty shines forth. For and in—

1. *Then from the need &c.*] Instead of "which they attach" <note>original: "ἣν ἀναπτόντων"</note> I would gladly read "they attached themselves." **VALENTIUS**. I would prefer: "they made them irrational" (previously a major punctuation mark was placed there) "since from the need—" He is responding to those who did not deny reason to animals, but maintained they had no relation to us. <column-break/>

There are some, however, who attempt to demonstrate, not poorly, from the places they have been allotted, that they are much more prudent than we. For evidently, excellence is not to be considered from location only in the case of the gods, while the same is not also to be done in the case of mortals.

2. *For just as those inhabiting the aether are rational...*] Perhaps "most rational." <note>original: λογικώτατα (logikōtata)</note> REISKE. Elsewhere, animals are commonly divided into those on land, in the sea, and in the heavens. See *Casaubon on Strabo:* p. 2. The ancient Philosophers taught that all regions of the world—the ethereal, aerial, aquatic, and terrestrial—produce, nourish, and foster living beings of their own kind, as is clear from Aristotle and others. See *Gataker on Antoninus:* XII, 24. and *Casaubon on Athenaeus:* VIII, 13. Also well known of old are those questions: which animals are more prudent, whether the land or the sea nourishes more and stronger ones, and others of that kind, concerning which see *Rittershusius on Oppian’s Cynegetica:* I, 239. and *Halieutica* V, 23. *Our author* [Porphyry] discusses this matter from *Plutarch* below in § 23. A little earlier, the *Leipsic Manuscript* incorrectly has "being shown" instead of "to show."

3. *We inhabit the dregs.*] "Dregs" <note>original: Ὑποστάθμην (Hypostathmēn)</note> (a word by which *Henri Estienne’s Thesaurus* may be enlarged) they call that which settles, and which stands at the bottom. *Wesseling* explains the nature of the word *on Diodorus Siculus:* III, 44. and *Gataker on Antoninus:* IX, 36. who, not forgetting *our author*, advises that the Stoics for the same reason called the earth "the dregs of all things." *Our author*, as I think, imitates *Plato in the Phaedo:* p. 81. D. "that these things are the dregs, and always flow together into the hollows of the earth."

# On Abstinence, Book III

<columns>2</columns>

§ 15. Since they <note>referring to non-human animals</note> even acquire skills—and human ones at that—learning to dance, to drive chariots, to engage in gladiatorial combat, and to walk on tightropes; and furthermore to write and read, to play the flute and the lyre, and even to shoot arrows and ride horses: can you still doubt whether they possess that faculty which receives such knowledge, when the knowledge received is clearly visible within them? For where do they receive it, if there is no underlying reason <note>original: *ratio* / *logos*</note> in which these skills can exist? For they do not hear our voices as mere noise, but they also have a perception of the diversity of signs, which arises from rational understanding. But, they say, they perform these human tasks poorly. Yet not even all humans perform them well; otherwise, it would be in vain that some are victors in contests while others are defeated. But they do not deliberate, they say, nor do they hold assemblies, nor sit in judgment—

<column-break/>

§ 15. When they take up skills, and human ones at that, learning to dance and to drive chariots, to fight as gladiators and to walk on ropes, and now even to write and to read, to play the flute and the lyre, to shoot arrows and to ride horses, will you still dispute whether the animal possesses the receptive faculty, when that which has been received is observed in them? For where does it receive these things if **1** reason <note>original: *logos*</note> were not present, in which skills are established? For it does not hear our voice as a mere sound, but there is in them a perception of the differences between signs, which already proceeds from rational intelligence. **2** But, someone says, the animal performs human tasks badly. Well, not even all humans do them well. **3** Or else it would be in vain that there were victors and vanquished in a contest. But they do not deliberate, they say, nor hold assemblies,

---

<columns>2</columns>

**1.** *Reason were present.*] Thus I have restored the text from the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, which the translator confirms. Previously it was read ridiculously as *reason to speak*. For which *Valentini* had substituted *was in*. Anyone can see how easily these words could be confused.

**2.** *But, someone says.*] This is correct. Namely, *the opponent*. Many have written much about this formula, and, if I am not mistaken, *Bentley* among them in his notes on *Horace*. However, the plural *they say* can also be approved, because it follows immediately after. REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 1716–1774, a noted German classicist.</note> The singular *says* is often used without an explicit "someone" when it is meant to indicate that someone is raising an opposing argument. See *Reiske* on *Dio Chrysostom* p. 187, and *Richard Bentley* on *Horace* (Satires I.4.79), who teaches that the Latins speak in the same way. Therefore, *Valentini* should not have substituted the plural *they say*.

<column-break/>

**3.** *Or else in vain a contest and victors...*] *The celebrated Abresch* (in *Dilucidationes Thucydideae Auctarium* p. 390) reads *well indeed and by...* <note>original: *καλῶς ἂν καὶ μὰ τὴν*</note>. It is certainly an ingenious conjecture. For as for what *Bos* thought (in *Animadversiones* ch. 3), that the formula *by the...* <note>feminine oath</note> is not found among the Greeks like the masculine version, I would not say that. See *Hemsterhuis* on *Aristophanes' Plutus* p. 120. If you prefer the common reading, the meaning is this: if both parties performed the task well, victors and vanquished could not be produced in the wrestling school. To "win a contest" <note>original: *νικᾶν ἀγῶνα*</note> is used also by *Epictetus* (Enchiridion 25), just as "to win a battle," "a song," and similar phrases, regarding which see *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus* XI.26 and XIII.74.

# PORPHYRY

4 ...nor do they hold trials. 5 For tell me, do all men do so? Do not many act before they have even deliberated? And how could anyone demonstrate that animals do *not* deliberate? No one is able to provide evidence for such a claim. On the contrary, those who have written detailed accounts concerning animals have shown that they do. As for the rest, the arguments declaimed against them are stale and outdated. 6 For instance, 7 that they have no cities; but I would say neither do the 8 wagon-dwelling Scythians <note>original: *Hamaxobii*, a nomadic tribe of Scythia known for living in wagons</note>, nor indeed do the gods. They say there are no written laws among the animals; 9 but there were none among men either, as long as they remained in a state of happiness <note>A reference to the "Golden Age" of humanity before the need for restrictive legislation</note>. 10

<column-break/>

...they practice. What wonder is it, since not even all men do this? Do not many act before they have consulted? Furthermore, from where can it be demonstrated that the other animals do not consult? Indeed, no argument exists for this matter that can be brought forward: but on the contrary, many arguments exist, which those who have written on every detail concerning animals supply to us. The rest of the things they shout against them are surely rotten. They say they have no cities: But neither do the Scythians, who wander about in wagons: nor even the gods. They have no written laws. But neither did men have any, while they persisted in happiness.

***

4. *Nor do they hold trials.*] I would prefer the reading "they seek justice for themselves" <note>original: *δικάζονται*</note>. They experience justice; then "they might deliberate" <note>original: *βουλεύσωνται*</note> in the subjunctive. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist</note>. The Meerman manuscript incorrectly reads "they wish."

5. *For if men, tell me.*] Rather "For either... all," as Abresch preferred. That formula "tell me" <note>original: *εἰπέ μοι*</note> is elegant in a challenge, when we want the person we are dealing with to prove something, as it were, and confirm it with examples. The Latins use "Say" and "Tell me" in this way. See the celebrated Burman on Ovid's *Heroides* XVI, 341.

6. *Declaimed against them.*] The word "to declaim" <note>original: *Ῥητορεύειν*</note>, like the Latin *rhetoricari*, is often used for futile and talkative chattering. See the notes collected by D'Orville on Chariton VI, 1, p. 503, who did not leave these passages of Porphyry untouched. It can be seen from here by what right that Distinguished Man thought, in Maximus Tyrius Dissertation IX, 5, that "battles and declamations" could not be rightly joined, since the brawls and contests of boys over their playthings can be called nothing less than "declamations."

7. *That they have no cities.*] Celsus, in Origen Book IV, p. 369, spoke in a slightly different way, saying that if men

<column-break/>

seem to differ from beasts for the reason that they inhabit cities, use laws, and appoint magistrates and leaders for themselves, that reasoning is entirely vain, for both ants and bees do the same.

8. *Wagon-dwelling Scythians.*] A matter well enough known from other sources. Hence they are called "wagon-dwellers" <note>original: *ἁμαξοικοὶ*</note> in Strabo Book VIII, p. 208. Mela expressed it in Latin (II, 1) as "called *Hamaxobii* because they have wagons instead of houses." If I consider that custom, I think nothing should be changed in Julius Capitolinus in *Maximinus* 13, where he says "he would display them in Scythian vehicles." Certainly, I cannot stomach Salmasius's reading of "dry vehicles." "Scythian vehicles," because placed in vehicles they were forced to travel day and night, as is said in Herodian VII, 3.

9. *Nor among men as long as they were happy.*] The Leipzig manuscript reads "For neither among..."—not badly, for he speaks that way a little earlier as well. Regarding the matter itself, see the observations made in Book I, § 8.

10. *Apis is said to be the first...*] In the Leipzig manuscript, this marginal scholion <note>A scholarly note written in the margin of a manuscript</note> is added: <margin>that Apis was the first lawgiver among the Greeks, being the King of the Argives.</margin> This refers to Apis, King of the Argives, who is usually held to be the son of Phoroneus. However, in Aeschylus's *Suppliants* 270, he is called a stranger—
