# PORPHYRY

The Egyptians also regarded these animals as gods, whether because they truly believed them to be gods, or because they intentionally fashioned the forms of the gods with the faces of oxen, birds, and other creatures, so that people might abstain from them just as they do from human beings, or perhaps for other more mystical reasons. In the same way, the Greeks attached the horns of a ram to the statue of Zeus <note>original: "Iouis" / "Διὸς"; the text refers to Jupiter Ammon</note>, and the horns of a bull to that of Dionysus <note>original: "Bacchi" / "Διονύσου"</note>. They composed Pan from a man and a goat, and they gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens; according to—

<column-break/>

The Egyptians, moreover, referred these same animals to the gods, whether because they truly thought they were gods, or because they purposefully assigned the faces of oxen, birds, and other animals to the gods, to warn that one must abstain from them no differently than from humans: or perhaps led by some other more hidden cause. Thus also the Greeks applied the horns of a ram to the statue of Jupiter, and those of a bull to the image of Bacchus: likewise they composed Pan from a man and a goat. They had equipped the Muses with wings, and the Sirens as well.

---

See *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> book I. *Socrates*, a not-uncelebrated writer of Cretan history whom an eminent man praises, is unknown to me. *Zenobius* and the *Scholiast on Aristophanes*: they have often misled learned men, in whose corrupted manuscripts "Socrates" is read instead of "Sosicrates." Compare *Kuster on Suidas* and *Fabricius, Greek Library* Book II, 23. p. 827.

5. **Whether because they truly believed them to be gods etc.**] That the Egyptians did not truly hold those animals to be Gods, but only as images and symbols of them, is shown among others by *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel* Book III, p. 117 and *Plutarch, Volume II* p. 379. Nevertheless, they held the same honor for the symbol as for the Divinities, on which matter see *Cuper, Harpocrates* p. 42. Soon *Meermann* reads *the forms of the gods*, omitting *the*.

6. **And of others.**] Perhaps it should read *and making others with similar faces*. And soon *that of them* (line 6.) REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>.

7. **Or for other reasons.**] Differently than other nations, the Egyptians worshipped not illustrious men, but animals with divine honors. This is indeed well-attested, but from where the practice took its origin is not so certain or explored. Both ancient and modern writers disagree greatly. *Diodorus Siculus* I, 86; *Mosheim on Cudworth’s Intellectual System of the Universe* p. 418; *Jablonski in the Prologue to the Egyptian Pantheon* § 35; *Warburton in The Divine Legation of Moses* Book IV, 4. etc. have dealt with this argument so at length that nothing ought to be added. Reiske rightly deleted *from* before *them* a little earlier; Abresch wanted the same.

8. **They attached the horns of a ram.**] Concerning Jupiter, or Ammon, *ram-faced* <note>original: "κριοπροσώπῳ"</note>, all things are well known, since the ancient theologians so often reproach the pagans for it. Read the *Learned Man on Minucius Felix* ch. 21. But you may wonder that this is attributed to the Greeks in this passage, which elsewhere is attributed to the Africans. *Suidas* indeed, under *Ammon*, says it is the *name of a Greek god*, but there Kuster thought one should read *Libyan* or explain it as *national*. But in truth, not only by Africans but also by Greeks was Jupiter worshipped as *ram-faced*. Spanheim discusses this beautifully in *On the Use and Excellence of Coins, Dissertation VII*.

9. **And of a bull to Dionysus.**] No one is ignorant of the horns of Bacchus. Hence he is called *bull-horned* and the *bull-horned god* <note>original: "ταυρόκερως"</note>, concerning which name see *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus III, 64*.

10. **And Pan—**] *Minucius Felix in Octavius* ch. 28: *You also dedicate gods mixed from a goat and a man, and gods with the faces of lions and dogs.* Where the interpreters have much on this matter. Compare *our author* <note>Porphyry</note> below, IV, 9.

11. **They gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens.**] They establish wings as common to the Sirens and the Muses (the daughters of one of them, as most relate). See *Spanheim, On the Use and Excellence of Coins, Dissertation V*. On the winged Sirens, Broukhuis writes most elegantly on *Tibullus V, 1, 69*. No one is unaware of the feathers of *Victory* and the others mentioned here.

# On Abstinence, Book III.
## Ii 2

In a similar way, they depicted both Victory and Iris <note>The messenger goddess of the rainbow</note>, as well as Cupid and Mercury <note>Hermes</note>, as winged. Pindar, certainly, in his odes, represented all the gods—when they were being pursued by Typhon <note>A monstrous giant in Greek myth who challenged Zeus</note>—not as resembling men, but as other animals. They assert that Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, captured by a love for Pasiphae, took the form of a bull; they tell stories of him becoming now an eagle, now a swan. By all these things, those ancients clearly displayed the honor which they judged should be shown to animals. And this is even more evident when they say that Jupiter was nursed by a goat. Furthermore, there was a law of Rhadamanthus <note>A legendary wise judge of Crete</note> among the Cretans, by which it was commanded that all animals be used in the taking of oaths.

<column-break/>

In the same way [they depicted] Victory, and Iris, and Eros, and Hermes. 12 Pindar, in his processional hymns, represented all the gods, when they were pursued by Typhon, as having been made like not to men, 13 but to the other animals; and that Zeus, having fallen in love with Pasiphae, 14 became a bull, and at other times an eagle and a swan. Through these things the ancients demonstrated their respect toward animals, and even more so when 15 they say a goat nursed Zeus. Among the Cretans there was a law of Rhadamanthus 16 to bring all animals into an oath.

---

<column-break/>

12. *Pindar in his processional hymns.*] The oldest editions have *prosodiois* <note>original: "προσόδιοis"</note>, which I would not have changed, as the manuscripts of many writers prefer both spellings. See Seber on Pollux IV, 53. Suidas under the letter P: *Prosodia: poems sung by lyric poets at the festivals of the gods.* But also the same: *Prosodion: the hymn.* In the entry for *Pindar*, he attributes to the poet *prosodia* and *parthenia* <note>maiden-songs</note>, which words perhaps ought to be joined there and understood as the *partheneia* which Plutarch attributes to Pindar.

13. *But to the other animals.*] The great scholar <note>referring to a specific commentator, likely Valckenaer</note> cites "But to the *irrational* animals" in his notes on Diodorus Siculus I, 86; I have not found this in the manuscripts. Many relate the fable which our author touches upon, concerning which matter see the Distinguished Man <note>a common scholarly honorific</note> in the same place, and the interpreters of Ovid, Metamorphoses Book V, 321. However, the claim added there by that Famous Man—that the shameful figures of the Egyptian Gods were born from this fable—is certainly not without controversy.

14. *Became now... and then...*] These things are unknown to no one, even from the mythographers. I will only cite Theodoret in his *Sermon on Sacrifices*, because he often echoes our author and joins these same points: "and the father of the gods himself, being likened to an eagle, a bull, and a swan," etc. However, it seems it should be read "became now indeed," as Abresch suggested. For others are accustomed to speak thus, as is our author above in section 5. See Reiske there.

15. *They say [a goat] nursed Zeus.*] I have restored the word "the" <note>original: "Τὸν"</note> to its place, from which it had been expelled by Valentinus, who published "the" in the feminine <note>original: "τὴν"</note>. The earlier editions and the Leipzig Manuscript demand this. Minucius Felix in *Octavius*, chapter 21: *And what are the sacred rites of Jove? A nanny-goat is his nurse, and the infant is stolen from his greedy father lest he be devoured.* See the learned men on this matter.

16. *To bring all animals into an oath.*] This expression is well-handled: to bring upon oneself, that is, to produce in one's own cause, every kind of living creature, so that they may be an "horkos" <note>original: "ὅρκος"</note> to oneself—that is, a religious obligation sanctioned by an oath. Valentinus had marked the passage with an asterisk as suspect, but the Illustrious Reiske defends it well. Hence the "brought-in oath" in Isocrates' *To Demonicus*, page 12, about which phrase the Grammarians disagree. Suidas says well: *An "epaktos" oath: one to which another person leads you.* Just as they call the help of foreigners and those sought from elsewhere an "epaktos" power. See Casaubon on Aeneas Tacticus; and "epaktos" wealth regarding a dowry in Euripides' *Melanippe*. Alberti has other things of this kind in his notes on Hesychius. This very subject occurred to us a little while ago.

# PORPHYRY

17 Nor was Socrates playing a game when he swore by the dog and the goose; 18 rather, he was making his oath according to the custom of the son of Zeus and Justice <note>original: "τὸν τοῦ Διὸς καὶ Δίκαιον παῖδα" - referring to Rhadamanthus, the judge of the underworld known for his integrity</note>. 19 Nor was he joking when he called the swans his fellow-servants. Mythology also hints that animals have the same soul as we do, 20 suggesting that through the anger of the gods, humans were changed from men into animals, and having been changed, they are thereafter pitied and loved. 21 For such are the stories told about dolphins, and those concerning kingfishers, nightingales, and swallows.

§ 17. And each of the ancients boasts that his vision was fortunate from the...

<column-break/>

Neither did Socrates, while he swore by the dog and the goose, do so as a joke: but he swore an oath in earnest according to the institution of the just son of Jupiter <note>Latin: Iovis</note>: nor did he call the swans his fellow-servants in jest. Furthermore, the fables which claim a transformation was made from humans into animals due to the indignation of the gods—and that the gods therefore followed them with mercy and loved them—seem to signify that other animals are endowed with the same soul as we are. For of such a kind are those things handed down concerning dolphins, kingfishers, nightingales, and swallows.

§ 17. Likewise, every one of the ancients who [experienced] a happy upbringing from animals...

---

<column-break/>

<margin>From this, therefore, the Cretans refrained from using divine names and swore by whatever living creatures were at hand. See *Meursius* in *Creta*, Book IV, chapter 1.</margin>

17. **Nor Socrates etc.**] Socrates swore by those things, not as if by Gods, but so that he might not swear by the name of God. This was mentioned above. *Tertullian, Apology, chapter 14: I am silent regarding the Philosophers, being content with Socrates, who, in contempt of the Gods, swore by an oak, a goat, and a dog.* See there *Havercamp* and *Menage* on *Diogenes Laertius II, 40.*

18. **But according to the [son] of Z. and J.**] "But according to the son of Zeus and Justice." Following the example of Rhadamanthus, who was born of Jupiter and Justice. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, a 18th-century philologist</note>. *The celebrated Jablonski in Egyptian Pantheon I, 5, 5* corrects this to "the son of Zeus and Maia." He suggests Socrates understood the Egyptian Anubis, or, as the Greeks interpret it, Mercury, whom they held to be the son of Jupiter and Maia. I will not say that these [theories] stray too far from the actual lettering; if the dog signified Mercury, what of the goose, the goat, etc.? Nor does the word "according to" <note>Greek: κατὰ</note> usually signify this when constructed in this manner. Since Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus are called "sons of the god" by our author in the *Life of Plotinus*, and Rhadamanthus is the son of Jupiter and Europa in *Plato's Minos p. 367 D*, and he emerged most famous for the praise of justice (as is known from *Meursius* in *Creta* III, 15 and others), I have decided nothing should be changed. For "he made" <note>ποιεῖτο</note>, read "he was making" <note>ἐποιεῖτο</note> from the *Leipzig and Meerman Codices*.

19. **Nor playing, fellow-servants —**] *Plutarch, Volume II, p. 975 B: "Socrates says privately that he makes himself a fellow-servant of the swans."* *Pausanias in Attica p. 58:* Socrates, on the night before Plato was to become his student, saw a dream of a swan flying into his lap. Perhaps for this reason Socrates said he made himself a fellow-servant of the swans, as *Spencer* writes on *Origen, Book VI Against Celsus, p. 635*; but this is of no weight and is refuted by our author, for he held swans and geese in the same regard.

20. **And by anger.**] Either something is missing before "and," or in its place one should read "saying," or a similar participle. Presently "having changed" <note>singular instead of plural</note>. <term>REISKE</term>.

21. **For such things etc.**] Concerning the Kingfisher <note>Halcyone</note>, turned into a bird by the anger of Jupiter, see *Didymus on Homer's Iliad I, 558*; concerning the swallow and nightingale, see *The Learned Man on Aelian, Various History XII, 20*, where Perizonius [notes] from Pausanias what gave occasion to the fable.

1. **A vision was fortunate.**] Perhaps "as each one" <note>Greek: ὡς τις</note>. <term>REISKE</term>.

### § 18.
Through these points and others—which we shall mention in order as we review the opinions of the ancients—it is demonstrated that other animals are indeed rational beings. Although in most of them reason is <gloss>1</gloss> imperfect, it is by no means considered to be entirely absent. Since justice exists toward rational beings (as our opponents themselves claim), why should justice not also extend from us to these animals? We do not extend the definition of justice to plants, <gloss>2</gloss> because in them there appears to be a great <gloss>3</gloss> lack of connection <term>asynkloson: literally "unspun together," meaning a lack of shared destiny or biological affinity</term> to reason. # On Abstinence, Book III.

No one would consume fish unless they were killed by force. In this matter, there is undoubtedly much injustice. Furthermore, as **Plutarch** <note>original: "Plutarchus"; referring to the Greek philosopher and essayist</note> also says, just because our nature lacks certain things and makes use of them, it does not follow that we should extend injury to all things. For it is granted that injury may be inflicted to a certain extent for the sake of necessity—since it is an injury to take anything even from plants, even if they remain alive. However, to take away and destroy other things out of insolence and to indulge in pleasures seems to be the height of ferocity and injustice, especially since abstaining from them is no hindrance to us either for living or for living well. For if, just as with air and plants and fruits, without which it is not possible to lead a life, so also—

<column-break/>

—those things which we also kill by force, no one would partake of them. Thus, there is much injustice in these things. To begin with, as **Plutarch** says, it is not because our nature requires some things and we use them that we must now extend injustice to everything and against all things. For nature allows and provides for a certain amount of harm for the sake of necessities (if indeed it is harm to take something from plants, even though they remain living). But to enjoy other things and destroy them out of excess <note>original: "ἐκ περιουσίας" (ek periousias); meaning from a position of surplus or luxury rather than need</note> and for the sake of pleasure, was a mark of absolute savagery and injustice. And abstinence from these things does not diminish us, neither in respect to living nor to living well. For if, as with air and water, plants and fruits, without which it is impossible to live, so also with slaughter—

---

<margin>Except for such things. VALENTINUS: Perhaps "except for the strong ones which also..." below in section 9. "Some things... as many as are strong." REISKE: *Thneseidia* <note>original: "Θνησείδια"; meat from animals that died of natural causes</note> which elsewhere is *thnesidia*. See Book IV, 16. The letters "ei" and "i" are frequently swapped in these texts, as mentioned elsewhere. Compare the learned scholar on Hesychius regarding *Thnetidia*. Foggeroll thought those words "except for fish" were badly inserted, and rightly so, in my opinion. Some foolish monk seems to have wanted us to eat fish—which are also killed by force (with respect to living creatures)—that died their own death out of the water. For the place we inhabit is like the underworld to them; as soon as they reach it, they die, as Plutarch beautifully says in Volume II, page 669 D.</margin>

6. **Plutarch says.** Read what he discusses regarding these matters in the *Symposiacs*, Book IX, 8. A little later, Valentinus had inserted "in" before "necessities," but against the evidence of the manuscripts and without necessity.

<margin>Critical Library X. 28.</margin>

7. **Out of excess.** By a common expression, those things are so called "whose presence is not necessary," as Suidas says in his entry. Diodorus Siculus, Book XX, 59: "they used all things abundantly out of excess." From there it is gracefully transferred to other things, concerning which there is a great Commentary. Sometimes it is also said of those things which are acquired easily and without labor. See Casaubon on Strabo, Book III, page 60. Our author in this passage seems to have had before his eyes those words of **Aristotle** in the *Topics*, Book III, 2: "To live well is out of excess; but life itself is a necessity."

8. **To enjoy for pleasure.** "To release for pleasure" <note>original: "ἀπολύειν" (apolycin)</note> meaning to lose or destroy, was created by the scribes from the letter A, as these two letters are often swapped. REISKE. A clever conjecture indeed, although I have preferred the common reading.

# PORPHYRY

...if we were in need of the slaughter of animals and the eating of flesh for the sake of our lives, nature would have a necessary entanglement with this injustice. But if many priests of the gods, and many kings of the **barbarians** <note>original: "βαρβάρων" (barbarōn); here referring to non-Greek peoples, often used by Porphyry to denote the Egyptians or Indians who practiced asceticism</note> live in purity, and countless races of animals live without ever touching such food at all, and they attain their natural end, how is he not absurd who commands that, if we are forced to be at war with some, we should not even live peacefully with those with whom it is possible? Does he think we must either live by practicing justice toward none, or not live at all by practicing it toward all? Just as among men, he who for the sake of his own safety, or his children, or his country, either takes away the money of some or crushes a region and a city, has necessity as a **pretext** <note>original: "πρόσχημα" (proschēma); a legal or moral excuse</note> for his injustice; but he who does these things for the sake of wealth, or satiety, or luxurious pleasures—

<column-break/>

...so if we also needed the slaughter of animals and the eating of flesh, our nature would necessarily be bound to this injustice. But if indeed many priests of the gods and kings of the barbarians lead a life piously and chastely—furthermore, if innumerable kinds of animals are not frustrated in reaching their natural end and good even though this kind of food is never tasted at all—how is he not absurd who, if we are forced to wage war with some, does not bid us live peacefully even with those with whom it is permitted? Or does he judge that we must either live by using justice toward none, or not live by using it toward all? Therefore, just as among men, he who for the sake of his own safety, and his children, and his country, either seizes the money of others or oppresses a region and a city, has a necessity which in some way excuses the injustice; but he who [does so] from the insolence of riches and pleasures, not—

---

<margin>
*To enjoy* <note>original: "Ἀπολαύειν" (Apolauein)</note> refers to pleasure, whether honorable or depraved and luxurious; hence *Hesychius* says: "He enjoys; he lives luxuriously." See *Alberti* on this. Hence *enjoyable things* <note>original: "ἀπολαυστικὰ"</note> are sometimes the same as *pleasurable things* <note>original: "ἡδονικὰ"</note>, just as men of this kind are called *pleasure-seekers* <note>original: "ἀπολαυστικοί"</note>, and their life is called a *life of enjoyment* <note>original: "βίος ἀπολαυστικὸς"</note>. See *Gataker* on *Antoninus* <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> III, 6. Thus there is a pregnant sense in those words of Paul in the First Epistle to Timothy VI, 17: "God provides *all things richly for enjoyment*."
</margin>

<margin>
9. *Of the barbarians. Living in purity.*] After the word *living in purity* <note>original: "ἁγνεύοντες"</note>, or rather *having lived in purity*, there seems to be missing a word like *are said*, or *are reported*, or *are recorded*, or something similar. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century philologist</note>. Concerning the word *to touch* <note>original: "θιγγάνειν"</note>, which follows, see the note at II, 33.
</margin>

<margin>
10. *Or toward all.*] The *Leipzig and Meermann Codices* <note>handwritten manuscript versions</note> read *toward all things* <note>original: "πρὸς πάντα"</note>, which I prefer. Recently, <term>Fogerolles</term> <note>a previous editor</note> inserted the word *the* <note>original: "τῆς"</note> instead of *his own*, without just cause.
</margin>

<margin>
11. *To have a pretext.*] In the earlier editions it was *to have* <note>original: "ἔχειν" (infinitive)</note>, and I do not see why <term>Valentinus</term> changed it to *he has* <note>original: "ἔχει" (indicative)</note>. It belongs to the following word *it seems*. The *Meermann codex* also protects the original reading.
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book III.
## K k

If a man, led by no necessity, does the same thing <note>original: "idem facit" - referring to the consumption of life</note>, he is considered unjust, lacking in self-control, and wicked. Thus, God allows men the use of plants, the consumption of fire and water, the shearing of sheep, their milk, and the yoking of oxen; and since men use these for their own safety and preservation, He forgives it. But to slaughter animals, and to eat their cut-up remains full of slaughter and blood—not for the sake of nourishment and satiety, but for the sake of pleasure and gluttony—that is indeed unjust and wicked beyond measure. For is it not enough that, although they ought to be oppressed by no labors, we use them even unto exhaustion?

<column-break/>

...and providing for the fulfillment of unnecessary desires, he seems to be unsociable, lacking in self-control, and evil. Thus, God grants pardon for the harm done to plants, the consumption of fire and streams, the shearing of sheep and their milk, and the taming and yoking of oxen for the safety and survival of those who use them. But to subject animals to slaughter and to cook them, becoming filled with murder—not for the sake of food or fullness, but making pleasure and gluttony the end—is extraordinarily lawless and dreadful. For it is enough that we use those who ought not to toil at all until they are weary with labor.

---

<columns>2</columns>

12. *He seems to be unsociable.*] <note>original: "Ἄμικτος εἶναι δοκεῖ"</note> An elegant expression. *Unsociable, unmixed, unapproachable, difficult to mix with*—all these refer to those who exclude strangers from the right of commerce and refuse their association and access, as **Wesseling** well notes on *Herodotus* I, 25. Therefore, *unsociable, lacking self-control, and wicked* are rightly joined, as in *Lucian's True History* I, 35: *harsh, heavy, unsociable, and wild.* Below, the term *difficulty of mixing* <note>original: "τὸ δυσεπίμικτον"</note> will occur to us in IV, 6.

13. *And of fire and of streams, the consumption.*] <note>original: "Καὶ πυρὸς καὶ ναμάτων ἀναλ."</note> Perhaps "and through fire and streams," meaning *the consumption of crops brought about by the aid of fire and water.* It signifies the cooking of them. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. I suspected *of wheat* <note>original: "πυροῦ"</note> or *of grains*, which words are often confused, as **Wesseling** shows on *Diodorus* I, 72. For why would he have omitted mention of grain here? But *streams* <note>original: "νάματα"</note> stands in the way, which, even if my hands itch to change it, I do not dare to touch. A little before, <term>MEERMAN</term> reads *thus the...*

14. *To subject animals.*] <note>original: "Ζῶα ὑπάγειν"</note> **Fogerolles & Valentinus** corrected this to *but to subject animals*, and the **Meerman Manuscript** also requires this. A little later, **Abresch** was refashioning it as *extraordinarily as*, as *Plato* often does.

15. *Weary with labor.*] <note>original: "Προκάμνουσι"</note> I substituted *for labors* <note>original: "πρὸς καμάτους"</note>. Previously, instead of *servant-substitutes* <note>original: "ἀντίδουλα"</note>, it was read as *if slaves*. See

<column-break/>

*Plutarch, On the Cleverness of Animals.* <term>VALENTINUS</term>. *Weary with labor* is a good reading. *To labor beforehand* <note>original: "προκάμνειν"</note> is to work in place of another, and by one's own prior effort to relieve the succeeding work of another of a great part of the trouble. But then one must read *and they toil, the teams of horses and donkeys.* For it is a six-foot line <note>iambic senarius</note> of **Aeschylus**, also frequently cited by **Plutarch**. <term>REISKE</term>. The earlier editions close the sense after *weary with labor*, and join *toils* <note>original: "μόχθους"</note>, which do not seem to belong to Aeschylus, to what follows. Yet our author could have said *the toils of horses*—calling them *servant-substitutes etc.*, just as they are called by that same **Aeschylus** in *Prometheus Bound* 463:
> Successors to mortals in the greatest toils.
What follows from the same author, **Plutarch** praises in Vol. II, p. 98 and p. 964, but in a different way. In the first place:
> Giving the teams of horses and donkeys, and the offspring of bulls,
> As substitute-gifts and receivers of toils.
In the other place, however, he has *teams, servant-substitutes, and receivers.* Therefore, in the first passage of **Plutarch**, *servant-substitutes* <note>original: "ἀντίδουλα"</note> should be read instead of *substitute-gifts* <note>original: "ἀντίδωρα"</note>, which in the latter passage **Pauw** would undoubtedly have asserted against **Xylander** in his *Fragments of Aeschylus* p. 1104, from **Porphyry**, if he had remembered our author—

# PORPHYRY

...and the labors of horses, the breeding of donkeys, and the offspring of bulls, as Aeschylus says, <note>original: "ὡς Αἰσχύλος φησὶν" - likely referring to a lost passage or Prometheus Bound regarding the domestication of animals.</note> having tamed them and brought them under the yoke to be servants and to take up our toils.

§ 19. But as for the man who deems that we should not use the ox for food, nor—by destroying and ruining breath and life—add seasonings for satiety and ornaments to the table: of what thing necessary for salvation, or what thing beautiful for virtue, does he deprive our life? Furthermore, to compare plants to animals is altogether forced. For the latter are by nature endowed with sensation, and can feel pain, and be afraid, and be harmed; for which reason they can also be treated unjustly. But for the former <insert>plants</insert> there is no sensation, and thus nothing is "alien" to them, nor is there evil, nor any injury or injustice. For the beginning of all "appropriation" <term>oikeiōsis: the Stoic concept of "making something one's own" or recognizing a kinship</term> and "alienation" is sensation. Now, the followers of Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> establish this "appropriation" as the principle of justice. But how is it not irrational, when we see many humans living by sensation alone, possessing neither mind nor reason, and many

<column-break/>

...for horses and donkeys to carry loads and the offspring of bulls, as Aeschylus says, *brought into servitude to become the receivers* of our labor, so that they might even undergo the yoke.

§ 19. For he who judges that we should not feed upon the ox, nor seek out seasonings for our tables from any destroyed breath or life, does not deprive the life of men of anything either necessary for health or honorable for virtue. Indeed, to wish to compare plants to animals seems exceedingly absurd and forced. Since animals feel, grieve, fear, and are offended, and therefore can be affected by injury; but in plants no sensation is present, and therefore neither "the alien," nor evil, nor any hurt or injury can happen to them. For sensation is the principle of all conciliation <note>Latin: "conciliationis" - translating the Greek 'oikeiōsis'.</note> and alienation. Indeed, Zeno established conciliation as the principle of justice. But truly, in what way is it not absurd, when we see many men living by sensation alone, while having almost no mind or reason; and likewise many

# On Abstinence, Book III.
->Kk 2<-

Likewise, there are those who, in cruelty, anger, and insolence, surpass even the most horrible wild beasts—murderers of parents, the wicked, and tyrants. Regarding these men, we assert that we have a right <note>original: "ius"; here meaning a legal or moral standing to judge or punish</note> to act against them. But regarding the ox that plows, the dog that lives in our home, and the flocks that nourish us with milk and clothe us with their wool, can we say we have no right of justice?

§ 20. But that argument of Chrysippus <note>A famous Stoic philosopher who argued animals were made solely for human use</note> is likely persuasive to those men: that we were made for our own sake and for the sake of the gods, but all other animals were made by the gods for our sake. Thus, horses were made to carry out war alongside us, and dogs to hunt with us; leopards, bears, and lions were made to provide us with manly exercise. As for the pig—

<column-break/>

—again, those who have surpassed the most fearsome of beasts in rawness, temper, and greed: child-killers and parricides, <gloss>2</gloss> tyrants and the servants of kings. Toward these men, we <gloss>3</gloss> think we have a standing; but toward the plowing ox, the companion dog, and the livestock that nourish us with milk <gloss>4</gloss> and adorn us with their fleece, how is it not the height of irrationality to say we have no bond of justice?

§ 20. But by Zeus, that point of Chrysippus might be persuasive: that the gods made us for ourselves and for one another, but made the animals for us—horses to fight alongside us, dogs to hunt with us, and panthers, <gloss>1</gloss> bears, and lions for the practice of courage. And the <gloss>2</gloss> pig, <gloss>3</gloss> [was born for nothing else but to be sacrificed...]

---

<column-break/>

<gloss>2. Tyrants and the servants of kings.]</gloss> These things ought to be explained according to the custom of those who, living in liberty, held the name of "king" in hatred. For since free kingdoms easily devolved into tyranny, they attacked that vice as if it were inherent to kingship. Hence the phrases *to live like a king* or *to act kingly and cruelly* and similar terms among the Latins; by the word "king," lack of self-control and tyranny itself are expressed, as *Schulting on Seneca's Controversies II. 15* shows. "King" and "tyrant" are usually joined for this same reason by *Demosthenes* and others.

<gloss>3. Think we have a standing.]</gloss> I have supplied the words "a right of justice" <note>original: "to dikaion"</note>. For the sense of the words demanded it. —VALENTIUS. Perhaps "think we have some kinship (or justice)." —REISKE. The *Lyons Edition* had already noted "justice" in the margin, and the matter itself speaks to the fact that the sense must be filled in that way.

<gloss>4. Adorn us with their fleece.]</gloss> The word *thremmata* <note>Greek for "nurslings" or "creatures"</note> denotes *livestock* in this passage; those who strive to assert the same meaning in the *Gospel of John 4:12* use this. Compare *Wetsten*: I agree with those who understand it there as *domestic animals*.

<gloss>1. And bears.]</gloss> In the *Leipzig Manuscript*, it was written *arkous* by the first hand, which a more recent hand corrected to *arktous*. He could have skipped that effort, for *arkos* was used no less than *arktos*. —REISKE. The *Meermann manuscript* also gives *arkous*.

<gloss>2. The pig — was born for nothing else but to be sacrificed.]</gloss> A little differently below: *the pig was born by nature for slaughter and being eaten.* Above, however, in *I. 14*: *nor is it useful for anything else but food.* Here the animal is said to be born for the sake of sacrifices. *Ovid, Metamorphoses XV. 111*:
> ...and the pig is thought to be
> the first victim to have deserved to die.

Elegantly, *Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies II. p. 405 D.*: "It is said, at least, that one of the philosophers, etymologizing the word for pig (*hys*), said it was so named as being fit only for sacrifice (*thysis*) and slaughter." *Varro, On Agriculture II, 4*: "The pig is called *hys* in Greek, formerly called *thys*... for the beginning of sacrificing seems to have first been taken from the swine species." Where for *thyfus* I rewrite *thys* following Clement. Nor do I doubt that the Philosopher whom *Clement* mentions, and whom *Scaliger* says he does not know in his notes on *Varro*, is *Cleanthes*, whose testimony will be produced immediately. Regarding pigs, *Aesop* speaks charmingly...

# PORPHYRY

For in this matter <note>referring to the pig</note> lies the most pleasant of favors; it was created for no other reason than to be sacrificed, and God mixed the soul into its flesh like a dash of salt, engineering a tasty dish for us. And so that we might have an abundance of broth and side-dishes, he provided all kinds of oysters, and purple-fish, and sea-nettles <note>anemones or jellyfish</note>, and various kinds of birds—not from any other source, but as if he had turned a great part of himself toward these sweet cravings, surpassing even wet-nurses in his care, and thickening this earthly place with pleasures and enjoyments. If these ideas seem to anyone to possess any probability or to be fitting for a God, let him consider what he will say in response to that argument—

<column-break/>

indeed, for here truly consists the most delightful grace; it was made for no other purpose, but God mixed the soul into its flesh in place of salt, so that he might procure a relish for us. Indeed, so that we might have a wealth of broth and delicacies, he produced various kinds of oysters, and purples, and nettles, and diverse species of birds; nor did he prepare them for us from elsewhere, but as if he had converted a great part of himself here toward sweetness, and surpassing nurses with the allurements of seasonings, he filled the whole place around the earth with pleasures and delights. Does it seem then that these things have any probability in them, or suit God in any way? But let anyone see what [he would say] to—

---

<column-break/>

<margin>He used to say it "cried out the loudest," for they [swine] are aware of nothing else useful for themselves when they are dragged along, except for sacrifice. Found in Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies*, Book VII, page 718 B.</margin>

3. *For in this lies the most pleasant of favors.*] Namely, it has long been believed that the pig has meat more pleasant than others, as Aelian says in *On the Nature of Animals*, IX, 28. It is well known how insolently the Jews were once regarded because they abstained from swine's flesh. I will just add the saying of Antiochus to Eleazar: "For why do you loathe the eating of this animal's flesh, when Nature has granted it as most beautiful? For it seems foolish not to enjoy pleasures that are without reproach, and unjust to turn away from the favors of Nature." Found in Josephus, *On the Maccabees* <note>4 Maccabees</note>, chapter 5.

4. *Mixed the soul in like salt.*] A saying of Cleanthes <note>Stoic philosopher</note>, that they have a soul instead of salt so that the meat does not rot; found in Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies*, VII, p. 718 B. "The soul was given to that beast for salt, lest it should putrefy," as Cicero says in the passage cited there by Sylburg, and Rittershusius in his notes on Porphyry’s *Life of Pythagoras*, I.

5. *And sea-nettles.*] This is better than the spelling used by others, *akaluphe*. See John Alberti on Hesychius under the letter V.

<column-break/>

6. *Not from any other source.*] This passage is sound, although it is a little obscure. "Not from any other source" is the same as "not from any other cause." *Not for any other reason, but as if he had contributed a great part of himself to this place.* That is, as if God had voluntarily contributed a great part of his own cares here, and in forming this universe, he had looked primarily to this: that he might supply man with the greatest possible abundance of pleasures. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>.

7. *Turning toward sweet cravings.*] I punctuate it thus: "turning toward sweet cravings, surpassing the wet-nurses" in his zeal to gratify our minds by bringing in the sweetness of things. Presently, "surpassing" <note>original: *hyperbalomenos*</note> is in the aorist tense. <term>REISKE</term>. On the contrary, I would prefer "nourishing" <note>original: *threp-sas* instead of *trep-sas*</note>, which also pleased the famous <term>ABRESCH</term>. These words are often confused due to the similarity of the letters.

8. *Will say to that argument.*] Plato in the *Sophist*, page 168: "One must consider what he will answer to the question asked." The expression seems to be taken from legal language.

# On Abstinence, Book III.

...let him answer that reasoning of Carneades <note>A skeptical philosopher known for challenging the dogmatism of the Stoics.</note>. He says that every single thing produced by nature, when it attains the end for which it was naturally made, attains its "utility." However, "utility" must be understood in a more common sense than the "good use" <note>original: *euchrestia*</note> which those men <note>The Stoics</note> name it. Now, the pig was made for this purpose: to be slaughtered and eaten. Therefore, when the pig is eaten, it attains its own end and is affected by utility. But if God produced animals for the use of men, for what use shall we have flies, mosquitoes, bats, beetles, scorpions, and vipers? Some of these are foul to the sight, filthy to the touch, intolerable in smell, and unpleasant and horrific in voice; others are altogether destructive—

<column-break/>

—the argument which Carneades used to speak. Each of the things born of nature, whenever it happens upon the end toward which it is by nature inclined and born, is benefited. One must listen to the more common sense of "benefit" <note>original: *opheleia*</note> rather than that which these men call "good use" <note>original: *euchrestia*</note>. For the pig is born by nature for the purpose of being slaughtered and devoured; and by suffering this, it happens upon that for which it was naturally inclined and is benefited. And indeed, if God has engineered animals for the use of humans, what use shall we make of flies, mosquitoes, bats, beetles, scorpions, and vipers? Of which some are hideous to see, and foul to touch, and hard to bear according to their smells, and sound terrible and unpleasant. Others are outright ruinous to those—

---

->**Notes**<-

...concerning those who respond to the arguments of an adversary, or have nothing they can oppose to them. *Lucian: in Jupiter the Tragedian:* "What then will you say to these things?" This is exactly the same formula (as Dr. *Marleus* opportunely contended regarding this passage) as that used by *St. Paul in Romans 8:31:* "What then shall we say to these things?" Where, as it seems, that Illustrious Man <note>referring to a previous commentator</note> wrongly wished to translate the word *pros* as "concerning," which it denotes here no more than in the passage he adduces *from the Epistle to the Hebrews 4:3.* There I understand it as referring to those who plead a case before a judge, as in *Dionysius of Halicarnassus VI. p. 374:* "The speech becomes necessary for me *to* [before] the people." Similar to our expression is also that of *Julian: to Themistius p. 256. B:* "To which it must be said." A little before, instead of "to whom," the Leipzig Manuscript has "in what way," and after "it seems" it omits "something." Both are poor readings.

9. **The benefit which they call good use.** Better, the celebrated *Abresch* says: "the matter of benefit." The Stoics used to call middle things <note>Things neither good nor evil in themselves</note> "useful" or "serviceable," but not "beneficial." *See Galen: to Antoninus VI, 45.*

10. **But the pig.** Perhaps "The pig indeed." <note>original: *he de* vs *he de*</note> *But if therefore the pig.* This is the beginning of a refutation led by the "reduction to absurdity." He concludes thus: if that which Carneades said is true, and if it is further true what you affirm—that animals were created for your sake—it will follow that it is expedient for the pig to be slaughtered; but this is absurd, therefore your decree is false. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a famous 18th-century German scholar.</note>

11. **What use shall we make of flies, etc.** *Jerome: Against Jovinian II, 6:* "For if everything that moves and lives was made for eating, let them answer me why there are elephants, lions, bears, leopards, wolves: why vipers, scorpions, bedbugs, mosquitoes, and fleas: why the vulture, the eagle... who among us ever ate a lion, a viper, a vulture, a stork, a kite, or the little worms crawling on the shores?"

12. **Ruinous to those who happen upon them.** To those who encounter them. "And venomous spiders" in the nominative case because of the following—

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from the previous section regarding the relationship between humans and animals, specifically challenging the Stoic view that all creatures were made solely for human benefit.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

to those who happen upon them. Regarding whales, sawfish, and other sea monsters—of which Homer says the loud-moaning Amphitrite <note>A Greek sea goddess, representing the sea itself.</note> feeds ten thousand—why has the Creator <note>original: "Demiurge," the divine craftsman of the universe.</note> not taught us in what way they have become useful to nature? But if they say that not all things were created for us and for our sake, then besides the fact that this distinction is full of confusion and obscurity, we do not even escape acting unjustly when we attack and harmfully use those things which were not made for us, but which—just like us—were brought into being according to the laws of nature. I pass over the fact that if we define "what is for us" by its usefulness, we would have to admit that we ourselves were created for the sake of the most deadly animals, such as crocodiles, whales, and dragons <note>original: "dracones," likely referring to large serpents or pythons.</note>. For we derive absolutely no benefit from them; instead, they seize and destroy any humans who happen to cross their path, using them for food—acting no more cruelly in this regard than—

<column-break/>

—those who happen upon them. What then? They behave just as we do, except that it is actual want and hunger that leads them to this injustice <note>original: "iniustitiam"; referring to the predatory behavior of wild animals</note>. We, however, out of insolence and luxury, often kill most animals for sport in theaters and during hunts. From this very habit, those who first dared to do such things strengthened the murderous, wild, and cruel instincts within us; likewise, they stripped away much of our gentleness. For habit has a wonderful power to lead a person further along in those affections which gradually take root.

<meta>This page continues a philosophical discussion regarding the nature of the soul and the balance of opposites in nature, specifically addressing the "irrational" element. The text presents a Greek passage from Porphyry (quoting Plutarch) alongside a Latin translation and philological commentary.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...that the irrational exists as an opposite and a counterpart. They claim that among so many pairings of opposites, this one alone should not be left incomplete or "maimed" <note>original: *πεπηρωμένην* (peperomenen) - meaning mutilated or defective</note>. As if we did not grant this, or could not point out many irrational things among existing beings! For there is surely a great and abundant amount of it in everything that lacks a soul, and we require no other opposite for the "rational." Rather, everything that is inanimate—being immediately without reason or intellect—stands opposed to that which possesses a soul, reason, and thought. Even if someone demands that it is not nature in general, but specifically *animated* nature that must have one part capable of imagination and another incapable of it, or one part capable of sensation and another devoid of it—so that nature might hold these opposing states and conditions <note>original: *ποιήσεις* (poieseis) - here referring to qualities or "makings" of a thing</note> in balance within the same genus—this would surely be absurd. For it is absurd to seek a part of the animated world that possesses sensation and another that is insensate, and—

<column-break/>

—that the irrational exists as an opposite, and they assert that this pairing of opposites must not be left defective. As if we were to deny this, or failed to show that many irrational things are found in the world. For a great and copious irrational force presents itself in all things that lack a soul: so that nothing else from any other source need be sought to oppose the rational. Since indeed everything inanimate, being immediately devoid of reason and mind, is opposed to that which is endowed with reason and mind. Even if there were someone who judged that it is not nature in common, but specifically animated nature, which should have one part endowed with imagination and another lacking it, and one part sensible and another insensible: so that nature might maintain the oppositions of these habits and privations as if in equilibrium within the same genus: this is certainly absurd. Indeed, he would be absurd who wished for one part of animated beings to be sensible and another insensible.

1. I interpose the word *not* <note>original: *μὴ* (me)</note> by conjecture. <term>VALENT.</term> <note>Valentinus, a previous editor</note> Nay, indeed, these preceding words are already those of <term>Plutarch</term>. I said so immediately.

2. *And maimed.*] Thus correctly. And so it is in <term>Plutarch</term>: previously it was incorrectly read as *filled* <note>original: *πεπληρωμένην* (pepleromenen)</note>. Rightly, therefore, <term>D'Orville</term> also restored this in our author: see his notes on *Chariton II, 9*, where there is more on this word.

3. *Or many irrational...*] <term>VALENT.</term> interposed the word *not*, as did <term>Fogerolles</term> before him: <term>Plutarch</term> also suggests this. The repetition of the same letter deceived the scribe, unless we think that *not* <note>original: *μὴ*</note> was originally written instead of *or* <note>original: *ἢ*</note>.

<column-break/>

4. *But the animated nature...*] Previously it was read as *innate* <note>original: *ἔμφυτον* (emphuton)</note>, but that has now been corrected. <term>Plutarch</term> has it in a slightly different way: *If someone demands that Nature not be mutilated, but that animated Nature...*

5. *These and opposite...*] The Florence edition and the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts read *to these*. <term>VALENT.</term> rightly restored *these* <note>original: *ταύτας*</note> from <term>Plutarch</term>. For *conditions* <note>original: *ποιήσεις*</note> the same editor suggests *privations* <note>original: *σερήσεις*</note>, which <term>Reiske</term> preferred; they commonly call these "qualifications" in a barbaric [Scholastic] style. Thus, no one can justly demand that among living beings, one should be granted to be rational and another irrational—especially when arguing against those men who believe that nothing partakes of sensation which does not also partake of intelligence <note>original: "intelligentiae"</note>; and that there is no animal that does not also possess some form of opinion and reasoning. This is because every sensation and every impulse exists according to nature. For Nature—which they rightly say does all things for the sake of something and toward some end—did not make the animal endowed with sensation merely so that it might simply experience and feel; rather, since many things are suitable and advantageous to it, and many are foreign <note>or harmful</note>, it could not exist for even a brief moment unless it had learned to avoid the latter and join itself to the former. Nature therefore bestowed the knowledge of both upon each creature by providing sensation in a similar manner. Those things which follow from sensation are the pursuit and grasping of useful things, as well as the repelling and fleeing of destructive and painful things.

# PORPHYRY

->**On Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

...seeing, there is no <gloss>10</gloss> means for it to be present in those who are not naturally disposed to reason, judge, and pay attention. For if you entirely take away expectation, memory, <gloss>11</gloss> purpose, preparation, hope, fear, desire, and grief, then there is no benefit from the eyes being present, nor the ears, nor any sense or imagination; if the faculty that makes use of them is not present, it would be better to be rid of them than to labor, grieve, feel pain, <gloss>12</gloss> and try to ward these things off when that faculty is absent. Indeed, there is an argument by Strato the Physicist <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Peripatetic philosopher known for his focus on natural science</note> demonstrating that it is not possible to perceive at all without the act of thinking. Often, letters <gloss>13</gloss> passing before our sight and words falling upon our hearing escape our notice and elude us when our mind is occupied with other things. Then later it returns...

<column-break/>

...means of escape can in no way be present, except in those things which are so constituted by nature that they are able to reason, judge, remember, and turn their attention. For those from whom you have entirely snatched away expectation, memory, attention, preparation, hope, fear, desire, and indignation, you will have left no use for the eyes, nor the ears, nor any of the other senses that are present. Indeed, it would be better to lack all sense and imagination if they have nothing that makes use of them, than to toil and suffer and have no ability to drive away these troubles. Furthermore, there is the reasoning of Strato the physicist, by which he demonstrates that no one can perceive anything at all without intelligence. For both letters meeting the eyes and speeches falling upon the ears are frequently accustomed to remain hidden from us and escape us when we have the mind intent on something else.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the rational capacities of animals, specifically focusing on memory, preparation, and conceptual thought. It draws heavily on Stoic terminology and compares readings with Plutarch.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

Once perception has internalised the difference between what is familiar and what is foreign, and has departed from the immediate experience, what is it that then remembers? It is that which fears things that cause pain, longs for things that are beneficial, and, when they are not present, devises ways for them to be provided. It prepares points of attack, refuges, <gloss>1</gloss> and snares; and again, it provides ways for those who have been caught to escape their attackers. Or <gloss>2</gloss> do not even those [the Stoics] <note>Porphyry is likely referring to Stoic philosophers, who often denied reason to animals while using these very technical terms.</note> wear us out by repeating these things in their introductions at every turn? They define "purpose" as the <gloss>3</gloss> marking of a completion; "approach" as an impulse before an impulse; "preparation" as an action before an action; and "memory" as the comprehension of a past proposition, the presence of which was first grasped by perception. For there is nothing among these things that is not rational, and they all belong to all living beings. Just as, of course, <gloss>4</gloss> is the case regarding "intellections" <note>original: *noeseis* (νοήσεις) — formal acts of the intellect.</note>, which, when stored away, are called "conceptions" —

<column-break/>

— and when they are set in motion and agitated, they are called "discursive thoughts" <note>original: *dianoeseis* (διανοήσεις) — the process of reasoning from one point to another.</note>. When a creature works out the difference between the advantageous and the alien, it already possesses the faculty of memory. It fears those things that bring trouble and desires useful things even when they are absent, taking care that they might be present. It prepares a method for pursuing and hunting, and conversely, for fleeing and avoiding those things which have attacked. Indeed, they themselves [the Stoics] also hammer these points home everywhere in their introductions to the point of boredom. They define "purpose" as the seal of perfection; "aggression" as the incitement before the incitement; "preparation" as the action before the action; and "memory" as the comprehension of a past thing which the sense had perceived as present. Truly, there is none of these things which is not rational, and all are present in all animals. This is clearly what they do regarding intellections, which, when stored, they call *conceptions* <note>original: *ennoias* (ἐννοίας) — innate or stored ideas.</note>, and while they are being moved and driven, they call *discursive thoughts*.

---

<margin>1. **And snares.** ---] Instead of "and snares, and again for those caught, escapes from attackers," the text in Plutarch reads: "and snares, and again for those about to be caught, and escapes from attackers." If Porphyry’s reading is better, I would rather translate it as --- *and nets, and again for themselves escapes from those who have captured them.* VALENTINI. <note>Federico Valentini, a 16th-century editor.</note> Nay, the reading of Plutarch is not only much better, but the only true one. Therefore, I did not hesitate to restore it to the "received text." It happened here, as we have seen happen often above, that two words *au tois* [again for them] were wrongly merged into one, *autois* [themselves]. Regarding the formula "again," we spoke at Book II, 40.</margin>
<margin>2. **Or do not even those wear us out.**] *Plutarch* reads "and these things indeed." But there some manuscripts read "and yet." And so Reiske <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German philologist.</note> restored it in his *Observations*, p. 548. Furthermore, *apoknaiein* means to *blunt* someone with annoying chatter, which the Greeks also call "wearing out the ears" or "the hearing." The use of the word was very skillfully explained by the celebrated Ruhnken <note>David Ruhnken (1723–1798), a head librarian and scholar at Leiden.</note> in his notes on *Timaeus' Lexicon*, p. 30, not forgetting our author, or rather Plutarch.</margin>
<margin>3. **The marking of a completion.**] Reiske writes "upon completion" as two words in his *Observations on Plutarch*, p. 548. I prefer "of completion" as one word. The old editions held it thus, and the Meerman manuscript alone; Valentini had pulled it apart.</margin>
<margin>4. **And regarding intellections.**] *Plutarch* reads "and the things regarding intellections," which Valentini and Reiske followed—</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book III.

->**On Abstinence, Book III.**<-

They call these "inclinations," or rather, "thoughts." Since they commonly admit that all passions are both corrupt natures and opinions, it is a wonder how they fail to notice many actions and movements of anger, fear, and—by Zeus—envy and jealousy in wild animals. They themselves punish dogs and horses when they do wrong, certainly not in vain, but for the sake of correction, instilling a distress through pain in them which we call *repentance* <note>original: "μετάνοιαν" (metanoia). The author argues that if animals can feel regret or learn from punishment, they possess a form of reason.</note>. Likewise, since the name for pleasure experienced through the ears is "enchantment," and that through the eyes is "sorcery," they are accustomed to use both upon animals. For stags and horses are enchanted by pipes and flutes. Likewise, they call crabs out of their hiding places by playing upon pipes. They even assert that the *thrissa* <note>A species of shad or similar fish believed in antiquity to be attracted by music and dancing.</note> fish emerges from its hollows at the sound of singing. Yet those who speak quite foolishly about these matters claim that animals neither feel joy, nor

anger <note>The Greek text on the right column mirrors the Latin on the left, providing the source for the translation above.</note>.

*Reiske preferred "just as certainly happens also concerning thoughts."* <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774) was a noted German physician and philologist who provided many emendations to classical texts.</note>

5. *Commonly corrupt natures ---]* Plutarch should be corrected here, for he has "judgments" instead of "natures." Reiske preferred "which commonly" in his *Critical Observations*, page 548. Previously, the text read "admitting" (in the accusative case), but Fogerolles had already corrected it. It remains thus, however, in the Leipzig Manuscript. Meermann is correct.

6. *How they fail to notice in animals]* More fully in Plutarch: "that they indeed overlook in animals." Reiske preferred "what things they indeed overlook." Presently in Plutarch: "yes, by Zeus, envy and jealousy."

7. *That which is through ---]* The author often cited

above [writes] "that which is through the ears... that which is through the eyes," but there it should be remodeled from our text to "the one... the other." 9. *Playing upon pipes ---]* Plutarch has "forcing them with flutes." The same author says "at the singing and clapping of the *thrissa* fish." I believe our author left it as "singing."

# PORPHYRY

Neither to fear, nor to prepare, nor to remember, but they say that the bee "as if" remembers, the swallow "as if" prepares, the lion "as if" grows angry, and the deer "as if" fears. I do not know how those who say this would respond to someone who claimed that animals do not see or hear, but "as if" see and "as if" hear; that they do not emit a voice, but "as if" emit a voice; and that they do not live at all, but "as if" live. For a fair-minded listener would easily perceive that these latter claims are no more contrary to evident reality than the former. # On Abstinence, Book III.

->**On Abstinence, Book III.**<-

...perfection, no appetite: I would certainly wonder why nature gave a beginning to those things which could not reach any end. But even to those very men <note>The Stoic philosophers, who argued that animals lack reason.</note> this does not seem at all absurd; for although they establish that love toward offspring is the beginning of society and justice in us, and they see that this love is powerful in other living creatures, they nevertheless judge that there is no justice or society shared with them. Furthermore, although mules lack none of the reproductive organs—for they have both a penis and a womb and use these with pleasure—they nevertheless do not achieve the end of generation <note>Mules are sterile, yet possess the biological drives and organs for reproduction; Porphyry uses this as an analogy for "imperfect" reason.</note>. In addition to this, does it not seem ridiculous if they say that the likes of Socrates, Plato, and Zeno behave no better than any common slave, but are in a similar way unwise, intemperate, and unjust; and then, because beasts do not conduct themselves exactly and exquisitely according to virtue, they ascribe this to a total privation <note>A complete lack of the faculty.</note>, rather than to a depravity or weakness of reason?

<column-break/>

...of animals, neither a clear aim, nor progress, nor appetite, I would be at a loss as to how Nature gave the beginning to those unable to reach the end. Or rather, this does not even seem strange to those men. At any rate, while they posit that natural affection toward offspring <gloss>14</gloss> <note>original: "philostorgia"</note> is the beginning of society and justice among us, and they see it present in great and strong measure in the animals, they say they do not, and should not, have a share in justice. Mules are not deficient in any of the generative parts; for having both genitals and wombs and the use of these with pleasure, they do not reach the end of procreation. Consider it another way: is it not ridiculous to claim that the likes of Socrates, Plato, and Zeno <gloss>15</gloss> are involved in a condition no lighter than that of any chance slave, but are equally foolish, licentious, and unjust, and then to blame the lack of purity and precision toward virtue in the beasts as a privation, rather than a defect...

...again with the partridges <note>original: "περδίκων"</note>. # On Abstinence, Book III.

-> Mm 2 <-

[We do not say that] a lion [is slower] than a deer. 12. For just as among things that lack all motion, one cannot be said to be slower than another, nor among those that have no voice can one be said to have a more slender voice than another: so too, nothing is called more cowardly, or more sluggish, or more intemperate where the faculty of understanding is not present in all by nature. <note>The author argues that you cannot rank things (like "slower" or "smarter") unless they possess the basic quality being measured.</note> Since this faculty is present in different beings in different ways—either more or less—it produces the differences we observe among animals. In this matter, it should cause us no wonder that man excels other animals by such a great interval in teachability, cleverness, and other things pertaining to justice and social life. For many of those animals also far surpass all men in body size and speed, as well as in sharpness of sight and keenness of hearing. Yet man is not therefore considered deaf, or blind, or weak. We also run, though more slowly than deer; and we also see, though not as—

§ 24. If many things had not already been collected and stated by many authors, I could bring forward ten thousand examples to demonstrate <margin>1</margin> the natural intelligence of animals. But this further point must be considered: it seems that whatever is naturally capable of receiving a certain state or power according to nature <margin>2</margin> is also capable of falling into a state that is contrary to nature, whether through being maimed or diseased. For instance, the eye can fall into blindness, the leg into lameness, and the tongue into stammering—but nothing else can. For there is no such thing as blindness in that which is not naturally intended to see, nor lameness in that which is not naturally intended to walk, <margin>3</margin> nor stammering

as acute as hawks: nor are we entirely deprived of strength and size by nature, although if we are compared to the elephant and the camel, we seem to be nothing in these matters. In a similar way, therefore, we must not say that beasts think and understand nothing at all, and are endowed with no reason, because they understand more dully and think worse than we do; but rather that they themselves possess it, though weak and troubled, just like a dim and disturbed eye.

§ 24. There are innumerable things which I could produce in proof of the character of animals, had not many things been previously collected and handed down to memory by many people on this subject. Besides that, this is worthy of consideration: It seems to belong to the same part or faculty which receives something according to nature, that it can also fall into that which is contrary to nature, either being impaired or sick. Just as the eye may run into blindness, the leg into lameness, and the tongue into stammering, for nothing else can do so. # On Abstinence, Book III.

<columns>2</columns>

->**Translation from the Latin**<-

We say that those born of the same father and mother are by nature related to one another. Therefore, we shall also say that those procreated from the same ancestors are related; likewise, the citizens of the same city are related because they share the same land and a mutual society with one another. For we do not consider these people to have a kinship among themselves simply because they were born of the same parents, unless perhaps some of the first progenitors were the same authors of their race, or descended from the same ones. Thus, indeed, we assert that Greek is related to Greek, and barbarian to barbarian, and likewise all men are related to one another, for one of two reasons: either because they are from the same ancestors, or because they share a fellowship of nourishment, customs, and the instruction of their whole life. And in this way, we establish that all men are related. Furthermore, the principles of the bodies of all animals are by nature the same. I do not think this should be understood regarding the primary elements—for plants also consist of these—but

<column-break/>

->**Translation from the Greek**<-

of the father and mother, we say they are by nature kin to one another; and therefore, we also consider those sown from the same ancestors to be kin to one another, and indeed our fellow citizens, by the fact of sharing the land and social intercourse with one another. $^2$ For we do not judge such people to be kin to one another because they were born from the same parents at that time, unless perhaps some of the first ancestors $^3$ were themselves the leaders of the race, or from the same ones. And so I think both the Greek to the Greek, and the barbarian to the barbarian, and all $^4$ men are kin and related to one another for one of two reasons: either by being from the same ancestors, or by sharing in food and customs and the same kind of life. In this way, we also place all men as kin to one another. And indeed, the principles of the bodies for all animals are by nature the same. I say this not by referring back to the first elements. $^5$ For from these even plants are made. But...

If one abstains from all living beings, even if they contribute nothing to one's own society, he will be much more careful to avoid inflicting harm upon those of his own kind. # On Abstinence, Book III.

->**On Abstinence from Animal Food**<-

It happens that we are made like unto God, so far as is possible, when innocence <note>original: "innocentia"; the Greek "τὸ ἀβλαβὲς" implies a state of doing no harm or being harmless</note> is preserved toward all things. In the same way, therefore, that a man led by his passions practices innocence only toward his children and his wife, while despising and harming all others—inasmuch as the irrational part of his soul dominates him and he is excited by and marvels at mortal things—so the man who is guided by reason conducts himself innocently toward his fellow citizens, and even more toward strangers and all mankind. Because he keeps his irrational faculty in subjection, he is more rational and more divine than the former man. Thus, he who does not limit the boundaries of innocence to humans alone, but extends them even to the other animals, is more like unto God; and if he were able to extend them even unto plants, he would preserve that image and likeness even further. Because he is unable to do so, from this point the deficiency of our nature—

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek source text for the Latin passage above</note>
—to be made like unto God, which is the ultimate goal, as much as is possible, harmlessness is preserved in all things. In the same way, then, as the man led by passions is harmless only toward his children and wife, but is contemptuous and grasping toward others—as the irrational part prevails within him, he is moved toward mortal things and is struck with awe by them—but the man led by reason maintains harmlessness toward the citizen, and even more toward strangers, and toward all men, having his irrationality in subjection; he is more rational than those others, and for these reasons more divine. Thus, he who has not only established harmlessness among men, but has extended it also to the other living beings, is more like God; and if it were possible even as far as plants, he would preserve the image even more. But if not, at least from this point the [deficiency] of nature—

# PORPHYRY

Our deficiency <note>original: ἐλάττωμα (elattoma) - a falling short or defect</note> is the source of that which was lamented by the ancients: that we are born from such strifes and contentions <note>original: ἐρίδων... νεικέων (eridon... neikeon)</note>, because we are unable to preserve the divine, pure, and harmless state in all things. For we were not without needs in all respects; the cause of this is our birth <note>original: γένεσις (genesis)</note> and our existence in a state of poverty, once the flow of abundance <note>original: πόρου (porou) - referring to 'Poros' or Plenty</note> had ebbed away. Now, poverty acquires its salvation and the order through which it receives its being from external things. Therefore, whoever requires more external things is more firmly nailed to poverty. And by as much as one is in need of more things, by so much is he without a share of God and a housemate to poverty. For that which is like God possesses true wealth immediately by virtue of that likeness. No one who is wealthy and in need of nothing commits injustice; for as long as he acts unjustly, even if he possesses all riches, and even if—

<column-break/>

the defect is perceived: hence the misery deplored by the ancients, that we are sprung from such adverse and discordant strifes, so that we lack the power to maintain divinity, incorruptibility, and innocence in all things. For we have not been without any want in all matters. The cause of this was our generation: and because, when plenty had already flowed away, we were established in want. Moreover, want acquires for itself safety and the adornment from which we received our being from foreign sources. He, therefore, who requires more external things, is more glued to want. And the more things anyone requires, the further he is from God, and the more addicted to want. For he who is like God, possesses true riches continually from that likeness. But no one who is rich, and in need of nothing, brings injury upon anyone. For as long as he does injury, even if he abounds in all money,

# On Abstinence, Book III.

-> O o <-

Even if a man possesses all the acres of the earth, since he is addicted to want, he is without doubt poor; and for that reason he is also unjust, and impious, and estranged from God, and finally liable to every vice. The nature of this vice was introduced by the soul’s sliding into matter <note>original: "delapsio animae in materiam"</note> through the deprivation of the Good. Therefore, all things are trifles as long as one has wandered from the first principle; likewise, every person is in need of all things as long as they do not look toward fullness <note>The Latin uses "satietatem" (satiety/fullness), translating the Greek "koron."</note>; and one indulges the mortality of their own nature as long as they do not truly know themselves. Moreover, injustice is quite skilled at employing persuasion upon itself and at judging those who are held under its power, because it maintains a <unclear>familiarity</unclear> <unclear>habit</unclear> with its foster-children and associates.

<column-break/>

...all the plethra <note>A Greek unit of land measurement.</note> of the earth, he is poor, dwelling together with poverty. Because of these things, he is indeed unjust, godless, impious, and **12** liable to every wickedness. # PORPHYRIUS

Just as in the 16 choice of lives, the more accurate judge is the one who has gained experience of both, rather than the one who has experienced only one; so too, in the choices and avoidances of duties, the safer judge is the one who judges the lower from the higher vantage point, rather than the one who judges 17 what lies above from below. Consequently, the one who lives according to the mind <note>original: "κατὰ νοῦν" — referring to the higher intellect or rational soul</note> is a more accurate definer of what is to be chosen and what is not than the one who lives according to irrationality; for the former has also passed through irrationality, having associated with it from the beginning. But the one who is inexperienced in the things of the mind persuades those like himself, 18 like a child talking nonsense among children. "But if everyone," they say, "were persuaded by these arguments, 19 what would become of us?" 20 Is it not clear that we would be happy, with injustice being banished from among men, and justice being practiced—

<column-break/>

—dwelling with its own people with pleasure. Indeed, just as in the choices of lives he is accustomed to judge more rightly who is skilled in both, rather than he who has been experienced in only one: so also, in the choices and avoidances of those things which are owed, the judgment of him is more certain who discerns the lower from the higher, than he who discerns from the lower those things which are placed above. Wherefore he who has established his life from the mind and intellect can more rightly and exquisitely pre-define those things which are to be sought, or avoided, than he who has been accustomed to live from the irrational faculty. For the former has indeed also passed through the irrational life, inasmuch as he was entwined with it from the beginning: but the latter, since he is unskilled in those things which proceed from the mind, being a child playing among children like himself, easily persuades them of everything. "But if all," they say, "should assent to these reasons, what [benefit] would there be for us then—"

---

<margin>he had corrected. I would change nothing, since all agree on *to judge* <note>original: "δικάζειν"</note>. And the following things confirm this, since he opposes the fairer judge, who established his life from the mind and intellect, and that one, who was accustomed to act from the irrational faculty. *To judge those things...* <note>original: "δικάζειν τοὺς ὑ. α. σ."</note> is therefore *to speak the law, to have subjects under oneself*.</margin>

16. *Choice of lives.* <note>original: "Βίων αἱρέσεσιν"</note>] *The kinds into which lives were divided* is what *Plutarch* calls them in *Volume I, page 91, C.* Indeed, *life* <note>original: "βίος"</note> signifies the kind and manner of living. We have seen this above; add *Hemsterhuis on Pollux IX, 33.*

17. *The things lying before.* <note>original: "Τὰ προκείμενα"</note>] Instead of *lying before*, I would prefer *lying above* <note>original: "ὑπερκείμενα"</note>, so that it may be opposed to *from below*. VALENTIUS. Recently, *Reiskius* desired *to be chosen* <note>original: "αἱρετέον"</note> instead of the common *chosen* <note>original: "αἱρετὸν"</note>.

18. *A child talking nonsense among children.* <note>original: "Παῖς ἐν παισὶ φλυαρῶν"</note>] Elegantly said. *Child* <note>original: "παῖς"</note> everywhere pertains to the character, and is applied to those who are children in mind, as words of this kind are accustomed to be used in both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note>. I add nothing to those things which the celebrated *Alberti* noted *on Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians IV, 14.*

19. *What will be for us?* <note>original: "Τί ἡμῖν ἔσται"</note>] This too is a beautiful way of speaking. *What reward shall we bring back?* exactly as *Peter* says, *what then shall be for us?* in the *Gospel of Matthew, chapter XIX, 27*, where see *Kypkius*, and join to him *Raphel on Mark XI, 24.*

But just as *Aristides* asserts that Justice and modesty returned to men during the reign of Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, the very same thing is clearly going to happen—

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book III of Porphyry’s "On Abstinence from Animal Food."
