# On Abstinence, Book III.

->**Page 291**<-

...what will happen? Without a doubt, this: that we shall be happy. For just as injustice is to be banished far from men, so shall justice dwell among us, even as it does in heaven. But as things stand now, it is just as if the **Danaids** <note>In Greek mythology, the fifty daughters of Danaus who were punished in Hades by having to forever carry water in leaky jars or sieves.</note> were to ask what kind of life they would lead if they were freed from that labor of drawing water in perforated jars. For people ask and doubt what would happen to us if we were to cease indulging our passions and desires—which all leak away—and instead settled for a life established in and for the sake of the necessities of life.

<column-break/>

...among us, just as in heaven. But now it is similar to as if the **Danaids** were at a loss as to what life they would live, having been delivered from the <gloss>21</gloss> service at the perforated jar by means of the sieve. For they are at a loss as to what will be, if we should stop piling things upon our passions and our desires, from which everything flows away <gloss>22</gloss> in an absence of evils, while we are content with <gloss>23</gloss> a life based on and for the sake of necessities.

---

Our author <note>Referring to Porphyry</note> means: if the human race could be brought back to a simple and harmless way of living. See: *Gataker on Marcus Aurelius* Book V. § 33.

21. **Regarding the perforated jar.**] A well-known fable. From this is derived the phrase "to draw water with a sieve" in *Theodoret's Sermon on Matter and the World*, p. 531; and "to draw into a perforated jar" in *Eunapius's Dialogues* I. p. 18. Others also call it a "worn-out" <note>original: "tetrimmenon"</note> jar, as the Illustrious **Wesseling** shows in his notes on *Diodorus Siculus* I, 97. But our author said "perforated" <note>original: "tetremenon"</note> jar following the example of his beloved **Plato** in the *Gorgias*, p. 336. D. Moreover, he took these ideas from **Plutarch**, Volume II, p. 160, as my very dear friend **Abresch** opportunely reminded me.

22. **In an absence of evils —**] The *Leipzig Manuscript* correctly gives "the [life]" and then "the necessary [life]," which I approve of so far as to read "and not beyond what is necessary." This whole [desire] perishes and vanishes when we lack evils (which one must necessarily endure when seeking a refined and sumptuous lifestyle), if we acquiesce to a life staying within the bounds of necessities—that is, only of necessary things, and on the condition that nothing superfluous is craved or sought out. I also wonder whether "inexperience" <note>original: "apeiria"</note> might be a better reading than "absence" <note>original: "aporia"</note>, as we are then free from the experience and knowledge of troubles. I myself would not claim that anything is missing after the word "evils." Finally, "and for the sake of necessities" could be defended, and the rest of the passage seen as sound, provided that in verse 20 "the" <note>original: "ton"</note> is admitted in place of "of the." We have said what a life "based on necessities" is: namely, one that rejoices in present

<column-break/>

necessities and is lived on the condition of being content with them. It remains to be said what a life "for the sake of necessities" is: it is surely that which labors only for the sake of procuring necessary things. <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a famous 18th-century German philologist.</note>. <term>Meermann</term> also reads "Necessary." I shall speak of this immediately.

**Of the evils, etc.**] It seemed that it ought to be read "of the beautiful things" <note>original: "ton kalon" instead of "ton kakon"</note>, and that this is the meaning of the passage: *We always try to fulfill our desires but in vain: because we do not seek the truly good things, which would fill the gaps and cracks of our soul better than those things which, among external matters, seem most necessary.* For I read "of those being content" <note>original: "stergonton"</note> instead of the [corrupt] "sergont." Those last words [in the previous edition] were absurd. The Illustrious **Reiske** excellently defends the common reading, and therefore I have restored "the" <note>original: "ton"</note> to its place, as **Fogerolles** had already emended it. **Felicianus** understood it no differently. Even so, I contend we must read "through an inexperience of beautiful things... our life of being content with necessities." Do not wonder why I have turned out so imperious: **Plutarch**, whom our author imitates here, says it in plainly the same words in the place cited above. From this, you should have no doubt about the restored "the." "Evil" <note>kakon</note> and "Beautiful/Good" <note>kalon</note> are often confused. We saw this already in Book I, § 9. **D'Orville** will give more examples in his notes on *Chariton* VIII, 4.

23. **Of us being content with a life.**] **Valentinus** absurdly wrote "segonton," although those words are sometimes confused with one another, as in *Diodorus Siculus* XI, 29. I have already noted that this is from Plutarch. To "be content with a life" is a phrase used like "to be content with present circumstances," "with fortune," and similar things, regarding which see **Wesseling** on *Diodorus* I. 1.

# PORPHYRY

"What then shall we do?" you ask, O man. Let us imitate the Golden Race <note>original: "χρυσοῦν γένος" — the first and best age of mankind in Greek mythology</note>; let us imitate those who have been set free. For with them, Shame, Indignation, and Justice walked together, because they were content with the fruits of the earth.

> For the grain-giving earth bore fruit for them
> Spontaneously, in great and plenteous abundance. <note>A quotation from Hesiod's *Works and Days*</note>

And those who have been set free now provide for themselves the very things they once provided while serving their masters. In no other way, then, shall you also—having been released from the slavery of the body and from the service to the passions caused by the body—nourish yourself. Just as you used to nourish that body in every way with external things, so now you shall nourish yourself in every way with internal things, justly reclaiming what is your own, and no longer taking away the property of others by force.

<column-break/>

...to cease indulging in disturbances and desires, from which all fruit flows away and perishes due to a lack of honorable things. What then are we to do, you ask? We shall imitate that Golden Age; we shall imitate those who have been asserted into liberty. For with them, Shame, Indignation, and Justice were familiar, because they were content with the fruits of the earth. *For the fertile Earth bore fruit for them of its own accord.* But those who have been gifted with liberty henceforth acquire for themselves those things which they previously prepared by ministering to their masters. In no other way shall you also—if you are freed from the slavery of the body and from that ministry which you exhibit to the passions—nourish yourself inwardly in various ways, just as you used to nourish that body outwardly. In this matter, your own things will justly be available to you, so that the things of others need no longer be taken by you through violence.

<margin>
See Gataker: on *Marcus Aurelius VI, 44*, who teaches that "to love" is used in the same sense in § 49. Eusebius in *Demonstratio Evangelica III, p. 119 B* says "having loved a hardy and laborious life."
</margin>

24. **Those who have been set free.**] "To set free" <note>original: "Ἐλευθεροῦν"</note> specifically means *to claim into liberty*, and is said of manumitted slaves. Our author [Porphyry] beautifully applied this from Plutarch to the liberty of the soul. Read the Learned Man <note>referring to a previous commentator</note> on those words of *John in the Gospel VIII, 32: "The truth shall set you free."*

25. **Shame and Indignation —**] He seems to be looking back at those words of Hesiod, whom Shame and Indignation <note>original: "Αἰδὼς καὶ Νέμεσις"</note> are said to have abandoned only in the Iron Age. *Works and Days, 198.* In this passage, Indignation and Justice are also well distinguished; for it is understood that this is not that "Nemesis" who was also called "Justice."

26. **For the fruit —**] *Hesiod: Works and Days, 117.*

<column-break/>

- - - - "and the grain-giving earth bore fruit." He uses this again in § 2 of the following book; see there.

27. **They provide in no other way.**] This is correct. *Without any doubt, without controversy, more certain than certainty.* Reiske, Fogerolles, and Valentinus had rashly corrected it to "for others." However, I have punctuated it differently than was previously done, as the major mark of distinction used to be placed after "in no other way." *Plutarch: "the things they used to do while serving their masters, these they now do for themselves and by themselves."* So the soul... if it should be released from service, etc.

28. **And you.**] An elegant formula, and therefore frequently used by others. See: *Markland on Maximus Tyrius, Dissertation XVII, 11*, who was not forgetful of this passage. Shortly after, instead of "you shall nourish him [the body]," the *Meerman manuscript* has "you shall nourish her [the soul]."

# PORPHYRY THE PHILOSOPHER

# PORPHYRY
## THE PHILOSOPHER
### ON ABSTINENCE FROM THE EATING OF ANIMALS
### *BOOK FOUR*

->SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT<-

*The fourth book is divided, like those preceding it, into three parts: the first of which contains the preface to Firmus Castricius <note>A student of Plotinus and friend of Porphyry to whom the work is dedicated</note>. The second part confirms, through the examples of the ancients, that abstinence from animals was practiced by great men—such as lawmakers, philosophers, and overseers of sacred rites—whereas, conversely, cruel and impious men utilized them for food. Examples of abstinence are drawn from the laws and customs of various nations: the Spartans (§ 3), the Egyptians (§ 6), the Jews (§ 11), the Syrians and Cyprians (§ 15), the Persians (§ 16), and the Cretan priests (§ 19). The exhortation which occupies the third place incites one toward chastity of the body, purity of the soul, and the sanctity of both.*

---

§ I. Against almost all the excuses of those who, in truth, for the sake of incontinence and pleasure—

<column-break/>

§ I. Against almost all the excuses of those who, in truth, for the sake of incontinence and licentiousness—

<note>The following section contains critical apparatus and commentary in two columns.</note>

1. *In truth.*] The *Leipzig Manuscript* gives "in truth indeed." Likewise in verse 8, it holds "the [practice] of meat-eating for them," with the rest omitted. It appears the passage is corrupt, which will be easily perceived by anyone attending to the phrase "in truth," to which no subsequent speech corresponds. It seems the author wrote to roughly this effect: "In truth indeed, for the sake of their own incontinence and licentiousness yielding to a friend... and having provided shameless excuses for meat-eating for themselves out of necessity." REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist known for his editions of Greek texts</note>. In truth indeed.

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

Since some admit the eating of flesh <note>original: "σαρκοφαγίαν" (sarkophagian) - literally "sarcophagy" or flesh-eating</note> for various reasons, yet shamelessly pretend they do so because of a physical need—attributing to our nature a greater deficiency than is actually the case—we have already answered them, O Castricius, in the preceding books. There remain, however, two specific questions still to be addressed. Of these, the promise of "utility" <note>The argument that eating meat is "useful" or "beneficial" for the body</note> most greatly deceives those whose judgment has been corrupted by pleasure. Furthermore, the claim that no wise man nor any nation has ever rejected this food leads listeners into a great injustice, due to their ignorance of true history. Intending to refute these claims, we shall now attempt to set forth the solutions regarding utility and the other remaining questions.

§ 2. Let us begin with the abstinence practiced by certain nations. Among these, the Greeks shall be brought forward first, as they are the most familiar witnesses of this matter. Therefore, from those who have written both briefly and accurately—

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

Among those who have accurately collected the history of Greek affairs is the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> Dicaearchus. In recounting the ancient life of Greece, he asserts that those early people—who by their antiquity stood closest to the gods, were of the best possible nature, and led such holy lives that their era was considered a "Golden Age" compared to our own, which is composed of adulterated and most wicked matter—were not accustomed to killing any animal. He says the poets also bear witness to this when they speak of that golden race of men: "To whom," as they say, "all good things were present, and the fruit was borne freely."

> The fertile earth bore much in lavish crops;
> They themselves, at peace and in quiet, 
> Enjoyed their own will amidst many blessings.

<column-break/>

Among those who have accurately collected the history of Greek affairs is also the Peripatetic <gloss>1</gloss> Dicaearchus, who, in describing the ancient life of Greece, [says] that the ancients, having been born near to the gods by nature, being the best by nature and having lived the best life, were considered a golden race when compared to those of today, who exist of a debased and most foul matter; [and] that they murdered no living thing. This is what the <gloss>2</gloss> poets represent <gloss>3</gloss> when they name it the golden race. "All good things," they say,

> Belonged to them, and the grain-giving earth bore fruit
> Spontaneously, both much and unstinting; and they, 
> Content and at peace, tended their works amidst many good things.

---

<columns>2</columns>

<gloss>1. Dicaearchus ---- the ancients, etc.</gloss> *Jerome: Against Jovinian, Book II, Chapter 13.* <note>original: "Hieron: II. Adv: Iovin: c. 13." Jerome was a Church Father who often quoted Porphyrius.</note> (In these books he expresses our author <note>Porphyrius</note> throughout, as has been said more often.) *Dicaearchus, in his books of Antiquities and his description of Greece, reports that under Saturn—that is, in the Golden Age—when the ground brought forth all things, no one ate meat, but everyone lived on the fruits and produce which the earth produced of its own accord.* Regarding Dicaearchus, of which name there were several, see *Suidas under the letter D, and Fabricius: Greek Library, Book III, Chapter 11.* Our author also praises him in the *Life of Pythagoras*, numbers 18 and 56, but there he seems to mean the books *On Lives*, which many confuse with the one he called *The Life of Greece*, mentioned here, of which a splendid fragment survives. See *Menagius on Diogenes Laertius III, 4,* who, in calling it a geographical book, perhaps confuses this work with Dicaearchus's geographical poem called *The Description of Greece*. Now, because *Varro, in On Agriculture II, 1,* excerpted the same things from Dicaearchus as our author, I ought to add them here: *It is necessary that human life descended by degrees from the highest memory to this age, as Dicaearchus writes; and the highest degree was the natural one, when men lived from those things which the earth brought forth untouched and of its own accord; from this life they descended into the second, the pastoral life, etc.*

<column-break/>

<gloss>2. The poets represent.]</gloss> The word "representing" <note>original: "παρισάντας"</note> is not in the *Leipzig Manuscript* from the ancient hand. For the person who, within the memory of our fathers, wrote "passing over" <note>original: "παρασάντας"</note> above the line, seems either to have been ignorant or to have forgotten the difference between "representing" and "passing over." I will not condemn "passing over," but it could be absent without damage to the meaning. For the word "which" <note>original: "ὃ"</note> often denotes the same as "wherefore." "Which" can also refer to "race." In either way of explaining, that word "representing" can be dispensed with. —REISKE. Shortly before, the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts erroneously had "debased" (plural) and "existing of the matter."

Explaining these matters, Dicaearchus says that life in the time of Saturn <note>The Roman name for Cronus, associated with the Golden Age</note> was of such a kind—if indeed we must accept that it truly existed and was not celebrated in vain. ...nutriments are produced: from which those people certainly kept their bodies perpetually purified. For they did not take in nourishment that was stronger than the nature of their bodies, but rather that which nature could easily master; nor did they take more than was moderate due to easy availability, but rather, for the most part, less than was sufficient due to scarcity. Furthermore, there were neither wars nor seditions among them, since there was no prize set out in their midst of such a kind that anyone would wish to undertake any contention to acquire it. Thus, the sum of their whole life was nothing other than leisure, and rest from providing for their necessities, health, peace, and friendship. Whence, to those of later generations who, because they had lusted after greater things, had fallen into many evils, a life of this kind deservedly appeared desirable. Moreover, the thinness of their diet, requiring no elaborate preparation, is sufficiently declared by what was said later: "Enough of the oak" <note>original: "ἅλις δρυὸς" (halis dryos). # On Abstinence, Book IV.

...they eventually descended into the labor of tilling the fields. And these are the matters which Dicaearchus <note>A student of Aristotle who wrote on the history of Greek civilization.</note> relates when recounting the ancient affairs of the Greeks, while he extols that blessed life of those ancients, to which indeed—no less than other virtues—abstinence from living creatures brought perfection. Whence there was no war in that age, since it was entirely free from all injustice. But afterward, together with the injustice toward animals, both war and the contention for having more <note>original: "plus habendi" / "πλεονεξία" (greed or graspingness)</note> crept in among them. For which reason I cannot sufficiently marvel, as they deserve, at the impudence of those who do not fear to call abstinence from animals the mother of injustice: since both history and experience clearly testify that luxury, war, and injustice invaded the lives of men at the same time as the slaughter of those creatures.

# PORPHYRY

->[The Lawgiver Lycurgus]<-

...did not define wealth by herds of oxen, sheep, goats, or horses, nor by an abundance of money, but rather by the possession of land. He prescribed that a plot should yield seventy measures <note>original: "medimnoi," a Greek unit of dry volume roughly equal to 1.5 bushels</note> of barley for a man and twelve for a woman, with a proportional amount of liquid produce <note>likely wine and oil</note>. For he believed that such an amount of food would be sufficient to maintain good health and physical fitness, and that they would require nothing else. 

Hence it is said that some time later, as he was traveling through the country upon returning from abroad, he saw the land recently harvested and the threshing floors standing parallel and equal to one another. He smiled and said to those present that all of Laconia <note>the region surrounding Sparta</note> appeared to belong to many brothers who had recently divided their inheritance among themselves. 

Consequently, having driven luxury out of Sparta, he was able to abolish the use of all gold and silver coinage, decreeing that they use only iron for money. Even this was of such great weight and bulk that...

it was established, it possessed such little value that an exchange of ten minae <note>A Greek unit of weight and currency; ten minae was a substantial sum, roughly 10 pounds of silver in other cities.</note> would require a very large storehouse in a house. For this reason, many types of injustices were banished from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>. For who would have wanted to steal, or to receive as a bribe, or to snatch away things which were neither easy to hide nor glorious to possess—and which, if they were broken into pieces, would offer no utility? At the same time, useless arts were also cast out along with these things, since the products of such labors could not be sold. For this iron currency could not be traded to other Greeks, nor was it held in any value. Therefore, it was not permitted to buy anything from foreigners or perfume-sellers, nor did any foreign merchandise sail into

<column-break/>

it possessed such little power; so that an exchange of ten minae required a large storehouse in a house, <margin>5</margin> even when a team of oxen brought it. Once this was ratified, many kinds of crimes fell away from Lacedaemon. For who was going to steal, or take bribes, or defraud, or plunder that which was neither possible to hide, nor enviable to possess, but not even <margin>6</margin> profitable to break up? And useless trades were also destined to be driven out with these, <margin>7</margin> as their works had no market. For the iron cargo was not exportable to the other Greeks, nor did it have value, being mocked; so that it was not possible to buy any foreign <margin>8</margin> or petty wares, nor did a cargo of merchants sail in.

5. *Even when a team of oxen brought it—*] <note>original: "Καὶ γευσοῦ ἀγαγόντος"</note> Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note> corrects this to "And a team of oxen bringing it, which being ratified..." Nothing is more absurd than what is currently read, in which the manuscripts nevertheless agree. Fogerolles and Maussac ridiculously interpreted it as "acting concerning taste." Our author <note>Porphyry</note> should be amended by Plutarch, and he in turn by the former: in Plutarch it is "and a team of oxen bringing it, this having been poured over." Those earlier words are to be restored to Porphyry. Then indeed one must read "which being ratified." Thus, with no letter changed, we have the true hand of the author. But also that last word in Plutarch ought to be restored: where it is published as "poured over." Xenophon, in *The Constitution of the Lacedaemonians* p. 682 D, says this: "for first, as for currency... it would require a large space and a wagon for transport." A little later, "nor enviable to possess" is in Plutarch and Meerman.

6. *Profitable to break up.*] The man from Chaeronea <note>Plutarch</note> adds: "For by quenching the edge of the red-hot iron in vinegar, he took away its use and power for other things, as it became weak and difficult to work." Iron could not receive an inscription or be forged if it were dipped in vinegar while glowing. Hence Lycurgus is said to have given "currency of iron spoiled by fire" in Plutarch Vol. I, p. 354 A. Felicianus translates, *if indeed they had been broken into pieces.* "To strike/cut currency" <note>original: "κόπτειν νόμισμα"</note> is said everywhere, but in this passage it does not mean to mint or engrave, but is mostly used for larger coins where weight gave the value, on which matter see Sperling, *On Uncoined Money*, chapter 28. Those things which follow are expressed by Plutarch in a slightly different way.

7. *As their works had no market.*] Translate: *with the works having no sale*, that is, *the works being unsellable.* Thus D'Orville on Chariton III, 3, who excellently cites the use of this word. Indeed, it is very widely applicable, as many have taught. But we have not assigned this labor to Plutarch.

8. *And petty wares.*] This scholium <note>marginal note</note> was added to the Leipzig Manuscript: "Petty wares: things of no value. For *rhopos* is all kinds of small or light freight, but also a mixture of color. From which also a *rhopopoles* is one who sells these things." You may read similar things in Suidas under the entries *Rhopos* and *Rhopikos*.

For the craftsmen, having abandoned useless works, displayed the excellence of their skill in necessary items.

§ 4. But when he had determined to suppress luxury even more and to remove the admiration of wealth, he introduced a third and most beautiful institution of fellowships and banquets: that they should dine together, coming together in a public place for common and prescribed side-dishes and foods. They were not to live at home, reclining on sumptuous couches at tables, indulging their bellies in the dark under the hands of builders and cooks, engorging themselves just like voracious animals, and thereby corrupting their very bodies along with their morals toward every desire and fullness.

<column-break/>

...the waters being drunk and offending the sight were hidden by the color, and as the muddy part was hindered and held back by the <gloss>15</gloss> rims, the liquid being drunk approached the mouth cleaner. The lawmaker was the cause of these things also, as Plutarch says. For the craftsmen, being freed from useless things, demonstrated fine artistry in the necessary ones.

§ 4. Intending to attack luxury still further and to take away the zeal for wealth, he introduced the third and finest political measure: the arrangement of communal meals <note>original: "syssitia"</note>; so that they would dine with one another, coming together for common and appointed meats and foods, and not take their meals at home, reclining on expensive bedding and tables, at the hands of craftsmen and cooks, <gloss>1</gloss> fattening themselves <gloss>2</gloss> in the dark like gluttonous animals; and destroying their bodies along with their characters, being abandoned to every desire and satiety,

# PORPHYRY

-> ...requiring long periods of sleep, hot baths, much rest, and a kind of 4 sedentary nursing of the sick. 5 This was indeed a great achievement; but even greater than this was making wealth "unenviable," as 6 Theophrastus says, and "unwealthy" through the communal nature of the dinners and the frugality of the diet. For there was no use for it, nor any enjoyment, 7 nor even any sight or display of all that preparation, since the rich man went to the same dinner as the poor man. Thus, that famous saying was fulfilled: 8 "In Sparta alone is Wealth <note>The god Plutus</note> seen to be blind," lying there like a painting, soulless and motionless. <column-break/>

...excessive: since satiety requires long sleep, hot baths, much rest, and a sort of medical treatment for the ill. This was a great thing in itself, but far greater was that which, as Theophrastus says, rendered riches both inglorious and impoverished by the community of meals and the parsimony of living. For there was no use for them, nor could anyone enjoy them: indeed, there could be no sight or ostentation of any great apparatus at all, since both the rich and the poor man approached the same table. Thus, that which is common in the proverb was seen: that in Sparta alone is Wealth blind, lying like an inanimate and motionless picture. 3. *Long periods of sleep ----*] Such are those of whom *Julian* speaks, citing Homer in *The Beard-Hater* <note>original: *Misopogon*</note> p. 342. D.
-> *They prefer warm baths and beds* <-
accepting these instead of what is holy.

4. *Sedentary nursing of the sick.*] *Plutarch* writes *nosēleias* <note>nursing/illness</note>. Many words of this kind are usually pronounced not only with the diphthong *ei*, but also with a simple *iota*, as we saw in Book I, § 14. From that source, however, I confidently restore the reading *kathēmerinēs* <note>daily</note>; I wonder if *Eiusdem deomenōn* <note>of those in need</note> might be better. Our text conveniently refers back to *plēsmonēn* <note>satiety/fullness</note>.

<column-break/>

...that even those illustrious men are inconsistent with themselves. *Menage* in his notes on *Diogenes V, 42* notes that *Meursius* thought the books *On Lives* were referenced; but as *the same author* writes at V, 47, he actually thought it was the book *On Wealth*. *Fabricius* in the place cited on p. 246 says it is from the books *On Lives*, but on p. 251 of the same work, they seemed to be taken from those *On Lawgivers*. Therefore, I determine nothing.

7. *Sight.*] This is correctly found in *Plutarch*. In *Vettori's* edition it was *opsas*, which was propagated into subsequent editions. Soon after, instead of *holēs* <note>whole</note>, *the same author* has *pollēs* <note>much</note>, and *tauto* instead of *to auto* <note>the same</note>.

See *Spanheim* on *Aristophanes' Plutus, 13.* In Plato, Wealth is numbered among the lesser goods—not the blind Wealth, but the one who sees most acutely, provided he follows Prudence as a guide. *Laws, Book I, p. 773. C.*, a passage excerpted by *Theodoret* in *Discourse on Divine Providence, p. 567.*

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

->**The Spartan Communal Meals**<-

to agree: for the others used to observe those who did not drink or eat with them very carefully, condemning them as lacking self-control <note>original: "incontinentes"</note> because they rejected the common way of life. For this reason, they also called these banquets *Phiditia*: either because they were a cause of mutual friendship and kindness—so that *Phiditia* was said instead of *Philitia*, with the letter 'd' taken for 'l', which you might interpret as "friendly gatherings"—or because they accustomed men to utility and thrift, being called *Phiditia* as if they were "frugal gatherings" <note>The author is playing on the Greek words for friendship (philia) and thrift (pheido)</note>. Moreover, they were accustomed to go together in groups of fifteen, or a few less or more than this; and each individual brought every month a bushel <note>original: "modium"</note> of meal, eight gallons <note>original: "choas"</note> of wine, five pounds of cheese, five half-measures <note>original: "heminas"</note> of figs, and in addition to these, a very small amount of money for purchasing relishes <note>original: "opsonia," referring to non-staple foods like fish or vegetables</note>.

§ 5. It was with good reason, therefore, that since they dined so meagerly and temperately, the children also frequented these communal meals, just as if they were being led to a school of temperance. For there they heard political discourses—

<column-break/>

<note>The right column contains the original Greek text of the passage translated above.</note>

...filled up, but the rest carefully watched the one not drinking or eating with them, and reproached him as one lacking self-control and becoming soft toward the common diet. Therefore they also addressed these as *Phiditia*: either as being causes of friendship and kindly feeling, taking the *delta* instead of the *lambda*, or as accustoming them to simplicity and thrift. And they came together in groups of fifteen, and slightly fewer or more than these. And each of the mess-mates brought per month a *medimnos* of barley-meal, eight *choes* of wine, five *mnae* of cheese, five half-mnae of figs, and in addition to these, some small amount of coinage for the buying of relishes.

§ 5. It was reasonable then, as they dined so simply and temperately, that the children also frequented the communal meals, as if being led to schools of temperance, and they listened to political discourses—

<margin>
9. **Filled up.**] *Plutarch:* "having been filled." And presently "watching closely." For "becoming soft," *Meermann's manuscript* has "soft things" and *tithia* for *Phiditia*. *Plutarch:* "becoming quite soft." But those things which follow there, our Author [Porphyry] did not divert into his own streams.
10. **Either as of Friendship—**] In *Plutarch* it is "either as being causes of friendship and kindly feeling." And he brings forward another reason for the name besides. In the *Leipzig edition*, "love of wisdom-feeling" is written poorly. Then for "accustoming" (plural), one should read "accustoming" (neuter singular). The common reading arose because in *Plutarch* "being" preceded it, for which when our Author had written "causes being," the "accustoming" of *Plutarch* was nonetheless retained. *The same author then* has "a little."
11. **Of the mess-mates.**] The author of these [notes] has "of the communal meals," where others however have "of the mess-mates," and the translator expressed that. Each of the guests therefore contributed these things per month. And so it is not defined whether these *Phiditia* were celebrated for only one month, or for each individual month. Compare *Meursius*: *Miscellanea Laconica* I, 10. Presently *Reiske* corrected "a small amount of coinage," omitting the "and." And so it is in *Plutarch*.

# PORPHYRY

-> [Page 306] <-

...of political matters, and they witnessed <gloss>1</gloss> liberal education <note>The Greek text uses 'paideia,' referring to the holistic upbringing of a citizen.</note>. They themselves were accustomed to play and to jest without scurrility <term>scurrility: buffoonery or coarse language</term>, and they did not take offense when they were the objects of jests. For this was also considered highly "Laconic" <note>Spartan</note>: to endure a joke; however, if one could not bear it, he was permitted to ask for it to stop, and the jester would cease. Such was the simplicity of the Lacedaemonians regarding their diet, even though it was established by law for the entire population. Therefore, those who emerged from this form of government are recorded to have been more manly, more temperate, <gloss>2</gloss> and more concerned with what is right than those from other states, <gloss>3</gloss> who were corrupted in both soul and body. It is clear that total abstinence is suited to such a government, while the habits of gluttony belong to those that are corrupted. But passing on to other nations, as many as possess good laws and a civilized nature...

<column-break/>

...they heard and observed liberal play. They themselves were accustomed both to joke and to speak witticisms without scurrility, and not to be indignant if they were stung by some sharpness of speech of this kind. For to tolerate a false thing said against oneself seemed very much the Spartan way. Nevertheless, it was permitted, if anyone did not endure it, to refuse, and the other would immediately desist from the taunting. And indeed, the thinness of the Lacedaemonians' living, although it had been instituted for the people, was of this sort. Whence also they are recorded to have been stronger and more temperate, and more eager for what is right—those who proceeded from this republic—than those from others, which were corrupted as much in mind as in body. It is evident that abstinence was peculiar to this state, while luxury of living was peculiar to the others. Now truly, if we cross over to other nations as well, among whom there is a regard for justice, gentleness, and piety...

---

<margin>1. **Liberal education.** The same author [mentions] "liberal educators." It is well known what "liberal studies" are. Otherwise, *Valentinus* reads "play" [paidiās] not badly. Next, instead of "they were accustomed" [ēthizonto], *Plutarch* has "they accustomed" [eithizon], but some manuscripts have "they were accustomed." Then, in the same place, "he had ceased" [pepauto], though other manuscripts prefer "they had ceased" or "they cease." To the word "scurrility" [bōmolochias] is added in the *Meermann* margin: "flattery of a jester's joke." It is said to be derived from "lurking [lochein] at the altars [bōmois]" in order to take from the sacrificial victims.</margin>

<margin>2. **And of the right.** I do not know what that "orthou" [of the right] means. Perhaps it should be read "koinou" [of the common good]. *VALENTINUS*. In the *Leipzig* Manuscript it is "orthrou" [of the dawn]. He seems to have intended "orthou" [of the right]. *REISKE*. Without doubt *Meermann* also intended "orthou," who gave "orthrou." And this is so true that, lest that filth wound your nostrils any longer, I have ejected the possession of "onthou" [dung], nor would I have done so unless *Felicianus* had also found what we have given. In *Hesychius*, under the entry "bombuthuleumata," it is "to season with dung [onthōi]," from which you might gather it was a type of seasoning. But that, even if you contend the writing there is intact, does not pertain to this. Next, *Meermann* erroneously has "melon" [apple] for "delon" [clear].</margin>

<margin>3. **Corrupted also in their souls.** Above, Book III, section 24, from *Plutarch*: "the thinking and reasoning part has been corrupted." He could also have used the accusative case, for the Greeks are accustomed to construct it in both ways. Compare the learned Doctor on those words of St. Paul in 1 Timothy 6:5, "corrupted in mind," and *Horreus's* Observations on Herodotus, chapter 9.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Qq 2 <-

...the care shown toward the gods was of primary importance, clearly perceiving that it contributes to the safety and benefit of cities that the precept of abstinence should apply, if not to all, then certainly to some: those who, by offering sacrifices and the remaining worship to the gods on behalf of the city, might atone for the sins of the people. For just as in the mysteries the one called the "child from the hearth" <note>original: "puer qui a Vesta dicitur" / "ὁ ἀφ’ ἑστίας παῖς." This refers to a youth chosen by lot to perform specific rituals in the Eleusinian Mysteries to win the gods' favor for the whole community.</note>, by exquisitely performing all things that have been commanded, appeases the divinity on behalf of all those being initiated: so in nations and cities the priests do the same, while they sacrifice for everyone, and through religion and piety implore the divinity to protect the safety of their people. To the priests, therefore, whether you look at the custom of the Greeks or the barbarians, it is commanded that some abstain from all animals, and others entirely from the eating of certain ones.

<column-break/>

...and if the record of piety toward the divine were inscribed, it would be clear that the command of abstinence was ordained for the safety of cities and for their advantage—if not for everyone, then at least for some—and that those sacrificing to the gods and serving them on behalf of the city were appeasing the sins of the many. For just as in the mysteries the so-called "child from the hearth" appeases the divine on behalf of all the initiates by accurately performing the things commanded, so throughout the nations and cities the priests are able to do this by sacrificing on behalf of all, and by drawing the divine to their guardianship through piety. To the priests, then, it has been commanded to abstain from food—to some from all animals, and to others from certain ones—whether...

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument for vegetarianism, specifically citing the priestly classes of various nations as moral exemplars. It transitions from a general discussion of customs to a specific historical account of Egyptian priests.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

Whether you look at Greek custom <note>original: "ἔθος" (ethos). A marginal note suggests "ἔθνος" (ethnos), meaning "nation" or "people."</note> or that of the barbarians, you will find things handled differently by different people. Thus, if one were to consider all people everywhere as a single group, it would appear that they collectively abstain from all animals <note>meaning that because every animal is considered sacred or forbidden by at least one culture, a universal observer would see a total abstinence</note>. If, therefore, those who preside over the safety of cities, and who are entrusted with piety toward the gods, abstain from animals, how could anyone dare to condemn such abstinence as being disadvantageous to cities?

§ 6. At any rate, in describing the customs of the Egyptian priests, Chaeremon the Stoic <note>A 1st-century scholar and tutor to Nero; he wrote on Egyptian history and hieroglyphs</note>—who says they were also regarded as philosophers among the Egyptians—explains that they chose the temples as the place to practice their philosophy. For, regarding their entire desire for the contemplation of the divine...

<column-break/>

And this is done differently among different peoples: so that if anyone considers all who are everywhere as if they were one, they would all seem to abstain from all things. If, therefore, those who preside over the safety of many, and to whom all piety and religion toward the gods is committed, abstain from the eating of animals: who is so impudent that he does not fear to condemn such abstinence as if it were useless to states?

§ 6. Furthermore, writing about the Egyptian priests, Chaeremon the Stoic, who says they were even considered philosophers among them, relates that they chose temples for themselves in which to live and philosophize. Indeed, since they were driven by a desire for the universal contemplation of the gods...

<margin>
9. **Greek custom.** I would prefer "nation." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar</note>.
10. **Who preside over the cities.** Exactly as those who take care of the sacred rites of others are called "those presiding" <note>Greek: <term>προϊστάμενοι</term></note> in the New Testament and "presidents" <note>Greek: <term>προεστῶτες</term></note> among the ancient Christians; they are called "Presidents" <note>Latin: <term>Praesidentes</term></note> in <term>Tertullian</term>. See <term>Kortholt</term> on <term>Justin Martyr, Apology I, p. 42.</term> <term>Felicianus</term> seems to have read "of many" <note>Greek: <term>πολλῶν</term></note> instead of "of cities" <note>Greek: <term>πόλεων</term></note>.
11. **Entrusted with piety.** A formula of speaking used by others and frequently by our author. See on the <term>Life of Plotinus, ch. 18.</term> <term>Fabricius, Greek Library, Book IV, ch. 26.</term> Who is ignorant of that passage of St. Paul to the <term>Romans 3:2</term>, "that they were entrusted with the oracles of God," where examples as numerous as dust are gathered by interpreters. Parmenion in <term>Diodorus Siculus</term> is said to be "entrusted with the king's treasures." Consult <term>Wesseling</term> on <term>Book XIX, ch. 59.</term>
1. **The priests, Chaeremon the Stoic, etc.** You may also read these things in <term>Jerome, Against Jovinian, Book II, 13</term>: "Chaeremon the Stoic, a most eloquent man, narrates concerning the life of the ancient Egyptian priests, that having set aside all the business and cares of life, they were always in the temple, and contemplated the natures of things and the causes and reasons of the stars; they never mixed with women, and never saw relatives or neighbors, not even their children, etc."
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
But the judgments of the ancients concerning Chaeremon differ greatly. See the end of § 8. The celebrated <term>Jablonski</term> gathered from this fragment that Philo the Jew took those things which he discusses regarding the Therapeutae <note>A Jewish ascetic sect in Egypt</note> from Chaeremon, with certain things changed and transposed with skillful artifice. See the illustrious <term>La Croze, Treasury of Letters, Vol. I, p. 180.</term> Concerning the priests of the Egyptians and the rule of life which they followed, read more in <term>Herodotus, Book II, 37.</term>
2. **To be regarded... he explains.** The Leipzig manuscript gives "to have been regarded," which <term>Reiske</term> deservedly preferred; <term>Meermann</term> orders the same. Then "he explains" <note>Greek: <term>ἐξηγεῖται</term></note>, not "to explain" <note>Greek: <term>ἐξηγεῖσθαι</term></note>, as was previously published, which error both <term>Fogerolles</term> and <term>Valentin</term> have already corrected. However, the manuscripts show no variation.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

it seemed to be natural <note>original: "cognatum esse"</note> for them to dwell near the statues of the gods. This rendered them secure through divine veneration, since everyone honored these philosophers as if they were certain sacred animals. It also brought them peace, as they only had to mingle with others during public festivals; for the rest of the time, the temples were almost inaccessible to others. Indeed, one could not approach them unless they had conducted themselves purely and abstained from many things. This is, as it were, a common law of the Egyptian temples. Having renounced all other crafts and human labors, they dedicated their entire lives to the contemplation and inspection of divine matters. From this inspection, they derived honor, safety, and piety; and from—

<column-break/>

it was natural <gloss>3</gloss> to dwell near their statues. This provided them with security arising from divine respect, as everyone honored the Philosophers like certain sacred animals. They remained quiet, since social mixing was carried out only during public assemblies and festivals. For the rest of the time, the temples were nearly inaccessible <gloss>4</gloss> to others; for it was necessary to approach only after having been purified and having abstained from many things, and this is like a common decree of the temples throughout Egypt. Having renounced all other work and human resources, <gloss>5</gloss> they devoted their whole life to the <gloss>6</gloss> contemplation and vision of divine things; through this, they provided for themselves what is honorable, secure, and pious, and through—

---

<margin>3. *It was natural.*] "It was characteristic." Doctor *Abresch* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch (1699–1782), a Dutch philologist</note> cited a passage from *Aeschylus’* Agamemnon, line 841: "For to few men is this natural." Regarding what they called "statues" <note>original: "Aphidrumata"</note>, see the notes on Book I, section 35. Shortly after, for "public assemblies" <note>Greek: panegyreis</note>, *Meermann* reads "at the public assemblies."</margin>

<margin>4. *For it was necessary to approach only after having been purified etc.*:] You see that those priests did not wish to mix even with their own countrymen unless they had undergone certain purifications. And so he relates a little later that during the time of purifications, lest they be defiled, they sequestered themselves from the company of friends and even from priests who were not "clean." This custom is very frequent today and in the past: that others, and especially priests, do not engage in commerce with foreigners, and restrain citizens from meeting and living with outsiders. There is nothing strange in this regarding the Egyptians, who so despised other nations and were accustomed to associate and eat with "those from outside" <note>original: "tois thyrathen"</note> only very rarely. It seems nature itself has engraved such a thing upon man. Hence *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), author of "De Legibus Hebraeorum"</note> in "Ritual Laws," Book III, Dissertation 3, illustrates the passage in Genesis 43:32 regarding *Moses*, and concludes that nations before the giving of the Law already had a custom of certain "uncleannesses" and consequently purifications to resolve them. The word "decree" <note>original: "thesmos"</note> is discussed below.</margin>

<margin>5. *They devoted their whole life.*] You might prefer "they gave themselves up to," which rightly pleased *Abresch.* Thus: "they gave their lives for the safety of the Greeks," in *Diodorus Siculus*, Book XI, 11, where *Wesseling* <note>Peter Wesseling (1692–1759), editor of Diodorus</note> says more. These compound words are often confused. See Book II, 30.</margin>

These words differ just as "to observe" and "to look at," or "observer" and "spectator," concerning which—</margin>

# P O R P H Y R I U S

...of contemplation, and knowledge. Through both of these, they acquired a certain hidden and **ancient-seeming** <note>original: ἀρχαιοπρεπῆ</note> discipline of character. For to be always engaged in divine knowledge and inspiration removes one from all greed, restrains the passions, and awakens the life toward understanding. They practiced simplicity and restraint, self-control and endurance, and in all things justice and freedom from avarice. Their **lack of social interaction** <note>original: τὸ δυσεπίμικτον</note> also rendered them venerable. Indeed, during the actual time of their so-called purifications, they hardly mixed even with their closest kinsmen and fellow tribesmen, nor were they seen by anyone else, except...

<column-break/>

...knowledge through trial: from both they prepared for themselves a certain hidden exercise of character, befitting ancient dignity. For to be always occupied in divine cognition and inspiration excludes one from all greed and insolence, represses the affections, and excites the mind toward intelligence. Likewise, they practiced parsimony, thinness of diet, continence, and tolerance, and justice and equity in all things. They were also rendered venerable by the fact that they mingled very little with others. For in the very time of chastity and purification, they did not even associate with those most closely related to them or their peers; nor were they seen by any other...

***

On which matters *Valckenaer* disputes beautifully in *Animadversions on Ammonius, Book II, ch. 3.*

$^7$. **Ancient-seeming.** <note>original: Ἀρχαιοπρεπῆ</note> This word is also ignored by the most copious treasury of the Greek language <note>The translator refers to the lack of this word in standard dictionaries of the time.</note>. It is also used by *Aeschylus in Prometheus, line 408.*

$^8$. **Divine knowledge and inspiration.** <note>original: Θείᾳ γνώσει καὶ ἐπιπνοίᾳ</note> It seems that "reflection" or "meditation" <note>original: ἐπινοίᾳ</note> might better suit this passage. **REISKE.** These words could very easily be confused, as happened in *Marcus Aurelius's Meditations I, 17* and others. Here I would change nothing. Thus we find "inspiration of the gods" in *Iamblichus, On the Mysteries III, 9*; "divine inspirations" in the same, chapters 6 and 21; and "daemonic inspirations" in chapter 7. Those priests, after certain sacrifices were duly and lawfully performed, were persuaded that they saw the god and received his breath, or that mysteries were revealed to them by him; on which matter see the celebrated *Jablonski, Egyptian Pantheon, Book V, 5, 12.*

$^9$. **Restrains the passions.** <note>original: Καταστέλλει δὲ τὰ πάθη</note> *Represses, settles.* He uses the word well, as it is primarily applied to those who are tumultuous and seditious, whence those who are *settled and modest* are called "katestalmenoi." See

<column-break/>

*Kypke on Luke, Acts of the Apostles XX, 36.* For whom, in *St. Paul’s First Letter to Timothy, ch. II, 9*, "katastole" is correctly defined as *modesty or restraint in clothing, gestures, gait* and other things falling under the senses, where more is said on this meaning. And I understand this in our author a little later through "katastole" (which word the *Meerman Codex* wrongly omits there), not as *thinness of diet*, as *Felicianus* gave it. Thus Pythagoras is said to have adorned himself with "reverence of soul and restraint of body" in *Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras, ch. II, no. 10*; also regarding character in *Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book VI, p. 659*: "unto the ordering of character and restraint."

$^{10}$. **Lack of social interaction.** <note>original: Τὸ δυσεπίμικτον</note> This word also escaped the diligence of the Lexicons. Among others, we have it in *Strabo, Book XI, p. 340*: "Nomads who are difficult to mix with others." The "lack of easy mixing" is mentioned *ibid. p. 346.* I have said more on related words *at Book III, 18.*

$^{11}$. **Nor seen by others.** <note>original: Οὐδὲ ἄλλων τῶν θεωρ.</note> In the *Leipzig Codex* it is "nor seen by others." It seems Porphyry wrote "nor otherwise seeing" or "being seen." That is, they were not seen in any other condition...

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

They did not associate with others, except when the necessary needs of those practicing abstinence required it; for they inhabited the inner sanctuaries, which were inaccessible to the impure and unpurified, and were considered holy for the performance of sacrifices. During all other times, they lived more freely among those like themselves, but they had no dealings with others who were outside the religious order. They were always seen near the gods and the statues of the gods, either carrying something, or presiding, or arranging things with modesty and gravity. This was not a sign of any pride, but an indication of natural reason. For they displayed a venerable gravity even in their very outward appearance. Indeed, their gait was orderly, and their gaze was steady, so that—

<column-break/>

<note>original Greek text of the passage above</note>
...unless for necessary needs they joined those practicing purity, or inhabited the inner sanctuaries as holy places for sacred rites, inaccessible to those not living purely. At other times, they mixed more simply with their peers; <gloss>12</gloss> but they did not live with any of those outside the religious worship; <gloss>13</gloss> they were always seen near the gods or the statues, either carrying them, or leading the way, <gloss>14</gloss> and arranging them with order and dignity; each of these actions was not vanity, but a demonstration of a certain natural principle. <gloss>15</gloss> Their dignity was also seen in their very posture. <gloss>16</gloss> For their gait was orderly, and their gaze was steady...

...giving to be made, than either among ---- Soon **perhaps** <note>original: "τοῖς συναγνεύουσι χρείας, ἢ πρὸς ἁγνευτήρια"</note> "the needs of those practicing purity, or toward the places of purification." <term>REISKE: Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century German physician and philologist known for his emendations of Greek texts.</term> *Manuscript:* <note>original: "οὐδὲ ἄλλων"</note> "nor of others." <term>Meermann Manuscript.</term> <note>original: "οὐδὲ ἀλλώντων"</note>. A little later I also rewrite from the *Leipzig* and *Meermann* manuscripts: <note>original: "καθαρεύουσιν"</note> "those who are pure."

<margin>12. Of those outside.]</margin> Others call them "those from without." <note>original: "οἱ ἔξω"</note> "Those outside," properly those who live *outside the house*; in the same style of speaking used by *Saint Paul*, they are those who did not belong to the Church of Christ, 1 Corinthians 5:12, where the *Interpreters* say much.

<margin>13. They were always seen etc.]</margin> These priests were indeed "exceedingly god-fearing, more than all other men," according to *Herodotus*, Book II, 37. For that reason, they were constantly near the images of the gods, which they either carried or arranged in a decorous order. See *Wesseling* <note>Peter Wesseling, a Dutch social and political scholar</note> on Diodorus Siculus, I, 73, who did not leave these passages of Porphyry untouched. Also, "carrying" is well-said; it was a very well-known custom that in processions and solemn rites they carried the Gods on their shoulders, or sometimes conveyed them placed on chariots. See *Cuper*: Harpocrates, p. 165, and *Spanheim* on Callimachus's Hymn to Pallas, 3.

<margin>14. and arranging.]</margin> **Perhaps** "or even arranging." The "or" <note>original: "ἢ"</note> easily fell out because of the preceding "i" at the end of the word "leading the way" <note>original: "προηγούμενοι"</note>. <term>REISKE.</term>

<margin>15. Dignity was also seen in their posture.]</margin> *Saint Paul* to Titus 2:3: "in behavior as becomes holiness," on which learned men will shed light from our Author. Regarding Gracchus, *Plutarch*, Vol. I, p. 824 F: "mild and composed in gaze and movement," exactly as our Author immediately explains "posture" <note>original: "κατάστημα"</note>. Regarding the form <note>original: "κἀκ τοῦ"</note> "and from the," see on I, 15, where I warned that those things which should properly be separated are frequently connected.

<margin>16. Orderly gait — steady gaze.]</margin> Indeed, a modest gait and a composed countenance create the "dignity of posture," on which matter see *Casaubon* on *Athenaeus*, Book I, 18. Just as "a composition of the face not broken into laughter, and a gentleness of gait, and a composure of dress" is praised by *Plutarch* in his Life of Pericles, Vol. I, p. 154 C. He elegantly calls it a "steady gaze" <note>original: "βλέμμα καθεστηκὸς"</note>, as *Philo* does in "On the Contemplative Life," p. 691 E: "with a steady gaze and a steady voice." In Latin, it is called a "standing face" <note>fixed or calm expression</note>. *Silius Italicus*, XV, 29: "A standing face, and in speech and gait more like a man." Where two...

# PORPHYRY

...practiced, 17 so that whenever they wished, they would not blink. 18 Laughter was rare, and if it ever occurred, it went no further than a smile. 19 Their hands were always kept inside their garments. 20 And there was a distinctive symbol for each person indicating the rank they held in the sacred rites; for there were several ranks. 21 Their diet was frugal and simple. 22 As for wine, some did not touch it at all, while others...

<column-break/>

...whenever they wished, they would blink their eyes very little: laughter was quite rare, and of such a kind that it did not progress beyond a cheerfulness of countenance: moreover, their hands were always kept within their clothing. Indeed, there was even a mark for each individual which signified the rank and status of each—for there were many—which each had been assigned in the temples. They used a thin and simple diet. For of wine...

---

...you see those two things are also joined. Compare there the Distinguished Scholar. The Greeks otherwise use "eyes" and "face" <note>original: ὄμματα & πρόσωπον</note> with a different sense, as the Celebrated *D’Orville* shows in his notes on *Chariton* Book III, 9 and V, 3, who was not unmindful of our author.

17. **So that whenever they wished, they would not blink.** <note>original: Ὡς ὅτε βουληθεῖεν μὴ σκαρδαμύττειν</note> *Abresch* in his notes corrected this to: "So that when they did not wish, they would not blink." <unclear>not</unclear> Now, "to blink" <note>term: σκαρδαμύττειν — to blink or twitch the eyelids</note> is to look entirely fixedly and never close the eyelid, to speak with *Heliodorus* Book III, p. 148. Thus *Synesius* in *In Praise of Baldness* p. 48 says that the "servants of the divine in Egypt" <note>referring to the Therapeutae or priests</note> do not even tolerate hair on their eyelids (a word which can be added to the riches of Henri Estienne). The Lexicographers and the Scholiast on *Aristophanes' Knights* 292 explain our word. What he adds there about the meaning of the word "to look without blinking" <note>original: ἀσκαρδαμυκτεῖν</note> fits beautifully with our author in *Life of Pythagoras* 10; from this, "to look without blinking" <note>original: ἀσκαρδαμυκτὶ βλέπειν</note> means to gaze with unmoving eyes, a sign of boldness and strength, which *Bentley* explains beautifully in his notes on *Horace* I, Ode 3, 18.

18. **Laughter was... as far as a smile.** <note>original: Γέλως δὲ ---- μέχρι μειδιάσεως</note> Just as *Isocrates* forbade "clinging to headlong laughter" in his *To Demonicus* p. 5. "To smile" <note>original: μειδιᾷν</note> is properly used for a gentle laugh. See the Celebrated *Lennep* in his observations on *Coluthus* II, 4; it is therefore rightly contrasted with "to laugh." *Aelian* in *Various History* VIII, 3 says that Anaxagoras was never seen either laughing or smiling. The word "smiling" <note>original: μειδίασις</note>, which *Estienne* writes occurs in the Lexicons without any author, is found in *Pollux* VI, 199.

19. **Hands inside the garment.** <note>original: Ἐντὸς τοῦ σχήματος χεῖρες</note> This too was a sign of modesty and shame. It was no different of old among the Greeks and Romans. See *Casaubon* on *Diogenes Laertius* p. 63. Regarding the Romans, *Seneca* in *Controversies* V. 6: *Among our fathers, who*

<column-break/>

*were beginning their legal careers, it was considered a sin to thrust the arm out of the toga.* I see these points have already been taken up by the Distinguished Scholar in his notes on *Valerius Maximus* VI, 9. External I, 6.

20. **There was a symbol... of the rank etc.** <note>original: Σύμβολόν γε ἦν ---- τῆς τάξεως</note> Concerning the Priests of the Egyptians, *Diodorus Siculus* I, 83 says: "they go about the cities and the countryside with their own signs." Those "ranks" <note>original: τάξεις</note> can be compared with the priests of the Hebrews, who were enrolled in several classes or families, concerning whom *Saint Luke* uses the same word in the Gospel I, 8, 9. The Famous *Abresch* had noted this passage.

21. **A diet frugal and simple.** <note>original: Δίαιτα δὲ λιτὴ καὶ ἀφ.</note> These things can also be compared with the institutions of the Jews. See *Marsham*, *Chronicus Canon* Section IX. Instead of "simple" <note>original: ἀφελὴς</note>, the *Meerman* Codex gives "secure" <note>original: ἀσφαλὴς</note>; not quite correctly.

22. **For of wine, some not at all—** <note>original: Οἴνου γὰρ οἱ μὲν οὐδ’ ὅλως</note> Just as for the Kings, most of whom were chosen from the priests, there was "a certain fixed measure of wine" according to *Diodorus* Book I, 70. *Wesseling* explains this from our author; but it was not truly unique or peculiar to the Egyptians, but common and familiar to all the priests and Philosophers of the Orient to detest wine as if it were brought forth for the destruction of men, from whence that persuasion flowed to others as well. Read *Jablonski*, *Egyptian Pantheon* II, 106. Hence, for some of the Pythagoreans it was the custom "to also use wine," while for others and the more rigid ones, "not to drink wine at all"; for in this way two passages of *Iamblichus* in the *Life of Pythagoras* numbers 98 and 107 are well reconciled. *Wetstein* compares these words of ours with the precept of *Paul* in 1 Timothy V, 23, and with the divine law in Leviticus X, 9. Compare the Incomparable *Grotius*.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

->R r<-

some [drank] nothing at all, others very little, on account of the damage it might do to the nerves <note>original: "nervorum laesionem"</note> and the filling of the head <note>congestion or "brain fog"</note>, which would be a hindrance to contemplation; also because it would incite the desires of Venus <note>sexual urges</note>. For this reason, they also behaved with great caution regarding other things they consumed: for they never tasted bread during their periods of ritual purification <note>original: "castimoniis"</note>, but when it was not a time of abstinence, they were accustomed to eat it crushed with hyssop; for they said the hyssop blunted the strength of the bread for the most part. Most of them abstained from oil generally, and many always: but if anyone used it occasionally with vegetables, he used very little, only as much as might slightly soften the taste.

§ 7. Furthermore, it was not lawful for them to touch those foods and drinks which were produced outside of Egypt; and thus they kept a great deal of room for luxury excluded.

For they said the hyssop destroyed much of its power. # PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

Indeed, all those who were in Egypt abstained from fish, and likewise from all quadrupeds that were solid-hoofed <note>animals like horses or donkeys</note>, or multi-cloven <note>animals with many toes, like dogs or cats</note>, or those without horns; they also abstained from birds that feed on flesh. Many also abstained entirely from all animals; and during periods of purification, everyone abstained, since they believed that at such times they should not even eat an egg. Furthermore, there was a great deal of other observation among them. For they rejected the females of cattle as food; and of the males, those that were twin—

<column-break/>

<margin>
Their seasoning was salt, which the more refined among them flavored with hyssop. They received this from the *Egyptians*.
1. *Of those in Egypt itself, they abstained from fish.*] One might gather from *Diodorus Siculus* (Book I, 43) that formerly all Egyptians used fish, as the river provided a large supply of them; but later, some abstained from certain kinds and others from others. "The priests abstain from all," as *Plutarch* says (Volume II, p. 353 C). Compare *Julian* (Oratory V, p. 176) and *Clement of Alexandria* (Book VII, p. 718 D), who also inquire into the causes why they had to abstain either perpetually or at least during <term>purifications</term> <note>original: "en tais hagneiais"</note>. On this matter, see also the *Learned Man on Horapollo* (Book I, ch. 15). From here, therefore, it was derived by the Pythagoreans. See *Athenaeus* (VII, 16) and *Plutarch* (Symposiacs, Question 8). *Iamblichus* (Life of Pythagoras, no. 98) seems to almost disagree, where they are said to "rarely use sea-foods." There, one should either rewrite it with *Kuster* as "sea-foods" (in the dative case), or rather with the learned *Koen* (on Gregory Pardus regarding Dialects, p. 122) as "rarely use the meat of sea animals" (the word being transposed here), unless "to use of foods" was said in the same way as "to eat of meats" or "to drink of wine" and similar phrases, but *Iamblichus* is not accustomed to using it that way. The former, therefore, either pertains to the more rigid observers, or signifies that they did not use every kind of fish, just as the Philosopher in our *Life of Pythagoras* (45) prescribes "abstaining from almost all sea creatures." In the same way, Pythagoras is said to have "rarely used sea creatures" by *Diogenes Laertius* (VII, 19), who in the same place (Section 34) prescribes "not to touch those fish which are sacred." A little before, *Abresch* corrected "a certain many" for "thus" in the *Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts*.
</margin>

<margin>
2. *Those that are solid-hoofed or multi-cloven.*] He says below in § 14 that this was also forbidden to the Hebrews. The law is well known in *Leviticus 11*. *Huet* (Demonstratio Evangelica IV, 11, 1) and many others have long ago noted those related institutions of both nations. Regarding the Jews and Egyptians abstaining from certain animals for religious reasons, yet observing different customs and laws in selecting and rejecting them, *Spencer* (Ritual Laws I, 5) discourses learnedly. To see how ancient theologians explain these things, read *Cotelerius* on the *Epistle of Barnabas* (Volume I, Apostolic Fathers, p. 36).

3. *They did not even admit an egg.*] The Jewish Masters relate similar things about the High Priest. See *Spencer* (Ritual Laws III, 5).

4. *They made a not un-slanderous refusal.*] I wish that "not" were deleted. VALENTINI. He calls the pride of the Egyptian priests in the selection of victims and the severity of their religious rites "not un-slanderous," which can hardly be freed from the mark of intemperance and malice, by which they rejected even those things which no one else would have ever marked as a fault. And they acted as "sycophants" <note>informers or false accusers</note> in religion, even plucking at and condemning things that were holy and harmless, whether by some error of will or judgment, just as slanderers harass the most holy and upright men with frivolous and unworthy accusations. REISKE.

5. *The females of cattle.*] See the note on Book II, § 11.

6. *Of the males, those that were twin—*] Nor were these things [forbidden] to the Jews—
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Rr 2 <-

...twins, or if they were spotted, or of different colors, or of an altered shape, or if they had already been tamed—as if they had already been consecrated to labor—and were similar to those that were honored: or if they represented anything by any other likeness: or if they were one-eyed: or if they tended toward a human resemblance. There are innumerable other observations which belong to the art of those who are called calf-

<column-break/>

...twins, or spotted, or of different colors, or varying in form, or tamed (as already consecrated to labors) and similar to those honored, or if it should be according to any sort of representation, or one-eyed, or leaning toward a human likeness. And there are ten thousand other observations, and of the art concerning them of those called calf- <note>original: "μοσχο-" (moscho-), the beginning of the word for "calf-sealers."</note>

---

...so dissimilar to the rites of the Hebrews. They examined the matter, but while being slaves to a hypothesis <note>original: "ὑποθέσει δουλεύοντες" (hypothesei douleuontes)</note>. *Marsham: Chronicus Canon, Section IX; and Spencer: De Legibus Hebraeorum Ritualibus, Book I, 5.*

7. **Similar to those honored.**] And "to those blamed," <note>original: "ἐπιμωμένοις" (epimōmenois)</note> meaning similar to those which had already been dishonored and depressed to the ignominy of servitude, deprived of their original honor and glory. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist.</note> *Valentius* had marked this place with an asterisk as suspect. I understand those brute animals which were nourished in sacred enclosures, to whom certainly greater honor was shown than to the others. *Plutarch* calls them such in various places, *Volume II, Page 359, and elsewhere.*

8. **According to any sort of representation.**] Perhaps those words can be read thus: "or if it should yield to any sort of representation." <term>VALENTIUS</term> I cannot settle this. I once thought "it might depart from custom," or "it might depart from the usual." That is, it might have exceeded custom, or withdrawn from the accustomed mode of nature: but I myself would not attribute much to this conjecture. Whether the simple "to go out" <note>original: "ἐξιέναι" (exienai)</note> was once used for the full "to go out from the usual," I would not dare to affirm for certain, but it almost seems so. <term>REISKE</term> Certainly these [readings] are sickly. A wound can be helped by various remedies, but who will be the guarantor of restored integrity? *T. Gale* reshapes it to "it might show" in his notes to *Iamblichus: On the Mysteries, p. 278.* *The Illustrious Abresch* suggests "extraordinary." *Hesychius* defines "Extraordinary" <note>original: "Ἐξείδεις" (Exeideis)</note> as "excessive" or "eminent." The sense then is, "as if it were... extraordinary." There was one for whom "representation" <note>original: "ἀπεικασμὸν" (apeikasmon)</note> was attractive, which I do not approve of because of the preceding "representation." What if "might be" <note>original: "εἴη" (eiē)</note> is read instead of "might go out" <note>original: "ἐξείη" (exeiē)</note>, which is surely a mild remedy and supplies the sense, which otherwise

<column-break/>

must be supplied by that same word. He says, therefore, that they abstained from all those animals which were similar to the honored ones, or were as if images of any thing whatsoever. Think of the Gods or the virtues, of which they were accustomed to be symbols. One could also refer "selected" to those things which preceded, "similar to those honored according to," etc. The Lexicons are ignorant of the word "representation" <note>original: "ἀπεικασμὸν" (apeikasmon)</note>. *Hesychius* explains "representations" <note>original: "Ἀπεικάσματα" (Apeikasmata)</note> as "likenesses." The *Author of the Book of Wisdom, XIII, 10*, calls the Gods of the Egyptians, as it seems, "representations of animals." This word appears more frequently in Plato.

9. **One-eyed.**] To sacrifice victims that are blind in their eyes, or spotted, was forbidden to the Hebrews just as much as to the Egyptians, as *Huet* teaches in *Demonstratio Evangelica IV, II, 1.* I would not believe that "one-eyed" <note>original: "ἑτερόφθαλμα" (heterophthalma)</note> should be translated as "various-colored eyes" in this place, as it seemed to the *Illustrious Man in his notes on Chariton VII, 5*, although he teaches that this meaning is in the word. *Moeris the Atticist* says: "one-eyed" <note>original: "ἑτερόφθαλμον" (heterophthalmon)</note> is Attic; "single-eyed" <note>original: "μονόφθαλμον" (monophthalmon)</note> is Common Greek. On this, consult the *Learned Man.*

10. **Observations.**] He uses this word well, for "observations" <note>original: "παρατηρήσεις" (paratērēseis)</note> are properly anxious and attentive observations, as "observing" <note>original: "παρατηροῦντες" (paratērountes)</note> above in III, 5 and 10. *Plutarch, Volume II, p. 363 B*, says "to make the observation accurate." The *Most Learned Kypke* excellently asserted the force of the word in his notes on *Luke’s Gospel XVII, 20.* The second to last syllable fell out in the *Meerman Manuscript.*

11. **And of the...**] "And" seems it should be deleted, and a little later "leading forward," for he returns to "observations." <term>REISKE</term>

# PORPHYRIUS

The **sealers of calves** <note>original: "μοσχοσφραγιστῶν" (moschospragistōn)</note>, whose duties extend even to the composition of books. They are even more meticulous regarding birds; for instance, they do not eat the **turtle-dove**. For they say that the **hawk** <note>original: "ἱέραξ" (hierax)</note>, having captured this creature on many occasions, lets it go free, granting its life as a reward for their mating. Therefore, lest they should unknowingly happen upon such a bird <note>i.e., one that had mated with a sacred hawk</note>, they have chosen to abstain from the entire species. These are some of the common religious observances, but they differ according to the classes of priests and are specific to each god. However, the **purifications** <note>original: "ἁγνεῖαι" (hagneiai)</note> of them all involved cleansing...

<column-break/>

The **sealers of calves** <note>original: "μοσχοσφραγισταὶ" (moschospragistai)</note>, that is, "calf-men" or "those who mark calves with a seal," are so named: a practice which proceeded even to the writing of books. This they do even more carefully regarding birds. For they believe that the turtle-dove, to cite this as an example, must not be eaten by them. For they say the hawk often, when it has caught that bird, lets it go unharmed, granting safety as a reward for sexual union. Lest, therefore, they should fall upon any such bird from among them, they judged that they must be forbidden from the entire genus. And indeed, there are some common rites.

---

They used sacred objects, for the sealing of which according to a certain ritual priests were employed, whom they thereafter call **sealers of calves**; the knowledge itself is called **the art of sealing calves**. See *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus*: I, 70, and what we said regarding Book II, 55. I would not dare to strike out "proceeding" <note>original: "προάγουσα" (proagousa)</note>. Truly, it refers to the "observation of the art," as in another matter above in III, 25.

13. **"For instance, not to eat the turtle-dove."**] Which for others is among the delicacies of the table, as is clear from *Plautus' Mostellaria* I, 1, 43 and *Athenaeus* IV, 1. We read, however, that the Tartars and other nations abominate their use. The Egyptians, out of a superstitious suspicion of impurity, drove them away from tables and altars, as *Spencer* writes in *Ritual Laws* I, 5, 3. Our author assigns another cause for the matter: lest they should by chance happen upon a turtle-dove released by a hawk (a bird sacred to them), just as their young sometimes escape, as *V. Aldrovandi* explains in *Ornithology* Book XV, 10, p. 245; which I learned from *Slichter's Dissertation on the Turtle-dove*, for that book is not at hand. But Porphyry indicates more closely the reason why the hawk releases the turtle-dove.

14. **"Giving back safety as a reward for mating."**] Those lines of *Flaccus* <note>Horace</note> in *Epode* XVI, 31 come to mind:
> *A wondrous love! It pleases that tigers lie with deer,*
> *And the dove is defiled by the kite.*
"Mating" <note>original: "Μίξις" (mixis)</note>, "to be mixed," and similar terms regarding sexual intercourse

<column-break/>

are quite frequent, and not only regarding a man who has a matter with a woman, as *M. Thomas* thought, but also regarding a woman with a man; even the **most Attic** <note>original: "Ἀττικωτάτοις" (Attikōtatois) - referring to the purest Greek style</note> writers employ that word, as was rightly observed by *Bosius* in response to *Thomas*. However, you will mostly find it in the former way. The Latin *miscere* (to mix) is very well known. The peoples of the East and others speak in the same way, for among most nations, with nature as the guide, the word has taken on that usage. Otherwise, the chastity of turtle-doves is common knowledge; those curious about nature report that they have one mate and do not admit another. See *Bochart: Hieroz:* II, I, 4.

15. **"They avoided."**] <note>original: "Περιΐξαντο" (Periixanto)</note> They shun, they beware of. *D'Orville* clearly brings out the force and power of the word in his notes on *Chariton* I, 13. The *Learned Men* <note>original: "V. D." (Viri Docti)</note> also have much to say for illustrating *Paul's* Second Letter to Timothy II, 16. Presently, the word "but" <note>original: "δὲ" (de)</note> after "classes" is missing in the *Meerman* manuscript.

16. **"They were purified of all things."**] The passage is correct. The meaning is that although religions were diverse according to the diversity of places, nevertheless all priests, wherever they were, when they performed their **purifications** <note>original: "ἁγνείας" (hagneias)</note> or "acts of chastity," then "they were purified" <note>original: "ἐκαθάρευον" (ekathareuon)</note>; what this "being purified" was, he explains a little later. *Reiske* says: "Excellent." *Valckenaer*, with poor judgment, had changed "of all things" <note>original: "πάντων" (pantōn)</note> into "altogether" <note>original: "πάντως" (pantōs)</note>, and had thrust that into the text itself against the consensus of everyone.

17. **"And this time..."**] Namely, of the purifications then when... — for those purifications...
