# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Rr 3 <-

None were the same: others differed according to the class of priests and were assigned to specific gods. However, rites of chastity and purifications were observed among all of them. The time for these occurred whenever they were about to perform some act of sacred worship, defined by a specific number of days—sometimes forty-two, sometimes more, or fewer—yet in such a way that it never fell below a seven-day period. During this time, they abstained from all living creatures <note>original: "animatis"; referring to meat</note>, from all pot-herbs and legumes, and above all from sexual intercourse with women; for they avoided the company of males at all other times as well. Three times a day they washed themselves with cold water: when they rose from bed, before they took their midday meal, and when they went to bed. If it happened by chance that they were defiled by a discharge in their sleep, they immediately <margin>This time was consecrated when they wished to perform the established sacred rites. "The time of the purifications was a predefined number of days" is the same as "the purifications began before the day of the general sacrifice by so many days." REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note> Soon after, the Meerman and Cambridge Manuscripts had "two" <note>original: "δύο"</note>; the older ones "of two" <note>original: "δυοῖν"</note>. In expressing the dual form, the ancients are not consistent; sometimes they write "duein," sometimes "duoin," for this should not be attributed everywhere to the negligence of scribes. Read Duker on Thucydides Book IV, 8, and Wesseling on Diodorus, p. 531.</margin> <margin>18. **And never falling short of seven:** From this, some conclude that the weekly cycle of days among the Hebrews was taken from mathematical discipline and the intimate storehouse of Egyptian antiquity. <margin>19. **From every living creature — from every pot-herb etc.:** These three things were required above all for purification: to fast, to wash, and to remain chaste. How these institutes of the Egyptians agree with those of the Hebrews is shown by Marsham, Section IX, and Spencer, *On Ritual Laws*, III, 5. # On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> <-

...moderate strength was also available for their labors; for they sustained many burdens in the performance of sacred rites, and undertook many services which seemed greater than what might suit common human strength. They divided the night for the observation of celestial bodies, and sometimes for sanctification <note>original: "sanctificationem" / "ἁγιστείαν" - referring to ritual purification or holy acts</note>. They distributed the day to the worship of the gods, during which three or four times—at morning and evening, when the sun reached the mid-heaven, and when it moved toward its setting—they honored him with hymns. For the rest of the time, being at leisure for arithmetic and geometric contemplations, they were always working on and thinking out something; and in general, they were occupied in empirical study. They were accustomed to use the same exercise even on winter nights...

...they remain wakeful, as they have no concern for providing for themselves, and they are liberated from that evil master: luxury. Indeed, their 8 unwearied labor and constant perseverance bear witness to the men's fortitude, while their lack of desire demonstrates their self-control. They considered it among the most impious of acts to sail away from Egypt, being cautious of foreign luxuries and habits; for it seemed holy only to those who were 10 compelled by 11 royal duties. There was 12 great concern among them to remain faithful to their ancestral customs. If they were found to have transgressed even in small matters, they were expelled. 13 And as for the truth—

<column-break/>

...they were wakeful in the study of letters, as those who had no care for any profit, and were free from the slavery of that troublesome mistress, luxury. Truly, their indefatigable labor and constant endurance manifest their patience, and their emptiness of all desires manifests their continence. Indeed, since they avoided foreign manners and luxury, they judged it to be a great impiety to depart from Egypt. For it seemed permitted only to those who were forced to handle royal business: yet even for these men, there was such great care for ancestral institutions that if they were caught violating them even a little, they were cast out. <margin>Even the wealthiest neglect these things. See Pollux: I, 71.</margin>

8. **Unwearied labor.** <note>original: "Πόνος ἀτρυτος"</note>] An elegant epithet. Look into *Suidas*, whom I see already cited by the illustrious *Alberti*, who presents another passage from *Herodotus* regarding *Hesychius* under the letter V.

9. **Bear witness.** <note>original: "Ἀπομαρτυρεῖ"</note>] That is, "sufficiently bears witness," as the prefix *apo-* usually functions in compound words. See the note on Book II, 30.

10. **Royal duties.** <note>original: "Βασιλικὰς χρείας"</note>] The word "duties" <note>original: "χρείας"</note> is missing in the *Leipzig* manuscript, which is an error. Unless in other books it was "by royal assemblies" or "by royal commands." —REISKE. *Chreia* means *business, office, or duty*, specifically the kind where the industry of others is necessarily required. Just like our author, *Josephus* attributes "royal duties" to those who take care of the king's business. Antiquities XVI, 8, 3. Read more in the best commentators on *Luke, Acts of the Apostles VI*, 3.

11. **Compelled.** <note>original: "Ἀπηναγκασμένοις"</note>] This must be explained according to a notable Greek custom. You have here not so much a compound word (which you would seek in vain in the Dictionaries, but which *Eunapius* also uses in *Maximus* p. 102) as a simple word whose full meaning must be sought from the context. For the sake of brevity, they often omit certain words, giving a hint through a preposition which, because it cannot stand alone, they attach to the verb. But as soon as you supply the omitted parts, the preposition changes its position and occupies its proper place. In Porphyry, therefore, "compelled" <note>original: "ἀπηναγκασμένοις"</note> is the same as if it read "compelled to sail away from Egypt," which preceded it. This passage can therefore shed light on those troubled words of *Luke* in the Gospel VI, 35: "lending, hoping for nothing in return" <note>original: "δαν. μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες"</note>, that is, "hoping for something back from the one to whom you lend." The learned *Abresch* explained this beautifully in his notes on *Matthew XXII*, 5.

12. **Concern to remain in ancestral [customs].** <note>original: "Λόγος ἐμμεῖναι τοῖς πατρίοις"</note>] The passage seemed corrupt and mutilated. Therefore I supplied and corrected it to "concerning the remaining." —VALENTINI. I wish it had not been done. He thought *logos* here meant "speech" or "word," when it actually means *care*, as in the phrase "to make a study of" or "to have regard for" in *Lucian's* Hermotimus 23 and others. However, I have restored "to remain" <note>original: "ἐμμεῖναι"</note> to the author from the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, whereas previously it was published as "remaining." "To remain in ancestral customs," just as elsewhere one "remains in the law, in faith," and similar things, regarding which see Book II, 25. That usage in *Euripides'* Medea 753 is rarer: "to abide by what I hear from you."

13. **And as for the [truth] etc.**] The discussion concerns the Egyptians.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

The true method of philosophizing was preserved among the prophets, the robe-keepers <note>original: "sacrificos" / "ἱεροσολισαῖς" - those responsible for the sacred vestments</note>, and the scribes, as well as the time-keepers <note>original: "horologos" - priests who observed the stars to determine the hours for rituals</note>. However, the remaining multitude of priests, shrine-keepers, and attendants also live purely and with abstinence, though not with such exacting diligence as the former. These are the things recorded concerning the Egyptians by a man who was a lover of truth and accurate, who practiced philosophy among the Stoics not in a vain manner, but with great solidity. <note>This refers to Chaeremon of Alexandria, a 1st-century Stoic philosopher and tutor to Nero.</note>

->§ 9.<-

The philosophy concerning the truth was found among the prophets, the robe-keepers, and the sacred scribes, and furthermore the time-keepers. But the rest of the multitude of priests, shrine-bearers <note>original: "παστοφόρων" (pastophoroi)</note>, temple-wardens, and servants of the gods, likewise keep themselves pure, though certainly not with such degree of accuracy and self-control. Such are the testimonies regarding the Egyptians by a man who loves truth and is precise, having philosophized most practically among the Stoics.

->§ 9.<-

***

<margin>On the Egyptians and other ministers of the sacred rites. Regarding these, see Caussin, *Observations on Horapollo's Hieroglyphics* 37 & 39, and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* Book VI, p. 456. VALENTINUS.</margin> Many orders and families of priests there cared for the worship of the Gods and all its rituals: the **Prophets**. Others were occupied with functions of lesser dignity, whom the Author mentions immediately. The celebrated Jablonski explains these most diligently in his *Introduction to the Egyptian Pantheon*, section 38.

14. **Robe-keepers and sacred scribes.**] The former are called *stolistai* <note>original: "σολισαὶ"</note> by Plutarch, Volume II, p. 366 E. Others are also called **sacred scribes**, as if they were the writers of sacred matters or of the more holy letters which were set forth in the sacred books. Jannes and Jambres <note>Traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note> are included in their number according to Eusebius. See Gale on Iamblichus' *On the Mysteries*, p. 183, and Wesseling on Diodorus II, 16.

15. **Time-keepers.**] These are the **hour-watchers** <note>original: "ὡρέσκοποι"</note> in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI, p. 633, who adds that they held a timepiece in their hand. In that passage, those presiding officers are mentioned in a nearly reversed order: but there he is speaking of the order in which they proceeded in ceremonies. The **singer** <note>original: "ᾠδὸς"</note> is said to proceed first, whom our Author does not mention here, but below in section 9, where he will be discussed.

16. **Shrine-bearers and temple-wardens.**] From carrying the *pastoi* <note>original: "παστοῖς"</note>—the bridal chambers or small shrines of the Gods, about which Cuper says much in *Harpocrates*, p. 129—they were called **pastophoroi** and **sacred-bearers**. In place of this name, Caussin tried to foist a new kind of word, *passophronous*, upon writers, but the assembly of learned men was indignant. See Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus I, 29. Regarding their dignity, there is more than one opinion among the learned. Since they carried the shrines or small temples on their shoulders, and since our Author joins them with the temple-wardens, and since Clement of Alexandria mentions them in the last place, and finally since Diodorus indicates they were almost equal to the Athenian **heralds**, I hardly doubt they were ministers of a lower rank. I know that F. Boerner, in *Ancient Egyptian Medicine* section 40, concludes the opposite from the passage in Clement, but he by no means persuades me that they were most eminent in dignity, since Clement himself in *The Instructor* III, 2, indicates they were attendants. Apuleius in *Metamorphoses* Book X, p. 719, says this was the name of a **most holy college** and indicates it was a venerable college on p. 776; but even so, they could be called this by Apuleius especially because they practiced medicine and took care of the human body, as Clement of Alexandria teaches. Physicians, moreover, belonged to the "clergy," as they call it, so it seems. In the Leiden and Meerman editions, the word for "attendants" is written as *hypepourgon* <note>original: "ὑπεπουργῶν"</note>, and the oldest editions are no different.

17. **By a man who loves truth...**] This seems otherwise to many, for the judgments of the ancients regarding Chaeremon are quite discordant. See the notes to section 6. Certainly Strabo and others report things in a different way. It is believed that Dionysius of Alexandria was his disciple and succeeded him in the School of Alexandria. See Suidas under "Dionysius of Alexandria" and—

Our author speaks according to the custom of the Platonists, by whom the body is frequently called a *tent* <note>original: "σκῆνος"</note> or *tabernacle* <note>original: "σκήνωμα"</note>. # On Abstinence, Book IV.

For among them, the statues of the gods display a human form as far as the neck, but they have the face of a bird, a lion, or some other animal set upon them; or conversely, they show the body of another animal placed beneath a human head. By these means, they clearly signify that, according to the judgment of the gods, these beings share a fellowship with one another: and that the animals—both the tame and the wild—are kindred to us, not without a certain divine will. Hence even the lion is worshipped as a god: and a certain part of Egypt, which they call a "nome" <note>original: *pascuum* / *nomon*. A 'nome' was an administrative district in ancient Egypt.</note>, is named Leontopolites <note>The "City of Lions."</note> after the lion, while another is named after the ox

<column-break/>

and of man; for one might see among them a figure that is human-shaped as far as the neck, but possessing the face of a bird, or a lion, or some other animal. And again, there is the human head with the parts of other animals placed either beneath or above it. Through these things they show that by the will of the gods these also have communion with one another, and that the wild among the beasts are our foster-brothers and tame, not without some divine purpose. Whence also the lion is worshipped as a god, and a certain part of Egypt, which they call a nome, has the name Leontopolites, and another

---

<margin>
They mixed beasts and men into the *likeness of the god*. <note>original: *homoiosin tou theou*</note> Or more briefly: *and in the likeness of a god*. They mingled beasts and men for the "assimilation" (that is, the likeness) of the deity: that is, they composed the image by which they wished to represent the God from a human image joined with a certain bestial one. **REISKE.** <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist.</note> I also follow **Eusebius**: *the likeness of the god and men*. Then he says *and of men*. **Tacitus** indicates this matter among others: *Histories, Book V. The Egyptians worship many animals and composite images.* **Minucius Felix**, chapter 28: *concerning gods mixed from a goat and a man, and dedicating gods with the faces of lions and dogs.* **Tertullian** aptly calls it a "two-formed deity" in *Apology, 16*. Even today, on the monuments of the Egyptians, the heads of diverse animals are seen, either alone or placed on other bodies. See the most refined **Shaw**, *Geographical Observations on Syria, Egypt, etc., chapter 5, page 112.*
</margin>

5. *The wild among the beasts.*] One might also read "and the wild," which would agree well with what follows; then "foster-brothers" <note>original: *syntropha*</note> should be understood in a broader sense, as if he spoke of every kind of living thing: *the whole living world was divided into the tame and the wild*, as **Plato** says in the *Statesman, page 532 D.* But nothing should be changed against the authority of the manuscripts.

6. *Is worshipped as a god and —*] There were certain animals which all Egyptians worshipped in common, and there were also those worshipped separately. Besides our author, **Strabo**, Book XVII, page 559, and others teach this. The Egyptians called the divisions according to the great parts of Egypt *nomous* <term>Nomes: administrative districts</term>, as **Proclus** says. See **Wesseling** on **Diodorus Siculus**, I, 73. **Lipsius** alone is correct here with *nomon* <note>distinguishing 'nomos' (law) from 'nomós' (district/pasture)</note>, which you see restored. The neglected distinction between *nómos* and *nomós* often leads interpreters into error, on which matter see **P. Leopardus**, *Emendations, VII, 18.*

7. *Leontopolites, another Ox, another Lycopolis.*] **Jerome**, Book II, *Against Jovinianus, 7*: *Almost every city in Egypt venerates beasts and monsters, whence also the cities among them are named from the vocabularies of animals: Leonto (Lion), Cyno (Dog), Lyco (Wolf), Busyris, Thmuis, which is interpreted as "he-goat."* There were therefore many cities of this mark, which worshipped those animals in particular from which they took their name. ...one is called Busirite, another Lycopolite. 8. For they thus venerated the force and power of God, which is diffused into all things, through the communal animals which each god had presented. <margin>...one Busirite.</margin>
It will be noted, add Leontopolis from *Diodorus* I, 84. *Eusebius* calls it Busirites. It is pronounced both ways, as is usual for variations in those names. Instead of Lycopolite, the same author says Cynopolite. It matters little, for there was a Nome <note>An administrative district in ancient Egypt</note> of each name. But the Lycopolite Nome should not be confused with the other Lycopolis in the Sebennytic Nome. This one of ours in the Thebaid seems to have been the birthplace of Plotinus. Read *Fabricius* on *Our Author* in the Life of Plotinus: Greek Library IV, 26. p. 92. *Meerman* incorrectly reads "another Busirite."

<margin>8. For the [power] over—]</margin>
Perhaps: "For they worshipped the universal power of God (namely, that which permeates all things) through the associated animals, but the partial powers through those which each of the gods provided." They worshipped the entire power of God pertaining to all things and remaining everywhere in domestic and tame animals, etc. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>.

<margin>9. Which each of the gods provided.]</margin>
In *Eusebius*: "which each of the gods provided." The learned Vigerus translates the whole period thus: *For indeed they are accustomed to worship the supreme power of God over all things through animals naturally joined and associated with them, which the individual gods declared.* I have rendered it as if "associated" <note>original: συννόμων</note> signified the animals that were raised in the individual Nomes, each of which provided a certain god. For just as one province provided a lion, another a wolf, etc., so the variety of divine power was represented by the various animals of these prefectures. I think the words can best be read as "which (i.e., the power) each of the gods showed." They worshipped that power which the individual gods displayed under the images of various animals. <term>VALENTINI</term>. The common reading holds up well, as rightly noted by *Victorius* and *Vigerus* on *Eusebius*. Valentini had ineptly corrected the text itself to "each god."

<column-break/>

<margin>10. Water and fire.]</margin>
See *Causin* on Hieroglyphics 41. Book I. <term>VALENTINI</term>.

<margin>11. In the opening—]</margin>
This is the same ceremony which they still employ in Egypt today, calling it <insert>Opening of the Canal</insert> <note>original Arabic: فتح الخليج (Fath al-Khalij)</note>, when they open the Nile canal led through the city of Cairo by tearing down the dam. There is no one who has published an account of his journey to Egypt who does not mention this ceremony. <term>REISKE</term>. See the most accurate *Shaw*, Geographical Observations on Syria, Egypt, etc. chapter 5. Moreover, Sarapis is the same as Serapis, as is well known. Compare *Vives* on *Augustine's* City of God XVIII, 5.

<margin>12. The singer of hymns.]</margin>
The "Hymn-singers" <note>original: Ὑμνῳδοὶ</note> are the same as those elsewhere called "Singers," concerning whose office see *Clement of Alexandria*, Stromata VI. p. 663. They were also called "Paeanists," such as the "Paeanists of Jupiter-Sun-Sarapis at Rome," in *Reinesius*, Inscriptions II, 68. We know that hymns were very frequent in the sacred rites of the ancients. See also *Spanheim* on *Callimachus'* Hymn to Jove 1, and what sort of hymn-singers other nations had in *Kuhn* on *Pollux* I, 36.

13. **Upon the road.**] In Eusebius: *threshold*. <note>original: "ουδοῦ"</note> Truly much better. See Scaliger on Tibullus: Book I, Elegy 3. Kircher in *The Pamphilian Obelisk*: Interpretation page 491. VALENTINI. Nothing is more true: what had been an error of the workmen in the *First Edition*, was ridiculously transcribed into the following ones as "upon the road." <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ"</note> Meerman: *standing upon the threshold*. Regarding the matter itself, see Cuper in *Harpocration* page 52. Moreover, the phrase "to awaken the god" <note>original: "ἐγείρειν τὸν θεὸν"</note> is a proper expression, and not unknown even to our own sacred rites. Iamblichus: *On the Mysteries* V, 23: *he awakens the gods*. Where see Gale. The Leipzig Manuscript gives "may he awaken."

14. **The participants.**] Perhaps "the providers," <note>original: "τὰ πάροχα"</note> and especially the more... when they worshipped those things, they then worshipped the deities from whom those things had proceeded, and those deities all the more, as they had found those things more numerous and fruitful for life. REISKE. Eusebius: *they worship the participants and especially more of the...* — The sense is clear enough, provided that it is punctuated as has now been done. They worshipped those things which were participants in the divine nature, and since these were many, they especially venerated those which participate most in the divine nature.

15. **They worship a human in Anubis.**] In Eusebius: *Anabis* page 94 and page 117 *Anamis*. VALENTINI. Not otherwise in the *Victorian Edition*, whose wandering typesetter the later editors rashly followed, for which reason I restored *Anabis* instead of *Anubis*. And so it is in the Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts. Theodore of Gaza <note>original: "Theodor: de Ang."</note> writes that this happens in the village of Anabis. Minucius Felix chapter 29: *The Egyptians certainly choose a human for themselves whom they may worship, him alone they propitiate, him they consult about all things, to him they slay victims*, where see more from Learned Men and on Clement in Cotelerius page 670. The matter was different among the Greeks, by whom "good men" <note>original: "ἄνθρωποι ἀγαθοὶ"</note> were not worshipped unless after they had been translated into "the higher powers." <note>original: "τοὺς κρείττονας"</note> Next, poorly in Eusebius: "of these is sacrificed." The same later more correctly: "is burned up." However, "is burned" <note>original: "κάεται"</note> is also in the Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts.

16. **Which indeed a little later he might eat...**] Eusebius: *But he might eat a little later those things prepared and set before him as his own, as if for a human.* This reading is to be preferred. The translator renders the passage thus: *But he, a little later, eats only those things which have been prepared and set before him from his private larder, just as for a human.* Those things which Porphyry has in the same place concerning the Hawk and the Beetle are illustrated by Causin in his notes on Horapollo, etc.

# PORPHYRY

...discovered which animals are more pleasing to the gods than even men: 17 as the hawk is to the Sun, possessing a nature entirely composed of blood and spirit <note>original: *pneuma*, the vital breath</note>, yet feeling pity even for man, and wailing over a prostrate corpse, 18 and casting earth upon the eyes, in which 19 they believe the solar light resides. They have observed that it lives for many years, 20 and after its life, it possesses the power of divination; and when it has been released from the body 21, it is most rational 22 and prophetic, and it can even consecrate statues...

<column-break/>

...they discovered which animals are more pleasing to the gods than men: as the hawk is to the sun: whose entire nature they say consists of blood and spirit. It takes pity on man, and laments over his corpse whenever it happens upon one, and sprinkles earth into the eyes, in which they believe the solar light dwells. And indeed, they have noticed that it lives for many years: but when it has departed from life, it obtains the power of divining, and when it has been released from the body, it is most rational and a foreteller of future things. For they assert that it can both perfect the statues of the gods and move temples.

17. **To the Sun, a hawk.**] Eusebius reads: "sacred things and," which ought to be corrected from our author. We have already seen above that the hawk was a bird sacred to the Sun. Our author and others bring forward various reasons for this. See the discussions by the most distinguished Cuper in *Harpocrates* p. 72.

18. **And casting earth.**] Eusebius reads: "casting," but incorrectly. See Viger there. Kuhn, on Aelian's *Various History* X, 4, illustrates from this the once very common custom of throwing some dust upon a dead person, which was a form of burial.

19. **The solar [light] resides—**] Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* X. 14: "For hawks alone of birds always look easily and without pain into the rays of the sun, being least of all troubled by the glare; they travel to the highest...

<column-break/>

...heights, and the divine flame does not hurt them at all." It is therefore no wonder that the Egyptians consecrated this bird to the Sun, whence Aelian (VII, 9) mentions the "Hawk-feeders" as Priests of Apollo <note>The Greeks identified the Egyptian Horus/Ra with Apollo</note>.

20. **And after its life—**] Because it was sacred to Apollo, the Egyptians attributed a prophetic power to this bird, which the license of superstition maintained even after death. Read Diodorus I, 87, and there see Wesseling and Gale on Iamblichus' *Mysteries* VI, 3.

21. **Released from the body.**] Using the same turn of phrase "to release the soul from the body" below in sections 10 and 18. 22. **And most prophetic.**] Perhaps "most prophetic and most fit to consecrate statues," and to prevail with the greatest power in instructing small seals or images (commonly called <term>apotelesmata</term> or <term>طلسمان</term> <note>Arabic: *talisman*</note> talismans) with <term>telestic</term> <note>The ancient art of consecrating statues to animate them with divine power</note> force (that is, by that power which, in hidden ways, can ward off certain evils from a person or place, or forewarn of future things) and to "move temples," that is, those small shrines in which they are sometimes displayed.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

->**The Scarab Beetle**<-

An ignorant person, unskilled in divine matters, might despise and loathe the scarab beetle; yet the Egyptians worship it as a living image of the Sun. For since the scarab is said to be of the male sex only, it discharges its seed into the dung, and having shaped it into a sphere, it rolls it backward with its hind legs, just as the sun moves across the heavens; it follows a cycle of twenty-eight days, which is the lunar period. In a similar manner, they philosophize about the ram, the crocodile, the vulture, and the ibis, and indeed about every single animal: so that from their prudence and divine wisdom, they proceeded to the veneration and worship of even these creatures. But the ignorant man does not even notice how they do not follow the common [path] of men...

<column-break/>

...and to move the temples. <note>original: "καὶ ναοὺς κινεῖν"</note> An ignorant man might be disgusted by the scarab beetle, being unacquainted with divine things. But the Egyptians revered it as a living image of the sun. For every scarab is male, and releasing its seed into a marshy place, and having made it spherical, it pushes it back with its hind feet, as the sun does the heaven. And it awaits a period of twenty-eight days, which is lunar. Thus also they philosophize something about the ram, and something else about the crocodile, and about the vulture, and the ibis, and generally concerning each of the animals; as if from wisdom and excessive divine knowledge, they came to the worship even of animals. But the ignorant man does not even suspect this very thing, how they did not [follow] the common...

# PORPHYRY

->On Abstinence from Animal Food<-

...carried away by a common current that perceives nothing, they clearly wandered into the path of ignorance themselves. However, having surpassed the ignorance of the masses—which is the first thing everyone encounters—they deemed those things worthy of veneration which to the many were of no value.

§ 10. In addition to what has been said, there was another factor that led them toward a belief in this veneration of animals: they understood that the soul of every animal, once released from the body, is rational <note>original: λογικήν (logikēn)</note>, possesses foreknowledge of the future, is capable of delivering oracles <note>original: χρηματιστικήν (chrēmatistikēn)</note>, and is effective in all the same ways as a human soul is when released from the body. Therefore, they rightly honored them and, as far as possible, abstained from them.

<column-break/>

...following a certain flux which perceives nothing, they themselves wandered into the way of folly. But having overcome the ignorance of the common people, into which every person first falls, they judged those things worthy of divine worship which were held in no esteem by most.

§ 10. It is added that, no less than the other things mentioned above, this also induced them to this cult of animals: that they had perceived the soul of every animal, when it had been released from the body, to be both rational and possessing foreknowledge of the future and the power of prophecy, and to be the achiever of all things which even a human being, free from the body, could perform. Whence they deservedly held them in honor, and from the eating of them, as far as was pos— <note>The Latin text cuts off at "fie-", matching the catchword "fie-" from the previous page's metadata.</note>

---

<margin>Which to most people seem worthy of contempt and ridicule. REISKE. On the "common current," see the notes on Book II, 40.</margin>

28. *Ignorance.*] I have restored "ignorance" <note>Greek: ἄγνοιαν</note> in place of "purity" <note>Greek: ἀγνείαν</note>. VALENTIUS. Most truly. The translator, as well as the Leipzig and Meerman Codices, agree; therefore, the lost reading rightly recovers its possession. It seems, however, that "first" <note>πρώτῃ</note> should be read, which I have given, as it does no violence to the Author; previously it was read as "the first" <note>πρώτη</note>, from which you could also read "the first [ignorance] which encounters everyone." Regarding the following phrase "deemed worthy of veneration," *Wetstein* compares Luke in the Gospel, 20:35.

It is well <unclear>erg</unclear> <note>likely "ergo" (therefore)</note> transferred to the power of prophesying in this place. Next, the *Meerman* manuscript has "they honored as," omitting the "and."

5. *A human being, released.*] See the notes on § 10.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> T t <-

...they were able to do so, they abstained. Since there are many other reasons why the Egyptians worshiped gods through animals, and because the discourse would turn out to be longer than seems appropriate for the present purpose if all were to be reviewed, let these suffice for now. However, one thing must not be overlooked: when they embalm the corpses of the noble-born, they take out the belly separately and place it in a chest; and along with other things they perform for the sake of the deceased's rational part, the chest is brought out toward the sun, and an oration is delivered by one of the embalmers on behalf of the one being buried, testifying for him. This oration Euphantus <note>original: "Euphantus," likely a historian of Egypt or a Pythagorean philosopher</note> translated from the native tongue in this manner: "O Lord Sun, and all you gods who have given life to men, receive me, and grant me a dwelling-place among the eternal gods..."

<column-break/>

...Since there is a long account of the reason why the Egyptians revered the gods through animals, and it is greater than the present undertaking, what has been revealed about them is sufficient. That, however, must not be passed over: that when they embalm <gloss>6</gloss> those of noble birth who have died, they take out the belly <gloss>7</gloss> separately and, placing it in a chest with the other things they perform for the dead, they hold the chest toward the sun and bear witness, while one of the embalmers makes a speech on behalf of the dead. And the speech, which <gloss>8</gloss> Euphantus translated from the native dialect, is as follows: <gloss>9</gloss> "O Lord Sun, and all gods, you who gave life to men, receive..."

<gloss>6. When they embalm.]</gloss> The Egyptian embalmers <note>original: "ταριχευταὶ" (taricheutai)</note> and the preservation of bodies are very well known, even from the sacred scriptures themselves. The custom was so frequent that even sacred animals had their own embalmers: hence the *Mummies*, as they are called, which physicians of our own and the previous age have examined most diligently, explaining the method of curing and preserving them. See *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus I, 91* and *Herodotus II, 86.*

<gloss>7. Taking out the belly.]</gloss> *Plutarch, Volume II, page 996 E:* "Just as the Egyptians, having taken out the belly of the dead and cutting it open toward the sun, cast it away as the cause of all the sins a man has committed." And concerning the same, page 159 B: "Those who dissect the corpse showed it to the sun, then threw those parts into the river. They then take care of the rest of the body, it having now become pure."

See the *Interpreters on Lucian, Alexander the False Prophet, IV, 24.* In Latin, they are called *Domini* a hundred times. # PORPHYRY
### P.

Receive me, and deliver me to the eternal gods as a fellow-dweller. For I have continued to worship the gods, whom my parents showed to me, for as long a time as I held my life in **that age** <note>original: *ἐκείνῳ αἰῶνι* — likely referring to the afterlife or the eternal realm</note>; and I always honored those who fathered my body. Of other men, I neither killed any, nor did I defraud anyone of a deposit <note>a legal term for property held in trust</note>, nor did I commit any other incurable evil. But if indeed I sinned at all during my life, either by eating or drinking things which were not lawful, I did not sin through myself, but through these—pointing to the chest in which the stomach was kept. And having said these things—

<column-break/>

—transfer me to the eternal habitation. For I have always pursued with piety the gods whom I received from my parents to be worshipped, as long as I led my life in that age: and I always honored those who procreated my body. Truly, of other men, I neither killed anyone, nor did I defraud anyone of a deposit, nor did I afflict anyone with any other destructive evil. But if I sinned in any way in my life, either by eating or drinking from those things which were not lawful, I did not sin through myself but through these—at the same time the chest in which the stomach was was pointed out: and when he had said these things, he would cast the chest into the river. Then the rest of the body, as—

***

<margin>
*Wesseling: on Herodotus, Book I, p. 100.* There are many things in this speech about worshipping the Gods, honoring parents, etc., which seem to regard the Table of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and the so-called "Precepts of the Sons of Noah" <note>Seven universal moral laws in Jewish tradition</note>. Other things are also worthy of note: the immortality of the soul is asserted, the sun is said to receive souls, and mention is made of *that age* <note>original: *ἐκείνου αἰῶνος*</note>, all of which *S. Le Moyne (Dissertation on Jeremiah 23:6)* surrounds with much light from the antiquities of the Hebrews; however, he is not everywhere as solid as he is ingenious. The words *those who gave life* are missing in the *Leipzig Manuscript*, and the *Meerman Manuscript* has *to receive* instead of *receive*, but that scribe frequently confuses the Greek letters *epsilon* and *alpha-iota*.
</margin>

10. **Eternal gods.**] Was Herodotus then mistaken, along with many others who report that the Egyptians believed the souls of men migrate into beasts? Shall we say they taught that the soul, having fallen from its seat, passes for a time through men and animals until it returns to its original place? This is the opinion of the *Celebrated Jablonski (Pantheon I, 2, 3)*. Or rather, was Egyptian Theology not the same throughout the whole kingdom, so that those priests whom *Herodotus* visited devised a circuit through various bodies, while others admitted the minds of the good immediately into the council of the Gods? This

<column-break/>

opinion is elaborated by the *Excellent Mosheim (on Cudworth’s System, Vol. I, p. 366)*. It is also possible that with the passage of time their Theology was changed in this part. Finally, a distinction can be made, as with the most ancient Philosophers, between the ethereal mind, which shares in reason, and the corporeal spirit, or sensing soul; of which the former did not migrate into men and beasts, but the latter did. The Distinguished Man <note>Wesseling</note> notes (ibid. p. 1042) that the difficulty can be removed by this observation. I am not permitted to be laborious here. Next, the *Leipzig Manuscript* does not have the words *the* and *whom*.

11. **In that age.**] I have already advised that these things are illustrated from Hebrew antiquities, who oppose *that age* to *this age*. This is commonly noted by *Interpreters on Matthew 12:22, Luke 20:35*, etc. See also *Huet on Origen’s Matthew, p. 497*. Instead of *that*, the *Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts* have *of those*.

12. **Defraud of a deposit.**] *To defraud* <note>original: *ἀποστερεῖν*</note> is to cheat or circumvent someone in any way. Hence it is joined with *to seize* above in section 3, and the word *to steal*, as in the *Gospel of Mark 10:19* and *Xenophon (Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, p. 685 B)*: *defrauders and thieves (Plato, Republic, p. 583 A)*. It is specifically said of those who deny they hold a deposit. Plato uses this very phrasing in *Republic IV*.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

...as if it were pure. And so they believed they needed to offer an excuse to the gods for those things which they had eaten or drunk, and for that reason, they judged that the belly should be treated with this manifest indignity <note>original: "uentrem manifesta hac contumelia afficiendum" - referring to the Egyptian practice of removing the intestines during mummification and casting them away as the source of sin</note>.

§ 11. But truly the Jews—before their institutions were first undermined by Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who attempted to Hellenize Jerusalem</note>, and later nearly destroyed by the Romans, when the temple in Jerusalem was captured and trampled by all those to whom it had been inaccessible, and the city was utterly overturned—they used to abstain from eating many other animals, but especially from the flesh of swine, a practice they observe even to this day. ...lived among themselves with such charity. Such were the Essenes, Pythagoreans, ancient Christians, and even many today. See *Holstenius* on our author’s *Life of Pythagoras* 20. For "matter" <note>original: πράγματι</note> *Meermann* reads "matter" <note>original: πράγματι</note>—foolishly.

10. **For to be unwashed—**] Since some trace the origin of Christian monks to these Essenes, the Jewish ascetics, it is no wonder that they once attracted such filth, a practice which has not yet fallen into disuse. See *Salmasius* on *Tertullian's On the Mantle*, page 68.

11. **And to wear white.**] There is a dispute regarding the Therapeutae <note>A similar ascetic group in Egypt.</note> as to whether they were Pagans, Jews (which is most likely), or Christians made from Alexandrian Jews. Certainly they led an ascetic life not much different from the Essenes. I will therefore add a passage from *Philo* saying the same thing with the same word: *On the Contemplative Life*, page 695 D: "whenever they come together, they are bright in their white garments."

12. **Administrators of common affairs.**] "The administrators" <note>original: Οἱ ἐπιμελ.</note> in *Eusebius*: This refers to the treasurers, about whom *Philo* speaks in the same way in *Eusebius's Preparation for the Gospel*, page 380 A: "each receiving their wages from such different tasks, they give it to the one elected treasurer."

<column-break/>

"and he, having received it, immediately buys the necessities, and provides abundant food, and the other things which human life requires."

13. **Undistinguished for—**] *Vigerus* explains what these words mean in his notes on *Eusebius*, though I do not think the word "into" <note>original: εἰς</note> should be deleted with him. The word "elected" <note>original: αἱρετοὶ</note> might be tempting, which is in the *Leiden Manuscript of Josephus*, but nothing should be changed against the consensus of so many others. The word "for" <note>original: πρὸς</note> can be construed with "elected." Indeed, he says the treasurers were created by common vote.

14. **But not one—they dwell as sojourners in each.**] Thus our author is correct, and *Eusebius* following him. *Josephus* has "they inhabit" <note>original: κατοικοῦσι</note>, but I would wish it rewritten in his text as well. Those words differ, and "to dwell as a sojourner" <note>original: μετοικεῖν</note> is properly said of inhabitants who do not enjoy the rights of citizenship, and hence it is applied to those who live in some city for a time, later to migrate elsewhere. See *Plato's Laws VIII*, page 919 E. By this observation, I believe the very serious controversy that occupies the Learned can be resolved: how *Josephus* can be brought into harmony with *Philo*, for whom (in the book *Every Good Man is Free*, page 678) the Essenes "dwell in villages, avoiding the cities." For they did not have a fixed domicile in any one city, but preferred to live in the fields; yet even so, when circumstances required, they were accustomed to stay and travel through cities for a time.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

Many of them live together in the same place; and for those of the same sect arriving from elsewhere, all things are open to them as if they were their own. Those who see them for the first time recognize them just like familiar friends. For this reason, whenever they travel, they are accustomed to carry nothing with them for the sake of expenses. They never change their shoes or garments unless they are either completely torn apart or consumed by age. They neither buy nor sell anything; instead, each person gives what they have to one in need and receives in return from that person what will be useful to themselves. Indeed, even without any such repayment, they are permitted to take what they need from whomever they wish.

They are so named. Just as the most learned *Brucker* <note>Johann Jakob Brucker, an 18th-century historian of philosophy</note> examines other matters of the Essenes, so he also interprets these things very gently in his *Critical History of Philosophy, Vol. II, p. 768*, regarding the phrase *on account of or in* <note>original: "propter vel in"</note>, so that they recited prayers composed *in or on account of* the rising of the sun, so that its light might fortunately shine upon them. Indeed, this could not be done more absurdly than if a Christian were to compose a song to the sun and praise that most excellent work. And there are things of this kind in the Holy Scriptures, as noted by *Aldrich in his edition of Josephus*. Those men waited impatiently for the sun to rise, and therefore, with a solemn formula, as if suppliants, they were able to ask repeatedly that it might put forth its light, just as they withdrew themselves with difficulty after sunset. *Philo, quoted in Eusebius, p. 379:* <note>original: "πρὶν δὲ ἥλιον ἀνασχεῖν..."</note> "Before the sun rises, they turn to their accustomed tasks, and after it sets, they return with difficulty." Remarkable is the passage of the *same author in On the Contemplative Life, p. 698, concerning the Therapeutae* <note>A Jewish ascetic sect in Egypt</note>: "Standing with their eyes and their whole body toward the dawn, when they behold the sun rising, they stretch their hands toward heaven and pray for prosperity and truth." # On Abstinence, Book IV.

Before the food is taken—which is chaste and pure—the priest offers a certain prayer, and it is not lawful for anyone to taste the food before this. After the meal, prayers are likewise offered by the same man. For they believe they must honor God both when beginning and when finishing. Afterward, laying aside these garments as if they were sacred, they return again to their labors. Having applied themselves to these until evening, they return and dine in the same manner, with guests also sitting at the table if any happen to have arrived. No shouting or tumult ever defiles the house. Instead, they grant one another the turn to speak or remain silent so modestly that to those on the outside, the silence of those within appears like some wonderful mystery. The cause of this is the constant sobriety of the men, who measure out their food and drink only to the point of sati-

<column-break/>

-faction for each. <note>The text here transitions from Latin to the original Greek source material being discussed.</note> The priest offers a prayer before the food, as it is holy and pure; and it is unlawful for anyone to taste it before the prayer. After they have dined, he prays again. Both at the beginning and at the end, they honor God. Then, laying aside their garments as sacred, they turn again to their works until evening. Returning, they dine <note>original: πίνουσι, literally "they drink," but used here for the evening meal</note> in the same way, with guests sitting with them if they happen to be present. Neither shouting nor noise ever defiles the house, but they yield to one another the turn to speak in an orderly fashion. And to those from the outside, the silence of those within appears as a formidable mystery. The cause of this is their continuous sobriety, and the fact that food and drink are measured out among them only until they are satisfied. To those who desire—

<margin>
The phrase "in linen coverings" is however missing in *Eusebius*: it seems therefore that in *Porphyry* three letters have fallen out. *Josephus* also uses "coverings" in reference to clothes in *Antiquities XV, 9, 2.* A little later, instead of "where," *Eusebius* has "in which."
</margin>

3. *Anyone before the—*] *Josephus* says "someone before," but there also the *Leiden Manuscript* has "before." *Eusebius* also has "someone." Next, the same author says "having dined, he prays," though some *Manuscripts* add "but," which *Valesius* changed to "at least," I know not by what authority. Certainly, the *Leipzig Manuscript* protects it, and in *Eusebius*, the word "rather" wrongly arose from the word "again." Then, after "they honor God," *Josephus* adds "as the provider of life."

<margin>

Because the Greeks gave a name to banquets from the inclination toward drinking, he seems to have used that word. It is well known
</margin>

<column-break/>

that passage of *Cicero: Letters to Friends IX. 24. "Our ancestors were wiser than the Greeks: they called them 'living together' (convivia), while the Greeks called them 'drinking together' (symposia) or 'dining together' (syndeipna), etc."* <note>original: "Sapientius nostri quam Graeci..." Cicero argues the Latin term emphasizes social life, while the Greek emphasizes consumption.</note> Hence, "symposium" is the same as "dinner." They also interpret our word in the sense of "feasting" in *Plutarch, Vol. I, p. 94. A.*

5. *Neither shouting—*] Thus I have restored it. Previously it was read as "so," which *Fogerolles* had also emended. *Valesius* had substituted "nor" from *Josephus*. Our reading is confirmed by *Eusebius* and the *Leipzig* and *Meerman Manuscripts*. *Valesius* soon uses "nor" again. We have given "neither," following the faith of the Hebrew and the Christian, although I am not unaware that no necessity compels us to reduce these particles to the same form. The *Leipzig* has "not noise," and so it is in the oldest *Editions*. The *Meerman* has "thurybos" <note>a misspelling of 'thorybos' (noise)</note>, by a perpetual confusion of letters.

6. *To those who desire.*] *Josephus* has "to the one who desires."

# PORPHYRY

For those who desire to join the sect, entrance is not immediately granted. Instead, the same rule of life is prescribed for them while they remain outside the community for a year. They are given a small axe <note>original: "axinarion/sarculo" - used for burying excrement, a practice of the Essenes</note>, a loincloth, and a white garment. 7 When the candidate has provided proof of his self-control during this period, he approaches closer to the way of life and 8 partakes in the purer waters for sanctification <note>referring to the ritual washings or baptisms of the sect</note>. However, he is not yet admitted into the communal life. For after this demonstration of endurance, his character is observed for two additional years. 9 If he then appears worthy, 10 he is thus admitted into the assembly.

§ 13. But before he may touch the communal food, he swears fearful oaths to them. First, that he will reverently worship the Divine; then, that he will observe justice toward men, and that he will harm no one, neither by his own intent nor by command, but will always hate the unjust and

<column-break/>

measured by their piety. For those who desire to be admitted into this society, the way is not opened immediately; rather, keeping the same diet, and having received a small hoe, a loincloth, and a white garment, a year must be spent outside. In which time, when they have now exhibited a trial of their continence, they approach nearer, and take from the purer waters for sanctification, although they are not yet admitted to the common living. For after this demonstration of continence, they spend two other years in the testing of their character. When these have passed, and if anyone has been seen to be worthy, he is thus elected into the college.

§ 13. Yet before he may touch the common food, he swears a certain horrendous oath. First, that he will piously venerate the deity; next, that he will preserve the laws toward men: that he will bring harm to no one, neither by counsel nor by command: that he will pursue the unjust with hatred:

---

<margin>Note the custom, once very frequent, that the character and disposition of those who were being admitted into a society were explored beforehand for some time; a custom which was also brought into the Christian Church. See *Holstenius on our author's Life of Pythagoras, 6.*</margin>

7. *When in this.*] "When indeed in this time." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. And it is thus in *Eusebius*.

8. *Purer — waters.*] To wash in common waters was once unlawful among the Jews and others, to which the *Author* seems to refer. *Epistle to the Hebrews 10:22.* See many things on this matter in *Spencer, Ritual Laws III, 1.* *Valentinus* restored the true reading from *Josephus*. Previously it was read as "more purely," which is also circulated in *Eusebius* and is in the *Meerman Manuscript*.

9. *Character is brought/tested.*] In the *Leipzig Manuscript* it is "is brought" (singular). He seems to have intended "is regulated" or "is adorned." <term>REISKE.</term> Since all the *Manuscripts of Porphyry* agree on "is brought" <note>original: "komizetai"</note>, which *Valentinus* also intended, I do not dare to punish it with exile. However, the uniquely true reading of *Josephus and Pamphilus* is "is tested" <note>original: "dokimazetai"</note>, which *Valentinus* had substituted; in his edition, it was read as "they are brought" (plural).

10. *Thus into —*] Was the fellowship of the *Freemasons* <note>original: "Francs Maçons"</note> therefore reborn from this institution? <term>REISKE.</term> See the note at § 11.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s discussion of the Essenes, specifically their initiation oaths and ethical standards regarding governance and honesty. It draws heavy parallels between the Essene lifestyle and early Christian teachings, particularly the writings of St. Paul.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> V v 2 <-

...that he will support the righteous, and show faith and obedience to all, but especially to those in power; for it is not without the will of God that dominion falls to any man. If he himself should rule, he will never use his power insolently: he will not surpass his subjects in clothing or any other more splendid ornament: he will always embrace the truth and prefer it to lies: he will keep his hands pure from theft, and his soul from unjust gain: nor will he hide anything from his fellow members, nor [reveal] anything to others—

<column-break/>

1 ...to fight alongside the righteous, to provide faithfulness to all, but especially to those 2 who rule; for without God, the right to rule does not come to anyone. And if he himself 3 rules, never to act insolently with his authority, nor to outshine those placed under him with clothing or any greater finery. To love the truth always, and to 4 reject those who lie; 5 to keep his hands clean from theft, and his soul from unholy gain. And neither to hide anything from the members of his sect, nor—

---

<column-break/>

<margin>1. *To fight alongside the righteous.*] <note>original: "Συναγωνίζεσθαι τοῖς δικ."</note> Eusebius reads: *to suffer injustice with*. Josephus reads: *to fight alongside*. Learned men use this to illustrate St. Paul’s letter to the Romans 15:30. A little before, those other two use the simple verb *to keep* instead of the compound form.</margin>

<margin>2. *To those who rule; for without God—*] <note>original: "Κρατοῦσιν, οὐ γὰρ δίχα θεοῦ —"</note> Compare Paul to the Romans 13:1: *For there is no authority except from God*, where see the most diligent interpreters. In that place, by "authority" <note>original: "ἐξουσίαν"</note> (the word our author uses immediately after), the office itself seems to be understood, and thus the form of the empire or Republic, which certainly has God as its author. Thus "royal authority" etc. is often said. "All beginnings and authorities" <note>original: "πᾶσαι ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι"</note> encompasses all forms of government, as in Plato’s *Alcibiades* p. 450 B. Others use "those who will exercise authority" <note>original: "ἐξουσιάσοντες"</note> in Luke 22:25. "Those who rule" <note>original: "κρατοῦντες"</note> are those who possess power over affairs, as is common. See Markland on Euripides' *Suppliants* 18. Instead of "to some" <note>original: "τισί"</note>, Josephus and Eusebius read "to someone" <note>original: "τινί"</note>. The former, a little before, says "always faithful to all."</margin>

<margin>3. *If he rules, never to act insolently.*] <note>original: "Ἄρχει μὴ δὲ πωπ. ἐξ."</note> Josephus reads: *if he should rule, never to be insolent*. Eusebius also uses the subjunctive "should rule," which seems proper to restore, although the construction "he rules" can be allowed, regarding which see Bergler on Alciphron Book II, Letter 58. More truly, Eusebius uses the past tense "to have acted insolently," for which Valentinus had given the present "to act insolently." For so it is in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts, as well as Victor's edition (for what is there as *exubrusai* I attribute to a printer's error, which, as often happened,</margin>

<column-break/>

Fogerolles followed). They therefore tolerated legitimate magistrates, but they did not want them to be proud in their dignity or to exalt themselves above others, being themselves the greatest haters of the condition of slavery. This is what Philo means in Eusebius' *Preparation for the Gospel* p. 382 A: *They condemn masters not only as unjust, for violating equality, but also as impious for destroying the law of nature, which brought forth all men equally* etc. He well uses the word "to be subject" <note>original: "ὑποτάσσεσθαι"</note> shortly after, which is proper in this context. From this, the Divine Man <note>A respectful reference to St. Paul</note> in the Epistle to the Romans 13:1 can be illustrated.</margin>

<margin>4. *To reject those who lie.*] <note>original: "Ψευδομένους προβάλλεσθαι."</note> Victor well defends the common reading; Markland gives more examples of this meaning in Maximus Tyrius 36:2. Josephus has: *to expose and reject*, where the "and" has fallen out.</margin>

<margin>5. *Hands from theft and soul—*] <note>original: "Χεῖρας κλοπῆς καὶ ψυχὴν —"</note> He joins "hands and soul," much like James joins "hands and heart" in chapter 4:8, which I wonder if they might be illustrated from here. Certainly, if "clean hands" are understood as men who are *not greedy*, which Raphel correctly notes are specifically called so. The Apostle might thus seem to touch upon three commandments of the Decalogue (verses 4, 8, 11). However, I would prefer to interpret it more broadly, for "pure hands" in both languages usually denote innocence and integrity of life.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

-> [The Essenes] will reveal nothing to others, even if one were to be tortured unto death. In addition to these things, <note>original: ἑτέροις αὐτῶν τι μηνύσειν / nunciaturum</note> he swears to transmit the doctrines to no one in any other manner than he himself received them; to abstain from robbery; and to likewise preserve the books of their sect and the names of the angels. <note>original: τῶν ἀγγέλων ὀνόματα / angelorum nomina</note> Such are their oaths. But those who are caught [in sin] and expelled perish by a miserable fate. For being bound by their oaths and customs, they are not even able to partake of food from others; so, eating grass and having their bodies wasted by hunger, they perish. Wherefore many... <-

<column-break/>

-> ...[the Essenes], moved by mercy, [receive back]... <-

***

6. *To reveal something to others.*] The *Meerman* manuscript <note>A famous 18th-century collection of manuscripts</note> incorrectly reads "to companions" (*hetairois*); these words are often confused, as shortly after "in another way" (*heteros*) is confused for "to companions" (*hetairos*). It was a very common custom among many peoples to take diligent care that the secrets of sacred rites not become known to the uninitiated. <note>original: τοῖς ἀμυήτοις</note> The Essenes held these things in common with the Pythagoreans, and received them from the Egyptians, about whom there is much testimony. This flowed down to the Christians, who did not betray the mysteries of religion to infidels; on which matter see *Milles* on *Cyril of Jerusalem, Preface p. 9.*

7. *He swears — than he himself received.*] *Josephus* writes: "In addition to these things they swear," and the *Meerman* manuscript reads "to transmit to no one." Then *Josephus* uses "partook of" (*metelaben*) instead of "received" (*parelaben*). But our reading is more emphatic. For "to receive" (*paralambanein*) is properly to receive a doctrine handed down by parents or teachers, just as to propagate it is "to hand down" (*paradidonai*). Saint Paul joins both in this way in 1 Corinthians 11:23: "For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered unto you." Our author and others do this a hundred times.

8. *The names of the angels.*] The word "the" is omitted by *Meerman*. *Scaliger* and others use this passage of *Josephus* to suggest that St. Paul in Colossians 2:18 condemns the "worship of angels" among the Essenes.

<column-break/>

On the contrary, many come forward and clear the other Jews of that age of this crime. Whether they are right, I do not inquire. *Origen in John p. 212* certainly seems to signify the opposite. But our author here says nothing about worship, only that they diligently guarded the names, which is not surprising in men devoted to superstition, since various ranks <note>original: τάξεις</note> of angels were believed in. Therefore, nothing should be changed against the will of the manuscripts of *Josephus*, *Porphyry*, and *Eusebius*, despite the Illustrious Man who conjectured the word "vessels" (*angeion*) instead of "angels" (*angelon*) in *Josephus*. <margin>† This word passed from the Jews and Christians to the Platonists, Hierocles, our author, and others. From this it is clear by what right the Learned Man <note>original: V. D. / Vir Doctus</note> noted in *Porphyry's Introduction ch. 3* that whenever that word occurs in our author, it is corrupt and the word "God" should be substituted. On the matter itself, compare *the celebrated Brucker: History of Philosophy Vol. II. p. 769.*</margin>

9. *But those who are caught.*] *Josephus* is more complete: "those caught in noteworthy sins." Our author departs a little from him in what follows.

10. *Eating grass.*] *Josephus* says: "eating grass and his body wasting away with hunger, he perishes." So too our Porphyry, except that "the body" is missing. It is more correctly edited there even now as "eating grass"—

<margin><insert>+ Haverkamp. see Odè on Angels p. 941.</insert></margin>

However, the construction better allows for *of God*. ...endurance, as if being racked, and twisted, and burned, and passing through all <margin>17</margin> the instruments of torture, rather than either blaspheme the lawgiver <note>Moses</note> or eat anything unaccustomed <note>non-kosher food</note>, they would not endure either option. ...drawn away by a natural flow and joined to bodies, but when they are released from these fleshy bonds, as if freed from a long slavery, they then rejoice and are carried upward. <margin>...that the matter is prepared, and that some part is living and perennial. Concerning which argument others [have written]. *Josephus* expresses the phrase "that spirit" in another way.</margin>

**21. But whenever they are released [Greek: Ἐπειδὰν δὲ ἀνεθῶσι].** There is no doubt that we should read *anethōsi* <note>the plural form</note>. I have very often found the letters alpha and epsilon interchanged in the Leipzig Manuscript of Porphyry. **REISKE.** The Meerman manuscript agrees, and Fogerolles had corrected it; Josephus and Eusebius read the same, so I have rightly restored his own text to Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name</note>. Immediately after, Eusebius has *hoia* instead of *hoion*.

**22. Delivered from slavery [Greek: Δουλείας ἀπηλλαγμένας].** Exactly as in the *Epistle to the Hebrews* 2:15: "delivered from slavery." For so it seems to me it should be construed there, as I said above, not "delivered from fear," which they usually supply and support with examples.

**23. From such [Greek: Ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς] etc.** These are also the words of Josephus, but Cyril [of Alexandria] copied them as if they were Porphyry's, up to the end of this section, in *Against Julian*, Book V. Soon after, the Leipzig manuscript simply has "they know," but all the rest agree on "they foreknow" [Greek: προγινώσκουσιν].

**24. Seldom however [Greek: Σπάνιον μέντοι] —** Josephus writes: "it is rare if they ever fail in their prophecies." Our text follows Eusebius, except that where he has "if," we have "however." Cyril also writes "but they seldom fail." The learned Kypke elegantly illustrates the word *asochein* <note>to miss the mark/fail</note> in his notes on Paul’s *1 Timothy* 1:6, using this passage of Josephus.

**1. To eat pig or fish without scales.** Regarding swine, see above, Book I, 14. Regarding fish, see the divine law in Moses, *Leviticus* 11:10. The scales of fish are properly called *lepides*, while those of serpents are *pholides*. See the celebrated Valckenaer on *Herodotus* VII, 61. Scaly fish [Greek: Φολιδωτοὶ ἰχθύες] are known from Suidas. The Lexicons are ignorant of our specific compound word. The Scholiast on Oppian’s *Halieutica* I, 638, says: "mollusks are without *pholides* and without *lepides*... but the *selachia*, though bony, are without *pholides*," and like our author, he says they are called *selachia*. Regarding solid-hoofed animals, see above, § 7.

**2. It was also forbidden [Greek: Ἀπηγόρευτο δὲ καὶ μὴ].** So in the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts.

It was also forbidden to kill those animals that act as suppliants <note>original: ἱκετεύοντα — animals seeking protection or "begging" for mercy</note>, and those that, as it were, flee to houses for refuge, let alone eating them. 3 Nor did the Lawgiver <note>Referring to Moses</note> permit the taking of parents along with their young; rather, he commands us to spare even in a hostile land those animals that work alongside us <note>beasts of burden like oxen</note> and to refrain from slaughtering them. 4 And he did not fear that the race of animals that are not sacrificed, by increasing in number, would cause a famine for mankind. 5 For he knew, first, that those which produce many offspring are also short-lived. A proof of this is that we abstain from many creatures, such as lizards and worms,

which have solid hooves. It was also forbidden to them to kill, much less to eat, those animals which were like suppliants and fled to their homes. <margin>*Meerman manuscript: "forbidden also not."* The little word "not" is commonly added to prohibitive expressions, as observed above. Certainly, the Jewish masters so taught. *Philo, On the Virtues (The Constitution of the Mosaic State):* "not to kill the supplication of animals, such as those which sometimes flee for refuge," found in *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, page 359, B.*</margin>

<column-break/>

4. *In a hostile land, those that work—*] Regarding the law not to cut down trees in an enemy's land, we have this in *Moses, Deuteronomy 20:19.* But on the contrary, God commands that the cities of enemies be utterly overturned, and does not even command that the beasts be spared, *ibid. 13:15.* Therefore, by the interpretation of custom, these rules seem to have been extended to animals as well. # PORPHYRY

-> Concerning Cyprus and Phoenicia, these are the facts. For at first, no living creature was sacrificed to the gods; nor was there any law concerning this, because it was forbidden by natural law. But they tell a story that at certain times <note>original: "ὑπὸ δέ τινας καιροὺς"</note> they first sacrificed a victim, asking for a soul in exchange for a soul <note>This refers to the concept of "life for life" or substitutionary sacrifice</note>. Then, after this had occurred, they would burn the sacrificed animal whole. Later, while a victim was being burned, a piece of flesh fell to the ground; the priest, picking it up and being burned by it, unintentionally brought his fingers to his mouth to soothe the burn. Having tasted the fat and juices <note>original: "κνίσσης" - the savory aroma or steam of burnt fat</note>, he desired it and did not abstain, but even shared it with his wife. 4. *At certain times.*] Perhaps it should read "by some occasion" and "being asked." Often the word *kairos* <note>time/occasion</note>, like the Latin *tempus*, signifies a calamitous and mournful condition of affairs, as I have explained at length in my notes on Polybius. They were forced to begin by some sinister and unlucky time demanding a soul, by which satisfaction might be made for another soul — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. A little later Meermann's manuscript says: *to burn the sacrifice whole*. Various accounts are handed down regarding the occasion on which mortals first began to use meat. See Castellan, *On the Eating of Flesh*, Book I, chapter 1. This much is certain: in the most ancient times, meat-eating <note>original: "κρεωφαγίαν"</note> was unknown, since victims were only slaughtered in honor of the Gods. Afterward they did indeed begin to use meat, but sparingly at first, and almost never unless it had been sacrificed. > some experience of the pleasure, from that beginning
> they increased the art of cookery to the greatest extent.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

...he took care to have it inscribed that he had been a teacher of the magical arts <note>original: "magicorum doctor"</note>. These men were divided into three classes, as stated by Eubulus <note>The OCR reads "Symbolus," but the marginal notes correctly identify this as Eubulus, a writer on the Mithraic mysteries</note>, who composed a history of Mithra in many books. Of these, the first and most learned neither ate nor killed anything with a soul <note>meaning animals</note>, but persevered in that ancient abstinence from living creatures. The second class did eat meat, but they would not kill any of the tame <note>domesticated</note> animals. The third class, however, did not refrain from any, but laid hands on all animals just as other men do.

<column-break/>

3. ...on his monument, among other things, that he had also become a teacher of the magical arts. 4. These were divided into three classes, 5. as Eubulus says, 6. who recorded the history of Mithra in many books. Of these, the first and most eloquent neither eat anything with a soul, nor do they kill, but they abide by the ancient abstinence from animals. The second use them, yet they do not kill any of the tame animals. Nor do the third, in the same manner as others, lay hands on all—

---

<column-break/>

<margin>XXIII. Near the end. *Zoroaster added much knowledge from the secrets of the Chaldeans, and then Hystaspes, a most wise King and father of Darius.* In which it is false that he calls Hystaspes "King": certainly if he means the parent of Xerxes, it is no other Hystaspes. But these matters are not clearly settled, whether that most ancient Magus Hystaspes was the same as the father of Darius or not. Persian writers, as Thomas Hyde has shown, consider him the same as Darius himself, the father of Xerxes. See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book I, chapter 14, 2.</margin>

<margin>3. On the monument — that [he was a teacher] of the magical arts —] The Most Distinguished Cuper says in *Observations* III, 30, that other editions have "of the Magi" <note>Greek: μάγων</note>, and he prefers that. To me, it is not clear: all my copies agree on "of the magical arts" <note>Greek: μαγικῶν</note>. Indeed, it is not surprising, since magic was taught among the first royal duties, as Apuleius says in *Apology* I, p. 148. For it was expedient for Kings to claim the guardianship of religion for themselves. "Teacher of the magical arts" here denotes not so much a teacher of magicians as an Arch-magus or sacred pontiff, as Brucker observes in *Critical History of Philosophy*, Vol. I, p. 159. Cuper, in the place cited, as well as Felicianus, takes this as if Darius ordered these things to be inscribed on *his own* monument. However, it seems it should be understood as his father's monument, for he, as was said, had deserved very well of the magical doctrine. Even so, it would better agree with the testimonies of the Persians, as we have seen.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>4. Divided — into three classes.] Just as they were described in three classes, so these and other things are common with the ancient Persians and Indians. Indeed, many Persians formerly settled in this region. It is therefore no wonder that Pausanias calls Isidore and the philosophers "Magi." Read La Croze, *Christian History of the Indies*, Book VI, p. 439.</margin>

<margin>5. As Eubulus says.] Instead of "Symbolus," it should be read as "Eubulus." See Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*. VALENTINUS. Lambecius confirms that "Eubulus" must be read in *Prodromus of Literary History*, p. 277; compare below, p. 253. REISKE. Most true. Thus also Fabricius restored it in *Greek Library* IV, 27, p. 205, and the Learned Gentleman in his notes on Jerome, who expressed our author's meaning in *Against Jovinian* II, 14: *Eubulus also, who explained the history of Mithra in many volumes, relates that among the Persians there are three classes of Magi, the first of whom, being the most learned and eloquent, take nothing more for food except flour and herbs.* Tollius thinks he is the same Eubulus mentioned in the fragments of Longinus, p. 246.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

For it is a primary doctrine held by all <note>original: "πάντων" (panton)</note>, that there is a transmigration of souls <note>The Greek term is "metempsychosis," the belief that the soul moves into different bodies after death.</note>. This is also what they seem to indicate in the mysteries of Mithras <note>Mithras was a Persian sun deity whose mystery cult became immensely popular across the Roman Empire.</note>; for hinting at our commonality with the animals, they are accustomed to identify us through animals. Thus, they call the initiates who participate in the same rites "Lions," the women "Hyenas," and those who serve "Ravens." And among the fathers—

<column-break/>

For the decree is held among the first regarding the transmigration of souls into diverse bodies. This they also seem to signify in the mysteries of Mithras. For in order to intimate that we have a communion with the other animals, they have accustomed themselves to indicate us by the names of other animals; while they call those who are participants in the same sacred rites "Lions," the women "Lionesses" <note>The translator notes a variation between "Hyenas" in the Greek and "Lionesses" in some Latin traditions.</note>, and the servants "Ravens." And among the fathers in a similar manner—

---

7. *For it is a primary doctrine* —] If the reading "of the first" <note>original: "τῶν πρώτων" (ton proton)</note> is correct, it signifies "a doctrine among the first and most ancient doctrines." However, I have sometimes suspected the reading should be "of those previously mentioned" or "of the Persians." *Of all those dictated above* (that is, the Magi) or *of all Persians*. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist.</note>. If you take it in the former sense, everything is clear. The <term>INTERPRETER</term> did not follow Porphyry's mind. The error arose from the fact that he had said the third class of Magi laid hands on all things indiscriminately, which would signify they did not use religion indiscriminately. Those who have dealt with the religion of the Persians explain the doctrine more broadly. That which Porphyry calls *metempsychosis* is described quite variously by the ancients, on which see the celebrated *Irkov*: *On the Palingenesis of the Ancients*, Book I, 1.

8. *In the mysteries of Mithras.*] There is a difference between *Mithra* and *Mithras*; the latter is the *Sun*, the former is *Venus*. They performed sacred rites in hidden caves, so that, always immersed in the dark squalor of shadows, they might not see the grace of the splendid and serene light, as *Julius Firmicus* says in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 414. Some think *Isaiah 45:19* refers to these. But those whom <term>REINESIUS</term> praises (*Inscriptions I, 48*) and <term>MOSHEIM</term> (in his notes to *Cudworth's Intellectual System*, p. 328) have examined these matters with such admirable erudition that to attempt anything after them might seem a "voyage of audacity, but not of mind," as the saying goes. Since both in this passage and in *The Cave of the Nymphs* and among others, the entire apparatus is described such that these things seem to have pertained uniquely to physical and astronomical reasoning, not—

<column-break/>

—yet has the illustrious man persuaded us that Mithras was a robust man, or a King and Hunter, who freed the province from robbers and beasts, and hence earned those honors. The *Meerman Codex* gives "which also seems to be."

9. *To call them Lions* —] I have translated this as "lionesses" on the authority of <term>KIRCHER</term> <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who studied oriental mysteries.</note>, whom I would wish you to consult, whoever would more fully understand the following things concerning the Persian mysteries. <term>VALENTINUS</term>. "They call the women lionesses." In the *Leipzig Codex* it is "hyenas." <term>REISKE</term>. Nothing is more certain; and thus it is correct. *Salmasius* writes in his commentary on *Lampridius* (Comm. 9) that some were even called "hyana," because they called women hyenas as they called men lions, but he seems to have been deceived by a faulty reading of this passage. Certainly, I do not remember reading it in any other author. Note in passing that humans of both sexes undertook those sacred rites, as we know was practiced among others as well.

10. *Ravens. And among the fathers* —] Those who were initiated into the "Patric" grade were called "Fathers," hence "Fathers of the unconquered Sun God" on inscribed stones, which word denoted eminence over the rest of the priests; and it is from this that they are nicknamed "Eagles" and "Hawks." A similar logic applies to the "Coracic" <note>Raven-grade</note> and "Leontic" <note>Lion-grade</note> rites, whence they call them "Ravens" and "Lions." An inscription in *Gruter* also joins these: Leontica, Coracica, and Patrica. Those rites were also called "Hierocoracica" and the ministers "hierocoraces" <note>Sacred Ravens</note>. Read <term>REINESIUS</term>: *Synthesis of Inscriptions I, 48*. You see, therefore, by what right the Great Man in *Ancient Monuments* p. 236 explains "among the fathers"—
