<gloss>11. Receives the Leontic rites.]</gloss> See Porphyry, *On the Cave of the Nymphs*. VALENTINI. Those who were initiated into the Leontic <note>Lion</note> grade were said to "receive the Leontic rites" in the Mithraic mysteries. Similarly, one is said to "undertake the Eleusinian rites" among the Greeks, and similar phrases exist among the Latins. See Casaubon on Lampridius' *Commodus*, chapter 9.

<gloss>12. Clothes himself in all kinds —]</gloss> Such a person is described in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* Book XI, page 748: *A precious cloak hung from his shoulders, and wherever you looked, it was marked all around with animals of various colors. Here were Indian dragons, there Hyperborean griffins* — the initiates call this the "Olympic stole" (Reinesius, page 96, preferred "Leontic"). Montfaucon and others display an image of this kind of beast, along with signs indicating Mithras, and a man girded in such wild skins, which was excavated at Zurich in Switzerland. Indeed, even after the Christian religion was introduced into Gaul, the custom persisted for a long time that on the Kalends of January (which were formerly sacred to Mithras), men would run about dressed in the skins of beasts; learned men believe this custom flowed from the rites of Mithras. See the great Mosheim, Book I, page 331. Just as with other things by which they wished to signify a kinship with animals, I am persuaded that the Persians received this also from the Egyptians. There is a notable passage in Diodorus Siculus, Book I, chapter 62: <note>original Greek: ἐν ἔθει γὰρ εἶναι...</note> *For it was the custom for the rulers in Egypt to place upon their heads the foreparts of lions, bulls, and dragons as signs of their authority.*

<column-break/>

<gloss>13. The common —]</gloss> Perhaps [the text should read]: *the common opinion of nature is to think they refer to the course of the sun through the Zodiac circle.* REISKE. See Book II, section 40.

<gloss>14. Dialect: wild boars, and scorpions —]</gloss> To confess frankly, I do not know what the word *lapourous* <note>Greek: λαπούρους</note> means. The French translator rendered it as *Lacertos* <note>Lizards</note>; I would have done the same if such a name occurred among the Romans. VALENTINI. The meaning is plain: among the Romans, many names are derived from animals. For certain illustrious Roman families use the name of Boars (*Apri*), others of Goats (*Capri*), others of Bulls (*Tauri*), others of Blackbirds (*Merulae*). But *lapourous* causes trouble; I find no such name in Roman families. It occurs to me to suspect that Porphyry wrote *lakertas* <note>Lizards</note>, and when someone had written *sauros* or *sauras* <note>Greek for lizards</note> above it, a faulty reading was conflated from them, representing neither a Greek nor a Roman name, but a part of each. REISKE. Cotelerius, in his notes on Clement, Volume I, *Apostolic Fathers*, page 673, thought it should be read as *strophous* and *laphous* <note>twisted ones and deer</note>, so that...

15. **Artemis as a she-wolf.** Just as her brother is "Wolf-like" <note>Apollo Lykeios</note>. See Book III, 17. Thus the name *Lykeia* was given to Diana. *Pausanias* investigates the cause of this in his *Corinthiaca*, p. 144.

16. **Lizard, lion—** Instead of "lizard" <note>sauros</note>, I believe it should read "bull" <note>tauros</note>; for I could prove with many examples, if it were worth the effort, that the Sun was sometimes called that. It is not yet clear to me that he was called a "lizard." **VALENT.** He rightly calls the sun a "lion," since that animal is dedicated to the sun and is its symbol among many nations. See *Cuper*: *Harpocrates*, p. 10. The **serpent** <note>draco</note> is also sacred to him for a specific reason, on which see the same, p. 62. Regarding the hawk, the matter is well known from earlier sections. "Bull," which fits better here than "lizard," also has a relationship to the sun, on which see *Cuper*: Book I, p. 12 and the *Scholiast on Statius* at the end of Book I; however, it relates more to the moon, as will be seen shortly.

He speaks of Hecate in the same way in Book III, § 17; see there.

From this is named the *Pherephattion*, a temple of Proserpina at Athens, concerning which see *Meursius*: *Attic Miscellany*, Book II, 16. More on this name shortly.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

->That is, she is the nurse of all things. For she is a goddess of the earth, who is also Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter</note>. To her they also consecrated the cock. From this it also followed that her priests abstain entirely from domestic birds. For it is also commanded in the Eleusinian rites that they abstain from domestic birds, fish, beans, and likewise from apples and pomegranates. By touching the stems of these, they are polluted just as if they had touched a dead body.<-

<column-break/>

->...and being a nurse. For the goddess is of the earth, and Demeter is the same. And they dedicated the cock to her. Wherefore her initiates also abstain from domestic birds. For it is commanded also at Eleusis to abstain from domestic birds, fish, beans, pomegranates, and apples; and it is equally a pollution to touch the stem [of the pomegranate] as it is to touch a dead...<- <note>The Greek text here mirrors the Latin translation provided in the first column, breaking off at the word "dead" (thne-).</note>

***

The readings differ entirely, as is evident from those who have written on animals. For *Phersophone* <note>A variant of Persephone</note>, the Meerman manuscript has *Persephone*, and it is so rendered above in Book I, 25. Moeris the Atticist says: *Pherephatta* is the Attic form; *Persephone* is used by the Greeks. Sometimes it is even called *Phersaphatta* and *Persaphatta*. See Pierson there.

20. **For the goddess is of the earth—** The names for Ceres and her daughter Proserpina <note>Persephone</note> are used almost interchangeably in the monuments of the ancients. See Spanheim on Callimachus's *Hymn to Ceres*, 133. It is singular that he says the Cock was consecrated to that Goddess, whom we know the ancients sacred primarily to Mars and Aesculapius. However, Ovid says in *Fasti* I, 455:
> At night, the crested bird is slain for the Goddess Night.

21. **Domestic birds.** Exactly as Pollux (Book X, 156) calls them "in-house" or "domestic" birds; shortly after he calls them "household" birds, as others often do. See Jungermann on Pollux, who teaches that these are hens, which are also simply called "birds." See Casaubon on Athenaeus I, 15. In Latin, they are called *aves* by writers on agriculture, such as Columella (VIII, 5) and others.

22. **Fish and beans.** Who has not illustrated the commands "to abstain from beans" and "not to taste fish," which were among the symbols of Pythagoras? One will not be surprised that these Eleusinian decrees were related to the teachings of Pythagoras, if one remembers they were derived from the same source. For "at Eleusis," the Lipsian manuscript erroneously gives *Eleusin*.

23. **Pomegranates and apples.** See Julian's *Oration 5* for the Mother of the Gods. *Valenti.* A distinction is made by Grammarians between *rhoia* (the pomegranate tree) and its fruit *rhoa*, though this distinction is not per-

<column-break/>

-petual. See Ammonius on this word, and there Valckenaer and Oudendorp on Thomas Magister. They are also joined by the Comic poet in *The Wasps*, 1259: "instead of an apple and a pomegranate," which the ancient critics explain as "abundant delicacies." Spanheim (in *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, Dissertation VI) shows that this fruit was held as a mystic object among the ancients, and that they abstained from it in the Thesmophoria and other sacred rites. There were also pomegranates in the chests which the women carried about in the Eleusinian rites. Read Meursius, *Eleusinia*, chapter 25.

24. **To touch the stem—** For *ou* (not) one should read *to* (the). *Valenti.* Perhaps: "and it equally pollutes to touch a woman in childbirth as it does a corpse." *Reiske.* Not otherwise Gale on Iamblichus's *Mysteries*, Section IV, 11: just as Pythagoras (according to Laërtius) kept himself pure "from mourning and from eating things that died of themselves," where you see those two things are also joined. Closer still to the common writing is the illustrious Abresch, who read "both the woman in childbirth." For a *lecho* is one who has "recently given birth," as Hesychius says; I do not know why Spanheim (on Callimachus's *Hymn to Jove*, 14) wished to change this word. It is well enough established that women in childbirth were once held to be impure. See Casaubon on Theophrastus, page 290. The Mosaic Law <note>The laws of Moses in the Bible</note> is very well known. Spencer (*On Ritual Laws*, I, 8) thinks this opinion proceeded from the Egyptians or the children of Noah. It is therefore no wonder that these things were approved by Pythagoras and his followers. There is a similar reasoning regarding menstruation, mentioned above in Book II, 5. If you wish to maintain the common reading, nothing is easier than to change *ou* (not) to *tou* (of the).

# PORPHYRY

...of those who have died naturally. <note>original: θνησιδίων / thnēsidion. But wickedness, as we have already said often, is suited in a wonderful way to act as its own patron, particularly when it speaks words among those who are ignorant of things. For it happens because of this, that those who are only moderately wicked think this kind of warning is a vanity, and what is in the proverb, "old wives' trifles," while others think it is superstition. # On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Yy 2 <-

They do not hesitate to slander [the holy men] as impostors and charlatans. But since these critics pay the deserved penalties for their crimes before both gods and men, they are sufficiently punished first by this very depravity of their own souls. We, however, having mentioned one more of the foreign nations that is famous and held to be just and pious toward the gods, shall then proceed to the remaining matters.

§ 17. For while the commonwealth of the Indians is divided into many parts, there is among them a certain race of wise men, whom the Greeks are accustomed to call Gymnosophists <note>original: "Gymnosophistas" — literally "Naked Philosophers."</note>. Of these there are two sects: one of the Brahmans, the other of the Samanaeans <note>original: "Samanaeorum" — likely referring to Buddhist or Jain monastics (Shramanas).</note>.

<column-break/>

[They slander them as] charlatanry and vanity. But these men, paying the penalty for their sins before both gods and men, first provide sufficient punishment for themselves by such a disposition. But we, after mentioning one more of the foreign nations—one indeed glorious and just, and believed to be pious in divine matters—will pass on to other things.

§ 17. ^1 For since the constitution of the Indians is divided into many parts, there is among them a race of God-wise men, whom ^2 the Greeks are accustomed to call Gymnosophists. Of these there are two schools: of which one, the ^3 Brah-

<margin>
The Meerman manuscript incorrectly reads *ektainontes* [stretching out] instead of *ektinontes* [paying a penalty], and then *aute* [by it].
</margin>

1. *For since the Indians &c.*] I think *Theophrastus* speaks of these in *History of Plants, Book IV, ch. 5*: "And the wise and abstaining men of the Indians use [this] food." *They translate this as: "the wise men of the Indians, who live naked, use this food." Indeed, those who are "wise but not abstaining" stop there. They cannot both eat and abstain,* says *Scaliger*: but *the "abstaining ones,"* those who are such by excellence, of whom our Author speaks, did not eat of that fruit. These Indians had many things in common with the Egyptians, and *La Croze* derives this from the idea that they were colonies of the Egyptians, as we observed above. However, that opinion is pressed by many difficulties, which can be read in *Brucker* in the *Treasury of Letters of La Croze, Vol. I, p. 70.* But if you think they migrated from India into Egypt instead, it would be because *Philostratus* places the Gymnosophists in Ethiopia near the Nile river. Compare *Ludovicus Vives on Augustine’s City of God, XIV, 17.* But they could also have received these customs through the Persians, to whom our Author joins the Indians here, and we have seen elsewhere that they had more things in common with the Egyptians. For the Persians, Arabs, and other northern Asian nations once enriched India with inhabitants, on which matter see *Illustrious La Croze, Book VI, History of Christianity in India.* Indeed, *Clearchus* says in *Diogenes Laertius's Prooemium* that the Gymnosophists *are descendants of the Magi.*

<column-break/>

2. *To call them Gymnosophists.*] *Jerome* expressed these things in Latin in *Against Jovinian, II, 14*: "Bardesanes, a man of Babylon, divides the Gymnosophists among the Indians into two dogmas, one of which he calls Brahmans, the other Samanaeans; who are of such great continence that they are nourished either by the fruits of trees near the Ganges river, or by a common meal of rice or flour." Regarding the reason for the name, and in what sense they were "naked," see the arguments of *Wolf on Origen’s Philosophy, ch. 24.* On the philosophers of the Indians, see also extensively *Diodorus Siculus, Book II, ch. 40*, where *Wesseling* has made many excellent observations.

3. *Brahmans — Samanaeans.*] The Meerman manuscript neglected the first syllable in *proistantai* [they preside] and immediately gives *hiereteian* [priesthood]. Concerning the Samanaeans, more a little later. Countless authors have dealt with the Brahmans; see as many as possible cited by *Wolf on Origen’s Philosophy, ch. 24*, regarding both those ancient ones and those of today.

# PORPHYRY

The Brahmans take the lead, and the Samanaeans <note>original: Σαμαναῖοι / Samanaei; likely referring to Buddhist or Jain monastics</note> follow. However, the Brahmans succeed to this divine wisdom <note>original: θεοσοφίαν / diuinam sapientiam; literally "theosophy" or knowledge of God</note> by birthright, just as one inherits a priesthood. The Samanaeans, on the other hand, are a selected group, composed of those who have chosen to devote themselves to divine wisdom. Their way of life is as follows, according to the account of Bardesanes <note>A Gnostic teacher from Edessa, c. 154–222 AD</note>, a Babylonian man who lived in the time of our fathers and met with the Indians who had been sent as ambassadors to Caesar. For all Brahmans are of a single race; they are all descended from one father and one mother. But the Samanaeans are not <margin>the same <note>original: ταυτοῦ</note>. 13. *A private hut.*] The Lexicographers and Kuhn explain this word in the notes to *Pollux: I, 73.* This matches the passage in *Achilles Tatius, Book V, p. 311: "there was a certain hut for me and Melite privately."*

14. *The Samanaeans, etc.*] The name still survives today among the Indians, whom they call *Schammanes* <note>likely a reference to Shaman or Shramana</note>. They admit that the worship of the Indian Brahmans succeeded that of a certain race whom they call *Samanaeans*, who were the most ancient inhabitants of India, and from whom they received all their arts and sciences. However, they consider these people as ignorant of the true God, because they were unaware of the "Supremely Perfect Being," as it is said. See *La Croze, Book I*, who observes that these things do not entirely agree with what our author [Porphyry] relates, who attributes almost the same law and religion to both Brahmans and Samanaeans. But although they agree well enough in their frugal way of life, it can be understood from our author that they followed a different system in many other respects. *Origen* also mentions the Samanaeans in *Against Celsus, p. 342*, as does *Clement of Alexandria* in *Stromata I, p. 305*, who has similar accounts of them. *La Croze* does not doubt that they are the same as those whom *Strabo* calls *Germanas*. To me it is certain that in *Strabo, Book XV, p. 489 & 490*, the text should be restored to *Sarmanas*, for they are also called *Sarmanae* by Clement. I can hardly bear what follows in *Eusebius*: *those called the Allobioi*; I think it should be rewritten as *Hylobioi* <note>meaning "forest-dwellers"</note> from *Strabo, p. 490*. The same word seems to have migrated into *Trakanoi* in *Philostratus, Life of Apollonius of Tyana, I, 18*, where *Olearius* edited it as *Germanas*; certainly *Hylobioi* could very easily be converted into *Trakanoi*, which is found there in the Codices and Manuscripts.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

And so, having no regard for wife or children, if he happens to have them, as if they no longer pertained to him at all, he departs to join the Samanaeans <note>original: "Samanaeos"; likely referring to Buddhist monks or Shramanas</note>. The care of educating the children is left to the King, and the care of the wife to her relatives. The life of the Samanaeans is of this sort: they dwell outside the city and spend the whole day in divine discourse. They have houses and temples built by the King, in which stewards are appointed who receive a certain fixed allowance from the King for the nourishment of those who gather there. Their food is prepared from rice, bread, fruit, and herbs. For when they have entered the house at the signal of a bell, the Samanaeans pour forth prayers; when they have done this, at a second signal, the servants offer a dish to each individual—for two do not eat from the same vessel—and they feed them with rice...

<column-break/>

...and he departs to the Samanaeans, making no further return or any account of wife or children, if he happened to possess them, <gloss>17</gloss> or considering them to belong to him at all. And the King takes care of the children, so that they have the necessities, while the relatives care for the wife. The life for the Samanaeans is such: they spend their time outside the city, passing the day in discourses concerning the divine. They have houses and sacred precincts built by the King, in which there are stewards, receiving a fixed portion from the King for the food of those who assemble. The preparation consists of rice, loaves, fruit, and vegetables. And when they have entered into the house <gloss>18</gloss> at the signaling of a bell, those <gloss>19</gloss> who are not Samanaeans depart, and the others pray. After they have prayed, the bell rings again <gloss>20</gloss>, and the attendants, having given a bowl to each (for two do not eat from the same one), feed them with the rice.

...preaching, each gives certain mandates to their dying kinsmen: so stable and true did they and many others believe the life of souls among one another to be after death. But those who have received the mandates committed to them, once the body is cast into the fire so that they may separate the soul in its purest state from the body, meet their death celebrated by all. For their friends and relatives dismiss them to death with a more tranquil mind than other men dismiss their own citizens on travels that are not even particularly long: and they bewail themselves who remain surviving in life, but they call those others blessed, as they have already received their immortal lot. # PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

asking, "If everyone imitates you, what will become of us?" Yet human affairs have not been thrown into disorder because of these people; for not everyone has imitated them, and those who have imitated them have been the cause of good order <margin>11</margin> rather than confusion among the nations. Furthermore, the law did not compel these people, but while permitting others to feed on flesh, it left these individuals to be self-governing <margin>12</margin>, and honored them as being superior to itself. Indeed, the law did not subject them to the penalties it imposes as if they were initiators of injustice, but rather subjected others. However, to those who ask what would happen <margin>13</margin> if everyone imitated such people, one must give the answer of Pythagoras: for if everyone were to become kings, he says, life would be difficult to manage, yet one must certainly not flee from kingship; and <margin>14</margin> if everyone were virtuous, it would be impossible to find a way to manage a state while maintaining the dignity appropriate to such excellence, yet surely no one would be so mad as to not wish for all—

->to be<-

<margin>11. Rather of Good Order.] "Good Order" <note>Greek: Eunomia</note> is beautifully defined by Diogenes Laertius, Book III, 103: "Good order is divided into three parts. First, if the laws are excellent, we say there is good order. Second, if the citizens abide by the established laws, we also call this good order. Third, if, in the absence of laws, they live well according to customs and practices." Thus, Suidas defines Good Order as "peace," putting the effect in place of the cause.</margin>

<margin>12. Left them self-governing.] Namely, "the law is not laid down for the righteous." <note>Latin: δικαίῳ νόμος οὐ κεῖται</note> See above at Book I, § 8. The Philosopher in Diogenes Laertius, Book VI, p. 371, says well: "The wise man should not live as a citizen according to established laws, but according to the law of virtue."</margin>

<column-break/>

if everyone imitates us, what will happen to us? Human affairs have not been thrown into confusion because of these men. For not everyone has imitated them: and those who have imitated them have stood as the cause of order and tranquility for peoples, rather than confusion. For indeed, the law did not bring any necessity upon these men, but while it permitted others to eat meat, it left these men to be their own masters, and venerated them as if they were superior to it. For it did not subject these men to the punishment it ordains as if they were perpetrators of injustice, but rather others. Yet to those who ask what would happen if all men imitated this kind of life, that saying of Pythagoras must be answered: "If all were kings," he says, "the result would be that life could only be carried on with difficulty, yet for that reason one must not flee from the throne." So also, if all were upright, no way would be found for managing and arranging a republic in which the proper dignity of their uprightness could be preserved. But no one would be so insane as not to wish for all—

->to be<-

<margin>13. If everyone imitated.] For the Philosopher did not dictate this norm of living to everyone indiscriminately, a point which he therefore emphasizes quite often. See at I, 27.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

The law does not forbid one from spending their life in taverns <note>original: καπηλίοις / cauponis. In antiquity, taverns were often associated with low social status or vice.</note>, and yet such a thing is a reproach to a man of moderate character. Something similar is evident regarding diet. One should not concede to the best men that which is permitted to the masses. A philosopher, above all, should prescribe for himself those sacred laws which the gods, and men following the gods, have defined. Now, sacred laws have appeared throughout nations and cities which command purity and forbid the eating of living things <note>original: ἐμψύχων / animatorum. Literally "things with a soul."</note> <gloss>21</gloss> to those engaged in sacred rites, and <gloss>22</gloss> even forbid the multitude from certain foods, either for the sake of piety or because of some harm arising from the nourishment. Therefore, one must either imitate the priests or obey all the legislators; for in either case, the man who is perfectly law-abiding and pious must abstain from all [flesh]. For if some people abstain from certain things in part for the sake of piety, then the man who is pious toward all things will surely abstain from all things.

->§ 19.<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book IV of Porphyry's "On Abstinence," focusing on the philosophical and ritual definitions of purity and the soul's relationship to the body.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

<column-break/>

They believed that the removal of souls <note>original: "ψυχῶν" - referring here to the departure of life or the dead</note> brought defilement upon the living; and much more so when a body that had possessed sensation was deprived of it, <gloss>3</gloss> and being dead, was brought into contact with the sensation of a living being. Therefore, in all things, sanctity and purity consist in the setting aside and abstinence from the many <gloss>4</gloss> and the contrary things, and in the isolation and reception of those things which are kindred and appropriate. For this reason, sexual acts also defile; for they are a union of female and male. Whether the seed is conceived, it brings defilement to the soul through its association with the body; or if it is not conceived, <gloss>5</gloss> it defiles through the "death" <note>original: "νεκρώσει" - referring to the loss of vital seed</note> of that which was offered. <gloss>6</gloss> Furthermore, the union of males with males contaminates doubly: both because it is spent in what is "dead" <note>i.e., non-reproductive</note> and because it exists contrary to nature. And in general, sexual acts and nocturnal emissions pollute because the soul is mixed with the body and is dragged downward toward pleasure. The passions of the soul also defile <gloss>7</gloss> through their entanglement, and <gloss>8</gloss> because the irrational part <note>the emotional or animalistic side of the soul</note> causes the internal male <note>the rational, governing principle</note> to become effeminate. For indeed, every <gloss>9</gloss> man who...

<column-break/>

<margin>3. And dead.] Perhaps "and having been deadened," and soon after "with the sensation of the living," according to Reiske.</margin>
<margin>4. And of contraries, isolation.] It should rather be read "by the isolation of contraries, and the reception of kindred things," according to Valent. The word "isolation" <term>monosis: a philosophical state of being alone or singular</term> is also used below and by others. See Spanheim on Josephus's Antiquities, Book II, 4.</margin>
<margin>5. By the death of that which was offered.] "Death" <note>nekrosis</note> is the proper term in this matter. It is exactly as used by Saint Paul in Romans 4:19, "a body having been deadened," with which Kypke rightly compared this passage.</margin>
<margin>6. Furthermore, the [union].] I have rewritten this based on the authority of the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts; previously it was read as "he who," but it refers back to either "union" or "intercourse."</margin>
<margin>7. Through the entanglement and.] The "and" after "entanglement" seems redundant, according to Valent.</margin>
<margin>8. The irrational part being made effeminate.] Since the female sex was considered weaker, philosophers were accustomed to compare the irrational part of the soul to a woman; on which matter see the illustrious Irhovius, "On the Transmigration of Souls," III, 5, 4.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and philological analysis of Porphyry’s text, specifically focusing on the concepts of purity, mixture, and "corruption" as understood by ancient painters and philosophers.</meta>

-># PORPHYRY<-

9 Defilement and pollution signify the mixing of one thing with another of a different kind, especially when 10 it becomes difficult to wash out. Hence, even in the case of dyes, which consist of mixtures where one form is entwined with another, 11 they say it "pollutes" <note>original: μιαίνειν (miainein)</note>.

12 *As when a woman stains ivory with Phoenician purple.* <note>A quote from Homer’s Iliad, Book 4, line 141.</note>

And conversely, painters call these mixtures 13 "corruptions" <note>original: φθοράς (phthoras)</note>, while common usage calls that which is unmixed and pure "uncorrupted," 14 "pure," and "undefiled." For even water mixed with earth is corrupted and is no longer pure. But that which—

<column-break/>

—is diminished. For the names of "staining" and "pollution" also signify, in a certain way, the mixture of things of a different kind among themselves, especially when a certain infection of this sort follows which can only be wiped away with great difficulty. Whence even in dyes, which arise from mixture, when one species is confounded with another, they call it "to stain." Not otherwise, says Homer, than a woman who stains ivory with Tyrian purple. Furthermore, painters call mixtures "corruptions." Common usage likewise says that what is unmixed and pure is "uncorrupted," "sincere," and "unpolluted." For water mixed with earth is corrupted, and sincere—

***

9. **The defilement etc.**] I ought to add a notable passage from *Plutarch* <note>Moralia, Vol II, p. 393 C</note> which our author refers to: "For pollution is the mixture of one thing with another; as Homer somewhere says that ivory is 'polluted' by being reddened with dye. And dyers call the mixing of colors 'perishing,' and name the mixture a 'corruption.'" Just as painters called the mixture of colors a "corruption," so philosophers call the mixture of any thing with another by that name, as is said immediately after. Compare: *Gataker on Antoninus [Marcus Aurelius], VI, 30.*

10. **Difficult to wash out.**] "Hard to wash out" <note>δυσέκπλυτοι</note> and "difficult to wipe away" <note>δυσέκνιπτοι</note> are joined in *Aelian: On the Nature of Animals, Book I, 48.* Our word is elegantly used regarding opinions that are plucked out with difficulty by *Plato: Republic, Book II, p. 605 A.* The "stain of sin" is called by *Stobaeus* a "dreg difficult to wipe away," by *Philo* an "impression hard to wash out," and by *Chrysostom* an "unwashable blemish." Read these and others in *Gataker: Adversaria, Book XI*, whom I see is already praised by *Wolf on Origen: Philosophumena, ch. 19.* To these can be compared the Hebrew <unclear>רחצ</unclear> <note>Rachatz - to wash/bathe</note>, which they rendered as "to wash out" in *Isaiah IV, 4.*

11. **They say it pollutes.**] This is the first and proper meaning of the verb: *to mix, to dye.* See *Bos: Critical Observations, ch. 30.* It is therefore rightly attributed to painters, like the Latin *inficere* [to dye/infect] and *inquinare* [to stain]. The passage of *Plutarch* just cited is notable.

12. **As when a woman—**] The poet in *Iliad, Book 4, line 141.* *Plutarch* refers to this, as I was just saying. *Virgil* imitates it in *Aeneid, Book 12, line 67*:
> *Just as if one had stained Indian ivory with blood-red purple.*

13. **Painters call them corruptions.**] Because a thing which is mixed with another is in some way corrupted and loses its natural power, painters call the mixture a "corruption," as *Plutarch* says in the cited place. From there it passed to the philosophers. To the notes add *Kuster on Aristophanes: Plutus, 530.*

14. **Pure and undefiled.**] He also uses the former in *Book I, 54* and "purely" in the same, section 40, which the *Scholiast on Thucydides II, 52* explains, where *Hudson* notes the error of *Dionysius of Halicarnassus*. "Undefiled" <note>ἀκήρατον</note> is also good and according to the usage of the ancients. See *on Book III, 27.* Elsewhere it is called "unmixed and undefiled" in *Theophrastus: On the Senses, p. 502* and *Plutarch* in the cited place, from which our author had taken certain things, "and always unmixed..."

<column-break/>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

...is no longer. But that water which flows and is borne along with a swift course rejects the earth it encounters; which, as Hesiod says, *flows unpolluted, streaming from an ever-flowing spring.* <note>original: "fluit illimis manans e fonte perenni"</note> For because it is incorrupt and unmixed, it provides a healthy drink. In the same way, a woman who has admitted no seminal exhalation or mixture into herself is called "uncorrupt." Therefore, corruption and defilement are the mixing of opposites. This is why the insertion of dead things into living animals—of things that once lived with sensation into those now living, and of dead flesh into living beings—rightly brings about a pollution and a defiler of our nature. Just as—

<column-break/>

—flowing and escaping, it strikes away the earth brought toward it, when, <margin>15</margin> as Hesiod says, it flows from an ever-running and out-pouring spring, which is untroubled. And the drink is indeed healthy, <margin>16</margin> because it is distinct and unmixed. And a female who has not received into herself the exhalation of seed <margin>17</margin> is called "uncorrupt." Thus, both corruption and defilement are the mixing of an opposite. <margin>18</margin> If, then, the insertion of dead things into living beings—and the <margin>19</margin> insertion of those things that lived with sensation into living beings, and of dead flesh into living flesh—reasonably brings a stain and <margin>20</margin> defilement to our nature <note>The Greek text here uses "physical nature," but see the marginal note regarding "soul."</note>, just as also...

---

<margin>It is fitting for the incorruptible and the pure. From which one might want the word "unmixed" <note>original: "ἄκρατον"</note>. I have restored the word "and," which *Valentinus* had omitted against the authority of earlier editions and the Leipzig Manuscript.</margin>
<margin>15. Hesiod says.] *Works and Days*, line 595: "From an ever-flowing and out-pouring spring, which is untroubled." *Ever-flowing* <note>original: "Ἀέναοι"</note> rivers and springs, as the Latins call them "eternal," are those which are properly so named, as the celebrated Burman beautifully shows in his notes on Rutilius, I, 109. Sophocles calls a spring "ever-running" in *Oedipus*, line 465, where the Scholiast explains it as "ever-flowing." Compare also the learned Goens in his notes on our author's *Cave of the Nymphs*, page 101.</margin>
<margin>16. Because it is distinct.] Read: "Uncorrupted" <note>original: "Ἀδιάφθορον"</note>. REISKE. This is excellent, and Abresch corrected it thus; a little later "uncorrupted water" is correctly used. First, an unskilled scribe corrupted it into "indifferent" <note>original: "ἀδιάφορον"</note>, then another, even more unskilled, gave "distinct" <note>original: "διάφορον"</note> to try to make sense of it. These words are often confused, as in Diodorus Siculus, where Wesseling correctly restored "corruption" for the "difference" found in others.</margin>
<margin>17. Is called uncorrupt.] Just as an "uncorrupted woman" <note>original: "ἀδιάφθορος γυνὴ"</note> is one who has not prostituted herself, in Diodorus, Book I, 59. Conversely, regarding debauchery, Dionysius of Halicarnassus says: "considering drunkenness the beginning of corruption." To "corrupt" and "to destroy" are very common terms in this matter.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Latins use "corruptors," "to corrupt a virgin," and similar terms, regarding which see Taubman on Plautus's *Casina*, Act I, scene 3.</margin>
<margin>18. If then to the—] Thus I read and punctuate this passage. "If then to living beings (supply 'it brings a stain' from what follows) the insertion of dead things..." That is: if the grafting of dead things brings some contamination to living creatures—even if it were that specific kind of grafting where things that seem to have once lived with sensation are brought into a living animal—it is necessarily also consistent that the intrusion of dead flesh into living flesh pollutes. REISKE.</margin>
<margin>19. Lived with sensation.] The same expression is found in Aristides, Vol. III, page 674, and Plato, page 423 C, which passages the celebrated Abresch had noted.</margin>
<margin>20. To our nature.] It seems that in some manuscripts it was "nature" <note>original: "φύσει"</note> and in others "soul" <note>original: "ψυχῇ"</note>, from which that faulty reading "physical" <note>original: "φυσικῇ"</note> emerged; but we should read "and a defilement to our **soul**," which the immediately following words prove. REISKE. *Valentinus* had corrected it to "nature," and the translator seems to have read it that way, unless it was "the physical [nature]," which my friend preferred.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

When the soul <gloss>21</gloss> is embodied, it is defiled. Therefore, <gloss>22</gloss> he who is born causes pollution through the mixture of the soul <gloss>23</gloss> with bodies; and he who has died, when he leaves behind a dead body, leaves something of a different nature and foreign to the living. The soul is also contaminated by anger, desires, and a multitude of passions, for which the diet is also in some way a contributing cause. Just as water flowing through rocks <gloss>24</gloss> is more pure than that which goes through marshes, because it does not pull along much mud; so also the soul, when it administers its own affairs through a dry body—one not irrigated by the juices of foreign flesh—is better, more incorruptible, and more ready for understanding. For they say that even for bees, the driest and most pungent thyme produces the best honey. Therefore, the intellect—or rather, the one who exercises intellect—is defiled when it is mixed with the faculties of imagination or opinion, and with their activities. <gloss>25</gloss> The

<column-break/>

In the same way, the soul also, when it is joined to the body, is stained. Whence also he who is born contracts pollution from the mixture of the soul with the body, as does he who dies, because he leaves behind a dead body which is foreign and different from the living. Likewise, the soul is contaminated by anger, and lusts, and a multitude of disturbances, of which the manner of living <note>original: "uictus"; referring here to diet and lifestyle</note> is also accustomed to be a cause in some way. For just as water which flows through rocks is more incorrupt than that which runs through marshes, inasmuch as it does not drag much mud; so the soul which administers its own affairs through a dry body, not through a flow of the juices of foreign flesh, is better, and more incorrupt, and more ready for intelligence. Indeed, they say that for bees also, the thyme which is driest and endowed with the greatest sharpness brings the best honey. Therefore, even thought—or rather the thinker—is stained when it is combined with the powers and operations of either imagining or opining.

---

<margin>21. **Is embodied.**] Either *ensomatoutai* <note>present tense</note> or *ensesomatotai* <note>perfect tense</note>. REISKE. Certainly one of the two is true. *Abreschius* also saw this. Instead of "is defiled" <note>memolytai</note>, the *Leipzig* and *Meermann Manuscripts* wrongly have the plural.</margin>
<margin>22. **He who is born.**] Perhaps "he who is being begotten" <note>gennomenos</note>, as pleased the Learned Man? But "to be born" <note>genesthai</note> is frequent enough. I add nothing to those things which *Alberti* noted regarding Paul's letter to the Galatians 4:4.</margin>
<margin>23. **Of the [soul] to the bodies.**] The word "of the" <note>tes</note> seems to have arisen from the last syllable of the word "soul" <note>psyches</note>, and thus one should read "of the soul to the body" or "by the mixture of the soul with the body." I also suspected</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>that this sentence was missing: "for souls are foreign to bodies." REISKE. I would believe that former suggestion to be most true. The *Meermann Manuscript* agrees beautifully, which has: "pollutes by the mixture of the soul with the bodies."</margin>
<margin>24. **Incorrupt of—**] After "incorrupt," the word "better" or "healthier" is missing. REISKE. Unless "more" is understood, which is familiar enough to our author, though rather harsh in this kind of structure. A little later also "and incorrupt," where *Reiske* prefers the comparative "more incorrupt" or "more so." The *Meermann* reading "incorrupt" is poor.</margin>
<margin>25. **The [connections] of this.**] Namely, of the intellect.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Aaa 2 <-

is mingled. Purification and holiness, however, consist in the separation from all these things; it is a state of solitude <note>original: "solitudo"; here meaning a soul standing alone, apart from material distractions</note>, and a form of nourishment that preserves each thing in its own essence. For in this way, you might rightly call the "food" of a stone that which causes it to persist in its own form; and the food of a plant, that which preserves it in its growth and fruit-bearing; and the food of an animal body, that which maintains its constitution. Indeed, it is one thing to nourish and provide necessities, and quite another to supply luxuries. Therefore, according to the diversity of things being nourished, the types of food are also diverse. And while all parts must certainly be nourished, effort must be given so that the most principal parts within us are fed and made robust. Thus, there is also a nourishment for the rational soul, which preserves it as rational: and this is the Mind <note>original: "mens" / "νοῦς" (nous); the higher intellect</note>. It must therefore be nourished by the Mind; and we must strive more to fatten the soul with the Mind than to fatten the flesh with foods. For the Mind preserves eternal life for us, whereas the body, when fattened, leads to—

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek source text for the passage above, with interlinear reference numbers.</note>

—mingled with these things. But purification <gloss>26</gloss> is the separation from all these, and holiness is the state of being alone, and nourishment is that which keeps each thing in being. For thus you might say the food of a stone is the cause of its staying together, and <gloss>27</gloss> its remaining in a state of cohesion. And of a plant, that which preserves it in growing or fruit-bearing; and of an animal body, that which preserves its constitution. But it was one thing to nourish, another to fatten; and one thing to give the necessary, another <gloss>28</gloss> to provide luxuries. Therefore the foods are different, <gloss>29</gloss> according to the difference of the things being nourished. And it is necessary to nourish all things, but to be diligent in fattening the most sovereign parts within us. And so the nourishment of a rational soul is that which keeps it rational. And this is Mind. So it must be nourished by Mind; and one must be diligent to fatten <gloss>30</gloss> from this rather than from the foods of the flesh; for the one maintains eternal life for us, but the body being fattened, 31 leads— <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "λί-" indicates the next page begins with "λιμόν" (famine/hunger) or a similar word.</note>

<margin>For "these things" refers back to the power of imagination and the power of opinion. I would also prefer the active form "might mingle," referring to the one who is thinking. — REISKE <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note></margin>
26. **The separation from these.**] Either the article "the" should be deleted entirely, or it should be placed before "all." — REISKE.

<margin>27. **Remaining in a state of cohesion.**] Thomas Gataker <note>English scholar, 1574–1654</note> beautifully explains what "state" <note>Greek: "hexis"</note> means in these matters in his notes on Marcus Aurelius, Book VI, Section 14. He thought that in this place we should read "and of the remaining in a state of cohesion," and not without merit.</margin>
28. **To provide luxuries.**] Thus the first editions correctly have it; the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts are wrong. Valentinus had mistakenly given "foods," unless it was a printer's error, for he translated it well.

<margin>29. **And the difference.**] Rather "according to some difference," or "according to the difference," as it is in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts; the translator expressed it no differently.</margin>
30. **From this rather than from.**] "Not from the [foods]"—evidently the word "not" was lost because of the "not" sound at the end of the word "this," and the letter "k" was swapped with "e," which often happens in handwritten books. — REISKE. It seems "rather" is understood, as we have often seen in this structure elsewhere.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry's argument regarding the purification of the soul through abstinence, specifically comparing the soul's attraction to the Divine with the physical attraction of iron to a magnet.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

It causes the soul to hunger for the blessed life, and increases our mortal nature, which, by becoming deranged, acts as an impediment to the immortal life. Likewise, by embodying the soul and dragging it down toward an alien nature, it stains and contaminates it. Now, the magnet stone <note>original: "magnes quidem lapis"</note> imparts a kind of soul to iron when it is placed nearby; and the iron, which is very heavy, is rendered light and runs toward it, lifted by the spirit of the stone. But will anyone who is suspended toward God—who is incorporeal and intellectual—worry much about food that merely fattens the body, which is an obstacle to the mind? Will he not rather, having contracted the necessities of the flesh into a very small and easily obtainable compass, be nourished himself by clinging to God more than iron clings to the magnet? For if it were possible, we would even abstain from the food of fruits without trouble, if our corruptible nature did not require it.

<column-break/>

<note>The following section contains scholarly commentary on the Greek and Latin text above.</note>

31. **The soul hungers.** <note>original: "Λιμώττειν τὴν ψυχήν"</note>] Read what was discussed on this matter above in Book I, 29, and what Philostratus <note>A 3rd-century Greek scholar</note> has in Book VIII, 12, and there Olearius <note>Gottfried Olearius, a 17th-century editor</note> has not forgotten our author. In place of "to hunger" <term>limōttein</term>, Fogerolles had given "to be a plague" <term>loimōttein</term>, though I do not know where he received that. We have said elsewhere that these words are confused, but here the former is uniquely true.

32. **Taking away.** <note>original: "Παραροῦν"</note>] Perhaps it should be "keeping in suspense" <term>paraōroun</term>. <margin>holding in suspense</margin> Holding it suspended and sublime. —REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a noted 18th-century philologist</note>. Certainly the letter omega could very easily have fallen out, as has often happened. However, I would not wish Markland to have consulted John the Evangelist, chapter 10, verse 24, in that way, reshaping "you take away" <term>aireis</term> into "you keep in suspense" <term>aiōreis</term>, as in Euripides' *Suppliants*, 89.

33. **Running toward.** <note>original: "Προσανατρέχων"</note>] This word is also missing from Henri Estienne's very copious *Thesaurus* <note>The standard Greek dictionary of the era</note>.

<column-break/>

Yet it occurs more often, as the examples collected by the celebrated Wesseling <note>Peter Wesseling, an 18th-century scholar</note> on Diodorus Siculus, Book IV, 60, will show you.

34. **Toward the thinking [body].** <note>original: "Πρὸς νοοῦν"</note>] The Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts read "mind" <term>noun</term>. Reiske preferred "toward that which thinks" <term>pros to nooun</term>.

35. **Without trouble.** <note>original: "Ἄνευ πραγμάτων"</note>] <term>Pragmata</term> are businesses or troubles, hence the phrase "to provide troubles" and similar ones, concerning which see above, Book I, section 46, and Gataker on Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, I, 12.

36. **If this were not.** <note>original: "Εἰ μὴ τοῦτ’ ἦν"</note>] The second "if" <term>ei</term>, like the first and third, is a sign of a wish. *O that this propensity of our nature toward destruction and ruin did not cling to us!* —REISKE.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

For if, as Homer says, we required neither food nor drink so that we might truly be immortal: for this was rightly stated by the poet <note>Homer, Iliad 5.341</note>, to signify that nourishment has brought about the occasion not so much for living, but also for dying. If, therefore, we had no need of this kind of nourishment, we would be as much more blessed as we were more immortal. But now, since we exist in a mortal state, we ignorantly render ourselves even more mortal (if it may be said so) by clinging to it: since the soul, as Theophrastus says, does not merely pay a small rent for its habitation in the body, but adds its whole self besides. But would that it were possible to lead that life spoken of in fables, entirely lacking hunger and thirst: so that each person, having restrained the flux of the body, might in the shortest time—

<column-break/>

For if, as <gloss>37</gloss> Homer says, we did not need food or drink, so that we might truly be immortal. The poet presented this well, showing that food was a <gloss>38</gloss> provision <note>original: "ephodion"</note> not only for living, but also for dying. If then we did not need this, <gloss>39</gloss> how much more blessed we would be, by as much as we were more immortal. But now, being in a mortal state, we make ourselves even more mortal, if one must say so, through our ignorance, <gloss>40</gloss> by the addition of this [mortal nature]; the soul <gloss>41</gloss> paying to the body not a great rent for its dwelling in it, as Theophrastus says somewhere, but adding its whole self. Would that it were easy to possess that fabled life free of hunger and thirst, so that one, having checked the <gloss>42</gloss> flowing away of the body, might quickly be among the best things,

# PORPHYRY

43 ...among whom, being also a god, he is a god. § 21. For those who, against the institutions of the nations which we have explained, oppose the Nomads, or the Troglodytes, or the Fish-eaters, they seem to be ignorant that peoples of this kind, due to the infertility of their region—

43. **Among whom being.** <term>Lipsius</term> <note>Justus Lipsius, 1547–1606, a famous Flemish philologist.</note> wanted *on* [being], which is without doubt true, and is read in the <term>Meermann</term> Codex. <term>Valerius</term> had indeed seen it, but with poor judgment had given *on* in the text. The <term>French Edition</term> followed, and here, according to its custom, the typographical error of the <term>Florentine Edition</term>.

44. **To sober up from drunkenness.** The word *ananephein* <note>Greek: ἀνανήφειν</note> is used everywhere of those who collect themselves from fear, anger, love, etc. See <term>D’Orville</term> on <term>Chariton</term>, Book III, 1, who also illustrates that passage of <term>St. Paul</term> in 2 Timothy 2:26, where the Philologists have gathered a harvest of examples. Specifically in this place it means to return to oneself from drunkenness, as in <term>Lucian's</term> *Hermotimus* 83: "sobering up from drunkenness," and many others whom I see already cited there. It is the same as *eknephein* in 1 Corinthians 15:34, where <term>Alberti</term> notes the <term>Meermann</term> manuscript corruptly has *anamenai*.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

...land which is so sterile and covered with rocks and sands that it produces no herbs at all; they were led to this form of nourishment by the necessity of food. A proof of this is that they cannot even use fire due to a lack of fuel and wood; instead, they roast their fish on stones glowing from the sun and in the hot sand. And these people, indeed, live this way because they are forced by necessity. But if certain nations are found who are of a cruel and savage nature, it is not fitting for a fair judge of things to bring a false accusation against the whole human race because of them. For in that way, not only the eating of other animals, but also the eating of humans and every other kind of wildness would come into dispute. For histories record that the Massagetae and the Derbicae <note>Ancient nomadic tribes of Central Asia often cited by Greek historians for their "barbaric" customs.</note> consider those of their kinsmen to be most mis-

<column-break/>

...since the land is so fruitless that it does not even bear grass, but only dunes and sand, they were reduced to this necessity of diet. The proof of this necessity is that they are unable to use fire, for lack of combustible material. Instead, they dry their fish upon the rocks or the dunes. These people do so out of necessity. # PORPHYRY

...the most wretched are those who die by a natural death. Therefore, they anticipate this by sacrificing and feasting upon those of their dearest kin who have grown old. 10 The Tibareni, however, cast down their nearest elderly relatives from cliffs while they are still living. The Hyrcanians and Caspians—some of them expose the living, others the dead, to be devoured by birds and dogs. The Scythians [bury] the living...

<column-break/>

...that this custom has now been abolished is stated by *Theodoret in his Sermon on Laws, p. 615, and Eusebius in Preparation for the Gospel, Book I, p. 11.* It was attributed to the institutions of the Romans by *Pliny, Book XXX, ch. 1.* However, the things written by the *learned Pelloutier in History of the Celts, Book II, ch. 3* to excuse the Scythians (whose <term>anthropophagy</term> <note>original: "ἀνθρωποφαγία" - the eating of human flesh</note> is noted everywhere) deserve to be read. Since nothing is more desirable than to depart by the fate of nature, you might rightly marvel at that insane love of violent death among some nations. That they themselves hastened their own fate can indeed be attributed to a zeal for glory. *For all cause for light is placed in arms, and to live for peace is condemned, as Silius Italicus says of the Cantabrians in Book III, 320.* The Cimbri and Celtiberians used to exult with joy in the line of battle, as if they were about to depart life gloriously and happily; they would lament in sickness, as if they were to perish basely and miserably. *Valerius Maximus, Book II, 6, 11.* But as for why they took the lives of their own people, it was from that persuasion by which they believed those who perished in such a manner would be more fortunate and blessed after this life. Concerning the Thracians, *Solinus in ch. 10* says they all agree on voluntary death, while some of them think the souls of the dying return, and others think they are not extinguished but become more blessed. Compare also *Pelloutier, as cited above, Book III, 18.*

9. **They feast upon those of their dearest kin who have grown old.** <note>original: "Ἑστιῶνται τῶν φιλτ. τοὺς γεγηρ."</note> *Sallust, in On the World, ch. 9*, also says the Massagetae "eat" their parents. If they reached extreme old age, they would slaughter and devour them; if they were extinguished by disease, they would hide them in a mound. Compare the *Learned Man on the Fragments of Pythagoras in Gale’s Mythological, Physical, and Ethical Works, p. 713.* Note also the word <term>to sacrifice</term> <note>original: "καταθύειν"</note> which he uses significantly, for he wishes it to be understood that those old men were slaughtered like sacrificial victims. For <term>to sacrifice</term> is to offer victims to the Gods on an altar, a part of which was eaten. See *Perizonius on Aelian, Various History, Book IV, ch. 1.* For "anticipating" <note>original: "φθάσαντες"</note>, the Meerman Codex has "those who anticipated."

10. **The Tibareni, however, [cast down] the living...** Such were the Cantabrians in *Silius Italicus, Book III, 318:*
> *A strange love possesses the people: when sluggish age turns grey,*
> *To anticipate the years already unfit for war with a stone.*

Those who are called *Tibareni* by our author are called *Tibari* by *Eusebius*. *Theodoret* calls them *Tibareni*, and they are usually expressed in that way, as in this place in the Meerman manuscript, although the codices vary everywhere on that name. See the *Learned Man on Stephanus of Byzantium and Wesseling on Diodorus, Book XIV, 30.* However, *Jerome* translated this poorly: *The Tibareni hang the old men they have loved on gallows*, when he ought to have said *they cast them down*, as *Cotelerius on the Recognitions of Clement, Vol. I, p. 584, and others* have noted. Nevertheless, those words are often confused. Certainly the simple *krēmnāō* and *krēmnēmi* are sometimes the same as *kremāō*, "I hang," on which matter see *Kuhn on Diogenes Laertius, Book VI, 50; Barnes on Euripides’ Heracles, 520; and others.* At any rate, among the Scythians, it was considered a blessed burial for the dead to be fixed to a cross or a stake, as *Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 499 C*, teaches among others. The Colchians hang those sewn in skins from trees, according to *Aelian, Various History, Book IV, ch. 1*, which however *Apollonius of Rhodes, Book III, 208*, suggests should be understood only of the men. Nor was it unusual for the Germans, the offspring of the Scythians, to end their lives with a noose, as *Bardesanes teaches in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book IV, p. 277 D.*

11. **Some to birds and dogs...** Many have noted that cruelty of the Hyrcanians. See *Menage on Diogenes Laertius, Book VI, 79.* *Theodoret, p. 615*, says the Hyrcanians and Caspians feed themselves on the corpses of men, which differs a little from...

12. The Scythians —] Above in Book III, 17, the Scythians are said to "eat their fathers." But as the name was applied very broadly, so their customs were diverse. For it is well known that it was a custom among the Scythians, as well as the Indians and other nations, to eat their own people; on which matter see *Perizonius* on *Aelian’s Varia Historia, IV, 1.* Our author spoke of this immediately regarding the Massagetae and Derbices.

Concerning the third law, he <note>The philosopher Xenocrates</note> thinks we must inquire what Triptolemus intended when he commanded that one must abstain from animals. Was it because he thought it altogether unworthy that kindred beings should be killed? Or because he perceived it happened that the most useful animals were being taken for food by men? Since he wished, therefore, to make the life of men mild, he took care that those animals which lived among men, and were especially tame, should be preserved. Unless perhaps, because he had commanded that the gods be honored with fruits, he judged that this worship would be more firmly established if sacrifices to the gods were not made from animals at all. # PORPHYRY, etc.

...driven by great necessity and involuntary sins, as we have demonstrated, they fell into this custom <note>The custom of animal sacrifice</note>. <margin>There were editors from Lyons and Cambridge who had omitted the word "to honor" <note>original: τιμᾷν (timan)</note>, which I have restored to its place as was done in the first edition, and the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts. 10. **An eternal decree.**] At Athens, laws were called *thesmoi*, but these laws of Draco were so called par excellence because they began with this word. See the learned author on Aelian's *Various History* VIII, 10, and Meursius in *Solon*, chapter 13.

<margin>11. **To honor the Gods and local heroes.**] The ancients often mention "local gods" and "following [ancestral laws]." See Cuper, *Observations* Book III, 16. They also frequently join "gods and local heroes," on which see Duker on Thucydides IV, 87. Since Draco ordained these things, Maximus Tyrius (Dissertation IV, 10) writes with little accuracy that neither Solon nor the laws of Draco handed down what the divine is, or how it should be honored.</margin>

12. **Following ancestral laws.**] Petit reads "punitive laws" <note>original: ἐμποινίμοις (empoinimois)</note> and in the penultimate line "and with annual cakes." See *Attic Laws* at the beginning. I would prefer "accordingly" <note>original: ἑπομένως (hepomenos)</note>. —VALENT. Petit's reading seems to have been approved even by the Honorable Cuper, *Observations* III, chapter 16, but it was rightly refuted by Wesseling in *Attic Laws*, page 69, who restored "following" <note>original: ἑπομένους</note> or rather "accordingly." The Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts give "following" <note>original: ἑπομένοις</note>, and thus Davis restored it in Cicero's *On Laws*.

<column-break/>

page 36, as the illustrious Abresch advised; I have made room for this word in the text. For that ridiculous "in-penalties" <note>original: ἐμποένοις</note> which was read previously was derived from a foolish error of the Florentine typesetter into subsequent editions, when he ought to have given "privately" <note>original: ἰδίᾳ</note>, which you now see. He rightly says "ancestral laws" <note>original: πατρίους νόμους</note>, which others also call *patroous*. See Book I, § 20. Moreover, the ancients studied nothing so much as ensuring that laws of this kind were not neglected. I will add only the response of Socrates in Xenophon, because it seems to look back to this law of Draco. When asked whether it was permitted for anyone to worship the Gods at his own whim, he replied: "No, but there are laws according to which one must do this." See Marcilius on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, page 344.

13. **Annual cakes.**] Rather "and with annual cakes" <note>original: καὶ πελάνοις ἐπετείοις</note>, as has long since been emended by learned men, Johannes Meursius in *Attic Themes* I, 1, P. Petit (whom G. Cuper follows), and others. However, the Leipzig manuscript brings no help, but the Meermann perhaps intended it, for it is accustomed to utter not only *-ous* but sometimes *-ois* in the manner done here. For what the *pelanoi* <note>thick, sacrificial cakes or libations</note> were, see at Book II, 6.

14. **And with cakes.**] Not a few things are missing at the end of this book: namely, examples of illustrious men from all Greek and Roman antiquity who abstained from flesh, together with the closing oration. —REISKE.

-> T H E  E N D. <-

<meta>This page begins a new correspondence (Letter I) from Johann Friedrich Thomas to Urban Gottfried Siber, dated September 18, 1715. It follows the previous gathering marked by the catchword "Epi-".</meta>

### Letter I.

->*To the Most Reverend Man*<-

## URBAN GODOFREDUS SIBER,

->*Sends Fondest Greetings*<-

## JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS.

I do not need to seek far for reasons to explain at length to you, Most Reverend Sir, why I have taken the liberty of sending this present writing as an obscure man not even known to you by name. Both the fame of your merits in literary as well as ecclesiastical affairs, and the renown of your singular kindness—by which you wonderfully adorn and assist the study of higher learning and its noble practitioners—have encouraged me. Relying on that goodwill of yours toward all, I send this small letter to you to modestly set forth my requests. As I am working on an edition of Porphyry’s work <term>On Abstinence from Animal Food</term> <note>original: "περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων" (peri apoches empsychon). Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher; this work is one of the earliest defenses of vegetarianism.</note>, I intend to prefix to the work a dissertation on the life and philosophical method used by Porphyry. I shall take up for particular treatment the vexed question of *Porphyry’s Apostasy* <note>The historical debate over whether Porphyry was originally a Christian who later abandoned the faith to become a fierce critic of Christianity.</note>, which is commonly believed even by Great Men such as *Fabricius*, *de la Croze*, and others; it is regarding this that I urgently and earnestly beseech you to write back your opinion to me. Concerning the *Porphyrians*—the name by which, as you know, the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arius, whose theological views were declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea. The Emperor Constantine ordered their books to be called "Porphyrian" to associate them with the pagan enemy of the Church.</note> were once designated—I am not yet sufficiently certain. For the opinions of both *Sandius* in his *Core of Ecclesiastical History* and *Godofredus* in his commentary on *Philostorgius* regarding them are displeasing to me. Likewise, the conjecture of *Cudworth*, which he puts forward in his excellent *Intellectual System of the Universe* on page 594, seems to me more subtle than true. Permit me, therefore, to learn the more correct view from you. Your love for and merits in historical investigations, which are well-celebrated, do not allow me to doubt that I shall experience your benevolence and favor in this matter; although I acknowledge myself plainly unequal to repaying it, I shall nonetheless do enough in proclaiming and cherishing it. Indulge my requests, therefore, Most Distinguished Man, and if any other materials are available to you which might be of use to my endeavors, even in illustrating the Work itself, allow yourself to be persuaded to grant them liberally. Farewell. Written at Schweidnitz in Silesia <note>original: "Suidnicii Silefiorum", modern Świdnica, Poland.</note>, the 14th day before the Calends of October, 1715 <note>September 18, 1715.</note>.

<summary>Johann Friedrich Thomas writes to the scholar Urban Gottfried Siber seeking academic guidance for his upcoming edition of Porphyry's treatise on vegetarianism. He specifically asks for Siber's opinion on Porphyry's alleged apostasy from Christianity and the historical labeling of Arians as "Porphyrians."</summary>

<keywords>Porphyry, Urban Gottfried Siber, Johann Friedrich Thomas, On Abstinence, Apostasy, Arians, Ralph Cudworth, Church History, Neoplatonism, 18th-century scholarship</keywords>

### Letter II.

->To the Illustrious and Most Distinguished Man,<-

# JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS,

->of Schweidnitz in Silesia,<-

->Sends Fondest Greetings.<-

# LUDWIG URBAN GOTTFRIED SIBER.

->*Most Distinguished and Noble Man, Patron to be honored with all respect,*<-

Since I am accustomed to value highly the conversations of learned men—from which not only friendship grows, but also various benefits often overflow for the public good—I cannot help but praise your kindness, with which you address me so blandly though I have been neither seen nor heard by you; indeed, you even seek my opinion on a vexed question <note>A "vexed question" refers to a long-standing scholarly debate that is difficult to resolve.</note>. I thank you, Most Distinguished Man, and likewise ask that, although your estimation of me may be excessive, you nevertheless maintain your benevolent spirit and promise yourself every kind of service from me. Furthermore, as for your endeavors, they are certainly to be praised in the highest degree; for such a task cannot be disparaged when men as great as Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661), a famous German humanist and geographer who served as the Vatican librarian.</note> were engaged in it with such labor and diligence. Truly, I believe that regarding the life of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher famous for his opposition to Christianity.</note>, hardly anything more accurate can be produced than what Holstenius has already published on the matter, being a man most well-versed in all literature and libraries. In saying this, I would not wish to interrupt your industry here, since it can happen that by excellent minds, even a "new world" may be discovered, and those things may be examined which we marvel were either not seen or neglected by others.

Regarding the *Apostasy* <note>original: "Αποστασίᾳ" (Apostasia). The act of renouncing one's religious faith.</note> of Porphyry, you first inquire and call it into doubt; I believe you do this not entirely without reason, since the older writers of Church History offer no sign that Porphyry was ever attached to the fellowship of Christians; indeed, they rather hold him to be a sworn enemy of the holy Religion. Sozomen <note>A 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note> is the first who reports that he, having been beaten by a Christian and seething with a weariness for revenge, defected; Theophanes (on page 45) copies him, drawing Nicephorus into the company of this opinion. Truly, the authority of these three men might seem so great to someone that Porphyry might indeed seem to have once embraced Christianity...

<summary>A letter from Ludwig Siber to Johann Friedrich Thomas discussing the scholarly biography of the philosopher Porphyry. Siber addresses the historical debate over whether Porphyry was ever a Christian before becoming a famous critic of the faith.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Friedrich Thomas, Ludwig Urban Gottfried Siber, Lucas Holstenius, Porphyry of Tyre, Sozomen, apostasy, church history, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 431 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the philosopher Porphyry’s alleged conversion to and subsequent apostasy from Christianity, following the previous analysis of historical sources.</meta>

...be able. Nevertheless, he could have been a Catechumen <note>A person receiving instruction in the Christian principles before baptism</note>, in whose rank even those who were held by a true zeal for our sacred rites used to remain for a long time. He could also have been delighted solely by the reading of the divine Oracles, a fact which is sufficiently attested not only by the consensus of the Church Fathers, but also by his own refutation of Christianity consisting of fifteen books. Perhaps, therefore, it happened that he approached intending to embrace Christianity if the arguments pleased him, but departed as an enemy when his mind, accustomed to the demonstrations of wise men, was provoked by the injustices of those whose lives fell short of the heavenly rule. But if we concede that he stood only on the border of Christianity and Paganism, but never actually entered the camp itself, it must be concluded that Sozomen, Theophanes, and Nicephorus <note>Early Christian historians</note> interpreted the term *apostasy* <note>original Greek: ἀποστασίας</note> too broadly, and that Porphyry was not branded with that disgrace by a fully accurate reasoning.

Indeed, I would not wish for such matters to be discussed too laboriously, lest the authority of the Ecclesiastical Writers collapse if we overturn those things which have been believed for so long and established by those to whom we are accustomed to turn as the stewards of Antiquity. Nor does it hinder the Christian cause that a Christian should act as an Apostate, since we acknowledge that even perfect beings and heavenly spirits deserted God himself. Furthermore, most distinguished Sir, you ask from where the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus was not co-eternal with God the Father</note> received the name "Porphyrians" as a term of disgrace? Do you recognize that the things Gothofredus said in his Observations on Philostorgius (page 420) are not sufficient for your accuracy? To those things I reply that, in my view, very abundant reasons were given in the Letter of Constantine the Great—provided that letter is truly Constantine's—namely, because the Arians were doing the same thing as Porphyry. Now, the efforts of Porphyry, like those of Celsus and Philostratus, aimed only at this: to recognize nothing divine in Christ, or if any such thing appeared, to destroy it. Since the Arians acted even more strongly in this regard, and perverted the very words testifying to his divinity with an unheard-of *distortion* <note>original Greek: στρεβλώσει</note>, they were most aptly and appropriately called Porphyrians. I have even thought that any evil thing was called *porphyrion* by the Greeks, and I recall that once a sea monster devastating the shores and long troublesome to fishermen was marked with the name of Porphyry; but I do not determine whether that beast drew its name from Porphyry the Apostate. Certainly, Constantine's reasons so pleased posterity that the Emperor Theodosius repeated or slightly changed them in a second edict for burning Porphyry's books, while simultaneously indicating that they had acquired that name from the equal and rival madness of the Arians and Porphyry.

Thus I think my respect for you, most distinguished Sir, has been declared. If it does not satisfy your accurate genius—which I am already beginning to perceive—consider that in that vast ocean of Ecclesiastical History, I prefer to avoid the rocks and seek out riches that may benefit the multitude. Meanwhile, I ask with all effort that you preserve for me the friendship you offered, and introduce me to the acquaintance of your other intimates, from whom I shall not cease to give and seek mutual signs of benevolence. May God preserve you. Given the 12th of October, 1715.

<summary>The author discusses whether the philosopher Porphyry was a true apostate or merely a student of Christianity, and explains why the Arian heretics were later disparagingly labeled 'Porphyrians' by Imperial edict.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Arians, Constantine the Great, Emperor Theodosius, apostasy, church history, heresy, polemics</keywords>

->To the Most Great, Reverend, and Distinguished Man<-

### URBAN GOTTFRIED SIBER,

->*Professor of Theology and Sacred Antiquities*<-

->Sends Fondest Greetings<-

### JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS.

Your reply brought me great joy, filled as it was with all kindness and erudition. You very benevolently indicated that my previous letters were not entirely unwelcome, and you remarkably declared your goodwill toward me. I certainly offer you the greatest thanks I can for your singular kindness, which was greater than my hope and expectation; I earnestly and zealously beseech you to preserve this favor toward me forever. 

Regarding the subject matter—the reason I so eagerly sought your friendship—I confess indeed that your ingenious conjecture pleases me greatly. In order to keep the tradition of the Church Fathers regarding Porphyry’s <term>Apostasy (falling away from the faith)</term> intact, you maintain that Porphyry was a <term>Catechumen (a convert under instruction but not yet baptized)</term>. Or, if this should displease anyone, you advise that the word "apostasy" <note>original: "ἀποστασίας"</note> ought to be interpreted a little more broadly, which seems to me the best course of all. 

But truly, since I still desire more certain proofs for this opinion of yours (which has a great appearance of truth), and since I do not think anything can easily be brought forward to this effect from the ecclesiastical writers or others who have handed down anything concerning Porphyry, you will not take it poorly if I choose "to withhold judgment" <note>original: "τὸ ἐπέχειν," a Skeptic philosophical term for suspending assent</note> here. Instead, I shall propose to you my own "divination" <note>meaning a scholarly guess or hypothesis</note> on this question, to be determined by your judgment. 

To be sure, the authority of the Church writers is sacred to me; however, I revere it in such a way that I have always thought the account of truth must be held in higher regard. Since those writers were very often stirred by a "gadfly of passions" <note>meaning they were often driven by intense emotion or bias</note>—as you yourself will acknowledge—and since they saw with resentment that Porphyry’s name was held in high esteem among his own people for his sharpness of mind and great store of learning, they certainly could not brand his reputation with a greater mark of shame than by passing on to their own and to posterity a story of Porphyry’s apostasy received from others. I could easily believe this story arose from our Philosopher’s familiarity with Origen Adamantius <note>A famous early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) whom Porphyry met in his youth</note>. 

As for the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, whose views on the nature of Christ were declared heretical</note>, it is well that you write that the most abundant reasons why they were called "Porphyrians" were noticed by you in the letter of Constantine; but it is better what you add: "if only that letter is truly Constantine’s own," about which there is still reason to doubt...

## Ccc 3

I understand these to be great men. I also judge it difficult to demonstrate from the writings of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher and opponent of early Christianity.</note> that he recognized nothing divine in Christ, or that if he perceived anything resembling divinity, he sought to destroy it.
