Furthermore, this also holds me in great doubt: that the Holy Fathers who disputed against the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who challenged the nature of the Trinity; the author argues they were more influenced by Plotinus than Porphyry.</note> never charged them with following the impiety of Porphyry. Such a charge certainly would have rendered the Arians much more hated; otherwise, it is well known that they so embraced the dogmas of Plotinus that they ought more rightly to have been called Plotinians than Porphyrians. 

Moreover, the observation you add regarding the word *porphyrion* <note>original: "πορφύριον"</note> is elegant; you think that any sort of evil was designated by this word among the Greeks, and for that matter you cite Procopius concerning a sea monster distinguished by the name of Porphyry. Unless everything deceives me, I remember reading this same history in Michael Glycas, Part IV of the *Annals*, page 270. To this one might also relate, in a certain way, the explanation of Porphyry's nickname, *the Bataneote* <note>original: "τοῦ βατανεώτου" — likely referring to his origin in Batanea</note>, which Stephen le Moyne gave on page 607 of the *Sacred Miscellany*. But I confess that this meaning of the word *porphyrion* is unknown to me, and I would greatly desire it to be proven from Greek authors. It has pleased me to mention these things, by your leave, though I wish nothing to be detracted from your opinion; I have intended solely to invite you to a further way of thinking on this matter.

In illustrating the Work of Porphyry itself—to add this as well—I have been most anxious concerning the collation <note>The process of comparing different manuscript copies to identify variations and errors.</note> of manuscript codices, by whose help the true reading, which is lacking in many places, might be restored. Nor has success been entirely absent from my prayers. For the illustrious Prefect of the Library of Vienna, Gentilotto ab Engelsbrun, procured for me not just a collation, but a complete description of a Vatican manuscript. And, to bestow a greater abundance of his favor upon me, he most kindly promised a collation of a Florentine manuscript, with the observations of the celebrated Salvini added, the unpublished remarks of Holstenius on the codex having only recently been sent. Likewise, the celebrated Lederlin gave a specimen of the variant readings of the Royal Parisian codex, which a collation of the entire codex will soon follow. 

Therefore, it has remained among my desires to obtain a collation of the Leipzig codex, which your Pauline Library preserves; I explained this to several celebrated men who dwell in Leipzig, and not long ago to the Magnificent Mr. Boerner. I now gather the sum of these requests anew and pour them into your bosom: that you might wish to care for this business, and make room for my petition—which is honorable, I think, and likely to benefit the public good—and aid my endeavors by your work. I ask that you forgive this audacity of mine, which assigns the burden of undertaking such a task to you, a man most occupied with other matters; nevertheless, comfort shall come to me from it, and the fruit of glory to you. Indeed, I have nothing with which to satisfy your inclined goodwill toward me; yet, as much as I am able, I shall strive and endeavor to prove all industry, which is placed both in piety and respect, and looks especially toward your honor and esteem. 

And so, farewell, most distinguished Sir, and—this I pray above all—preserve your benevolence toward me forever. 

Written at Schweidnitz, Silesia <note>original: "Suidnicii Siles."</note>, the 13th day before the Kalends of December, 1715. <note>November 19, 1715.</note>

### Letter IV.

->To the most Distinguished and learned Gentleman<-

## JOHN FREDERICK THOMAS,

->of Schweidnitz,<-

->Sends Fondest Greetings.<-

## URBAN GODOFRED SIBER,

->*Professor of Theology and Sacred Antiquities, and Priest at St. Thomas Church.*<-

That you might defend Porphyry of Tyre—a Phoenician and indeed a supreme Philosopher, yet the worst of Christians and a deserter—from the stain of *apostasy* <note>original: "ἀποστασίας"; the act of renouncing one's faith</note>, and draw me into agreement, you employ numerous arguments; they are plausible, but not true, and I shall review them here in summary. First, you think the Christian writers were driven by a frenzy of emotion; 2) that, inflamed by envy, they fruitlessly reproached Porphyry with that crime; 3) that the Letter of Constantine, in which he wished the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ</note> to be called "Porphyrians," seems to be a forgery; 4) that Porphyry’s Christianity was merely inferred from his familiarity with Origen; 5) that it cannot be demonstrated that the divinity of Christ was attacked by him; 6) nor that any insults were spoken against Christ; 7) that the Church Fathers never cast "Porphyrianism" in the teeth of the Arians. 

Before I weigh or discuss these points according to your demand, I for my part declare once more that it matters little to me, and perhaps to the entire Christian community, whether Porphyry acted the part of an Apostate or not. Nevertheless, lest I seem to have made light of your reasoning or to be insufficiently intent on the duties of my office, I respond to and defend that most widely accepted affirmation of the Fathers regarding Porphyry’s apostasy. Firstly, I plainly deny that the Ecclesiastical writers, from whom that tradition has come down to us, were driven by a frenzy of emotion—or what is the same, by the stings of hatred and fury—to fabricate such a thing about Porphyry. For the more I observe the modesty and *bridling of the tongue* <note>original: "χαλιναγωγίαν"</note> of those ancient men in their writing, the more I perceive their utmost tranquility in accusing the gentiles; so much so, that I would assert that Suetonius, Tacitus, and other secular writers inveighed much more strongly against the crimes of their own people. Nay, even when peace was obtained, they considered it a law unto themselves that no *loose-tongued speech* <note>original: "ἀθυρόγλωσσα"</note> should appear, but rather they should restrain the intemperance of the tongue, *the lack of linguistic control* <note>original: "τὸ ἀκρατὲς τῆς γλώσσης"</note>,

They held it to be the <note>original: "νοσημάτων αἴσχισον" (nosēmatōn aischiston)</note> **most shameful of diseases**. (*) This is quite evident from the first public writings of the Christians, their *Apologies*, in which, while they were pleading against the crimes charged to them, they nevertheless spoke with great verbal chastisement regarding the vices of the Deities whom [the pagans] worshipped and the crimes of mortals; nor did they publish anything unless it was plainly certain and common knowledge. And what gain, I ask, would the Christians have had if they had charged Porphyry with **Apostasy** <note>The act of renouncing one's religious faith.</note> out of mere madness, when his efforts against Christianity were going to be equally worthless whether he acted as a Philosopher or as a treacherous Christian? Certainly, the Christian Republic was not so helpless or ignoble that, because of one man being denied access, they would break the reins of Christian moderation and hurl falsehoods at those who had wandered astray.

And I use the same argument against your second reason: as if the Christians, looking upon the fame of Porphyry with envious eyes, had fabricated the charge of Apostasy? Certainly, they had no reason to envy the Greeks for such a man, who—whatever he knew in the human or philosophical arts and sciences, or wrote with greater sobriety—he had drawn from the company of Christians and his familiarity with **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note>, and from there he had amended the dogmas of the other Philosophers. This is asserted by **Augustine** in Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 30, and by Baltus in *Platonism Defended by the Fathers*. If he [Porphyry] misused these things against his Masters, they had weapons, displayed from heaven and strengthened by a divine edge, with which they could overthrow and defeat entire cohorts of Porphyrys. This was indeed done, since at that time more than one person endowed with Porphyry's talent was attempting to undermine the Church. **Arnobius**—whose disputations against the heathens Ciacconius claims were born chiefly from Porphyry’s Apostasy—beautifully says in Book 3 of *Regarding the Church*: *She [the Church] is content with her own strengths and rests upon the foundations of her own truth; nor is she stripped of her power, even if she has no defender: indeed, even if all tongues speak against her and strive against her, and conspire with the animosity of a united consensus to abolish faith in her.* From this it is clear that the Christians burned with no envy toward Porphyry; however, this will be even more abundantly clear if you look closely at the citations made here and there by the Fathers. These are so far from breathing envy that they sometimes seem to exhale praise instead, except when the truth had to be sacrificed for. **Eusebius**, in his books on the *Preparation for the Gospel*, commends his talent; and **Cyril**, in his books against Julian, spoke with a most composed mind only those things which, if Porphyry had survived until Cyril’s time, he would not have wished said otherwise. Now as pertains to your third reason—that the letter of Constantine, in which he orders the name "Porphyrians" to be imposed upon the Arians as a mark of ignominy, is a forgery—I ask that you allow me to clear away my earlier suspicions. Nevertheless, since I have not known anyone who supported those suspicions with certain reasons, and since Eusebius and others praise the genius of Constantine, and the Hymn-writers even rank him among the Apostles for that very reason, I certainly think it more certain to conclude that Constantine the Great wrote them; or, even if he used the words of someone else, the mind and the commands of the Emperor were nonetheless instilled into them. Nor was it unusual for Emperors, both contemporaries of Constantine and those older, to commit to memory speeches written by others and subsequently recite them in public gatherings.

Fifthly, you think that Apostasy cannot be demonstrated from the writings of Porphyry himself, for the reason that he said nothing against the divinity of Christ. To these points I reply, that the writings which bear witness to Porphyrian Impiety do not survive, for the reason that Christians, according to a solemn custom, would give them to the pyre and glory in such a conflagration. I recall that in the work of Ciampinus <note>Giovanni Giustino Ciampini (1633–1698), an archaeologist who studied Christian antiquities.</note> regarding the Church at Ravenna, such an image engraved in bronze was discovered, in which the books of Heretics are consumed by flames. Even if those insane writings do not survive, will you deny credit to Cyril, who pronounces that *bitter words, fighting against the glory of God, foul-mouthed, and mocking* <note>original Greek: λόγους πικροὺς & τῇ θεοῦ δόξῃ μαχομένους & ἀθυροστόμους & κατορχουμένους</note> were written by him? It was enough to overthrow the divinity of Christ that he introduced substances subordinated and subjected to one another—a custom which the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who believed Jesus was a created being subordinate to God the Father.</note> subsequently followed. *He showed the subsistence of one from another, beginning from the King, and the descent and decrease of those after the first; but for those who think like Arius, he divides and establishes the subsistences as sitting beneath one another in equal measure, and he thinks there are three gods separately, rather than the holy and consubstantial Trinity.* <note>original Greek: Δεδήλωκε τὴν ἐξ ἀλλήλων ὑπόστασιν... καὶ τρεῖς οἴεται θεοὺς εἶναι διῃρημένως τὴν ἁγίαν καὶ ὁμοούσιον.</note> To this may be added what Augustine brings forward concerning him in *The City of God*, Book 10, Chapter 23, since he had established two principles: *But as for what he says are the Principles, as a Platonist, we know he speaks of God the Father and God the Son, whom he calls in Greek the "paternal intellect": of the Holy Spirit he says either nothing or nothing clearly. And this he said as he was able, or as he wished: for Philosophers use free words.* Soon in Chapter 24, he refutes this further. Indeed, how much he departed *from our strictness* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς παρ' ἡμῖν ἀκριβείας</note> by that assertion, the praised Cyril declared in Book 8, pages 270 and 271, as did Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 10, who in Chapter 29 called those words undisciplined. Besides Cyril and Augustine, Theophylact exposed the sophisms of Porphyry against the divinity *of the Word* <note>original Greek: τοῦ λόγου</note> in his *Exposition of the Gospel on the Nativity*, which I have read only in Latin in the collection of Combefis <note>François Combefis (1605–1679), a Dominican scholar and editor of patristic texts.</note>, Volume 1, page 351. These things, along with others, must be diligently collected, lest you defend the enemy and adversary of Christ too kindly. For even if it could be demonstrated that he not only did not insult the divinity of the Savior, but even granted him something of divinity, even that would not suffice for his defense; since *something divine* <note>original Greek: θεῖόν τι</note> was ascribed even to Philosophers and excellent Artisans according to Plato, who called such men—especially if they were engaged in reforming the Republic—*reproving gods* <note>original Greek: θεοὺς ἐλεγχτικούς</note>, a role which Porphyry undertook. *Porphyry maintains that there is a certain race of gods, whom he says also turn into men at times, as if they were playing among us.* <margin>(*) Cyril, Book 8, p. 287.</margin> (*) But since Christians were not concerned with acknowledging merely "something divine" in Christ, but rather *the whole fullness of the deity* <note>original Greek: πᾶν πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος</note>, it was enough to charge him with *apostasy* if he once acknowledged and then denied His full divinity, such as we confess in the Creeds following the guidance of Scripture.

# IV.

Nor indeed is the stain of **apostasy** <note>original: *ἀποστασίας* (apostasias)</note> washed away even if the slanders spread by him against Christ cannot be demonstrated, although the testimonies of Cyril sufficiently declare that he acted otherwise. But if you should disregard those, it must be known that Christ had adversaries of different kinds: some who insulted him in a common, vulgar manner—which was done in the theaters both before Julian and during the reign of that treacherous prince—and others who, with more learned reasoning, desired to see His Majesty overthrown. These were the Philosophers, whose **dignity** <note>original: *σεμνότης* (semnotēs)</note> and credibility would have perished if they had betrayed any lack of restraint in their speech. Thus Julian usually restrained himself from speaking too impudently; his Satire was poured out only so far as to contemptuously call Christ a "Galilean" and the "son of a carpenter," although Cyril <margin>(*) Cyril, Book I, p. 38.</margin> called these very words **ill-omened voices** <note>original: *παλιμφήτους φωνὰς* (palimphētous phōnas)</note>. However, the moderation of these men was all the more dangerous because, under the appearance of **impassivity** <note>original: *ἀπαθείας* (apatheias)</note>, they won all the greater applause for themselves, which Augustine graphically describes in *The City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 23. Indeed, what would you say if you read through the Quran? Although no one denies it was written to prostrate the divinity of Christ, is there any railing against Christ present there? You will find scarcely a shadow of detraction, but rather many praises and other things that can be turned to his glory. Will these things truly persuade you, most learned Sir, to free the Author and his followers from the crime of Apostasy?

Finally, it will be of little use if you assert that the Fathers rarely charged the Arians with "Porphyrian arts." It is enough that Arius, in the first birth of his heresy, followed the dialectical arts of Porphyry—which Rufinus so greatly reproached Jerome for—and that he held the same hypotheses as Porphyry, as Cyril taught a little earlier. It is enough that the Arians imitated the **ways** <note>original: *τοὺς τρόπους* (tous tropous)</note> or manners of Porphyry (which are the words of Constantine), and **changed like chameleons** <note>original: *ὡς χαμαιλέοντες μετεβάλλοντο* (hōs chamaileontes meteballonto)</note>, and thus expressed both of Porphyry's crimes: his disputations and his Apostasy. Later writers, when they saw that Porphyry had been surpassed in many ways by Arius and his followers, thought it more advisable to call the abominable heresy by its own Author, or by the principal heads of its errors, rather than referring back to Porphyry. This was especially true since the successors of Arius had peculiar marks by which they were distinguished from Porphyry, just as it seemed better to the Church to call the Nestorians by their own name rather than by the name of Simon Magus, even though Theodosius had commanded this with the same severity as Constantine had commanded the name "Porphyrians."

With your opinions discussed in this manner, I should think you must look for stronger arguments if you require even a mere probability that Porphyry was not an Apostate. Therefore, I repeat again and again that the authority of the Ecclesiastical Writers is not only not to be despised, but rather every stone must be turned to ensure it remains sound and protected. For that reason, I urge you to weigh carefully: First,

# Book IV, Chapter 11

When I was summoned to Bithynia <note>A Roman province in modern-day Turkey</note> to teach rhetorical literature, it happened that at the same time the Temple of God was being destroyed. Two men emerged there who insulted the prostrate and cast-down Truth, I know not whether more proudly or more shamelessly. One of these professed himself a *High Priest of Philosophy*. This was Hierocles, as all learned men agree. Lactantius continues: *The other described the same material more bitingly; he was then among the number of the judges, and was a primary author of the persecution being carried out. Not content with this crime, he also pursued with his writings those whom he had afflicted. For he composed two small books, not "against the Christians," lest he seem to pursue them as an enemy, but "to the Christians," so that he might seem to advise them humanely and kindly. In these books, he attempted to prove the falsehood of Holy Scripture as if it were entirely self-contradictory; for he set out certain Chapters which seemed to oppose one another, enumerating so many and such intimate details that at times he seemed to have been from that same school of discipline.*

Thus far the words of Lactantius. Regarding these, I advise you of a disagreement among the learned, who have sometimes confused these two philosophers with one another, such that they referred things belonging to Hierocles to Porphyry, and attributed things belonging to Porphyry to Hierocles. This is what Theophilus Raynaud did when, in his book *On Judas the Traitor*, Chapter 15, Section 7, he says: *Hierocles and Porphyry—in the same year that Diocletian was overseeing the destruction of Christian churches and the burning of books at Nicomedia—having previously professed the Christian religion, became traitors to the faith whose name they had put on and the Sacrament they had received, representing the traitor Judas.*

I have used in part the words of Lactantius; although he mentions neither by name while reviewing their virulent writings against the Christian religion, nevertheless, from the circumstances he relates, he sufficiently signaled who they were. He clearly noted Hierocles when he said the title of the two books written by him "to the Christians"—he who was one of the judges and an instigator or even author of the persecution against the Christians—was *Philalethes, Lover of Truth* <note>original: "Philalethes veri amator"</note>. We learn that all these details apply to Hierocles from Eusebius, who refuted that study by Hierocles. However, Baronius conjectures (under the year 302 AD) that the other philosopher and enemy of Christians mentioned there is Porphyry. That he was a deserter of Christianity is established from Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian</note>, Book 3, Chapter 9. Therefore, both are rightly counted among the brothers of the traitor Judas, as I related was done by Lactantius.

So says Raynaud; though I am entirely of the opinion that Lactantius's latter character description pertains rather to Porphyry. But before that is determined, let us meanwhile embrace the opinion of the great Bishop Pearson, who, in his *Prolegomena to Hierocles*, thinks these two philosophers were discussed by Lactantius. Although I know this is contradicted by Holstenius, and those same contradictions are repeated and approved by Needham <margin>(*) Needham, Preface to Hierocles, p. 14.</margin> in his notes to Pearson's *Prolegomena*, you will see, most illustrious Sir, that the arguments of Holstenius are not of great weight, and by an accurate measure of chronology and a correct reconstruction of Porphyry's biography...

<meta>This page continues the chronological and biographical defense of the claim that the philosopher Porphyry was an apostate from Christianity, following the previous discussion of his age and historical context.</meta>

# Page 396

...can be very easily overturned. For how will they prove that in the 19th year of Diocletian <note>303 AD</note>, Porphyry had passed his 69th year of age? Or, even if that premise is admitted, how will they prove he had not become a nonagenarian or a centenarian, he who is called by the singular surname "the Elder"? Indeed, it contributes much toward embracing the words of Lactantius <note>Early Christian author, c. 250–325 AD</note> and applying them to Porphyry, that Jerome likewise, and all others, testify that these same things were written by Porphyry. Furthermore, Cyril, in his books against Julian, seems to have translated Lactantius's words concerning Porphyry as if into the Greek language, when he expressed that impudent insult by the term *tēs katorchēseōs* <note>original: "τῆς κατορχήσεως" — meaning a mocking dance or triumphing over a fallen foe</note>, which is always joined, according to Strabo, with *anaideia* <note>original: "ἀναιδείᾳ" — shamelessness</note>.

Furthermore, the account of Eusebius of Caesarea—that Porphyry, unable to endure injuries, returned to the camp of the heathens—is not to be despised. For Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian</note> drew this from Eusebius's books written against Porphyry, although those have long since been lost. By what reasoning will you render that account void? Socrates would have to be accused of fiction, and his entire credibility overthrown; everyone sees how much danger to historical truth is joined to such a view. But if you believe that Socrates took those details from Eusebius, you must simultaneously believe Eusebius; no one would assert that Eusebius was ignorant of the events occurring in his own Church, unless they intended to wrongly insult such a great man.

Added to this is the Emperor's Edict concerning the name of Porphyry being held in ignominy; and this was chiefly on account of his **Apostasy**, since such a stigma was burned into none of the other philosophers for mere paganism. Now indeed, that edict, held as genuine, was repeated by Theodosius, and its authenticity was never questioned by Jacques Godefroy (*) or any other learned men—a certain sign that those who approved it also believed the reasons that brought such disgrace upon Porphyry. Now, where will you dismiss Socrates? (**) He who, with deliberate purpose, reports that Apostasy from the books of Eusebius, and who, leaning upon such a great man as Eusebius was, could most confidently assert the same. If you think he mocked the world with lies, you would in one moment do away with the rest of the things he left to memory. And thus Hardouin and his followers, who have long since striven to undermine the authority of the Ancients, will triumph securely. But if your mind is otherwise, then by Hercules, Socrates will please you all the more because he soon compares Julian the Apostate with the same man, and establishes that both fell into the same impiety: *amphoteroi oun dyssebēsantes en gnōsei hamartias to epitimion echousin* <note>original: "ἀμφότεροι οὖν δυσσεβήσαντες ἐν γνώσει ἁμαρτίας τὸ ἐπιτίμιοv ἔχουσιν" — "Both therefore, having acted impiously with knowledge of their sin, have their punishment"</note>. Departing from the interpretation of Valesius, I translate these words thus: they shall be struck with a greater punishment because, having been better and more rightly instructed, they wandered from the true path against their conscience. Nor did Socrates alone do this, but also the Sophist Libanius himself, who joined Porphyry and Julian on account of that desertion; a fact which Nicephorus (***) rightly observed, who, in the manner of Cyril, called Porphyry the *patera kai didaskalon* <note>original: "πατέρα καὶ διδάσκαλον" — father and teacher</note> of Julian, even in regard to his Apostasy.

<meta>The previous page likely discussed the early life of Porphyry and initial arguments regarding his departure from the Christian faith. This page continues the catalog of historical authorities who identify him as an apostate.</meta>

calling him by name. A little while later, joining the two together again, he says: *Julian leaned toward the madness of Porphyry, and both, having chosen impiety with full knowledge, are abominable, paying the penalty for their voluntary sin.* <note>original Greek: Ἰουλιανὸς πρὸς τὴν Πορφυρίου λύσσαν ἀπέκλινεν...; the author is quoting Nicephorus Callistus</note> Johannes Langus translates this as: *Julian in the same manner declined into the rage of Porphyry. Both are to be detested, since they embraced impiety while being prudent and knowing, and they therefore hang under the punishment of a voluntary and deliberately admitted sin.* Very well put indeed. For from this we see 1) an equality between the two, 2) knowledge, namely of sound doctrine, and 3) a voluntary sin <note>original Greek: ἑκούσιον ἁμαρτίαν</note>, and thus a perfect apostasy <term>apostasy: the formal abandonment of a religious belief</term>. This is what moved Nicephorus to call them both "abominable" <note>original Greek: ἀποτροπαίους</note>, that is, according to the testimony of Stephanus: to be averted, detested, horrendous, terrible, and abominated. Nor would I wish to scorn the authority of Nicephorus, since he follows Cyril and Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian</note>, and doubtless many others besides, who with unanimous consent recognized that apostasy. And I conveniently join to them Theophanes, who, since he collected his Chronology from the most excellent writers, gives us confidence that this was the belief among all the writers of his nation. After Theophanes comes Elias of Crete in his commentary on the 4th Oration of Gregory Nazianzen, where he called him "the Apostate" without any veil over his speech in number 69. Almost alone among all the Greeks is Theophylact, though he is somewhat negligent in Ecclesiastical History; he calls Porphyry a "gentile philosopher," looking toward the later period of the Apostate's life, yet he did not deny the crime that had gone before.

Indeed, the greatest and most influential part of the learned Latin writers have likewise recognized this apostasy. Jerome joined him with Julian, and in this followed the Greeks most closely, in Chapter 16 on Hosea: *The mouth of fools bubbles over with folly, such as were Porphyry and Julian, who poured out floods of their own folly against the teachers of the Church.* Rufinus, in his invective against Jerome, says: *Brother, you have made a bad omen in that your introducer is Porphyry. Where does that Faithless one lead you? If to that place where he himself is, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth; for there the Apostates, and the enemies of God, and perhaps the perjurers dwell.* <margin>(*) Rufinus said these things having stayed a long time among the Greeks both in Alexandria and in Palestine and Caesarea, so that he was able to know well whether these things were being tossed about truly or falsely concerning Porphyry. Nor would he have dared to do so, having such an adversary as the man from Stridon <note>Jerome, who was born in Stridon</note>, who, if Rufinus had used fables as a weapon, would have quickly crushed that "leaden fig."</margin> Furthermore, Augustine must certainly be brought forward, by whom many things have been preserved from the books which Porphyry wrote against Christ after his apostasy. He himself indicates several times that the Philosopher, just as he was about to approach the Religion, recoiled from its simplicity. *If you had truly and faithfully loved the Wisdom of Christ, you would have known the power of God and Wisdom, nor would you have recoiled, puffed up in your usual way, from his most wholesome humility.* <margin>(**)</margin> These words prove: 1) there was a time when Porphyry loved that Wisdom, 2) but that love was not constant, 3) and thus he recoiled.

# Page 398

from the faith to which he had crossed over. Indeed, he adds (*) that after his apostasy from the Faith, he did not even adhere sincerely to Paganism, but was trembling, feigning, and as if blushing (Chapter 24). The recent editors of Augustine have seen that the apostasy of the philosopher was known to the Holy Prelate <note>Augustine of Hippo</note>, and for that reason, they added that he was first a Christian and later a deserter. The more closely I examine the Prelate's writings, the more I suspect the primary incentives for Porphyry’s desertion were the Incarnation of Christ and the Resurrection; he believed the former to be unbecoming and the latter to be impossible. Let Cassiodorus follow Augustine, who confirms this very point—a man skilled in Greek literature and preserving those things he had learned among the Greek Fathers. 

But if that entire number of witnesses still seems too small to you to restrain Porphyry among the apostates, remember: 1) in Porphyry’s age, the word "apostate" was not yet sufficiently established as a formal term; 2) nor was <term>apostasy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποστασίαν; the act of renouncing one's faith</note> considered shameful among philosophers, if you except the Pythagoreans; 3) and by prudent reason, one’s mind and judgment sometimes had to be hidden, as Lactantius mentions when he says: "For the sake of the times, the Christians were sometimes silent." See the Valesian Edition, page 573.

I think these points will suffice, Distinguished Sir, to convince you not to grant more credit to your own conjectures than to the manifest evidence of such great men, whom I can hardly—if at all—persuade myself were fed on fables and dreams. As for your other requests, I am sending you various readings gathered from the Leipzig Manuscript <note>Codex Lipsiensis</note>, which the Illustrious Boerner very kindly shared with me. However, you will need to compare them with the French edition by Fogerolles from Lyon, against which I ordered the manuscript to be collated. The manuscript book is made of paper, neatly written, not very old, and not of such a nature that I think much trust can be placed in it. Sometimes several lines that appeared in Fogerolles were omitted; sometimes syllables were neglected. Nevertheless, I hope these readings will not be entirely useless to you, but that "grapes may be gathered from these thorns." May God prosper your efforts in editing Porphyry and render your other labors happy and auspicious with a large harvest of fortune. 

Leipzig, the 5th day before the Calends of January <note>December 28</note>, 1716.
